countdown:
Why it matters

About 2 weeks to go. Gear and practice take longer than you think. This is the order that works.

• Week 1 (now): licences, buy the shotgun, buy and mount the scope.
  • Week 2: sight in the rifle, pattern the shotgun, buy clothing, scout on the map.
  • Hunt week: final checks, pack, go.
  • Dates are a plan, not a rule. Move them to fit your life.
My lean (opinion)

Licences and the scope come first. Without a sighted in rifle there is no deer hunt. Without a federal permit there is no duck hunt.

• Buy where you can handle the gun and get help mounting the scope. (Tip)
  • Ask the store about a range near Kamloops. Many have sighting in days. (Tip)
  • One ammo load for the rifle. Do not mix brands after zeroing. (Tip, 85% the zero changes between loads)
  • Practice loading and unloading at the car until it is boring. (Tip)
Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Buy once, practice twice. The rifle you shot 60 times beats the fancy one you shot 6 times.

Common mistakes
  • Mounting the scope the night before the hunt.
  • Buying 5 kinds of ammo and never zeroing any of them.
  • Spending every evening shopping and none on the range.
Do this in the field

Tonight: put your hunt date in More. Then tick off the first 3 boxes above.

• Licence facts: see Session 2 sources (official synopsis pages 5 to 8, read directly 2026-10-02).
  • In season changes: the synopsis says to check gov.bc.ca/huntingregulations before your hunt, page 7 99%. Checked 2026-10-02.
  • Everything else in this session is a plan and tips (opinion), not rules.
licences:
Why it matters

No licence, no hunt. Deer tags by mail take about 14 days. Buy them in person.

• Mule deer and white tailed deer are separate tags 99%.
More: the table and the fine print
HuntingYou need
DeerBC hunting licence + deer species licence (tag) for that species
Ducks and geeseBC hunting licence + federal bird permit
Quail and grouseBC hunting licence only
  • Residents need no species licence for quail or grouse 99%.
  • Ducks and geese need no BC species licence, only the federal permit 99%.
  • Mule deer and white tailed deer are separate species licences 99%.

• (Fish and Wildlife ID) = your old hunter number + 3 digits 99%.
  • Carry photo ID. Know the number. No card needed (95 to 99%).
More: how to find it
  • Your old hunter number is now the FWID 99%.
  • It is your old hunter number with 3 extra digits 99%.
  • No card or printout needed. Knowing the number is enough 95%.
  • You must carry photo ID and be able to give your FWID number when an officer asks 99%.
  • Not sure of yours? Log in to WILD (Wildlife Information and Licensing Data) and use Find my FWID 99%.
  • No luck? FrontCounter BC: 1 877 855 3222 99%.

• Good 1 April to 31 March. $32 plus GST (Goods and Services Tax) 99%.
  • Electronic only. Buy it online tonight 99%.
More: cost and where to buy
  • It is good for the licence year, 1 April to 31 March. It expires 31 March 99%.
  • Adult resident cost: $32. That is a $25 fee plus a $7 conservation surcharge 99%.
  • GST is not included in that price 99%.
  • It is electronic only. You need no paper copy while hunting 99%.
  • Buy online, or at Service BC, FrontCounter BC or a participating store 99%.

• Hunting in the next 2 weeks? Buy in person 99%.
  • $15 each plus GST (Goods and Services Tax). Carry all your tags, used and unused 99%.
More: prices, mail times, waiting periods
  • Mule deer: $15. White tailed deer: $15. Each is a $12 fee plus a $3 surcharge 99%.
  • Plus 5% GST 99%.
  • Cannot be printed at home. They are printed on special paper with unique numbers 99%.
  • Online orders are mailed. Allow about 14 business days to a BC address 95%.
  • Hunting in the next 2 weeks? Buy in person at Service BC, FrontCounter BC or a licence vendor. You get them right away 99%.
  • No waiting period for deer. The 2 day wait applies only to bobcat, caribou, cougar, lynx, mountain goat, mountain sheep and wolverine 99%.
  • Carry all your species licences for the year, used and unused 99%.
My lean (opinion)

Buy both a mule deer and a white tailed deer tag. $30 plus GST. You will not know which deer walks out first.

• Needed every time you hunt ducks or geese 99%. Buy online, save it on your phone (85 to 99%).
More: name, dates and tax
  • Name: Migratory Game Bird Hunting Permit 99%.
  • The habitat conservation stamp must be on it. You pay for it with the permit 99%.
  • Cost: $17. That is $8.50 for the permit plus $8.50 for the stamp 99%. Plus tax 80%.
  • It expires 30 June after you buy it 99%. The 2026 e permit runs 1 August 2026 to 30 June 2027 80%.
  • Buy online 99%. Save the e permit on your phone 85%.
  • Carry it every time you hunt ducks or geese 99%. Paper or phone both count 85%.

• His own licence, deer tags and bird permit. No sharing 99%.
  • The hunter who kills cancels his own tag, right away 99%.
More: helpers and party hunting
  • He has CORE (Conservation and Outdoor Recreation Education), a PAL (Possession and Acquisition Licence) and an FWID (Fish and Wildlife ID). He can hunt too.
  • He needs his own BC hunting licence, his own deer species licences and his own federal bird permit 99%.
  • Licences cannot be lent, shared or transferred 99%.
  • Each hunter fills their own tags. The hunter who kills cancels his own licence, right away 99%.
  • You cannot notch your tag for his deer. BC has no party hunting rule 95%.
  • Anyone without a licence can still come along to watch and help pack out, if they carry no firearm or other weapon 99%.
  • The licensed hunter stays with the meat, unless the helper carries a Record of Receipt 99%.

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Licences in a zip bag, same pocket every time. Check the pocket before you leave the truck.

Common mistakes
  • Deer tags ordered online a week before. Too late.
  • Thinking the BC licence covers ducks.
  • Used tags left at home.
Do this in the field

Open WILD tonight. Find your FWID. Pencil it on the back of your PAL card.

shotgun-guide:
Why it matters

One 12 gauge does ducks with steel and grouse and quail. Know its parts, action, chokes and plug.

• One 12 gauge, 3 inch chamber, screw in chokes 70%.
  • A gas semi auto is softest with heavy steel loads 70%.
More: budget and the full short answer
  • You need one 12 gauge with a 3 inch chamber and screw in chokes 70%.
  • That gun covers ducks with steel and upland birds 70%.
  • A gas semi auto is the softest shooting choice with heavy steel loads 70%.
  • Budget: entry about $420 to $900, mid about $850 to $1,870, premium about $1,950 to $2,900 65%. Price checked 2026-10-01.
  • Prices are in CAD (Canadian dollars), from search previews of retailer pages. Verify at checkout.

• Pump kicks most. Gas semi auto kicks least 70%.
More: the full table

Gas semi autoSoftest recoil. Best with 3 inch steelMore parts to clean. Needs the gas system kept clean

  • Gas semi auto: spreads recoil, so 3 inch steel feels softer 70%.
  • Inertia semi auto: stays clean and runs in cold weather 70%.
  • Over/under: weak as a one gun for ducks plus upland, check steel rating 65%.

• 3 inch chamber fires 2 3/4 and 3 inch shells 75%. 28 inch barrel for one gun 65%.
More: 20 gauge, 3 1/2 inch, finish
  • Gauge: 12 gauge has the widest choice of steel loads in every shop 70%.
    • 20 gauge kicks less but steel loads are weaker for ducks 65%.
  • Chamber: 3 inch is enough. It fires 2 3/4 inch and 3 inch shells 75%.
    • 3 1/2 inch adds recoil and cost for little gain on ducks 65%.
  • Barrel: 28 inch is a good compromise for one gun 65%.
    • 26 inch swings faster in thick grouse timber 65%.
  • Finish: synthetic stock and a coated or camo finish for rain and salt (Tip).

• A squeezes the shot at the muzzle 85%.
  • With steel: nothing tighter than Modified unless marked steel safe 75%.
More: how chokes work, numbers
  • A choke is a short tube at the muzzle. It squeezes the shot to control spread 85%.
  • Tighter choke means a smaller, denser pattern at range 85%.
  • Steel is hard. It does not squeeze like lead. Tight chokes can damage the choke or barrel 75%.
  • Rule of thumb: nothing tighter than Modified with steel unless the choke says steel safe 75%.
  • IC (Improved Cylinder) for ducks over decoys and close grouse. M (Modified) for longer passing ducks 70%.
  • Squeeze in a 12 gauge: IC about 0.25 mm (0.010 in), M about 0.5 mm (0.020 in) 70%.
  • Full about 0.76 to 1 mm (0.030 to 0.040 in). Makers differ 70%.
  • Classic benchmark at 37 m (40 yd): Cylinder 40%, IC 50%, M 60%, Full 70% of pellets inside a 76 cm (30 in) circle 70%.
  • You test your own gun on paper in Session 5 (patterning).

• Your gun's manual wins (Tip). Learn the notches or stamps on your tubes (Tip).

More: length of pull and shims
  • LOP (length of pull) is trigger to the end of the stock. Most adults need about 14 to 14.75 inches 65%.
  • A winter jacket makes the stock feel longer. Try guns on in your hunting jacket (Tip).

• Ducks and geese: 3 shells max, one piece plug 99%.
  • Quail and grouse in BC: plug in too, magazine 2 max 99%.
More: the exact law and non toxic shot
The rule

For migratory birds (ducks, geese), the shotgun may hold no more than 3 shells in magazine and chamber combined 99%. The must be one piece and removable only by taking the gun apart 99%. A detachable magazine may hold no more than 2 99%.

  • Most new semi autos and pumps ship with the plug installed. Check before every duck hunt (Tip).
  • Quail and grouse too: in BC a pump, semi auto or other repeating shotgun needs a plug so the magazine holds no more than 2 shells 99%. Leave it in all season (Tip).
  • (steel, bismuth, tungsten, tin) is required for ducks, geese, coots and snipe 99%. Pigeons and doves are the exception 99%.

scope-guide:
Why it matters

Your Tikka T3x Arctic has iron sights only. A good scope shows a deer clearly at dawn, for one clean shot.

• A 3 to 9x40 or 3.5 to 10x40 covers BC deer to about 300 m 65%.
  • It must clear the rear drum sight: expect high rings (60 to 75%).
More: budget and the full short answer
  • A 3 to 9x40 or 3.5 to 10x40 scope covers BC deer out to about 300 m 65%.
  • Second focal plane, simple duplex crosshair, capped turrets (Tip).
  • Your Arctic has a tall rear drum sight. The scope must clear it 75%.
  • Expect high rings, and dry fit before you pay 60%.
  • Prices are in CAD (Canadian dollars).
  • Budget: entry about $270 to $690, mid about $765 to $1,300, premium about $1,700 to $3,300 65%. Price checked 2026-10-01.

• "3 to 9x40": zoom 3 to 9 times, 40 mm front lens 85%.
  • More zoom is not better. It shrinks your view (Tip).
More: low power, high power, lens size
  • "3 to 9x40" means zoom 3 times to 9 times, with a 40 mm front lens 85%.
  • Low power (2.5 to 3x) gives a wide view for close deer in timber 65%.
  • 9 to 10x is plenty for a deer at 300 m 65%.
  • Objective 40 to 44 mm is the sweet spot. Bigger sits higher and weighs more 65%.
  • More zoom is not better. It shrinks your view and adds weight (Tip).

• Beginner pick: SFP (second focal plane) with a duplex crosshair 70%.
More: SFP, FFP, BDC explained
  • SFP (second focal plane): crosshair stays the same size when you zoom 70%.
    • Simple. Best for beginners. Hash marks are only true at one power 70%.
  • FFP (first focal plane): crosshair grows with zoom. Marks are true at every power 70%.
    • Better for long range dialing. Thin crosshair at low power in dim light 65%.
  • Reticle: duplex (thick outer posts, thin centre) is simplest 70%.
  • BDC (bullet drop compensator) hash marks help only after you confirm drops on paper 70%.
  • The distances on the BDC drawing are an example only. Every scope and load differs.

• 1 click = 1/4 MOA (minute of angle), about 0.73 cm at 100 m (70 to 85%).
  • Eye relief 9 cm (3.5 in) or more. A .308 kicks 65%.
More: turrets, eye relief, parallax
  • Turrets: the knobs that move the crosshair. Capped turrets cannot get bumped in the bush 65%.
    • Most hunting scopes move 1/4 MOA per click 70%. Session 5 has the math.
  • Eye relief: distance from your eye to the rear lens for a full picture 85%.
    • Look for about 9 cm (3.5 in) or more. A .308 kicks, and short eye relief cuts your brow 65%.
  • Parallax: the crosshair seems to shift if your eye is off centre 80%.
    • Fixed at 100 yd (91 m) is fine for hunting out to about 300 m 65%.

• Bring the rifle to the store. Dry fit scope and rings before you pay (Tip).
More: rail, sight and ring notes
  • 20 inch stainless barrel, 1 in 10 twist (Sako spec page, 95%; check the stamp on your barrel), removable rail 80%.
  • Rail is short, about 12 to 13 cm (4.75 to 5 in), to make room for the rear sight 70%.

More: the full steps and torque table
  1. Prove the rifle unloaded. Bolt out ().

sighting-in:
Why it matters

A new scope is not aimed until you shoot it. A shotgun is not understood until you see its pattern.

• 3 shot groups from a solid rest. Adjust from the group centre 70%.
  • Same load you hunt with. Different bullets hit different spots 75%.
More: full plan and what to bring
  • Rifle: , then 25 m to get on paper, then 100 m (109 yd) for the real (Tip).
  • Shoot 3 shot groups from a solid rest. Adjust from the centre of the group, not one shot 70%.
  • Use the same load you will hunt with. Different bullets hit different spots 75%.
  • Shotgun: at 37 m (40 yd) on a 76 cm (30 in) circle 70%.
  • Bring: ammo, targets, stapler, rest or bags, ear and eye protection, tools for the turrets (Tip).
  • Let the barrel cool between groups. A hot barrel can shift shots (Tip).

Bore sight in 3 steps1 of 3
More: the full steps
  1. Prove the rifle unloaded. Bolt out ().
  2. Set the rifle solid in a rest or sandbags, target at 25 m.
  3. Look through the bore from the back. Move the rifle until the target is centred in the bore 70%.
  4. Without moving the rifle, look through the scope.
  5. Turn the turrets until the crosshair sits on the same spot 70%.
  6. A shop laser bore sighter does the same job. It still is not a zero (Tip).
▶How to Sight in a Rifle Scope Presented by Larry Potterfield | MidwayUSA GunsmithingBore sight first, then fine tune at 100 m.
MidwayUSA, YouTube, 4 min. Needs internet.

Zero in 4 steps1 of 4
More: the full steps
  • At 25 m: fire 1 shot, check, then a 3 shot group. Get it centred left and right (Tip).
  • Move to 100 m (109 yd). Fire a 3 shot group at the bullseye.
  • Find the centre of the group. Measure how far it is from the bullseye, in cm.
  • Turn the turrets the right number of clicks (next screen).
  • Fire another 3 shot group to confirm. Repeat until centred.
  • Then shoot from sitting and kneeling with sticks. That is how you will shoot a deer (Tip).
▶How to Zero a Riflescope in 3 Shots or LessZero your scope in three shots with a solid rest.
Vortex Optics, YouTube, 3 min. Needs internet.

• Clicks = cm off ÷ 0.73, at 100 m 85%. Check the turret cap says 1/4 MOA (minute of angle) 70%.
More: MOA, yards, 25 m and MRAD
  • MOA is a tiny angle: about 2.9 cm at 100 m 85%.
  • Most hunting scopes move 1/4 MOA per click 70%. Check the turret cap.
  • So 1 click moves the shot about 0.73 cm at 100 m 85%.
    • At 100 yd (91 m): about 0.66 cm per click 85%.
    • At 25 m: about 0.18 cm per click. You need 4 times the clicks 85%.
  • Example: group is 6 cm low and 3 cm left at 100 m.
    • Up: 6 ÷ 0.73 = about 8 clicks "UP".
    • Right: 3 ÷ 0.73 = about 4 clicks "R".
  • Turn the knob the way the arrow says to move the bullet (UP, R) 70%.

My lean (opinion)

More: pros and cons of each way

Decoys over water

  • Pros: birds come to you, slow and close. Best shots. Best way to learn.
  • Cons: need decoys (6 to 12 is enough to start), a hide, and a way to fetch birds.

Jump shooting

  • Sneak along a creek, slough or pond edge. Ducks flush close.
  • Pros: cheap, active, no decoys. Good with 2 hunters.
  • Cons: hard fast shots. Birds may fall into deep or fast water. Safety needs a plan.

Pass shooting

  • Stand under a flight line between roost and food.
  • Pros: no gear.
  • Cons: long, crossing shots. More wounded birds. Hard for beginners.
  • My lean in full: jump shoot small calm water first. Then a small decoy spread on a pond with a shallow shore. Skip pass shooting until you are hitting clay targets well. Pick water where any bird you drop can be reached by wading or by boat.

More: the eight steps in words
  1. Night before: check sunrise, legal start (half an hour before), and the wind forecast.
  2. Pack: licences, ID, both federal permits, steel shells, PFDs, waders, net, game bag, headlamps.
  3. Arrive 1 hour before legal light. Set 6 to 12 decoys in a J hook with flashlights only.
  4. Hide on shore with the wind at your side or back. Unload guns on the walk in until set.
  5. Zones of fire agreed. Phone on silent. Watch the clock: no shot before legal time.
  6. Let ducks commit to the pocket. Call the shot. Shoot your own side only.
  7. Fetch each bird before the next flock if you can. Count birds by species.
  8. Done by 10:00 or at your bag. Pick up every decoy and every empty shell.

Why it matters

Quail are fast, fun and live close to farms and homes. Most of the skill is getting permission and keeping every shot safe.

  • Residents need only the BC hunting licence for quail. No species licence 99%.
More: trip assumptions
  • Trip: the Okanagan, Region 8. Two hunters with shotguns.
  • Assumption: no landowner permission yet. No dog.
  • Residents need only the BC hunting licence for quail. No species licence 99%.

More: season and limits in full
  • Region 8 quail, synopsis page 68: 1 October to 30 November 99%. The row says only "QUAIL"; California quail is the one you will see (Tip).
  • Daily bag 10. Possession 30 99%.
  • Open in MUs (Management Units) 8-1 to 8-15 and 8-21 to 8-26 99%.
  • Legal hours: 1 hour before sunrise to 1 hour after sunset 99%.
  • Lead shot is legal for quail. The shot ban covers ducks, geese, coots and snipe, not upland birds 99%. BC lists one non toxic shot only area, the Delta and Surrey dykes, far from the Okanagan 99%. Steel works fine (Tip).
  • Each hunter has a personal bag limit 99%. Birds you shoot count in your own bag, so you cannot fill your partner's limit 90%.
• They would rather run than fly. Pushed, they burst up with whirring wings 75%.

More: habitat and habits in full
  • In BC, mostly in the Okanagan and Kettle valleys and on southeast Vancouver Island 75%.
  • They live in farm and suburban edges with lots of cover, and in brushy creeks, grassland and open forest 75%.
  • Fall and winter flocks are called coveys. Often family groups, sometimes very large 75%.
  • They feed mornings and evenings. They rest in shrubs midday and roost in trees 75%.
  • A lookout bird, often a male, watches while the rest feed 75%.
  • They would rather run than fly. When pushed, they burst up with loud whirring wings 75%.

• Listen at first light. Their call carries far (Tip).
  • After the first flush, singles hold tighter (Tip).
More: where to look in full
  • Brushy draws, blackberry and rose thickets, creek edges near grain or orchards (Tip).
  • Listen at first light. Their call carries far (Tip).
  • Look for dusting spots and tracks on dirt roads near cover (Tip).
  • After the first flush, singles hold tighter. Mark where they landed and follow up (Tip).
  • Best time, my opinion: the first 2 hours after legal light and the last 2 hours before sunset, on calm days. Late October and November, after leaves drop, you can see them better.

  • Walk in a straight line, side by side, 15 to 25 m (16 to 27 yd) apart (Tip).
  • Each hunter takes birds on their own side of centre (Tip).

  • Never swing through your partner. Stop the swing, gun up, safety on (Tip).
  • Blaze orange hat and vest on both of you in brush (Tip).

No shooting across, or hunting on, the road allowance of a numbered highway or a 2 lane public road the province maintains 99%. No loaded firearm in or on a vehicle or (all terrain vehicle) 99%.

after-the-shot:
Why it matters

The shot is 1 second. The next 3 hours decide if you find the deer and if the meat is good.

Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

  • Each of you notches only your own licence, for your own kill 99%.
More: the fast order
  • Fast order: wait, mark, track, approach, notch, evidence, dress, cool, transport, report.
  • Tagging and evidence rules are law. Tracking and dressing steps are skills (Tip).
  • Your brother hunts too. Each of you notches only your own licence, for your own kill 99%.

• Stay still, watch, listen for a crash. Pin both spots (Tip).
  • Wait about 30 minutes. Longer if the hit was far back (Tip).
More: wait and mark details
  • Stay still. Watch where it runs. Listen for a crash. Tip.
  • Rifle reloaded and on safe. Watch for 5 minutes in case it stands. Tip.
  • Drop a phone map pin where you shot from and where the deer stood. Tip.
  • Note a landmark at the last place you saw it (a tree, a rock). Tip.
  • Wait about 30 minutes before you follow. Longer if you think the hit was far back. Tip, common hunter practice, not law.

• Bright pink and bubbly: lungs. Dark or gut matter: back out (Tip).
  • You must make all reasonable effort to find it 99%.
  • Fence or posted land: stop. No tracking exception 99%.
More: tracking details and the law
  • Go to where it stood. Look for blood, hair, scuffed ground. Tip.
  • Bright pink, bubbly blood often means a lung hit. Dark blood or gut matter: back out and wait hours. Tip.
  • Mark each blood spot with tape or a phone pin. Tip.
  • Lost the trail? Go back to the last blood. Search in slow circles. Get your brother to help. Tip.
  • Trail goes into fenced or posted private land: stop. The Trespass Act has no exception for tracking wounded game. Get the owner's permission first, in writing if you can 99%.
  • Trail goes into a No Shooting Area or a park closed to hunting: no shooting there 99%. Call a conservation officer. Tip. See Phase 2 Session 5.
  • You must make all reasonable effort to find, finish and retrieve a wounded animal, and count it in your bag limit 99%.
• Slow circles from the last blood. Get your brother to help (Tip).

Approach and notch in 3 steps1 of 3
  • Notch the licence immediately, before you handle the animal 99%.
  • Follow the instructions printed on your licence 99%.
More: notch rules in detail
  • Come from behind the back, rifle ready. Touch the eye with a stick. No blink means dead. Tip.
  • Notch (cancel) the species licence immediately after the kill and before you handle the animal 99%.
  • Cancel it the way the instructions printed on that licence say 99%. The synopsis does not list the steps 95%.
  • A cancelled licence records the date, the region number and, where it applies, the antler configuration 95%.
  • Read the instructions on your own licence before the hunt. Tip.
  • Keep the notched licence with you. Carry all licences for the year 99%.
  • Take photos: the deer, the notched licence, the spot. Tip.

• Unskinned tail and sex parts stay naturally attached 99%.
  • Antlers are not on the deer list. Keep the tail and parts on a buck too 95%.
More: evidence of sex in detail
  • Evidence of sex stays naturally attached to the carcass, or to one part of it, until it is home and butchered there, at a meat cutter or cold storage plant, or inspected 99%.
  • Buck: the unskinned tail and a testicle or part of the penis 99%.
  • Doe: the unskinned tail and part of the udder and teats 99%.
  • Antlers on the head are not on the deer list. Keep the tail and sex parts even on a buck 95%.
  • Antler restricted season (like 4 point): keep the antlers naturally attached to part of the upper skull, together with the species licence, while you return from hunting 99%.
  • Do not cut these off during field dressing. Plan your cuts around them. Tip.

  • Gloves on. Do not cut the stomach or guts 75%.
  • Leave the evidence of sex attached (Tip). Full steps: Phase 5.

  • If gut contents touch meat, wipe them off right away with a clean cloth 75%.
  • Do it fast. Remove the guts as quickly as you can 75%.
  • Leave the evidence of sex attached. Check before each cut. Tip.

  • Reach in behind the last rib for the tenderloin. Tip.

  • Prop it open, shade, off the ground (Tip).

4 safe carries1 of 4
  • Pick the carry that keeps the muzzle off your partner (Tip, hunter education).

• Agree left and right before first light. Never shoot across your partner.
  • Boat: back to back, sit to shoot 70%.
More: blind and boat details

In a blind

  • You and your brother agree who takes the left side and who takes the right side before first light.
  • Shoot only birds or deer on your side. Muzzles out the front, never across your partner.
  • Guns rest muzzle up or out the front when not shooting. Never leaned on the wall behind you.

In a boat or canoe

  • Two hunters sit back to back: bow shooter faces forward, stern shooter faces back (70%, hunter education guidance).
  • Shoot sitting. Never stand. See the water safety session.
  • Only one person moves at a time. Unload before anyone changes seats.
  • Loading in a boat is a legal question too. See the water safety session.

Cross a fence step by step1 of 5
  • Never climb a fence, log or bank with a loaded firearm.
More: the steps in words
  • Alone: unload, PROVE it, lay the firearm under or through the fence, muzzle pointed away from you 75%.
  • Cross well away from the muzzle, then pick it up by the stock 75%.
  • With a partner: one unloads and holds both firearms, actions open. The other crosses, then takes both. Then the first crosses (Tip, common hunter education method).
  • Never climb a fence, log or bank with a loaded firearm in your hands.
▶How To Safely Cross a Fence With a FirearmUnload, pass it under, cross away from the muzzle.
Hunter Ed, YouTube, 1 min. Needs internet.

• No loaded firearm in or on a vehicle or boat in BC 99%. Load only where you may lawfully shoot 99%.
  • Unload facing away from the car, partner and road.
More: the exact law
  • Load only where you may lawfully shoot. Federal rules allow loading, or handling a loaded firearm, only in a place where it may lawfully be discharged (federal transport regulations, section 15) 99%.
  • In BC, you must not transport, carry or store a loaded firearm in or on a vehicle or boat (Firearm Violence Prevention Act, section 4(1)) 99%. The synopsis says the same for vehicles (page 11, item 28, 2 October 2026 edition) 99%.
    • Boats only: from 1 October 2026, a BC hunting exemption allows a loaded firearm in a boat with no motor, or while the motor is not moving the boat, when hunting or retrieving wildlife (Designation and Exemption Regulation, section 18) 95%. See the water safety session.
  • "Unloaded" means no cartridge in the chamber, and none in a magazine attached to or inserted in the firearm (federal transport regulations, section 1) 99%.
  • So: magazine out, chamber empty, before the firearm goes in the car or on the (All Terrain Vehicle). Both count as vehicles (Firearm Violence Prevention Act, section 1) 95%.
  • Leaving the car? Non restricted firearms go locked in the trunk or a lockable compartment. No trunk: out of sight, car locked (federal transport regulations, section 10(2)) 99%.
  • Unload facing away from the car, partner and road. Load the same way, at the start of the walk.
Warning

BC's Firearm Violence Prevention Act (FVPA) came into force 1 October 2026, including the vehicle and boat rules in sections 4 and 5(1) (Order in Council 156/2026) 99%. Its hunting exemptions cover boats only (Designation and Exemption Regulation, sections 18 and 19) 95%. No exemption for cars, trucks or ATVs was found 90%.

• Only one of you shoots at a deer unless you agreed a backup plan (Tip).
More: roles, and a non hunting companion
  • Both of you hold (Conservation and Outdoor Recreation Education) and a (Possession and Acquisition Licence). Each carries your own licences and tags (owner confirmed).
  • Before every walk, agree three things: who covers left, who covers right, and the stop signal.
  • Only one of you shoots at a deer unless you agreed a backup plan first (Tip).
  • Neither one steps in front of the other's muzzle. Ever.
  • After a shot, both unload, then walk up together. The shooter leads.
  • First hunt for him? Swap roles at midday so each practises spotter and shooter (Tip).

General case: a non hunting companion

  • A person who only watches carries no firearm. Searching for or following wildlife while carrying a firearm counts as hunting (page 3, definition of hunt) 95%. See the Licences session.
  • They walk behind or beside you, never ahead, and freeze on your signal.
Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Grandpa's rule (wisdom): The safety is a mechanical device. Your muzzle and your finger are the real safety.

Common mistakes
  • Muzzle on your partner while unloading at the tailgate.
  • A round in an attached magazine. That counts as loaded.
  • Following a running deer past your arc.
Do this in the field

At the car, each runs PROVE out loud while the other watches. Walk 50 m (55 yd) unloaded, side by side, and point out each other's arc.

water-safety:
Why it matters

October water in the Interior is cold. A small boat tips fast. The cold, not swimming skill, is what kills.

Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

• Use the 10 minutes for one job: get out, or onto the hull (Tip).
More: where 1 10 1 comes from
  • The "1 10 1 principle" is a name, not exact timing. It was made by physiologist Dr. Gordon Giesbrecht 80%.
  • 1 minute: cold shock. You gasp and breathe hard. Get your breathing under control 80%.
  • 10 minutes: of useful muscle movement before hands and arms stop working 80%.
  • 1 hour: before hypothermia makes you unconscious 80%.
  • Real times vary with water temperature, body and clothing. Some experts say it is too neat 70%.
  • The first gasp is the killer. If your head is under water when you gasp, you inhale water 75%.
  • Tip: use the 10 minutes for one job: get out of the water or onto the hull. Do not swim for shore unless it is very close.
▶Cold Water Boot Camp - 1-10-1 PrincipleFall in cold water? 1 minute breathe, 10 minutes move, 1 hour.
SmartBoater, YouTube, 8 min. Needs internet.

• A (personal flotation device) only works if you wear it. My lean: wear it, zipped, every minute.
  • Try it on over all your hunting layers.
More: what the law says
  • Canadian law requires an approved PFD or lifejacket of the right size on board for each person 99%.
  • The law requires carrying it, not wearing it 95%. One exception: an inflatable PFD must be worn in an open boat 99%. My lean: wear it, zipped, every minute on the water.
  • About 87% of boaters who drowned were not wearing one, per the Lifesaving Society 75%.
  • Pick one that fits over your hunting jacket. Try it on with all layers before the trip.

• Any motor, even a small electric: carry a PCOC (Pleasure Craft Operator Card) or other proof of competency (95 to 99%).
  • Never lean out for a bird. Bring it along the hull to the middle.
More: boat, kayak and retrieving
  • Any boat fitted with a motor needs the operator to have proof of competency on board, usually a PCOC 99%. The rule sets no minimum motor size, so a small electric counts 95%.
  • 10 ft boat: check the capacity plate. Count you, your brother, gear, guns and a deer (VERIFY plate numbers on your own boat).
  • Load low and in the middle. Heavy items on the floor, centred side to side.
  • Kayak: one person, guns cased and strapped, dry bag clipped in. Hard to shoot from and easy to tip.
  • No dog? Retrieve birds with the boat, motor off and gun unloaded, or with a long handled landing net (Tip).
  • Never lean out over the side to grab a bird. Bring it along the hull to the middle.

• Motor pushing the boat: every gun unloaded 95%. Ducks: no hunting from a moving motor boat 99%.
More: the exact rules, BC and federal
  • BC (Firearm Violence Prevention Act), in force 1 October 2026, section 4: you must not transport, carry or store a loaded firearm in or on a vehicle or boat 95%.
  • Section 5 of the same Act: no shooting "in, on or from a vehicle or boat" 95%.
  • Hunting exemption, in force the same day: a loaded gun, and shooting, are allowed in a boat with no motor, or in a motor boat while the motor is not propelling it, when you are hunting or retrieving wildlife 95%. For ducks and geese, the federal moving boat rule below also applies 99%.
  • So while the motor pushes the boat, every gun aboard is unloaded 95%.
  • BC synopsis, page 11, item 23 (2 October 2026 edition), deer and other game: no hunting from a boat unless it is not being propelled by a motor, or is held still in current, tide or wind by the motor 99%. Item 22: no hunting wildlife from a motor vehicle 99%.
  • Federal, ducks and geese: no hunting from a moving boat with a motor or sail. Drifting on momentum from the motor still counts as moving 99%.
  • BC synopsis, page 11, item 24 (2 October 2026 edition), ducks and geese: no hunting "from or by using a moving boat that is equipped with a motor or sail" 99%. Same as the federal rule. This replaced the old power boat rule on 1 October 2026 (99%, B.C. Reg. 66/2026).
  • Safe habit: gun unloaded and in a case while moving. Load only once you are stopped and set (Tip). Federal transport rules require a non restricted firearm to be unloaded, not cased 95%.
My lean (opinion)

Use the boat as a ride to a shore blind or a point. Shoot from land. It removes most of the legal and tipping risk.

• Sit square, feet flat. Shoot only inside your arc. One person moves at a time.
More: why boats tip
  • Small boats and canoes tip when weight goes high or to one side.
  • Recoil pushes you back. Standing turns that into a fall over the side.
  • Sit square, feet flat, shoot only inside your own arc. See the firearm safety session.
  • One person moves at a time. Everyone else sits still.

If you go in1 of 5
More: the steps in words
  1. Expect the gasp. Mouth closed if you can. Float in your PFD and get breathing under control for about 1 minute 80%.
  2. Stay with the boat. It is bigger to see and helps you float 75%.
  3. Climb onto the hull to get as much of your body out of the water as you can 75%.
  4. Can't get out? Use the HELP (Heat Escape Lessening Posture): arms crossed on chest, knees up, ankles crossed 75%.
  5. Two people? Huddle, chests together 75%.
  6. Once out, stay out. Water pulls heat away about 25 times faster than air 70%.
  7. Let the gun go. It is replaceable.
Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Grandpa's rule (wisdom): The PFD in the bow locker is a cushion. The PFD on your chest is a lifejacket.

Common mistakes
  • PFD under the seat "to put on if we tip".
  • Motoring after a crippled duck with a loaded gun.
  • Standing up to shoot or to pull in a bird.
Do this in the field

Both wear PFDs over hunting layers. In shallow water, practise sitting back to back and reaching for a bird, gun unloaded.

bush-safety:
Why it matters

Most bad days in the bush start small: a wrong turn, wet socks, dark at 6 pm. A plan and a few tools keep them small.

Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

Lost? STOP1 of 4
  • STOP: Stop, Think, Observe, Plan (AdventureSmart) 75%. Lost, disoriented or hurt 75%.
More: the details
  • AdventureSmart teaches STOP: Stop, Think, Observe, Plan 75%.
  • Some AdventureSmart material uses Sit instead of Stop. Same idea 70%.
  • Stop: do not keep walking. Most people make it worse by pushing on.
  • Think: where did you last know where you were?
  • Observe: map app, compass, sun, creeks, the sound of a road.
  • Plan: stay put, or move only if you are sure. Shelter and fire before dark.
  • Use it when lost, disoriented or hurt 75%.
▶Hug-A-Tree & Survive filmLost? Stop. Stay put. Shelter and signal.
AdventureSmart, YouTube, 12 min. Needs internet.

• Always leave a trip plan with someone at home 75%. List the car, the and the boat.
More: the 3 Ts and the app
  • AdventureSmart's 3 Ts: Trip planning, Training, Taking the essentials 75%.
  • Always fill out a trip plan and leave it with someone at home 75%.
  • AdventureSmart has a free trip plan app that sends your plan to a contact 70%.
  • Write: who, vehicle and plate, where you park, route, return time, when to call for help.
  • Say who to call if you are late: 911, and police will start a search (Tip: confirm with your local police).
  • Assumption: you hunt from the car, the ATV and the boat. List all three in the plan.

• iPhone 14 or later: Emergency SOS via satellite in Canada, iOS 16.1 or later 85%.
  • Needs open sky 75%.
More: iPhone details and messengers
  • Much of the backcountry near Sun Peaks has no cell signal (Assumption: check with your carrier map).
  • iPhone 14 or later can send Emergency SOS via satellite in Canada with iOS 16.1 or later 85%.
  • Messages via satellite and Find My via satellite also work in Canada on iPhone 14 or later 80%.
  • Apple says it is free for two years from activation of the phone 80%. After that: VERIFY.
  • It needs open sky. Trees, hills and canyons slow or block it 75%.
  • A dedicated satellite messenger (two way texting and SOS) works on any phone. Needs a paid plan.
My lean (opinion)

Both carry iPhone 14 or later? That covers SOS. If not, buy or rent a satellite messenger so each hunter can call for help alone.

• Shivering that stops is an emergency 75%.
More: first aid and October risk
  • Mild: shivering, cold, and the "umbles": fumbles, mumbles, stumbles, grumbles 75%.
  • Moderate: violent shivering, confusion, poor judgment 75%.
  • Severe: shivering stops, stiff muscles, glassy stare, slow breathing. This is an emergency 75%.
  • First aid: out of wind and wet, dry layers on, cover head and neck, rewarm gently 75%.
  • Warm sweet drinks only if fully awake and able to swallow (Tip, common first aid advice).
  • October risk: wet from sweat or rain, then sitting still glassing as the sun drops.
▶How to spot and treat hypothermiaSpot hypothermia early: shivering, fumbling, confusion.
Canadian Red Cross / Croix-Rouge canadienne, YouTube, 1 min. Needs internet.

• Turn back 1 hour before sunset. Dry layer and toque every trip.
More: fire rules and the numbers
  • Interior October can go from sun to sleet in an afternoon. Pack a dry layer and a toque every trip.
  • Daylight is short. Turn back time = 1 hour before sunset.
  • Kamloops Fire Centre campfire and open fire rules changed in late September 2026 75%. Today's status: VERIFY on the BC Wildfire Service app before any fire.
  • Report a wildfire: 1 800 663 5555 toll free, or *5555 on a cell 80%.
  • Never park a hot vehicle or ATV on dry grass. The exhaust can start a fire (Tip).
• Spray on the hip belt or chest, not in the pack (Tip).

More: spray range, grizzlies, and who to call
  • Black bears live around Kamloops and Sun Peaks 75%.
  • Grizzlies: the Thompson Nicola region holds about 317 grizzlies 65%. A Sun Peaks visitor site says only black bears at the resort 60%. My lean: carry spray as if both are there.
  • Bear spray: point it at the ground a few metres in front of the bear, then sweep up to its face 70%.
  • Do not spray into the wind. It will blow back on you 70%.
  • Range: about 3 m to 10 m depending on the can. Read your can 70%.
  • Black bear attack: defensive (cubs or food) is the most common type. Spray. If it makes contact, play dead (75%, Parks Canada).
  • Predatory attack (stalks you, or at night): spray, stand big, fight back. Do not play dead (75%, Parks Canada).
  • Cougar: never run, look big, back away slowly, keep eye contact. If attacked, always fight back (75%, WildSafeBC).
  • A gut pile draws bears. Move the meat away from it fast and watch your back.
  • Report a dangerous bear or cougar: RAPP (Report All Poachers and Polluters) 1 877 952 7277, open 24/7, for wildlife and human conflicts where public safety is at risk (synopsis page 2) 95%.
▶How to Use Bear Spray - Banff National ParkRemove the clip, aim low, spray a cloud between you and the bear.
Parks Canada, YouTube, 2 min. Needs internet.▶How to Use Bear SprayOne minute bear spray demo.
AlbertaParks, YouTube, 1 min. Needs internet.

• Firm pressure first. Life threatening limb bleed and pressure fails: tourniquet, 5 to 10 cm (2 to 4 in) above 70%.
More: Red Cross steps and the kit
  • The big killer after a fall, knife slip or gunshot is bleeding from an arm or leg.
  • Red Cross guidance: firm direct pressure first. If bleeding from a limb is life threatening and pressure fails, use a tourniquet 70%.
  • Place it about 5 to 10 cm (2 to 4 in) above the wound, between wound and heart. Tighten until bleeding stops. Write the time 70%.
  • Buy a commercial windlass tourniquet, not a homemade one. The Red Cross training kit uses the SOFTT (Special Operations Forces Tactical Tourniquet) type 65%.
  • Kit carried by each hunter on the body: tourniquet, gauze, pressure bandage, gloves, emergency blanket, lighter.
  • Take a first aid course. A kit you do not know how to use is weight.
Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Grandpa's rule (wisdom): Tell someone where you went. Pack like you will sleep out. Leave the bush an hour before dark.

Common mistakes
  • No trip plan, "only up the road".
  • Bear spray buried in the pack.
  • Sweating on the climb, then sitting still wet.
Do this in the field

Fill out the AdventureSmart trip plan. Test SOS demo mode on your iPhone. Practise drawing bear spray in under 2 seconds, safety clip on.

atv-rules:
Why it matters

An unregistered quad, a loaded rifle on the rack or a ride into a closed area each cost more than the hunt. Learn the rules once.

Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

  • (all terrain vehicle) means your quad. (Off Road Vehicle) is the law's wider word 98%.
More: about this session
  • Most lines here were read directly in the official synopsis, the Off Road Vehicle Act and its regulation, and ICBC (Insurance Corporation of British Columbia) pages. Those lines show 95% or more.
  • ATV means a quad here. ORV is the law's wider word: quads, dirt bikes, side by sides and snowmobiles 98%.
  • Your ATV's registration status is unknown. The checklist at the end sorts that out.

• FSR (Forest Service Road) = Crown land: the ORV (Off Road Vehicle) Act applies 90%.
  • Private land: only with the owner's consent 98%.

LawWhat it coversWhere it applies
Off Road Vehicle Act and RegulationRegistration, plate, helmet, lights, photo ID (identification), kids 98%Crown land, including resource roads 98%

The rule

Synopsis page 11, item 28 (2 October 2026 edition), exact words 99%: "To discharge, carry or have in possession a firearm containing live ammunition in its breech or in its magazine attached to the firearm, in or on a railway car, motor vehicle, sleigh, aircraft, bicycle or other conveyance."

Why it matters

Deer bed on benches, cross at saddles and feed on edges. A topo map shows all three from your kitchen table.

  • Each contour line is one flat slice of the hill 98%.
  • Close lines: steep. Far apart: gentle 98%.
More: topo map basics
  • A topo (topographic) map shows the shape of the ground with contour lines 95%.
  • Canada's standard sheets are the NTS (National Topographic System) at 1:50,000 and 1:250,000 98%.
  • Every phone map app draws the same contours. Learn them once, use them everywhere.

• 1 cm on the map is 500 m on the ground 98%.
  • A thumb, about 2 cm, is 1 km: 20 to 30 minutes of walking (Tip).
More: scale details
  • 1:50,000 means 1 unit on the map is 50,000 units on the ground. 1 cm on the map is 500 m on the ground 98%.
  • 1:250,000: 1 cm is 2.5 km 98%. Good for driving, useless for picking a bench.
  • One 1:50,000 sheet covers about 1,000 square km 95%.
  • Rule of thumb at 1:50,000: a thumb width, about 2 cm, is 1 km (Tip).
  • Walking speed in hills is about 2 to 3 km per hour, so a thumb is 20 to 30 minutes (Tip).
  • North is at the top of an NTS (National Topographic System) map 98%.

• The thick line carries the height. The top of the number faces uphill 98%.
  • The height step between lines is printed in the map margin 90%.
More: contour line details
  • A contour line joins points of equal elevation 98%.
  • Lines close together: steep. Lines far apart: gentle 98%.
  • The contour interval is the height step between lines. It is printed in the map margin and varies by sheet 90%. Newer sheets use 20 m 70%. Check the margin.
  • Every fifth line is thicker, the index contour, and carries a number 90%.
  • The numbers read uphill: the top of the number points up the slope 98%.
  • Colours on NTS (National Topographic System) sheets: brown contours, blue water, green wooded, white open ground 98%.
  • Water runs in draws. Arrows and falls symbols show which way it flows 95%.

Five shapes to find on any topo1 of 5
More: every shape, in words
  • Ridge: a long high spine. Contours make U or V shapes that point downhill 90%.
  • Draw: a small valley running down a slope. Contours make V shapes that point uphill, toward the high ground 90%. Draws carry water, cool air and deer.
  • Saddle: the low point on a ridge between two highs. Two sets of closed loops with an hourglass between them 90%. Deer cross ridges at saddles 65%. Hunter observation.
  • Bench: a flat step on a slope. A wide gap between lines with tight lines above and below 90%. Deer bed on benches with a view 65%. Hunter observation.
  • Spur: a short ridge running off the main ridge. Contours point downhill, like a tongue 90%.
  • Cliff: lines touch or merge. Do not plan a route through them 90%.
  • Knob or peak: small closed loops. A glassing seat if it looks across a bench (Tip).
• Find each shape here before you go on.

• Saddles are crossings. Benches are beds (65%, hunter observation).
  • Glass benches from across the draw (Tip).

• Count lines per cm before a dawn climb (Tip).
  • Follow one contour line to stay flat and quiet (Tip).

Grandpa's rule (wisdom): Read the lines before you read the leaves. The map tells you where to look. Your boots confirm it.

More: the mistakes in full
  • Mixing up ridge and draw. The V points uphill for a draw and downhill for a ridge. Water runs in draws, never on ridges.
  • Trusting the colour green. Green means trees on the day the map was made. Cutblocks and burns change it.
  • Planning a straight line that crosses ten lines in a centimetre.

Why it matters

Phones die, fog comes in, every draw looks the same at dusk. A compass and one bearing get you back to the truck.

  • Phone with offline maps, baseplate compass, paper map of the block (Tip).
  • Set the compass for local declination once a season.
More: acronyms on this page
  • GPS (Global Positioning System), UTM (Universal Transverse Mercator), NTS (National Topographic System), (Management Unit), NRCan (Natural Resources Canada).
  • Carry three things: a phone with offline maps, a baseplate compass, and a paper map of the block (Tip).
  • Set the compass up once for local declination and it is done for the season.

• Red end of the needle points to magnetic north 95%.
  • Buy one with adjustable declination.
More: each part, in words
  • Baseplate: the clear plate with a ruler and the direction of travel arrow 95%.
  • Bezel: the ring that turns, marked 0 to 360 degrees 95%.
  • Orienting arrow: the outline arrow inside the bezel. Hunters call it the shed (Tip).
  • Needle: the red end points to magnetic north 95%.
  • Index line: the mark at the top where you read the bearing 95%.
  • Buy one with adjustable declination. A sighting mirror helps. Prices: VERIFY at a local store.

Take a bearing and walk it1 of 6
More: the six steps in words
  1. Point the direction of travel arrow at the object: the saddle, the truck, the far knob.
  2. Turn the bezel until the orienting arrow boxes the red needle. Red in the shed.
  3. Read the number at the index line. That is your bearing 95%.
  4. To follow it: hold the compass flat, turn your body until red is in the shed, walk toward the direction of travel arrow.
  5. Pick a tree on that line, walk to it, repeat. Do not stare at the needle while walking (Tip).
  6. Back bearing to return: add 180, or subtract 180 if the bearing is over 180 95%.

More: declination details and sources
  • True north is the pole. Magnetic north is where the needle points. The angle between them is declination 98%.
  • Heffley Creek, October 2026: about 15.1 degrees east, falling about 0.13 degrees a year 80%. Computed with the World Magnetic Model 2025. Mission: about 15.2 degrees east 80%.
  • East declination means the needle points to the right of true north 98%.
  • NRCan (Natural Resources Canada) rhyme 98%: "declination west, magnetic best (add); declination east, magnetic least (subtract)."
  • So: map bearing to compass bearing, subtract 15. Compass bearing to map bearing, add 15 90%. My reading of the rhyme for east declination.
  • Adjustable compass: set 15 degrees east once and read map bearings straight off the bezel 90%.
  • Printed NTS (National Topographic System) maps show grid declination for the year printed plus a yearly change. Old maps drift 98%.
  • Phone apps correct declination for you 85%. Your compass does not.

• UTM (Universal Transverse Mercator): read right, then up 95%.
  • Kamloops is zone 10U. East of 120 degrees west is 11U 90%.
More: UTM, latitude and longitude details
  • Latitude and longitude: degrees north and west. Three formats get mixed up: decimal degrees, degrees and minutes, degrees minutes seconds 90%. Pick decimal degrees and stick to it.
  • UTM (Universal Transverse Mercator): a metric grid. NTS (National Topographic System) maps are drawn on it 98%. Zone, easting (metres east), northing (metres north).
  • Kamloops and Heffley Creek are in zone 10U. East of the 120 degree west line, roughly Sun Peaks and the Shuswap, is zone 11U 90%. Zones are 6 degrees wide. A wrong zone puts you hundreds of kilometres out.
  • Read right, then up: easting first, northing second 95%.
  • The blue grid on a 1:50,000 sheet is 1 km squares, 2 cm on the paper 85%.
  • Datum: Canadian maps use NAD83 and phones use WGS84. For hunting they agree within a couple of metres 75%.
  • Search and rescue wants one line: zone, easting, northing, or decimal degrees. Write both formats on your (Tip).

• GPS (Global Positioning System) needs no cell signal 95%.
  • Map tiles do. Download them at home.
More: GPS details
  • GPS works with no cell signal. The satellites are free 95%. The map tiles are not: download them at home.
  • Accuracy is a few metres in the open, worse under thick timber and in narrow canyons 80%.
  • Airplane mode on: GPS still works and the battery lasts longer 85%.
  • Cold kills batteries. Phone in an inside pocket, power bank in the pack (Tip).
  • Mark the truck as a waypoint before you walk. Mark the deer before you start cutting (Tip).
  • Paper map and compass go anyway. Every time (Tip).

More: cutblock and burn details
  • Cutblocks and burns grow feed. Edges where a 5 to 15 year old block meets timber are deer country 60%. Hunter observation.

More: elevation and snow details
  • Region 3: no motor vehicles above 1,700 m except on existing roads and trails 98%. Plan the walk, not the ride, up high.
  • October: mule deer start down from summer range when snow and cold arrive. Most are back on by late October to November 85%. Interior deer can stay high into December 80%. The two sources conflict. Plan both elevations.
  • Winter range is south and west facing, old Douglas fir 85%. Deer struggle in snow over about 30 cm, and snow deeper than about 50 cm pushes them off a slope 75%.

  • Elevation on the map: contour numbers. Elevation on the phone: GPS (Global Positioning System) altitude, often 10 to 20 m off 75%.

wind-thermals:
Why it matters

A deer that smells you is gone before you see it. You cannot hide scent, but you can put it where deer are not.

  • Keep the deer upwind: the wind blows from the deer to you.

• Your scent drifts with the air, like smoke from a campfire.
  • Deer rely heavily on smell to detect danger 70%.
More: how scent moves, in full
  • Your scent drifts with the air, like smoke from a campfire.
  • Deer rely heavily on smell to detect danger 70%.
  • Deer often travel with the wind at their back or side so they can smell behind and look ahead (60%, hunter observation).
  • Steady wind is your friend. Shifting, light wind is the danger.
  • Rule of thumb: keep the deer upwind of you. The wind blows from the deer to you.

• Morning sun warms slopes: air rises uphill 75%.
  • Evening slopes cool: air sinks downhill 75%.
More: thermals in full
  • Thermals are air currents made by the ground warming and cooling 75%.
  • Morning: the sun warms slopes and air rises uphill 75%.
  • Evening: slopes cool and air sinks downhill, into draws and valley floors 75%.
  • Shaded north slopes and timber stay cool longer, so the switch comes later there (Tip).
  • On calm days, thermals beat the light breeze. In strong wind, the wind wins (Tip).

• Morning: be above the deer. Evening: be below (Tip).

• Wind swirls in draws, saddles, valleys and thick timber 70%.
  • In a swirl, no setup is safe. Back out.
More: swirls in full
  • Wind swirls in draws, saddles, valleys and thick timber, where air bounces off terrain 70%.
  • Swirl also happens around the switch time, mid morning and near sunset, as thermals change direction (Tip).
  • Lakes and creeks: cold air often slides down creek bottoms in the evening (Tip).
  • In a swirl, no setup is safe. Back out and come back with steadier air.

Four ways to see the wind1 of 4

More: wind check tools in full
  • Puffer bottle: a squeeze bottle of unscented powder. One puff shows drift and direction 70%.
  • Milkweed fluff: floats far and shows thermals and swirls over terrain 70%.
  • Lighter flame: quick check, shows only the air right at your hand (Tip). Mind fire risk in dry grass.
  • Thread on your bow or rifle sling: always on, no hands (Tip).
  • Check every few minutes and at every new terrain feature, not just at the truck.

Tip (opinion)

Milkweed is the best teacher. Watch one tuft for 30 seconds.

• Plan an A and B spot for each wind. Wrong wind? Go to B.
  • Walk in with the wind in your face or across you.
More: the six planning steps
  1. Check the forecast wind direction and speed the night before.
  2. On the map, mark likely bedding and feeding areas.
  3. Mornings: come in from above or from the side so rising air carries scent up and away.
  4. Evenings: sit below or to the side so sinking air carries scent down and away.
  5. Plan an A and B spot for each wind. Wrong wind on the day? Go to B, do not force A.
  6. Walk in with the wind in your face or across you, never at your back toward the deer.

Grandpa's rule (wisdom): Hunt the wind you have, not the wind you wanted.

  • Checking wind once at the truck, then hunting a swirling valley.
  • A morning seat above deer bedded higher up still.
  • Ignoring the evening switch.
More: the mistakes in full
  • Checking wind once at the truck, then hunting a valley where it swirls.
  • Sitting on a morning ridge above deer that are bedded higher up, so rising air takes your scent right to them.

glassing:
Why it matters

In open Interior country you find more deer with your eyes than with your boots. lets you see them before they see you.

  • Sit, brace, glass slowly in strips. Look for parts of deer.

Get steady glass1 of 3
  • Move the binoculars, not your eyes inside them (Tip).
More: binocular technique in full
  • Set the eye cups and the right eye dial (diopter) once at home. Mark the setting.
  • Brace. Elbows on knees, back on a tree or pack. Shaking binoculars hide deer.
  • Hold still and let the view settle. Move the binoculars, not your eyes inside them (Tip).
  • Look through the binoculars for a long time, rest your eyes for a few seconds, then go back (Tip).
  • Use a hat brim or hand to cut glare when the sun is low in front of you.

• A tripod steadies the view and stops arm fatigue 65%.

Use the binoculars you have plus a cheap tripod adapter. Upgrade glass later.

  • Many western hunters rate a tripod as a bigger upgrade than better glass (60%, hunter opinion).

  • Steady glass shows small movement: a tail flick at 800 m (875 yd) you would miss handheld (Tip).
  • My lean in full: start with the binoculars you have plus a cheap tripod adapter. Upgrade glass later, once you know what you use.

More: the seven grid steps
  1. Pick a spot with a wide view and the wind right (see Wind and thermals).
  2. Quick scan first: open slopes, cut blocks, edges where deer are easy to see 65%.
  3. Then split the view into a grid in your head 65%.
  4. Start at one corner. Glass one strip slowly, left to right 65%.
  5. Overlap each binocular view by about a third so nothing falls in a gap 60%.
  6. Drop down one strip and come back right to left 65%.
  7. Then glass it again. Deer stand up, move and turn as light changes.

More: what to look for, in full
  • Do not look for a whole deer. Look for parts 65%.
  • A horizontal line in a world of vertical trees: a back or belly 65%.
  • Vertical legs under a shape that does not belong 65%.
  • An ear flick or tail twitch. Movement is the giveaway.
  • The white rump of a mule deer, or the flash of a white tail (Tip).
  • A shape that is the wrong colour: grey brown body against green or yellow.
  • Antler tips catching light, or a shiny black nose.
• Find each deer, then name the part you saw first.

• Glass at first light and in the last hour (Tip).
  • Deer legal hours: 1 hour before sunrise to 1 hour after sunset 99%.
More: times and places in full

  • You work out sunrise and sunset yourself, for each date and place (synopsis page 12) 99%.
  • Midday: glass shade, timber edges and benches where deer bed (Tip).
  • Glass from above, with the sun behind you, so deer are lit and you are not (Tip).
  • Near Sun Peaks: cut blocks, burns, open grass slopes and timber edges (Tip, check on your map).
• Glass from above with the sun behind you. Deer are lit, you are not (Tip).

Grandpa's rule (wisdom): Sit longer than you think. When you want to move, glass it one more time.

  • Looking only for a whole standing deer in the open.

still-hunting:
Why it matters

Most beginners walk through the bush at a hiking pace. Deer hear and see them long before. Slow down and the woods change.

• Still hunting: slow walking through cover to find a deer 70%.
  • Stalking: closing in on a deer you have already seen 70%.
More: still hunting vs stalking, in full
  • Still hunting: walking very slowly through deer cover, hoping to see a deer before it sees you 70%.
  • Stalking: you have already seen the deer. You close the distance for a shot 70%.
  • Still hunting suits thick timber and wet, quiet days.
  • Stalking suits open country after .
  • Both depend on wind. Read the wind session first.

• Move 2 or 3 steps, then stand and look 20 seconds or more (Tip).
  • A few hundred metres an hour is normal (Tip).
More: pace in full
  • Move 2 or 3 steps, then stand and look for 20 seconds or more. Some hunters stop for minutes (Tip, hunter method).
  • Look much more than you walk 65%.
  • Expect to cover very little ground: a few hundred metres an hour is normal (Tip).
  • Look near as well as far. A bedded deer may be very close 65%.
  • Before each step, pick where your foot goes next.
  • Heel down softly, roll to the ball, test before putting weight on it 65%.

• Move from cover to cover. Pause at each.
  • Stay in shade, off the skyline.
More: using cover, in full
  • Move when the deer's head is down feeding or behind a tree (Tip).
  • Stay in shade. Avoid the skyline on ridges.
  • Keep a tree or bush between you and where deer may be, then look around it, not over it (Tip).

• Keep a tree between you and the deer. Look around it (Tip).

• Deer hear higher pitch than people 75%.
  • A steady crunch, crunch sounds like a person (Tip).
More: hearing studies and noise, in full
  • White tailed deer hear about 0.25 to 30 kilohertz in one study, best at 4 to 8 kilohertz 75%.
  • People hear up to about 20 kilohertz. Deer hear higher pitch than we do 75%.
  • A second study found deer can hear even higher, past 50 kilohertz 65%.
  • Sharp, high sounds are the giveaway: zippers, Velcro, nylon scrape, metal on metal (Tip).
  • A snapped stick can sound like a deer. A steady crunch, crunch rhythm sounds like a person (Tip).
  • Mule deer hearing studies: none found. Assumption: similar.

• Jump up and down at the truck. Fix anything that rattles.
More: clothing and kit, in full
  • Wool and brushed fleece are quieter in brush than hard nylon shells (Tip).
  • Tape or wrap metal parts that clink: sling swivels, buckles, knife sheath (Tip).
  • Swap Velcro pockets for buttons or magnets, or leave them open.
  • Before you leave the truck, jump up and down. Fix anything that rattles.
  • Keep the gun's action and safety quiet. Practise moving the safety slowly at home.

Grandpa's rule (wisdom): If you think you are going slow enough, halve it.

Common mistakes
  • Hiking pace, called still hunting.
  • Looking only far and walking past a bedded deer at 20 m (22 yd).
  • A swishing nylon jacket and a Velcro rip near a feeding deer.

Still hunt 200 m (219 yd) of timber. Aim for 30 minutes or more. Your brother walks behind and names every noise.

weather-moon:
Why it matters

Hunters blame the moon, the pressure and the front. Know which ones the science backs, so you spend your days off on the things that matter.

  • The best day to hunt is the day you can go. Weather picks where, not whether (Tip).
More: the evidence summary in full
  • Strong evidence: snow and cold move mule deer, the moves bucks, hunting pressure changes deer.
  • Weak or mixed evidence: barometric pressure and fronts.
  • Almost no evidence: moon phase.
  • GPS (Global Positioning System) collar studies give the best data. Most are on white tailed deer in the United States (Tip: Interior mule deer may differ).
  • Bottom line (Tip): the best day to hunt is the day you can go. Weather picks where, not whether.

• Snow and cold trigger mule deer migration to 85%.
  • First real cold snap: glass lower slopes and south faces (Tip).
More: snow and cold, in full
  • Snow and cold, not the rut, trigger mule deer migration to (85%, Monteith 2011, via Hunt Mentor research notes).
  • In the BC Wildlife Federation mule deer study, most collared deer migrated and returned to winter range in October to November (85%, SIMDeer, search preview).
  • Deer have trouble in snow deeper than about 30 cm (85%, BC government deer account) and leave slopes where it passes about 50 cm (80%, University of British Columbia thesis).
  • Fresh snow shows you tracks: you learn what moved last night, and how fresh (Tip). See Snow tracking.
  • First real cold snap of the fall: glass lower slopes and south faces (Tip).
  • Deer reduce movement during an actual storm (80%, Penn State Deer Forest Study).

• Deer slowed during storms, not before them (80%, Penn State).
  • Pressure: weak, mixed evidence. Do not cancel a hunt for it (Tip).
More: fronts and pressure studies, in full
  • Hunter belief: deer feed hard before a front and when pressure falls or rises (Tip, not proven).
  • Penn State tracked collared does through 30 winter storms, 2015 to 2017. "Data show no statistical or biological significance of oncoming winter storms on behavior or movement of our collared deer." (80%, read directly)
  • Deer slowed down during storms, not before them (80%, same study).
  • A Mississippi State team found temperature explained most of the change in movement in an Oklahoma collar study, with no clear weather pattern (65%, search preview).
  • A South Carolina study of 116 collared deer found weather, temperature, wind and pressure each mattered in some seasons and hours, not all (65%, search preview).
  • Honest rating: barometric pressure is weak and mixed evidence. Do not cancel a hunt for it (Tip).

field-first-aid:
Why it matters

A rifle, a knife and steep ground: your partner is the ambulance for the first hour. What you do in the first 3 minutes decides the rest.

  • Big bleeding kills in minutes. Everything else can wait a little (Tip).
  • This session: bleeding, wounds, sprains, breaks, shock and the trauma kit.
More: what this session covers, and what it is not
  • Order of care, the bleeding control steps (press, pack, tourniquet), cleaning cuts, shock, sprains, splints, and the kit you carry.
  • The short version lives in Bush safety and Pack and car kit. This session is the deep dive.
  • Cold injuries are next: Hypothermia, frostbite and cold weather.
  • This is a study aid, not a first aid course. Take a hands on course with tourniquet practice before the season (Tip). A kit you have never used is just weight.
  • Assumption: you hunt with your brother, often out of cell range, an hour or more from an ambulance. That is why the partner is the first responder.
Warning

Study aid only. Not a substitute for a certified first aid course.

• Scene safe, call, then stop the bleeding 75%.
  • Press, pack, tourniquet: in that order for most wounds 75%.
More: the 8 key points in full
  1. Make the scene safe first: unload every gun, look for the hazard (a bear on a carcass, a loose rock) (Tip).
  2. Call early: 911 on any phone, or SOS on a satellite device. 911 can connect through any carrier's tower in range (75%, BC Search and Rescue Association).
  3. Life threatening bleeding comes before everything else except your own safety (75%, Canadian Red Cross bleeding sheet).
  4. Firm direct pressure stops most bleeding 75%.
  5. Deep wounds in the groin, armpit or neck, where a tourniquet cannot go, get packed with gauze (70%, Stop the Bleed and military training cards).
  6. A limb bleed that pressure cannot stop gets a 75%.
  7. Flush cuts with at least 1 litre of drinkable water (75%, Wilderness Medical Society).
  8. Keep every injured person warm: shock and cold make each other worse 75%.

The first minute1 of 4
  • Your own safety first. A second casualty helps no one (Tip).
More: Check, Call, Care in full
  • Check (Tip): stop. Unload your gun and the injured person's gun. Look for what caused this: a slope, a bear near a carcass, a loose rock, ice. Then go.
  • Call 75%: 911 on any phone. BC Search and Rescue Association: a phone can reach 911 through any tower in range, even another carrier's. Turn on location services so you can read out your coordinates.
  • No signal: satellite SOS (iPhone 14 or later in Canada, or a satellite messenger). See Bush safety 85%.
  • Say your location first, then what happened, how many hurt, and what you have done. If the call drops, they still know where to send help (Tip).
  • Care: life threatening bleeding first, then breathing, then everything else 75%.
  • Write the times: injury, tourniquet on, pills given, changes. Medics need them (75%, Canadian Red Cross skills sheet: document tourniquet times).
  • Phone in an inside pocket: cold kills phone batteries fast (70%, see Lost).

• Any one sign: act now. Do not wait to see if it slows (Tip).
More: the signs in full
  • Life threatening bleeding signs taught in bleeding control courses (70%, Stop the Bleed course material via university and fire department pages):
    • Blood spurting or pulsing out.
    • Blood flowing that will not slow with pressure.
    • Blood pooling on the ground.
    • Clothing or bandages soaking through.
    • A partly or fully missing arm or leg.
    • The person is confused, pale or weak: they have already lost a lot.
  • An adult has about 5 litres of blood 70%. Losing a big share of it fast is what kills (Tip: no exact number is needed in the field. If it looks like a lot, it is a lot).
  • A rifle wound to the thigh or upper arm can hit a big artery. These are the wounds a tourniquet was made for 70%.

Stop bleeding with your hands1 of 4
  • Gloves on if you have them. No gloves? Do not wait (Tip).
More: pressure and packing in full
  • Expose the wound. Cut or pull clothing away so you press on the real source, not on a jacket 70%.
  • Press: gauze or any clean cloth on the wound, both hands, arms straight, body weight over it (75%, Canadian Red Cross skills sheet step 1: direct pressure).
  • Still bleeding through? Add a pressure bandage over the first layer. Do not lift the first layer (75%, Canadian Red Cross step 2).
  • Pack 70%: for a deep wound where a tourniquet cannot go (groin, armpit, side of the neck), push gauze into the wound with one finger, following it to the bottom, until the hole is full.
  • Training cards say fill the cavity so gauze stands 2.5 to 5 cm (1 to 2 in) above the skin, then press on top for at least 3 minutes (65%, military training cards via search).
  • Do not pack wounds of the chest or belly 65%.
  • Haemostatic gauze (gauze with a clotting agent) can work faster. Plain gauze or a clean cloth still works 65%.
  • After 3 minutes: wrap tight with a pressure bandage. If blood soaks through plain gauze, add more gauze and press again 65%.

Tourniquet in 5 steps1 of 5
  • It will hurt. That means it is working 70%.
More: the tourniquet steps in full
  • When: life threatening bleeding from an arm or leg that direct pressure cannot control (75%, Canadian Red Cross and American Red Cross).
  • Where: on the limb, between the wound and the heart, not on a joint. If the wound is close to a joint, go above the joint (70%, Stop the Bleed guidance from fire department pages).
  • How far above: see the next screen. The sources differ.
  • Pull the strap as tight as you can before twisting. A loose strap means you run out of turns 70%.
  • Twist the windlass rod until the bleeding stops, then lock it in the clip so it cannot unwind (70%, American Red Cross search preview).
  • Still bleeding with the first one as tight as it goes? Put a second tourniquet above the first, closer to the heart (70%, American Red Cross search preview).
  • Write the time it went on. Medical staff need it 75%.
  • Do not loosen or remove it yourself. Only medical staff do that (70%, American Red Cross search preview).
  • Note: an older Canadian Red Cross skills sheet (2012) says to slowly release after 10 minutes if bleeding has dropped a lot. Newer American Red Cross and Stop the Bleed material says leave it on. VERIFY with your course instructor.
  • Buy a real one: a CAT (Combat Application Tourniquet) or SOFTT (Special Operations Forces Tactical Tourniquet) style windlass tourniquet. Fakes exist (60%, see Pack and car kit).

• Two numbers in our sources: 5 to 8 cm, and 5 to 10 cm. VERIFY.
  • Both agree: above the wound, heart side, never on a joint 75%.
More: the two numbers and where they come from
  • 5 to 8 cm (2 to 3 in): American Red Cross (search preview) and several Stop the Bleed guides 70%. Also used in Pack and car kit.
  • 5 to 10 cm (2 to 4 in): Canadian Red Cross workplace skills sheet, Controlling External Bleeding, 2012 (75%, read directly). Also used in Bush safety.
  • This is an open question for the owner. Ask your first aid instructor which number they teach and use that one. VERIFY.
  • Some military guidance teaches "high and tight" (as high on the limb as it goes) when you cannot see the wound well. One vendor blog says so; not confirmed in an official source here. VERIFY.

More: why each line matters
  • Slack in the strap uses up the windlass turns before the artery closes 70%.
  • A joint has bone in the way; the band cannot squeeze the artery 65%.
  • A second tourniquet is the standard fix when one is not enough (70%, American Red Cross search preview).
  • Loosening it lets blood flow out again and can wash out a clot (Tip).
  • A tourniquet under a jacket gets missed at the hospital handover. Leave it visible, write TQ and the time (Tip).
  • Counterfeit tourniquets can snap. Buy from a known medical seller 60%.

• Lay them flat, keep them warm, nothing to eat or drink 70%.
More: shock in full
  • Shock here means the body cannot get enough blood to the organs, often after bleeding 70%.
  • Signs: pale, cold, clammy skin; fast weak pulse; thirst; anxiety; confusion 70%.
  • Care 70%:
    • Stop the bleeding first. That is the real treatment.
    • Lay the person flat on a pad: a pack, foam, spruce boughs. The cold ground steals heat.
    • Cover them: emergency blanket, jacket, toque.
    • Nothing to eat or drink while they may need surgery, and if they are not fully awake (Tip).
    • Talk to them. Keep them still and calm.
  • Shock and hypothermia feed each other. A hurt hunter lying on frozen October ground gets cold fast (Tip). See cold injuries.

• Most knife injuries hit fingers and thumbs 70%.
  • Cut away from you. Wipe the handle (Tip).
More: knife cut prevention in full
  • In a United States study of emergency department knife injuries (1990 to 2008), fingers and thumbs were hurt in about 66% of cases, and 94% were cuts (70%, PubMed abstract via search). Not hunters only.
  • A bloody, wet handle lets the hand slide onto the edge (60%, patent filing describing the problem).
  • Habits (Tip):
    • Cut away from your body and away from your partner's hands.
    • Keep the hand that holds the hide behind the blade.
    • Use a sharp knife. A dull one needs force and slips.
    • Wipe the handle and your glove often.
    • Work in daylight. Headlamp gutting doubles the risk.
    • Wear thin nitrile gloves under a cut resistant glove on the holding hand if you own one.
  • See Field dressing for the cuts themselves.

Clean a cut in 3 steps1 of 3
  • Drinkable water works. No soap or iodine in the wound needed 75%.
More: the Wilderness Medical Society advice
  • Wilderness Medical Society wound guideline (2014): irrigate with at least 1 litre, strong recommendation (75%, abstract via search).
  • Drinkable (potable) water is the preferred fluid in the wilderness 75%.
  • High pressure beats low pressure for removing dirt and bacteria 75%. Make pressure: squeeze a soft bottle hard, or poke a pin hole in a clean zip bag and squeeze.
  • No additives in the flush water needed, except rabies prone bites 75%.
  • Water from a creek? Treat it first. See Water.
  • Cover with a clean dressing. Change it daily (Tip).
  • Infection signs: spreading redness, heat, swelling, pus, a red streak up the limb, fever. Get to a doctor 70%.

More: more detail
  • Tip: a cut on the hand while gutting is easy to shrug off. A deep hand cut can cut a tendon; if a finger will not bend or straighten normally, end the hunt and get it seen.
  • Tetanus: ask your doctor when your last booster was before the season (Tip).
  • Animal fluids in a cut: wash well. Wear gloves while field dressing (Tip, see Field dressing).

Rolled ankle in 3 steps1 of 3
  • Can walk? Wrap, poles, partner carries gear (Tip).
More: sprains in full
  • RICE: Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation. Widely taught; the evidence for it alone is thin (65%, Wikipedia review of sprain research).
  • Newer sports medicine says PEACE for the first days: Protection, Elevation, Avoid anti inflammatories, Compression, Education. Then LOVE: Load, Optimism, Vascularisation, Exercise (65%, British Journal of Sports Medicine, Dubois and Esculier, 2020).
  • Ice timing varies by source: British Red Cross says no more than 10 minutes; UK hospital sheets say 10 to 20 minutes with breaks 65%. Always a cloth between ice and skin 70%.
  • In the field: cold creek water in a bag, or snow, wrapped in a buff.
  • A firm wrap (elastic bandage) gives support to walk out 65%.
  • The "4 steps" test comes from the Ottawa ankle rules, a doctor's tool for deciding on an X ray image: unable to take 4 steps, or bone tenderness at the ankle knobs, means get it imaged (70%, MDCalc). Here it is only a rough walk out guide (Tip).

• Never split up in the dark to "go get help" without a plan (Tip).
More: the decision in full
  • Can walk 4 steps on it: wrap it, use trekking poles or a stick, empty the injured hunter's pack into the partner's, go slow on the easiest route, not the shortest (Tip).
  • Cannot: stay put, splint, build warmth and shelter, call 911 or SOS. Search and rescue can carry a person; you two cannot carry each other far (Tip).
  • Bone through the skin, a limb that is cold, blue or numb below the injury, or a suspected broken thigh: call for help now 70%. A broken thigh can bleed a lot inside 65%.
  • Leaving to get help: only if there is no signal, the hurt person has shelter, warmth, water and a light, and you can mark your route back (Tip). Write the GPS (Global Positioning System) point before you leave.

Splint in 3 steps1 of 3
  • Splint: trekking poles, sticks, a rolled foam pad (Tip).
More: splinting in full
  • Splint it in the position you found it. Do not try to straighten it (70%, military first aid lessons via search).
  • Cover the joint above and the joint below the break 70%.
  • Pad between the splint and the skin 70%.
  • Tie above and below the break, never on it 70%.
  • Check circulation below the splint before and after: warm, pink, can feel touch, can wiggle fingers or toes. Cold, pale, numb or tingling: loosen the ties 70%.
  • Take off rings and watches early. Swelling makes them a tourniquet 70%.
  • Neck or back injury after a fall: do not move them unless you must (danger, cold). Call for help 70%.

• Kit on your body. Same pocket every hunt (Tip).

More: the kit list and why each item

  • Pressure bandage (an emergency trauma dressing with a built in pad): wraps and presses in one move (Tip).
  • Packing gauze, plain or haemostatic 65%.
  • Nitrile gloves: protect you from blood and from game fluids (Tip).
  • Trauma shears: cut clothing to expose the wound (Tip).
  • Marker and tape: write TQ and the time 75%.
  • Emergency blanket and lighter: from Bush safety.
  • Extras for a long day: elastic wrap for sprains, blister care, pain pills you know you tolerate, any personal medicine (Tip).
  • Prices for kits: VERIFY at a Canadian outdoor or medical store before buying. Not checked here.

• Both of you carry one. Show your partner where yours is (Tip).
More: why on the body
  • You may be the one bleeding. Your partner must find your tourniquet in seconds, without digging through your pack (Tip).
  • Either hand must reach it: if your right arm is hit, your left hand applies it (Tip).
  • Cold hands: practise in gloves (Tip).
  • Store it ready: strap pre routed, rod folded in, not sealed in plastic that needs scissors (Tip).

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Grandpa's rule (wisdom): Blood first, then breath, then warmth. And carry the tourniquet where your brother can find it.

Common mistakes
  • Tourniquet in the truck "for emergencies".
  • Loosening a tourniquet to check.
  • Gutting by headlamp with a wet, bloody handle.
More: the mistakes in full
  • The kit stays at the truck because the day hunt is "short". The bleeding happens 3 km in (Tip).
  • Loosening a tourniquet to see if the bleeding stopped. Leave it to medical staff 70%.
  • Gutting tired, in the dark, with a dull knife and a slippery handle (Tip).
  • Splitting up after an injury with no plan and no light (Tip).
  • Owning a tourniquet but never practising with it (Tip).

Do this in the field

Before the first hunt: each of you puts a tourniquet on your own arm, then on your own leg, one handed, in gloves. Time it.
