cold-injuries:
Why it matters

October and November hunts mean sweat on the climb, then hours sitting still at 0 °C. Cold does not need a blizzard to hurt you.

  • Wet plus wind plus sitting still: that is the hunter's cold (Tip).
More: what this session covers
  • How you lose heat, the numbers for your hunting months, staying dry, the 3 stages of hypothermia and what to do at each, frostbite, wind chill, and the cold kit.
  • Short version: Bush safety. Layers: What to wear. Falling in: Ice and cold water.
  • Assumption: you hunt Heffley Creek and the Kamloops hills mid October to November, and the Fraser Valley in wet cold rain.

• Shivering is good: the body fighting. Shivering that stops is an emergency 75%.
More: the 8 key points in full
  1. You lose heat 4 ways: conduction (cold ground), convection (wind), radiation (open sky), evaporation (sweat and wet clothes) (75%, physics, Wilderness Medical Society treatment logic).
  2. Insulation and a barrier from the ground and weather are the core of all hypothermia care (75%, Wilderness Medical Society via American Family Physician).
  3. Mild: alert, shivering strongly. Moderate: drowsy, shivering slows or stops. Severe: unconscious, no shivering 75%.
  4. Mild hypothermia can be treated in the field with shelter, insulation, heat to the trunk, and food if alert 75%.
  5. Moderate and severe: gentle, horizontal, no food or drink, wrap, warm the upper trunk, evacuate 75%.
  6. Frostbite: do not rub, do not thaw if it may refreeze, rewarm in 37 to 39 °C water 75%.
  7. Wind makes skin freeze much faster (70%, US National Weather Service chart).
  8. The trap: sweating on the climb, then sitting still (Tip).

DateSunriseSunsetDark

• Kamloops times, my calculation 80%. BC no longer changes clocks: it stays on daylight time all year (95%, BC government news release, 2 March 2026).
More: the numbers in full
  • Kamloops Airport averages, 1991 to 2020: October high 13.6 °C, low 3.5 °C; November high 5.8 °C, low minus 1.1 °C (75%, Wikipedia climate table from the national climate normals).
  • Record lows: October minus 17.1 °C, November minus 30.0 °C (75%, same table).
  • The airport sits low in the valley. Hunting ground higher up is colder: Sun Peaks village is at about 1,255 m 70%, and one source gives October lows near minus 2 °C there 60%.
  • Sun times: calculated by me with the standard sunrise formula for Kamloops (50.67 N, 120.33 W). BC stays on daylight time (UTC minus 7) all year from March 2026, so there is no fall back on 1 November (95%, BC government news release 2 March 2026). "Dark" here means end of civil twilight (sun 6 degrees below the horizon). Accuracy about 2 minutes 80%.
  • Legal shooting hours are a separate rule: see the Rule Book. Do not use this table for legal hours.
  • Half a day of light is gone by mid November. A wounded deer at 16:00 means tracking in the dark and cold (Tip).

• Damp base layer plus a long sit is how October hunters get hypothermic (Tip).
More: why it happens
  • Wet clothing loses much of its insulation, and evaporation pulls heat from you 70%.
  • A long glassing sit in a breeze adds convection, and a cold rock or wet ground adds conduction (75%, physics).
  • Classic sequence (Tip): fast climb in a heavy jacket, soaked back, then 2 hours still on a cold ridge as the sun drops.
  • Also see the round 1 animation on layers: What to wear.

Stay dry in 4 habits1 of 4
More: the habits in full
  • All 4 habits are Tip (hunter and mountaineer practice, not a study).
  • Start a little cold: you warm up within minutes of walking.
  • Vent early: zips open, toque in the pocket, gloves off on the climb.
  • Carry a spare dry base layer top in a dry bag. Changing at the top takes 2 minutes and pays for hours.
  • Puffy (insulated jacket) on before you feel cold. Keep it at the top of the pack.
  • Sit on a closed cell foam pad. Cold ground pulls heat by conduction 75%.
  • Wool or synthetic, never cotton next to the skin: see What to wear.

• Judge by what you see, not a thermometer 75%.
More: the stages in full
  • Wilderness Medical Society 2019 guidelines, summarized by American Family Physician 75%:
    • Mild: core 35 to 32 °C. Movement impaired, but alert and shivering.
    • Moderate: core 32 to 28 °C. Shivering slows or stops. Not alert, but conscious.
    • Severe: under 28 °C. No movement, no shivering, not conscious.
  • Shivering slows around 32 °C and stops by about 30 °C 75%.
  • In the field you cannot measure core temperature. Stage by what the person does 75%.
  • Bush safety covers the same scale in short: Bush safety.

• Your partner sees the umbles before you feel them (Tip).
More: the umbles in full
  • Early signs often taught as the "umbles": stumbles, mumbles, fumbles, grumbles (75%, Red Cross material via Bush safety).
  • Fumbles test: can they work the zip and load a cartridge? If not, stop (Tip).
  • Hypothermia dulls judgment, so the cold person often says "I'm fine". Trust the signs, not the words (Tip).
  • Alcohol: hypothermia is common with alcohol or other intoxicants (75%, American Family Physician). Leave the flask at camp (Tip).

Mild hypothermia in 4 steps1 of 4
  • Alert and shivering? You can fix this in the field 75%.
More: mild treatment in full
  • Wilderness Medical Society advice, via American Family Physician 75%:
    • Insulate with a vapour barrier (a layer that stops moisture and wind, like a tarp or plastic), especially head, neck and the ground contact area.
    • Wet clothes: keep them on until you are in a warm place, then change. In wind and rain, a wrap over wet clothes beats stripping 75%.
    • Warm, high calorie food or drink only if alert, shivering well and able to swallow safely.
    • Sit or lie down at least 30 minutes, then watch.
    • Active heat to armpits, chest and back. Check the skin every 20 to 30 minutes so the heat packs do not burn.
    • Exercise can come back slowly after warming and food.
  • Shivering burns fuel. Food is heat (Tip).

The hypothermia wrap1 of 4
  • No food or drink. Handle like glass 75%.
More: moderate and severe in full
  • Wilderness Medical Society advice, via American Family Physician 75%:
    • Handle gently. Keep the person horizontal.
    • No food or drink.
    • Insulate and actively warm the upper trunk. This is essential.
    • Use large heat sources. Small chemical hand warmers are not enough for the core; use them only on hands and feet in transport.
    • Evacuate carefully. Call 911 or send SOS.
  • Severe (unconscious): check breathing and pulse for up to 60 seconds; pulses are hard to feel through cold skin. Start CPR (cardiopulmonary resuscitation) if there are no signs of life 75%. Take a CPR course (Tip).
  • The wrap order, from inside out (Tip, common wilderness first aid practice): pad, sleeping bag or all spare layers, heat on the chest, then a tarp or emergency blanket outside.

• Rubbing limbs or warming hands first can make it worse 75%.
More: afterdrop in full
  • Warming or moving the arms and legs can send cold blood back to the core, dropping core temperature and raising the risk of a dangerous heart rhythm (75%, American Family Physician summary of the Wilderness Medical Society).
  • Keep moderate hypothermia patients horizontal to prevent it 75%.
  • After a cold water rescue, a person can collapse soon after being pulled out ("circumrescue collapse") 75%. Handle gently, keep them flat. See Ice and cold water.

FrostnipFrostbite
WhatSkin surface onlyTissue freezes
LooksPale, numbWhite, waxy, hard
After warmingBack to normal fastRed, swollen, blisters
ActionWarm it nowProtect, plan rewarm
More: the difference in full
  • Frostnip: superficial, no freezing inside the tissue. Numbness and paleness go away quickly after warming (75%, American Family Physician summary of the Wilderness Medical Society).
  • Frostbite: tissue freezes. Mild cases are numb, red, swollen; the deepest reach muscle and bone 75%.
  • Common spots: fingers, toes, ears, nose, cheeks (70%, US National Weather Service).
  • Frostnip is your warning. Warm it now: hands in armpits, a warm hand on the cheek (Tip).

Frostbite in 4 steps1 of 4
  • Thaw then refreeze is the worst outcome 75%.
More: frostbite care in full
  • Wilderness Medical Society advice, via American Family Physician 75%:
    • Keep a frozen part frozen if it could refreeze. Field rewarming only if care is more than 2 hours away and refreezing can be prevented.
    • Water at 37 to 39 °C. No thermometer: put an uninjured hand in for 30 seconds; it should feel comfortable.
    • Done when the area is red or purple and soft, usually within 30 minutes.
    • Air dry or blot. Do not rub.
    • Ibuprofen early: up to 600 mg four times a day in the field (check your own health first).
    • Bulky gauze dressing, raise the part above the heart if you can.
    • Do not walk or climb on a frozen foot until care is reached, if you can avoid it.
  • Prevention: keep skin dry and out of wind, mitts instead of gloves, check hands and feet often 75%.
  • Skin creams may raise the risk 75%.

• The same air feels far colder in wind. Faces and fingers freeze first 70%.
More: wind chill in full
  • US National Weather Service chart examples (70%, search preview; my conversion to metric):
    • 0 °F (minus 18 °C) with a 20 mph (32 km/h) wind: wind chill about minus 30 °C; exposed skin can freeze in about 30 minutes.
    • Minus 10 °F (minus 23 °C) with 5 mph (8 km/h) wind: about 30 minutes.
    • Same temperature with 30 mph (48 km/h) wind: about 10 minutes.
  • The chart has 3 bands: 30, 10 and 5 minutes to frostbite 70%.
  • Riding the (all terrain vehicle) or a boat makes your own wind. A 40 km/h ride in November adds wind chill to your face and hands (Tip).
  • Canadian wind chill guidance exists from Environment and Climate Change Canada, but canada.ca was not available here. VERIFY against it.

• Mitts are warmer than gloves 75%.
More: the kit in full
  • Mitts beat gloves; add layers as needed (75%, Wilderness Medical Society prevention advice).
  • Toque and buff: cover head and neck, big heat loss areas when the body is covered (Tip).
  • Puffy jacket at the top of the pack (Tip).
  • Dry socks in a zip bag (Tip).
  • Closed cell foam sit pad: stops conduction into a cold rock or log (75%, physics).
  • Chemical heat packs: good for hands, feet, or trunk care in mild hypothermia 75%.
  • Thermos of hot sweet drink and extra food: fuel for shivering (Tip).
  • Shooting mitts: a mitt with a fold back finger flap keeps the trigger hand warm (Tip).

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Grandpa's rule (wisdom): Be bold, start cold. Stop, then puffy on before your teeth tell you to.

Common mistakes
  • Climbing in the warm jacket and soaking it.
  • "I'm fine" from a partner who is fumbling.
  • Rubbing a white frozen cheek with snow.
More: the mistakes in full
  • Climbing in the heavy jacket: it gets wet from the inside, then cannot keep you warm at the top (Tip).
  • Believing the cold person's words over their actions. Hypothermia dulls judgment (Tip).
  • Rubbing frostbite or rubbing snow on it damages tissue 75%.
  • Thawing feet at camp, then walking out on them. Thaw then refreeze, or walking on thawed feet, adds damage 75%.
  • No foam pad: hours of conduction into a frozen log (Tip).

Do this in the field

On the first cold sit, every 30 minutes: check your partner's face for white spots, and ask them to work a zip. Then swap.

lost-survival-kit:
Why it matters

Being lost is not the danger. Panic, wandering and a night without kit are. A plan turns a scary night into a story.

  • Hunters get lost doing hunter things: chasing, tracking, staying till dark (Tip).
More: what this session covers
  • How hunters get lost, STOP, why you walk in circles, stay or move, calling for help, signals, being found, prevention, and the survival kit.
  • Short version: Bush safety. Navigation skills: Maps 2: navigation.
  • The night itself: Fire in wet BC weather, Shelter, Water.
  • Assumption: you hunt the Heffley Creek hills and the Okanagan, often out of cell range, often just you and your brother.

• Stop early. Call early. Stay put if in doubt 75%.
More: the 8 key points in full
  1. STOP: Stop, Think, Observe, Plan (75%, AdventureSmart via BC Search and Rescue Association).
  2. Staying put reduces the time and the area searchers must cover (75%, BC Search and Rescue Association).
  3. Without sun or landmarks, people walk in circles without knowing it (75%, Max Planck Institute study, 2009).
  4. If you need help, your first action is to call 911 (75%, BC Search and Rescue Association).
  5. A phone can reach 911 through any carrier's tower in range 75%.
  6. Signal in threes: whistle, mirror, horn, fires or rock piles 75%.
  7. For aircraft: a V or SOS on the ground at least 3 m long 75%.
  8. Carry the essentials on you, not in the truck (75%, AdventureSmart Three Ts).

Lost? STOP1 of 4
▶Hug-A-Tree & Survive filmLost? Stop. Stay put. Shelter and signal.
AdventureSmart, YouTube, 12 min. Needs internet.
  • Sit down for 5 minutes. Eat something. Then think (Tip).
More: STOP in full
  • BC Search and Rescue Association, emergency steps 75%:
    • Don't panic: stay calm and keep a positive attitude.
    • S.T.O.P.: Stop. Think. Observe. Plan. Then act.
    • Stay put: it reduces time and search area for the people looking for you.
    • Seek shelter: stay warm and dry.
  • North Shore Rescue: stay put once lost; wandering usually takes you farther from your last known point 75%.
  • North Shore Rescue: avoid going downhill into ravines. They are steep, unstable and hard to climb out of 75%. This matters in the gullies above the Thompson too (Tip).
  • Sitting stops the "walk faster" panic loop. A snack and water help you think (Tip).

• In a 2009 study, forest walkers under cloud crossed their own path 75%.
More: the study in full
  • Max Planck Institute researchers tracked walkers by GPS (Global Positioning System) in the Sahara and in a German forest (75%, Max Planck press release, Current Biology, 2009).
  • With sun or moon visible, people walked fairly straight. Under cloud in the forest, they curved and some crossed their own path without noticing 75%.
  • Blindfolded, most walked in circles, some under 20 m across 75%.
  • Cause: small errors in the sense of "straight ahead" add up. A visible landmark resets it 75%.
  • Lesson (Tip): in fog, snow or thick timber, use the compass or GPS for every leg, and aim at a tree you can see, then the next one.

• Doubt means stay (Tip).
More: when moving makes sense
  • Moving can be right when (Tip):
    • You know the way back to your last known point and can reach it in daylight.
    • You can follow your own fresh tracks in snow back the way you came.
    • Your position is dangerous: avalanche path, rising water, fire.
  • If you move: mark your route (broken branches pointing the way, flagging tape, a note with time and direction at your start point) (Tip).
  • Do not "follow water downhill" by default in steep country. Creeks drop into canyons and ravines (75%, North Shore Rescue advice on avoiding ravines).
  • Moving at night in the bush is how ankles break. Settle in before dark (Tip). See the sunset table in Cold injuries.

• Area grows with the square of the distance (75%, geometry).
More: the math
  • A search circle's area is pi times the radius squared. Double the radius, the area is 4 times as big. Triple it: 9 times (95%, geometry).
  • That is why staying put helps: your trip plan tells searchers where to start, and every kilometre you walk away grows the area they must cover (Tip).
  • Your with the truck location, route and return time is the start point for every search 75%.

Call for help in 4 steps1 of 4
  • 911 dispatches police, who call in Search and Rescue 75%.
More: calling in full
  • BC Search and Rescue Association: if you need help, your first action is to call 911. The operator dispatches the RCMP (Royal Canadian Mounted Police), who request Search and Rescue 75%.
  • Your phone can connect to any cell tower in range, even another provider's, for 911 75%.
  • Turn on location services and learn to read your coordinates on your phone 75%.
  • North Shore Rescue: call as soon as you know you are lost or injured. Early calls help find you before conditions get worse 75%.
  • No signal: iPhone 14 or later can send Emergency SOS via satellite in Canada (85%, see Bush safety). A satellite messenger works too.
  • Tip: agree on check in times with dispatch or family. Phone off between, on at the hour.
  • Search and rescue in BC does not charge the lost person (Tip: North Shore Rescue says rescue has no cost; VERIFY for your area).

• Inside pocket, against your body 70%.
More: phone battery in full
  • Apple lists an iPhone operating range of 0 to 35 °C. Outside it, battery life can drop and the phone can shut off (70%, Apple spec via forum and news; Apple page not read directly).
  • A cold shutdown is usually temporary. Warm it slowly against your body 65%.
  • Battery savers (Tip): low power mode, screen dim, close navigation apps you do not need, airplane mode between check ins (it stops the phone searching for a tower).
  • Carry a small power bank in an inside pocket (Tip).
  • Keep the phone's map of the area downloaded for offline use before you go (75%, Bush safety).

• 3 of anything means help 75%.
More: signals in full
  • BC Search and Rescue Association: whistle blasts times 3, mirror flashes times 3, horn blasts times 3, signal fires times 3, or rock piles times 3 75%.
  • Ground to air: a V or SOS, at least 3 m long, big and high contrast 75%.
  • North Shore Rescue: blow 3 blasts for help 75%.
  • A whistle carries farther than a voice and costs no energy. Clip one to your jacket zip (Tip).
  • Gunshots: 3 shots are a well known signal among hunters (Tip). Keep enough ammunition for the walk out and for any animal. A fire or whistle is better if you are short.
  • At night: a headlamp flashed in threes (Tip).

Be found in 3 steps1 of 3
  • Hidden in thick timber, you are warm but invisible 65%.
More: being found in full
  • Dense cover can keep you warm but make you hard to see. Making yourself visible outside the shelter matters as much as the shelter (65%, hiking safety source via search).
  • Hug a Tree program: stay put, keep warm and dry, and answer searchers' calls (70%, Canadian Geographic Education).
  • Blaze orange is already on you. Hang the vest in the open (Tip).
  • A smoky fire by day and a bright fire by night help aircraft (Tip). See Fire and the fire rules there.
  • Leave a note at your start point if you do move: time, direction, your name (Tip).

• Pin the truck before you leave it (Tip).
More: prevention in full
  • Drop a GPS pin at the truck, the (all terrain vehicle) and each junction (Tip). See Maps 2: navigation.
  • Turn around at each junction and landmark. The way out looks different from the way in (Tip).
  • Note a "handrail": a creek, road or ridge you can follow back, and a "backstop" you must not cross (Tip).
  • Set a turn back time 1 hour before sunset (Tip, from Bush safety).
  • Tracking a wounded animal: mark last blood with flagging and a GPS pin, and stop if dark comes with no plan. See Blood trailing.
  • Carry a paper map and compass as backup to the phone (75%, AdventureSmart essentials).

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Grandpa's rule (wisdom): The minute you wonder where you are, sit down. The bush is not going anywhere, and neither should you.

Common mistakes

  • Following a creek down into a canyon.
  • Kit in the truck, phone in the pack pocket.

  • Following water downhill into a ravine (75%, North Shore Rescue).
  • Waiting until dark to call. Call early 75%.

  • Letting the phone die in a cold pack pocket 70%.

fire-wet-weather:
Why it matters

A fire dries you, warms you, signals for you and calms you. In cold October rain, getting one going is a skill you practise before you need it.

  • Heat, fuel, air. Wet steals heat, so prepare twice the small stuff (Tip).
More: what this session covers
  • The fire rules first, where dry fuel hides, the fuel ladder, feather sticks, the build, lighting in wind and rain, signal fires, and putting it out cold.
  • Fire kit lives in your pockets: Lost and the survival kit.
  • Wildfire danger and smoke: Wildfire, smoke and heat.
  • Assumption: you hunt Interior pine and fir country (Kamloops) and wet coastal forest (Fraser Valley). Both need the same skills; the coast needs more patience.
Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law. Fire rules come from BC Wildfire Service orders, not the hunting synopsis.

• Check bans before any fire. Every time 80%.
More: the 8 key points in full
  1. Fire needs heat, fuel and air. Take away one and it dies (75%, basic science).
  2. A Category 1 campfire is no bigger than 0.5 m high by 0.5 m wide (80%, BC Wildfire Service brochure, search preview).
  3. Keep at least 8 litres of water or a hand tool on hand the whole time it burns 80%.
  4. Fire bans change. Check the BC Wildfire Service before each fire 80%.
  5. Dry fuel in rain: dead, off the ground, and split to the inside (Tip).
  6. Birch bark and pitch wood (resin soaked wood) burn even when wet 65%.
  7. Gather 2 big handfuls of each size before you strike the lighter (Tip).
  8. Out means cool to the touch: drown, stir, feel, repeat 80%.

• Check the ban status for your fire centre before every fire 80%.
  • Kamloops Fire Centre status today: VERIFY.
More: the rules in full
  • Category 1 campfire: an open fire burning material in one pile no larger than 0.5 m high and 0.5 m wide, lit for recreation (80%, BC Wildfire Service Category 1 campfire brochure, search preview). Bigger is a Category 2 open fire 80%.
  • Water or tool: at least 8 litres of water or a hand tool on hand at all times while it is lit 80%. One fire centre notice says "a shovel or at least eight litres of water" 75%. The exact wording varies: VERIFY on the current order.
  • Fuel break: clear the area around the fire of debris and anything that burns 80%. One fire centre advises a pit or ring at least 3 m from trees, shrubs and debris 70%.
  • During a campfire ban: only a CSA (Canadian Standards Association) or ULC (Underwriters Laboratories of Canada) approved portable campfire apparatus with a flame no higher than 15 cm may be used 75%.
  • Fines: up to $1,150 for breaking an open fire ban 80%. An escaped fire that causes a wildfire can bring a fine up to $1 million, up to 1 year in jail and the firefighting costs 75%.
  • Kamloops Fire Centre 2026: Category 1 campfires were allowed again from noon 3 September 2026; Category 2 and 3 open fires stayed banned until noon 9 October 2026 unless rescinded earlier (70%, District of Logan Lake release, 3 September 2026). After 9 October: VERIFY.
  • Survival fire during a ban: whether a life threatening emergency changes the rule is not confirmed here. VERIFY with BC Wildfire Service. My lean: carry a small stove and an emergency bivy so you rarely need a fire in a ban.
  • Not in the Rule Book: the hunting synopsis does not carry fire bans. The Rule Book covers hunting rules only.

• Dead, off the ground, and split (Tip).
  • Snap test: dry dead wood snaps; wet or green wood bends (Tip).
More: dry fuel in full
  • Standing dead wood stays drier than wood lying on wet ground (Tip, common bushcraft advice).
  • Dead twigs on the lower trunk of big spruce and fir stay dry under the canopy (Tip).
  • Split a wet piece: the core is often dry (65%, wet weather fire guides).
  • Birch bark: the oily layer burns even when damp 65%. Paper birch grows in the BC Interior (Tip). Take bark from dead or downed trees only (Tip).
  • Pitch wood (also called fatwood): resin soaked wood from old pine or fir stumps and knots. The resin makes it burn even when the outside is wet 65%.
  • Pine needles can still burn when damp 60%.
  • Coast tip: in the Fraser Valley rain, bring your own tinder. Cotton balls with petroleum jelly in a pill tube, or wax fire starters (Tip).

• Have 2 big handfuls of every size before you light (Tip).
More: why the ladder matters
  • Small pieces have more surface for their weight, so they heat and catch faster (75%, basic science).
  • The most common failure: lighting with only tinder and big wood. The tinder burns out before the big wood gets hot (Tip).
  • Sizes, smallest first (Tip): tinder fluff, matchstick, pencil, thumb, wrist.
  • In rain, double the matchstick and pencil piles. Wet wood needs more heat to dry before it burns (Tip).
  • Leave gaps. Fire needs air 65%.

Make a feather stick1 of 3
  • Your hunting knife can do this. Cut away from you (Tip).
More: feather sticks in full
  • Split the thickest, driest dead wood into quarters, then shave a fine feather stick or a pile of shavings (65%, bushcraft sources via search).
  • Feather sticks give a big surface for the flame to grab 65%.
  • Use the knife's straight edge, long strokes, thumb behind the spine (Tip). Knife safety: First aid.
  • Practise at home on dry wood first, then in the rain (Tip).

Build a fire in 5 steps1 of 5
More: the build in full
  • A platform of dry sticks or bark keeps tinder off wet ground or snow (65%, wet weather fire guides).
  • Lay out piles in the order you will need them, within reach 65%.
  • Tipi: kindling leaned over tinder with gaps for air and a door on the upwind side (Tip).
  • Light the bottom of the tinder. Flame climbs (Tip).
  • Your body and pack make a wind wall (Tip).
  • Add wood gradually: small to big, never jump straight to logs 65%.
  • On snow: a platform of green or wet logs under the fire stops it melting down into a hole (Tip).

• Two ways to light, in two pockets (Tip).
More: lighting tools in full
  • Lighter: fast. Cold can weaken it and wet fingers slip on the wheel. Keep one inside your jacket (Tip).
  • Matches: stormproof matches burn in wind and wet. Strike surface must stay dry (Tip).
  • Ferro rod (ferrocerium rod): throws hot sparks even wet, but needs very fine dry tinder like birch bark shavings or cotton (Tip).
  • Fire starter: wax cubes, gel or cotton with petroleum jelly. Burns several minutes to dry the kindling (Tip).
  • My lean: lighter plus fire starter in one pocket, stormproof matches or a ferro rod in another.

• A tarp goes high above the fire, never close (Tip).
More: rain and wind in full
  • A sheet of birch bark or your hat can shield the first flame from rain 65%.
  • Use a rock or log as a wind wall on the windward side (Tip).
  • Do not light a fire in strong wind. The BC Wildfire Service advises against campfires in windy conditions 75%.
  • Tarps melt and catch fire. Keep it high, and the fire small (Tip).
  • Keep spare tinder in a zip bag inside your jacket so body heat dries it (Tip).

• Smoke by day, flame by night. Three fires mean help 75%.
More: signal fires in full
  • BC Search and Rescue Association lists signal fires times 3 as a distress signal 75%.
  • Green boughs on a hot fire make thick white smoke (Tip).
  • Build it in the open where aircraft can see it, and keep it inside the rules and under control (Tip). An escaped signal fire becomes a wildfire.
  • More on being found: Lost.

Put it out in 4 steps1 of 4
  • Fully out before you leave. Not smoky, not warm 80%.
More: putting it out in full
  • Stir water into the ashes until they are cool to the touch. Hot coals can reignite (80%, BC Wildfire Service brochure, search preview).
  • The fire must be fully extinguished before you leave the area 80%.
  • A fire with water on it, thought to be out, can stay lit underground (75%, Cariboo Fire Centre notice).
  • No water? Mineral soil stirred in, then more stirring. Water is far better (Tip).
  • See smoke or flames you did not start? Report a wildfire: 1 800 663 5555 toll free, or *5555 on a cell 80%.

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Grandpa's rule (wisdom): Gather twice what you think, light once. And drown it till you could sleep on the ashes.

Common mistakes
  • Lighting before the kindling pile is ready.
  • Smothering the flame with big wet wood.
  • Leaving a fire that is "mostly out".
More: the mistakes in full
  • Lighting with only tinder ready, then running for kindling while it dies (Tip).
  • Piling on wood too fast and too big: no air, too much water to boil off (Tip).
  • Building on wet ground or snow with no platform (Tip).
  • Not checking the ban 80%.
  • Walking away from warm ashes 80%.

Do this in the field

On a rainy scouting day, legal campfire conditions only: light a fire with one lighter and only what you find, in under 15 minutes. Then put it out cold and feel it.

shelter-night-out:
Why it matters

A blood trail at dusk, a twisted knee, fog on the ridge: one day you will sleep out. Shelter is what makes that a cold night, not a rescue.

  • Bed under you first, roof over you second (Tip).
More: what this session covers
  • Choosing a spot, insulating from the ground, a tarp shelter, a debris hut, foil blankets versus bivy bags, using fire with shelter, the night routine, and sharing heat.
  • Why you lose heat: Cold injuries. Fire: Fire in wet weather. Being found: Lost.
  • Assumption: October nights near 0 °C in the Kamloops hills, wet nights near 5 °C in the Fraser Valley.

• Start building at least an hour before dark (Tip).
More: the 8 key points in full
  1. Insulation and a barrier from the ground and weather are the core of preventing and treating hypothermia (75%, Wilderness Medical Society via American Family Physician).
  2. The ground pulls heat by conduction. A thick bed matters more than a roof on a dry night (75%, physics; Tip on the order).
  3. Wind and wet speed heat loss a lot 70%.
  4. Cold air sinks into valley bottoms at night (75%, see Wind and thermals).
  5. A tarp or bivy is faster and safer than building from the bush when tired or hurt 65%.
  6. Foil blankets reflect radiant heat but do little against conduction from the ground 65%.
  7. A shelter hidden in thick timber can hide you from searchers. Put a signal in the open 65%.
  8. Two people sharing one bed and cover stay warmer (Tip).

• Bench part way up, near trees and fuel. Not the valley floor (Tip).
  • Look up: no dead trees or hanging branches (Tip).
More: choosing a site in full
  • Choose the driest spot you can, out of the wind, away from low points where cold air and water collect (65%, shelter guides via search).
  • Cold air sinks downhill at night and pools in draws and valley floors (75%, thermals, Wind and thermals).
  • Ridge tops are windy (Tip).
  • Look up for dead standing trees and broken branches that can fall in wind (Tip).
  • Not in a gully, a creek bottom or an avalanche path. See Avalanche awareness (Tip).
  • Near firewood and water, and near an opening where you can be seen (Tip).

• Thicker than you think. It squashes flat under you (Tip).
More: the bed in full
  • Insulate the ground contact area: it is one of the key places to protect (75%, Wilderness Medical Society via American Family Physician).
  • Bed materials (Tip): closed cell foam pad, your pack, spruce or fir boughs, dry grass, dry leaves, layered thick.
  • Build it so it is still a hand or more thick when you lie on it (Tip).
  • Sit on your pack while building to stay off the ground (Tip).
  • Cutting boughs: take a few from many trees, not one tree stripped. Check land rules where you are (Tip).

Tarp shelter in 4 steps1 of 4
  • A 2 m by 3 m tarp and 10 m of cord cover two people (Tip).
More: tarp in full
  • Tarps and bivy bags are among the most effective shelter tools for their weight, and often safer than building when tired, hurt or short of light (65%, shelter guides via search).
  • Open side away from the wind. Windward side pinned to the ground with rocks, logs or stakes (Tip).
  • Steep pitch sheds rain and snow (Tip).
  • Carry a light tarp in the day pack in October (Tip). An emergency bivy bag works alone if you have no tarp.
  • Lean to version: tie only the top edge to the cord and stake the bottom edge on the windward side. More open, good with a fire in front (Tip).

More: what the sources say
  • Foil blankets reflect radiant heat, but the "reflects 90%" claim on packets is marketing 65%.
  • The thin film does almost nothing against conduction into the ground (65%, medical equipment supplier and gear reviews).
  • They need an air gap to work against radiation; touching skin, they act like a thin plastic sheet 60%.
  • They do not breathe: moisture gets trapped 60%.
  • A bag shape (bivy) wraps you fully and stops wind; you still need a pad or bed under it (Tip).
  • My lean: carry an emergency bivy bag in the pack and a foil blanket in the pocket kit.

Debris hut in 4 steps1 of 4
  • Takes hours and lots of material. Start early 65%.
More: debris hut in full
  • Debris shelters can give emergency insulation when time is short, but they are uncomfortable and need large amounts of dry material (65%, shelter guides via search).
  • Make it just big enough for you: a small space warms faster (Tip).
  • Thickness: "as thick as your arm is long" is a common bushcraft rule (Tip, not tested here).
  • In the dry Interior you may not find enough leaves. Boughs and needles work (Tip).
  • My lean: a tarp in the pack beats 3 hours of building.

• Small fire, safe gap, and only when fire is legal 80%.
More: fire and shelter in full
  • A wall of logs or rocks behind the fire bounces heat toward you (Tip).
  • Keep the fire small and the tarp high above and away (Tip). See Fire for the size limit and ban checks 80%.
  • Feed it through the night, or let it die and rely on the bed. A big fire next to a sleeping hunter is how sleeping bags and tarps burn (Tip).
  • Carbon monoxide: never burn a stove or fire inside a closed shelter (Tip).

• Food is fuel. Eat before you sleep (Tip).
More: the routine in full
  • All Tip unless marked:
    • Eat something with fat before sleeping. Shivering burns fuel.
    • Pee before you settle. Holding it costs heat.
    • Dry socks on. Wet socks inside your shirt to dry from body heat.
    • Toque and buff on all night. Hood up.
    • Boots in a bag or under you, so they do not freeze stiff.
    • Cold in the night: clench big muscles, eat, sit up and move, add a layer.
  • Keep the headlamp and whistle in a pocket you can find in the dark (Tip).
  • Keep the phone warm for the morning check in. See Lost.

• One bed, one cover, back to back (Tip).
More: sharing heat in full
  • Two people huddling share body heat. In cold water, huddling is a taught technique (75%, see Water safety). On land, the same idea works under one cover (Tip).
  • Put the colder or hurt person in the middle of all the insulation (Tip).
  • Swap who gets up to feed the fire (Tip).

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Grandpa's rule (wisdom): When the light turns gold and you are still far from the truck, start building. The dark will not wait for you.

Common mistakes
  • Building after dark.
  • A roof but no bed.
  • Camping in the valley bottom.
More: the mistakes in full
  • Starting the shelter after dark. Everything takes 3 times longer by headlamp (Tip).
  • A great roof and bare ground under you. The ground wins 75%.
  • The valley floor: coldest air, and often wet 75%.
  • Under a dead tree (Tip).
  • A shelter hidden so well no one can see you. Put orange in the open 65%.

Do this in the field

Before the season, pitch your tarp in the backyard or a legal camp spot in under 10 minutes, then sleep one cold night under it with only your day pack kit.

water-safe-drinking:
Why it matters

A long day climbing for deer drains you, and the clear creek looks perfect. One mouthful can mean weeks of "beaver fever" after the hunt.

  • Treat every lake, creek and spring. Clear is not clean 75%.
More: what this session covers
  • Finding water in dry Interior hills, picking the best source, the germs, and the 4 ways to treat it: boil, filter, chemicals, UV light. Cloudy water, water no method fixes, and toilet distance.
  • Water is also for wounds: First aid says flush cuts with drinkable water.
  • Assumption: you carry water from the truck most days. This is for long days, nights out, and backup.

• Boiling kills everything that makes you sick from germs 75%.
More: the 8 key points in full
  1. Do not drink untreated water from lakes, streams, rivers, ponds or springs (80%, HealthLink BC File 10).
  2. Giardia ("beaver fever") symptoms usually start 1 to 3 weeks after infection and can last 2 to 6 weeks 80%.
  3. Boil at least 1 minute; above 2,000 m, at least 2 minutes (80%, HealthLink BC File 49b).
  4. A filter for Giardia needs a pore size of 1 micron or smaller, certified 80%. Jug filters like Brita do not remove it 80%.
  5. Chlorine bleach: 2 drops per litre, wait 30 minutes; cloudy or cold water: double, wait 1 to 2 hours 80%.
  6. Chlorine is generally not effective against Giardia (80%, HealthLink BC File 10). Filter first, then disinfect (75%, CDC).
  7. Cloudy water: settle and strain before treating 80%.
  8. Boiling and disinfecting do not make water with chemicals or toxins safe (75%, CDC).

• Symptoms start 1 to 3 weeks later, often after you are home 80%.
More: Giardia in full
  • Giardia is a parasite of the gut in humans and animals. The illness is giardiasis, often called "beaver fever" (80%, HealthLink BC File 10, updated 10 July 2026).
  • You get it mainly from contaminated water, including swallowing lake or stream water 80%.
  • Symptoms: diarrhea, cramps, gas, bloating, pale greasy stools, nausea, vomiting, weight loss, tiredness. Some people have none 80%.
  • Symptoms usually appear 1 to 3 weeks after infection and can last 2 to 6 weeks 80%.
  • Cryptosporidium is another parasite in surface water; HealthLink names both Giardia and Cryptosporidium as reasons boiling is best 80%.
  • Sick after a trip? Tell your doctor you drank surface water (Tip).

• Look for green: a line of brush in a draw often marks water (Tip).
More: finding water in full
  • All Tip (hunter and outdoor practice):
    • A line of green shrubs or a different colour of grass down a draw.
    • Cottonwood, willow and red osier dogwood grow along water.
    • Seeps and springs below rock outcrops and at the toe of slopes.
    • Game trails heading downhill in the evening often go to water.
    • Snow and ice in November: melt them in a pot. Add a little water to the pot first so it does not scorch.
  • Food, water and cover for game: Food, water and cover.
  • Your map shows creeks and lakes, but small creeks dry up by October in the grassland (Tip). Check on the map scouting day: Map scouting.

• Upstream of cattle and beaver dams when you can (Tip).
More: ranking sources
  • All Tip: there is no official ranking. Any source can carry germs.
  • A spring right where it comes out of the ground is usually cleanest.
  • Fast clear creeks beat still water.
  • Lakes: away from the shore and from inlets.
  • Ponds, sloughs and cattle troughs: last choice. Interior range land has cattle; manure washes into water.
  • Beaver ponds: the nickname "beaver fever" exists for a reason, though people and other animals spread Giardia too (Tip).
  • Then treat it anyway 80%.

• Boil or filter for Giardia. Chemicals alone are weak on it 75%.
More: the full table
  • From the US Centers for Disease Control (CDC) backcountry water page, read directly 75%:
    • Boiling: protozoa (Giardia, Cryptosporidium) yes; bacteria yes; viruses yes.
    • Filter 1 micron or smaller, NSF (National Sanitation Foundation) Standard 53 or 58 cyst reduction: protozoa yes; bacteria not all; viruses no.
    • Filter 0.3 micron or smaller: protozoa yes; bacteria yes; viruses no.
    • Chlorine bleach or iodine: protozoa not well; bacteria yes; viruses yes.
    • Chlorine dioxide tablets: Giardia yes; Cryptosporidium somewhat; bacteria and viruses yes.
    • Portable UV (ultraviolet) light: all three, but only in small amounts of clear water.
  • Filter first, then disinfect, is the safest combination (75%, CDC).

Boil in 3 steps1 of 3
  • The surest method. Costs fuel and time 80%.
More: boiling in full
  • HealthLink BC File 49b, updated 25 July 2025 80%: boil at least 1 minute; above 2,000 m (6,500 ft), at least 2 minutes. Boiling is the most effective method, especially for Giardia and Cryptosporidium.
  • The US CDC says 3 minutes above 6,500 ft 75%. The two differ. Boiling longer does no harm: my lean, 3 minutes up high.
  • Most of your hunting ground near Kamloops is below 2,000 m (Tip: check the map).
  • Let it cool covered (Tip).

Filter in 3 steps1 of 3
  • A filter alone does not stop viruses 75%.
More: filters in full
  • HealthLink BC: use an NSF certified filter with a pore size of 1 micron or less, or a certified UV or distillation unit (80%, File 10).
  • Jug style filters like Brita do not remove Giardia 80%.
  • Viruses: filters alone do not stop them (75%, CDC). In BC backcountry, protozoa and bacteria are the usual worry; add a chemical step if the water is near camps or people (Tip).
  • Many hollow fibre filters can be damaged if they freeze. Read your filter's instructions and keep it warm in November (Tip, VERIFY with the maker).
  • Back flush or clean the filter as the maker says (Tip).

• Good backup in the pocket kit. Weak on Giardia 80%.
More: chemicals in full
  • Bleach (HealthLink BC File 49b) 80%: 2 drops (0.1 mL) of unscented household bleach (about 5.25% chlorine) per litre. Cover, wait 30 minutes. No slight chlorine smell? Add 2 more drops and wait 15 more minutes. Cloudy water or water colder than 10 °C: double the bleach and wait 1 to 2 hours.
  • Iodine 80%: 6 drops of 2% tincture of iodine per litre, wait 30 minutes (several hours if cold); cloudy water 10 drops. Short term use only. Not for children or pregnant women.
  • Chlorine is generally not effective against Giardia (80%, HealthLink BC File 10). That is why boiling or a filter comes first.
  • Chlorine dioxide tablets: Giardia yes, Cryptosporidium somewhat (75%, CDC). Follow the label contact time.
  • In October, creek water is often below 10 °C: double dose and long wait (Tip, based on File 49b).

• Mud shields germs from chemicals and UV 80%.
More: cloudy water in full
  • Cloudiness reduces how well disinfectant works. Clarify first: strain through a clean cloth or coffee filter, let the rest settle, pour the clear water into a clean container, then disinfect (80%, HealthLink BC File 49b).
  • UV light needs clear water; particles shield germs (75%, CDC).
  • A bandana over the pot works as a strainer (Tip).

• Find other water 75%.
More: toxins and chemicals in full
  • Boiling and disinfecting cannot make water with harmful chemicals, toxins or radioactive material safe (75%, CDC).
  • Algae blooms (blue green algae) can make toxins. Scummy, paint like or bright green water: do not drink it (Tip; the toxin point is from the CDC chemical and toxin line).
  • After a wildfire, ash and runoff can change water quality (70%, HealthLink BC topic "Wildfire: its effects on drinking water quality", title only). See Wildfire.
  • Fuel sheen near roads, ATV crossings and boat launches: avoid (Tip).

• Toilet at least 30 m from any water source 80%.
More: hygiene in full
  • HealthLink BC: when camping, do not urinate or have a bowel movement within 30 m of a water source (80%, File 10).
  • Dig a small cat hole for solid waste (Tip).
  • Wash hands, or use sanitizer, before eating and after field dressing (Tip). Hand sanitizer does not replace washing off blood (Tip).
  • Gut piles away from water too (Tip). Rules on leaving parts: Rule Book: after the kill.

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Grandpa's rule (wisdom): The creek always looks clean. Boil it anyway, and thank yourself in three weeks.

Common mistakes
  • One "quick sip" from a clear creek.
  • Bleach in cold, cloudy water with a 5 minute wait.
  • A frozen filter trusted the next morning.
More: the mistakes in full
  • Drinking untreated because it looks clear (80%: clear water can carry germs).
  • Short contact time with chemicals in cold or cloudy water 80%.
  • Relying on chlorine alone for Giardia 80%.
  • Dipping the clean bottle in the creek after filtering (Tip).
  • Leaving the filter in the truck overnight at minus 5 °C (Tip).

Do this in the field

On a scouting day, find water on the map, walk to it, treat 1 litre two ways (filter, then boil), and time each.

  • "1, 2, 30": boil 1 minute, 2 drops a litre, 30 minutes wait, 30 m toilet 80%.
  • "1 to 3 then 2 to 6": weeks until Giardia symptoms, then weeks they last 80%.

bear-cougar-encounters:
Why it matters

Hunters do everything that draws bears: move quietly at dawn and dusk, carry blood, and leave gut piles. Knowing what to do turns a bad moment into a story.

  • Most encounters end with the bear leaving. Your job: do not make it worse (Tip).
More: what this session covers
  • Avoiding bears, reading what a bear is doing, bear spray by distance, spray versus guns, defensive and predatory attacks, the kill site, camp, and cougars.
  • Short version and the spray animation: Bush safety. Hunting bears: Black bear. Cougars and wolves as game: Predators.
  • Assumption: black bears around Heffley Creek and the Okanagan; grizzlies possible in the Thompson Nicola uplands. Carry spray as if both are there (see Bush safety).
Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

• Never run from a bear or a cougar 75%.
More: the 9 key points in full
  1. If you meet a bear: stop, stay calm and never run (75%, WildSafeBC).
  2. Make noise near running water, thick brush, berry patches and in high wind 75%.
  3. Found a carcass you did not kill? Leave and report it 75%.
  4. Bear spray: use it when the bear is within about 5 to 10 m (75%, WildSafeBC).
  5. Defensive attack, contact made: lie on your stomach, hands over the back of your neck, legs apart 75%.
  6. Predatory attack: fight back hard, at the face, eyes and nose 75%.
  7. Cougar: never run, look big, back away slowly; if attacked, always fight back 75%.
  8. Move meat at least 200 m from the gut pile; hang it 3.5 m up (70%, Alberta bear and hunter guidance).
  9. Report aggressive bears and cougars: 1 877 952 7277 (99%, synopsis RAPP line; also the Conservation Officer Service line per WildSafeBC).

• Colour does not tell you the species. Hump and face do 75%.
More: ID and numbers
  • Full ID lesson: Black bear, screen "black bear or grizzly?".
  • BC black bears: estimates range from 120,000 to 150,000 (70%, WildSafeBC).
  • BC grizzly bears: about 15,000, about a quarter of North America's (70%, WildSafeBC).
  • Grizzly hunting is closed in BC (see Black bear). A grizzly near your kill is a safety problem, not a target (Tip).

• Calls and decoys can bring in bears as well as game 75%.
More: why in full
  • Distress or mating calls, decoys and cover scents can attract bears as well as game (75%, Alberta: Bears and hunters).
  • Be extra careful at dusk, at night and at dawn, when it is noisy, or when sight lines are short 75%.
  • Gut piles and carcasses draw bears, which then defend them 75%.
  • Quiet stalking is good hunting and bad bear safety. Balance it: quiet when hunting, noisy when travelling, packing or working on a kill (Tip).

Avoid bears in 4 steps1 of 4
  • WildSafeBC says do not rely on bear bells 75%.
More: avoiding in full
  • WildSafeBC 75%:
    • Watch for scat, tracks, freshly torn logs and fresh claw marks.
    • Talk or sing to avoid surprising a bear, especially near running water, in thick brush or high wind. Not bear bells.
    • No headphones, do not hike alone, keep pets leashed.
    • Pack out all food waste.
    • Extra caution where sight lines are poor: berry bushes, salmon streams.
    • Found a carcass? Leave the area and notify the Conservation Officer Service.
  • Sign photos: Black bear and Reading sign.

• Watch what it does, then match it 75%.
More: each case in full
  • WildSafeBC 75%:
    • Unaware of you: leave quietly the way you came, keep watching it, check your bear spray.
    • Aware but not reacting: speak softly, back away slowly. Do not follow it if it leaves.
    • Agitated (jaw popping, moaning, woofing, stomping, bluff charging): speak calmly, back away slowly, do not make direct eye contact but keep it in sight, spray ready.
    • Approaching steadily: yield slowly. If it keeps coming, it may be predatory. Yell, move to higher ground, be ready to fight.
  • In every case: never run 75%. You cannot outrun a bear (Tip).
  • Holding a loaded rifle: a bear is not a target unless it is legal game in season, or a real threat to life. Follow up rules: Rule Book: unlawful acts (Tip).

• These are warnings, not attacks. Give it room 75%.
More: warning signs in full
  • Jaw popping, moaning, woofing, stomping and bluff charging are signs of an agitated bear (75%, WildSafeBC).
  • Most bluff charges stop short of contact (75%, WildSafeBC).
  • A defensive bear wants you gone. Backing away slowly gives it what it wants (Tip).

▶How to Use Bear Spray - Banff National ParkRemove the clip, aim low, spray a cloud between you and the bear.
Parks Canada, YouTube, 2 min. Needs internet.
  • Spray on the chest or hip, never in the pack 75%.
More: spray in full
  • WildSafeBC: carry it where you can reach it fast, like a hip holster, not in your pack. Use it when the bear is within about 5 to 10 m 75%.
  • Alberta guidance by distance 75%:
    • 9 to 15 m: a half to 1 second warning blast, aimed slightly down.
    • 6 to 9 m: 1 to 2 second bursts, aimed slightly down in front of the head, until it leaves.
    • 0 to 6 m: 1 to 2 second bursts at the head, into the nose and mouth, until it leaves.
    • Keep some in reserve. After spraying, back away while watching the bear. Bears may be drawn to spray residue.
  • Do not spray into the wind (70%, Bush safety).
  • Can range: about 3 to 10 m depending on the can. Read yours 70%.
  • Cold weakens spray pressure (Tip: keep it inside your jacket on frozen mornings, VERIFY on your can's label).

• Studies found spray stopped bears more often than guns 70%.
More: the studies in full
  • Smith and Herrero (2008): bear spray stopped aggressive bear behaviour in about 92% of cases (70%, news coverage via search; some coverage says 90%).
  • Firearms: one report gives 67%; a 2014 article quoting the firearms paper gives 84% for handguns and 76% for rifles (65%, figures differ by source).
  • The firearms study found people with guns had about the same injury rate in close encounters whether or not they fired 65%.
  • Stopping a charging bear with bullets took on average about 4 hits in that work 60%.
  • My lean: spray in hand first, rifle as backup. Your partner must never be in the line of fire (Tip).

• Defensive: lie still once it makes contact. Predatory: fight 75%.
More: attacks in full
  • Defensive (usually a surprise, the bear protecting itself, food or cubs): if knocked down, lie still on your stomach, hands clasped over the back of your head, feet slightly apart. Stay still until the bear has left (75%, WildSafeBC).
  • Predatory (the attack does not stop and the bear tries to eat you): fight back with everything, at the face, eyes and nose 75%.
  • Parks Canada adds: a bear that stalks you or comes at night is predatory; fight (75%, from Bush safety).
  • Keep your pack on; it protects your back (Tip).

Kill site safety in 4 steps1 of 4
  • Get the meat out fast. Avoid dressing at dusk if you can 75%.
More: kill site in full
  • Alberta: Bears and hunters (70% for BC use; same bears, other province's advice):
    • Make noise while field dressing; scent may draw a bear. Remove the carcass as quickly as possible.
    • Move the carcass at least 200 m from the gut pile before you leave, if you can. Bears often go to the gut pile first.
    • Hang it at least 3.5 m (11.5 ft) off the ground and 1.5 m (5 ft) from nearby trees, where you can see it from a distance.
    • Coming back: approach from upwind, check with binoculars, make noise.
    • Bear at the site, or the carcass moved or buried? Do not approach. Leave and report.
    • Do not drag the carcass back to camp: it lays a scent trail to you.
  • Montana says at least 100 yards (91 m) from the gut pile and hang 10 ft (3 m) up 65%. Rules differ by place; the bigger number is safer (Tip).
  • Idaho: do not try to scare a bear off a carcass 65%.
  • BC law: a carcass is an attractant. Do not leave one where people are, or likely to be, in a way that draws dangerous wildlife (99%, see Rule Book: after the kill).

• Put something bright on the meat so you can see from afar if it moved 65%.
More: more detail
  • Montana State University guide: put something noticeable on the carcass so you can tell if it was disturbed 65%.
  • Leave the area if the carcass is moved or buried: a bear has claimed it 70%.
  • Plan the pack out so no meat sits overnight if you can. Dusk, night and dawn are the high risk times 75%. See Packing out.

• Food, cooking and meat at least 100 m from where you sleep 75%.
More: camp in full
  • Alberta guidance 75%: food and toiletries in airtight containers at least 100 m from where you sleep; hang food at least 3.5 m up and 1.5 m from trees; harvested animals at least 100 m from camp; cook and wash up at least 100 m away and downwind; never keep food in the tent.
  • It is unlawful in BC to intentionally feed dangerous wildlife, including bears and cougars (99%, see Rule Book: legal methods).
  • The truck: lock food and coolers inside, not in the box (Tip).
Cougar encounter in 4 steps1 of 4

• Cougars rarely attack people. Never play dead with one 75%.
More: cougars in full
  • WildSafeBC 75%:
    • Stay calm, never run. Look as large as possible and back away slowly.
    • Keep it in view and leave it a clear exit. No sudden moves, do not turn your back.
    • Watching you: keep eye contact, speak loud and firm. Bear spray out, safety off.
    • Aggressive or following: be aggressive back. Yell, make noise, arm yourself with sticks or rocks without crouching down.
    • Attacked: fight back, aim for the face and eyes. Spray, rocks, sticks.
    • Found a kill site (often covered with debris)? Leave at once and report it.
  • Cougars can sprint over 70 km/h 70%. The Conservation Officer Service gets about 2,500 cougar calls a year, many of them other animals 70%.
  • Cougar tracks: big round pads, usually no claw marks (75%, see Tracks).

• Aggressive bear or cougar, attack, or a kill site near people: call 1 877 952 7277 99%.
More: who to call
  • RAPP (Report All Poachers and Polluters) line: 1 877 952 7277, open 24/7, for wildlife and human conflicts where public safety is at risk (99%, synopsis page 2, from Bush safety).
  • WildSafeBC lists the same number for the Conservation Officer Service: report aggressive behaviour, kill sites, urban sightings 75%.
  • Injury: 911 first 75%.
  • Killed a bear or cougar in self defence: report it to an officer promptly (99%, see Rule Book: unlawful acts).

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Grandpa's rule (wisdom): Quiet when you hunt, loud when you work. And look before you walk back to your meat.

Common mistakes
  • Spray in the pack.
  • Walking straight back to the hanging meat at dusk.
  • Running from a bear or cougar.
More: the mistakes in full
  • Spray buried in the pack, or the safety clip stuck with cold fingers 75%.
  • Walking straight in to the kill without glassing or calling out 70%.
  • Dragging a carcass back to camp 70%.
  • Running 75%.
  • Playing dead with a cougar or a predatory bear 75%.
  • Calling elk or predators in thick cover with no partner watching your back (Tip).

Do this in the field

With an inert practice can, draw and fire in under 2 seconds from the chest holster, in gloves. Then walk a creek bottom and call out every minute.

  • "If it's brown, lie down; if it's black, fight back" is a common rhyme, but colour does not tell the species and the right action depends on the attack type (Tip; colour point 75%).
  • Use instead: defensive (surprised, cubs, food): lie still once it makes contact. Predatory (stalks, keeps coming, at night): fight 75%.

wildfire-smoke-heat:
Why it matters

BC fire seasons now run into the early hunting season. Closures, smoke and heat can end a hunt, or put you in danger, if you do not check first.

  • Check fires, closures, bans and air quality before every trip in fire season 75%.
More: what this session covers
  • Checking before you go, area restriction orders, how fire moves, escape, not starting a fire, hunting burned ground, smoke and the AQHI (Air Quality Health Index), and heat illness.
  • Lighting your own fire safely: Fire in wet weather.
  • Assumption: September and early October hunts in the Kamloops and Okanagan grassland and pine country, where fires are common.
Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

• Fire runs uphill fast. Escape down, sideways or into ground that already burned 65%.
More: the 8 key points in full
  1. Area restriction orders under section 11 of the Wildfire Act close Crown land around fires to everyone without written permission, including hunters (75%, BC Wildfire Service notices via search).
  2. Restrictions can stay after evacuation orders are lifted 75%.
  3. Violation tickets of $1,150 have been issued for entering restricted areas 75%.
  4. Fire races uphill; slope and wind speed it up (70%, University of British Columbia Okanagan study coverage).
  5. Plan two ways out 65%.
  6. Report a wildfire: 1 800 663 5555, or *5555 on a cell 80%.
  7. AQHI 10+: everyone should avoid strenuous activity outdoors (80%, BC Centre for Disease Control fact sheet).
  8. Heat stroke: call 911, cool the whole body fast (80%, HealthLink BC).

Check 4 things before you go1 of 4
  • Check the night before and the morning of (Tip).
More: where to check
  • BC Wildfire Service: the wildfire map and dashboard, fire bans and area restrictions for each fire centre 80%. Heffley Creek and the Okanagan are in the Kamloops Fire Centre (75%, Kamloops Fire Centre ban pages cover from Blue River to the US border).
  • Air quality: the BC Air Quality website and the national AQHI app. Do not rely on other apps; their values may not match BC measurements (80%, BC Centre for Disease Control).
  • Local government burning rules can add to provincial ones 75%.
  • Hunting rules and closed areas: Rule Book: where you can hunt.

• Inside a restricted area, no hunting, even if evacuation orders were lifted 75%.
More: what the orders say
  • Orders are made under section 11 of the Wildfire Act. Unless an exemption applies, a person must not remain in or enter the restricted area without prior written authorization from an official (75%, order wording via search).
  • Exemptions listed in one order include travelling to or from your home, using a highway, and acting in an official capacity 75%.
  • A 2009 order said the restriction applied to all purposes, including recreation and hunting. More recent BC Wildfire Service statements said the same for specific fires 75%.
  • A Kamloops area official noted hunters thought downgraded evacuation orders meant they could hunt there. They could not (70%, news coverage).
  • A recent fire centre notice: failure to comply may bring a violation ticket of $1,150 75%.
  • Orders get extended and their boundaries change. Read the current order and map before going 75%.

• Afternoon heat and wind make fires most active (Tip, VERIFY).
More: fire behaviour in full
  • Fires race uphill (70%, University of British Columbia Okanagan study coverage). Slope effects vary with fuel, wind and terrain 70%.
  • Wind and slope are two critical variables for how fast fire spreads (70%, Forest Science comparison).
  • The BC Wildfire Service rates fire behaviour on a scale of 1 to 6; higher ranks mean faster spread and fire in the crowns 75%.
  • Chimneys (narrow draws), saddles and steep upslopes funnel heat and wind (Tip: wildland firefighting teaching, not read directly here).
  • Afternoons are often the most active part of the day (Tip, VERIFY).
  • Ash or sparks falling around you suggests the fire is probably within about 1.6 km (1 mile) (60%, hiking safety source).

Escape a wildfire in 4 steps1 of 4
  • Avoid getting trapped at all costs: survival odds are low 65%.
More: escape in full
  • Experts say hikers should avoid being trapped by a wildfire at all costs; odds of survival when trapped are low (65%, hiking safety sources).
  • Leave early. Stay upwind. Watch for smoke and ash 65%.
  • Plan at least two routes out wherever you are; routes on or near burned areas are an option because changing winds can reverse a fire 60%.
  • Move downslope and upwind when you can; fire spreads fast uphill 60%.
  • Cornered: find a spot with nothing to burn, clear what you can, lie face down in a low spot with feet toward the flames until they pass. Cover your airway with cloth. Do not soak your clothes unless there is a lot of water: it can turn to scalding steam 60%.
  • Air 1.5 m above the ground is far hotter and smokier: stay low 60%.
  • Vehicle: a road and the truck are often your best way out. Park facing out in fire season (Tip).
  • Call 911 if threatened (Tip).

• Never park a hot truck or (all terrain vehicle) on dry grass (Tip).
More: prevention in full
  • Hot exhaust on dry grass can start a fire (Tip, from Bush safety).
  • Cigarette butts: put them out and carry them out (Tip).
  • Campfires: check bans, keep 8 litres of water or a tool, drown, stir, feel 80%. See Fire.
  • Dragging chains and metal on rock can throw sparks (Tip).
  • Report a wildfire: 1 800 663 5555 toll free, or *5555 on a cell 80%. Note where it is, size, colour of smoke, wind (Tip).

• New growth draws game. Look up and watch your feet (Tip).
More: burned ground in full
  • Burns grow fresh feed that deer, elk and bears use (Tip, see Food, water and cover).
  • Roots can smoulder deep in the ground and reignite without warning (60%, hiking safety source).
  • Fire weakened trees can fall without wind; avoid camping or sitting under them (Tip).
  • Ash pits: burned out stump holes can hide hot coals (Tip).
  • Bare slopes can slide and flood after rain (Tip).
  • Check that the burn is not inside an area restriction order 75%.

• At 10+, the air is extremely poor. Everyone should take action 80%.
More: the AQHI in full
  • The AQHI runs 1 to 10+ (80%, BC Centre for Disease Control fact sheet, read directly).
  • In BC the AQHI is calculated two ways each hour, and the higher value is reported: the usual 3 pollutant formula, and fine particles (PM2.5, particles smaller than 2.5 micrometres) alone 80%.
  • PM2.5 is the biggest health risk in wildfire smoke 80%.
  • Messages 80%:
    • Low (1 to 3): ideal for outdoor activity.
    • Moderate (4 to 6): no change needed unless you have symptoms; people at higher risk consider easing off.
    • High (7 to 10): consider reducing or rescheduling strenuous outdoor activity if you have symptoms; higher risk people should reduce or reschedule.
    • Very high (10+): reduce or reschedule strenuous activity, especially with symptoms; higher risk people avoid it.
  • No cleaner air? Consider a well fitted N95 respirator 80%.
  • Being too hot is more risky than breathing smoke for most people (80%, the same fact sheet). Do not overheat in a closed truck to avoid smoke.
  • Adults breathe up to 10 times more air when exercising, so slowing down cuts the dose (65%, news quoting BC Centre for Disease Control).

ProblemDo this
Hard climb in heavy smokeSlow down or reschedule
Cough, chest tightStop, rest, leave the smoke
Asthma or heart troubleStay home on high days

More: why each row
  • Strenuous activity raises the smoke dose 80%.
  • People with lung or heart disease, pregnant women, infants, children and older adults are at higher risk 80%.
  • Smoke can hide people and buildings behind game. Only shoot what you can fully see, with a safe backstop (Tip, see Firearm safety).
  • Thickening smoke can mean a fire is moving toward you. Check before you go deeper (Tip).

• Confused and hot: heat stroke. Call 911 80%.
More: heat in full
  • Heat stroke happens when the body cannot control its temperature and it keeps rising, often to 40 °C or higher (80%, HealthLink BC).
  • Warning signs of fast progressing heat stroke: unconsciousness more than a few seconds, seizures, trouble breathing, temperature above 40 °C, confusion or aggression, fast heartbeat, heavy sweating or sweating that has stopped, red hot dry skin, severe vomiting and diarrhea 80%.
  • Heat exhaustion: move to shade, remove extra clothes, cool wet cloths on head and neck, fluids. Stop cooling if they start to shiver (70%, BC Forest Safety Council).
  • Early season (September) hunts in the Okanagan can be hot (Tip). Carry more water than you think. See Water.
  • Heat spoils meat fast. Cool it quickly: Meat care.

Heat stroke in 4 steps1 of 4
  • Cool first, ask questions later (Tip).
More: the steps in full
  • HealthLink BC heat stroke first aid 80%:
    • Call 911 or other emergency services.
    • Move the person to a cool place out of direct sun.
    • Remove unnecessary clothing; lay them on their side to expose skin to air.
    • Cool the whole body by sponging or spraying cold water, and fan them.
    • Ice packs on the neck, groin, back and armpits.
    • Do not give aspirin or acetaminophen for the high temperature.
    • Awake and able to swallow: fluids, about 1 to 2 litres over 1 to 2 hours, sitting up. Not fully awake: nothing by mouth.
  • In the field: a creek, wet shirts, a game bag soaked in water and fanned (Tip).

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Grandpa's rule (wisdom): In fire season, know where the fire is, which way the wind blows, and which road gets you out.

Common mistakes
  • Hunting inside an area restriction because "the evacuation was lifted".
  • Parking on tall dry grass.
  • Climbing hard in heavy smoke.
More: the mistakes in full
  • Entering a restricted area to hunt. It is closed for safety and tickets have been issued 75%.
  • Hot exhaust on dry grass (Tip).
  • Strenuous effort at high AQHI 80%.
  • Running uphill ahead of a fire 65%.
  • Leaving meat in the sun on a hot afternoon (Tip).

Do this in the field

At the truck, before every fire season hunt: open the wildfire map, name two ways out, and say them to your partner.

  • AQHI bands: 1 to 3, 4 to 6, 7 to 10, 10+ 80%.

avalanche-hunters:
Why it matters

Late season goats, sheep and high country deer put hunters on steep snow before the avalanche forecasts even start. A small slope over a gully can bury you.

  • Most avalanches start on slopes of 30 to 45 degrees 80%.
More: what this session covers
  • When avalanches matter to hunters, slope angle, terrain traps, warning signs, the danger scale, terrain ratings, the forecast, rescue gear, travel habits, what to do if caught, and companion rescue.
  • This is awareness only. Before travelling in avalanche terrain, take an AST 1 (Avalanche Skills Training 1) course (Tip, Avalanche Canada training).
  • Assumption: you will mostly hunt below avalanche terrain in October. Late fall goat, sheep or alpine deer hunts, and any snowmobile access, change that.

• No signs of instability does not mean safe 80%.
More: the 9 key points in full
  1. The vast majority of avalanches happen on slopes between 30° and 45° (80%, Avalanche Canada Avy Savvy, read directly).
  2. They can happen on 25° to 30° slopes, less often 80%.
  3. A slope of about 10 m by 10 m can hold enough snow to be dangerous (80%, Avalanche Canada).
  4. Avalanches that start on steep ground can run across flat ground and even uphill 80%.
  5. Terrain traps (gullies, creek beds, cliffs, trees, flats under steep slopes) make the result worse 80%.
  6. Signs of instability: recent avalanches, whumpfs, shooting cracks 75%.
  7. The forecast gives a danger rating from Low to Extreme 80%.
  8. Everyone carries a transceiver, probe and shovel, and is trained 75%.
  9. Fully buried: over 90% survive the first 15 to 20 minutes, then survival drops fast (75%, Canadian Medical Association Journal commentary).

• Early season snow on grass or rock slabs can slide with little snow 70%.
More: when it matters
  • Late season mountain goat and sheep hunts are in steep alpine terrain (Tip). See Mountain goat and Mountain sheep.
  • Avalanche Canada has warned that rock slabs, grassy slopes, glaciers and slopes with leftover summer snow need only about 30 cm for avalanches to form (70%, Avalanche Canada blog via search).
  • Gullies are natural walking and pack out routes, and they are terrain traps (Tip, 80% for the trap part).
  • Snowmobile access: probe and shovel go in the backpack on your back, not on the sled (70%, Avalanche Canada forecaster quoted in news).
  • The Kamloops grassland hills near Heffley Creek are mostly gentle. Steep cutbanks and gully walls still count if they are 30° or more and big enough (Tip).

• Measure it: a phone clinometer app works 80%.
More: slope angle in full
  • Avalanche Canada (80%, read directly):
    • "The vast majority of avalanches take place on slopes between 30° and 45°."
    • Slides happen on 25° to 30° slopes but less often.
    • Over 45°, snow usually slides off often, so slabs form less.
    • A slide that starts on steep ground can run across a flat slope and even travel uphill.
    • Use a clinometer or a phone app to measure.
  • Avalanche Canada also reported slab avalanches on slopes around 26° with certain buried weak layers (70%, blog via search).
  • Convex rolls on a slope are trigger points, and the area right below them is exposed 80%.
  • Being below a steep slope counts: you can trigger it from the flat beside or below 75%.

• A small slide into a gully can bury you deep 80%.
More: terrain traps in full
  • Avalanche Canada: a terrain trap is any terrain feature that makes the consequences of an avalanche more serious. Examples: gullies, creek beds, ditches, cliffs, flat areas under steep slopes, and trees or rocks in slide paths (80%, read directly).
  • Steep sided gullies and creek beds trap moving snow so it piles much deeper in a small area 75%.
  • Hunter angle (Tip): we glass from benches and walk creek bottoms. Do not sit or camp in a gully under a loaded slope.

• See one? Stay off and out from under steep slopes (Tip).
More: signs in full
  • Avalanche Canada glossary, signs of instability (75%, search preview): recent slab avalanches (especially in the last 48 hours), remote triggered avalanches, whumpfs, shooting cracks. Also hollow sounds and snow shedding from trees.
  • A whumpf is a buried weak layer collapsing, often with a loud sound 75%.
  • Shooting cracks run away from your boots or skis 75%.
  • Remote triggering often happens from flatter ground next to avalanche slopes: ridge crests, benches, or right below avalanche paths 75%.
  • The absence of signs does not mean there is no danger 75%.
  • Heavy new snow, strong wind and rapid warming load or weaken slopes (Tip, VERIFY with Avalanche Canada avalanche problem types).

• Considerable (3) is where the most deaths happen 75%.
More: the scale in full
  • Avalanche Canada forecasts rate danger as low, moderate, considerable, high or extreme, for each region, for today and the next two days (80%, read directly).
  • Low: be cautious, use smart travel habits on steep slopes, avoid shallow rocky start zones 80%.
  • Moderate: pay careful attention to the avalanche problems in the forecast 80%.
  • Considerable: many slopes should be avoided 80%. The most avalanche deaths happen at this level (75%, search preview).
  • High: avoid all avalanche terrain; stick to very mellow slopes or dense trees free of overhead hazard 80%.
  • Extreme: avalanches run even into forest 80%.

More: terrain ratings in full
  • The ATES (Avalanche Terrain Exposure Scale) sorts terrain into simple, challenging and complex (80%, Avalanche Canada Avy Savvy outline).
  • Simple: low angle or primarily forested; under most conditions you can move confidently, but watch small slopes with traps, forest openings and paths above you (80%, read directly).
  • Challenging and complex: definitions not read directly here. The table lines for them are my summary (Tip, VERIFY on Avy Savvy).
  • The Avaluator trip planner pairs a terrain rating with the day's danger rating, and is the basis of the AST 1 course 75%.

Travel habits in 4 steps1 of 4
  • Before forecasts start: read Avalanche Canada's early season conditions page 70%.
More: forecasts and travel in full
  • Check the avalanche forecast before planning your trip (80%, Avalanche Canada).
  • Forecast season start dates in past years: 22 to 25 November (70%, search preview). Your October hunts may have no daily forecast. Early season forecasts can say there is not enough data to rate the danger 70%.
  • The Mountain Information Network takes observations from anyone 70%.
  • Travel habits (Tip, standard avalanche course teaching):
    • One at a time on any slope that could slide, partner watching.
    • Safe spots: ridges, thick trees, high ground away from runouts.
    • Do not stop in runout zones or gullies.
    • Turn back when you see signs of instability.
  • Avalanche Canada's daily process: get the forecast, make a trip plan, check gear, verify conditions, good travel habits, watch signs, evaluate slopes, reflect (80%, Avy Savvy outline).

• All three, every person, and practice 75%.
More: gear in full
  • Avalanche Canada: the transceiver, probe and shovel are the three key pieces of rescue gear everyone should carry in winter backcountry. One or two of the three is not good enough (75%, search preview).
  • Wear the transceiver in its harness and switch it on at the start of the day. Probe and shovel in the pack 75%.
  • Snowmobile: probe and shovel in the backpack on your back, not on the sled 70%.
  • Training in companion rescue is critical 75%.
  • Prices: VERIFY at a Canadian outdoor store. Not checked here.

If caught in 4 steps1 of 4
  • There is no sure way to escape. Avoiding the slope is the real plan 80%.
More: what Avalanche Canada says
  • For skiers, read directly 80%, adapted for a hunter on foot (Tip):
    • Yell "AVALANCHE!" to warn others.
    • Move to the side at about 45° down and across the flow.
    • Near the top: try to dig hands into the bed surface.
    • Near a tree: hug it or shelter on its downhill side.
    • In the flow: get rid of skis, poles; for a hunter, the rifle and heavy pack can pull you down (Tip: a pack can also protect you; judgment call).
    • Fight to stay near the surface, swim upward.
    • As it slows: clear snow in front of your mouth with one hand and reach toward the surface with the other.
  • Avalanche Canada notes there is no surefire way to escape an avalanche 80%.

• Your partner is the rescue. Help is too far away (Tip).
More: survival in full
  • Swiss data: over 90% of fully buried people survive the first 15 to 20 minutes, then survival drops steeply to about 35% by about 35 minutes, mostly from lack of air (75%, Canadian Medical Association Journal commentary, 2011).
  • A Canadian study of 301 burials found a faster drop in Canada; the authors suggest about 10 minutes may be a better companion rescue target 75%.
  • Fast companion rescue is the main survival tool 75%.

Companion rescue in 4 steps1 of 4
  • Call 911 or SOS once someone is searching, not before you look (Tip, VERIFY in your course).
More: rescue in full
  • Avalanche Canada's companion rescue order: signal search, coarse search, fine search, probing, shovelling, when to call for help (80%, Avy Savvy outline, steps not read in detail).
  • Watch the person as they go down; the last seen point narrows the search (Tip).
  • Probe and shovel details (Tip, standard course teaching): probe perpendicular to the slope in a spiral around the strongest signal; leave the probe in on a strike; dig from the downhill side; clear the airway first.
  • Learn this in an AST 1 course with real practice. Reading is not enough (Tip).

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Grandpa's rule (wisdom): A goat is not worth a gully full of snow. If the slope talks to you (crack, whumpf), listen and leave.

Common mistakes
  • "It's only October, no avalanche risk."
  • Glassing from the bottom of a loaded gully.
  • Two hunters, one shovel.
More: the mistakes in full
  • Thinking early season means safe. About 30 cm on a smooth slope can slide 70%.
  • Sitting, camping or packing meat out in terrain traps 80%.
  • Partial gear: one or two of three is not enough 75%.
  • Crossing a slope together instead of one at a time (Tip).
  • Ignoring whumpfs and cracks because the sun is out 75%.

Do this in the field

Before any late season alpine hunt, measure 5 slopes with a phone clinometer app and guess first. Learn what 30 degrees looks like.
