ice-cold-water:
Why it matters

Late season ducks sit on the last open water. Ponds skim over in November. A shortcut across the ice, or a step after a downed bird, is how hunters go through.

  • Fall ice is new, thin and uneven. Treat it as unsafe (Tip).
More: what this session covers
  • How thick ice must be, ice colour, where it is thin, testing it, the ice kit, birds that fall on ice, getting yourself out, helping someone else, warming up, and wading cold creeks.
  • Boats, PFDs, capsizing and the 1 10 1 principle: Water safety. Rewarming: Cold injuries.
  • Assumption: you hunt ducks from the 10 ft boat and the kayak, and walk pothole ponds near Kamloops in November as they freeze.

• Floating ice is never 100% safe 75%.
More: the 8 key points in full
  1. Canadian Red Cross thickness for clear blue ice: 15 cm to walk or skate alone, 20 cm for a group, 25 cm for a snowmobile 75%.
  2. Clear blue ice is strongest; white opaque ice is about half as strong; grey ice is unsafe 75%.
  3. Floating ice on ponds, rivers and lakes is never considered 100% safe 75%.
  4. Ice over springs and outlets is thinner; ice on moving water cannot be trusted (75%, Lifesaving Society).
  5. Waterfowl keep patches open, so ice near where birds sit can be very thin 70%.
  6. Carry ice picks, an ice staff (chisel), a rope and a phone (75%, Lifesaving Society).
  7. Fell in: turn back the way you came, arms on the ice, kick, slide out, roll away (75%, Minnesota Department of Natural Resources).
  8. Someone else in: call 911, then preach, reach, throw, row. Go only as a last resort 75%.

• Measure several spots. Thickness changes in a few steps 75%.
More: thickness in full
  • Canadian Red Cross (75%, search preview): at least 15 cm for walking or skating alone, 20 cm for skating parties or games, 25 cm for snowmobiles.
  • These numbers are for clear blue ice (75%, Lifesaving Society).
  • Thickness varies with springs, currents, air and water temperature, location, depth and size of the water body 75%.
  • Ice sections close together can have very different thickness 75%.
  • In October and November the ice is new. Most potholes will not reach 15 cm until well into winter (Tip).
  • An (all terrain vehicle) on ice: no number found in these sources. VERIFY. My lean: never in fall.

• On white ice, double the numbers 70%.
More: colour in full
  • Clear blue ice is strongest (75%, Canadian Red Cross).
  • White opaque or "snow ice" is about half as strong as clear blue ice (75%, Lifesaving Society). It forms when snow on the ice melts and refreezes (70%, Minnesota Department of Natural Resources).
  • Some guidance says double the thickness guidelines on white ice 70%.
  • Grey ice often holds water from a thaw and is unsafe (75%, Lifesaving Society).
  • White ice with very little air can be nearly as strong as clear ice, so colour is a clue, not a measurement 70%.

• Where ducks sit is where ice is thinnest 70%.
More: thin spots in full
  • Ice above a spring or an outlet pipe is thinner and weaker (75%, Lifesaving Society).
  • Ice on creeks and rivers cannot be trusted; current and changing water levels weaken it 75%.
  • Areas used by ducks and geese can have very thin patches because the birds kept the water open longer (70%, municipal advisory).
  • Edges near reeds, logs, rocks and docks melt first (Tip).
  • Pressure cracks and slush: stay off (Tip).

Test ice in 3 steps1 of 3
  • Any doubt, stay off (Tip).
More: testing in full
  • Measuring is the best way to judge ice (75%, Canadian Red Cross: thickness is the best measure).
  • An ice chisel (spud) or auger shows thickness; a tape or marked stick measures it (Tip).
  • Check more than one spot; ice can be thin in places (75%, Red Cross spokesperson).
  • Walk apart, not side by side. One person through is better than two (Tip).
  • Wear a PFD (personal flotation device) on the ice; it floats you and pads a fall (Tip; also Water safety).

• Ice picks around your neck, not in the pack (Tip).
More: kit in full
  • Lifesaving Society "Check the ice" material: carry ice picks, an ice staff, a rope and a cell phone 75%.
  • Ice picks give the grip you need to pull out; nails or sharpened screwdrivers also work (75%, Minnesota Department of Natural Resources).
  • Carry picks for quick access (70%, Colorado Parks and Wildlife).
  • Phone in a dry bag or zip bag, on your chest (Tip).
  • Dry clothes and a towel in the truck, and the heater ready (Tip).
  • Prices: VERIFY. Not checked here.

• Let it go. No duck is worth falling through (Tip).
More: birds and ice in full
  • A common pattern in hunting accidents: a downed bird or a dog on thin ice, and the hunter goes out after it (70%, waterfowl safety coverage).
  • Plan shots so birds fall on open water you can reach by boat, or on land (Tip).
  • The boat on ice edges: do not push a small boat onto thin ice to retrieve; it can tip as the ice breaks (Tip). See Water safety.
  • The law asks for "all reasonable effort to locate, dispatch, retrieve" game you hit (99%, synopsis page 12, see Rule Book: unlawful acts, retrieval screen). My reading: walking onto unsafe ice is not a reasonable effort (Tip, VERIFY with a conservation officer).
  • Retrieval by boat has its own rules (loaded guns, motors). Read them on the same Rule Book screen 99%.

Get yourself out in 5 steps1 of 5
  • Keep your winter clothes on. They trap air 75%.
More: self rescue in full
  • Minnesota Department of Natural Resources (75%, read directly):
    • Do not remove your winter clothing; heavy clothes trap air for warmth and flotation.
    • Turn toward the direction you came. That ice is probably the strongest.
    • Place your hands and arms on the unbroken surface. Ice picks, nails or sharpened screwdrivers help grip.
    • Kick your feet and dig in your picks to work back onto solid ice. Lots of water in your clothes? Lift up on your elbows to let it drain first.
    • Lie flat once out and roll away from the hole to spread your weight.
    • Get to a warm, dry, sheltered place and rewarm right away.
  • Cold shock gasp, then about 10 minutes of useful movement: use them to get out (80%, the 1 10 1 principle, see Water safety).
  • Can't get out? Get your arms up on the ice and keep still; arms may freeze to the ice and help keep your head up (Tip, VERIFY).

• Do not run to the edge of the hole 75%.
More: helping in full
  • Minnesota Department of Natural Resources (75%, read directly):
    • First, call 911.
    • Resist the urge to run up to the edge of the hole.
    • Preach: shout to encourage them to fight to survive; help is coming.
    • Reach: from shore, a rope, ladder, branch or pole. Let go if they start pulling you in.
    • Throw: a rope or floating object; have them tie it on before the cold weakens their hands.
    • Row: push a light boat across the ice to the hole, climb in, pull them over the bow.
    • Go: a non professional should not go out on the ice unless every other option is ruled out.
  • The partner who rushes out often becomes a second victim (Tip).

• Handle gently. Collapse can happen after rescue 75%.
More: after the rescue in full
  • Moderate to severe cold water hypothermia needs medical care (75%, Minnesota Department of Natural Resources).
  • Cold blood from the limbs can rush back to the heart as you rewarm and cause a dangerous rhythm 75%. See afterdrop in Cold injuries.
  • After cold water rescue, a person can collapse suddenly ("circumrescue collapse"). Keep them flat and handle gently (75%, Wilderness Medical Society via American Family Physician).
  • Wet clothes off once sheltered, dry layers on, insulate under and over, heat to the trunk 75%.

• Over the knee and fast: find another crossing (Tip).
More: wading in full
  • All Tip (outdoor and hunter practice, not read in an official source here):
    • Scout for a wide, shallow, slow spot. Not above a logjam or a drop.
    • Face upstream at an angle; shuffle; one foot moves at a time.
    • A stout pole or trekking pole as a third leg, on the upstream side.
    • Undo the pack hip belt and sternum strap so you can shed it if you fall.
    • Rifle unloaded and slung, action open or cased (see Firearm safety).
    • Cross early in the day; glacier and snow fed creeks rise in the afternoon.
  • Wet feet in November: change socks right away (see Cold injuries).
  • Waders can fill and pull you down if you fall. Wear a wading belt cinched tight (Tip, see What to wear).

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Grandpa's rule (wisdom): Fall ice is a liar. If you have to ask whether it will hold you, it won't.

Common mistakes
  • Walking out after a duck on skim ice.
  • Two hunters side by side on the ice.
  • Taking off the coat in the water.
More: the mistakes in full

  • Walking together instead of apart (Tip).
  • Shedding winter clothing in the water; it traps air 75%.
  • Running to the hole to help, and going in too 75%.
  • Trusting white or grey ice like clear ice 75%.

Before late season duck hunts: hang ice picks around your neck and practise pulling yourself onto a dock or pool edge with them, then the roll away.

rifle-mechanics:
Why it matters

Know what every part does and you can fix a jam, trust your safety, and spot trouble before it hurts you or a deer.

  • Five jobs: action, barrel, trigger, safety, stock.
  • The example is your Tikka T3x Arctic in .308 Winchester.
More: what this lesson covers
  • Your rifle: Tikka T3x Arctic, .308 Winchester (owner's gear list).
  • Sako's own spec page for the Arctic in .308: 508 mm (20 inch) barrel, 1:10 inch twist, 4.1 kg, two stage trigger, two position safety, Picatinny rail, birch laminate stock, open sights with a rear wheel stepped out to 600 m 95%.
  • Tikka rifles are made by Sako in Finland, and every Tikka must group three shots under 1 MOA (minute of angle) at 100 m before sale (95%, Tikka manual).
  • Parts names come from the firearm safety refresher. Scope and rings live in choosing and mounting your scope.
  • Assumption: your rifle matches Sako's Arctic spec. Read the stamp on your barrel and check.

• Bolt: up, back, forward, down 95%.
  • Safety ON locks trigger, sear and bolt on the Tikka 95%.
  • Click, no bang: wait 1 minute 95%.
More: all key points
  • The bolt action works in four moves: lift, back, forward, down. Lifting unlocks, back extracts, forward feeds, down locks and cocks (95%, Tikka manual).
  • The barrel's rifling spins the bullet. Your 1:10 twist means one full turn every 10 inches 95%.
  • The trigger lets the sear go, the firing pin hits the primer, the powder burns, the bullet leaves 85%.
  • Tikka safety ON locks the bolt closed, the firing pin cocked, and the sear and trigger (95%, Tikka manual).
  • A safety is a mechanical device. It is never a substitute for safe handling (95%, Tikka manual).
  • Misfire: keep it pointed safe and wait at least one minute before unloading with great care (95%, Tikka manual).
  • Action screws: 7 Nm (newton metres), 62 in lb, with a metal trigger guard. Max 5 Nm (44 in lb) with a plastic one (95%, Tikka manual).
  • Changes in feel, sound or function: stop shooting, see a gunsmith (95%, Tikka manual).

• Up unlocks. Back pulls the case out. Forward feeds. Down locks 95%.
  • Run the bolt hard and full length. Short strokes jam (Tip).
More: the cycle in full
  1. Lift the handle (up). The locking lugs turn out of their seats in the receiver. Lifting also cocks the firing pin: the cocking piece moves back as you lift (95%, Tikka manual).
  2. Pull back. The extractor claw drags the fired case out and the ejector flips it out the ejection port 85%.
  3. Push forward. The bolt face strips the top round from the magazine and pushes it into the chamber (95%, Tikka manual).
  4. Turn down. The lugs lock. The rifle is cocked and ready to fire once the safety comes off (95%, Tikka manual).
  5. Tikka: "This rifle can have a live round in the chamber and can fire even if the magazine is empty or has been removed" (95%, Tikka manual). Magazine out never means unloaded.
  6. Short stroking: pulling the bolt only part way back. The case does not clear and the next round jams on it (Tip).
  7. Practise the cycle with snap caps or dummy rounds, never live ammunition, until it is smooth without looking (Tip).

• Lugs lock. Pin strikes. Claw extracts 85%.
  • Do not strip the bolt for routine cleaning 95%.
More: bolt parts in full
  • Locking lugs: at the bolt head, they turn into recesses in the receiver and hold the pressure of the shot 85%.
  • Firing pin and spring: inside the bolt. Cocked when you lift the handle (95%, Tikka manual).
  • Cocking piece and shroud: at the back. The cocking indicator shows when the pin is cocked (95%, Tikka manual).
  • Extractor and ejector: pull the case out and throw it clear 85%.
  • Tikka: "Generally, disassembling the bolt is not necessary." Strip it only if oil has got inside, which matters most in cold or harsh weather (95%, Tikka manual).
  • Grease points: Tikka says keep the locking lug surfaces, cocking cam and head of the cocking piece lightly greased 95%. See gun care.

• Trigger, sear, pin, primer, powder, bullet 85%.
  • Follow through: keep pressing until the recoil ends 85%.
More: the chain in full
  1. You press the trigger.
  2. The trigger releases the sear, the catch that holds the cocked firing pin 85%.
  3. The firing pin springs forward 85%.
  4. It dents the primer, a small charge in the case head that ignites when struck (85%, hunter education).
  5. The primer flash lights the powder. It burns fast and turns to expanding gas (85%, hunter education).
  6. The gas drives the bullet down the barrel and out the muzzle 85%.
  7. The whole chain is over in a few thousandths of a second (Tip: order of magnitude, not a measured number).
  8. Anything that moves the rifle during that chain moves the shot. That is why hunter education teaches a slow, steady squeeze and follow through 85%.
  9. More on each part of the round: how a cartridge works.

• Chamber, throat, bore, muzzle. Each matters 85%.
  • A dinged crown can open groups. Protect the muzzle (Tip).
More: barrel parts in full
  • Chamber: the cut at the back that holds the cartridge. Shaped exactly for .308 Winchester. The calibre is marked on the side of the barrel (95%, Tikka manual).
  • Throat: where the bullet leaves the case and meets the rifling 70%.
  • Bore: the inside of the barrel, with rifling 85%.
  • Muzzle and crown: the last edge the bullet touches. Damage here can spoil accuracy 70%.
  • Arctic barrel: 508 mm (20 inch), stainless (95%, Sako spec page).
  • Threaded muzzle: some Tikkas have one. Keep the thread protector on when no brake or suppressor is fitted (95%, Tikka manual). Suppressor and brake law is not covered here: VERIFY before fitting anything.
  • Obstruction check before loading: bolt out, look through from the back. Any obstruction is a gunsmith job (95%, Tikka manual).

• Grooves are cut. Lands are the ridges between 85%.
  • Land to land across the bore is the calibre 85%.
More: rifling in full
  • "The spiral channels cut into a bore are the grooves, and the metal ridges between them are the lands. Together, the grooves and lands make up the rifling" (85%, hunter education study guide).
  • Calibre: the barrel diameter measured land to opposite land (85%, hunter education).
  • The bullet is a touch bigger than land to land, so the lands bite into it and force it to turn 70%.
  • Shotguns have no rifling and are called smoothbores (85%, hunter education).
  • Copper from bullet jackets can build up in the rifling. Tikka recommends removing copper fouling in periodic maintenance (95%, Tikka manual).

• 1:10 means one full turn in 10 inches 95%.
  • Faster twist suits longer, heavier bullets 70%.
More: twist rate in full
  • Twist rate is the barrel length the rifling needs for one full turn. Lower second number = faster spin (70%, MeatEater).
  • Your Arctic in .308: 1:10 per Sako's spec page 95%.
    • Note: the scope session lists 1 in 11 80%. Sako's own page says 1:10. Trust the maker, and check the barrel stamp. VERIFY on your rifle.
  • Common .308 twists: 1:10 and 1:12 (70%, MeatEater).
  • Spin rate math: 2,820 fps (feet per second) × 12 inches per foot ÷ 10 inches per turn = about 3,400 turns a second, or about 200,000 rpm (revolutions per minute) (95%, arithmetic).
  • Too slow a twist for a long bullet: it wobbles, keyholes (hits sideways) and groups open 70%.
  • Factory rifles use twists that stabilise the common bullets for the cartridge 70%. A 1:10 .308 handles 150 to 180 gr (grain) hunting bullets 65%.

  • Adjust range 2.5 to 4 lb. Never below 2.5 lb 95%.
More: the trigger in full
  • Tikka: the trigger is adjusted at the factory and needs no adjustment. Factory weight 13 to 15 N (about 3 lb) (95%, Tikka manual).
  • Adjustable 11 to 18 N (2.5 to 4 lb) with a 2.5 mm Allen key through the magazine well (95%, Tikka manual).
  • "For safety reason do NOT attempt to reduce trigger weight below 11 N (2,5 lbs)" (95%, Tikka manual).
  • Sako lists a two stage trigger on the Arctic (95%, Sako spec page). Two stage: light take up, then a firm wall, then the break.
    • Most T3x models have a single stage trigger. Dry fire yours with a snap cap to learn which you have (Tip).
  • Do not make any other trigger adjustment. Changes in feel: gunsmith (95%, Tikka manual).
  • Single set trigger (optional on some Tikkas, not the Arctic per Sako): when set, about 2 to 2.5 N, and any shock may fire it (95%, Tikka manual).
My lean (opinion)

Leave the trigger at the factory setting your first season. Learn it with dry fire instead of changing it.

• Tikka: red dot showing = ready to fire 95%.
  • CZ 457: bolt opens with the safety on. Tikka: it does not 95%.
More: the safety in full
  • Tikka: the safety catch is beside the bolt. Back is ON. ON locks the bolt closed, the firing pin cocked, and the sear and trigger (95%, Tikka manual).
  • The safety can only go ON when the firing pin is cocked (95%, Tikka manual).
  • Red dot visible = safety OFF, ready to fire. No red dot = safety ON (95%, Tikka manual).
  • Some Tikkas have a three position safety with a bolt release button. Sako lists a two position safety on the Arctic 95%.
  • So on the Arctic, to unload you push the safety OFF with the muzzle pointed safe, then lift the bolt (95%, Tikka manual unloading steps).
  • CZ 457: safety back shows a white dot and locks the trigger. You can pull the bolt out "even with the safety engaged" (95%, CZ 457 manual).
  • The manual safety "is merely a mechanical device and is in no way a substitute for the Basic Safety Rules" (95%, Tikka manual).
Warning

Two rifles, opposite habits. Say it out loud when you switch: "Tikka: safety off to unload. CZ: safety stays on."

Prove the Tikka unloaded in 4 steps1 of 4

More: the manual's steps in full
  1. Finger away from the trigger, barrel in a safe direction 95%.
  2. Disengage the safety: push it forward, red dot showing 95%.
  3. Remove the magazine with the magazine release button 95%.
  4. Remove the bolt: lift the handle, press the bolt stop and pull it fully out 95%.
  5. Check the chamber is empty. If not, follow "Unloading the rifle" 95%.
  6. Put the bolt back and close it. The firing pin is now cocked. With the barrel pointed safe, decock by pulling the trigger 95%.
  7. Source: Tikka T1x and T3x instruction manual, v5.3, "Load check" 95%.
  8. Hand the rifle to your brother only with the magazine out, the bolt open and the chamber checked (95%, Tikka manual).

  • Never force an extra round in 95%.
More: magazines in full
  • Load: hold the magazine, place a round on the follower in front of the lips, press down and slide it fully under the lips. Repeat (95%, Tikka manual).
  • "Do not try to force more cartridges than the maximum capacity of your magazine" (95%, Tikka manual).

  • Tikka: "If the rifle doesn't fire after pulling the trigger, wait at least one minute and unload the rifle with extreme care" (95%, Tikka manual).
  • Why wait: a slow ignition (hang fire) can fire late 70%.

Tikka says stop shooting immediately and see an authorised gunsmith if (95%, Tikka manual):

  • the trigger mechanism works differently
  • the rifle misfires
  • the safety does not operate

cartridge-anatomy:
Why it matters

The bullet is the only part that touches the deer. Know the round, pick the right bullet, and never load the wrong one.

  • Four parts: case, primer, powder, bullet 85%.
  • Memory: CPPB.
More: the four parts, in hunter education words
  • Case: "The container that holds all the other ammunition components together." Usually brass (85%, hunter education).
  • Primer: "An explosive chemical compound that ignites the gunpowder when struck by a firing pin" (85%, hunter education).
  • Powder: "A chemical mixture that burns rapidly and converts to an expanding gas when ignited" (85%, hunter education).
  • Bullet: "A projectile, usually containing lead, fired through a rifle or handgun barrel" (85%, hunter education).
  • A cartridge is one complete round: primer, powder, case and bullet together (80%, Massachusetts hunter education lesson).
  • Which load to buy: ammo for your guns. How the rifle fires it: how a rifle works.

• Barrel stamp, box and headstamp must all match 85%.
  • Hunting bullets must expand. Full metal jacket is illegal for hunting in BC 99%.
  • Tikka: no ammunition over 10 years old 95%.
More: all key points
  • Compare "the barrel stamp on the firearm against the description on the ammunition box and the stamp on each cartridge" (85%, hunter education).
  • Smokeless powder burns, it does not explode in the open. Gas pressure in the chamber is what drives the bullet (85%, hunter education).
  • Centrefire primers sit in the centre of the base. Rimfire priming is inside the rim (85%, hunter education).
  • Five hunting bullet designs: cup and core, bonded, partition, all copper, polymer tip 70%.
  • BC: "It is unlawful to hunt or trap with a rifle using a full metal jacketed non expanding bullet, or a tracer, incendiary, or explosive bullet" (99%, Rule Book: legal methods).
  • Tikka: do not fire ammunition over 10 years old, and inspect every round (95%, Tikka manual).
  • 7,000 grains make one pound 95%.

• The headstamp on the base names the cartridge 85%.
  • .308 Win in a .308 Win rifle. Nothing else 95%.
More: case parts in full
  • Rim: the edge at the base. The extractor grabs it 85%.
  • Extractor groove: the cut in front of the rim on rimless cases like .308 70%.
  • Body: the main tube that holds the powder 85%.
  • Shoulder: the slope down to the neck. On a .308 it sets how far the round goes into the chamber 70%.
  • Neck: grips the bullet 85%.
  • Headstamp: maker and calibre stamped on the base 85%.
  • Tikka: "Make sure that the ammunition is of the appropriate caliber and loading for the firearm and is clean, dry, and in good condition. The caliber designation for your rifle is marked on the side of the barrel" (95%, Tikka manual).
  • Tikka also says use only factory ammunition made to CIP (the European proof commission) or SAAMI (the US standards institute) standards 95%.
Warning

.308 Winchester and 7.62x51 NATO are close cousins but not identical in every chamber. Use what your barrel stamp says, and ask a gunsmith before mixing (60%, Tip).

The shot in 5 steps1 of 5
  • All five happen in a few thousandths of a second (Tip).
  • The case seal keeps hot gas off your face 70%.
More: the five steps in full
  1. The firing pin strikes the primer (85%, hunter education).
  2. The primer compound ignites and sends a flash through a small flash hole into the powder 85%.
  3. The powder burns very fast and turns into a large volume of hot gas (85%, hunter education).
  4. Pressure swells the brass case against the chamber walls. This seals the gas so it can only push forward 70%.
  5. The gas pushes the bullet out of the neck, into the throat and rifling, and down the barrel 85%.
  6. This is why a bulged or split case, a pierced primer or gas spitting back means stop shooting (95%, Tikka manual).
  7. Ammunition that is wet, oily or dirty can change pressure. Tikka asks for clean, dry rounds and a dry chamber before shooting 95%.

• Centrefire: primer in the centre. Your .308 85%.
  • Rimfire: compound in the rim. Your .22 LR (long rifle) 85%.
More: the difference in full
  • "Centerfire ammunition is used for rifles, shotguns, and handguns." The primer sits in the centre of the casing base. Most centrefire ammunition can be reloaded (85%, hunter education).
  • "Rimfire ammunition has the primer contained in the rim of the ammunition casing." Low pressure only. Cannot be reloaded (85%, hunter education).
  • BC legal methods treat them differently. Rimfire for grouse, ptarmigan and turkey only among game birds; no rimfire for deer (99%, Rule Book: legal methods).
  • The .22 LR in depth: the .22 rimfire.

• Smokeless powder burns slowly in the open air 85%.
  • Locked in a chamber, the same burn makes huge pressure 85%.
More: powder in full
  • "Modern smokeless powder will burn slowly when ignited in the open (outside of the case)" (85%, hunter education).
  • "Black powder is less stable and can be explosive when impacted or ignited in the open" (85%, hunter education).
  • In the chamber, the gas has nowhere to go but forward, so pressure climbs fast 70%.
  • Heat and cold change how fast powder burns, and so the speed of the bullet 65%. See ballistics deep dive for what that does to drop.
  • Store ammunition cool and dry. Tikka asks you to store it in a separate locked place 95%.

• Tip, ogive, shank, base 70%.
  • Jacket outside, core inside on most hunting bullets 70%.
More: bullet parts in full
  • Tip: soft point (exposed lead), hollow point, or a plastic tip. All start expansion 70%.
  • Ogive: the curved nose. A long ogive cuts the air better 65%.
  • Shank: the full width part that the rifling grips 70%.
  • Base: flat or boat tail (tapered). A boat tail drags a little less at long range 65%.
  • Hunter education bullet types: pointed soft point (flat shooting, excellent mushrooming), round nose soft point (low speed, tube magazines), protected tip (accurate, good expansion), full metal jacket (no expansion) 85%.
  • BC (ballistic coefficient) on the box tells you how well the bullet cuts air. Higher drifts less 85%. More in .308 ballistics made simple.

• 150 gr (grain) = 9.7 g. 165 gr = 10.7 g. 180 gr = 11.7 g 95%.
  • Heavier: slower, carries energy, more recoil 70%.
More: weights in full
  • 7,000 grains = 1 pound = 453.6 g, so 1 grain = 0.0648 g (95%, unit definition).
  • 150 gr = 9.7 g. 165 gr = 10.7 g. 168 gr = 10.9 g. 180 gr = 11.7 g. 40 gr .22 LR = 2.6 g (95%, arithmetic).
  • Powder charges are also weighed in grains. Do not confuse bullet weight and powder weight on a box (Tip).
  • In a .308: 150 gr leaves faster and shoots flatter. 165 to 180 gr leaves slower, keeps more energy, and penetrates more 70%.
  • The ammo session gives the picks by animal: 150 gr for deer, 165 to 168 gr all round, 178 to 180 gr for elk and moose 65%.

• Cup and core: cheap, opens fast 70%.
  • Bonded, partition, copper: hold together for bone and big game 70%.

ballistics-deep:
Why it matters

Every miss and every wounded deer past 200 m has a number behind it. Learn the numbers and you know when to shoot and when to close the gap.

  • The scope looks straight. The bullet arcs 85%.
  • 100 m zero: 13 cm low at 200 m, 48 cm at 300 m 75%.
More: what this deep dive adds
  • The basics are in .308 ballistics made simple: Federal's tables, MPBR (maximum point blank range), the 20 inch barrel and the 1,000 ft lb rule. Read it first.
  • This lesson adds: why the bullet crosses the crosshair twice, holds in MOA (minute of angle) and mils, the wind clock, uphill and downhill shots, time of flight, cold and altitude, and building your own dope card.
  • Numbers marked "Hunt Mentor model" come from a point mass ballistic solver (py ballisticcalc 3.0, G1 drag model) fed with Federal's published data. It matches Federal's drop table within 1 cm at 300 yd (91 m to 274 m) and its wind drift within about 10% 75%. The wind tables below use the simple session's Federal based numbers.
  • Assumption: Federal Power Shok 150 gr (grain), 2,820 fps (feet per second), BC (ballistic coefficient) .313; scope 3.8 cm (1.5 in) above the bore, as Federal assumes.

• Internal: in the barrel. External: in the air. Terminal: in the animal 85%.
  • You control external by knowing range, wind and angle.
More: the three in full
  • Internal ballistics: pressure, the bullet engraving into the rifling, the twist. Covered in how a rifle works and how a cartridge works.
  • External ballistics: gravity, air drag, wind, angle, temperature and altitude. This lesson.
  • Terminal ballistics: what the bullet does in the animal: expansion, penetration. See the cartridge lesson and shot placement.
  • The hunter controls external ballistics mostly with three numbers: distance, wind and angle (Tip).

• The bore points slightly up at the line of sight 85%.
  • 100 m zero: first crossing near 25 m, peak about 1 cm high 75%.
More: the arc in full
  • The scope sits above the bore, about 3.8 cm. To hit where the crosshair points at 100 m, the bore must tilt slightly upward 85%.
  • So the bullet starts 3.8 cm below the line of sight, climbs through it, peaks, and falls back through it at your zero 85%.
  • 100 m zero, Hunt Mentor model: crosses near 25 m, about 1 cm high at 60 to 75 m, 0 at 100 m 75%.
  • That is why a 25 m target is a quick check for a 100 m zero: the bullet should hit near the aim point at 25 m 70%. Your sighting in session uses this.
  • Gravity starts pulling the instant the bullet leaves. It never "rises" against gravity; the barrel was simply pointed up 85%.

• 150 m: 4 cm. 200 m: 13 cm. 250 m: 28 cm. 300 m: 48 cm 75%.
  • Past 300 m the curve gets steep fast 75%.

judging-distance:
Why it matters

Your drop table is only as good as your distance. A 50 m mistake at 300 m puts the bullet under the heart.

  • Guess 250 m, deer at 300 m: about 20 cm low 75%.
  • Laser first. Reticle second. Eye third.
More: the cost of a wrong guess
  • Drops with a 100 m zero, 150 gr (grain) .308: 28 cm at 250 m, 48 cm at 300 m (75%, ballistics deep dive).
  • Hold for 250 m on a deer at 300 m: about 20 cm low, the full height of the vital zone 75%.
  • Inside 150 m, a 25 m mistake costs about 2 to 4 cm. That is why close shots forgive bad guesses 75%.
  • Hunters estimate badly without practice, so a laser rangefinder is the primary tool and the reticle is the backup (70%, Vortex: reticle ranging "provides a good back up should your laser rangefinder fail").

Scope reticleAbout 400 m with practice (Tip)Always with youNeeds known size and steady hold
Eye methodsTo about 400 m 80%Free, silentEasy to fool
  • Learn all three. Batteries die on the coldest day (Tip).
More: why the order matters
  • Canadian Army fieldcraft lists other ways too: maps, pacing, the mil formula, range cards and rangefinders 80%.
  • In the field: laser, then confirm with the reticle or the map if the reading looks odd (Tip).
  • Your phone mapping app can measure distance between two points, a good check before or after (Tip). See maps 2: compass, GPS and apps.

• It times a light pulse to the target and back 70%.
  • Deer range is about half the box number 65%.
More: rangefinder specs explained
  • The big number on the box is usually the reflective range, on a bright, flat target 65%.
  • Example: Vortex Ranger 1800: reflective 9 to 1,800 yd, deer 9 to 900 yd, accuracy plus or minus 3 yd at 1,000 yd, angle reading to plus or minus 60 degrees, 6x22 (65%, retailer listing).
  • Its HCD (horizontal component distance) mode shows the flat distance for your hold 65%.
  • Rain, snow, fog and low light shorten range (Tip).
  • Angle: see ballistics deep dive for why flat distance matters.

Use a laser rangefinder in 4 steps1 of 4
  • Range landmarks before the deer comes (Tip).
More: the steps in full
  1. Brace the unit on a tree, pack or knee, two hands. A shaking box hits the brush beside the deer (Tip).
  2. Put the aiming box on the deer's shoulder, mid body. Edges let the beam slip past onto the hill behind (Tip).
  3. Range at least three times. Two that agree within a few metres are the answer (Tip).
  4. Read the angle or the flat distance mode, and use that for your hold 65%.
  5. Before any deer shows, range three landmarks: a rock, a bush, a fence post. Write them down. When a deer stands near one, you already know (Tip).
  6. Quiet: rangefinders are silent, but your arm movement is not. Range landmarks early, move little when the deer is there (Tip).

• A reading much shorter than you expect: branch or grass (Tip).
  • Much longer: the beam missed and hit the hill (Tip).
More: how to beat it
  • Many rangefinders have a "last target" or "distant target" mode that ignores near objects like brush. Check your manual (60%, VERIFY by model).
  • Move a step left or right to find a clear gap (Tip).
  • Range a solid object right beside the deer, like a tree at the same distance (Tip).

• Metres = size in metres × 1,000 ÷ mils 85%.
  • Yards = size in inches × 95.5 ÷ MOA (minute of angle) 85%.
More: the formulas in full
  • Vortex mil formula: "Known Width or Height of Target (Meters) × 1000 ÷ Target Width or Height (Measured on Reticle in MRADS) = Range (Meters)" 85%.
  • Vortex MOA formula: size in inches × 95.5 ÷ MOA = range in yards. Using 100 instead of 95.5 overestimates by about 5% 85%.
  • A steady hold matters: brace on a rest, bipod or sling when measuring (85%, Vortex).
  • Second focal plane scopes: the marks are only true at one power, usually the highest. Check your manual (70%, scope session).
  • Duplex reticles: the gap between the thick post tips covers a set number of MOA at a set power, which varies by model. VERIFY yours in the scope manual.

More: the method in full
  • "A known accurate distance is visualized (e.g., a football field or the distance between two telephone poles), and that unit is applied repeatedly between the observer and the target until the range is determined" (80%, Canadian Army fieldcraft).
  • You must see the ground between you and the target. "This method is not accurate beyond 400 metres" 80%.
  • Build your unit: a Canadian football field is 110 yd (101 m) goal line to goal line (60%, VERIFY), close enough to 100 m. Any measured 100 m works better: walk one at the range (Tip).

• Learn what a deer looks like at 100, 200, 300 m 80%.
  • These pictures are tips. Build your own with a laser (Tip).
More: the method in full
  • The appearance method compares how an object looks at 100 m and farther. As distance grows, it gets smaller, the outline blurs and details fade (80%, Canadian Army fieldcraft).
  • The Army's guide is for a person: at 200 m all parts of the body are distinct, at 300 m the face blurs, at 400 m the face is hard to see, at 500 m the body tapers, at 600 m the head is a dot 80%.
  • For deer, the panel above is a Hunt Mentor tip, not a source. Range every deer you see this fall and say the detail you see out loud (Tip).

• Bright light, snow, water, clear air: looks nearer 80%.
  • Fog, dusk, part showing, lying down: looks farther 80%.
More: the full lists

Objects seem nearer (80%, Canadian Army fieldcraft):

  • in bright light or with the sun behind you
  • when the colour contrasts sharply with the background
  • looking over water, snow or a uniform surface
  • in the clear air of high altitudes
  • with dead ground (a hidden dip) between you and it
  • when bigger than things around it

Objects seem farther 80%:

  • looking over a depression you can fully see
  • in poor light, fog, or with the sun in your eyes
  • when only a small part shows
  • looking down a street or tree lined road
  • when it blends in with the background
  • when smaller than things around it
  • when you are lying down
  • Field meaning: a deer across a snowy cutblock on a bright morning is farther than it looks. A deer in a shady draw at dusk may be closer (Tip).

• Halving: judge to halfway, then double 80%.
  • Bracketing: "more than X, less than Y", call the middle 80%.
More: aids in full
  • Halving: "A point is chosen halfway to the target and the distance is estimated to the point and doubled" (80%, Canadian Army fieldcraft).
  • Bracketing: add the near and far limits and halve the sum 80%.
  • Key ranges: know the range to one landmark, judge others from it 80%.
  • Unit average: you and your brother both guess, take the average 80%.

• Know your pace count for 100 m 80%.
  • Map measure before the hunt (Tip).
More: pacing and maps in full
  • Pacing and maps are on the Army's list of other methods 80%.
  • Pace count: walk a measured 100 m three times, counting each left foot, and average (Tip). Uphill, brush and snow shorten your pace (Tip).
  • After a shot, pace to the spot where the deer stood. It tells you the true range and trains your eye (Tip).
  • Map: measure from your glassing point to the far edge of a cutblock before the hunt. Then you know the "edge is 280 m" before any deer steps out (Tip).

field-positions:
Why it matters

Deer never stand in front of a bench. The steadier you get in grass, sage and timber, the farther you can ethically shoot.

  • Lower and more supported is steadier 85%.
  • Pick the steadiest the grass and time allow (Tip).
More: what this lesson adds
  • The four basic positions, sticks, breath and trigger, the dry fire plan and the max range test are in shooting skills. Start there.
  • This lesson goes deeper: bone support, natural point of aim, packs, bipods, sitting styles, trees, slopes, slings, speed into position, and drills you can run at the range and at home.
  • Hunter education ranks prone steadiest, then sitting, then kneeling, then standing 85%.
  • The ladder above mixes in rests. Its order is a Hunt Mentor ranking, not a measured fact (opinion).

• Bone support, not muscle (Tip).
  • Find your natural point of aim, then shoot 80%.
  • Pad between rifle and rest. Never the bare barrel on rock 85%.
More: all key points
  • Support the rifle with stacked bones and the ground, then relax the muscles (Tip).
  • Natural point of aim (NPOA): "the point where the barrel naturally orients when the shooter's muscles are relaxed and support is achieved" (80%, US Army TC 3-22.9 via American Rifleman).
  • Hunter education: the safest and most accurate field shots come from a stable rest like a log or rock, but "Don't rest the barrel directly on a hard surface, or the rifle will fire higher than normal." Pad it with a hat or jacket 85%.
  • Get into position in under 5 seconds with practice (Tip).
  • Practise from the clothes and pack you hunt in (Tip).
  • Drills beat bench groups for hunting skill (opinion).

Find your natural point of aim in 4 steps1 of 4
  • If you hold the crosshair on with muscle, the shot drifts 80%.
  • Groups that string left and right can mean a bad NPOA 70%.
More: the method in full
  • American Rifleman (Matt Robertson, January 2026): pick a fixed pivot, like a foot or an elbow supported on something, and move the rest of your body around that point to adjust your NPOA 80%.
  • Test: crosshair on target, relax slightly, a small "shimmy" of the body. "If they settle back on the target, you're good to go!" 80%
  • Keep your eyes open during the test. Instructor John Simpson advises against closing them (75%, American Rifleman).
  • Prone: shift your hips left or right to swing the rifle. Sitting: shuffle your seat. Sticks: move your feet (Tip).
  • A group that drifts left to right can point to a bad NPOA (60%, search preview of NPA articles).

• Pack under the forend, not under the barrel 85%.
  • Rear hand fine tunes the height (Tip).
More: prone with a pack in full
  • Lie in line with the rifle, slightly angled, both elbows down (85%, hunter education on prone).
  • Pack under the forend. Push it into the pack slightly for a solid feel (Tip).
  • The rear hand makes a fist, or squeezes a sock of sand, under the butt to raise or lower the aim (Tip).
  • Grass and sage often block a prone view at deer height. Check the bullet path, not only the scope view: the barrel sits about 4 cm below the scope (Tip).
  • Hard rests shoot high, soft rests low. Learn yours on paper (70%, from the shooting skills session).

• Lean gently forward to load the legs (Tip).
  • Same pressure every shot (Tip).
More: bipod in full
  • A rifle mounted bipod works prone and sitting, or braced against a tree (70%, shooting skills session).
  • Tikka's front sling swivel stud can take a bipod (95%, Tikka manual).
  • Loading: push your shoulder gently forward so the legs press into the ground. The rifle stops hopping (Tip).
  • Bipod on hard rock shoots differently from soft dirt. Practise both (Tip).
  • Bipods add weight on the hill. Many hunters carry sticks and use the pack as a prone rest instead (opinion).

• Crossed ankle: lowest and steadiest (Tip).
  • Open leg: fits slopes (Tip).
  • Sticks: over grass 70%.
More: sitting in full
  • Sitting is the next steadiest after prone (85%, hunter education).
  • Elbows go inside the knees, flat of the arm against the soft knee, not the point of the elbow on the kneecap (Tip, shooting skills session).
  • Crossed ankle: legs crossed at the ankles, body leaning forward. Low, very steady, slow to get into (Tip).
  • Open leg: feet apart, knees up. Quick, works on uneven ground (Tip).
  • With sticks: tripod or bipod sticks in front, elbows on knees. Clears grass and sage 70%.
  • Bring the position to the ground: on a slope, face downhill and sitting becomes almost a bench (Tip).

• Kneeling clears low brush, one arm braced 85%.
  • Standing on a tripod makes a hard shot workable 70%.
More: kneeling and standing in full
  • Kneeling: sit on the heel of your rear foot, support elbow on the raised knee. Less steady than sitting 85%.
  • Standing with three leg sticks: two legs toward you, one toward the deer, top about armpit height, feet nearly square (70%, Richard Mann, Field and Stream).
  • Rest the back of your hand on the sticks, hold the forend as normal 70%.
  • Offhand: only when the deer is close and there is no time to sit (Tip).

• Hand or glove between rifle and bark 85%.
  • Hard surface under the barrel: shoots high 85%.
More: trees and rocks in full
  • Hunter education: "Don't rest the barrel directly on a hard surface, or the rifle will fire higher than normal." Pad it 85%.
  • Against a tree: press the side of your support hand against the trunk, rifle in that hand (Tip).
  • On a rock or log: hat, glove or pack between the forend and the rock 85%.
  • Sit beside a tree, not in front of it. The trunk breaks your outline and gives a side rest (Tip).

• Downhill: sit facing down, heels dug in (Tip).
  • Uphill: prone or kneel with the pack (Tip).
More: slope positions in full
  • Heffley Creek and Okanagan side hills give lots of angled shots (Assumption, based on the owner's areas being hilly).
  • Downhill sitting: heels dug in, elbows inside knees. The slope raises your knees to the right height (Tip).
  • Steep uphill: prone becomes hard as the muzzle points up. Kneel, or sit with sticks (Tip).
  • Recoil on a steep slope can push you downhill. Brace your feet (Tip).
  • Hold correction for angles: ballistics deep dive.

• Sling around the support arm pulls the rifle tight (Tip).
  • Practise it dry before you trust it (Tip).
More: sling in full
  • This is a common rifleman's technique, shown here as a tip: Hunt Mentor has no hunter education source for it this session 55%. VERIFY with a range officer or instructor.
  • Hasty sling: support arm goes between sling and rifle, sling wraps the upper arm, hand forward on the forend. The sling tension pulls the butt into the shoulder (Tip).
  • Works sitting and kneeling. Changes your zero slightly for some rifles: test on paper (Tip).
  • Carrying with the sling: safe carries.

• Say the position out loud. Then do it (Tip).
  • Safety off only when the crosshair is settled on the deer 95%.
More: speed drill in full
  1. Stop. Find the deer again with your eyes or binoculars.
  2. Say it: "Sitting. Sticks." It stops the panic offhand shot (Tip).
  3. Sticks out, sit down, elbows in.

shotgun-mastery:
Why it matters

A shotgun throws a cloud, not a bullet. Match choke, shell and range, swing ahead of the bird, and the cloud does the work.

  • The cloud spreads with distance 85%.
  • Choke controls how fast it spreads 85%.
More: what this lesson adds
  • Basics first: choosing your shotgun (actions, chamber, plug, steel safe chokes), ammo for your guns (shells by bird) and shotgun skills (stance, mount, swing, clay plan).
  • This lesson goes deeper: what constriction really is, pattern percentages, patterning step by step, pellet counts, how much lead and why, angles, eye dominance, and setups for upland and waterfowl.
  • Assumption: your 12 gauge has a 3 inch chamber and screw in chokes, as the shotgun session recommends. Your exact model is not chosen yet; read its manual for steel and choke ratings.

More: all key points
  • Choke is a slight narrowing at the muzzle that controls spread 85%.
  • One maker's lead shot chart, 76 cm (30 in) circle at 40 yd (37 m): cylinder 40%, IC (improved cylinder) 50%, modified 60%, improved modified 65%, full 70% (85%, Trulock). "This chart should be used as a starting point only" 85%.
  • Big steel through tight chokes can cause "choke creep" and lock a choke in the barrel (85%, Trulock).
  • Pattern at least 5 shots per choke and shell (85%, Trulock).
  • Lead (forward allowance) at a 30 m crossing duck: roughly 1 to 2 m 65%.
  • Most misses are behind (70%, shotgun skills session).
  • Aim with the dominant eye (85%, hunter education).
  • Ducks and geese: non toxic shot, plug, 3 shells total (99%, Rule Book: legal methods).

  • Trulock rates most of its chokes for steel from cylinder through improved modified 85%. Your gun maker's rating is what counts for your gun (Tip).
  • Shotgun session rule of thumb: nothing tighter than modified with steel unless the choke says steel safe 75%.
  • Trulock's steel pairings, number size shot: about 30 yd Skeet 1, about 35 yd Skeet 2 (light modified), 35 yd plus improved modified. For BB and BBB: cylinder, IC, modified for close, mid, long 85%.

Pattern a shotgun in 5 steps1 of 5
  • Pattern where you will shoot: 35 m for ducks, 25 m upland (Tip).
More: Trulock's method in full
  1. Target about 4 ft (1.2 m) square. Butcher paper or flooring paper works 85%.
  2. Mark the centre. Shoot from a padded bench with your head and eye where they are when you shoot offhand 85%.
  3. At least 5 shots, each on its own sheet, for each shell and choke 85%.
  4. Draw a 30 in (76 cm) circle around the densest part of each pattern. Count pellets inside, divide by total pellets in the shell 85%.
  5. Average all sheets 85%.
  6. Look for holes big enough for a target to slip through. "The goal is multiple hits" 85%.
  7. Pellet count in your shell: shot weight × pellets per ounce (next screen), or cut one shell open and count (Tip).
  8. Your first pattern session is in sighting in and patterning.

  • Dense core kills. Thin fringe cripples 70%.

  • Example: 1 1/8 oz of steel #2 is about 141 pellets. At 65% that is about 92 in the circle (70%, arithmetic from Wikipedia's 125 per oz).

firearm-care:
Why it matters

A rusty bore, a frozen firing pin or a snow plugged barrel can cost you the deer or your face. Ten minutes after each hunt prevents all three.

  • Tikka: corrosion can begin within 24 hours 95%.
  • Clean after every use, even if you never fired 95%.
More: what the manuals say
  • Tikka: "Routine cleaning should always take place right after use of the rifle (even without shooting). Maintenance should not be neglected even in case of the 'All weather' or 'Stainless' models. Corrosion can begin within 24 hours if the rifle is not cleaned after use" (95%, Tikka manual).
  • Your Arctic is stainless with a laminated stock (95%, Sako). Stainless resists rust; it is not rust proof (Tip).
  • CZ: clean each time you use it, if it gets wet, as soon as possible after shooting, at least once a year (95%, CZ manual).
  • Shotgun: your model is not chosen yet. Follow its manual; the steps here are general (Tip).

• Rod from the breech, through a guide 95%.
  • Wet: dry it warm, out of the case 95%.
  • Deep cold: less oil, or a cold rated lube 95%.
More: all key points
  • Use a straight, smooth one piece rod with a bore guide, and clean only in the direction the bullet travels (95%, Tikka manual).
  • Leave a thin coat of oil in the chamber for storage, and wipe it dry before shooting (95%, Tikka manual).
  • Use a CLP oil (clean, lubricate, protect) (95%, Tikka manual).
  • Grease lightly: locking lugs, cocking cam, cocking piece head (95%, Tikka manual).
  • Check action screws after cleaning: 7 Nm (newton metres) with a metal trigger guard (95%, Tikka manual).
  • After any fall in snow or mud: unload and look through the bore before firing (95%, Tikka obstruction check).
  • Transport: unloaded in any vehicle or boat, by BC and federal rules. See the transport screen 99%.

Clean the Tikka in 6 steps1 of 6
  • About 10 minutes once you know it (Tip).
More: Tikka's 11 steps in full
  1. Ensure the rifle is unloaded; remove bolt and magazine 95%.
  2. If used in wet conditions, dry it with compressed air or let it dry in a warm, dry place without a protective cover 95%.
  3. Straight, sturdy, smooth rod, bronze brush soaked in bore solvent, push pull about 10 to 15 times. Use a rod guide 95%.
  4. Clean felt pellets wet with solvent, one after another, until they come out clean, about 5 to 10. Only in the bullet direction 95%.
  5. Clean the inside of the receiver with pellets or a brush and solvent 95%.
  6. Small solvent wet brush on the bolt 95%.
  7. Nylon brush or chamber pellet with solvent for the chamber 95%.
  8. Pellet wet with rust preventive oil through the bore. Thin oil in the chamber, and wipe it dry before shooting 95%.
  9. Very light rust preventive oil on touching surfaces of receiver and bolt 95%.
  10. Wipe the stock dry. Wooden stocks: light stock oil 95%.
  11. Check the receiver screws 95%.
  12. Source: Tikka T1x and T3x manual v5.3, routine cleaning and maintenance 95%.

• Never push a rod in from the muzzle on the Tikka or CZ 95%.
  • A bore guide keeps the rod off the throat 95%.
More: why the direction matters
  • Tikka: "Clean only in the direction of bullet movement" and use a guide so the rod does not drag on the bore and receiver 95%.
  • CZ: insert rod and brush from the chamber "to prevent wear or damage to the muzzle." Push the brush all the way through before reversing 95%.
  • The crown is the last thing the bullet touches. A nick there opens groups (70%, see how a rifle works).

• Grease: lugs, cocking cam, cocking piece head 95%.
  • Oil: a thin film everywhere else 95%.
More: lubrication in full
  • Tikka asks that the locking lug surfaces, cocking cam and head of the cocking piece be lightly greased 95%.
  • New rifle: wipe the factory oil from the bore with a dry patch from the breech, and clean extra oil from bolt and chamber before first use (95%, Tikka manual).

  • CZ: never put bore cleaner on other parts; it can stay in joints and cause corrosion 95%.

• Once a year, or more with heavy use 95%.
  • Remove copper fouling from the bore 95%.
More: Tikka periodic maintenance in full

At least once a year, more often with heavy use or severe conditions, and before long storage (95%, Tikka manual):

  1. Do the routine clean.
  2. Remove copper fouling from the bore with a copper solvent, following its maker's instructions. "Badly fouled barrels can shoot inaccurately and will corrode much easier" 95%.
  3. Lubricate all metal surfaces with a lightly oiled rag.
  4. Lubricate sling swivel mounts and check them.
  5. Strip the bolt as the manual shows, clean, lightly oil, grease lugs, cam and cocking piece head.
  6. Reassemble the bolt and check extractor and ejector.
  7. Check sights and scope mounts.
  8. Clean accessories.
  9. Check all screws, including stock and receiver screws.
  10. Reassemble and check function.
  11. Wooden stocks: stock oil.
  12. Spare parts: original factory parts only 95%.

optics-mastery:
Why it matters

You find deer with glass, not with legs. Good optics, set up right and used right, show you the buck before he shows you his tail.

  • Binoculars find. Spotting scope judges. Rifle scope aims (Tip).
  • Never glass with the rifle scope (Tip).
More: what this lesson adds
  • How to glass (grid, tripod, where to look): glassing.
  • Rifle scope choice, rings and mounting: choosing and mounting your scope.
  • This lesson: what the numbers mean, how to choose binoculars and a spotting scope, how to set them up for your eyes, rifle scope focus and parallax, power choice in the field, price tiers, care, and the legal line on thermal optics.
  • Main source: Vortex Optics' "All About Optics" guide 85%. Brand neutral facts; Vortex is used because it publishes the basics clearly.

• Exit pupil = objective lens ÷ power 85%.
  • 8x42 or 10x42 binoculars suit BC hunting (Tip).
  • Set the diopter once for your eyes 85%.
More: all key points
  • "10x50": 10 is the magnification, 50 is the objective lens diameter in mm (85%, Vortex).
  • Exit pupil: objective ÷ magnification. 10x50 = 5 mm 85%.
  • Your pupil: about 2 to 3 mm in bright light, 4 to 5 mm at dawn or dusk, 7 to 8 mm in the dark (85%, Vortex).
  • More magnification: narrower view, more shake, shallower depth of field (85%, Vortex).
  • "7x or 8x magnification is considered adequate for woodland settings, while 10x is preferred for viewing at greater distances" (85%, Vortex).
  • Fully multi coated optics have every air to glass surface coated with multiple films: the best image 85%.
  • Spotting scopes must sit on a tripod 85%.
  • Infrared optics, such as thermal scopes and monoculars, are banned on the hunt (99%, Rule Book: unlawful acts).

• At dawn and dusk your pupil opens to about 4 to 5 mm 85%.
  • An exit pupil bigger than your pupil adds little 70%.
More: exit pupil in practice
  • "A larger exit pupil will deliver brighter images, especially under low light conditions" (85%, Vortex).
  • In daylight your pupil shrinks to 2 to 3 mm, so almost any binocular is bright enough 85%.
  • At legal light at dawn, an 8x42 (5.25 mm) or 10x50 (5 mm) matches your eye. A 10x42 (4.2 mm) is a touch dimmer (70%, arithmetic plus Vortex pupil sizes).
  • Pupil size shrinks with age. Older hunters gain less from huge exit pupils (60%, Tip).
  • Twilight factor (the square root of power × objective) is often quoted, but it is a maths number, not real brightness. Glass quality matters more 65%.

• 8x: wider, steadier, brighter 85%.
  • 10x: more detail at long range, more shake 85%.

Fit binoculars to your eyes in 4 steps1 of 4
  • Note your diopter number. Then only use the centre wheel 85%.
More: Vortex's steps in full
  1. Interpupillary distance: rotate the barrels in or out until you see a single image with no shading 85%.
  2. Eyecups: extend them without glasses; twist or fold them down with glasses, or you see a "tunnel" 85%.
  3. Pick an object about 20 yd (18 m) away. Close the right eye or cover the right lens; turn the centre focus until the left eye sees it sharp 85%.
  4. Close the left eye; turn the diopter ring, usually on the right eyepiece, until sharp. Note the setting. From then on, use only the centre wheel 85%.
  5. Some diopters lock: lift to unlock, push down to lock 85%.
  6. Your brother's eyes differ. Write both diopter numbers on tape on the strap (Tip).

  • Rule Book definitions: infrared optics means any optic that can detect infrared radiation: thermal scopes and thermal monoculars (99%, page 3, via Rule Book: definitions).
  • Rule Book: no thermal scope or thermal monocular on the trip, not even in the pack (99%, page 11, via Rule Book: unlawful acts).
  • No light or illuminating device to hunt by (99%, page 11, Rule Book: legal methods).
  • Illuminated reticles light the crosshair inside the scope. Whether that counts as a light is not addressed in these lessons: VERIFY with a conservation officer before relying on one 55%.

• Caps on, lens cloth or pen, never your shirt (Tip).
  • Dry optics out of the case after rain (Tip).
More: care in full
  • Blow off grit first, then a lens brush, then a lens cloth or pen. Grit wiped with a shirt scratches coatings (Tip).
  • Fogging on the outside lens in cold: breathe away from the eyepiece, warm it slowly (Tip). Inside fog means a broken seal: warranty (85%, waterproofing explained by Vortex).
  • A binocular harness keeps glass dry, quiet and at hand (Tip).
  • Check scope ring screws after a fall or a rough ATV ride; see gun care.

Grandpa's rule (wisdom): Buy the best binoculars you can afford, then sit behind them twice as long.

topo-deep-dive:
Why it matters

Every bench, saddle, pinch and hidden fold where a deer can bed is already drawn on the map. Learn to read the lines and you scout 10 km of country before you leave the couch.

  • A contour line joins points of the same height 98%.
  • Read the pattern, not the single line.
More: what this lesson adds
  • The basics (scale, the five shapes, steepness, aspect) are in Maps 1: reading terrain. This lesson goes deeper: every pattern, what it looks like on the ground, and what a hunter does with it.
  • Think of a contour as the shoreline of a lake that rises one step at a time (Tip, classic teaching picture).
  • Contours are drawn by mappers from elevation data. They are a picture of the ground's shape, not a photo of it (90%, orienteering coaching text, Cory Wright 2000).
  • Practise every pattern in the Hunt Map: The Hunt Map like a pro.

PatternMeans
Lines closeSteep
Lines wideGentle or flat
V pointing uphillDraw or creek
U pointing downhillRidge or spur
HourglassSaddle
Wide gap in tight linesBench
Lines touchingCliff
Ticked loopHole
More: the key points in full
  1. Contours join points of equal height. They never cross; they only merge at a vertical cliff (95%, USGS Topographic Map Symbols).
  2. Close lines are steep, wide lines are gentle, no lines is flat (95%, USGS).
  3. Every fifth line is a thicker index contour with its height printed on it (90%; the step can vary by map series).
  4. The contour interval, the height step between lines, is printed in the map margin 95%. The Hunt Map draws a line every 20 m and a thick index line every 100 m (99%, read in the app's map code).
  5. Closed loops are tops. Loops with small ticks on the inside are holes, called depressions (90%, USGS US Topo specification).
  6. Contours bend into a V where they cross a creek. The V points upstream, uphill 90%.
  7. Shape matters more than any one line: a bench, a saddle, a convex roll (Tip).
  8. Small features can hide between two lines. A 20 m interval can miss a 15 m cliff (95%, simple maths).
  9. Every pattern has a hunting use: beds, crossings, glassing seats, stalking cover (Tip, hunter observation).

Five rules that never change1 of 5
  • Learn these five and every map makes sense.
More: the five rules in full
  • Never cross: each contour is one height, so two can only meet where the ground is vertical, at a cliff (95%, USGS: "contours never cross").
  • Close is steep: "Contours that are very close together represent steep slopes. Widely spaced contours or an absence of contours means that the ground slope is relatively level." (95%, USGS Topographic Map Symbols)
  • Index lines: wider lines with the height printed in several places (95%, USGS). On most maps every fifth line 90%. Some series use every fourth (85%, USGS 250K specification).
  • Closed loops: a ring with no ticks is a knob or summit. A ring with short ticks on the inside is a closed depression; the ticks point down into the low spot (90%, USGS US Topo specification).
  • The V rule: where a contour crosses a creek it bends upstream, making a V that points uphill (90%, standard map reading; also in Maps 1).
  • Colours: brown contours, blue water (95%, USGS; same on Canadian NTS, National Topographic System, sheets, see Maps 1).

• Plain rings: a knob, high ground.
  • Ticked rings: a hole. Often wet, a pond or a sinkhole (Tip).
More: knobs and holes for hunters
  • A small knob in a flat bench is a natural glassing seat: you sit a few metres higher than the cover around you (Tip).
  • Small depressions in grassland and parkland often hold water after rain or snowmelt. Kettle ponds and potholes draw deer and ducks (Tip). Lac du Bois grassland north of Kamloops has pothole lakes in hollows like these (see the photo on this screen and Habitat tour: ducks) (Tip).
  • A depression can be too shallow to show at a 20 m interval. Satellite view and the Slope steepness tool fill the gap (Tip).

• Draw: Vs point up, into the hill. Water runs here.
  • Ridge or spur: Us point down, out of the hill.
More: draws, gullies, ridges and spurs
  • Draw (also gully or reentrant): a small valley on a slope. Sharp Vs pointing uphill 90%.
  • Ridge: a long high spine. Rounded U or V shapes pointing downhill 90%.
  • Spur or finger ridge: a short ridge sticking off a bigger one, like a finger. Us pointing downhill 90%.
  • A spur and a draw always sit side by side, like fingers and the gaps between them (Tip).
  • Hunter use: deer and elk often travel the edge of a draw or along a spur, and cool evening air sinks down draws (Tip; thermals 75%, see Wind and thermals).
  • Picture water dropped on the map. It always runs down the middle of the V, through the open end (Tip).

The five big shapes (from Maps 1)1 of 5
  • Say each name out loud as you scroll a map.
More: what each one is on the ground
ShapeOn the groundHunter use (Tip)
RidgeA long spine you can walkTravel line, glass both sides
DrawA dip with a creek or wet bottomCool, shady, evening thermals sink here
SaddleLow pass between two highsAnimals cross ridges here 65%
BenchFlat shelf on a slopeBeds with a view 65%
CliffRock faceBarrier and funnel. Plan around it
  • Saddle and bench lines are hunter observation from the deer research notes, 65% (see Maps 1).

• Convex: spacing goes wide to tight. The slope rolls away below you.
  • Concave: tight to wide. The slope flattens into a bowl you can see.
More: convex and concave in full
  • Convex slope: gentle on top, steepening below. On the map: wide spacing near the top, tight near the bottom 90%.
  • Concave slope: steep on top, flattening below. Tight spacing near the top, wide near the bottom 90%.
  • Uniform slope: even spacing all the way 90%.
  • Why it matters: from the top of a convex slope you cannot see the bottom. From the top of a concave slope you see the whole face (95%, line of sight geometry).
  • Hunter use: a convex roll is perfect stalking cover. You can walk down to the edge unseen, then peek over (Tip).

• Dead ground is any ground you cannot see from where you stand.
  • Rolls, folds and draws hide whole herds.
More: dead ground in full
  • Dead ground is a military and stalking term: ground hidden from view by the shape of the land (75%, common usage).
  • Below every convex roll there is dead ground. A deer feeding there cannot see you either (95%, geometry). Use it to close distance.
  • Before a stalk, find a fold that hides you from the animal all the way in (Tip).
  • The Hunt Map's What can I see tool shades hidden ground for you. See The Hunt Map like a pro.
  • Bare ground only: trees and brush hide even more (99%, the app says so).

• A horseshoe of lines open downhill: a bowl or basin.
  • Tip: wind swirls in bowls. Approach from the side.
More: bowls in full
  • A bowl is a rounded hollow with steep sides on three sides and an open bottom 90%.
  • High bowls hold snow, shade and often thick timber on the north side (Tip).
  • Air drains down and out of a bowl at night and swirls in it on light wind days (70%, slope wind behaviour; see Wind mastery).
  • The head of a draw is where a draw starts below a ridge. Animals often cross there because it is the easy way around the steep draw below (Tip, hunter observation).

• Where cliffs, water or steep ground squeeze travel into a narrow gap (Tip).
  • Look for tight lines beside a lake, river or second cliff.
More: pinch points in full
  • A pinch point (also funnel) is any spot where terrain or water squeezes animal travel into a narrow strip (Tip, hunter term).
  • On the map: two barriers close together. Cliff bands (lines touching), a lake or river, a steep draw, or a fence line from satellite view (Tip).
  • Pair it with the wind before you sit it (Tip). See Trails, funnels and pinch points.

• Number tops face uphill 98%.
  • Water runs in the bottom of the V.
More: three clues in full
  1. Index numbers are printed so the top of the number faces uphill (98%, NRCan Topographic maps tips, see Maps 1).
  2. Creeks and lakes are low. Water never runs along a ridge 98%.
  3. Closed rings with no ticks are tops 90%.
  4. In the Hunt Map: the elevation readout under the scale bar shows the height at the map centre. Pan up a line and watch it change (99%, app feature).

• A 15 m cliff can fit between two 20 m lines.
  • Check steep ground with the Slope tool and satellite view (Tip).
More: what hides between lines
  • Any feature smaller than the contour interval can vanish: rock bands, cut banks, small knobs, small depressions (95%, maths).
  • The Hunt Map draws 20 m lines (99%, app code). Its terrain data is about 24 m between points, so small cliffs, cut banks and rock bands do not show in the slope colours either (99%, the app says so).
  • Belt and braces: topo plus satellite plus your eyes (Tip).

Draw a profile in 4 steps1 of 4
  • The Hunt Map's Elevation profile does this for you 99%.
More: profiles in full
  • A profile shows the ups and downs along a line: how hard a climb is, and what you can see from where 95%.
  • Paper method: edge of a sheet of paper on the line, tick each crossing, write the height, transfer to a graph (90%, standard map reading).
  • App method: Tools, Elevation profile, Draw a line. The chart shows climb and drop along it (99%, app feature).
  • Use it before every dawn climb: where is the steep bit, where is the bench to rest and glass? (Tip)

More: the steepness maths
  • Slope percent = rise divided by run times 100. Degrees = the angle whose tangent is rise over run (98%, maths).
  • 20 m of rise over 50 m of ground is 40 percent, about 22 degrees 98%.
  • Most avalanches start on slopes of 30 to 45 degrees (95%, Avalanche Canada glossary, slope angle).
  • The Hunt Map's Slope steepness tool colours this for you: yellow 15 to 25°, orange 25 to 30°, red 30 to 45°, purple over 45° (99%, app code).
  • More on steepness and walking speed: Planning a route.

More: the hunter use table in full

  • South and west faces catch October sun: feed and warmth (85%, Maps 1, deer research notes).
  • Interior mule deer winter range sits on south and west aspects 85%. See Maps 1.
  • Check every spot on the map for land status and closures before you plan it: Maps 3: land status.

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Grandpa's rule (wisdom): The map shows the bones. Your eyes add the meat. Read both before you take a step.

Common mistakes
  • Reading one line, not the pattern.
  • Trusting the map to show every small cliff.
  • Planning a stalk without checking for dead ground.
More: the mistakes in full
  • Reading one line, not the pattern. A single bend means little; a stack of Vs means a draw.
  • Trusting the map to show every cliff. A cliff shorter than the interval can hide between two lines.
  • Planning a stalk across open ground when a fold 100 m over would have hidden you all the way in.
Do this in the field

Pick one draw near Heffley Creek on the Hunt Map. Draw its profile. Then walk it and stop at every bench you predicted. Score yourself.

  • 35 is 30: 20 m lines 35 m apart on the ground make a 30 degree slope, the avalanche line.
  • Hourglass, hold the pass: a saddle is the hourglass; animals cross there.

compass-mastery:
Why it matters

A compass never runs out of battery. With five skills (declination, map bearings, triangulation, handrails, aiming off) you can walk to a bench in fog and back to the truck in the dark.

  • 1 degree off misses by 17 m per km (98%, maths).
  • Forget declination and you miss by 268 m per km.
More: what this lesson adds
  • Compass parts, red in the shed and a simple bearing are in Maps 2: compass, GPS and apps. Do that lesson first.
  • This one adds: setting declination, bearings off the map, finding yourself (triangulation), and the orienteer's tricks: handrails, catching features, attack points, aiming off, pace counting and detours.
  • Error maths: miss distance = distance walked times the tangent of the error angle 98%. Per km: 1 degree is 17 m, 5 degrees 87 m, 10 degrees 176 m, 15 degrees 268 m, 30 degrees 577 m.

SkillOne line
DeclinationSet 15° east once a season
Map bearingRing lines to map north, ignore the needle
Orient the mapTurn the map so north lines run with the needle
TriangulateTwo bearings, two back lines, one cross
HandrailFollow a line feature
Catching featureBig line just past the target
Attack pointGo big, then go small
Aiming offMiss on purpose to one side
Pace countKnow your 100 m
More: the key points in full
  1. Near Heffley Creek and Mission the needle points about 15 degrees east of true north (95%, NOAA World Magnetic Model calculator, October 2026).
  2. An adjustable compass set to 15 east gives true bearings straight off the ring 90%.
  3. Map bearings: line the compass edge from you to the target, turn the ring until its north lines match the map's north lines, read the number. The needle plays no part (95%, orienteering coaching text).
  4. Two or more bearings to known landmarks, drawn back on the map, cross at your position. Best when they cross near 90 degrees (85%, resection method).
  5. Handrails, catching features, attack points and aiming off are core orienteering techniques (85%, Little Book of Orienteering Techniques; British Orienteering use since the 1970s).
  6. Pace counting is a backup for distance, never used alone (75%, same source).
  7. Keep steel and electronics away from the needle (Tip).

• Heffley Creek and Mission: about 15° east 95%.
  • South Okanagan: about 14.6° east 95%.
More: declination values and maths
  • NOAA (National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration) World Magnetic Model calculator, 15 October 2026 (95%, read directly):
    • Heffley Creek, 50.858 N 120.269 W: 15.17 degrees east, changing minus 0.13 degrees a year.
    • Mission, 49.13 N 122.31 W: 15.20 degrees east, minus 0.13 a year.
    • Osoyoos area, 49.03 N 119.47 W: 14.58 degrees east, minus 0.12 a year.
    • Model uncertainty: about 0.4 degrees 95%.
  • These match Maps 2's earlier figure of about 15.1 to 15.2 (80% there, now confirmed at 95%).
  • East declination means the needle points right of true north 98%.
  • No adjustable compass? Map to compass: subtract 15. Compass to map: add 15 (90%, NRCan rhyme "declination east, magnetic least", see Maps 2).
  • Paper NTS (National Topographic System) maps: the blue grid lines are UTM (Universal Transverse Mercator) grid north, not true north. Near Heffley Creek grid north is about 2.5 degrees east of true north, so the needle sits about 12.7 degrees east of the grid lines (85%, my calculation from the UTM zone 10 central meridian at 123 degrees west). The map margin prints this angle for its year. Use it when you take bearings off an NTS grid.
  • The Hunt Map and most phone maps draw true north up when the map is not rotated 90%.

Set an adjustable compass to 15° east1 of 3
  • Do it at home, once a season (Tip).
More: how adjusters differ
  • Models differ: some use a tiny screw and a key on the lanyard, some a click ring. Read your compass's own sheet (Tip).
  • Set east, not west. Setting 15 west puts you 30 degrees out, 577 m per km (98%, maths; see the mistakes in Maps 2).
  • Round to the nearest degree. A compass is good to about 2 degrees in the hand anyway (Tip).
  • Check it each spring and fall: declination drifts about 1 degree every 7 or 8 years here (95%, NOAA yearly change).

Map bearing in 4 steps1 of 4
  • Ignore the needle while on the map 95%.
More: map bearings in full
  1. Put the compass on the map with its long edge joining where you are to where you want to go. Travel arrow toward the target (95%, Little Book of Orienteering Techniques).
  2. Turn the ring until its north lines run parallel to the map's north lines, N toward the top of the map 95%.
  3. Read the number at the index line 95%.
  4. Declination set to 15 east? Walk it as it is. Not set? Subtract 15 for an east declination 90%.
  5. Hold the compass flat at your belly, turn your whole body until red is in the shed, pick a tree on the line, walk to it, repeat (95%; see Maps 2).
  6. On paper NTS maps use the grid lines and allow for the grid angle in the map margin 85%.
  7. On the phone: Tools, Measure in the Hunt Map shows the bearing of the last leg in degrees from true north (99%, app feature). Use it to check your paper work.

• Turn the map, not yourself, until north lines run with the needle.
  • Then the map looks like the land.
More: orienting in full
  • "Make sure you are holding the map the same way as the ground features." Turn the map so its north lines run the same way as the needle, red end to north (95%, Little Book of Orienteering Techniques).
  • You do not need to turn the compass ring to do it (95%, same source).
  • You can also orient by the land: line up a ridge or road on the map with the real one 95%.
  • Hold the map and compass in the same hand, thumb on where you are (Tip, orienteering habit "thumb the map").

Two bearings, one cross1 of 4
  • Pick landmarks about 90° apart 85%.
More: triangulation in full
  • Proper name: resection. With three lines people call it triangulation (85%, Wikipedia, Resection).
  • Steps: take magnetic bearings to two or more mapped features, correct for declination, convert each to a back bearing (add or subtract 180), draw each line from the feature, and the crossing is your position 85%.
  • Accuracy is best when the lines cross near 90 degrees and poor when they are nearly parallel 85%.
  • A third line usually makes a small triangle. You are most likely inside it (Tip). Big triangle? Retake the bearings.
  • Easier version: on a known handrail (a road, a creek), one bearing to a landmark is enough. Where the back bearing crosses the handrail is you (Tip).
  • Or just ask the phone. Then use this skill to check the phone (Tip).

• A line you can follow without the compass: creek, road, fence, ridge, timber edge 85%.
  • Worth a detour to use one 85%.
More: handrails in full
  • "Easy line features to lead you on your route." They can be tracks, vegetation edges, fences, streams or clearings, or point features joined into a line (85%, Little Book of Orienteering Techniques).
  • "It is worth going a bit out of your way to follow them" (85%, same).
  • Hunter handrails near Heffley Creek: forest roads, creeks, power lines, cutblock edges (Tip; check each on the map).
  • A ridge or a contour line is a handrail too. Following one contour keeps you flat and quiet (Tip).

• A big line just past the target.
  • Hit it and you know you went too far 85%.
More: catching features in full
  • A catching feature is an obvious feature beyond your target that tells you that you have overshot (85%, orienteering sources; Little Book: "features beyond the control to bounce back off").
  • Pick one before every leg: a road, a lake shore, the bottom of a valley (Tip).
  • For the walk out at dark: the main road is the catching feature for the whole hunt (Tip). See Night navigation.

• Aim well left of the truck. Hit the road. Turn right 85%.
More: aiming off in full
  • "Aiming deliberately to one side of a feature to know which way to turn when you hit it." (85%, Little Book of Orienteering Techniques)
  • Why: a straight bearing at a point on a line is always a little off, and you do not know which way. Aim off and you do (95%, logic).
  • How much: enough to beat your error. At 2 km with a 5 degree error you could be 175 m out, so aim off 200 to 300 m (Tip, from the error maths).
  • Classic hunter use: the truck on a road, a canoe on a lake shore, a camp on a creek (Tip).

• Walk fast to something big and easy, then take a careful short bearing.
More: attack points in full
  • An attack point is a large or obvious feature near the target. The safest is where two handrails cross (85%, Little Book of Orienteering Techniques).
  • Use it as a preview: go big, then go small (Tip).
  • Hunter use: a road bend, a lake corner or a big knob near the bench you want to glass from (Tip).

• Count each left foot on a measured 100 m. Count it again uphill and in brush.
  • A backup for distance, never on its own 75%.
More: pace counting in full
  • Count double paces, every time one foot lands (75%, Little Book of Orienteering Techniques).
  • Know your count for 100 m on a road, flat bush, rough ground and hills. Pace in 100 m blocks and adjust as you go 75%.
  • "Never use pacing in isolation, read the map too." 75%
  • Keep track with ranger beads or knots in a cord, one bead per 100 m (Tip).
  • Your phone's track distance is another check, if the GPS is good (Tip).

• Box around it: 90° off, count, walk your bearing past it, 90° back, same count.
  • Or bearing to a tree across it, walk around, carry on (Tip).
More: detours in full
  • Box method: turn 90 degrees, count paces, turn back to the bearing, pass the obstacle, turn 90 degrees the other way, walk the same count, then resume (Tip, standard land navigation habit).
  • Sight method: take a bearing to a tree on the far side of the swamp, walk around to the tree, then carry on from it (Tip).
  • Do not guess a new line around big obstacles. Small errors add up (Tip).

ErrorFix
Steel nearbyStep away from the rifle and the truck
Phone in the same handPocket it

Staring at the needlePick a tree, walk to it
Declination wrong wayCheck 15 east at home
More: errors in full
  • Steel, magnets, phones and vehicles bend the needle (80%, common compass guidance). Step a few metres from the truck and lean the rifle away (Tip).
  • A tilted compass drags the needle. Hold it level (Tip).
  • Sighting at a landmark and walking to it beats walking with your eyes on the needle (95%, see Maps 2).
  • Every leg, check against the land: does the ground look like the map? (Tip)

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Grandpa's rule (wisdom): Trust the compass over your gut. Your gut has never been to this draw.

Common mistakes
  • Aiming straight at the truck on a road. Aim off.
  • Using the needle while taking a bearing off the map.
  • Taking a bearing next to the truck or the rifle.
More: the mistakes in full
  • Aiming straight at the truck on a road, then reaching the road and not knowing which way to turn.
  • Using the needle while taking a bearing off the map. On the map, only the ring's lines and the map's north lines matter.
  • Taking a bearing beside the truck or with the rifle leaning on you. Steel moves the needle.

On the Heffley Creek block: pick a knob 1 km off. Take the map bearing, walk it, then triangulate from two landmarks. Your brother checks you with the phone.
