gps-phone-battery:
Why it matters

Your phone is your map, your track home and your SOS. Cold, a bright screen and a hunt for cell signal can kill it by noon. Set it up right and it lasts the day.

  • Screen and track recording eat the most (Tip).
  • Cold makes a full battery quit early 95%.
More: what this lesson adds

  • This lesson: why GPS is off sometimes, how cold kills batteries, a setup routine, a battery budget, backups, and what to do when the phone dies.
  • The drain order in the chart is a field rule of thumb (Tip). It changes by phone, app and weather.

More: the key points in full
  1. GPS needs no cell signal. Map tiles do, so save the area offline first (95%; Hunt Map Offline Maps, 99% app feature).
  2. Phone GPS is typically within about 4.9 m (16 ft) in open sky, worse near trees, buildings and bridges (90%, gps.gov).
  3. iPhones are designed for 0 to 35°C. In the cold the battery can drain fast and the phone can shut off; it recovers when warm (95%, Apple support).
  4. Lithium ion batteries should not be charged below freezing (75%, Battery University).
  5. The Hunt Map keeps the screen awake while recording a track, and iPhone web apps cannot record with the screen off (99%, read in the app).
  6. iPhone 14 or later can text emergency services by satellite in Canada with no cell or wifi, with a clear view of the sky (95%, Apple support).
  7. Carry a paper map and compass every time (Tip).

• Open sky: about 5 m 90%.
  • Thick timber, cliffs and canyons: worse. Wait for the dot to settle (Tip).

  • The Hunt Map shows the accuracy: the blue circle around your dot, and Go & Track says "GPS good (8 m)" or "GPS is weak" and skips weak points (99%, app).

  • In cold conditions battery life can drop for a while, the device may turn off, charging may stop, and it returns to normal when it warms up 95%.

More: charging in the cold in full
  • Battery University: lithium ion can be fast charged from 5 to 45°C; below 5°C reduce the current, and no charging at freezing temperatures, because metal lithium plates on the anode and permanently harms the battery (75%, BU 410).

  • Practical: warm the phone and bank against your body for 15 minutes, then charge (Tip).

route-planning:
Why it matters

Most bad days in the hills start with "it looked close on the map". Put numbers on the walk and set a turnaround time, and you stop being surprised by the dark.

  • 1 hour per 5 km, plus 1 hour per 600 m of climb 75%.
  • Off trail: about 4 km an hour 75%.
More: what this lesson adds
  • Map reading: Topo deep dive. Compass and legs: Compass mastery.
  • This lesson: how long a walk takes, how light works in late October, a turnaround time, breaking the route into legs, and the trip plan.
  • Naismith's rule, 1892: one hour per 5 km of distance, plus one hour per 600 m of ascent (75%, several secondary sources agree).
  • Aitken, 1977: 5 km an hour on paths and roads, 4 km an hour elsewhere 75%.

StepTool
DistanceHunt Map Line or route
ClimbElevation profile
TimeNaismith, plus extra for packs and dark

More: the key points in full
  1. Measure the real route, not a straight line (Tip).
  2. Climb costs more than distance: 600 m up is worth 5 km of flat walking in Naismith's rule 75%.
  3. Naismith is a minimum. One source suggests adding about 50 percent in practice; it ignores rest, weight, bad weather and rough footing (60%, search preview of a navigation FAQ).
  4. Legal hunting light ends 1 hour after sunset for big game and upland birds (99%, Rule Book). Hunting, including tracking with a firearm, stops then.
  5. A turnaround time is a clock time you decide at home and keep (Tip).
  6. Break the route into legs with checkpoints you will recognise (Tip, from orienteering).
  7. Leave a trip plan: route, start and return times, where the truck is, and when to call for help (75%, AdventureSmart guidance via search and rescue groups).

• Fastest on a gentle downhill. Flat is about 5 km an hour 75%.
  • Steep up or down is slow 75%.
More: Tobler's curve in full
  • Tobler's hiking function: speed in km an hour = 6 times e to the power of minus 3.5 times the absolute value of (slope plus 0.05), with slope as rise over run (75%, Wikipedia and research papers).
  • Peak 6 km an hour on a 5 percent downhill; 5 km an hour on the flat 75%.
  • Off path, Tobler multiplies by 0.6: about 3 km an hour on the flat 75%.
  • Researchers say the sharp peak is not realistic, but the shape is right: steep is slow both ways 70%.
  • Langmuir adds a descent rule: on slopes over about 12 degrees, add 10 minutes per 300 m of descent 70%.
  • Steep descents with a meat pack are slow and risky (Tip). See Packing out.

• 3 km off trail, 400 m up: about 1 h 25 min 75%.
  • With a pack in the dark, allow 2 h (Tip).
More: the example maths

  • Climb: 400 m at 600 m an hour = 40 minutes (Naismith, 75%).
  • Total: about 1 hour 25 minutes, a minimum.
  • Add about 50 percent for a heavy pack, brush, dark or rests: about 2 hours (60% plus Tip).
  • Walking out is mostly downhill, so faster in theory. With meat or in the dark it is often slower (Tip).
  • Still hunting is far slower: a few hundred metres an hour (Tip, see Moving quietly).

night-navigation:
Why it matters

In late October, legal light ends about an hour after sunset, when it is already dark. Almost every deer hunt ends with a walk out at night. Plan it like a second hunt.

  • Night routes are big and simple: handrail to catching feature (Tip).
  • Prepare in daylight: waypoint, back bearing, lamp.
More: what this lesson adds
  • Light times and turnaround: Planning a route. Compass tricks: Compass mastery. Phone and battery: GPS, phone and battery.
  • This lesson: night eyes, lights and the law, the before dark routine, walking out, finding north by the stars, and what to do when unsure.
  • Mid October at Heffley Creek: sunset about 18:08, legal light ends about 19:08, civil twilight ends about 18:41 (85%, my calculation).

More: the key points in full
  1. Big game and upland bird hunting ends 1 hour after sunset (99%, synopsis page 11, see the Rule Book).
  2. It is unlawful to hunt with the aid of a light 99%. A headlamp to walk in or out is not hunting with a light (90%, Rule Book, my reading).
  3. Following a wounded animal with a firearm after hours, or with a headlamp, is hunting outside hours and with a light (85%, Rule Book reading in Blood trailing).
  4. Night vision takes 20 to 40 minutes to build and a few seconds of bright light breaks it down (90%, US National Park Service).
  5. Dim deep red light preserves night vision (90%, same).
  6. In the dark, use handrails and catching features, not long straight bearings (Tip, from orienteering).
  7. Lost: stop, stay put, shelter, call (75%, AdventureSmart).
Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

• 20 to 40 minutes to see well in the dark 90%.
  • A few seconds of bright light resets it 90%.
More: night eyes in full
  • Rods in the eye use a pigment, rhodopsin, that builds up in low light. It starts after about 20 minutes and full benefit takes 20 to 40 minutes (90%, NPS, dark adaptation article).
  • "A few seconds of bright light" breaks it down and the rods stop working until it rebuilds 90%.
  • Older aviation guidance gives 20 to 30 minutes for useful dark adaptation 70%.
  • Tip: on a clear night with snow or a moon you may not need a lamp on an open road. In timber you will.

• White for walking hard ground. Red, low, for maps and near your brother (Tip).
  • Never shine a light in another hunter's eyes (Tip).
More: lights in full
  • Deep red light does not break down rhodopsin. Bright red still can, so dim red is best (90%, NPS).
  • Red light makes red ink on a map hard to see (65%, older aviation handbook).
  • Headlamp habits (Tip): beam on the trail at your feet, not at the horizon; turn your head, not your whole body; warn before you switch to bright.
  • Animals react to a moving light as pure motion (Tip). See Deer senses and mind.
  • Two lights each, plus spare lithium cells (Tip). Energizer lists its lithium AA from minus 40 to 60°C 75%.

• Walking in before light? Point the lamp at your boots (Tip).
  • Using a light to find or hold game is illegal 99%.
More: lights and the law

  • Rule Book: Legal methods and Unlawful acts.

field-weather:
Why it matters

The forecast is for the valley. You are on the ridge. Clouds, pressure and wind give you hours of warning about snow, rain, thunder and wind shifts, so you change the plan before the weather changes it for you.

  • High wisps, mid grey sheets, low puffs: three levels 95%.
  • Watch which way they change: lowering and thickening means wet weather coming 70%.
More: what this lesson adds
  • How weather moves deer (snow, fronts, moon) is in Weather, moon and what moves game. This lesson is about reading the sky and air for your own plan and safety.
  • Ten basic cloud types by level (95%, NOAA JetStream, World Meteorological Organization classes):
    • High: cirrus, cirrocumulus, cirrostratus.
    • Mid: altocumulus, altostratus, nimbostratus.
    • Low: stratocumulus, stratus, cumulus, cumulonimbus.
  • Wind is the next lesson: Wind mastery.

More: the key points in full
  1. Ten cloud types in three levels (95%, NOAA).
  2. Warm front sequence: cirrus, cirrostratus (halo), altostratus, nimbostratus (70%, Met Office and textbook sources agree on order, not timing).
  3. Cumulonimbus is "the thunderstorm cloud", tall with an anvil shaped top (95%, NOAA). It can bring hail 95%.
  4. Behind a cold front winds shift from south to west or northwest, the dewpoint drops and pressure rises (70%, NWS text via secondary source).
  5. With your back to the wind, low pressure is on your left in the northern hemisphere (75%, Buys Ballot's law, Wikipedia).
  6. Cold air drains down slopes at night and pools in valleys (75%, USDA Forest Service Fire Weather handbook via Forest Encyclopedia).
  7. Thunder heard? Go to a hard topped vehicle and wait 30 minutes after the last thunder (85%, US National Weather Service).

Four skies before the rain1 of 4
  • The sky lowers and thickens over hours 70%.
More: warm fronts in full
  • Order: cirrus, cirrostratus, altostratus, nimbostratus 70%.
  • The Met Office says cirrostratus can produce rings, spots or arcs of light around the sun or moon, and that one type means an incoming warm front will bring persistent rain within a day (75%, Met Office cirrostratus page, search preview).
  • Timing varies: sources give 12 to 24 hours from halo to rain, some less 60%. Treat it as "within about a day".
  • Ahead of a warm front pressure falls steadily and the rain is widespread and steady (70%, secondary source).
  • Hunter use (Tip): halo at evening glassing means plan B for tomorrow, rain gear in the pack, meat care plan for wet weather.
• Warm air rides up over cold air, so clouds come first, rain last 70%.

• Tall clouds, gusts, a short burst of rain or snow 70%.
  • After: wind W or NW, colder, clearing, pressure rising 70%.
More: cold fronts in full
  • Before: winds often from the south, warm and humid 70%.
  • At the front: towering clouds, gusty winds, heavy showers or snow squalls 70%.
  • After: wind shifts west or northwest, temperature and dewpoint drop, pressure rises, skies clear (70%, NWS text via secondary source).
  • In the mountains, terrain channels wind and can hide the classic wind shift (75%, Fire Weather handbook: "the effect of the mountains on the windflow usually overshadows this").
  • Hunter use (Tip): the clear, cold morning after a cold front is a classic glassing morning. Snow after it brings fresh tracks; see Snow tracking.

• Flat bottomed puffs that stay small: fair weather 70%.
  • Puffs that tower and spread an anvil: thunder, hail, gusts 95%.
More: thunder in full
  • Cumulonimbus: heavy, dense, shaped like a mountain or huge tower, with an anvil or plume top and a dark base; can bring hail (95%, NOAA).
  • "When thunder roars, go indoors." Shelter in a substantial building or a hard topped vehicle and stay until 30 minutes after the last thunder (85%, US National Weather Service).
  • Lightning can strike well away from the rain (70%, US Army safety document).
  • Thunderstorms are less common in late October than in summer (Tip). Still: get off ridges and away from lone trees when you hear thunder.

• Falling: weather coming. Rising: clearing, often colder 75%.

  • Phone or watch barometer: sitting still, if your altitude reading climbs, the pressure is falling (85%, physics: about 8 m of altitude per hPa near sea level).
  • Pressure trends are general rules. Mountains and local winds can fool them (Tip).
  • Do deer care about pressure? The evidence is weak and mixed (65 to 80%). See Weather, moon and what moves game.

• Back to the wind: low pressure on your left 75%.
  • The low is where the bad weather lives.
More: Buys Ballot's law in full
  • In the northern hemisphere, with your back to the wind, low pressure is to the left and high pressure to the right (75%, Wikipedia, Buys Ballot's law, 1857).
  • Near the ground and in mountains it is approximate 75%. Use the upper clouds' direction for a better read (Tip).
  • Use (Tip): if the low is to your west, weather is usually on its way, since systems here mostly move from the Pacific eastward. VERIFY with the forecast.

• Clear calm nights: cold air drains down into valleys 75%.
  • Morning fog or frost below, milder and clear above (Tip).
More: inversions in full
  • Downslope flow starts first along the valley floor in the evening, deepens through the night and becomes the down valley wind; as cold air pools, pressure rises in the valley (75%, Fire Weather handbook via Forest Encyclopedia).
  • Down valley flow lasts through the night and weakens after sunrise 75%.
  • Kamloops sits in a deep valley. Fall mornings often have valley fog or haze (Tip).
  • Hunter use (Tip): climb above the fog to glass; the sun hits upper slopes first and deer move to it on cold mornings. See Sun and shade in the Hunt Map.

• About 6.5°C colder per 1,000 m up in standard air 85%.
  • Rain at the truck can be snow on the ridge 85%.

  • Example: 8°C at a 400 m valley floor is about 1.5°C on a 1,400 m ridge (85%, maths).
  • Wind makes it feel colder still. See hypothermia in Bush safety.
  • Pack for the top of the hunt, not the truck (Tip).

• Look up every hour. Write it in your journal (Tip).

  • Ignoring a halo and a falling barometer the night before.

wind-mastery:
Why it matters

Wind is the one thing a deer trusts more than its eyes. Learn how terrain bends it and how the sun flips it hour by hour, and you can predict where your scent goes before you take a step.

  • Slope winds flip almost right at sunrise and sunset 75%.
  • Valley winds lag by hours 75%.
More: what this lesson adds
  • The basics (keep the deer upwind, morning up, evening down, puffer and milkweed) are in Wind and thermals. Do that first.
  • This lesson adds the timing by slope and by hour, the speeds, what ridges, saddles, draws, timber and junctions do to the wind, how to read wind strength on the land, and a five step read before every move.
  • Main source: the USDA Forest Service Fire Weather handbook (Schroeder and Buck, 1970), written for firefighters who must predict exactly this (75%, via Forest Encyclopedia).
  • Mountain science review: the switch from night downslope to day upslope happens "almost immediately after sunrise", and the reverse after sunset; valley winds switch "several hours" later (75%, boundary layer research review, search preview).

FactHunting meaning (Tip)

More: the key points in full
  1. "Upslope winds begin as a gentle upflow soon after the sun strikes the slope." East facing slopes start first (75%, Fire Weather handbook).
  2. Up valley flow waits until the whole valley air warms, usually "middle or late forenoon", peaks early afternoon and runs into the evening 75%.
  3. On slopes going into shade: the upslope wind dies, a brief calm, then gentle downslope flow begins 75%.
  4. Down valley flow lasts through the night and fades after sunrise 75%.
  5. On dense forested slopes, upslope flow may rise above the treetops while a shallow downslope flow persists under the canopy 75%.
  6. Eddies "may form at canyon bends and at tributary junctions"; along upper ridges wind speed and direction may change quickly 75%.
  7. On the lee side of a peak a turbulent reversal or eddies are possible (70%, NWCG, search preview).
  8. Beaufort speeds are at 10 m; at 2 m wind may be only 50 to 70% of them (90%, Royal Meteorological Society).

• East faces first. South strongest near midday. West mid afternoon 75%.
  • North faces stay weakest, and sink first in the evening 75%.
More: timing by aspect in full
  • South slopes peak "soon after midday", west slopes by about mid afternoon (75%, Fire Weather handbook).
  • South and southwest slopes heat most and have the strongest upslope winds, several times stronger than on north slopes 75%.
  • Bare and grassy slopes heat faster than brush or tree covered slopes, so upslope winds are weaker under vegetation 75%.
  • Where slopes of different aspects drain into one basin, the shaded slopes start downslope first, and late afternoon up valley winds can turn up to 180 degrees after sunset 75%.
  • Find aspect fast with the Hunt Map's Slope direction tool, and the sun's position with Sun and shade 99%. See The Hunt Map like a pro.

• Clear calm day: slopes up from soon after sun to shade 75%.
  • Switch times are swirl times. Be set up before them (Tip).

  • Do not sit just behind the crest (Tip).
More: ridges in full

  • Some acceleration of the general wind is likely over the tops and flanks of isolated peaks (70%, NWCG).
  • On the lee side, a turbulent reversal or eddies are possible 70%.
  • Along upper ridges "wind speed and direction may change quickly" 75%.
  • Tip: glass from the windward side or well down the lee side, not in the tumble just behind the crest.

• Wind speeds up through low gaps (Tip).
  • Your scent pours through the saddle with it.
More: saddles and draws in full
  • Air flowing over a ridge is channelled through low gaps and along valleys (75%, Fire Weather handbook: "The windflow is channeled").
  • Saddles are where animals cross ridges (65%, Maps 1). If you sit a saddle, sit off to the downwind side, not in the gap (Tip).
  • Draws act like gutters for cool evening air (75%; Wind and thermals).

• Sun on the canopy: air rises above the trees.
  • Shade on the floor: a thin cool layer still sinks 75%.

  • "On dense forested slopes, upslope flow may rise above the treetops while a shallow downslope flow persists at the surface under the canopy shade." (75%, Fire Weather handbook)
  • "A dense understory blocks nighttime downslope flow, which is diverted or confined to openings such as streams and roads." 75%
  • Hunter meaning (Tip): at 10 am in thick north timber your scent may still creep downhill along the floor, and at night cold air runs down creeks and roads like water.
  • Puffer at your feet as well as at chest height (Tip).

• Eddies form at canyon bends and side draw junctions 75%.
  • A junction is a swirl trap. Sit above or away from it (Tip).
More: eddies in full
  • Strong up valley and up canyon winds can be turbulent because the air is unstable and the terrain rough; eddies may form at canyon bends and tributary junctions (75%, Fire Weather handbook).
  • Bowls swirl too. See Topo deep dive.
  • Cold air pools where draws meet the valley floor at night 75%. See Reading weather in the field.

  1. Forecast wind: Hunt Map, Weather and wind: direction, speed, gusts 99%.
  2. Terrain: what will the ridge, saddle, draw or timber do to it? (this lesson)

  4. Real check: puffer bottle or milkweed, every few minutes and at every new feature (Wind and thermals).
  5. Decide: steady and right, commit. Swirling or wrong, go to plan B. Never force a bad wind (Tip).
  6. Map tool: Scent cone from my location shows where forecast wind takes your scent; the app reminds you the real cone is wider in timber and around ridges 99%.

stay-unseen:
Why it matters

A deer that sees you first is gone. Expensive camo is not the answer: outline, flash, shadow, skyline and above all movement give you away. Fix those and plain wool works.

  • Six ways you get seen. Movement is number one (Tip).
  • Pattern and stillness beat colour 75%.
More: what this lesson adds
  • How deer see and why: Deer senses and mind. How to move: Moving quietly and Stalking footwork.
  • The six words come from military concealment teaching: the Australian Army lists shape, shine, shadow and silhouette among its "Seven S's of Tactical Concealment"; older guides add spacing and movement (70%, Australian Army CoVE and older field guides, search preview). Using them for hunting is Tip.
  • Scent and sound are the other two ways: see Wind mastery and Moving quietly.

FixHow (Tip)
ShapeBrush in front, tree behind, sit low
ShineMask or paint, matte gear, glasses in shade
ShadowSit in shade, watch where yours falls
SilhouetteNever on a skyline
SpacingTwo hunters move one at a time
MovementMove when heads are down, freeze when up
ColourAvoid blue; orange looks dull to deer 75%
More: the key points in full
  1. Deer have two cone types, not three, and lack the long wavelength "red" cone: likely red green colour blind like some people (75%, National Deer Association on the University of Georgia study, Jacobs and others).
  2. They likely tell blue from red, but not green from red or orange from red 75%. Clothing in green, red or orange is equal to them; blue is a disadvantage 75%.
  3. "The actual color of the fabric is relatively unimportant as long as the pattern blends with your surroundings." (75%, NDA)
  4. Scent and movement matter far more than clothing colour or UV brighteners (75%, NDA).
  5. Deer lack the UV filter in the human eye and see UV better than we do, but poorer fine detail (75%, NDA). A 2014 behaviour study found some UV sensitivity (70%, Wildlife Society Bulletin, search preview).
  6. More rods than people: better night vision, poorer daytime colour vision (75%, NDA).

The six, one at a time1 of 6
  • Run through the six every time you sit (Tip).
More: the six in full
  • Shape: a person's outline, head and shoulders above a straight body, is what animals learn to fear (Tip). Brush in front, a tree behind, sit or kneel to lose the vertical line (Tip).
  • Shine: skin, glasses, rifle bluing, scope lenses and phone screens flash in low sun (Tip). Face mask or paint, gloves, matte finishes, a scope cover, glasses in the shade of a brim (Tip). Binocular glare: see Glassing.
  • Shadow: your shadow moves when you move and stretches long at dawn and dusk (Tip). Sit inside shade, not at its edge (Tip).
  • Silhouette: a figure on a ridge against the sky is visible a long way (Tip). Cross ridges at a low spot, crawl the last metres, glass from below the crest (Tip).
  • Spacing: even, regular shapes look man made; nature is random (70%, military concealment teaching). Two hunters side by side are two shapes; move one at a time (Tip).
  • Movement: deer have "an amazing ability to detect movement" (75%, NDA, hunter consensus). Move when the head is down or behind cover; freeze when it looks (Tip; see Moving quietly).

• Blue pops. Orange, red and green look like dull browns and greys 75%.
  • The drawing is an illustration, not a measurement (Tip).
More: colour in full
  • Two cone pigments: short wavelength sensitivity around 450 to 460 nm (blue) and middle wavelength around 537 nm in white tailed deer (75%, Jacobs and others, via search previews).
  • Missing the long wavelength cone: red and orange fall in a range deer barely separate from green and brown 75%.
  • Blue jeans and blue jackets are a bad idea (75%, NDA: "disadvantaged in blue").
  • Mule deer were not in these studies. Assumption: similar, as both are deer (Tip).
  • Deeper detail: Deer senses and mind.

• Orange looks dull to a deer but bright to other hunters 75%.
  • Wear it walking in and out, and when others hunt nearby (Tip).
More: blaze orange in full
  • BC rule: the Hunt Mentor Rule Book lists no blaze orange clothing rule for BC hunters (85%, my reading). VERIFY in the synopsis before relying on it.
  • Other places do require it (New Brunswick, Washington State, Missouri), so check the rules when you hunt outside BC (85%, those regulations, search preview). See the trip lessons.
  • Deer see orange as dull, close to brown or grey; motion and outline give you away, not the colour (75%, see Deer senses and mind).
  • Tip: an orange toque and vest for walking, packed away when you sit in a safe spot with no other hunters around. Wrap a carried deer or turkey in orange.
  • Firearm safety with your brother: Firearm safety.

• Brim low, glasses shaded, turn your head slowly (Tip).
More: shine fixes
  • Face: mask, net or paint (Tip).
  • Hands: thin gloves, they move the most (Tip).
  • Rifle and scope: matte finish or a cover, lens caps on while walking (Tip).
  • Phone: screen off and away when deer are close; a lit screen in shade is a flash (Tip).
  • Glass: shade the objective lenses of binoculars with your hand or a hood in low sun (Tip). See Glassing.

• Back against a tree, rock or bush wider than you (Tip).
  • A little brush in front breaks your middle (Tip).
More: seats in full
  • The backdrop hides your outline; the brush in front hides your hands moving (Tip).
  • Shade over the seat hides shine and your shadow (Tip).
  • Leave a clear shooting lane through the brush in front. Clear it in the off season or quietly, not on the morning (Tip).
  • Sit, do not stand. A seated hunter is a smaller, wider, less human shape (Tip).
  • Check the wind before you choose a seat: Wind mastery.

Check your hunting clothes1 of 3
  • Evidence is mixed. It costs little to check (Tip).
More: UV in full
  • Deer lack the UV filter in the human lens and likely see UV better than people (75%, NDA). The 1990s retina work found little UV response; a 2014 behaviour study with 7 deer found some sensitivity (70%, search previews).
  • No direct test found that UV brightened clothing spooks deer (60%: not a fact). Treat it as cheap insurance, labelled Tip.
  • Many household detergents add optical brighteners (Tip). Read the label or test with the light.

• One moves, one watches. Then swap (Tip).
  • Hand signals, not voices (Tip).

  • Moving together doubles the shapes and the noise (Tip).
  • The watcher keeps the animal in view and signals when its head goes up (Tip).
  • Agree signals at the truck: stop, down, come, deer, buck, shoot lane clear (Tip).
  • Safety first: zones of fire and where each of you is at all times. See Firearm safety.

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Grandpa's rule (wisdom): Camo hides you when you are still. Nothing hides you when you move at the wrong time.

Common mistakes

  • Bare face and hands in low sun.
  • Fidgeting while a deer is looking.

  • Bare face, bright hands and glasses catching the low October sun.

Have your brother sit in three spots: open, against a tree, against a tree in shade with brush in front. Walk away 100 m and glass each one. Then swap. Score which you saw first.

stalking-footwork:
Why it matters

Your feet are the loudest thing you own. The last 100 m of a stalk is won or lost one step at a time, and quiet feet are a skill you can train on the living room floor.

The fox walk in 4 moves1 of 4
  • Weight stays back until the new foot is quiet 65%.
More: what this lesson adds
  • Pace, the heel to toe step, cover and what deer hear: Moving quietly. Do that first.
  • This lesson adds the fox walk, when to use which step, balance, rhythm, using wind noise, crawls, ground types, and a drill plan to practise at home before the season.
  • The fox walk: set the outside of the ball of the foot down lightly, roll onto the whole foot with partial weight, then shift full weight; it lets you feel the ground and slowly compress leaves and sticks (65%, Princeton outdoor action nature observation guide, search preview).
  • Camp Kawartha's stalking guide: carry your weight on the back leg, test with the front toes for crunchy leaves or sticks, roll along the outside of your foot onto the heel once the ground is clear (65%, search preview).

SkillOne line
Weight backYou can freeze mid step
Feel firstThe foot finds the stick before your weight does
Two stepsHeel first for pace, edge first for the stalk
Short stridesBalance and less noise
Broken rhythmNo steady crunch, crunch
Wind coverMove in gusts
CrawlsKneel, hands and knees, belly
DrillsTen minutes a day before the season
More: the key points in full
  1. Keep your weight on the back foot until the front foot is set and quiet (65%, stalking guides).
  2. Feel through the boot: thin, flexible soles feel sticks better than stiff mountain boots (Tip).
  3. Heel first works at normal still hunting pace on quiet ground (65%, see Moving quietly); outside edge first is quieter but very slow (60%, hunter forum, search preview).
  4. "A good stalker will take a long time to silently move 50 metres." (65%, Camp Kawartha)
  5. A steady crunch, crunch rhythm sounds like a person; a deer's steps come in uneven bursts (Tip).
  6. Deer hear about 0.25 to 30 kHz with best hearing at 4 to 8 kHz, above much of what we hear well (75%, see Moving quietly).
  7. Every drill here is hunter or tracker practice, labelled Tip.

• Heel first: quiet trails, still hunting pace (Tip).
  • Edge first: crunchy ground and the last 100 m of a stalk (Tip).
More: choosing a step
  • Heel first, rolling to the ball and testing before full weight, is the step in Moving quietly 65%.
  • Outside edge of the ball first, rolling in, then the heel, lets the foot find sticks before the heel crushes them (65%, Princeton and Camp Kawartha).
  • Edge first is "quieter but really slow travelling" (60%, BC hunting forum, search preview).
  • Mix them: heel first to cover ground between glassing stops, edge first once you are inside 200 m (Tip).

• Weight back means you can stop on one leg when a head comes up (Tip).
  • Train it with the balance drill below.
More: balance in full
  • Short strides keep your centre over the back foot (Tip).
  • Knees soft, not locked (Tip).
  • Hands quiet. Rifle on the sling or held across the body so it does not swing into brush (Tip). Safety first: muzzle control at all times, see Firearm safety.

• Two steps, a long look, two steps. Never a steady beat (Tip).
More: rhythm in full
  • People walk at a steady beat. Deer step, stop, feed, step again (Tip, hunter observation).
  • Two or three steps, then stand and look for 20 seconds or more (Tip, see Moving quietly).
  • If you snap a stick, stop. Wait a few minutes. A deer may accept one crack from another animal, not a steady series (Tip).

• Wind noise in the trees covers footsteps (Tip).
  • Calm air: slow to almost nothing (Tip).
More: wind and noise in full
  • Strong wind: you cannot hear well either, and scent spreads unpredictably (Tip, see Weather, moon and what moves game).
  • Creek noise, rain on leaves and gusts all cover your steps (Tip).
  • Wind direction still rules: see Wind mastery.

  • Pine cones and dry twigs hide under needles. Feel first (Tip).

Three ways to get low1 of 3
  • Knee pads or thick pants save your knees on rock (Tip).

  • Keep the muzzle out of the dirt and pointed safely. Check the barrel for snow and mud after any crawl (Tip; see Firearm safety).
  • Move the rifle first, then your body, so it never swings (Tip).
  • Peek around a rock or tree, not over it: Moving quietly.

  • Fast where it cannot see you, slow where it can (Tip).
More: the stalk in full
  • Plan the approach from where you glassed: landmarks, dead ground and the wind (Tip). See dead ground in Topo deep dive and What can I see in The Hunt Map like a pro.
  • Stalking is "a chess game", alternating fast and slow movement (65%, Princeton guide).

Five drills, ten minutes a day1 of 5
  • Start three weeks before the season (Tip).
More: drills in full
  • Balance: 30 seconds each leg, then with eyes on a far point, then in hunting boots (Tip).
  • Cereal box: spread crushed cereal on a sheet. Cross it in socks, then boots, with no crunch (Tip).
  • Leaf strip: your brother sits with eyes closed at the end of a 10 m strip of dry leaves and points at every noise (Tip).
  • Freeze game: while you fox walk, your partner calls freeze at random. Hold 60 seconds without a wobble (Tip).
  • Timed stalk: still hunt 100 m of timber in 30 minutes or more. Moving quietly sets 200 m in 30 minutes for a first drill; this one is slower (Tip).
  • Rifle drill: kneel, sit and rise again with an unloaded rifle, no clink, muzzle safe (Tip).

hunt-fitness:
Why it matters

Tired legs make bad decisions: a rushed stalk, a shaky shot, a fall on the way down. Fitness is a safety skill.

  • Hills, a pack, long days, and meat out at the end.
  • This lesson: a safe 12 week plan you can start today (Tip).
More: what this lesson covers
  • What a hunt day asks of your body: climbing, carrying, long hours, moving meat, cold and wet, and steep downhill (Tip, from the packing and meat lessons in this app).
  • October days near Heffley Creek run from about 11 h 43 min of daylight on 1 October to about 9 h 51 min on 31 October (90%, NOAA solar equations, see Weather, daylight and season timing).
  • A hunt day can fill all of that light, plus the walk in and out in the dark (Tip).
  • A whole gutted deer is about 50 kg to drag; boneless meat from one deer is about 25 kg (Tip, from Packing out).
  • The plan here is a Hunt Mentor plan built on the national movement guidelines and on what mountain hunting coaches teach. It is opinion, labelled Tip, not a medical prescription.
  • Related: Packs and carrying loads, Food and water for long hunt days.

• Train three engines: heart, legs, carry (Tip).
  • Base first, pack later. Every fourth week easier (Tip).
  • Moderate pace: you can talk but not sing 70%.
More: the key points in full
  • Canadian adults: at least 150 minutes a week of moderate to vigorous aerobic activity, and muscle strengthening of the major muscle groups at least twice a week (95%, Canadian 24 Hour Movement Guidelines, CSEP (Canadian Society for Exercise Physiology), read directly).
  • The same guidelines: 7 to 9 hours of good quality sleep with consistent bed and wake times 95%.
  • Talk test: moderate means you can talk but not sing; vigorous means only a few words before a breath (70%, CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) talk test via news report).
  • Mountain hunting coaches build the aerobic base first and save weighted pack carries for the last 8 weeks of a long plan (65%, Uphill Athlete coach statements on their forum).
  • They also use every fourth week as a lighter recovery week (65%, TrainingPeaks plan summary by Uphill Athlete coaches).
  • The famous "10% a week" rule has weak research support. Small steady steps still make sense (65%, secondary summaries of running studies). Tip: when in doubt, add less.
  • Strength twice a week protects knees and back on steep ground and under a pack (Tip).
  • Break in boots and socks during training, not on the hunt (Tip).

• Today is 11 October. Your first hunts are mid to late October.
  • 12 weeks from today ends about 3 January.
  • So: start now, gain safely, and peak for the late season and next year (Tip).
More: what to do this week and next
  • You cannot build 12 weeks of fitness in 10 days. Trying to cram it is how people get hurt (Tip).
  • This week (Tip):
    • Walk 30 to 45 minutes most days, with some hills or stairs.
    • Wear your hunting boots and socks on every walk.
    • Do one short strength session (screen "Strength moves").
    • Carry your real day pack on two of the walks, not heavier.
    • Sleep 7 to 9 hours (95%, CSEP).
  • On the hunt: pace yourself, rest before steep climbs, and pass on any shot you reach out of breath (Tip).
  • Deer buck seasons in Region 3 close on 10 December (99%, from The BC hunter's year). Weeks 1 to 8 of this plan land before that date.
  • Next season: start the 12 weeks in early July and finish before the September and October openers (Tip).

More: who should check first
  • The Canadian movement guidelines say adults who are pregnant or who have a disability or medical condition should consider the Get Active Questionnaire, condition specific advice, or a health professional (95%, CSEP, read directly).
  • Chest pain, dizzy spells or fainting with effort are reasons to stop and get checked before training (Tip, standard first aid caution).
  • Sore is normal. Sharp pain, joint pain that gets worse, or pain that changes how you walk is not. Stop and get it looked at (Tip).
  • Training alone on trails: leave a like you would on a hunt (75%, AdventureSmart, see Bush safety).

More: the talk test in full

  • Vigorous intensity: you cannot say more than a few words without pausing for a breath 70%.
  • Uphill hiking is listed as a vigorous example 70%.
  • Why moderate for most sessions: you can do more of it, recover faster, and it builds the base that lets you climb all day (65%, mountain hunting coaches; Tip).
  • Field use: if you cannot talk on a climb, slow down. You will arrive with steadier hands (Tip).

  • Pack weight starts in week 5 and grows in small steps (Tip).
  • Weeks 4, 8 and 12 are easier on purpose (Tip).

More: what METs mean and your calories
  • A MET (Metabolic Equivalent of Task) compares an activity with sitting still, which is 1 MET (90%, Compendium of Physical Activities).
  • Compendium values, read directly: hunting from a stand with limited walking 2.5; hunting, general 5.0; hunting deer, elk, large game 6.0; hunting, hiking with hunting gear 9.5; hunting large game, dragging a carcass 9.8; hunting pheasants or grouse 6.0 (95%, 2024 Adult Compendium, codes 04085, 04100, 04080, 04125, 04081, 04110).
  • Rough calories: METs x body weight in kg x hours (85%, standard way MET tables are used).
  • Example, 80 kg (Assumption): 6 hours hiking with gear at 9.5 METs = about 4,560 kcal for those 6 hours (Tip, estimate).
  • Food plan: Food and water for long hunt days.

• Sleep 7 to 9 hours 95%.
  • Easy week every fourth week (Tip).
More: recovery in full
  • 7 to 9 hours of good quality sleep, consistent bed and wake times (95%, CSEP).
  • Fitness grows during rest, not during the workout (Tip).
  • Eat a real meal with protein after long sessions (Tip).
  • Sick or injured: drop back a week, do not push through (Tip).
  • Hunt week: no hard training in the 3 days before (Tip).

More: why these tests

  • Getting up from the ground with a pack is the lift you will do 20 times a day (Tip).
  • A steady hold after a climb is what fair, clean shots need. The synopsis ethics code says do not shoot unless you have a clear shot of a vital part (99%, synopsis page 77).
  • If a test fails: repeat weeks 9 and 10 and try again (Tip).

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Grandpa's rule (wisdom): The mountain does not care how strong you were in June. Train for the hill you will climb, with the pack you will carry.

Common mistakes

  • Only flat ground. Hunting is hills.
  • New boots on opening day.
More: the mistakes in full

  • Only flat ground. Train on hills, stairs or step ups every week (Tip).
  • New boots on day one. Break them in over weeks (Tip).
  • Bonus mistake: training alone with no trip plan on remote trails (Tip, see Bush safety).

On your next scouting trip, carry your full hunting pack for 2 hours on the real hills. Note where you got tired and how long the climbs took. Plan your hunt day around those times.

packs-carrying:
Why it matters

A pack that fits puts the weight on your hips, not your shoulders. A bad lift from the ground can end a season. Both are skills you can learn in an evening.

  • Day pack for short hunts, frame pack for long days and meat (Tip).
  • Fit, pack, lift: three skills, this lesson.
More: what this lesson covers
  • Choosing the right pack for the job (Tip).
  • Measuring your torso and adjusting the fit (70%, REI (Recreational Equipment Inc.) fit guide via search).
  • Packing order: what goes low, close, high (65%, outdoor guides).
  • How heavy is too heavy (70%, REI guideline; Tip for meat loads).
  • Safe lifting from the ground (85%, BC Forest Safety Council).
  • What goes in the pack: Day pack and car kit. Moving meat: Packing out. Getting strong enough: Fitness for hunting.

• Most of the weight rides on your hip bones 70%.
  • Heavy close to your spine, light low, quick items on top 65%.
  • Lift with your legs, load close, never twist 85%.
More: the key points in full
  • Torso length, not your height, decides pack size (70%, REI).
  • Hip belt centred on the top of your hip bones (the iliac crest) (70%, REI, via search summary).
  • "You'll carry most of your pack weight on your hips" (70%, REI sizing guide, search preview).
  • Heaviest items in the middle of the pack, close to your spine (65%, several outdoor guides agree).
  • A loaded backpacking pack should weigh no more than about 20% of body weight, a day pack about 10% (70%, REI pack fit specialist).
  • Meat loads: 20 to 30 kg per trip is sustainable for a fit adult on rough ground (Tip, from Packing out).
  • Safe lifting: firm footing, good grip, bend knees, tighten your core, keep the load close, lift with the legs, back upright, turn with your feet (85%, BC Forest Safety Council crew talk citing WorkSafeBC).

More: choosing in more detail
  • Day pack: carries the 10 essentials, a layer, water, game bags and rope (75% for the essentials list, AdventureSmart; see Day pack and car kit).
  • Frame pack: a stiff frame and a padded hip belt let the hips take the load. Built for heavy, awkward loads like meat (Tip).
  • Load shelf: some frame packs let meat ride between the frame and the bag, against your back. Meat stays out of the bag and close to your spine (Tip).
  • Try packs on in a store with weight in them. Every brand fits differently (70%, REI: torso ranges vary between brands).
  • Price tiers: VERIFY in store. Prices change; check the day you buy.

Torso length in 3 steps1 of 3
  • You need a friend and a soft tape (Tip).
  • Torso length picks the size, not your height 70%.
More: measuring in full
  1. Tilt your head forward. Find the bony bump where your neck meets your shoulders (the C7 vertebra, "C" for cervical, the neck bones). That is the top of your torso length (70%, REI, via search summary).
  2. Put your hands on top of your hip bones (the iliac crest), thumbs pointing to your spine. A line between your thumbs is the bottom 70%.
  3. A friend measures along your spine from the bump to the thumb line, while you stand up straight 70%.
  4. Hip size: wrap the tape around the top of your hip bones. That is a little higher than your belt line (70%, REI).
  5. Between sizes? Try both on with weight in them (70%, REI).

Adjust a loaded pack1 of 5
  • Always hips first, sternum last (Tip).
  • Re adjust when the load changes, like after meat goes in (Tip).
More: fit checks
  • Gap between the shoulder straps and the top of your shoulders: torso setting too long (65%, outdoor fit guide).
  • All the weight on your shoulders: torso setting too short or hip belt too low 65%.
  • The middle of the hip belt should sit right on top of your hip bones 65%.
  • Load lifters pull the top of the load toward you. Snug, not cranked (Tip).
  • Sternum strap at a comfortable height across your chest so you breathe freely (Tip).
  • On a long climb, loosen the shoulder straps a little and let the hips work. On a side hill, snug everything (Tip).

• Light and bulky at the bottom 65%.
  • Heavy in the core, against your spine 65%.
  • Quick things on top and in the lid 65%.
More: why this order
  • Heavy items close to your back and centred keep the load from pulling you backward (65%, Andrew Skurka and other guides).
  • Heavy items too low make a pack feel saggy 65%.
  • Off trail, some guides put heavy items a little lower for balance. On steep hunting ground, centred and close is a safe default (Tip).
  • Things you need fast (rain shell, headlamp, first aid, map) go on top or in the lid 65%.

More: the lifting guide in full

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Grandpa's rule (wisdom): Hips carry, shoulders steady, legs lift. Your back just comes along for the ride.

  • Heavy gear at the bottom or far from your back.

fsr-vehicles-radio:
Why it matters

Most of your hunting ground is reached by gravel resource roads built for logging trucks. Knowing how those roads work keeps you out of a head on crash and out of trouble with the law.

  • Read the sign at the start of every road 95%.
  • The sign in the field beats any map 95%.
More: what this lesson covers
  • How resource roads and (Forest Service Road) traffic work (85%, BC Forest Safety Council).
  • The radio call: road name, kilometre, up or down (95% that BC standardised up and down calling; 65% for the exact wording).
  • Which radios need a licence (85%, ISED (Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada)).
  • Firearms, vehicles and roads: only the rules in the app's Rule Book 99%.
  • What to carry and what to do if you get stuck (Tip and 85%).
  • Radio channels: this lesson never gives channel numbers. Use the channel posted on the sign at the road entry (95%, BC government).
  • Related: ATV rules in BC, Maps 3: land status and access, Hunter etiquette.

• Lights on, keep right, yield to industrial traffic 85%.
  • No posted limit? Never over 80 km/h 85%.
  • Firearm unloaded in or on any vehicle 99%.
More: the key points in full
  • Resource roads are gravel, often one lane, with tight curves, steep grades and soft shoulders (85%, BC Forest Safety Council Resource Road User Safety Guide, 2017).
  • They are built for industrial vehicles. Yield to them 85%.
  • If no limit is posted, the maximum speed on a resource road in BC is 80 km/h (85%, same guide).
  • Drive with head and tail lights on; drive on the right; do not overtake industrial vehicles unless the driver pulls over and signals 85%.
  • Where posted, mobile radio users "must use the posted channels and call protocols" (95%, BC government resource road radio page).
  • Most resource roads are "radio assist": radio use is not mandatory and not everyone has one (95%, BC government).
  • A loaded firearm in or on any vehicle is unlawful (99%, synopsis page 11, item 28).
  • An ATV (All Terrain Vehicle) on an FSR needs a valid driver's licence and at least $200,000 third party liability insurance (99%, synopsis page 9).

hunting-camp:
Why it matters

A good camp means real sleep, dry gear and no bear visits. A bad one means a cold night, a tired hunter and a bear that learned where people keep food.

  • Sleep, cook and store food apart: about 100 m each 85%.
  • Nothing with a smell in the tent 85%.
More: what this lesson covers
  • Picking a site (85% WildSafeBC, rest Tip).
  • The bear triangle and food storage (75 to 85%, WildSafeBC).
  • Meat, garbage and carcasses in camp: what the law says (99%, synopsis).
  • Campfire rules (95%, BC Wildfire Service).
  • Sleeping warm: bag ratings, pad R values, tricks (70 to 75% sources, rest Tip).
  • Carbon monoxide: the danger of heaters and stoves in tents 80%.
  • Related: Bush safety, Hypothermia, frostbite and cold weather, Black bear, Meat care.

• Tent upwind, kitchen and food downwind (Tip).
  • Food in a vehicle, locker, or hung 4 m up and 3 m out (75 to 85%).
  • Campfire: 0.5 m by 0.5 m max, 8 L water or a hand tool 95%.
More: the key points in full
  • WildSafeBC: in undeveloped areas, set tent, cooking area and food storage about 100 m apart in a triangle (85%, WildSafeBC Camping in Bear Country brochure, 2018).
  • Where possible, hang food at least 4 m off the ground and 3 m from the nearest tree (75%, same brochure, text partly damaged in the PDF).
  • With no lockers, keep food in the trunk of a vehicle or a hard sided RV 85%.
  • "Never take food with you into your tent, not even a small snack" 85%.
  • "Cook in clothes other than those you will sleep in" 85%.
  • Carcasses are attractants in law. Leaving one where people are likely to be and where dangerous wildlife can reach it can be fined up to $50,000 (99%, synopsis page 15).
  • A Category 1 campfire is no larger than 0.5 m high by 0.5 m wide, with at least 8 L of water or a hand tool on hand and a fuel break around it (95%, BC Wildfire Service).
  • Never run a fuel burning heater or stove in a tent (80%, Technical Safety BC and Vancouver Coastal Health).

• Look up for dead trees before you pitch (Tip).
  • Not on a trail, not by a creek animals travel 85%.
More: site choice in full
  • Inspect the area for bear sign: scat, claw marks, fresh digging, tracks (85%, WildSafeBC).
  • Camp away from waterways or other features that may be travel routes for wildlife (85%, WildSafeBC).
  • Bears have long memories: a site that gave a bear food before may get a visit again (85%, WildSafeBC).
  • Dead standing trees and hanging limbs fall in wind and snow. Never pitch under them (Tip).
  • Cold air sinks into hollows and valley bottoms at night (75%, same physics as Wind and thermals). A bench a little above the bottom is warmer (Tip).
  • Flat, high and dry: check where rain water would run (Tip).
  • Respect private land and closed areas: Maps 3: land status.

• Tent upwind of the kitchen and food (Tip).
  • Kitchen and food about 100 m from the tent 85%.
More: the triangle in full
  • Tent, cooking area and food storage about 100 m apart, in a triangle (85%, WildSafeBC).
  • Sleeping area upwind of the kitchen and food storage, at least 100 m apart (65%, Princeton Outdoor Action, citing Gary Brown, Safe Travel in Bear Country).
  • Wind shifts. Pick the most common night wind for the spot; valleys often flow downhill at night (75%, see Wind and thermals).
  • At a truck camp, a 100 m triangle may not fit. Then: food locked in the truck, cook downwind, clean up right after (Tip and 85% for the truck).

• Lockers first, then the vehicle, then a hang 85%.
  • Never in the tent. Not a snack, not toothpaste 85%.
More: storage in full
  • Use bear resistant storage where it is provided (85%, WildSafeBC).
  • None provided: trunk of a vehicle or a hard sided RV 85%.
  • Backcountry: hang food at least 4 m up and 3 m from the tree 75%.
  • Other guides give 3 to 5 m up, 2 to 3 m from the trunk and 1 m below the branch (60%, Girl Guides of Canada BC camping sheet). Use the bigger numbers when you can (Tip).
  • Bear resistant containers: an option where trees are poor (Tip). Price tiers: VERIFY in store.
  • Attractants are more than food: soaps, toothpaste, dish rags, pots, grey water, garbage, fuel containers, pet food (85%, WildSafeBC list).
  • Keep camp free of attractants whenever you leave it, even for a short walk 85%.

  • It is unlawful to intentionally feed or attempt to feed dangerous wildlife (cougar, coyote, wolf and bear), except where baiting is authorized for cougar, coyote and wolf (99%, synopsis page 11, item 20).
  • Gut piles: leave them away from camp, trails and roads (Tip, plus the attractant rule above).

  • Where you can see the meat from camp, you notice a bear early. Approach meat with noise and the wind in your face (70%, see Packing out).

  • Wet clothes steal heat. Change into dry ones at night (Tip).

  • Food is fuel. A meal with fat and protein before bed helps (Tip, see Food and water).
  • A full bladder makes you colder and wakes you (Tip).
  • Sweaty clothes steal heat; sleep in a dry base layer and a toque (Tip, see What to wear).
  • Breath carries moisture. A cracked vent cuts frost inside the tent (Tip).
  • Hot water bottle: lid tight, in a sock, never boiling into a soft bottle (Tip).

Warning

Never run a stove, heater, lantern or generator inside a tent or a closed truck cab. Opening the flap is not enough 80%.

More: carbon monoxide in full
  • CO (carbon monoxide) comes from fuel burning appliances: portable stoves and heaters, barbecues, firepits, lanterns, generators (80%, Technical Safety BC and Vancouver Coastal Health).
  • They should never go in enclosed spaces such as tents and RVs (80%, same).
  • Opening tent flaps or doors is not enough to prevent dangerous build up (80%, US CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention)).
  • Symptoms: headache, dizziness, breathlessness, nausea, tiredness, confusion; easy to mistake for flu 80%.
  • Suspect it: turn appliances off, get everyone outside, call 911 80%.
  • Wall tents with stove jacks are a different set up with a proper flue. If you ever use one, learn it from someone who does; VERIFY the maker's instructions (Tip).

Next scouting trip, pitch your camp for one night as if it were the hunt: triangle, hang, fire rules, sleep system. Write in the journal what was cold, wet or awkward, and fix it at home.

hunt-food-water:
Why it matters

Hungry, thirsty hunters get cold, slow and careless. A pocket of snacks and a planned drink schedule keep your head clear for the shot that matters.

  • Eat before you are hungry, drink before you are thirsty (Tip).
  • A hard hunt day can burn several thousand calories 85%.
More: what this lesson covers
  • How much energy hunting takes (95% Compendium values, 85% for the maths).
  • When and what to eat on a long day (Tip, with 95% energy facts).
  • How much to drink, and how to find your own number 65%.
  • Water in the cold, and treating stream water (95%, HealthLink BC).
  • Food safety in camp and in the truck (95%, HealthLink BC).
  • Full water treatment lesson: Water: finding it and making it safe.

• Something to eat every 2 to 3 hours (Tip).
  • Fat has 9 calories a gram, carbohydrate and protein 4 95%.
  • Treat all stream water 95%.
More: the key points in full
  • Hiking with hunting gear is rated 9.5 METs (Metabolic Equivalents); deer hunting 6.0; stand hunting 2.5 (95%, 2024 Adult Compendium of Physical Activities).
  • Rough calories = METs x body weight in kg x hours 85%.
  • Energy factors: fat 9 kcal per gram, protein 4, carbohydrate 4, alcohol 7 (95%, FAO (Food and Agriculture Organization) food energy report).
  • Hunters often struggle to eat enough on hard days and forget to eat (65%, outfitter and boot maker blog). Set a snack timer (Tip).
  • Weigh before and after a training hike: 1 kg of weight lost is about 1 L of fluid not replaced (65%, sports nutrition summaries).
  • Boil water at least 1 minute (2 minutes above 2,000 m) or use 2 drops of household bleach per litre and wait 30 minutes (95%, HealthLink BC File 49b).
  • Keep perishable food at 4 °C or colder; the danger zone is 4 °C to 60 °C; no more than 2 hours out (95%, HealthLink BC).
  • Do not consume alcohol or drugs while hunting (99%, synopsis ethics code, page 77).

• Walking hills with a pack: about 760 kcal an hour for an 80 kg hunter (Tip, estimate).

hunting-partner:

Two hunters see more, carry more and get help faster. Two hunters with no plan can also shoot toward each other or lose each other at dark. The plan is the difference.

The law sets the floor. Ethics is how you hunt when nobody is watching. Every hunter is judged by the worst thing people see a hunter do.

  6. The wrong animal. Stop, do not hide it, and report promptly. Item 18 covers accidental kills 99%; my reading is that the honest path for a wrong animal is the same report 80%.   • This session: track shapes for 11 animals, sizes in cm, the gaits and the patterns they leave, aging a track, and direction of travel.
  • Carry a small tape or know the length of your knife and your boot. Measure, never guess (Tip).
  • Sign that is not a track (scat, rubs, beds) is the next session: Reading sign.

Read a track in 5 steps1 of 5
  • Photograph every good track with a coin, knife or tape for scale (Tip).
More: the 6 steps in full
  1. Count the toes. 2 toes: hoofed (deer, elk, moose). 4 toes: cat or dog family. 5 toes: bear 85%.
  2. Look for claws. Dogs, wolves, coyotes and bears show claws. Cats usually do not 80%.
  3. Measure length and width of one clear print. Front prints are usually bigger than hind on deer and bears 75%.
  4. Measure the stride: same foot to same foot, for example left front to left front 75%.
  5. Measure the straddle: the width of the whole trail from outer edge to outer edge 70%.
  6. Look at the whole trail, not one print. Pattern and spacing tell you the gait and the mood (Tip).
Tip (opinion)

Photograph every good track with something for scale: a coin, your knife, a tape. Note date, time, weather and place in the Journal.

• Measure the front print, then find its bar.
  • Bars overlap: use toes, claws and the trail too (Tip).

• The pointed end points the way it went 85%.
  • Mule deer and white tail prints overlap; the trail tells them apart 60%.

  • Dewclaws (the two small bumps behind the hoof) show in deep mud, snow, or when the animal runs 75%.
  • Mule deer and white tail tracks overlap too much to tell apart from one print 60%. Use the trail: a stotting trail is a mule deer 85%.
  • A buck track is often bigger, rounder at the tips and deeper, with a wider straddle, but a big doe fools people (hunter lore) 60%.
  • Cattle tracks are round, blunt and wide, and in Region 3 grassland they are everywhere. A cow print has no pointed tip 75%.

• Toes in a straight row, long claws far ahead: grizzly 70%.
  • Grizzly track on your trail: change your plan (Tip).
Warning

Grizzly until proven otherwise: make noise, spray on your belt, do not follow.

More: black bear and grizzly sizes
  • A bear track with long claw marks and toes in a straight row is a grizzly until proven otherwise. Make noise, keep bear spray on your belt, and do not follow it.
  • Black bear: 5 toes in a curved row, short claws (about 3 to 5 cm) that print as dots close to the toes 70%.
  • Black bear front track about 10 to 16 cm long and 10 to 14 cm wide. Hind track about 15 to 18 cm long, like a flat human foot 70%.
  • Grizzly: front track about 18 cm long and 13 cm wide. Hind about 28 cm long. Claw marks sit well ahead of the toes 65%.
  • The toe line test: lay a straight edge across the top of the palm pad, under the toes. Black bear: the outer, smallest toe falls below the line. Grizzly: all 5 toes sit above it 70%.
  • Grizzlies live in the Thompson. A fresh grizzly track on your trail means change your plan (Tip). See Bush safety.

• No claws and a 3 lobe heel: cougar 75%.
  • Coyote is about half a wolf 70%.
  • Cougar tracks mean deer country (Tip).

  • A coyote track is about half the size of a wolf track 70%. A wolf track outsizes almost any dog 70%.
  • Dog or wild canid? A dog trail wanders, toes splay, and the track is rounder. A wolf or coyote walks a straight, purposeful line with toes tight (tracker lore) 60%.
  • A cougar track is as wide as it is long, shows no claws, and the heel pad is bigger than the 4 toes together. A dog's pad is about the size of 3 toes 70%.
  • Cougar is the top killer of mule deer in the southern Interior 85%. Where you find cougar tracks, you have found deer country (Tip).

• Hare: a Y of prints, big hind feet in front 75%.
  • Grouse: 3 toes forward, 1 back, in one line 65%.
More: hare and grouse details
  • Snowshoe hare: hind track long and triangular, up to about 12 cm, in winter up to 15 cm with the fur spread. Front track round, about 4.5 cm 70%.
  • Hare pattern: two big hind prints side by side, ahead of two smaller front prints. The group looks like a letter Y pointing the way it went 75%.
  • Hare runways in brush are 10 to 15 cm wide and packed down in snow 65%.
  • Grouse: 3 toes forward, 1 short toe back, about 5 to 7 cm long 65%. The bird walks in a line, often zig zag, and you may find wing marks in snow where it flushed 65%.
  • In winter grouse grow comb like fringes on their toes, so the snow track looks wider and fuzzy 65%.

Watch the 3 gaits1 of 3
  • The pattern tells you the mood.
  • Stot groups from a bed: you bumped that deer (Tip).
More: all 5 gaits and the stot tip
  • Walk: the everyday gait. A zig zag line. The hind foot lands on or just behind the front print on the same side 75%. A relaxed animal, feeding or travelling (Tip).
  • Trot: longer stride, narrower trail, prints nearly in one line. Hind lands on or past the front 70%. Moving with purpose, not panicked 65%.
  • Bound: hind feet land side by side ahead of the front feet. Hares and squirrels live in this gait 75%.
  • Stot: the mule deer bounce. All 4 feet land close together in a group, then a gap of about 2.4 to 4.6 m to the next group 60%. This deer saw or smelled you 85%.
  • Gallop: groups of 4 prints in a line with the hind prints beyond the front, long gaps between groups 70%. White tails, elk and moose run this way 70%.
  • Speed shows in stride. A walking deer step is roughly 40 to 60 cm; a running deer covers metres between groups 65%.
Tip (opinion)

Stot groups leading away from a bed on a ridge mean you bumped that deer within the last hour. Mark the bed on your map. Mule deer come back to good beds (hunter lore).

• Walk, trot, bound, stot, gallop, side by side.
  • Hare bound: big hind prints land ahead of the front 75%.

• Crisp walls: hours. Rounded: days. Debris inside: a week (Tip).
  • Cold shaded ground keeps tracks crisp for days 65%.
More: every aging clue
  • Edges: fresh prints have crisp, sharp walls. Sun, wind and rain round them off 75%.
  • Debris: leaves, needles, insect trails or spider web inside the print mean time has passed 70%.
  • Frost: frost crystals grown inside the print mean it was made before the frost, usually last night or earlier 65%. A print pressed through the frost crust was made after the frost, this morning 65%.
  • Rain: rain pits inside the print mean it was made before the rain. A clean print on rain spattered ground is after the rain 70%.
  • Dust and mud: in fine dust a fresh print has a thin raised rim that collapses within hours 60%. In mud, fresh means the walls are still shiny and wet (Tip).
  • Snow: see Snow tracking. Cold still nights in the Interior keep a track crisp for days, so crisp does not always mean fresh 65%.
  • Best test: make your own boot print right beside it and compare (Tip).

• Hoof: the point leads 85%. Paw: toes and claws lead 80%.
  • Loose soil or snow piles up at the back 65%.
More: more direction clues
  • Hoofed animals: the pointed end leads 85%. Toes dig deeper than the heel when climbing or pushing off 65%.
  • Paws: the toes point the way and the claws lead 80%.
  • Pushed material: the animal shoves soil or snow backward on push off, so a lip of loose material sits at the rear of the print 65%.
  • Snow: drag marks run into the print from behind. A small spray of kicked snow lies ahead of it 65%.
  • Bent grass and bent twigs lie in the direction the animal moved 65%.
  • Lost the line? Walk a slow circle 10 m out around the last clear print and find where the trail leaves the circle (Tip).

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

One track is a guess. Three tracks are a direction. Ten tracks are a story. Read the story.

Common mistakes
  • Calling every big heart shaped track a buck. Measure it, then look at the trail.
  • Judging age by one print on a shaded north bank, where tracks stay crisp for days.
  • Following a fresh grizzly track just to see.

sign:
Why it matters

Scat, beds, rubs and chewed twigs tell you what lives here, what it eats, and when it was here.

  • Sign is everything an animal leaves except the track.
  • Gloves and a stick for scat, never bare hands (Tip).
More: what this session covers
  • Sign is everything an animal leaves behind except the track itself.
  • This session: scat by species, beds, rubs, scrapes, wallows, browse lines, hair on fences, grouse sign, kill sites, and how to judge freshness.
  • Tracks are in Tracks. Where sign adds up to a trail or a funnel is in Trails and funnels.
  • Carry nitrile gloves and a stick. Do not handle scat bare handed (Tip).

• Size overlaps: check the tracks beside the pile (Tip).
  • Piles are not a count of deer 70%.

  • Pellet size overlaps between a big deer and a small elk. Look at the tracks beside the pile (Tip).
  • Mule deer and white tail pellets look the same 60%.

• Deer hair and bone: wolf or cougar. Mouse hair: coyote 70%.
  • Big fresh berry scat on the trail: go loud (Tip).

  • Fresh bear scat draws flies within hours, then lightens and cracks as it dries 65%.
  • Big fresh bear scat full of berries on a trail: a bear fed here in the last day. Go loud (Tip).

• Wet and shiny: hours. Faded with moss: weeks 60%.
  • Mixed ages in one spot: a place used again and again (Tip).
More: every aging clue
  • Hours: wet, shiny, warm, strong smell, flies 60%.
  • A day or two: dull surface, a dry crust, still soft inside 60%.
  • Days to a week: dry, lighter colour, cracks 65%.
  • Weeks: faded, crumbling, moss or mould, insect holes 60%.
  • Cold slows all of this. Frozen pellets in November can look fresh for a week (Tip).
  • Pellets in a pile that are all one colour and one age were dropped at once. A mix of ages means a bed or a feeding spot used again and again (Tip).

• Deer bed: an oval 0.9 to 1.2 m long 70%. Elk beds are bigger, in groups 65%.
  • Warm bed means minutes. Do not linger (Tip).
More: bed sizes and the snow test
  • A deer bed is an oval of flattened grass, duff or snow about 0.9 to 1.2 m long, often with pellets and a few hairs 70%.
  • Elk beds are bigger, about 1.2 to 1.5 m, and come in groups 65%.
  • Moose beds are bigger again and often alone, in willow or timber near water 60%. Typical size: VERIFY.
  • Day beds sit where the animal can see below and smell what comes from above: benches, the top third of a slope, under a tree with a view (hunter lore) 60%.
  • In snow a used bed melts and refreezes into an icy bowl. A bed with a dry crisp floor and no refreeze is recent 65%.
  • Warm bed test: put your hand in it. Warm means minutes. Do not sit down to think about it; the animal may be watching you (Tip).
  • Bedding areas have many beds, trails between them, and pellets of mixed age (Tip).

• The rubbed side faces where the buck came from 60%.
  • A line of rubs is his road between bed and feed 60%.

• : pawed bare dirt under a chewed licking branch 65%.
  • White tails scrape, mule deer rarely do 60%.
More: rub and scrape details
  • A is bark stripped from a sapling by a buck's antlers and forehead. Most rubs sit about 30 to 105 cm above the ground 65%.
  • Rub height says more about buck size than tree size. A rub centred 75 cm or higher suggests a mature buck 60%.
  • Tree thickness still helps: 2.5 to 5 cm trees are often yearlings; over 10 cm is usually an older buck 60%.
  • The rubbed side faces where the buck came from. A line of rubs facing one way is his route between bed and feed 60%.
  • White tails make many rubs. Mule deer make fewer, on small conifers and shrubs 60%.
  • A is a pawed bare oval of dirt under an overhanging licking branch about 1.2 to 1.5 m up 65%. The buck chews the branch and urinates in the scrape 70%.
  • About 80% of scraping in the north happens from mid October to mid November 65%. White tails scrape; mule deer rarely do 60%.
  • Fresh scrape: dark moist soil, pawed leaves thrown back, a urine smell, branch tip chewed (Tip).

• Moose dig rut pits, elk roll in wallows 65%.
  • Sharp ammonia smell and muddy water: used within hours 60%.
More: rut pits, wallows and Region 3 notes
  • Bull moose dig rut pits: a pawed hole about 45 to 105 cm long and 8 to 15 cm deep, soaked with urine, strong smell 65%.
  • Bulls thrash shrubs and small trees with their antlers many times an hour in the rut. Look for broken, stripped willow and alder 65%.
  • Bull elk wallow: a muddy depression the size of a bathtub at a seep or spring, stinking of urine, with mud rubbed on nearby trees 65%.
  • A wallow with muddy water, wet edges and a sharp ammonia smell was used within hours 60%.
  • Elk rub and strip bigger trees than deer, often above your head (Tip).
  • Region 3 moose and elk: most hunts are (Limited Entry Hunting). Spike fork bull moose general seasons exist in some (Management Unit) areas 95%. Details in The rut.

• Torn end: deer. Clean 45 degree cut: hare 75%.
  • The height of the line tells you who ate 65%.
More: browse details and 3 plants to learn
  • Deer have no upper front teeth. They tear twigs, leaving a ragged, shredded end 75%.
  • Hares and rabbits cut twigs clean at 45 degrees, like pruning shears, on stems under about 1.2 cm 75%.
  • Fresh browse: the torn end is pale green or white and moist. Old browse: grey and dry (Tip).
  • A browse line is the height below which every twig is eaten. Deer reach to about 1.2 m. A line at 1.5 to 1.8 m says elk. 1.8 to 2.4 m says moose 65%.
  • Shrubs that look clipped into a hedge mark heavy winter use. You are standing on 65%.
  • Learn three plants first: saskatoon, red osier dogwood and Oregon grape. Browsed saskatoon in October means deer are feeding here now (Tip).

• Same crossing, night after night 65%.
  • Fences often mean private land: consent first 95%.
More: crossing details and the land rule
  • Deer and elk cross fences at the same spots. Look for a hard packed path running straight at the wire and a polished, sagging top strand 65%.
  • Hair caught in the barbs is the giveaway. Brown or grey deer hair, coarse black or brown bear hair 65%.
  • Hair in the barbs is usually a doe, fawn or young buck going through. A big buck often jumps and leaves nothing 60%.
  • Pull the hair out. Next visit, new hair means the crossing is in use (Tip).
  • Elk and moose push wire down. A broken top strand with hair on it is big animal sign (Tip).
Warning

Fences often mean private or leased land. Cultivated land, and grazing leases with livestock on them, need consent to hunt 95%. See BC rules.

• Dusting bowl: a 20 cm scrape in fine dirt with feathers 65%.
  • A pile of droppings marks a night roost 70%.
More: bowls, roosts, feathers and seasons
  • A dusting bowl is a round to oval scrape in dry fine soil, about 20 cm across, often on a trail or road edge, with a few feathers in it 65%.
  • Grouse droppings in a pile mark a night roost. In winter, a hole in soft snow with a pile of droppings inside is a snow roost 70%.
  • Feathers: a hawk or owl plucks and leaves whole feathers with clean quills. A fox or coyote bites, so quills are chewed or cut 60%.
  • A few loose feathers and a dusting bowl near Douglas fir, aspen and rose thickets: come back with the shotgun (Tip).
  • Grouse are upland game birds in the with their own seasons and limits. Check your MU before you carry the shotgun 85%.

• Covered carcass: the owner is close and coming back 75%.
  • Back out the way you came, talking loudly. Tell your brother (Tip).
More: kill site details
  • Cougar: drags the kill into cover, eats the chest and organs first, then covers it with leaves, snow, dirt or sticks 75%. It stays nearby and feeds for 6 to 8 days 70%.
  • Wolves: the carcass is torn apart in the open, bones crushed and scattered, many tracks 60%.
  • Bears: cache by raking dirt and debris over the carcass. The ground looks rototilled. Bears defend caches 70%.
  • Scavengers: ravens, magpies and eagles circling or calling in one spot often mark a kill (Tip).
  • Cougar scrapes: a small pile of pine needles or dirt with scat or urine on it, on a ridge trail 65%.
Warning

A covered carcass means a cougar or bear is close and will come back. Do not touch it. Back out the way you came, talking loudly, and tell your brother where it is.

More: freshness in words
  • Fresh, minutes to hours: wet scat, warm bed, green browse ends, crisp track walls, dew knocked off grass (Tip).
  • Today: track edges still sharp, scat dull but soft, scrape dark and damp (Tip).
  • This week: dry scat, grey browse ends, track softened, bed with refrozen snow (Tip).

funnels:
Why it matters

The land squeezes deer onto a few lines. Sit beside one and the deer comes to you.

  • A trail is where animals walk again and again.
  • A funnel is where the land forces them onto one trail.
More: what this session covers
  • A trail is where animals walk again and again. A funnel is where the land forces them onto one trail.
  • This session: trails, funnels, pinch points, saddles, benches, edges, bedding versus feeding, and how to turn all that into a stand or a glassing point.
  • Nearly all of this is hunter craft, not science. Treat it as a strong Tip and test it on your own ground.
  • Wind and thermals decide where you sit. Read Wind and thermals first.

• Packed, bare, 15 to 30 cm wide, with prints and pellets 65%.
  • Find where it comes from and where it goes (Tip).
More: how to read a trail
  • A game trail is a bare, packed line 15 to 30 cm wide through grass or duff, with hoof prints and pellets along it 65%.
  • Cattle trails are wider, deeper and churned, with cow pies. In Region 3 grassland many trails are shared (Tip).
  • Count the sign per 10 m of trail. Lots of fresh pellets and crisp prints: a highway. Old faded sign: a back road (Tip).
  • A trail that splits into many faint lines is entering a feeding or bedding area. A trail that gathers many lines into one is heading for a crossing (Tip).
  • Deer trails run on the easiest line: along a bench, round the head of a draw, through the low spot in a ridge 65%.
  • Follow a trail far enough to answer two questions: where does it come from and where does it go (Tip).

• Funnel: land that narrows the routes 65%.
  • Pinch point: the narrowest spot in it 65%.
More: saddles, benches, edges and crossings
  • A funnel is any feature that narrows the possible routes: a strip of timber between two openings, a creek bottom, a bench, a cut block edge 65%.
  • A pinch point is the narrowest spot in a funnel: a creek crossing, a gap in a cliff band, an open gate or a downed fence, the inside corner of a field 65%.
  • Saddles: the low dip between two high points on a ridge. Deer cross ridges here, hidden from the skyline and using the least effort 65%.
  • Benches: flat shelves on a hillside. Deer walk them and bed on them 65%.
  • Edges: where two cover types meet, like timber against grassland or an old burn against green forest. Deer feed on the edge and bed just inside 65%.
  • Water crossings: deer cross creeks where banks are low and gravel is firm. One crossing may serve a whole slope (Tip).
  • In the , bucks cruise funnels between doe groups. A saddle between two bedding ridges is a November classic 60%.

• Feed in the open at dusk and dawn, bed hidden by day 85%.
  • Never hunt inside the beds. Hunt the line 60%.
More: bed and feed in detail
  • Feeding areas are open: grassland, cut blocks, hayfields, burns with new shrubs, a south slope with saskatoon and bitterbrush 75%.
  • Bedding areas are hidden: timber on a north slope, a bench with a view below, the top third of a ridge, thick regrowth 70%.
  • Deer feed in the open at dusk and dawn, then move to bed as the light grows 85%. Morning trails run uphill, evening trails run downhill (Tip).
  • Mule deer near Heffley Creek: grassland and open Douglas fir benches to feed, timber and broken rock above to bed 75%.
  • White tails: hayfields and cottonwood bottoms to feed, thick brush and willows to bed 80%.
  • Never hunt inside the bedding area. Hunt the line between bed and feed: closer to the bed in the morning, closer to the feed in the evening (hunter lore) 60%.

Pick a stand in 4 steps1 of 4
  • Check the earth behind every lane (Tip).
More: all 7 steps and my lean
  1. Find the line: a trail or funnel between a known bed and a known feed (Tip).
  2. Check the wind and the thermal for the hour you will sit. Morning: sit above or beside the line. Evening: sit below or beside it 75%.
  3. Pick a spot 100 to 200 m off the line with a long view and a solid rest for the rifle. Past 200 m you are a watcher, not a shooter (Tip). See Glassing.
  4. Check the behind every lane you might shoot. Earth, not sky (Tip).
  5. Plan a quiet approach that does not cross the trail, the feed or the bed. Come in the back way (Tip). See Moving quietly.
  6. Pick a B spot for the opposite wind. Never force A (Tip).
  7. Mark it on your map and note where the sun will rise. A low sun in your face kills glassing (Tip).
My lean (opinion)

For your first October trips, pick a glassing point above a grassland edge with timber behind you. Sit from 45 minutes before legal light. Learn the lines first, then move closer.
