food-water-cover:
Why it matters

Every animal needs to eat, drink and hide. Find all three close together and you have found where it lives this week.

  • The overlap moves with the season.
  • Learn 5 plants this month (Tip).
More: what this session covers
  • Food, water and cover change with the season. The deer of September are not where the deer of December are.
  • This session: what deer eat in Region 3 (Thompson) and Region 2 (Fraser Valley) by season, the plants to learn, berries and mast, farm fields, water in a dry fall, thermal cover in cold, and how snow changes it all.
  • Plant names here are the ones BC biologists and hunters use. Learn 5 plants this month and you are ahead of most beginners (Tip).

• The deer of September are not where the deer of December are.
  • Frost kills the feed, snow moves the deer 85%.

• Browse: shrub twigs, leaves, green forbs 85%.
  • Dry fall: deer stay near water 70%.
More: September details
  • Deer are browsers: twigs, leaves and buds of shrubs plus forbs, with little grass in fall 85%.
  • Early fall feed near Kamloops: forbs still green on north slopes and in draws, shrub leaves, the last berries 85%.
  • Key shrubs: saskatoon, red osier dogwood, willow, rose, snowbrush, bitterbrush, Oregon grape, rabbitbrush, sagebrush 80%.
  • Mule deer are often still high in September: subalpine meadows, old burns and cut blocks 75%.
  • Water matters now. In a dry Interior fall, deer stay within reach of seeps, springs, stock ponds and lakes 70%.
  • Cover: shade. Deer bed in timber on north slopes and in draws on warm days 80%.

• Shrub twigs become the main meal 80%.
  • Hayfields pull white tails every evening 80%.
More: October and November details
  • Green feed fades. After fall rain, grassland greens up again and deer use new grass shoots and forbs 75%.
  • Shrub twigs and leaves become the main meal: saskatoon, red osier dogwood, willow, rose hips 80%.
  • Douglas fir needles enter the diet in late fall and peak in December and January 85%.
  • Hayfields and alfalfa in the North Thompson valley pull white tails every evening and mule deer in hard weather 80%.
  • Bucks eat less and move more as the nears 70%. See The rut.
  • Cover shifts to thermal cover as nights freeze: mature Douglas fir on south and west slopes 85%.

• Snow and cold, not the rut, push deer down 85%.
  • Do not push deer on winter range for fun (Tip).
More: winter range details
  • Snow and cold, not the rut, push deer down to : south and west facing slopes with old Douglas fir, often below about 760 m north of Kamloops 85%.
  • Deer have trouble in snow deeper than about 30 cm and leave slopes where it passes about 50 cm 75%. Moose move freely to about 40 cm and are restricted by 40 to 70 cm 70%. Elk sit between 65%.
  • Winter diet: Douglas fir, shrubs, and whatever bunchgrass is blown clear on windy ridges 80%.
  • Winter range shows browse lines and hedged shrubs, trails between beds and feed, and pellets everywhere 65%.
  • Many Region 3 mule deer general seasons end 10 December (65%, VERIFY your (Management Unit) in the ). Late season means hunting winter range in snow (Tip).
  • Do not push deer on winter range for fun. Every run costs them fat they cannot replace (Tip).

• Learn these 6 plus Oregon grape (Tip).

• Interior mast is berries, rose hips and conifer seed 70%.
  • Fresh seedy bear scat marks a patch (Tip).
More: berries, bears and grouse
  • Mast is the fruit and nuts of trees and shrubs. In the Interior there are no acorns; the mast is berries, rose hips and conifer seed 70%.
  • Berry season for bears and grouse: saskatoon and soopolallie in July and August, huckleberry in August and September, rose hips and snowberry into winter 70%.
  • Bears work berry patches hard in September to fatten up. Fresh bear scat full of seeds marks a patch (Tip).
  • Grouse eat rose hips, snowberry, kinnikinnick berries and clover along roads in October 65%.
  • Fraser Valley: Himalayan blackberry fruits August to September; wild crabapple, hazelnut and old orchard apples draw black tailed deer and bears 60%.
  • Cottonwood, aspen and alder leaves on the ground in October are a quick deer snack (Tip).

• White tails live on farm edges 80%.
  • Same corner most nights, wind in their favour 60%.
  • Cultivated land: owner's consent first 95%.
More: fields, edges and asking a farmer
  • White tails live on farm edges: alfalfa and hay regrowth, grain stubble, and the brushy fence lines between 80%.
  • Mule deer come to hayfields too, mostly in hard weather and in the rut 65%.
  • Fraser Valley: corn stubble, berry fields, pasture and hay draw black tailed deer at dusk, and ducks and geese in winter 65%.
  • Field deer come out the same corner most nights, from the nearest thick cover, with the wind in their favour (hunter lore) 60%.
  • Hunting cultivated land needs the owner's consent 95%. Many farms welcome a polite ask for deer; ask in person, early, and offer to share (Tip).
  • Never shoot toward buildings, roads or livestock. Field hunting is backstop hunting (Tip).

• When feed dries, deer need surface water 75%.
  • Sit a pond at dusk until the big rain (Tip).
More: water details
  • Deer get much of their water from green feed. When the feed dries, they need surface water 75%.
  • Studies elsewhere found deer rarely live more than about 2.4 km from water and prefer it within about 1 km 65%.
  • In the Thompson grassland in October, water means seeps, springs, stock ponds (dugouts), small lakes and the river (Tip).
  • Tracks at a muddy pond edge tell you who drinks here. Deer drink at dawn and dusk 70%.
  • Sitting water is a good evening stand in a dry October, until the first big rain refills every puddle (Tip).
  • Moose live by water: willow swamps, lake edges, beaver ponds 85%.

• Closed canopy above 3 m: warmer, less wind and snow 80%.
  • Cold snap: timber by day, sunny edge in the afternoon 75%.
More: thermal cover details
  • Thermal cover is forest that keeps an animal warmer: a closed canopy above 3 m that traps heat, cuts wind, and catches snow 80%.
  • Mule deer winter survival in the Interior depends on mature or old Douglas fir on warm aspects, with a mix of open and closed canopy 85%.
  • Cold snap: look for deer in the timber by day and on the sunny open slope right beside it in the afternoon 75%.
  • Thermal cover for the hunter means wind blocks and sun. Pick a stand with a tree at your back and the sun on your chest (Tip).
  • Elk and moose stand cold better than deer. They stay higher, longer 70%.

• Columbian black tailed deer, rut November to early December 80%.
More: Fraser Valley details
  • The deer of Region 2 is the Columbian black tailed deer, a coastal mule deer 85%. Its is November to early December 80%.
  • Fall and winter food: salal, red huckleberry, trailing blackberry, Douglas fir, western red cedar, deer fern and tree lichens 80%.
  • Spring and summer: grasses, fireweed, salmonberry, willow, maple and many forbs 80%.
  • Winter pushes them to low, warm, south facing slopes and floodplains with little snow 80%.
  • Cover: thick second growth, blackberry tangles, cedar and hemlock. Edges along cut blocks and power lines are the feed (Tip).
  • Ducks: Fraser Valley fields, sloughs and the delta are a major wintering area; fields flood after rain and ducks feed on stubble and grass 70%.

the-rut:
Why it matters

For a few weeks a year, careful bulls and bucks get careless. Know the calendar and be there when it happens.

  • Elk first, then moose, then deer 80%.
  • Your October hunts land in the deer 75%.
More: what this session covers
  • The is the breeding season. Males roam, fight, call and lose their caution 85%.
  • Each species has its own calendar. Elk first, then moose, then deer. From late September to December something is rutting somewhere in BC 80%.
  • This session: timing for elk, moose, mule deer, white tails and black tails; , calling and scents; the (Chronic Wasting Disease) rule on lures; and what changes for you week by week.
  • Your first hunts in mid to late October land in the deer and the tail end of the moose rut 75%.

• Day length sets the date. Weather sets how much you see 75%.
  • Cold, calm mornings: rutting animals on their feet 70%.
More: the timing table and Region 3 notes
SpeciesRut windowPeak
Elkearly September to mid October 70%about the third week of September, a smaller second wave in early October 70%
Mooselate September to mid October, young bulls later 70%last week of September to first week of October 70%

  • Timing is driven by day length, so it barely moves year to year. Weather changes how much you see, not when it happens 75%.
  • Cold, crisp, calm mornings put rutting animals on their feet in daylight. Warm wind hides them 70%.
  • Region 3: no elk general open season is printed in the Region 3 pages, and moose general seasons are spike fork bulls only in some (Management Unit) areas 95%. For you, the rut matters most for deer (Tip).

• Pre rut: rubs and bucks checking does at dusk 70%.
  • Peak: does lead, bucks follow. Hunt the does (Tip).
More: each phase in detail and my lean
  • Pre rut, mid October to early November: bucks leave bachelor groups, rub, scrape (white tails), and start checking doe groups at dusk and dawn 70%.
  • Seeking and chasing, first half of November: bucks travel, cruise funnels between doe groups, and show up in daylight 75%.
  • Peak, mid November: a buck tends one doe at a time, follows her for a day or two, and fights rivals 75%. Does lead, bucks follow: hunt the does (Tip).
  • Post rut, December: bucks are thin, tired and back in cover. A second, smaller rut comes when unbred does cycle again about 28 days later 65%.
  • Mule deer bucks rut on winter range, so the rut and the snow bring them down to the same open slopes 80%.
  • White tails rut near the fields and bottoms where the does live 80%.
My lean (opinion)

Your October hunt is pre rut. Glass doe groups at dusk. The first bucks will be nosing around them. In November, sit a saddle or bench between doe groups from first light until 11.

• Call little, listen a lot (Tip).
  • Rattling: best in peak rut, cool calm mornings 70%.
More: rattling, grunts, elk and moose calls
  • copies two bucks fighting. In a Texas radio collar study about 65% of rattling sessions pulled in a buck, best in the peak rut, in the morning, cool and calm 70%.
  • Rattling works best where bucks compete for does, so it is less reliable for mule deer and on heavily hunted ground 50%.
  • Grunt tube: short soft grunts every 15 to 20 minutes in November. A doe bleat can stop a cruising buck (hunter lore) 60%.
  • Elk: a cow call is the safest call for a beginner. Bugling can pull a herd bull in or push him away (hunter lore) 60%.
  • Moose: a long cow moan at dusk, and raking a shoulder blade or paddle on brush to sound like a bull (hunter lore) 60%.
  • Recorded or electronic calls are unlawful for hunting wildlife except wolf, coyote, cougar, lynx, bobcat and Schedule C birds 95%. Mouth and hand calls only for deer, elk and moose.
  • Scents: skip deer urine lures. The rule is on the next screen 95%.

  • (Chronic Wasting Disease) can ride in urine scents 95%.
More: the CWD rules in full and my lean
  • It is unlawful to use, for the purpose of hunting wildlife, any part or derivative of a deer, elk, moose or caribou if the part or derivative originated from outside British Columbia 95%. Synopsis page 12, item 51.
  • It is unlawful to possess any part of a Cervidae (caribou, deer, elk, moose) killed outside BC, other than the edible meat of the four quarters, loins, neck and ribs, or the hide, antlers and skull plate cleaned of all tissue 95%. Synopsis page 12, item 50.
  • The synopsis names urine based scents as a material that can carry CWD prions into new areas 95%. Synopsis page 81, Chronic Wasting Disease.
  • Bottled deer urine on store shelves is almost always from farms outside BC, so using it for hunting is an offence under item 51 (85%, interpretation). A synthetic lure is not a cervid derivative (80%, interpretation).
  • CWD was confirmed in BC in January 2024 in the Kootenay. Deer, elk and moose harvested in the CWD Management Zone (MUs 4-1 to 4-8 and 4-20 to 4-25) have mandatory testing and transport limits 95%. Synopsis page 15 (transport restrictions), page 81, and the Region 4 pages.
  • Region 3 is outside the zone, but the Region 3 pages ask hunters to submit deer, elk and moose heads for CWD testing and list a Kamloops drop off 95%. Region 3 synopsis page 32. See BC rules.
My lean (opinion)

No urine lures at all. The upside is small and the rule is clear. Your scent control is the wind, not a bottle.

snow-tracking:
Why it matters

Fresh snow writes down everything that moved last night. For a beginner it is the best teacher there is.

  • Who, how many, which way, how long ago, and what it did.
  • Late Region 3 deer season is mostly snow hunting 75%.
More: what this session covers
  • Snow turns every animal into an open book: who, how many, which way, how long ago, and what it did.
  • This session: reading a snow track, aging in snow, backtracking versus following, tracking a wounded animal, tracking safely, and when to stop.
  • Late season Region 3 deer hunting, November into early December, is mostly snow hunting on 75%.
  • Track basics are in Tracks. Winter feed and cover are in Food, water and cover.

• Find the clearest print in shallow snow (Tip).
  • Wide straddle, big prints, drag marks: a buck worth following 60%.
More: drag marks, counting and urine lore
  • Snow shows size and shape clearly in the first few centimetres. Deep powder blurs everything into holes; look for the clearest print in a shallow spot (Tip).
  • Hoof drag marks run into each print from behind. Bucks and older deer drag more; a long drag in shallow snow suggests a heavy animal (hunter lore) 60%.
  • A wide straddle, big prints and drag marks together is buck sign worth following. A big doe can fool you 60%.
  • Deer in snow walk in each other's prints. Count the trails leaving a bed area, not the prints (Tip).
  • Stot groups in snow are easy to read: 4 holes close together, a long gap, 4 more 85%.
  • Urine in snow: a doe squats, so the stain is behind the hind prints. A buck dribbles while walking, so the stain is between or ahead of the hind prints (hunter lore) 60%.

• Loose crumbs: fresh. Bonded crumbs: hours 65%.
  • Your own test print is your clock (Tip).
More: every snow aging clue
  • Fresh: sharp walls and loose crumbs of snow scattered around the print that have not bonded 70%.
  • The crumbs bond into a crust within hours. Trackers call this sintering. Poke a crumb; if it holds together, time has passed 65%.
  • Sun rounds the edges and glazes the floor. Wind drifts snow into the print. New snow fills it 75%.
  • Compare the snow in the print with the snow on the ground. 2 cm of fresh snow in a print after a 10 cm fall means it was made early in the storm (Tip).
  • Cold clear Interior nights with no wind keep a track crisp for days. In that weather trust the snow crumbs and your own test print, not the edges 65%.
  • Melt and refreeze: a print with an ice floor and ice walls was made before last night's freeze 65%.
  • Make your own print beside it every hour. Watch how yours ages; that is your clock (Tip).

• Backtrack to learn its life. Follow to catch it (Tip).
  • Look ahead, not down. Glass every few steps (Tip).
More: backtrack or follow in detail
  • Backtrack (walk the trail the way it came) to learn where the deer fed, bedded and crossed. You will not catch the deer, but you will learn its life (Tip).
  • Follow (walk the way it went) to catch up with it. The trail tells you when you are close: feeding turns to walking, then a single line going uphill, then a bed (hunter lore) 60%.
  • Follow with the wind in your face or across you. If the trail turns downwind, loop around rather than walking your scent to the bed (Tip).
  • Go slow when the track shows the deer slowed: meandering, nibbling, a dribble of urine, a short stand. It is near its bed 60%.
  • Look ahead, not down. Every few steps stop and glass the cover ahead and above (Tip). See Glassing.
  • Scouting rule: backtrack in the morning after a snowfall, follow in the afternoon toward beds that face the sun (Tip).
Tip (opinion)

Big woods trackers walk a buck track until he beds, then stalk the bed from above. It takes all day and fails more often than it works. For a beginner, backtracking teaches more.

• Mark where it stood and where you last saw it. Then wait (Tip).
  • You must make all reasonable effort to find it 95%.

More: wounded animal details
  • Mark the spot where the animal stood when you shot and the spot where you last saw it, then wait (Tip).
  • Wait about 30 minutes for a heart or lung hit; hours for a single lung, liver or gut hit 65%. Pushing a wounded animal makes it run farther 70%.
  • Blood: bright pink and frothy is lungs. Dark red is liver or muscle. A green or brown smear is gut 65%.
  • Snow makes blood easy to see and shows the bed, the stumble, and the drag of a leg. Mark every blood spot with flagging you will remove later (Tip).
  • Lost the blood? Walk small circles out from the last spot and check every trail leaving it. A wounded deer often heads downhill and toward water or thick cover 60%.
  • You must make all reasonable effort to locate, dispatch and retrieve game you kill, cripple or wound 95%. Synopsis page 12, Retrieval.
  • Full after the shot steps: After the shot.

• Set a turn around time and keep it (Tip).
  • Leave a . Carry a (Tip).
Warning

Region 3: no motor vehicles except snowmobiles above 1,700 m off roads and trails 95%. Never shoot from a vehicle 95%.

More: safety details and the snowmobile rules
  • Snow tracking pulls you far from the truck. Set a turn around time before you start and keep it (Tip).
  • Leave a with someone at home. Carry a in the Thompson backcountry (Tip). See Bush safety.
  • Avalanche terrain starts around 30 degrees of slope once there is enough snow to slide. Open slopes, gullies and the run outs below them can slide in November 70%. Avalanche Canada forecasts cover the North Columbia and South Columbia regions near Kamloops 65%.
  • An AST (Avalanche Skills Training) level 1 course is 2 days. Take it before you hunt steep snow country (Tip).
  • Cold: wet feet and a sweaty back at dusk are the start of hypothermia. Layer, stop to vent, carry a dry base layer (Tip). See What to wear.
  • River and lake ice in November is not trustworthy. Do not cross to save a kilometre (Tip).
  • Driving: FSRs (Forest Service Roads) in snow need chains, a shovel and a tow strap. Tell your brother which road (Tip).
Warning

Region 3: motor vehicles except snowmobiles are prohibited above 1,700 m except on existing roads and trails 95%. Snowmobiles may not be used for hunting year round in (Management Unit) areas 3-45 and 3-46, and from 1 April to 14 December in MU 3-28 95%. Shooting wildlife from a motor vehicle is unlawful anywhere 95%.

• A buck is not worth a night out (Tip).
More: when to stop, in words
  • Stop when legal light ends: one hour after sunset for game other than migratory birds 95%. Mark the track and come back at first light (Tip).
  • Stop when the track crosses into terrain you cannot handle: avalanche slopes, cliffs, ice, or private land without consent (Tip).
  • Stop when the animal is walking steadily in a straight line and the day is half gone. It is not bedding; you will not catch it 60%.
  • Stop when you are tired, wet or unsure of the way out. A buck is not worth a night out (Tip).
  • Stop and back out if you find fresh grizzly or cougar tracks on top of your own (Tip).
  • A wounded animal changes the rule: keep going while there is light and safe ground, and return at first light if you lose it (95% on the duty to retrieve, Tip on the method).

• December to February teaches you deer numbers (Tip).
  • Keep your distance: deep snow costs deer fat (Tip).
More: winter scouting details
  • December to February on winter range teaches you more about deer numbers than any October walk (Tip).
  • Count trails, beds and browse lines on south and west slopes below about 760 m north of Kamloops 80%.
  • Note where tracks cross roads; those are year round crossings (Tip).
  • Bucks drop antlers from late December into March. Shed hunting in spring shows you where bucks wintered 70%.
  • Keep your distance in winter. Pushing deer in deep snow costs them fat they cannot replace (Tip).
  • Snowshoe hare and grouse tracks tell you where small game lives for a .22 LR (Long Rifle) or shotgun day (Tip). Check seasons in the 85%.
Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Snow tells the truth. Walk the track backward to learn, forward to hunt, and home before dark either way.

Common mistakes
  • Reading a 3 day old track as fresh on a cold shaded slope.
  • Following a wounded deer 10 minutes after the shot. It runs a kilometre and you lose it.
  • Chasing a track onto steep open snow with no avalanche training or gear.
Do this in the field

After the first snow, pick a deer trail and backtrack it for 1 hour. Find where it fed, where it crossed a road or creek, and where it bedded. Draw the route on your map and in the Journal.

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Snow tells the truth. Walk the track backward to learn, forward to hunt, and home before dark either way.

Common mistakes
  • Reading a 3 day old track as fresh on a cold shaded slope.
  • Following a wounded deer 10 minutes after the shot. It runs a kilometre and you lose it.
  • Chasing a track onto steep open snow with no avalanche training or gear.

Do this in the field

After the first snow, backtrack one deer trail for 1 hour. Find where it fed, crossed and bedded. Draw the route in the Journal.

sign-drill:
Why it matters

Reading sign is a skill, and skills are built on your feet. One walk with this list teaches more than ten sessions on the couch.

  • One walk, 2 to 3 hours, 10 kinds of sign. Score yourself.
  • Do it before your first hunt and again after the first snow (Tip).
More: the drill in full
  • The drill: one walk of 2 to 3 hours near Heffley Creek or anywhere in Region 3 (Thompson). Find 10 kinds of sign, record each, score yourself.
  • Do it before your first deer hunt, then again after the first snow. Compare scores (Tip).
  • Take your brother. Two sets of eyes find twice the sign and it is safer (Tip).
  • Everything you need is in the last four sessions: Tracks, Reading sign, Trails and funnels, Food, water and cover.

• An edge with water: grass against fir, cut block against timber (Tip).
  • Mid morning: deer are bedded, you will not bump them (Tip).
More: where, when and the land rules
  • Pick ground with an edge: grassland against Douglas fir, a cut block against timber, a hayfield against cottonwoods (Tip).
  • Include water: a creek crossing, a stock pond, a lake edge (Tip).
  • Go mid morning. Deer are bedded, you are not hunting, and you will not bump them if you stay out of thick timber (Tip).
  • Crown land is open to walk. Cultivated land and grazing leases with livestock need consent to hunt, and enclosed land is trespass without permission 85%. See BC rules.
  • Lac du Bois grassland inside the City of Kamloops boundary: no firearm discharge 95%, but it is a superb sign walk (Tip).
  • Heffley Creek (Management Unit): VERIFY on the official map before you carry a rifle.

• A ruler in every photo (Tip).
  • Carry a firearm and you are hunting: all the rules apply 95%.
More: the kit list in full
  • Small tape measure or ruler, nitrile gloves, a stick, phone for photos, a notebook or the Journal (Tip).
  • Binoculars, water, bear spray, a map with the walk marked, a satellite messenger if there is no signal (Tip).
  • A ruler in every photo. A track without scale is a guess later (Tip).
  • Flagging tape only if you take it out again (Tip).
  • If you carry a firearm, you are hunting: licences on you, the season open in that MU, legal hours, and no loaded firearm in the truck 95%.

More: photos, Journal lines and bonus items
  • One photo per item with the ruler, plus the time and a map pin (Tip).
  • Write one line per item in the Journal: what, who, how old, which direction (Tip).
  • Bonus items: a kill site seen from a distance, a browse line, a shed antler, a stot trail, a snow roost (Tip).

• One point per item found, named and aged (Tip).
  • Walked through a bedding area at midday? Lose all points (Tip).
More: the full scoring rules
ScoreRatingNext step
0 to 3Beginner eyesWalk slower. Stop every 50 m and look at the ground for a full minute (Tip)
4 to 6Getting itYou see sign. Now age it and say which way it went, every time (Tip)
7 to 8ReaderPick a glassing point from what you found and sit it at dusk this week (Tip)
9 to 10TrackerDo the drill again after snow and add 3 bonus items (Tip)
  • One point per checklist item found, named and aged. A guess with no reason scores half (Tip).
  • Lose a point for every item you touched bare handed or knelt over (Tip).
  • Lose all points if you walked through a bedding area at midday to find beds (Tip).
  • Two extra points if you can draw the walk from memory: trail, water, feed, bed and your stand (Tip).

Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

  • Close every gate you open. Give bulls room (Tip).
  • Leave a covered carcass alone (Tip).
More: safety and the rules in full
  • Bears are feeding hard in October. Talk, keep spray on your belt, and leave a covered carcass alone (Tip).
  • Cattle on Crown range: close every gate you open and give bulls room (Tip).
  • Hunting on cultivated land, or on Crown land under a grazing lease with livestock on it, needs the consent of the owner, lessee or occupant 95%. Synopsis page 12, item 53.
  • It is unlawful to intentionally bait or feed ungulates within 200 m of a dwelling, school yard or playground in Region 3 95%. Region 3 synopsis page 33.
  • Discharge of firearms and bows is prohibited on the part of Lac du Bois Grasslands Protected Area and Crown land inside the City of Kamloops boundary 95%. Region 3 synopsis page 33.
  • A wireless camera for hunting is unlawful from 1 August to 10 December, and all year in Region 1 99%. Synopsis page 11, item 30 (2 October 2026 edition). A drone on a hunting expedition is unlawful 99%. Item 36.
Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Look at the ground until the ground looks back. Then look up, because the deer already has.

Common mistakes
  • Walking fast to cover ground. Sign is found at a crawl.
  • Photographing a track with nothing for scale.
  • Scoring yourself 10 because you saw lots of deer poop.
Do this in the field

Book the drill for this week: 3 hours, mid morning, an edge with water. Take the list, the ruler and your brother. Score it in the Journal.

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Look at the ground until the ground looks back. Then look up, because the deer already has.

Common mistakes
  • Walking fast to cover ground. Sign is found at a crawl.
  • Photographing a track with nothing for scale.
  • Scoring yourself 10 because you saw lots of deer poop.

Do this in the field

Book the drill this week: 3 hours, mid morning, an edge with water. Take the list, the ruler and your brother. Score it in the Journal.

habitat-deer:
Why it matters

You cannot hunt deer until you can see deer country. Learn the look of the land, the plants and the sign, and every walk turns into scouting.

  • This is a photo walk. Look first, then read the bullets under each set of photos.
  • Three kinds of deer country near our bases: Kamloops grassland and fir edge, burns and cut blocks up the North Thompson, and the wet coast forest around Mission (Tip).
  • Mule deer and white tails live in the Interior; the Columbian black tailed deer lives on the coast and in the Fraser Valley 85%.
  • Plants here are the ones from Food, water and cover. Now you see them.
  • Photos come from many places with the same plants. Captions say where (Tip).
• Look for the line where grass meets timber. That edge is where mule deer feed at dusk and dawn (Tip).

• Winter range is the steep south and west facing slopes with old Douglas fir, often below about 760 m north of Kamloops 85%.
  • Draws and gullies hold shrubs, shade and the last green feed in a dry fall 80%.
  • Lac du Bois itself is a no shooting area inside the City of Kamloops boundary 95%. It is a classroom, not a hunting spot (Tip).
• Bitterbrush: grey green shrub on dry slopes, tiny 3 toothed leaves 75%. Key mule deer browse on dry grassland 80%.

• Sagebrush: deer eat little of it, but it marks the dry, low country deer use in winter 70%.
  • Snowbrush (ceanothus) springs up after fire and logging and is good deer browse 75%. Source: E Flora BC and Parish and others, Plants of Southern Interior BC.
  • Look for twigs that end in a torn, ragged tip. Deer have no top front teeth, so they tear 80%.
• Saskatoon: shrub 1 to 4 m, oval leaves toothed on the top half, purple berries in July 80%. Top deer browse all year 80%.

• Rose: thorny stems and red hips; hips and twigs are eaten in fall and winter 75%.
  • Red osier dogwood: bright red stems, white berries, wet ground; a favourite fall and winter browse 80%.
  • A draw with these shrubs plus water is a deer kitchen. Glass it at first light (Tip).
• After a fire or logging, shrubs and forbs sprout for years. Burns and cut blocks are feed 80%.

• Mule deer often stay high in September in subalpine meadows, old burns and cut blocks 75%.
  • Douglas fir: soft flat needles, cones with 3 pointed bracts 85%. Winter food and thermal cover 85%.
  • Kinnikinnick: evergreen mat, leathery spoon shaped leaves, red berries 80%. It tells you the ground is dry and open (Tip).
• Black tailed deer fall and winter food: salal, red huckleberry, trailing blackberry, Douglas fir, western red cedar, deer fern and tree lichens 80%.

• Spring and summer: grasses, fireweed, salmonberry, willow and maple 80%.
  • Thick second growth and blackberry tangles are cover; cut block and power line edges are feed (Tip).
  • Winter pushes coast deer to low, south facing slopes and floodplains with little snow 80%.
• A deer track is a split heart, pointed end forward, about 5 to 9 cm long for an adult 80%.

• Trails run from beds to feed to water. Follow one and you learn the daily loop (Tip).
  • Fresh: sharp edges, no debris in the print. Old: crumbled edges, leaves or rain marks inside 75%.
  • In snow, deep drag marks between prints mean deep snow and a tired deer. Leave winter range deer alone (Tip).
• Deer pellets are about 1 to 1.5 cm long, oval, often with a point at one end 75%.

• Shiny and soft means hours old; dull, hard and pale means days to weeks 70%. Many piles in late fall mark winter range 65%.
  • Clumped pellets mean soft green feed; separate pellets mean dry browse 70%.
  • Rubs: bucks strip bark off saplings with their antlers from late summer through the rut 80%. A line of rubs marks a buck's travel route (Tip).
Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Grandpa's rule (wisdom): Find the edge, find the water, find the shade. The deer are where all three touch.

Common mistakes
  • Walking the open grass at noon. The deer are bedded in the trees beside it.
  • Calling every twig a browse sign. Check for the ragged deer tear, not the clean hare cut.
  • Learning plants from photos only. Touch, crush and smell them once in the field.
Do this in the field

Walk one draw from bottom to top. Find saskatoon, rose and snowberry, one deer track and one pellet pile. Photograph each with your hand for scale. Then find the nearest water and the nearest fir patch.

habitat-ducks:
Why it matters

Ducks live by water, food and shelter from wind. Learn to read a pond, a marsh and a wet field, and you know where ducks will land before they do.

  • This is a photo walk. Look at the water, the plants on its edge and the fields around it.
  • Two kinds of duck country near our bases: Interior ponds, potholes and lake marshes around Kamloops and the Okanagan, and the farm fields and sloughs of the Fraser Valley near Mission (Tip).
  • Dabbling ducks, like mallards and pintails, feed in shallow water by tipping up 85%. Diving ducks dive for food in deeper water 85%.

• Interior fall migration mostly ends by late November with freeze up 75%. On the coast, ducks stay all winter 70%.
  • Species ID is in Ducks. This session is the places.
• Shallow water with plants on the edge beats deep, bare water for dabblers 80%.

• Look for the calm side. On a windy day ducks sit in the lee of a point or a tall reed bed (Tip).
  • Small ponds freeze first. Big lakes and the rivers stay open longer and hold late ducks 75%.
  • Tranquille, at the head of Kamloops Lake, is a staging marsh and a No Shooting area on Map C17 85%.
• Cattail: tall, flat leaves and a brown sausage shaped head 85%. Cover and nesting, not much food 75%.

• Pondweeds: leaves float on the surface; ducks eat the seeds and the plants 80%. Source: Ducks Unlimited Canada and E Flora BC.
  • A gap in the cattails with pondweed in the open water is a landing spot. Set up with the wind at your back facing that gap (Tip).
• Fraser Valley fields, sloughs and the delta are a major wintering area. Fields flood after rain and ducks feed on stubble and grass 70%.

• Bert Brink Wildlife Management Area: open fields "partly flooded in the winter" draw wigeon and Canada geese 90%.
  • Pitt Addington Marsh, at the south end of Pitt Lake, is wintering, migration and breeding habitat for waterfowl 90%.
  • Field hunting needs the farmer's consent 95%. Ask early, in person (Tip).
• Webbed tracks, droppings and loose feathers on a mud bar mean ducks loaf there 75%.

• Beaver dams make flooded timber and shallow edges that ducks love 75%.
  • A pond with fresh sign at noon is a pond to sit at dawn (Tip).
  • Never hunt near bait: not within 400 m of a place where bait was put out, unless it has been bait free for at least 7 days 95%.
Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Grandpa's rule (wisdom): Ducks land into the wind. Sit with the wind at your back and let them come to your face.

Common mistakes
  • Setting up on the windy side of the pond. The ducks are on the calm side.
  • Picking deep, bare water. Dabblers want shallow water with plants.
  • Scouting at noon and hunting the same spot without checking where they actually fly at dawn.
Do this in the field

Visit one pond or slough near home at sunrise. Note the wind direction, where ducks sit, where they land, and what plants grow at that spot. Draw it in the Journal.

habitat-upland:
Why it matters

Upland birds live in small, exact places. Learn to see the brushy edge, the aspen draw and the berry slope, and you stop walking empty country.

  • This is a photo walk through four kinds of bird cover near our bases (Tip).
  • California quail: Okanagan valley bottoms, farms and towns 85%.
  • Ruffed grouse: aspen, creek bottoms and mixed forest edges 80%.
  • Dusky and spruce grouse: higher conifer forest, ridges and the subalpine 80%.
  • Bird ID is in Grouse and Quail, chukar, partridge and pheasant. This session is the places.
• California quail live mainly in the Okanagan and Kettle valleys, mostly at 250 to 500 m and rarely above 750 m 85%.

• They seldom go more than 15 to 30 m from thick cover 75%. Find the brush and you find the birds.
  • They favour farmland and suburbs 85%. Most coveys sit on private land: ask first 75%.
  • There is no quail season in Region 2 (Lower Mainland) or Region 3 (Thompson) 90%. Quail are a Region 8 (Okanagan) bird.
• Ruffed grouse are most common at 750 to 1,250 m in BC 85%.

• They stay in a small area all year, often 2.4 to 16 ha 70%.
  • Aspen: smooth white bark, round leaves that shake in the wind 85%. Buds are winter grouse food 80%.
  • Walk old roads and trails through aspen and berry brush in October. Grouse come to the edges to pick grit and clover (Tip).

• Dusky grouse move uphill in fall into dense conifers and eat needles in winter 70%.
  • Many dusky grouse are seen at 1,500 to 2,250 m 85%.
  • Spruce grouse are conifer specialists that eat pine and spruce needles 85%.
  • Spruce grouse sit tight and trust their camouflage. Look up and look slowly (Tip).
• Grouse tracks show 3 long toes forward and a short one back, about 5 cm long 75%.

• In deep, soft snow ruffed grouse dive in and roost under the snow for warmth 80%.
  • A hole with wing marks beside it means the bird flew out from under the snow 75%.
  • Fresh tracks in new snow mean the bird is close. Follow slowly and be ready (Tip).
Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Grandpa's rule (wisdom): Hunt the edges, not the middle. Birds live where two kinds of cover meet.

Common mistakes
  • Walking the open field for quail. They are in the brush beside it.
  • Hunting grouse in dark timber in October when they are out on the berry and aspen edges.
  • Rushing a fresh track line in snow. Slow down; the bird is often within 50 m (Tip).
Do this in the field

Find one aspen stand with berry shrubs on its edge. Walk its border slowly at mid morning. Note every grouse you flush, the plant it came from and the height. Write it in the Journal.

habitat-big-game:
Why it matters

Big animals leave big sign. Learn their food, their water and their marks, and you can tell from one walk whether a moose, an elk or a bear lives there.

  • This is a photo walk: moose country, elk country, bear food, then the tracks and sign of each.
  • Moose: willow swamps, lake edges, beaver ponds, burns and cut blocks 85%. The Bonaparte Plateau north of Kamloops is a provincial moose study area 90%.
  • Elk: few near our bases; about 1,350 in the Thompson Okanagan area in 2000 85%. Roosevelt elk were released near Chehalis, not far from Mission 85%.
  • Black bears: everywhere near our bases, following the food from spring greens to fall berries and fish 85%.
  • Carry bear spray on every walk in this country (Tip).
• Winter moose browse: red osier dogwood, cottonwood, birch, aspen, willow and subalpine fir 85%.

• On plateaus, summer moose spread out near lake shores, swamps and beaver ponds; in winter they gather in river valleys, burns, logged areas and wetland complexes 85%.
  • Moose move easily in snow up to 40 cm deep and often winter where the snow is 50 cm or more 85%.
  • Willow: long narrow leaves, grows in wet ground and cut blocks 80%. Look for broken twig tops up to 2 m high (Tip).
• A moose track is about 13 to 15 cm long, more than twice a deer track 75%.

• Moose step over deep snow and logs; the trail is a trough with deep holes, not a line of prints (Tip).
  • Moose pellets are big, oval, about 2.5 to 3 cm long, and piles are large 75%.
  • Fresh tracks at a beaver pond edge at dawn: sit there the next evening (Tip).
• The elk rut is mid September; most cows are bred mid to late September 85%.

• Bull elk dig and roll in wallows and rub trees with their antlers in the rut 80%. Fresh mud and bright wood mean a bull is near (Tip).
  • Elk tracks are about 9 to 11 cm long, rounder than a deer track 75%.
  • Interior elk spend summer in subalpine basins and avalanche tracks and move down with autumn snow 85%.

• Spring bear food: meadows, estuaries, stream sides, skunk cabbage, avalanche chutes, grassy south slopes and burns 85%.
  • Fall bear food: berries and spawning fish 85%.

• Soopolallie berries ripen in July and August; huckleberries in August and September 70%.
  • Huckleberry: shrub to about 1.5 m, thin oval leaves, dark purple berries, in mountain forest and old burns 80%. Source: E Flora BC.
• Bear tracks show 5 toes and a wide pad; the hind track looks like a short, wide human foot 80%.

• Berry filled scat on a trail means a berry patch is close and in use (Tip).
  • Black bears den in mid October to late November in the Interior and come out in April and May 75%.
  • Fresh sign, a carcass smell or ravens circling: back out, talk loudly, and keep bear spray ready (Tip).
Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Grandpa's rule (wisdom): Find the groceries and you find the big animals. Willow for moose, wet meadows for elk, berries for bears.

Common mistakes
  • Calling every big track a moose. Check the size: elk tracks are smaller and rounder.
  • Walking into a berry patch with the wind at your back. The bear smells you; you do not see it.
  • Hunting dry timber for moose. They want water and willow.
Do this in the field

Walk the edge of one wetland or beaver pond. Find browsed willow or dogwood, one big track and one scat. Measure the track and photograph everything with a ruler. Decide: moose, elk, deer or bear?

• BC Ministry of Environment species accounts (2000 to 2001): Moose in BC, Elk in BC, Black Bears in BC, checked 2026-10-03 85%.
  • BC moose research progress report 2016 (Bonaparte Plateau study area), checked 2026-10-03 90%.
  • Habitat Conservation Trust Foundation, Return of the Roosevelts, checked 2026-10-03 85%.
  • Gaines 2003, Canadian Field Naturalist, and WildSafeBC black bear page: den dates 75%.
  • Elbroch, Mammal Tracks and Sign (Stackpole, 2003): track and pellet sizes, wallows, rubs, claw marks (75% to 80%).
  • E Flora BC: willow, dogwood, huckleberry, soopolallie (75% to 85%). Berry timing is local knowledge 70%.
  • Photos: Wikimedia Commons, credits under each photo and on the Photo credits page. Checked 2026-10-04.
migration:
Why it matters

The deer you scouted in August can be 50 km away by November. Know where each animal goes and when.

  • Snow depth, cold and food move them 85%.
  • General patterns, not mapped routes. Your valley can run 2 weeks early or late (Tip).
More: the 4 groups and the map slider
  • Three ways animals use the year (my grouping of the sources below):
    • Up and down migrants: mule deer, black tailed deer, moose, elk, bighorn sheep, mountain goats. Summer high, winter low.
    • Upside down migrant: dusky grouse. Breeds lower and more open, winters higher in dense conifers.
    • Residents: white tailed deer, ruffed and spruce grouse, California quail, chukar, black bear. Short moves only.
    • Long distance migrants: ducks and geese on the Pacific Flyway.
  • What moves them: snow depth, cold and food 85%. For mule deer the rut does not trigger the move down; snow and cold do 85%.
  • Everything here is a general pattern for southern BC, not a mapped route. Your valley can run 2 weeks early or late (Tip).
  • The Spot Finder map's month slider uses this same data. Set the month, read the elevation band, then scout it.

• Valley grass and pine low, spruce and subalpine fir high 90%.
More: the zones and their elevations
  • Zones from the valley up (90%, BC Ministry of Forests):
    • BG (Bunchgrass): valley floor to 700 to 1,000 m.
    • PP (Ponderosa Pine): 335 to 900 m.
    • IDF (Interior Douglas fir): about 350 to 1,450 m.
    • MS (Montane Spruce): about 1,100 to 1,700 m.
    • ESSF (Engelmann Spruce Subalpine Fir): about 1,200 to 2,300 m. Alpine above.
  • Near Heffley Creek: valley grass and pine benches are the low band; spruce and subalpine fir toward Sun Peaks are the high band (my reading of the zone map, 65%).

• Summer high, winter low 85%.
  • The move down: October to December, earlier in a snowy fall 75%.

More: month by month
  • December to March: . Steep south and west facing slopes with shrubs and old Douglas fir, below deep snow 85%. Near Kamloops the studied range sits below about 760 m 80%.
  • April: green up on low south facing grass, the best month to see big groups 85%.
  • April to May: most migrants head for summer range 85%.
  • June to September: moister high country 85%. Openings, cutblocks and burns are the feed to check (Tip). Fawns are born late May to June 85%. Some deer stay low all year 85%.
  • October to November: back to winter range. In 2019 nearly all collared deer were back by mid October 85%. An older BC account says many stay high until December 85%. Plan on October to December, earlier in a snowy fall (my reading, 75%).
  • Rut: November and early December 85%. See .

• Same path down in fall as up in spring 85%.
  • Trouble past 30 cm of snow, gone by 50 cm 75%.
More: distances, triggers and winter range maps
  • In the SIMDeer (Southern Interior Mule Deer Project) study, 74% of collared deer that could migrate did, averaging 47.2 km a year 85%.
  • An earlier update put the average trip at 55 km. One doe went 102 km in a straight line, from near Apex Mountain to west of Aspen Grove, in 11 days 85%.
  • Most deer use nearly the same path down in fall as up in spring 85%.
  • The trigger is snow and cold, not the rut 85%.
  • Deer struggle in snow over about 30 cm and leave a slope by about 50 cm (75%, two sources combined).
  • No official winter range is mapped around Kamloops and Heffley Creek. The mapped ones sit south toward Merritt and in the Okanagan (90%, provincial map layer).

• White tails: valley bottoms all year, short moves 85%.
  • Black tails: some migrate, some stay put 80%.
More: white tail and black tail details
  • White tails: valley bottoms with farmland all year. Short moves only: up or down the valley, or across it from north slopes in summer to south slopes in winter (85%, BC account built on Kootenay data).
  • White tail summer: floodplains, river terraces, hay and alfalfa. Early winter: aspen, cottonwood and willow along rivers, then conifer patches as snow deepens 85%.
  • White tail rut peaks in November. Fawns are born late May or June 85%.
  • Black tails (Mission, Hope): some migrate within one watershed, some stay put. Migrants use about 1,770 hectares a year, residents about 140 hectares 80%.
  • Black tail winter: low old forest, warm south slopes and floodplains. Above 1,000 m is rarely used in winter 80%. Rut in November and early December 80%.
  • Black tail dates come from Vancouver Island studies. No Fraser Valley collar study was found, so treat the dates as rough (Tip).

• Moose stay high longest and handle 40 cm of snow 85%.
  • Elk: up in May and June, down with autumn snow 85%.
More: moose and elk details
  • Moose in the mountains: summer high, winter in valley bottoms; some stay in the valleys all year 85%.
  • Moose on plateaus (the Bonaparte is one): summer spread out near lakes, swamps and beaver ponds; winter packed into river valleys, burns, cutblocks and wetland complexes 85%.
  • Moose stay high in fall longer than deer, elk or sheep and drift down slowly 85%. They walk easily in 40 cm of snow and often winter in 50 cm or more 85%.
  • Most moose calves are conceived in late September and early October, and born in late May and June 85%.
  • Elk: up to subalpine basins in May and June, bulls first; autumn snow pushes them back down 85%. Rut in mid September 85%.
  • Few elk near your bases: about 1,350 in the Thompson Okanagan area in 2000 (85% for that year).

• Bighorn: low steep south grass in winter, alpine in summer 85%.
  • Goats stay within 400 to 500 m of cliffs 85%.
More: sheep and goat details
  • Bighorn: winter and spring on low, steep south to southwest grassland, 300 to 1,825 m 85%.
  • Lambs are born from the last week of April to early June, in cliffs near winter range 85%.
  • Migratory herds go to alpine pastures in May or June and return in late September or October when snow covers the feed. Many Fraser River sheep stay low all year 85%.
  • Bighorn rut: early November to mid December 85%.
  • Goats: interior goats summer at or above treeline, drop lower in spring for green up and mineral licks, then winter on windswept high slopes or bluffs near treeline. Coastal goats winter lower, in old forest near cliffs 85%.
  • Goats rarely go more than 400 to 500 m from cliffs. Rut runs early November to early December, peak 15 to 20 November 85%.

• Not a migrant: follows food in its home range 85%.
  • Interior bears den about 5 to 7 months 85%.
More: den and food details
  • Not a migrant. Bears follow food inside home ranges of about 5 to 150 km2 85%.
  • Asleep: interior bears den about 5 to 7 months, south coast bears 3 to 5 85%. Cubs are born in January or February 85%.
  • Out: a study in the northeast Cascades of Washington, just south of BC, had males out 4 April to 7 May and females 4 April to 22 May 80%.
  • Spring: grassy south slopes, meadows, riparian strips, avalanche chutes and burns 85%.
  • Summer and fall: berries, then spawning fish on the coast; fall is a feeding binge 80%.
  • In: the same study had dens entered 15 October to 19 November 80%. WildSafeBC says most bears are denned December to April 75%.

Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

  • Fall migration: late September to late November, as lakes freeze 75%.
  • Tranquille: No Shooting 85%. Vaseux Lake: no hunting 99%.
More: flyway details and named water
  • Fall migration is well under way by late September and mostly over by late November, when interior lakes freeze (75%, Ducks Unlimited).
  • High plateau lakes freeze first; birds then crowd onto open valley water and the coast (my reading, 60%).
  • Named wintering water: the South Thompson River from Little Shuswap Lake to Kamloops Lake, Vaseux Lake, and the Fraser delta and valley marshes (80 to 90%, Important Bird Area and Wildlife Management Area pages).
  • Tranquille, at the head of Kamloops Lake, is spring and fall staging for geese and swans 90%. It is a No Shooting area (85%, synopsis Map C17). Vaseux Lake is a bird sanctuary with no hunting (99%, synopsis page 67).
  • Snow geese reach the Fraser delta by early October, peak mid October to mid December, mostly shift to the Skagit in Washington late December to February, return mid March to mid April, then fly home to Wrangel Island, Russia 80%.
  • Mallard, goldeneye and wood duck nest on interior wetlands such as Tranquille 90%.

• Dusky grouse climb into conifers in fall 70%.
  • Ruffed grouse stay home; young birds scatter 70%.
More: grouse details
  • Ruffed grouse: resident on a home range of about 2.4 to 16 hectares (70%, US agency data). In fall the young birds scatter to new ground, the "fall shuffle"; adults stay put 70%.
  • Most ruffed grouse in BC live at 750 to 1,250 m 85%.
  • Dusky (blue) grouse: in fall they walk and fly from open breeding ground up into dense conifers and eat needles all winter, up to about 48 km but usually much less 70%.
  • They come back down to breed in late March or April 70%. In BC many breed high anyway, at 1,500 to 2,250 m 85%.
  • Spruce grouse: resident in conifers; on the ground late spring to early fall, in the trees eating needles in winter 75%. Some move up to 9.5 km between summer and winter ranges 70%.
  • Around Mission the blue grouse is the sooty grouse. Washington sources say it also moves to higher conifers in fall, but not everywhere 60%.

• Quail stay within 15 to 30 m of cover 75%.
  • Chukar drop onto low south slopes in heavy snow 75%.
More: quail, chukar, pheasant and turkey
  • California quail do not migrate 75%. A stays on a small range all winter, about 7 to 18 hectares in a California study 75%.
  • In BC they live in the Okanagan and Kettle valleys, mostly below 750 m and most often at 250 to 500 m, on farm, orchard and suburban edges with thick brush 85%.
  • They seldom go more than 15 to 30 m from cover 75%. Winter coveys grow larger, and a hard winter is what kills them (60 to 70%).
  • Chukar stay too, but drop lower and onto south slopes in heavy snow 75%. In 1962 they ran from Lytton to Kamloops at 195 to 610 m 80%.
  • Chukar winter flocks break up in late February; coveys form again from mid June 80%.
  • Pheasant: resident, mostly below 500 m 80%. Wild turkey: resident, spreading into the south Okanagan 80%.

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Wisdom, not law: follow the snow line and the green line. Fall snow pushes them down, spring green pulls them up. Hunt the edge between.

Common mistakes
  • Scouting a high basin in August and hunting it in late November. The migrants left.
  • Thinking the rut brings mule deer down. Snow and cold move them; the rut changes how they act.
  • Hunting grouse only in the valley in October. Dusky grouse are climbing into the conifers by then.

Do this in the field

Every trip: date, snow line, lowest green feed, each animal and its elevation. One season makes your own map.

• BC Ministry of Environment species accounts, read directly 2026-10-03: mule and black tailed deer, white tailed deer, moose, elk, bighorn sheep, black bear 85%.
  • Management Plan for the Mountain Goat in BC, 2010, read 2026-10-03 85%.
  • BC Wildlife Federation, Southern Interior Mule Deer Project pages: project, 2020 update, 2019 update, read 2026-10-03 85%.
  • Monteith and others 2011, migration trigger; Willms 1976, Kamloops winter range; checked 2026-10-01 (80 to 85%).
  • Ungulate Winter Range layer, queried 2026-10-03 90%.

• Meidinger and Pojar 1991, Ecosystems of BC, zone chapters, read 2026-10-03 90%.
  • Black tails: Gold River wildlife report and McNay and Voller, read 2026-10-03 80%.
  • Bears: Gaines 2003 80% and WildSafeBC 75%, read 2026-10-03.
  • Waterfowl: Ducks Unlimited 2024 and 2025 field reports 75%; Reifel snow geese 80%; Important Bird Areas South Thompson River and Vaseux Lake (80 to 85%); Tranquille Wildlife Management Area page 90%; all read 2026-10-03.
  • Synopsis 2026 to 2028, 2 October 2026 edition, pages 35 and 67, read 2026-10-03 (85 to 99%).

  • Grouse movement: Audubon, Colorado Parks and Wildlife, Vermont ruffed grouse, Birdweb sooty grouse, Vermont Spruce Grouse Recovery Plan citing Herzog and Keppie 1980 (60 to 70%); read 2026-10-03.

landforms-101:
Why it matters

Animals move, bed and feed by the shape of the land. Name the shape and you can guess the animal.

  • Seven shapes run almost every hunt: ridge, spur, draw, saddle, bench, knob, bowl.
  • You will learn each one three ways: topo map, Hunt Map in 3D, on the ground.
More: what this lesson covers and how it builds
  • This lesson goes deeper than Maps 1: reading terrain. That lesson taught contour lines, scale and steepness. This one is a field guide to the shapes.
  • For each shape: what it is, how it looks on a topo map, how it looks on the Hunt Map tilted in 3D, how it looks when you stand on it, and why animals and hunters care.
  • A contour line joins points of the same height. Picture water rising around a hill: every shoreline is a contour 98%.
  • On the Hunt Map in metres, contour lines are every 20 m with a thicker index line every 100 m (99%, app settings, read from the app code).
  • Animal use of each shape is mostly hunter observation, not science. It is labelled Tip or given a certainty under 80%.
  • Next lessons build on this: Slope and aspect, Elevation bands, Bedding terrain, Pinch points.

• Topo map: shape from above, in lines.
  • 3D map: the same lines draped over the hills.
  • Ground: what your eyes see from where you stand.
More: why three views
  • A topo map is exact but abstract. The 3D view on the Hunt Map turns the lines back into hills. Your eyes on the ground see only what faces you (Tip).
  • Train all three together. Every time you look at a shape on the map, tilt it in 3D, then find it on the skyline on your next drive (Tip).
  • The Hunt Map 3D view is built from terrain data with about 24 m between height samples, so small cliffs, cut banks and rock bands may not show (95%, app notes).
  • The drawings in this lesson labelled "3D sketch" are hand drawn to show the idea. Your screen will look like a shaded, tilted map, not a painting.

FamilyShapesContour clue
HighRidge, spur, knob, topVs or Us point downhill; closed rings on tops
LowDraw, valley, bowlVs or Us point uphill
Steps and gapsSaddle, bench, cliffHourglass; wide gap; lines touching
  • Learn the families first. The names come easily after.
More: the military list and the hunter list
  • Land navigation manuals use 5 major shapes (hill, saddle, valley, ridge, depression), 3 minor ones (draw, spur, cliff) and 2 made by people (cut and fill) (75%, land navigation references).
  • Hunters add words the manuals do not use: bench, knob, bowl, finger, point. They are plain names for common shapes (Tip).
  • A depression is a low spot with higher ground all around. Its contour rings have small tick marks pointing in 75%. Rare in hunting country, except sinks and potholes.
  • A cut is a road or rail cut through high ground. A fill is a built up bank across low ground. Both show on maps near roads and rail 75%.

• V points uphill: a draw. Water runs down its middle 90%.
  • V points downhill: a ridge or a spur 90%.
More: the V rule in full
  • Where contour lines cross a draw or valley, they bend into a V or U that points uphill, toward higher numbers 90%.
  • Where they cross a ridge or spur, the V or U points downhill, toward lower numbers 90%.
  • Check with water. A blue creek line sits in the V of a draw. A creek never runs along the crest of a ridge 95%.
  • Check with the numbers. The top of each contour number faces uphill 98%.
  • Sharp Vs mean a narrow, steep draw. Round Us mean a broad, gentle one 75%.

Ridge: map, 3D, ground1 of 3
  • A long line of high ground, higher than the land on both sides 90%.
  • Deer and elk travel just below the crest, not on top (Tip).
More: ridge details and how animals use it
  • A ridge is a long strip of high ground. Its crest is higher than the ground on both sides 90%.
  • On a topo map the contour lines make long Us or Vs that point downhill, away from the crest 90%.
  • On the Hunt Map in 3D, a ridge is the line where a sunny face meets a shady face. Turn the map so the sun lights one side (Tip).
  • On the ground, it is the skyline you see from the valley road.
  • Animals: deer and elk often travel a ridge a little below the top, on the side away from the wind, so they are not outlined against the sky (Tip, hunter observation).
  • You: a ridge is a highway for walking and a seat for . Walk just below the crest so your outline does not show (Tip).
  • Morning thermals rise up both faces toward the crest 85%. A ridge top seat in the morning puts your scent above the animals. See Wind and thermals.

Spur: map, 3D, ground1 of 3
  • A short ridge that runs down off a bigger ridge 90%.
  • Each spur has a draw on both sides 90%.
More: spur details and how animals use it
  • A spur is short, sloping high ground that juts out from the side of a ridge 90%. Hunters also call it a finger or a point.
  • On the topo map it is a tongue of U or V shapes pointing downhill, sitting between two draws that point uphill 90%.
  • On the Hunt Map in 3D, spurs look like the knuckles of a hand running off the main ridge (Tip).
  • Animals: the point of a spur, just below the top, gives a bedded deer a view down both draws and the wind from below in the morning (Tip, hunter observation).
  • Trails often climb a spur because the slope is even, then cross into the next draw at the top (Tip).
  • You: a spur is a natural glassing seat. From the end of one spur you can see the faces of the next spur across the draw (Tip).

Draw: map, 3D, ground1 of 3
  • A small valley that runs down a slope 90%.
  • Draws hold water, brush, shade and travel routes 75%.
More: draw details and how animals use it
  • A draw is a small, steep sided valley with little or no flat ground in the bottom. Contours make Vs or Us that point uphill to its head 90%.
  • On the Hunt Map in 3D a draw is a trough. The shady side and the sunny side meet in the bottom (Tip).
  • On the ground, look for a line of darker green: shrubs, aspen, willow, red osier dogwood, chokecherry. They need the extra water 75%.
  • Animals: draws give cover close to food. Mule deer, white tails, grouse and quail use brushy draws to move and hide 70%.
  • Evening thermals and cold air drain down draws 85%. Do not sit at the bottom of a draw in the evening with animals below you.
  • The head of a draw, where it starts near the top, is a common crossing point (Tip). See Pinch points.

Saddle: map, 3D, ground1 of 3
  • The low point on a ridge between two higher points 90%.
  • Animals cross ridges at saddles: least climb, least skyline 65%.
More: saddle details and how animals use it
  • A saddle rises on two sides and falls on two sides. Other names: col, pass, gap, notch 90%.
  • On the topo map it is an hourglass: two sets of closed rings with the lines pinched between them 90%.
  • A saddle can also be just a dip along a level ridge, not always between two big tops 75%.
  • On the Hunt Map in 3D it is the dip in the skyline. Rotate the map to look along the ridge and it pops out (Tip).
  • On the ground it is the low notch on the skyline.
  • Animals: deer and elk cross a ridge at the saddle because it is the easiest climb and keeps them off the high skyline (65%, hunter observation).
  • In the rut, bucks cruise saddles between groups of does 60%. See The rut.
  • You: saddles are classic stand sites. Wind swirls in saddles because air pours through the gap, so check it often (Tip).

Bench: map, 3D, ground1 of 3
  • A flat or gentle shelf on a steep slope 90%.
  • Deer bed and travel on benches 65%.
More: bench details and how animals use it
  • A bench is a flat step on a hillside. On the topo map: tight lines above, a wide gap, tight lines below 90%.
  • A bench can be big (a whole grassland terrace) or tiny (one contour gap). Small ones may not show on 20 m contours: use the 3D view with the height boost up (Tip).
  • On the Hunt Map in 3D a bench is a pale shelf across a dark face. The Slope steepness tool shows it as an uncoloured strip between coloured slopes (95%, app tool shows slopes under 15 degrees uncoloured).
  • On the ground it is the place where you suddenly stop climbing and catch your breath.
  • Animals: a bench gives a bedded deer flat ground, a view down the slope and wind from below in the morning (65%, hunter observation).
  • Trails run along benches because walking on the level costs less energy 65%.
  • You: benches are where to look first when glassing a big face (Tip).
  • Many Thompson valley sides have big flat terraces left by glacial lakes and rivers. They are benches on a giant scale (65%, VERIFY with a local geology source).

Knob: map, 3D, ground1 of 3
  • A small rounded hill or high point 85%.
  • Your best lookout on rolling ground (Tip).
More: knob details and how animals use it
  • A knob is a small top: on the map, a small set of closed contour rings, sometimes only one ring 85%.
  • Hunters also say knoll, hump or high point (Tip).
  • A knob smaller than 20 m tall may not show on 20 m contours at all. Look for a bump in the 3D view or a small closed ring on the satellite with hill shading (Tip).
  • Animals: on rolling grassland, deer often bed on the shoulder of a knob, just below the top, where they can see and smell (Tip, hunter observation).
  • You: climb the back of a knob and glass over the top. Keep your head below the skyline and use the grass or a tree as a screen (Tip).

Bowl: map, 3D, ground1 of 3
  • A rounded basin with high ground on three sides 85%.
  • Hides animals from below. Glass it from the rim (Tip).
More: bowl details and how animals use it
  • A bowl is a rounded basin at the head of a draw or valley. Contours wrap around it in big U shapes, open toward the low side 85%.
  • A high mountain bowl carved by ice is called a cirque. Many hold a small lake or meadow 80%.
  • On the Hunt Map in 3D a bowl looks like an amphitheatre. Turn on Slope steepness: the rim is often coloured red or purple, the floor uncoloured (Tip).
  • Animals: bowls hold feed (meadows, wet seeps) and shade, and wind in a bowl swirls (Tip). Elk and mule deer use high basins in early fall before snow 70%.
  • You: glass a bowl from the rim or from across the valley. Walking the floor puts you in a swirl with eyes above you (Tip).

• Lines touch or merge: a cliff. Plan around it 90%.
  • Small rock bands may not show at all 95%.
More: cliff details
  • A cliff is a vertical or nearly vertical drop. Contour lines merge or nearly touch 90%.
  • On 20 m contours a 15 m rock band can hide between two lines. The 3D view and satellite base help, but trust your eyes on the ground (Tip).
  • On the Hunt Map, Slope steepness colours ground over 45 degrees purple: cliffy, scrambling (99%, app tool key).
  • Cliffs are escape terrain for sheep and goats and a barrier that funnels other animals 85%. See Escape terrain.
  • Never plan a route down a gap you have not seen. Many gaps end in a drop (Tip).

• Find each number before you go on.
  • Then find the same seven on your own hunting map.
More: answer key
  1. Ridge: the skyline from left to right.
  2. Saddle: the dip between the left tops and the big top.
  3. Spur: the finger running down off the ridge on the left.
  4. Draw: the blue creek line with trees.
  5. Bench: the flat brown band across the left face.
  6. Knob: the small rounded hill low on the right.
  7. Bowl: the green basin below the big top.

Find the shapes on the Hunt Map1 of 5
  • Open the Hunt Map at Heffley Creek
More: how the Hunt Map shows each shape
  • 3D: tap 3D in the pill at the bottom right. Tilt with two fingers or the tilt buttons on the left; rotate with the rotate buttons (99%, app).
  • Height boost: tap the base button (Topo), then slide 3D height boost. It runs 1 to 2.5 times, default 1.5 (99%, app). Higher makes benches and saddles pop, but makes slopes look steeper than they are (Tip).
  • Slope steepness colours: 15 to 25 degrees yellow (steady climb), 25 to 30 orange (steep), 30 to 45 red (very steep, avalanche terrain in snow), over 45 purple (cliffy). Under 15 degrees no colour (99%, app key).
  • Elevation profile: the button at the top left. Draw a line and read the climb and drop (99%, app).
  • When the map is tilted past a set angle, minor contour lines hide so the view stays readable (99%, app). Tilt back to see every line.
  • The link above opens the map at the Heffley Creek base point from the app settings (99%, app). Assumption: this is near your main hunting area in MU (Management Unit) 3-27.

• Flat stretch on a climb: bench. Dip between tops: saddle.
  • Sharp drop to a low point: draw.
More: profile tips
  • An elevation profile is a side view of the ground along a line you draw (99%, app).
  • Draw your line straight up a slope, across the contours, to find benches. Draw it along a ridge to find saddles (Tip).
  • The profile also gives the climb in metres. Over 300 m of climb before first light is a hard morning for most beginners (Tip).

• Knuckles are tops. Dips between knuckles are saddles.
  • Fingers are ridges and spurs. Gaps between fingers are draws.
More: using the fist trick
  • This is an old land navigation teaching trick (Tip). Make a fist, knuckles up, and look at it from the side and from above.
  • Draw contour rings on your knuckles with a pen if you like: you will see Vs point down your fingers (spurs) and up the gaps (draws).

ShapeAnimals doYou do
RidgeTravel just below the topWalk below the crest, glass
SpurBed on the pointGlass the next spur
DrawHide, travel, drinkStill hunt into the wind
SaddleCross the ridgeSit downwind of it
BenchBed, travel levelGlass benches first
KnobBed on the shoulderGlass over the top
BowlFeed, rest in shadeGlass from the rim
  • Everything in this table is hunter observation (Tip).
More: why these patterns happen
  • Animals save energy: they avoid climbing when a level route exists, which is why trails follow benches and cross at saddles 65%.
  • Animals want to see danger and smell it: high beds with a view below and wind from below in the morning (Tip).
  • Animals hide: draws and timbered faces give cover close to food 70%.
  • These are patterns, not laws. Pressure, wind, snow and food change them every day (Tip).

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Grandpa's rule (wisdom): The land has a few doors. Learn where they are and you stop chasing the animal and start waiting for it.

Common mistakes
  • Reading a draw as a ridge. Check which way the V points.
  • Trusting 20 m contours for small benches and rock bands.
  • Glassing the whole hill instead of benches, spurs and saddles first.
More: the mistakes in full
  • Reading a draw as a ridge: the V points uphill for a draw, downhill for a ridge. Find the creek line to check.
  • Trusting 20 m contours: a bench, cliff band or knob under 20 m can sit between two lines. Check the 3D view, the satellite base and then your eyes.
  • Glassing everything evenly: start with the shapes animals favour (benches, spur points, saddles, draw edges) and work out from there (Tip).

Do this in the field

On your next drive, name three shapes on the skyline out loud. Then find the same three on the Hunt Map in 3D that night.

• V points to the Very top: a draw. V points down: a ridge.
  • Hourglass, cross the pass: a saddle is where trails cross.
  • Wide gap, take a nap: benches are beds.
  • Fist test: knuckles tops, dips saddles, fingers spurs, gaps draws.
  • RSD SBKB (Ridge, Spur, Draw, Saddle, Bench, Knob, Bowl): "Really Smart Deer Sneak Between Knobs and Bowls".
More: why hooks help
  • Short rhymes and pictures are easier to recall under pressure than definitions (Tip).
  • Say one hook every time you see the shape on a map or a skyline.
