slope-aspect:
Why it matters

Steepness decides where animals feel safe. The way a slope faces decides how warm it is, what grows, and where snow lies.

  • Slope: how steep the ground is.
  • Aspect: which way the slope faces 95%.
More: what this lesson covers
  • Slope and aspect are the two numbers every hillside has. Together they set sun, snow, plants, cover and wind on that slope.
  • This lesson: degrees and percent, reading steepness on the map and the Hunt Map, why south faces are warm in October, what grows on each face, how animals use each face by season and time of day, and safety on steep ground.
  • Builds on Landforms 101 and Maps 1: reading terrain.
  • is in the glossary.

• Percent = rise divided by run, times 100 98%.
  • 45 degrees is 100 percent 98%.
More: the conversion table
DegreesPercentFeels like (Tip)
59Gentle walk
1018Steady walk
1527Hard with a pack
2036Steep, short steps
2547Very steep, zig zag
3058Hands sometimes
3570Scramble
4084Hands and care
45100Climbing
  • Percent = tan(degrees) x 100 (98%, trigonometry). The two scales are not the same: 30 degrees is 58 percent, not 30.
  • Forestry and wildlife reports usually give slope in percent. Avalanche and climbing guides use degrees 85%. Check which one a source means.
  • The feel column is a beginner guide, not a measurement (Tip).

• On the Hunt Map each contour line is 20 m of height (99%, app).
  • Lines per 100 m of ground x 20 = slope in percent 95%.
More: how to measure slope on the Hunt Map
  • Use Measure (in Tools) or the scale bar at the top left to mark 100 m. Count the contour lines crossing it (Tip).
  • Each line is 20 m of rise in metres mode, so 1 line is about 20 percent, 2 lines 40 percent, 5 lines 100 percent (95%, maths).
  • On a 1:50,000 paper map with 20 m lines, count lines per cm instead: 5 lines per cm is 100 m over 500 m, 20 percent. See the table in Maps 1.
  • Faster: turn on Slope steepness and read the colour (next screen).

• Yellow, orange, red, purple: steeper and steeper (99%, app).
  • No colour on a coloured face: a bench or flat (Tip).
More: both colour keys in words
  • Slope steepness: under 15 degrees no colour, 15 to 25 yellow (steady climb), 25 to 30 orange (steep), 30 to 45 red (very steep, avalanche terrain in snow), over 45 purple (cliffy, scrambling) (99%, app key).
  • Slope direction (aspect): north blue, northeast teal, east green, southeast lime, south yellow, southwest orange, west red, northwest purple. Ground flatter than 8 degrees gets no colour (99%, app key).
  • Both are worked out on the phone from terrain samples about 24 m apart. Small cliffs, cut banks and rock bands do not show (95%, app notes).
  • Both work offline in areas you saved with Offline Maps (99%, app).
Turn on the slope tools1 of 3

• Aspect is the way water would run off the slope 95%.
  • A south slope faces south: it looks at the sun.
More: how to read aspect on any map
  • Picture water poured on the slope: the direction it runs downhill is the aspect 95%.
  • On a topo map, aspect is at right angles to the contour lines, toward the lower numbers 95%.
  • On the Hunt Map, turn on Slope direction: the colour tells you the face at a glance (99%, app).
  • On the ground, use your compass: face straight downhill and read the bearing 95%.
  • Forestry guides group aspects: warm is about 135 to 270 degrees (southeast through west), cool about 315 to 90 degrees (northwest through east) (85%, BC silviculture practices for mule deer winter range, 2004).

• Mid October noon sun near Kamloops: about 30 degrees up 95%.
  • A 30 degree north face gets almost no direct sun at noon 90%.
More: the sun maths
  • Noon sun height = 90 minus your latitude plus the sun's declination (98%, astronomy).
  • Heffley Creek is about 50.9 degrees north (99%, app base point). Mid October the declination is about minus 9 degrees, so the noon sun is about 30 degrees up 95%. On 21 December it is about 16 degrees 95%.
  • A south slope tilted 30 degrees toward that sun meets it at about 60 degrees: about 87 percent of full strength. Flat ground gets about 50 percent. A north slope tilted 30 degrees away gets almost nothing (90%, simple noon geometry; real slopes and times vary).
  • In October the sun rises south of east and sets south of west 90%, so a steep north face stays in shade all day.
  • Result: south and west faces dry out, melt snow first and grow grass. North faces stay cool and moist and grow thick timber 80%.

FaceNear Kamloops (typical)
South, southwestBunchgrass, sagebrush, open Douglas fir, ponderosa pine 75%
WestWarm and dry, open timber 70%
EastMixed, first morning sun (Tip)
North, northeastThick Douglas fir and spruce, moss, late snow 75%

• Drive any valley and you see it: grass on one side, timber on the other (Tip).
More: why the plants split
  • Warm aspects lose more water to sun, so trees are fewer and grass and shrubs take over 75%.
  • North aspects "support denser stands of higher crown closures" (85%, BC wildlife habitat rating account, mule deer, 2004).
  • In the Thompson, valley bottoms and warm faces carry bunchgrass, cool faces carry Douglas fir first 75%. See Habitat tour: deer.
  • The same split shows on the Hunt Map Satellite base: pale grass on one face, dark timber on the facing slope (Tip).

AnimalWarm south and west facesCool north faces
Mule deerWinter range, spring green up 85%Hot day beds, deep snow refuge under thick timber 75%
White tailed deerWinter on low warm slopes and floodplains 80%Thick cover beds (Tip)
Bighorn sheepWinter on steep south to southwest grass 85%Rarely (Tip)
Mountain goatWarm aspect winter range 85%Shade in summer heat 70%
Black bearSpring green up (Tip, app)Cool shade, berries later (Tip)
Chukar, quailSouth slopes in snow 75%Rarely (Tip)
  • The colder it gets, the more animals crowd onto warm faces 80%.
More: sources for each row
  • Mule deer: spring feeding "on moderate to steep, south and west facing slopes"; winter in Douglas fir "with south facing, warm aspect slopes where the snowpack is lower"; north aspects used "during severe weather conditions" because their thick timber catches snow (85%, BC wildlife habitat rating account, mule deer, 2004).
  • Mule deer winter range definition: "10 to 45 % slope, having a south and/or west aspect, and below 1500 m" in shallow to moderate snow zones (85%, same account citing US Forest Service 1998).
  • Mule deer summer beds: in Montana and Idaho study sites, deer chose cooler northeast and east aspects with overhead cover (60%, thesis via search preview).
  • White tails: winter on "low, south facing warm slopes or floodplains" (80%, BC account, as logged in research/2026-10-03).
  • Bighorn sheep: winter ranges "tend to be steep, south to southwest facing" bunchgrass (85%, Bighorn Sheep in BC, 2000).
  • Mountain goat: "warm aspect" is a main factor in winter range choice (85%, BC Mountain Goat Management Plan, 2010).
  • Chukar: may move onto south facing slopes in heavy snow (75%, USDA Fire Effects Information System).
  • Black bear spring: Hunt Map Slope direction tip (Tip).

• Cold morning: deer often bed where the first sun hits (Tip).
  • Warm midday: they slide into shade (Tip).
More: daily aspect pattern
  • On cold sunny days, deer often bed where the first sun hits, then move into shade as it warms up (Tip, app Sun and shade tool note).
  • Glass east faces at sunrise and sunny faces early. Glass shady timber edges in the heat of the day (Tip).
  • On warm October afternoons, west faces get the hottest sun: animals bed elsewhere until evening (Tip).
  • The Hunt Map Sun and shade tool lights the map by the real sun for any time today, and shows sunrise and sunset at the map centre (99%, app).

• Steep, broken ground is security cover for mule deer 85%.
  • Gentle ground is easy feeding and easy travel (Tip).
More: slope and animals in detail
  • "Areas of steep broken terrain can also be used as security habitat" for mule deer (85%, BC habitat account citing Nyberg and Janz 1990).
  • When coyotes come, mule deer move to and up slopes; white tails move down and away (75%, Lingle 2002, abstract). See Escape terrain.
  • BC guidance for mule deer winter range timber: moderate to steep slopes, about 40 percent and more (85%, BC silviculture practices, 2004).
  • Hunters avoid steep ground: in one Pennsylvania public forest study, hunters were 1.25 times more likely to use an area for every 10 degree drop in slope (85% for that forest). Steep ground near you may hold less pressured animals (Tip). See Islands of habitat.

• Most avalanches start on 30 to 45 degree slopes 85%.
  • Red on the Hunt Map means avalanche terrain in snow (99%, app).
More: steep ground safety
  • Avalanche Canada: the vast majority of avalanches start on slopes of 30 to 45 degrees; they can happen from about 25 to 60 degrees (85%, search preview).
  • A slide that starts above can run far out onto flat ground below. Do not stop under a red slope after heavy snow (Tip, app note).
  • The Hunt Map slope colours are not an avalanche forecast. Check Avalanche Canada before entering snowy mountains (99%, app note).
  • Shooting on steep ground: hold for the uphill or downhill angle. See the steep stalk lessons in the species section (Tip).
  • Packing meat: a 25 degree slope is hard work loaded. Plan the pack out before the shot (Tip).
  • Wet grass, frost and pine needles on 20 degrees plus are slippery. Unload before steep scrambles (Tip).

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Grandpa's rule (wisdom): Cold morning, look to the sun. Hot noon, look to the shade.

Common mistakes
  • Mixing up percent and degrees.
  • Glassing the shady north face at sunrise in a cold snap.
  • Ignoring a red slope above you after fresh snow.
More: the mistakes in full
  • Percent and degrees: 30 percent is only about 17 degrees. 30 degrees is 58 percent. Check which one your source uses.
  • In a cold snap, deer move to warm aspects and sunny beds: glass the south and east faces first at dawn (Tip).
  • Avalanche terrain is 30 to 45 degrees. In snow, stay off and out from below red slopes (Tip, app note).

Do this in the field

Pick one valley. Name the aspect of both sides, then say what grows on each and where deer would be at dawn, noon and dusk.

• South is the stove, north is the fridge.
  • Cold day, sun face. Hot day, shade face.
  • 45 is 100: 45 degrees is 100 percent.
  • Times 20: contour lines per 100 m x 20 = percent slope on the Hunt Map.
  • 30 to 45, avalanches thrive.
  • Aspect: where the water goes.
More: using the hooks
  • Say "stove or fridge" every time you look at a slope. It makes you think of sun, snow and cover in one word (Tip).

  • BC Forest Investment Account, Silviculture best management practices, 7.6.1 Mule deer winter range, February 2004, PDF, read directly, checked 2026-10-11 85%: warm aspects 135 to 270 degrees, cool 315 to 90, slopes about 40 percent and more.
  • Bighorn Sheep in BC, 2000, PDF, read directly, checked 2026-10-11 85%.
  • Management Plan for the Mountain Goat in BC, 2010, PDF, read directly, checked 2026-10-11 85%.

• Avalanche Canada, slope angle, glossary, search preview, checked 2026-10-11 85%.
  • Lingle 2002, coyote predation and habitat use of mule deer and white tails, abstract via search preview, checked 2026-10-11 75%.
  • Luloff, Diefenbach, Stedman and others, Pennsylvania hunter movement report, August 2004, PDF, read directly, checked 2026-10-11 (85% for that forest).

elevation-snowline:
Why it matters

Height sets the cold, the snow and the food. In October the snowline starts pushing animals down. Know the band and you know where to look.

  • Each band of height has its own plants, weather and animals 85%.
  • The snowline moves down through the fall, and animals move ahead of it 85%.
More: what this lesson covers
  • Elevation bands: what grows at each height near Kamloops, Heffley Creek and the Okanagan.
  • Why it gets colder as you climb, and why valleys can be colder at night.
  • The snowline: what it is, how aspect bends it, and how to read its height from the truck.
  • Which animals live at which height in October.
  • The Hunt Map: elevation readout, Habitat zones layer, and month by month layers.
  • Builds on How animals move through the year. For the zones themselves see BC habitat zones made simple.

• Low: bunchgrass. Middle: pine and Douglas fir. High: spruce and subalpine fir. Top: alpine 90%.
  • Bands overlap and shift with aspect and rain 85%.
More: the zones and their heights
Zone (BEC, Biogeoclimatic Ecosystem Classification)Typical height in the southern Interior
BG, BunchgrassValley bottoms up to about 700 to 1,000 m
PP, Ponderosa PineAbout 335 to 900 m
IDF, Interior Douglas firLower edge 350 to 600 m, upper edge 900 to 1,450 m
MS, Montane SpruceAbout 1,100 to 1,700 m
ESSF, Engelmann Spruce Subalpine FirAbout 1,200 to 2,300 m
AlpineAbove about 1,650 to 2,250 m
  • Source: Meidinger and Pojar 1991, Ecosystems of British Columbia, as logged in the Hunt Mentor research notes 90%.
  • The ranges overlap because warm south faces push each band higher and cool north faces pull it lower 80%.
  • Near the coast, the bands are different: Coastal Western Hemlock from sea level to about 900 to 1,050 m 90%.

• About 6.5°C cooler per 1,000 m, on an average day 80%.
  • Rain at the truck can be snow on the ridge (Tip).
More: lapse rate details
  • In the standard atmosphere, air cools about 6.5°C for every 1,000 m you climb (80%, weather teaching sources). Real days vary a lot.
  • So a 1,000 m climb from the valley to a ridge can turn 4°C rain into wet snow (Tip).
  • Pack for the top, not the truck. See Layering and the weather lessons (Tip).
  • The temperatures in the drawing are an example day, not a forecast.

• Cold air drains down at night and pools in the valley 75%.
  • Frost and fog sit low; the bench above can be warmer 75%.
More: inversions and cold air pools
  • On clear, calm nights the ground loses heat fast and cold, heavy air slides down slopes into the valley 75%. Air higher up stays warmer: an inversion.
  • Studies in western mountain valleys measured cold pools many degrees colder than the air above 75%.
  • Animals may bed above the frost line on cold clear nights (Tip).
  • The same downhill drain carries your scent down at dusk and before dawn. See Wind and thermals.
  • Thompson and Okanagan valleys often hold fog or haze under an inversion in late fall (Tip). Glass from above the fog if you can.

• September to November, snow creeps down the mountains 85%.
  • Deep snow pushes deer, then elk and moose, to lower ground 85%.
More: timing in the southern Interior
  • BC mule deer study (BCWF, BC Wildlife Federation, Southern Interior Mule Deer Project): most deer return to winter range in October and November; in 2019, "by mid October ... nearly all the collared deer in each study area were back in their winter range" 85%.
  • The trigger is snow and cold, not the calendar or the rut (85%, Monteith 2011, as logged).
  • Moose "stay on high elevation ranges much longer than elk, deer or mountain sheep" (85%, BC moose account, 2000).
  • No source found for the usual snowline height by month near Kamloops. Watch it yourself and log it in the Journal (VERIFY each year).
  • See Migration routes in BC and Winter ranges.

• Deer struggle past about 25 to 30 cm, avoid over 50 cm 80%.
  • Moose move freely to about 40 cm 70%.
More: snow depth numbers
  • Deer spend the most energy in soft, crustless snow where they sink more than 25 cm (85%, BC habitat account citing Nyberg and Janz 1990).
  • "If snow accumulations exceed 50 cm then an area is generally avoided" by mule deer (85%, same account).
  • Moose move freely to about 40 cm, are restricted at 40 to 70 cm 70%. Elk sit between deer and moose 65%. As in Food, water and cover.
  • Crusted snow that holds a deer is easier for it; crusted snow that breaks under a deer but holds a coyote is deadly for deer (Tip).

• Snow melts first and lies thinnest on sunny south faces 85%.
  • The first bare ground below new snow pulls deer (Tip).
More: why it bends
  • Winter range for mule deer is on south and west aspects because "the snowpack is lower" there (85%, BC habitat account).
  • After an early storm, look for deer on the sunny face just below the snow edge (Tip).
  • North faces hold snow longer but their thick timber catches snow in the branches, so the ground under the trees can be shallower than in the open 85%. Deer use that in deep snow years.

• Quail and chukar stay low. Dusky grouse go high in fall 80%.
  • Ruffed grouse live in the middle band 85%.
More: where each number comes from
  • California quail: breeding mostly 250 to 500 m, usually below 750 m, some to 1,250 m (85%, BC Breeding Bird Atlas). They do not migrate 75%.
  • Chukar: 195 to 610 m in a 1962 Thompson study; they move lower in heavy snow (80%, Demarchi 1962; 75%, US Fire Effects Information System).
  • Bighorn sheep winter and spring ranges: 300 to 1,825 m (85%, Bighorn Sheep in BC).
  • Mule deer winter range: below about 1,500 m in shallow and moderate snow zones, below 1,000 m in deep snow zones (85%, BC habitat account citing US Forest Service 1998).
  • Ruffed grouse: most abundant 750 to 1,250 m (85%, BC Breeding Bird Atlas).
  • Dusky grouse: "many observations in the 1,500 to 2,250 m range"; they move uphill to dense conifers in fall (85% and 70%).
  • Moose and elk: no single height band; they follow food and snow (Tip). See the species lessons.

• Find the snow edge on the mountain.
  • Find the same spot on the Hunt Map and read the contour (Tip).

Put a number on the snowline1 of 3
More: how to do it well
  • Pick a landmark at the snow edge: a rock band, a cutblock corner, a meadow. Find it on the map (Tip).
  • Put the map cross on it. The readout at the top left shows the ground height under the cross (99%, app).
  • Write it in the Journal with the date and aspect. Over a season you will see the line march down (Tip).
  • Hunt the band just below fresh snow on the warm faces in a cold snap (Tip).

Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

  • Region 3: above 1,700 m, motor vehicles stay on existing roads and trails, snowmobiles excepted 99%.
  • Region 8 has its own 1,700 m rule. Read it in the Rule Book.
More: the exact rule and where to read it
Region 3, region wide

"The operation of all motor vehicles, excluding snowmobiles is prohibited in region 3 above 1,700 m elevation, except on existing roads and trails."

  • Carried in full with page numbers in Rule Book: Region 3 and Rule Book: Region 8 (99% as carried there).
  • The Hunt Map readout tells you when you are near 1,700 m (99%, app). Use it before you leave a road with the ATV (All Terrain Vehicle).

Elevation on the Hunt Map1 of 4
  • Long press a spot and open Insights for zone, height and species (99%, app).
More: layer names and what they show
  • Habitat zones: the BEC (Biogeoclimatic Ecosystem Classification) zone of the ground (99%, app layer list).
  • Mule deer by month, White tailed deer by month, Moose by month, Elk by month, Bighorn sheep by month: general seasonal patterns, not collar data (99%, app layer names).
  • Winter range layers for mule deer, white tails, moose, elk, sheep and goats (99%, app). See Winter ranges for what they mean.
  • Insights says its likelihood is an estimate based on habitat, never a fact (99%, app).

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Grandpa's rule (wisdom): Hunt the edge of the snow, not the middle of it. The animals live where the white stops.

Common mistakes
  • Hunting the high summer range after a big October storm.
  • Dressing for the valley and climbing into snow.
  • Driving off road above 1,700 m in Region 3.
More: the mistakes in full
  • After the first big storm, much of the high summer range empties. Move down to the snow edge and the warm faces (Tip).
  • Air cools about 6.5°C per 1,000 m: pack for the top 80%.
  • Above 1,700 m in Region 3, vehicles stay on existing roads and trails (99%, Rule Book).

Do this in the field

Every trip, log the snowline height and which face it is on. Compare it with where you see deer.

• Snow drops, deer drop.
  • 6 and a half per thousand: degrees cooler per 1,000 m.
  • 25 to struggle, 50 to leave: cm of snow for deer.
  • Clear and calm, the valley's the freezer.
  • Hunt where the white stops.
  • 17 hundred, stay on the road (Region 3).
More: why these numbers matter
  • 6.5, 25, 50 and 1,700 are the four numbers in this lesson worth knowing by heart (Tip).

water-on-land:
Why it matters

Every animal drinks. In a dry October, a little water in a big dry hill tells you where they will be.

  • Water shapes trails, beds, browse and crossings 75%.
  • The smaller and rarer the water, the more it is worth (Tip).
More: what this lesson covers
  • The water types you will meet: rivers, creeks, dry creeks, springs, seeps, wallows, dugouts and ponds, beaver ponds, marsh and lake edges.
  • How each looks on a topo map, on the Hunt Map and Satellite base, and on the ground.
  • Why animals use each one, and when water matters most.
  • Safety and the law near water.
  • For the plants and birds of wet places see Wetlands, marshes and riparian strips and Habitat tour: ducks. For drinking it yourself see Safe drinking water.

WaterWhat to look forWho uses it
CreekBlue line, brush stripEverything 75%
Dry creekDashed line, pools in bendsDeer in dry spells (Tip)
SpringWet spot, green patchDeer, elk, birds (Tip)
SeepDamp ground, aspen, sedgeDeer, grouse, bears (Tip)
WallowMuddy pit, rank smellElk, moose in the rut 75%
Dugout or pondRound, on ranch landDeer, ducks, geese (Tip)
Beaver pondDam, flooded willowMoose, ducks, deer 75%
Marsh, lake edgeCattail, reedsDucks, moose 85%
More: definitions
  • Spring: a place where groundwater comes out of the ground on its own and flows 90%.
  • Seep: groundwater that oozes out slowly over a patch, keeping it damp but rarely making a flowing stream 85%.
  • Intermittent creek: flows only part of the year, after snowmelt or rain 90%.
  • Dugout: a pond dug for cattle on ranch land 85%. Most are on private land or grazing leases: permission and the rules apply. See Rule Book: where you can hunt.
  • Wallow: a muddy pit dug and rolled in by bull elk in the rut; bull moose dig rut pits too 75%. See Reading sign.

• Dashed blue: the creek may be dry (99%, app).
  • Springs and seeps are often missing from maps (Tip).
More: reading water on maps
  • On the Hunt Map Topo base: solid blue lines for creeks, dashed blue for intermittent ones, a pale green grey fill for wetlands, blue fill for lakes and ponds (99%, app map style).
  • The map data comes from OpenStreetMap; small springs, seeps and dugouts may not be drawn (Tip). Check the Satellite base.
  • Layers: Wetlands shows mapped wetlands; Duck staging and winter waters shows key duck water (99%, app layer list).
  • Water always runs in the V of a draw, never on a ridge 95%. If a draw has no blue line, the bottom may still hold a seep (Tip).
  • Paper map symbols vary by series: check the legend on your sheet (VERIFY).

• In a dry fall, the greenest spot is usually the wettest (Tip).
  • Aspen, willow, red osier dogwood and cottonwood mean water near 75%.

More: plants that point to water
  • Willows, red osier dogwood, cottonwood and alder need wet roots and line creeks and seeps 75%. See Habitat tour: deer.
  • On open grassland, a lone clump of aspen often marks a seep or high water table (65%, Tip).
  • Sedges and rushes in a patch of grassland mean damp soil 70%.
  • On the Hunt Map Satellite base, these show as dark or bright green spots in pale grass. Mark them and walk to check (Tip).

Find a spring1 of 3
  • Springs often appear where a slope eases: the foot of a bench or a draw head (Tip).
  • Fresh tracks in mud tell you who drinks here 75%.
More: why springs are gold
  • Rain soaks in, meets a tight layer of rock or clay, and runs along it until it comes out of the slope 85%.
  • In the dry Interior, springs and seeps are small and scattered. One spring can serve a whole slope (Tip).
  • Deer in desert studies gathered near permanent water as other sources dried (60%, desert data). Thompson grassland deer also get water from green feed, dew and snow (Tip).
  • Read the mud: count species, aim the tracks, age them. See Tracks and Aging tracks and sign.
  • Never sit right on a small spring: sit downwind where you can see the trails coming in (Tip).

• Trails follow creek bottoms and gather at easy crossings 65%.
  • Evening air drains down creek bottoms 85%.
More: creek details
  • Brushy creek bottoms are travel lanes with cover, food and water in one strip 70%.
  • Animals cross where banks are low and the bottom is firm: one crossing may serve a whole slope (Tip). See Pinch points.
  • Cold air flows down creek bottoms at dusk and before dawn 85%. Your scent goes with it.
  • A creek is also noise: running water hides your footsteps, but hides an animal's too (Tip).
  • Crossing yourself: unload first, use a pole, unbuckle the pack belt, never cross fast deep water (Tip). See Water safety.

• Bull elk dig and roll in wallows in the rut 85%.
  • A fresh wallow is a classic afternoon sit (Tip).
More: wallow details
  • Fresh wallow signs: muddy water, fresh tracks, mud splashed on nearby trees, a strong musky smell 75%.
  • Wallows sit in wet meadows, seeps and spring heads, often in timber near feed 70%.
  • Bull moose dig shallow rut pits and urinate in them; cows are drawn to them 75%. See Moose.
  • In October the elk rut is mostly over in the Interior; old wallows still mark where elk live (Tip). See Elk.

• Ranch ponds pull deer, ducks and geese (Tip).
  • Most are on private land: ask first (99%, Rule Book).
More: ponds and the rules
  • On private land you need permission to enter and hunt (99%, Trespass Act, as carried in the Rule Book).
  • No hunting or shooting within 100 m of a dwelling or an occupied farm building (99%, Rule Book).
  • Ducks: for puddle ducks on small ponds see Habitat tour: ducks and Ducks.
  • Dugout banks are often steep and slippery. Retrieving a duck from one needs a plan (Tip).
Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

• Water, browse and cover in one place 75%.
  • The dam is often a crossing (Tip).
More: beaver pond details
  • Beaver ponds flood timber and grow willow, a moose favourite 85%. See Habitat tour: moose, elk and bears.
  • Ducks use the quiet water and flooded edges 80%.
  • Dams look solid but can collapse. Never stand on a dam with a pack and rifle in deep water (Tip).
  • Old dried beaver meadows grow lush grass and sedge: good feed 70%.

• Reeds and cattails: duck cover and feed 85%.
  • Moose feed in shallow lakes and marsh edges 85%.
More: marsh edge details
  • Moose live by water: willow swamps, lake edges, beaver ponds 85%.
  • In the south Okanagan, marsh edges also hold quail cover in the thorny brush nearby (Tip). See Habitat tour: quail and grouse.
  • Soft marsh bottoms can trap a wader. Test every step (Tip).
  • Many valley wetlands are private, parks or bird sanctuaries. Check the land status layers and the Rule Book 99%.

• Dry spell: water is a magnet. Sit it at dawn and dusk (Tip).
  • After rain or snow: water is everywhere. Hunt food and cover (Tip).
More: timing water
  • Deer drink at dawn and dusk 70%.
  • Deer get much of their water from green feed; when feed dries, they need surface water 75%.
  • The first big fall rain refills every puddle and ends the water stand season (Tip).
  • In freezing weather, open water at springs and fast creeks becomes valuable again (Tip).

Find water on the Hunt Map1 of 4
  • Then go look. Many small water sources are not on any map (Tip).
More: Hunt Map water tips
  • Switch bases with the Topo button in the pill at the bottom right (99%, app).
  • Satellite with hill shading on makes draws and benches stand out next to the green (99%, app setting "Shade hills on satellite").
  • Saved areas work offline, including the Wetlands layer and terrain (99%, app).

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Grandpa's rule (wisdom): In a dry year, the smallest water on the mountain is the biggest thing on it.

Common mistakes
  • Trusting the map to show every spring.
  • Sitting right on top of the water instead of the trail in.
  • Sitting a water hole after the rain filled every puddle.
More: the mistakes in full
  • Maps miss most springs and seeps. Use the satellite, the plants and your boots (Tip).
  • Sit downwind of the trails coming in, with a view of the water, not at the edge (Tip).
  • Water stands lose value after a big rain (Tip).

Do this in the field

Find three green spots in a brown hill on the Satellite base. Walk to one. Read every track in the mud.

• Green in brown, water's found.
  • Dashed line, maybe dry.
  • Dry year: sit the drink. Wet year: sit the food.
  • Dam is a bridge (but test it).
  • SWAMP check: Springs, Wallows, Aspen clumps, Marsh edges, Ponds.
More: using the hooks
  • SWAMP is a scan list for any new map: find one of each within walking distance of the truck (Tip).

  • Spring, seep and intermittent stream definitions: plain English hydrology (85 to 90%).
  • Deer and water: as cited in Food, water and cover (65 to 75%); desert mule deer gathering at permanent water, Texas Parks and Wildlife and Borderlands Research Institute, search preview, checked 2026-10-11 60%.
  • Moose, elk and wallows: BC species accounts and the app glossary, as cited in the species lessons (75 to 85%).

  • Plant indicators: Habitat tour: deer and BC habitat accounts (70 to 75%); aspen clump as seep marker is hunter observation (Tip).

edges:
Why it matters

Most animals need two things at once: food in the open and cover close by. The line where they meet is where you see them.

  • An is where two cover types meet 75%.
  • Deer, grouse, quail, bears and elk use edges every day 70%.
More: what this lesson covers
  • What an edge is, hard and soft edges, the six edges to look for, the shapes that hold game, how far animals go from cover, and where to sit.
  • How edges look on the map, on the Hunt Map Satellite base and layers, and on the ground.
  • Builds on Food, water and cover and Trails and funnels. For burns in detail see After fire.

• Edge: "the juncture of two or more different cover types" 75%.
  • A wide, blended edge is called an ecotone 75%.
More: edge, ecotone, interspersion
  • "Edge is defined as the juncture of two or more different cover types" (75%, Alabama Cooperative Extension, 2022).
  • Where forest and open land blend through shrubs and small trees, it is an ecotone or transitional edge (75%, same source).
  • Aldo Leopold wrote in 1933 that game which needs two or more cover types is most common where those types are mixed close together. Later writers say he meant interspersion (a fine mix of types), not simply more edge (70%, extension sources via search preview).
  • So the real lesson: animals want food and cover within a short walk. Edges are where that happens (Tip).

• Hard edge: tall timber stops in a straight line 75%.
  • Soft edge: shrubs and young trees blend the two 75%.
More: which is better
  • A soft edge gives browse and hiding cover right beside the open feed (Tip).
  • A hard edge is easy to see and easy to sit: animals step out of a wall of trees (Tip).
  • Cutblock edges start hard and soften as shrubs and young trees grow in (Tip). See the cutblock age screen below.

• Timber and grass, cutblock, burn, field and brush, creek strip, treeline.
  • Each one is a feeding line next to a hiding line (Tip).

More: each edge type
  • Timber and grass: the Interior classic. Mule deer feed on bunchgrass slopes and bed in the fir 75%.
  • Cutblock: shrubs and young trees feed deer, elk and moose for years after logging 75%. See Map scouting for cutblock age.
  • Burn: new grass, forbs and shrubs grow under the dead trees 75%. See After fire.
  • Field and brush: hayfields and orchards next to brush hold white tails and quail. Mostly private land: permission first (99%, Rule Book).
  • Creek strip: a ribbon of willow and dogwood through open ground: cover, browse and water 75%.
  • Treeline: forest meets alpine. Mule deer and elk use it in early fall 70%.
Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

• Inside corners, points of timber and islands of cover beat a straight line (Tip).
  • These shapes bunch the travel (Tip).
More: why shapes matter
  • An inside corner is where an edge turns back on itself. Animals cutting across the open come close to the corner (Tip).
  • A point or finger of timber pushing into the open lets animals stay in cover longer before they step out (Tip).
  • An island of cover in the open is a safe stop between two edges. Small islands get overlooked by hunters too. See Islands of habitat.
  • The more turns an edge has, the more edge there is per hectare (Tip).

• In daylight, feeding hugs the edge (Tip).
  • At night animals feed farther out (Tip).
More: the numbers
  • BC mule deer habitat ratings call for security and thermal cover "near forage habitat (i.e. within 200 m)" in spring (85%, BC habitat account, 2004).
  • California quail "seldom ventures more than 15 to 30 m from cover" (75%, California Department of Fish and Wildlife life history).
  • Mule deer security cover hides 90% of a deer at 60 m or less, in patches 180 m or more across (85%, same BC account). That is the cover they run back to.
  • Hunting pressure pushes the feeding line closer to cover and later into the dark (Tip). See Hunting pressure.

AnimalFavourite edge (October)
Mule deerBunchgrass against fir, burns, cutblocks 75%
White tailed deerHayfields and cottonwood bottoms against brush 80%
ElkMeadows and burns against timber 70%
MooseWillow flats and cutblocks against conifers 75%
Black bearBerry slopes, cutblock and road edges 75%
Ruffed grouseAspen and brush against conifer, road edges 70%
California quailBrushy draws and hedges against open ground 75%
  • Edges hold the most kinds of game 75%.
More: sources for the table
  • Mule deer and white tails: Trails and funnels and Habitat tour: deer (75 to 80%).
  • Elk and moose: BC species accounts and Habitat tour: moose, elk and bears (70 to 75%).
  • Black bear: glass berry slopes, cutblocks and road edges at dawn and dusk (75%, app area lessons from the black bear lesson).
  • Ruffed grouse and quail: Habitat tour: quail and grouse (70 to 75%).
  • Extension sources: edges support the greatest diversity and abundance of wildlife, particularly game species (75%, Alabama Cooperative Extension, 2022).

• Young cutblocks fill with shrubs: feed for years 75%.
  • Old cutblocks close in and the edge fades (Tip).
More: cutblocks on the Hunt Map
  • Layers: Cutblocks by age shows when each block was cut (99%, app layer list). Burns by year does the same for fires 99%.
  • Pair the layer with the Satellite base to see what is growing there now (Tip).
  • New logging roads into cutblocks bring hunters. The edge far from the road is often the one that holds game (Tip). See Islands of habitat.

• Edges are busy: predators hunt them too 75%.
  • Every hunter knows the field edge at dusk (Tip).
More: the downside of edge
  • Edges attract predators and nest parasites; ground nesting birds near edges can lose more nests (75%, Alabama Cooperative Extension, 2022).
  • Too much edge can hurt forest birds that need big blocks of forest 75%.
  • For you: the obvious edge by the road gets sat by everyone. Look for the edge one bench up, one draw over, or across the creek (Tip).

• View of a corner or point, wind from the edge to you, sun at your back (Tip).
  • Sit 100 to 200 m off it with a rest (Tip).
More: how to set up
  • Pick the inside corner or point where trails come out (Tip).
  • Check the wind and the thermal for the hour you sit: evening air drains downhill 85%. See Wind and thermals.
  • Sit far enough off the edge that animals stepping out do not see or smell you, close enough for a sure shot: 100 to 200 m for most beginners (Tip). See Judging distance.
  • Have a behind every lane (Tip).
  • Get there early: 45 minutes before legal light in the morning, 2 hours before dark in the evening (Tip).

Find edges on the Hunt Map1 of 4
  • Mark three corners before you leave home (Tip).
More: more map tips
  • On the Satellite base the edge is a colour line: dark timber, pale grass, bright green fields (Tip).
  • Aspect makes edges: grass on the warm face, timber on the cool face, an edge along the ridge or the valley bottom 80%. See Slope and aspect.
  • Check Private land before you plan any field edge (99%, app layer).

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Grandpa's rule (wisdom): Don't sit in the field or in the woods. Sit where you can see both.

Common mistakes
  • Sitting a straight edge instead of a corner or point.
  • Walking the edge you plan to hunt.
  • Sitting the road edge everyone else sits.
More: the mistakes in full
  • Straight edges spread the animals out. Corners and points bunch them (Tip).
  • Walking the edge leaves your scent right where animals step out. Come in from the open or the back side (Tip).
  • Find the edge one step farther from the road (Tip).

Do this in the field

On the Satellite base, find one inside corner, one point of timber and one island of cover within 2 km of your truck. Sit the best one with the wind right.

• See both, sit both: a view of the open and the cover.
  • Corners collect.
  • 200 m to the bedroom: mule deer cover within about 200 m of feed.
  • Quail stay a stone's throw from cover: 15 to 30 m.
  • EDGE: Eat in the open, Duck into cover, Go at dusk, Exit at dawn.
More: using the hooks
  • EDGE is the daily loop of most deer: say it when you pick an evening sit (Tip).

  • Leopold 1933 and the interspersion reading: Oklahoma State University Extension and McConnell, Martin and Burger, search preview, checked 2026-10-11 70%.
  • Wildlife habitat rating account, Mule deer, BC Ecological Reports Catalogue, 2004, PDF, read directly, checked 2026-10-11 85%: cover within 200 m, security cover 60 m and 180 m.
  • California quail cover distance: California Department of Fish and Wildlife life history, as logged in research/2026-10-03-migration-and-areas.md 75%.

  • Animal edge use: the habitat tour lessons and species lessons (70 to 85%); where to sit is hunter craft (Tip).
  • Photo credits show under each photo. Research log: research/2026-10-11-rl.md.
bedding-cover:
Why it matters

Animals spend most of the day lying down. Know the ground and cover they pick, and you know where to glass at noon and where never to walk.

  • A good bed gives a view below, wind from behind and cover close (Tip).
  • Thermal cover keeps an animal warm or cool for less energy 85%.
More: what this lesson covers
  • This lesson is about the ground and the cover: which terrain makes bedding areas, what thermal cover and security cover are, with numbers, and how weather moves the beds.
  • How to read a single bed (size, hair, buck or doe) is in Beds and bedding areas. How to hunt near beds without busting them is there too.
  • Builds on Landforms 101 and Slope and aspect.

NeedHow the ground gives it
See dangerA view downhill or across open ground (Tip)
Smell dangerWind or rising air from below, a slope or cover behind (Tip)
Hear dangerQuiet ground, away from roads and creeks (Tip)
HideShrubs, young trees, rocks, tall grass 85%
Stay warm or coolSun or shade, wind shelter, canopy 85%
  • The best spots give all five at once (Tip).
More: why each need matters
  • Bedded deer rely on sight downhill and smell from behind and above (Tip, hunter observation). See Beds and bedding areas for the research on deer bed choice.
  • Mule deer summer day beds in an Arizona pine study were cooler, shadier spots: "Site temperature and canopy closure were the most influential attributes" (80%, Germaine and others 2004).
  • Security cover and thermal cover are separate needs, often met by the same thick stand (85%, BC habitat account).

• Below the crest of a spur or ridge, on benches, at the head of a draw, in thick cool timber (Tip).
  • Mountain mule deer often bed about two thirds of the way up 60%.
More: each spot
  1. Below the crest: on the point of a spur or just under a ridge top, where the deer sees down and the morning thermal brings scent from below (Tip). A field guide article says mountain mule deer routinely bed about two thirds of the way up slopes in front of vegetation (60%, search preview).
  2. Benches: flat ground on a steep face with a view (65%, hunter observation).
  3. Head of a draw: brush, shade and an escape route over the top (Tip).
  4. Thick cool timber: north and east faces on warm days 75%.
  5. Plains and grassland deer often bed just below the rim of a coulee, plateau or hill (60%, same article).
  6. Bedding areas are rarely on the valley floor in hill country, except in thick bottomland brush for white tails 75%.

• Mule deer security cover hides 90% of a deer at 60 m or less 85%.
  • Patches 180 m or more across 85%.
More: security cover details
  • "For Mule Deer the most effective security cover hides 90% of the animal at a distance of 60 m or less, and security patches need to be 180 m or more in diameter" (85%, BC habitat account citing Nyberg and Janz 1990).
  • Mature and old forest with a dense shrub or patchy conifer understory meets this 85%.
  • "Areas of steep broken terrain can also be used as security habitat" 85%. See Escape terrain.
  • Elk hiding cover in US studies: vegetation that hides 90% of a standing elk at 61 m (70%, Thomas and others 1979, as cited).
  • Test it yourself: stand 60 m from a thicket. If you can see a deer sized shape through it, it is not security cover (Tip).

• Night: a closed canopy above 3 m holds heat and cuts wind 85%.
  • Day: rock bluffs gather heat; canopy blocks hot sun 85%.
More: thermal cover in the BC sources
  • Night thermal cover "should trap long wave radiation and maintain warmer air temperatures (occurring under a closed canopy above a deer's head or above 3 m), reduce wind at deer height ... and intercept precipitation" (85%, BC habitat account citing Bunnell and others 1985).
  • "Daytime thermal requirements are met by areas that gather heat (on or near rock bluffs) or intercept excessive solar radiation (canopy closure)" (85%, same).
  • Elk thermal cover in US studies: conifer stands at least 12 m (40 ft) tall with over 70% crown closure (70%, Thomas and others 1979, as cited).
  • Caution: a Blue Mountains study (Cook and others 1998) found thermal cover did not improve elk condition. Animals may choose those stands for food or safety instead (70%, US Forest Service paper via search preview).
  • Thermal cover for you: a tree at your back and the sun on your chest makes a long sit bearable (Tip).

• Tall closed conifers keep the snow up in the branches 85%.
  • Deer walk and feed under them in deep snow years 85%.
More: snow interception numbers
  • "Canopy closure (i.e., stands taller than 10 m with greater than 60% crown completeness) exerts the most influence on snow interception" (85%, BC habitat account citing Bunnell and others 1985).
  • Mule deer winter range in the Interior relies on old Douglas fir with closed, multi layered canopies, generally over 60% canopy closure, on moderate to steep warm slopes (85%, BC silviculture practices, 2004).
  • Douglas fir foliage and lichen falling from those big trees is winter food too: 62 to 89% of the winter diet at Knife Creek near Williams Lake (85%, Waterhouse and others 1994, as cited).
  • See also Food, water and cover and Winter ranges.

WeatherWhere to look
Cold and clearSunny south and east faces, below rock, out of wind 75%
HotNorth and east timber, shady benches, draw heads 75%
WindyLee side just below the top, in timber (Tip)
RainUnder big conifers, edges of thick timber (Tip)
Snow stormThick timber, then sunny faces after (Tip)

More: the evidence behind the table
  • Cold: deer in an Ontario study picked sun exposed day beds in winter (60%, Armstrong and others 1983, white tails, search preview). On cold sunny days deer often bed where the first sun hits (Tip, app tool note).
  • Hot: mule deer in a Montana and Idaho study picked cooler northeast and east aspects with overhead cover 60%; summer day beds in Arizona were cooler and shadier than random spots 80%.
  • Severe weather: north aspects with dense, high crown closure stands "may be used during severe weather conditions" (85%, BC habitat account).
  • Wind and rain rows are hunter observation (Tip). See Weather fronts and game movement.

• Wind pours over a ridge and swirls on the lee side 75%.
  • Bedded animals may sit just over the top, out of the wind (Tip).
More: lee side details
  • The lee side is calmer but the wind eddies there. Your scent can swirl back to a bedded animal from any side 75%. See Wind and thermals.
  • On very windy days, deer may bed in thick cover and move little. A slow still hunt into the wind can work because noise is covered (Tip). See Moving quietly.

AnimalTypical October bed ground
Mule deerBenches, spur points, broken rock, fir timber above feed 75%
White tailed deerThick brush, willow and cottonwood bottoms, field edge thickets 80%
ElkDark timber on north faces, high basins 70%
MooseThick conifer or willow near water and browse 75%
Black bearThick cover near berries and water (Tip)

More: sources for the table
  • Mule deer and white tails: Trails and funnels bed and feed screen (70 to 80%).
  • Elk and moose: BC species accounts and the species lessons (70 to 75%).
  • More on each species' beds: Beds and bedding areas.

Find bedding terrain in 5 steps1 of 5
  • Use What can I see from here to find a glassing seat with a view of the beds (99%, app tool).
More: how the tools fit
  • Slope steepness shows benches as gaps in the colour (99%, app key: under 15 degrees uncoloured).
  • Slope direction shows aspect by colour: pick warm faces for cold days and cool faces for hot ones (Tip).
  • What can I see from here shades the ground you can likely see from a spot, worked out from bare ground only, so trees block more than the map shows (99%, app notes).
  • Sun and shade shows which faces are in sun at any time today (99%, app).

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Grandpa's rule (wisdom): Glass the beds, hunt the trails. Walk into a bedroom only when you are ready to lose it.

Common mistakes
  • Walking the ridge top right over the beds.
  • Looking in the open at noon.
  • Forgetting that weather moves the beds every day.
More: the mistakes in full
  • Beds sit just below crests and on spur points. Walking the very top puts you above them with your scent and outline (Tip).
  • At midday, animals are bedded in cover. Glass shade, timber edges, benches and below rocks (Tip).
  • A cold clear morning and a hot afternoon put the same deer on different faces 75%.

Do this in the field

Pick one face. Mark three likely beds on the map from slope, aspect and cover. Glass them at midday from across the draw.

• View below, wind behind, cover close.
  • 90 at 60: security cover hides 90% of a deer at 60 m.
  • 10 and 60: trees over 10 m, crowns over 60% closed catch snow.
  • Cold day, sun bed. Hot day, shade bed.
  • Two thirds up is a good first glass on a mountain face (Tip).
More: using the hooks
  • Say "view, wind, cover" as you scan each bench or spur point. Mark the ones that have all three (Tip).

escape-terrain:
Why it matters

Every animal has a plan for danger. Know where it will run and you can stalk smarter, shoot safer and find it after.

  • Escape terrain is the ground an animal runs to when threatened 85%.
  • Each species has its own: cliffs, rough slopes, thick cover, distance, water 80%.
More: what this lesson covers
  • What escape terrain is for mule deer, white tails, elk, moose, sheep, goats, bears and birds.
  • How to predict where an animal will run before you stalk.
  • How hunting pressure pushes animals into escape terrain.
  • Safety: shooting near cliffs and steep ground.
  • Builds on Slope and aspect and Bedding terrain.

AnimalRuns toCertainty
Mule deerUp slopes into rough, broken ground; bunch up75%
White tailed deerDown and away, fast, into thick cover75%
ElkDistance and dark timber, far from roads65%
MooseThick timber, willow, sometimes waterTip
Bighorn sheepCliffs and broken rock near grass85%
Mountain goatCliffs of 40 degrees or more90%
Black bearThick brush; can climb trees75%
QuailRun to thorny brush, rarely 30 m from it75%

More: sources per row
  • Mule deer and white tails: when coyotes came, mule deer "moved to and up slopes", white tails "moved down and away from slopes"; mule deer often stand and bunch, white tails flee (75%, Lingle 2002, abstract via search preview). Stotting is thought to work best on uneven ground (70%, Dellinger 2019).
  • Mule deer: "Areas of steep broken terrain can also be used as security habitat" (85%, BC habitat account).
  • Elk: elk security area ideas (big blocks of cover far from open roads) are widely used but debated 60%. See Hunting pressure.
  • Bighorn: "best suited ... to rugged, mostly treeless terrain"; lambs born in "rugged lambing cliffs" (85%, Bighorn Sheep in BC, 2000).
  • Goats: escape terrain is "generally steep slopes usually 40 degrees or more ... of shear or broken cliffs" (90%, BC Mountain Goat Management Plan, 2010).
  • Quail: "seldom ventures more than 15 to 30 m from cover" (75%, California Department of Fish and Wildlife).
  • Black bears climbing trees: general wildlife knowledge 75%; see the bear claw marks photo in Reading sign.

• Mule deer use slopes and broken ground to escape 75%.
  • They often stop and look back from a high spot (Tip).
More: mule deer escape in detail
  • Stotting lets a mule deer bounce up steep, rocky, brushy ground faster than a dog can follow 70%.
  • Mule deer standing high on slopes were less likely to be attacked by coyotes than those standing low (75%, Lingle 2002).
  • A spooked mule deer often stops at the top or behind cover to look back. That pause is the reason to stay ready, but never take a running or rushed shot (Tip). See Legal to shoot.
  • On the map, rough escape ground shows as orange, red and purple on Slope steepness, often with rock bands (Tip).

• White tails rely on early warning and speed 75%.
  • They head for thick bottomland cover 80%.
More: white tail escape in detail
  • White tails flee at a gallop on gentler ground and rely on detecting threats early (70%, Dellinger 2019 via search preview).
  • In valleys they run for willow, cottonwood bottoms and brushy field edges 80%.
  • A flagging white tail rarely stops in the open. Watch where it enters cover: that is the trail to remember (Tip).

• Goats rarely go more than 400 to 500 m from escape terrain 90%.
  • Bighorns live where steep rock meets grass 85%.
More: sheep and goat escape terrain
  • Mountain goats "are usually reluctant to venture more than 400 to 500 m from escape terrain, often less distance during winter" (90%, BC Mountain Goat Management Plan, 2010).
  • Along river valleys, goats also use steep mud and clay banks as escape terrain (90%, same).
  • Bighorn winter ranges are steep, south to southwest facing grasslands with "rugged breaks and terraces along river valleys, rocky outcrops" (85%, Bighorn Sheep in BC).
  • Young sheep learn where escape terrain is by following older sheep (85%, same).
  • Sheep and goat hunting has its own licences and rules: see Mountain sheep and Mountain goat.

• Pressured elk move far and into timber away from roads 65%.
  • Moose stand in thick cover or move off steadily (Tip).
More: elk and moose in detail
  • Elk security areas in US planning: big blocks of cover at least about 0.8 km (half a mile) from open roads; the exact numbers were never validated (60%, Hillis 1991 as cited and debated).
  • Elk often cross a ridge and keep going: one spooked herd can leave a basin for days (Tip).
  • Moose often stand and stare, then trot off into the thickest timber or willow (Tip). See Moose.
  • See Hunting pressure for where pushed game goes.

• Quail run to thorny brush, then flush 75%.
  • Grouse flush into trees or curl back past you (Tip).
More: upland escape
  • California quail stay within 15 to 30 m of cover 75%. They run first, then flush in a burst 75%. See Quail.
  • Ruffed grouse often flush to put a tree trunk between you and them (Tip). See Grouse.
  • Chukar run uphill ahead of you, then flush back downhill: climb above them first (Tip, as in the upland lessons).

• Before every stalk, ask: if it busts, where does it go? (Tip)
  • Stalk so the wind and the exit both work for you (Tip).
More: how to use the prediction
  • Mark the likely exits on the map: uphill to timber, over a saddle, down a draw (Tip).
  • If you hunt with your brother, one of you can watch the main exit while the other moves (Tip). Agree on zones of fire first. See Firearm safety.
  • Never shoot at an animal on the skyline or running toward rough ground you cannot see beyond (Tip).
  • After a shot, a hit animal often runs toward its escape cover. Start your search there (Tip). See After the shot.

• Hunters favour flat ground near roads 85%.
  • Steep and far is where pressured animals end up (Tip).
More: the evidence
  • In a Pennsylvania public forest, hunters were about 3 times more likely to use an area for each km closer to a road, and 1.25 times more likely for every 10 degree drop in slope (85% for that forest).
  • So steep, rough ground far from roads gets the least pressure (85% there, Tip for BC).
  • More in Hunting pressure and Islands of habitat.

• Never shoot an animal on a cliff edge or above a drop you cannot reach (Tip).
  • Your own escape plan: no stalks onto ground you cannot climb back up (Tip).

More: steep ground safety
  • An animal shot on a cliff falls: the meat can be lost and the retrieval can kill you (Tip). Wait for it to move to safer ground.
  • Unload before scrambling (Tip). See Firearm safety.
  • Red and purple on Hunt Map Slope steepness mean 30 degrees and more; in snow, red is avalanche terrain (99%, app key).
  • Tell someone your trip plan before steep country (Tip). See Bush safety.

Find escape terrain on the Hunt Map1 of 4
  • Feed close to escape terrain is prime (85% for goats, Tip for deer).
More: map notes
  • The terrain behind the map is about 24 m apart, so small cliffs may not show. Check the satellite and your eyes (95%, app notes).
  • The Area report (Insights) flags cliffs for mountain sheep and goats (99%, app).

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Grandpa's rule (wisdom): Before you take one step, know where the animal will go. Then make sure you are not standing in the doorway, and not shooting into it.

Common mistakes
  • Stalking from the side the animal wants to run to.
  • Shooting an animal above a cliff.
  • Chasing a mule deer straight uphill.
More: the mistakes in full
  • If your approach pushes the animal past you or over the skyline, you get no safe shot (Tip).
  • Animals shot near cliffs fall and are lost or ruined (Tip).
  • A spooked mule deer uphill is gone. Back out, let it settle, come back another day (Tip).

Do this in the field

For every animal you glass, say out loud: its exit, your approach, your backstop. Then decide to stalk or not.

• Mulie up, whitey out.
  • Goats stay a short walk from the rock: 400 to 500 m.
  • Quail: a stone's throw to thorns, 15 to 30 m.
  • EXIT before entry: know the exit before you start the stalk.
  • No shot over the edge.
More: using the hooks
  • "Mulie up, whitey out" covers most deer escapes you will see in the Thompson and the Fraser Valley (Tip).

  • Wildlife habitat rating account, Mule deer, BC Ecological Reports Catalogue, 2004, PDF, read directly, checked 2026-10-11 85%.
  • Pennsylvania hunter movement report, August 2004, PDF, read directly, checked 2026-10-11 (85% for that forest).

pinch-points:
Why it matters

A pinch point turns a whole mountain of choices into one narrow path. Find it, sit it right, and the animal walks to you.

  • Funnel: land or cover that narrows the routes 65%.
  • Pinch point: the narrowest spot in a funnel 65%.
More: what this lesson covers
  • This is the deep dive after Trails and funnels. That lesson defined funnels and pinch points. This one shows every kind, how to find them on the map and the Hunt Map in 3D, how to rank them, and how to sit them.
  • Nearly all of this is hunter craft, not science (Tip). Treat each pinch as a guess until tracks and trails prove it.
  • Builds on Landforms 101, Water on the land and Edges.

FamilyExamples
TerrainSaddle, bench ledge, head of a draw, gap in a cliff band, narrow ridge
CoverTimber strip between openings, brushy creek strip, hedge, point of timber
WaterCreek crossing, beaver dam, lake narrows, strip between lake and cliff
PeopleGate, fence gap, culvert, gap between yards or roads
  • The best pinches stack two or more families in one spot (Tip).
More: why animals use pinches
  • Animals take the easiest, safest route between bed, feed and water: less climbing, more cover, firm footing 65%.
  • When the land or cover leaves only one easy route, most animals that pass use it (Tip).
  • Use is not constant: wind, pressure, snow and season change which pinch is hot (Tip).

Five terrain pinches1 of 5
  • Each one shows on a topo map and pops in 3D (Tip).
More: each terrain pinch
  • Saddle: an hourglass on the map. Animals cross ridges here 65%. In the rut, bucks cruise saddles between doe groups 60%.
  • Bench ledge: wide gaps between contour lines that pinch to a thin gap where cliffs above and below come close (Tip).
  • Draw head: animals walk around the top of a steep draw rather than dropping in and climbing out (Tip).
  • Cliff gap: a break in a rock band. On 20 m contours a small band may hide: check 3D, satellite and your eyes 95%.
  • Narrow ridge or spur: where a ridge is just a few metres wide, everything walking it passes one spot (Tip).

• Animals cross open ground where cover connects 65%.
  • A strip of timber, a brushy creek, a hedge (Tip).
More: cover pinches in detail
  • A strip of trees or brush between two blocks of timber across open ground is a travel lane, especially in daylight (Tip).
  • Creek strips: willow and dogwood through grassland or farmland 75%.
  • Leave strips in cutblocks: narrow bands of standing timber left by logging (Tip). See Cutblocks by age on the Hunt Map.
  • Points of timber: the place where cover reaches farthest into the open (Tip). See Edges.

• Trails gather at the easy creek crossing (Tip).
  • A lake against a cliff leaves a narrow shore strip (Tip).
More: water pinches in detail
  • Low banks and firm gravel collect crossings from a whole slope (Tip). See Water on the land.
  • Beaver dams are bridges for many animals (Tip).
  • Lake narrows and the strip between a lake and a cliff squeeze trails, as in the opening animation (Tip).
  • Rivers: shallow riffles are crossings; deep pools are barriers (Tip).

• Open gates, downed fence, fence corners, culverts (Tip).
  • Usually on or near private land: permission first 99%.
More: people pinches and the rules
  • Deer cross fences where they are low or broken. Look for hair on the wire 65%. See Reading sign.
  • Most farm gates and fence lines in the valleys are on private land: you need permission (99%, Rule Book).
  • No hunting or shooting within 100 m of a dwelling or an occupied farm building, and never within a road allowance (99%, Rule Book). See Rule Book: where you can hunt.
Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

• One feature is good. Two or three in a line are gold (Tip).
  • Example: saddle above a timber strip above a creek crossing.
More: how to rank a pinch
Score each pinch 0 to 2012
How narrowWideMediumOne trail
Between bed and feedNoMaybeYes
Fresh signNoneOldFresh
Wind works for a seatNoSome windsMost winds
PressureRoad sideSomeFar or awkward
  • 8 to 10: sit it. 5 to 7: test it with sign. Under 5: keep looking (Tip).
  • This scorecard is a beginner aid, not science (Tip).

• Packed trails, tracks both ways, pellets, rubs 75%.
  • No sign, no sit (Tip).
More: what to look for
  • Trails 15 to 30 cm wide, packed and bare 65%. See Trails and funnels.
  • Tracks going both ways mean a daily route; one way can mean a seasonal move (Tip).
  • Rubs along a pinch in late October and November mean bucks travel it in the rut 60%. See Rubs and scrapes.
  • In snow, a pinch tells you exactly how many animals passed and when 75%. See Snow tracking.

• Downwind or crosswind, 100 to 150 m off, a clear lane (Tip).
  • Never walk through the pinch to reach your seat (Tip).
More: set up in detail
  • Check the wind and the thermal for the hour you sit. Morning air rises, evening air drains 85%. Sit where both carry your scent away from the trail (Tip). See Wind and thermals.
  • Saddles swirl: wind pours through the gap. Have a second seat for the other wind (Tip).
  • Pick a seat with a rest, a backstop for every lane and a range you know. Use Range rings on the Hunt Map to see 100, 200, 300 m (99%, app).
  • Be in before first light or 2 hours before dark, and come in the back way (Tip).
  • If you hunt with your brother, sit two pinches on the same route or one pinch from two angles with agreed zones of fire (Tip).

• Quail and grouse run along hedges and brushy strips to the end 75%.
  • Ducks fly the same lines between roost and feed 75%.
More: birds and pinches
  • In upland hunting, the end of a hedge or brushy strip is where birds flush. Post a blocker there with clear zones of fire (Tip). See Habitat tour: quail and grouse.
  • Ducks and geese follow flight lines between roosting water and feeding fields, often over low points and along rivers 75%. See Waterfowl daily flights.
  • Grouse in fall walk logging roads and creek edges for grit and greens 65%.

Find a pinch in 6 steps1 of 6
  • Mark every candidate, then score it on the ground (Tip).
More: Hunt Map details
  • Range rings show 100, 200 and 300 m from a spot (99%, app).
  • The Scent cone shows where your scent goes with the forecast wind from a spot (99%, app tool name). It needs signal for the forecast (99%, app notes).
  • What can I see from here shows which lanes you can see from a seat; trees are not included (99%, app).
  • Recreation trails and Forest Service roads layers show where people walk and drive: human pinches and pressure (Tip).

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Grandpa's rule (wisdom): Don't hunt where the animals are. Hunt where they have to go.

Common mistakes
  • Sitting right on the trail in the pinch.
  • Walking through the pinch to get to your seat.
  • Sitting a pinch with no fresh sign.
More: the mistakes in full
  • On the trail you are in the animal's face and in its nose. Sit off it (Tip).
  • Your boots and scent on the trail warn every animal that follows (Tip).
  • A pinch on the map is a guess. Tracks, pellets and packed dirt make it a fact (Tip).

Do this in the field

Find five pinches on the Hunt Map in one MU (Management Unit). Score them. Walk the top two and read the sign.

• Hunt where they have to go.
  • Two in a line, that's fine. Three in a row, that's the spot.
  • Off the trail, not on it.
  • No sign, no sit.
  • PINCH: Paths join, Into cover, Narrow ground, Check the wind, Hide off the line.
More: using the hooks
  • Run PINCH on every candidate before you commit a morning to it (Tip).

  • Rut cruising on funnels 60%: as cited in Trails and funnels and The rut.
  • Thermals: as cited in Wind and thermals 85%.
  • Waterfowl flight lines 75%: Waterfowl daily flights.
  • Rules on private land, the 100 m rule and road allowances: Rule Book: where you can hunt, 2 October 2026 edition (99% as carried there).
  • Hunt Mentor app tools (3D, height boost, Slope steepness, Range rings, Scent cone, What can I see from here, layers), read 2026-10-11 99%.
  • The scorecard, seat distances and mnemonics are hunter craft and teaching aids (Tip).
  • Research log: research/2026-10-11-rl.md.
habitat-islands:
Why it matters

Most hunters walk past small, awkward, close spots on their way to the big obvious one. Animals learn that. You can too.

  • An island of habitat is a patch of good cover others skip (Tip).
  • Close to a road does not mean empty, if it is legal and safe (Tip).
More: what this lesson covers
  • Where hunters actually go, and the gaps they leave.
  • What islands of habitat look like near roads: small timber patches, brushy draws, sloughs, steep pockets, river islands, the far side of the creek.
  • The rules near roads, buildings and parks, first.
  • How to find islands on the Hunt Map, and how to hunt them without pushing them.
  • The full story on pressure is in Hunting pressure. This lesson is the small spot side of it.

• In one Pennsylvania forest, 73% of hunters were within 0.5 km of a road 85%.
  • Hunters thought they went 2.5 times farther than they did 80%.
More: the study in full
  • Luloff, Diefenbach, Stedman and others tracked deer hunters with GPS (Global Positioning System) units on Sproul State Forest, Pennsylvania, 2001 and 2002 85%.
  • 56% of the study area was within 0.5 km of a road open to vehicles, and the model estimated 73% of hunters hunted there: hunter density near roads was over 2 times higher 85%.
  • "The average maximum distance hunters reached from a road open to public vehicles was 0.84 km"; they walked 5.48 km a day 85%.
  • Hunters were 1.25 times more likely to use an area for every 10 degree drop in slope 85%.
  • Hunters reported going more than 2.5 times farther from the road than their GPS showed (80%, journal abstract via search preview).
  • This is one forest in Pennsylvania. BC patterns are likely similar but not measured here (60%, Tip).

• A timber patch, a brushy draw, a slough, a steep pocket (Tip).
  • Small, close, awkward, or between two busy spots (Tip).
More: more island types
  • A small patch of fir or aspen in open grassland (Tip).
  • A brushy draw or creek strip running down to a road or a field (Tip).
  • A cattail slough or beaver pond in a farm or ranch corner: often private (99%, permission needed).
  • A steep pocket of cover just below a road where nobody wants to climb back up (Tip).
  • An island in a river or the far shore of a lake, reached by your kayak or boat (Tip). See the water rules below.
  • The far side of a creek or a fence nobody wants to cross (Tip).
  • A thicket between two popular parking spots (Tip).

• Too small, too close, too awkward, in between (Tip).
  • Each is a reason to look twice (Tip).
More: how animals use them
  • Pressured deer and elk move away from people, often into thick cover, steep ground or areas far from roads 75%. See Hunting pressure.
  • Some animals do the opposite: they sit tight in small cover close to roads while hunters walk past (Tip, hunter observation).
  • Elk security area ideas in US planning focus on big blocks far from open roads (60%, Hillis 1991, debated). Small islands work better for deer, birds and bears than for elk (Tip).

Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

  • No shooting across or within a road allowance, and no hunting within it 99%.
  • 15 m each side of the middle on roads under 3 lanes 99%.
More: every rule that bites near roads
  • Road allowance: no discharge across or within it, and no hunting within it, on numbered highways and 2 lane or greater public roads maintained by the province or others 99%. See Rule Book: where you can hunt.
  • Listed highways also have 400 m bands. Example: Hwy 5 between Hope and Kamloops bans single projectiles within 400 m of the road allowance; Hwy 5 north of Kamloops is not on that list (95%, my reading in the Rule Book).
  • 100 m: no hunting or shooting within 100 m of a dwelling, an occupied farm or ranch building, a school, a church, a playground or a regional district park 99%.
  • Inside a BC Park: no hunting or shooting within 400 m of a park road or highway 99%.
  • No hunting from a motor vehicle (99%, item 22). No loaded firearm in or on a vehicle (99%, item 28).
  • Private land needs permission 99%. Check the Private land layer and Reserves on the Hunt Map (99%, app layers).
  • Local No Shooting Areas and bylaws: check the Rule Book region pages 99%.

• Every answer must be yes before you load (99%, Rule Book).
More: where the flowchart lives
  • The full flowchart and every rule behind it: Rule Book: where you can hunt and Legal to shoot.

• Earth backstop behind every shot. Never toward a road, house or trail (Tip).
  • People see and hear shots near roads (Tip).
More: safety and ethics
  • A .308 bullet can travel kilometres if it misses or passes through. Only shoot into a solid earth backstop (Tip). See Firearm safety.
  • Walk well past the road allowance before you load, and unload before you return (99% for the allowance rule; Tip for the habit). See the road walk animation in the Rule Book.
  • Gut piles in view of a road upset people. Move them or hide them where allowed (Tip).
  • Close spots get checked by conservation officers too. Have your licence and tags ready (Tip).

• A kayak or your 10 ft boat reaches islands and far shores others skip (Tip).
  • Boat rules are strict: read them first 99%.
More: boat rules and safety
  • No hunting wildlife other than migratory birds from a boat being propelled by a motor (99%, item 23).
  • Migratory birds: no shooting from or with a moving boat with a motor or sail; a boat still gliding from the motor counts as moving (99%, item 24).
  • Since 1 October 2026 a loaded firearm in a boat is banned except when it is not being propelled by its motor (99%, FVPA (Firearm Violence Prevention Act), as carried in the Rule Book). See Rule Book: it is unlawful.
  • River islands may be private, parks, reserves or sanctuaries. Check land status before you land 99%.
  • Cold water kills. Wear a PFD (Personal Flotation Device) and know the 1 10 1 principle (Tip). See Water safety.

Find islands in 5 steps1 of 5
  • Look for cover between 100 m and 500 m from a road, legal and safe (Tip).
More: map tips
  • Range rings from your truck spot show 100, 200 and 300 m (99%, app). Anything inside 100 m of a house is out (99%, Rule Book).
  • Forest Service roads and Recreation trails layers show where other people drive and walk (99%, app layers).
  • What can I see from here shows whether a road or a house can see your spot: if they can, so can people, and your shots point that way (Tip).

Hunt a small island1 of 3
  • Hunt it once and well. Small cover burns out fast (Tip).
More: options
  • Option A, sit: watch the island's edge at dawn or dusk from downwind (Tip).
  • Option B, walk it: one hunter walks slowly through into the wind while your brother watches the far exit, both with agreed zones of fire (Tip). See Firearm safety.
  • Option C, glass: glass it from the road or a pullout without a firearm in hand, then plan (Tip). Searching for wildlife with a firearm in your possession counts as hunting (99%, definition in the Rule Book), so never do it from the truck.
  • My lean: start with A. It disturbs the least.

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Grandpa's rule (wisdom): The spot everybody drives past is the spot nobody hunts.

Common mistakes
  • Shooting toward a road, a house or a trail.
  • Hunting inside the road allowance or 100 m of a house.
  • Walking a small patch over and over until it is empty.
More: the mistakes in full
  • No earth backstop, no shot (Tip).
  • Road allowance and 100 m rules apply to every island near a road 99%.
  • Small cover holds few animals. Pick the right wind and hunt it rarely (Tip).

Do this in the field

On your next drive, list three small patches of cover within 500 m of the road. Check each on the map for rules and land status before you set foot.

• 73 near the road: 73% of hunters within 0.5 km in one study.
  • Small, close, awkward, between: the four skipped spots.
  • 15, 100, 400: road allowance metres, house ring metres, listed highway band metres.
  • Backstop or nothing.
  • ISLAND: Is it legal, Safe backstop, Look at land status, Approach with the wind, Never overhunt, Dawn or dusk.
More: using the hooks
  • 15, 100 and 400 are the three distances to know near roads. Read the exact wording in the Rule Book 99%.
