  • Journal of Wildlife Management 2004 paper on the same study, abstract via search preview 80%.
  • Hillis 1991 elk security areas and the debate, search preview, checked 2026-10-11 60%.

• Rules near roads, buildings, parks and boats, and the definition of hunting: Rule Book: where you can hunt, Rule Book: definitions, Rule Book: it is unlawful, BC Hunting and Trapping Regulations Synopsis 2026 to 2028, 2 October 2026 edition (99% as carried there; item 22 and the definition applied to glassing from a truck is my reading, 85%).
  • Hunt Mentor app layers and tools, read 2026-10-11 99%.
  • Island types and hunting options: hunter craft (Tip).
  • Research log: research/2026-10-11-rl.md.
read-land-truck-map:
Why it matters

Every hour on the map and every slow kilometre on the road saves you a wasted morning on foot. Read the land before you walk it.

  • The map shows the shape. The drive shows what is growing and what is moving (Tip).
  • Together they tell you where to walk first (Tip).
More: what this lesson covers
  • The 10 minute map read: the same 8 checks every time.
  • What to notice from the truck: faces, edges, burns, benches, saddles, water, tracks on the road, other hunters.
  • The rules that apply to glassing and driving.
  • Turning a drive into waypoints, and waypoints into a plan.
  • This lesson pulls together lessons 13 to 21. For a full map build see Build your own hunting map and Map scouting from home.

• Same 8 checks, same order, every new piece of ground (Tip).
  • Law first. Wind last. Everything else in between.
More: each check in detail
  1. Law: MU (Management Unit), open season, land status, parks, reserves, No Shooting Areas. See Rule Book.
  2. Access: roads, gates, Motor vehicle closures, the 1,700 m rule in Regions 3 and 8 (99%, Rule Book).
  3. Shape: ridges, spurs, draws, saddles, benches, knobs, bowls. See Landforms 101.
  4. Face: aspect for today's weather. See Slope and aspect.
  5. Water: blue lines, dashed lines, green spots. See Water on the land.
  6. Cover: edges, cutblocks by age, burns by year. See Edges.
  7. Pressure: roads, trails, rec sites, where trucks park. See Islands of habitat.
  8. Wind: forecast wind and thermals for your seat and approach. See Wind and thermals.
▶How To E-Scout For Whitetails: Key Terrain FeaturesKey terrain features to find on a map before you go.
onX Hunt, YouTube, 4 min. Needs internet.

The 8 checks on the Hunt Map1 of 6
  • Save the area for offline use before you leave home (99%, app).
More: Hunt Map details
  • Offline Maps saves Topo, terrain, hillshade, contours, 3D, hunting layers and your spots for an area (99%, app).
  • Satellite tiles you have looked at stay saved for a while but are not part of Offline Maps (99%, app note). Look at your area on Satellite at home on wifi.
  • Insights gives a quick area report for any point, with a likelihood that is an estimate, never a fact (99%, app).
  • See Hunt Map pro for every tool.

• Faces: grass on warm faces, timber on cool ones 80%.
  • Burns, cutblocks, benches, saddles on the skyline (Tip).
More: the driving scan
  • Name the aspect of each face you pass and what grows on it (Tip). See Slope and aspect.
  • Find the snowline and put a height on it (Tip). See Elevation bands.
  • Look for green in brown: springs, seeps, brushy draws (Tip).
  • Note burns and cutblocks, and how old they look (Tip).
  • Note where other trucks park: that is where the pressure starts (Tip).
  • Note gates, closure signs and road conditions for the next trip (Tip). See Forest roads, vehicles and radio.

• A dirt road is a tracking strip: count the crossings (Tip).
  • Fresh crossings mark live trails between bed and feed (Tip).
More: reading road crossings
  • Best right after rain or fresh snow: every track is new 75%. See Snow tracking and Aging tracks.
  • Mark each fresh crossing with a waypoint and the direction of travel (Tip).
  • Two crossings close together often mean a pinch nearby (Tip). See Pinch points.
  • Drive slowly and pull fully off the road to look. Logging trucks have the right of way on many Forest Service roads (Tip). See Forest roads, vehicles and radio.

Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

  • No hunting from a motor vehicle. No loaded firearm in or on one 99%.
  • Searching for wildlife with a firearm in your possession counts as hunting 99%.
More: the exact rules and my reading
Item 22

"To hunt wildlife from a motor vehicle."

Item 28

"To discharge, carry or have in possession a firearm containing live ammunition in its breech or in its magazine attached to the firearm, in or on a railway car, motor vehicle, sleigh, aircraft, bicycle or other conveyance."

Definition of hunt

"HUNT AND HUNTING - includes shooting at, attracting, searching for, chasing, pursuing, following after or on the trail of, stalking, or lying in wait for wildlife or attempting to do any of those things, whether or not the wildlife is then or subsequently wounded, killed or captured: (a) with intention to capture the wildlife, or (b) while in possession of a firearm or other weapon."

  • My reading (85%, VERIFY with a conservation officer): glassing for game from the truck with a firearm in it can count as hunting from a motor vehicle. Scout from the truck without a firearm, or step away from the truck to glass with the rifle unloaded and cased inside.
  • When you decide to hunt: walk away from the truck and out of the road allowance before you load (99% for the allowance rule).
  • Rules carried in full: Rule Book: it is unlawful, Rule Book: definitions, Rule Book: where you can hunt.
  • No hunting with a light: no spotlight, headlamp or truck lights to hunt by (99%, item 38).

Glass from a pullout in 4 steps1 of 4
  • Glass the faces that fit the time and weather first (Tip).
More: glassing tips from the road
  • Early morning: sunny east faces and edges. Midday: shade and benches. Evening: west faces and feeding edges (Tip). See Glassing.
  • Use the truck hood, a fence post or a tripod for a steady view (Tip).
  • Put a number on every animal you see: where, when, which face, which way it went (Tip). It goes in the Journal.
  • Other people use pullouts too. Never point binoculars or a scope at houses or people (Tip).

• Match what you see to the map: the snow edge, a burn, a bench (Tip).
  • The Hunt Map height readout puts a number on it (99%, app).
More: matching view to map
  • Centre the map on the feature you see, tilt it in 3D, and rotate it to face the same way you do. The match becomes obvious (Tip).
  • Use your phone compass: point the top of the map where you are looking (Tip). See Compass mastery.
  • Draw an elevation profile from the road to the bench you see: it tells you the climb before you leave the truck (99%, app tool).

Turn a drive into a plan1 of 4
  • Write the plan in the Journal and your trip plan (Tip).
More: planning details
  • Route: follow benches and contours, approach from downwind, stay off the skyline and out of the bedding cover (Tip). See Route planning.
  • Time: be at the seat before first light or 2 hours before dark (Tip).
  • Leave a trip plan with someone at home (Tip). See Bush safety.
  • Plan B for the opposite wind (Tip).

• Map at home, drive, mark, walk, journal, back to the map (Tip).
  • Each lap makes your map truer (Tip).
More: why the loop matters
  • Maps go out of date: new cutblocks, new burns, closed roads, new houses (Tip).
  • Your Journal is the real map: where you saw animals, sign, other hunters, the snowline by date (Tip).
  • After three laps you will know a piece of ground better than most people who drive past it (Tip).

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Grandpa's rule (wisdom): The truck is for looking. Your boots are for hunting. Never mix them up.

Common mistakes
  • Glassing from the cab with a rifle beside you.
  • Driving the same road at dawn and calling it scouting.
  • Trusting the map over fresh tracks on the road.
More: the mistakes in full
  • With a firearm in your possession, searching for wildlife is hunting, and hunting from a motor vehicle is unlawful (99%; applying it to the cab is my reading, 85%).
  • Driving at prime time moves animals and wastes the best light. Drive midday, hunt dawn and dusk (Tip).
  • Fresh sign beats old maps (Tip).

Do this in the field

Do the 10 minute map read for one new area at home. Then drive it slowly at midday, without a firearm, and drop five waypoints.

bec-zones:
Why it matters

BC is split into habitat zones by climate. Know the zone and you know the trees, the food, the snow and the game before you take a step.

  • Interior zones stack up the hill like floors in a building 85%.
  • Each floor has its own trees, food and game.
  • Learn 6 Interior floors and 1 coast floor. That covers your hunts.
More: what this session covers
  • BEC (biogeoclimatic ecosystem classification) is how BC sorts land by climate, plants and soil 90%. Bio = living things, geo = ground, climatic = climate.
  • BC uses 14 zones in the classic book (Meidinger and Pojar 1991) 95%. The current provincial map legend shows 16 units because it splits the alpine into 3 kinds (80%, search preview).
  • Zones are named after the main tree of mature forest on an average site 85%.
  • This session: the zones you will hunt, how to read a zone code, why the coast is wet and the Interior dry, your bases by zone, and how to tell the zone in the field.
  • The next sessions go deep on each kind of country: Grasslands, Dry forests, Wet forests, Wetlands.
  • Assumption: elevation numbers are the ranges given for each whole zone. Your local slope can differ by a few hundred metres.

• Zone letters, then 2 small letters, then a number 95%.
  • First small letter: how wet. Second: how warm 90%.
  • IDFxh2 means Interior Douglas fir, very dry, hot 95%.
More: the letter key in full
  • Zone code: capitals, for example IDF (Interior Douglas fir) 95%.
  • Subzone: 2 small letters 90%.
    • First letter, how much rain and snow: x very dry, d dry, m moist, w wet, v very wet (80%, BC Species and Ecosystems Explorer, search preview).
    • Second letter in the Interior, how warm: h hot, w warm, m mild, k cool, c cold (90%, read off the names in the BC zone map data: PPxh is Very Dry Hot, IDFdk is Dry Cool, IDFmw is Moist Warm, MSdm is Dry Mild, ESSFdc is Dry Cold).
    • On the coast the second letter tells how maritime the climate is. CWHdm is Dry Maritime, CWHvm is Very Wet Maritime (90%, BC zone map data).
  • Variant: a number for a local version of the subzone, for example the 2 in IDFxh2 90%.
  • Why care: a dry hot subzone in late October means open slopes, little snow and deer that need water. A wet cold one means deep snow early (Tip).

• Wet Pacific air hits the Coast Mountains and drops its rain 90%.
  • The Interior sits in the rain shadow behind them 95%.
  • A station near Mission gets about 9 times the rain of Kamloops 85%.
More: rain shadow details and numbers
  • The rain shadow of the Coast Mountains makes the southern Interior Plateau dry. It is driest in the deepest valleys, so grassland wins there (95%, Bunchgrass zone chapter).
  • Representative stations (Meidinger and Pojar 1991, Table 4) 85%:
    • Haney, UBC (University of British Columbia) Research Forest, Maple Ridge, CWH: 2,140 mm a year.
    • Kamloops, BG: 242 mm a year.
    • 2,140 divided by 242 is about 8.8. Call it 9 times.
  • The CWH is on average the rainiest zone in BC, about 2,228 mm a year, ranging 1,000 to 4,400 mm 95%.
  • The Bunchgrass zone gets most of its moisture in winter. Plants dry out as summer goes on 95%. So by October, green feed in the Thompson is in draws, north slopes and near water (Tip; see Food, water and cover).

• Coast forest: wettest. Grassland: driest 85%.
  • Wet zones grow thick brush. Dry zones are open and easy to glass (Tip).

  • One station is not the whole zone. Ranges inside a zone are wide: the IDF runs from about 300 to 750 mm, over 1,000 mm in its wettest parts 95%.

• High zones get the most snow: ESSF far ahead 85%.
  • Deer struggle in snow deeper than about 30 cm 85%.
  • Snow is what pushes deer down to the low zones 85%.
More: snow and what it does to game
  • Yearly snowfall at the same stations (Table 4, 85%): Boss Mountain ESSF 782 cm, Revelstoke ICH 422 cm, Brenda Mines MS 398 cm, 150 Mile House IDF 145 cm, Kelowna PP 97 cm, Haney CWH 82 cm, Kamloops BG 67 cm.
  • ESSF: 50 to 70% of precipitation falls as snow; the snowpack peaks at about 1 to nearly 4 m 95%.
  • Mule and black tailed deer have difficulty moving in snow deeper than 30 cm (85%, BC Ministry of Environment, Mule and Black tailed Deer in BC).
  • Moose move freely in snow to about 40 cm and with slight difficulty at 40 to 70 cm (85%, BC Ministry of Environment, Moose in BC).
  • Moose sometimes winter in the drier ESSF but usually leave to escape deep snow 95%. Most ungulates in the MS move lower in winter 95%.
  • Ungulates: hoofed animals (deer, elk, moose, sheep, goats).

• Heffley Creek sits in the hot dry pine zone 90%.
  • Mission is coast forest. Oliver and Osoyoos are grassland 90%.
More: how these were read
  • I read each town centre point off the official BC zone map data (BC Geographic Warehouse, BEC zone polygons) on 2026-10-11 90%.
  • One point is one point. Walk 3 km uphill and you are in another zone. See the next screen.
  • Heffley Creek base point in this app: 50.86 N, 120.27 W (approximate). Mission: 49.13 N, 122.31 W. Kelowna: 49.89 N, 119.49 W.
  • Your (Management Unit) 3-27 spans several zones. Use the zone map before you scout (Tip). See Map scouting.

• Drive 27 km uphill and you pass 4 zones 90%.
  • Pine valley, fir slopes, spruce plateau, subalpine at Sun Peaks.
  • Each band is a different hunt (Tip).

• Look at the oldest, tallest trees. They name the zone 85%.
  • Pine parks: PP. Fir: IDF. Spruce spires: ESSF. Cedar: wet zones.
More: tree clues in full
  • PP (Ponderosa pine): big pines with long needles and orange plated bark in open, park like stands with grass under them 95%.
  • IDF (Interior Douglas fir): Douglas fir dominates. Open stands with bunchgrass on dry sites, dense fir with pinegrass on moister sites 95%. Douglas fir cones have 3 pointed bracts sticking out like mouse tails 85%.
  • MS (Montane spruce): hybrid spruce and subalpine fir at climax, but huge young lodgepole pine stands from old fires are the look you will see most 95%.
  • ESSF (Engelmann spruce and subalpine fir): narrow spire shaped trees, meadows and parkland near the top 95%.
  • ICH (Interior cedar and hemlock): western redcedar and western hemlock; devil's club and skunk cabbage in wet spots 95%.
  • CWH (Coastal Western Hemlock): western hemlock most common, western redcedar, coast Douglas fir on drier sites, red alder where logged 95%.
  • Young forest after fire or logging can fool you. Aspen and lodgepole pine pioneer in many zones 90%. Look for the old survivors (Tip).

• South slopes are hotter and drier. They act like a lower zone 85%.
  • North slopes act like a higher zone 85%.
  • The edge between them is prime deer country (Tip).
More: aspect in the zone book
  • In the Bunchgrass zone, rough or Idaho fescue often grows on steep north and east slopes, while bluebunch wheatgrass and sage hold the hot ones 95%.
  • In the IDF, ponderosa pine persists on dry, south facing slopes even in moister subzones 95%.
  • Low elevation, south facing slopes in the IDF attract many animals in winter 95%. See and .
  • Tip: on a cold October morning, deer feed on the sunny south face. On a hot afternoon, they bed in the shade of the north face timber.

Read the zone in 5 steps1 of 5
  • 2 minutes at every stop. It becomes automatic (Tip).
More: the 5 steps in detail
  1. Elevation and aspect: your phone map or GPS gives metres. Aspect is the way the slope faces (Tip).
  2. Big trees: ponderosa pine, Douglas fir, spruce and subalpine fir, cedar and hemlock 85%.
  3. Ground plants (85%, zone book plant lists):
    • Bunchgrass, sagebrush, antelope brush (bitterbrush): BG or PP.
    • Pinegrass, kinnikinnick, soopolallie: IDF.
    • Black huckleberry, grouseberry, white rhododendron: MS or ESSF.
    • Devil's club, ferns: ICH.
    • Salal, red huckleberry, sword fern: CWH.
  4. Hanging tree lichen and late snow in shade mean cold and wet (Tip).
  5. Map: BC publishes the zone map free. Links in Sources.

• Summer and early fall: high zones (MS, ESSF) 85%.
  • Winter: low south slopes in PP and IDF 95%.
  • Some deer travel up to 80 km to winter there 95%.
More: movement through the zones
  • Mule deer, white tailed deer, bighorn sheep and elk can migrate up to 80 km to winter in the PP and IDF (95%, zone book).
  • In the northern IDF, mule deer need old Douglas fir for winter food (litterfall) and snow interception 95%.
  • Most ungulates leave the MS for lower ground in winter; caribou and some moose stay 95%.
  • Full story with timing: How animals move through the year.

• BC rates each zone by how often fire comes back 90%.
  • Dry low zones: frequent small ground fires kept them open 90%.
  • Coast forest: big fires, centuries apart 90%.
More: natural disturbance types
  • NDT (natural disturbance type), from the Forest Practices Code Biodiversity Guidebook, 1995 (90%, BC Ministry of Environment restoration guidelines page):
    • NDT1: ecosystems with rare stand initiating events.
    • NDT2: ecosystems with infrequent stand initiating events.
    • NDT3: ecosystems with frequent stand initiating events.
    • NDT4: ecosystems with frequent stand maintaining fires.
    • NDT5: alpine tundra and subalpine parkland.
  • The BC zone map data gives each subzone an NDT 90%: Heffley Creek PPxh2 is NDT4, the MSdm3 plateau and ESSFdc3 at Sun Peaks are NDT3, Mission CWHdm3 is NDT2, Harrison CWHvm2 is NDT1.
  • Stand initiating means the fire kills most trees and a new forest starts. Stand maintaining means ground fire clears brush and small trees but old thick barked trees live 90%.
  • More: After fire.

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not fact): Know your floor. Every 300 m up the hill is a different house with different tenants.

More: why this works
  • Elevation changes zone faster than distance does. On the Heffley transect, 4 zones fit in 27 km 90%.
  • When you find game in one zone, look for the same zone on the map elsewhere (Tip).

Common mistakes
  • Thinking one valley is one habitat. Zones change every few hundred metres of height and with every slope turn.
  • Hunting high zones in late fall snow. The deer already moved down.
  • Reading a young pine stand as the zone. Look for the old trees.
More: more mistakes
  • Trusting a 1991 number as today's weather. Use it to compare zones, not to plan a day (Tip).
  • Forgetting the north slope. It acts a zone higher and holds snow longer 85%.

Do this in the field

On your next drive from Heffley Creek toward Sun Peaks, stop 4 times. At each stop: height, big tree, ground plant, zone guess. Check on the map at home.

  • 30 and 40: deer struggle past 30 cm of snow, moose shrug to 40 cm.
  • Rhyme: South is hot and grassy, north is cool and mossy.

grassland-country:
Why it matters

Grassland is where you can see deer a kilometre away, and they can see you. Learn its belts, draws and edges and you hunt it instead of just looking at it.

  • BC grassland is tiny but packed with game 70%.
  • Deer use the draws and edges, not the open middle (Tip).
  • This is the country right outside Kamloops and Heffley Creek.
More: what this session covers
  • Grasslands cover less than 1% of BC but hold about 30% of the province's species at risk (70%, conservation groups, search preview).
  • Most Interior grassland sits in the BG (Bunchgrass) zone and in the grassland phases of the IDF (Interior Douglas fir) zone 95%. See BC habitat zones.
  • This session: the three belts, healthy versus worn out range, where deer are in October, stalking open country, hazards, and the access rules on leased range.
  • Grassland plants for deer: Browse plants. Water and fall food: Food, water and cover.

• Lower grassland: sage on the valley floor 95%.
  • Middle grassland: no sage, thicker grass 95%.
  • Upper grassland: fescue, inside the fir zone 95%.
More: the belts in the zone book
  • BGxh (Bunchgrass, very dry hot), the lower grassland: valley bottoms to about 700 m. Widely spaced bluebunch wheatgrass, big sagebrush, lichen crust on the soil 95%.
  • BGxw (Bunchgrass, very dry warm), the middle grassland: about 700 to 1,000 m. Generally no big sagebrush; bluebunch wheatgrass grows closer together 95%.
  • Upper grasslands above about 900 to 1,000 m are mapped as grassland phases of the IDF 95%. Rough fescue dominates in the central part of the IDF, Idaho fescue in the south 95%.
  • Undisturbed climax grassland is about 60% bunchgrass, 10 to 15% shrubs and 25 to 35% soil crust (mosses, lichens) 95%.
  • Moisture comes mostly in winter. Plants dry out as summer goes on 95%. By October the grass is cured brown (Tip).
  • Source: Meidinger and Pojar 1991, Bunchgrass zone and Interior Douglas fir zone chapters.

• Bunchgrass grows in clumps with bare soil between 95%.
  • Sagebrush marks the hottest, driest ground 95%.
  • Deer eat little sage but use sage country in winter 70%.

• Tall bunchgrass: good range, good feed 95%.
  • Sage, cheatgrass, cactus, knapweed: overgrazed 95%.
  • Elk and sheep follow good grass (Tip).
More: range condition in the zone book
  • Overgrazing raises unpalatable or weedy plants at the expense of bunchgrass, especially bluebunch wheatgrass 95%.
  • Sites in fair to poor range condition often have more big sagebrush, low pussytoes, needle and thread grass, brittle prickly pear cactus and cheatgrass 95%.
  • Extreme disturbance brings knapweeds and cheatgrass 95%.
  • Bighorn sheep and elk use grassland in good condition; overgrazing and weeds have hurt them 90%.
  • Tip: cheatgrass seeds work into dog paws, ears and noses. Check your quail dog after every hunt.

More: more on grassland wildlife
  • The Bunchgrass zone is one of the smallest in BC but supports a tremendous diversity and density of wildlife, because grassland, shrub steppe, riparian strips and forest sit side by side 95%.
  • Mule and white tailed deer graze IDF grasslands in early spring 95%.
  • Shrub steppe adds mule and white tailed deer to the grassland species 95%.
  • California quail, ring necked pheasant and chukar were introduced; gray partridge came in from Washington 95%.
  • Sage grouse once lived in the Bunchgrass zone and are gone from BC 95%.
  • Bighorn sheep use low cliffs next to grassy forage as lambing grounds 95%.
  • Source: Meidinger and Pojar 1991, Tables 18, 20 and 22.

• Draws, timber edges and water. Not the open middle (Tip).
  • Dawn and dusk on the grass, midday in cover 80%.
More: why the draws and edges
  • Draws, moist depressions and north slopes keep green feed longest. Ponderosa pine and Douglas fir grow in moist draws 95%.
  • Brushy draws hold saskatoon, chokecherry and rose: browse plus cover (Tip). See Browse plants.
  • Water: when feed dries, deer need surface water. Studies elsewhere found deer prefer water within about 1 km 65%. See Food, water and cover.
  • Grassland lakes and potholes are first to thaw in spring and are duck and goose staging water 95%.
  • Tip: on a calm cold morning, check the sunny side of a draw. On a warm afternoon, check the shady side.

• In the open, your route is the hunt (Tip).
  • Stay below the skyline in a draw or fold (Tip).
  • Wind from the deer to you, always 75%.
More: stalking open country
  • Deer rely heavily on smell 70%. See Wind and thermals.
  • On grassland slopes, morning air rises uphill and evening air sinks 75%. Approach from above in the evening, from below in the morning, when the wind allows (Tip).
  • A skylined hunter is seen from far away (Tip). Cross ridges where a tree, rock or saddle breaks your outline.
  • Move when the deer has its head down feeding; freeze when it lifts its head (Tip).
  • Full method: Moving quietly and Glassing.

Hunt a grassland basin in 5 steps1 of 5
  • Most of the work is the glassing (Tip).
More: the 5 steps in detail
  1. Glass from a high seat at first light, binoculars braced (Tip). Scan order (near first or far first) is your choice; both are covered in Glassing.
  2. Look in the draws, at timber edges, under lone trees and on north slopes (Tip).
  3. Plan with the wind and thermals. Pick 2 landmarks to find the deer again from below (Tip).
  4. Close in using draws, folds, rocks and cattle trails. Head down: move. Head up: freeze (Tip).
  5. A bullet that misses on open grass can travel a long way. Shoot only with hillside behind the animal (Tip). See Firearm safety.

Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

  • Leased range with cattle on it: no hunting without consent 99%.
  • Leased land is under the Trespass Act even with no cattle 99%.
  • Leave every gate as you found it (Tip).
More: the rule words and courtesy
BC Hunting and Trapping Regulations Synopsis, page 9, 2 October 2026 edition

"A person is not permitted to hunt on cultivated land or on Crown land which is subject to a grazing lease while the land is occupied by livestock, without the consent of the owner, lessee, or occupant of the land."

  • Plain English: cultivated land always needs consent. A needs consent while livestock are on it 99%.
  • Note on page 9: leased land is subject to the Trespass Act whether or not livestock are present 99%.
  • Full rules: Where you can hunt.
  • Lac du Bois Grasslands near Kamloops is a no shooting area inside the city boundary (95%, from Habitat tour: deer). Use it as a classroom.
  • Courtesy (Tip): leave gates as found, never drive on wet range, never shoot near cattle, and tell the rancher what you saw. Ranchers remember hunters.

• Nearly all rattlesnakes are in their dens by mid October 85%.
  • Badger holes, grass fire, cattle, long shots (Tip).
More: hazard details
  • Western rattlesnakes live in the dry valleys of the Fraser Canyon, Similkameen, Thompson, Okanagan and Kettle 80%.
  • They spend about 180 days a year in communal dens. They come out in March and April. Virtually all are back in the dens by mid October (85%, BC Identified Wildlife account).
  • Dens are often near the base of warm, sunny slopes in rock. Snakes seldom move more than about 1.5 km from a den 85%. On a warm October day, watch your hands and feet near rock piles (Tip).
  • Badger holes and ground squirrel burrows twist ankles and catch ATV wheels (Tip).
  • Hot exhaust on dry grass can start a fire. Park on bare ground or gravel (Tip). See ATV rules.
  • Give cattle and bulls room. Never get between a cow and calf (Tip).

• Quail: brush next to grass, near water (Tip).
  • Sharp tailed grouse: open bunchgrass country 90%.
More: birds in more detail
  • California quail are an introduced species in the Bunchgrass and Ponderosa pine zones 95%.
  • Sharp tailed grouse are listed for Bunchgrass grasslands and IDF grassland 90%.
  • Check seasons and open areas in the Rule Book before you hunt either: Region 3, Region 8.
  • Quail tactics: First quail trip and Habitat tour: quail and grouse.

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

  • Hunting leased range with cattle on it without asking (99%, rule above).

Why it matters

Most of your October deer hunting near Heffley Creek happens in open pine and Douglas fir. Read this forest well and you know where deer feed, bed and winter.

More: the full tree key
  • Ponderosa pine: tree to 40 to 50 m. Needles mostly in threes, 12 to 20 cm long, yellow green, clustered at branch ends. Old bark cinnamon red in loose plates. Cones 8 to 14 cm with prickly scale tips (85%, E Flora BC).
  • Douglas fir: needles 2 to 3 cm, single, soft, spreading around the twig. Bark very thick, rough, dark brown. Interior cones 4 to 7 cm 85%. The 3 pointed bracts that stick out of the cone scales look like mouse tails 85%.
  • Lodgepole pine: needles in pairs, 2 to 7 cm, often twisted. Small lopsided cones 3 to 6 cm that can stay shut until fire opens them 85%.
  • Western larch, in the southeast and some IDF: needles in bunches of 15 to 30 that turn yellow and fall in autumn 85%.
  • Why care: pine means the hottest, driest ground. Thick fir on a north slope means shade and a cool bed (Tip).

More: fire in the dry forest
  • Ponderosa pine is well adapted to fire, and fire has played an important role in the PP zone 95%.
  • In the IDF, ground fires were common historically, favouring mature trees with thick bark and open canopies 95%. Where crown fires ran, you get mixed Douglas fir and lodgepole pine with scattered big fir veterans 95%.

  • A fire history at Trout Creek Ecological Reserve near Summerland (PPxh1, 75 ha) found a mean fire interval of 18 years from 1715 to 1952 (80%, Gayton 2013, search preview).
  • The open canopy lets light through for shrubs like ceanothus and saskatoon that wintering deer and elk eat 95%.

• Less fire for about 100 years means thicker forest 85%.
  • Thickets of young fir cut your view and the deer's feed (Tip).
  • Burns and thinning open it again 85%.
More: fire suppression and what it changed
  • The IDF grasslands have been influenced by reduced fire frequency since the turn of the 20th century (95%, zone book).
  • BC restoration guidelines say decades of fire control let dense, even aged stands spread, which later fed beetle outbreaks 85%.
  • Restoration work in the dry Interior uses logging, thinning and prescribed burning to reopen fire maintained forests (80%, Kootenay Boundary NDT4 guidelines, search preview).

Why it matters

  1. Ducks usually face into the wind. Coming from downwind means they flush toward you (Tip).
  2. Every cattail band, willow clump or bank fold is cover. Crawl the last part if needed (Tip).
  3. Glass first: you may find a moose, a deer drinking, or a pair of mallards in the far corner (Tip).
  4. Retrieve: a dog, chest waders in shallow water, or a wind that drifts the bird to shore. If none, do not shoot (Tip).
  5. Cold water kills. See Water safety and the .

  • Wallows in wet meadows: bull elk in the rut 85%. See Reading sign.

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Common mistakes

  • Shooting a duck over deep cold water with no way to get it back.

burn-country:
Why it matters

BC burns a lot, and a burn changes month by month for 20 years. Know what each age of burn looks like and who feeds there, and a burned hillside becomes a map of where game will be.

  • New green feed grows under the dead trees 85%.
  • Each age of burn feeds different animals 70%.
  • Burns are also dangerous ground 85%.
More: what this session covers
  • This session: a burn year by year, who uses it when, why burns are patchy, how to hunt one, and the safety rules of burned ground.
  • Fire in the dry forest: Dry forests. Fire types by zone (NDT, natural disturbance type): BC habitat zones. Logging, the other big disturbance: Cutblocks.
  • Evidence on how game uses burns is mixed and varies by place and burn severity. Numbers here are from studies, mostly outside BC, so certainty is 60 to 75% unless marked.
  • Assumption: "year 1" means the first growing season after the fire.

A burn from year 0 to 201 of 5
  • Black, then green, then shrubs, then thicket 75%.
  • The best feed years are roughly 2 to 10 65%.
More: the stages in detail
  • Year 0: ash, black soil, standing dead trees (snags). Ash pits can stay hot long after the flames (85%, BC Wildfire Service).
  • Years 1 to 2: grasses and herbs flush green. Seeds of snowbrush (ceanothus) and lodgepole pine germinate in response to fire (90%, BC restoration guidelines). Elk use of burned grassland went up in the first 1 to 2 years after prescribed burns in Montana 70%.
  • Years 3 to 5: shrubs and sprouts. Trembling aspen regenerates abundantly from root suckers that quickly form a dense shrub layer (85%, E Flora BC). Willow, saskatoon and rose resprout 75%.
  • Years 6 to 10: young lodgepole pine and aspen rise. Most fire killed snags break or fall in the first 15 years; lodgepole and ponderosa pine snags fall sooner than Douglas fir (65 to 70%, Pacific Northwest studies, search preview).
  • Years 10 to 20: dense regeneration. In the MS (Montane spruce) zone, dense lodgepole regeneration thickets give moose and mule deer thermal and hiding cover (95%, zone book).
  • In BC's structural stages, burned and cut areas pass through herb (stage 2) and shrub (stage 3) stages, usually under 20 years for herbs and under 40 years for tall shrubs, before the pole and sapling stage 90%.

• Bears and elk: early green years 70%.
  • Deer and moose: shrub years 70%.
  • Woodpeckers: dead trees first 90%.
More: the evidence, study by study
  • Black bears forage burned areas in spring for succulent green plants (85%, BC Ministry of Environment, Black Bear in BC).
  • Elk in sagebrush grassland (Montana): use rose in years 1 to 2 after prescribed burning, then fell back to pre burn levels over 3 to 10 years as forage quantity and protein dropped (70%, Van Dyke and Darragh 2007, search preview).
  • Elk in Yellowstone used burned grassland more after the 1988 fires but avoided burned forest for the first 3 winters (65%, search preview).
  • Mule deer in an Arizona ponderosa pine burn: use passed the unburned area after 2 years, tied to palatable plants, not total plant mass (65%, Kruse 1972, search preview).
  • Moose in BC's Mount McAllister burn (26,500 ha, about 5 years old, north central BC): moose used low and medium severity patches, especially wet sites (75%, McNay and others 2021, Alces 57).
  • Boreal moose in Alberta, Saskatchewan and northeast BC showed low use of burns up to 40 years old (65%, DeMars and others 2019, search preview). Burns do not always mean more moose.
  • ICH (Interior cedar and hemlock) clearcuts and burns: moose, mule deer, white tails, elk, cougar; ruffed grouse; black backed and three toed woodpeckers (95%, zone book Table 24).

• Unburned islands, light burn, black burn 85%.
  • Hunt the edges between patches (Tip).
  • Moose favoured low and medium burn patches 75%.
More: reading severity
  • Low severity: ground burned, many trees alive with green crowns, black trunks (Tip).
  • High severity: everything black, crowns gone (Tip).
  • Unburned islands are bedding and escape cover beside new feed (Tip).
  • The Mount McAllister moose study recommends prescribed burns for moose focus on low to medium severity on moist sites 75%.
  • Satellite images in mapping apps show burn patches clearly (Tip). See Map scouting.

  • Fireguards open new access into game country 70%.

  • Before every trip in fire season, check the BC Wildfire Service for area restrictions and the Rule Book for in season closures (Tip). Region 3 rules: Region 3.

  • Ash pits stay hot. Floods and slides follow rain 85%.
  • Risks can last 2 years or more 85%.
More: the BC Wildfire Service list

  • Ash pits: hard to detect and can stay hot long after the flames die down 85%.
  • Burned ground sheds water: floods and debris flows. In severely burned areas this risk can last much longer than the others 85%.

More: snag rules of thumb

  • Windy days and wet soil after rain are the worst times to be among snags (Tip).
  • Look up before you sit, glass or field dress (Tip).
  • Leaning snags hung up in other trees are the most dangerous (Tip).

Hunt a burn in 5 steps1 of 5
  • Burns are glassing country: open and wide (Tip).
More: the method in detail
  1. Age the burn from the map date or the plants: grass and fireweed (1 to 2 years), knee to chest shrubs (3 to 5), head high pine and aspen (6 to 10) (Tip).
  2. Burns are open. Glass from across the valley or from a high corner (Tip). See Glassing.
  3. Island edges give food and cover side by side (Tip).
  4. Deadfall makes noise and twists ankles. Old roads and game trails are quieter (Tip).
  5. Fresh beds and droppings at the edge of thickets show where deer and moose lie up (Tip). See Reading sign.
  6. Grouse love burn edges with berries and young trees (Tip).

  • Walking the deadfall instead of the roads and trails.

cutblock-country:
Why it matters

Logging has made a patchwork of cutblocks of every age across your hunting country. Each age is a different kitchen. Learn to age a block at a glance and you know who eats there.

  • A cutblock grows through stages, like a burn 90%.
  • Young blocks feed deer. Middle aged blocks feed moose (65 to 85%).
  • Old dense blocks are cover, not food 90%.
More: what this session covers
  • This session: BC's forest stages, a block year by year, moose and block age, reading a logged landscape from above, roads and access, and how to hunt blocks.
  • Fire does the same job in nature: After fire. Strips left along creeks: Wetlands and riparian strips.
  • Assumption: ages are years since the block was cut. Growth is faster in wet zones and slower in dry or high ones.

• 7 stages from bare ground to old forest 90%.
  • Food peaks in the shrub stages 85%.
  • The pole stage is dark and bare 90%.
More: the official definitions
  • Source: BC structural stages, Standards for Terrestrial Ecosystems Mapping 1998, reprinted in Accounts and Measures for Managing Identified Wildlife, Appendix 5, 2004 90%.
  • Stage 1, sparse or bryoid: mosses and lichens, under 20 years after disturbance in normal forest.
  • Stage 2, herb: grasses, forbs, ferns; trees under 10% cover; under 20 years.
  • Stage 3, shrub and herb: shrubs over 20% cover; 3a low shrub under 2 m (under 20 years), 3b tall shrub 2 to 10 m (under 40 years). Recent cut or burned areas regenerating to forest are stage 3.
  • Stage 4, pole and sapling: trees over 10 m, densely stocked, overtopping shrubs and herbs; usually over 10 to 15 years old and under 40 years since disturbance; stagnant dense stands up to 100 years.
  • Stage 5, young forest: self thinning and layering; generally 40 to 80 years.
  • Stage 6, mature forest: understories well developed as the canopy opens; 80 to 140 years in group A zones (for example MS, SBPS), 80 to 250 years in the others.
  • Stage 7, old forest: snags and logs of all ages, patchy understories; over 140 or over 250 years.
  • : a broad leaved herb that is not a grass.

• About years 3 to 10: deer feed (Tip).
  • About years 10 to 30: moose feed 65%.
  • About years 25 to 40: dark poles, few animals 85%.

A cutblock from stumps to forest1 of 5
  • Age a block from the height of the young trees (Tip).
More: who uses each stage
  • Young seral forest (stages 2 to 4) in the MS: moose, mule deer, black bear, lynx, coyote, snowshoe hare; ruffed grouse, northern goshawk (95%, zone book Table 26).
  • Dense young lodgepole regeneration gives moose and mule deer thermal and hiding cover 95%.
  • Logging may temporarily benefit moose when willows and other shrubs become abundant in cutblocks, but removing too much forest cover can hurt them. Moose need cover to hide from predators and hunters, for shade and for shelter in blizzards (85%, BC Ministry of Environment, Moose in BC).
  • Logging creates early seral forage for elk, but it disappears once the canopy closes (85%, Elk in BC).
  • Coast black tailed deer make frequent use of logged habitats in spring and summer 80%.
  • Snowshoe hares and grouse use the thick shrub and sapling stages (Tip, see Small game).
  • Height guide (Tip): knee high seedlings about 3 to 5 years; head high about 8 to 12; twice your height about 15 to 20; closed dark canopy about 25 plus. Varies by zone.

• One BC study: moose chose blocks 10 to 30 years old 65%.
  • They avoided blocks under 10 and over 30 years 65%.
More: the studies
  • UBC thesis using GPS data from 46 mostly adult female moose, 2004 to 2019: moose strongly selected cutblocks 10 to 30 years since cut and avoided 0 to 9 and over 30 year blocks in every season (65%, search preview; study area not confirmed).
  • Near Logan Lake (Region 3), a study found plants in cutblocks had more tannins and less digestible protein than plants in forests, and summer forage was short of protein for nursing cows (65%, search preview). Good looking browse is not always good food.
  • Moose basics: Moose.

  • Stars: young feed blocks touching timber or creek strips (Tip).

farm-country:
Why it matters

Valley bottom farms grow the richest feed in BC, and deer, elk, quail, ducks and geese know it. But every field belongs to someone. Read the farm, then ask.

  • Farms sit on old winter range in the valley bottoms 95%.
  • Deer, elk, geese and quail all use farm edges 95%.
  • Cultivated land: no hunting without consent 99%.
More: what this session covers
  • In the PP (Ponderosa pine) and IDF (Interior Douglas fir) zones, agriculture is restricted to low valleys and riparian areas, which ungulates historically used as winter range (95%, zone book).
  • Elk, mule deer and white tailed deer are often considered pests because of crop damage 95%.
  • This session: crops and who eats them, reading a field, Okanagan orchards, Fraser Valley winter fields, the rules, asking permission and farm safety.

  • Elk relish cultivated forage crops such as alfalfa and clover (85%, BC Ministry of Environment, Elk in BC).
  • Hayfields and alfalfa in the North Thompson pull white tails every evening and mule deer in hard weather (80%, from Food, water and cover).
  • Agricultural areas in the BG (Bunchgrass), PP and IDF list elk, mule deer, white tailed deer, coyote, pocket gopher, Canada goose, kestrel and magpie (95%, zone book Tables 18, 20, 22).
  • Fraser Valley: corn stubble, berry fields, pasture and hay draw black tailed deer at dusk, and ducks and geese in winter (65%, from Food, water and cover).
  • Deer and elk chew buds, spurs, shoots and leaves of all fruit tree varieties (85%, BC Tree Fruit Production Guide).
  • Bears are drawn to fruit trees in fall; BC conservation programs ask residents to pick ripe and fallen fruit daily (70%, WildSafeBC via news).

  • Hedgerows and ditches are travel lanes (Tip).

More: field reading in detail
  • Field deer come out the same corner most nights, from the nearest thick cover, with the wind in their favour (hunter lore, 60%).
  • Look for trails worn into the field edge, fence crossings with hair, and droppings at the corners (Tip). See Reading sign and Trails and funnels.
  • Creek strips through farmland link timber to fields (Tip). See Wetlands and riparian strips.
  • Glass fields from public roads at last light. Never shine lights or shoot from the road (Tip; road rules in Where you can hunt).

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

  • No hunting or shooting within 100 m of an occupied house or farm building 99%.
  • Cultivated land: always ask 99%.

No Shooting or Hunting Areas, page 10, 2 October 2026 edition

"It is unlawful to hunt or discharge a firearm within 100 m of a church, school building, school yard, playground, regional district park, dwelling house, or farm or ranch building that is occupied by persons or domestic animals."

Wildlife Act, page 9

"A person is not permitted to hunt on cultivated land or on Crown land which is subject to a grazing lease while the land is occupied by livestock, without the consent of the owner, lessee, or occupant of the land."

  • Many valley towns and districts add discharge bylaws and No Shooting areas. Check Region 8, Region 2 and the local sessions before every new farm (Tip).

More: orchard deer facts
  • Deer and elk chew buds, spurs, shoots and leaves of all fruit trees. Small damaged trees may never become productive. Antler rubbing breaks branches and strips bark (85%, BC Tree Fruit Production Guide).
  • The guide calls a properly built fence the only long term solution 85%.
  • South Okanagan orchardists have asked for deer culls because of damage (70%, BC Fruit Growers' Association via news).

  • Electric: 1.5 to 2.1 m high, 7 to 9 high tensile wires spaced 20 to 30 cm apart. Okanagan research found vertical designs work better than slanted ones 85%.
  • Tip: a fence pushes deer along it to the end, a gate or a washout. That is where to look for tracks.

rs-track-measuring:
Why it matters

A guess says "deer". A tape says "big mule deer, walking, relaxed, heading for the timber".

  • Five numbers turn a print into a story.
  • Measure the same way every time (Tip).
More: what this session covers
  • Tracks taught shapes, rough sizes and the 5 gaits. This session goes deeper: how to measure like a biologist, and how to read speed, mood and body size from the trail.
  • You will learn: length, width, step, stride, straddle, group and gap; front versus hind; the 3 ways a hind foot lands; walk, trot, lope, gallop, bound and stot patterns; the wolf or dog size rule; and how to log it.
  • Kit (Tip): soft tape in centimetres, a straight stick with 2 rubber bands (a track stick, see Following a track), notebook, phone, and your knife for scale in photos.
  • Field biologists record length, width, stride and straddle, plus the ground type, date, time and weather (70%, Jack Raven Bushcraft and Murray State University mammalogy pages).
  • Different guides measure stride in different ways. Pick one way, write it down, and stick to it 70%.

#Key point
1Measure length, width, stride, straddle, group 80%
2Measure the floor, never the rim 80%
3Average 3 to 5 prints and strides 80%
4Front prints are a little bigger, except bears and hares 80%
5Faster gait: longer stride, narrower straddle 85%
6Wolf if front 10 cm or hind 9 cm, no claws 85%
7A change in pattern marks an event (Tip)
  • Seven points. The rest of the session is the detail behind them.

Measure a trail in 5 steps1 of 5
  • Measure 3 to 5 prints and average 75%.
  • Claws register on and off. Leave them out of length 80%.
More: the 5 measurements in full
  1. Length: from the tip of the furthest forward toe to the back of the heel pad, along the foot's own line (80%, Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife). On hoofs: tip of the hoof to the back of the heel. Dewclaws are noted separately, not added in (Tip).
  2. Width: from the farthest outside point to the farthest inside point, at right angles to the length (80%, Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife).
  3. Step and stride: a step is one print to the next print. A stride is the same foot to the same foot, which is 2 steps. This app uses stride = same foot to same foot, as in Tracks. Some guides measure heel to heel, others toe to toe. Always measure like to like 70%.
  4. Straddle (trail width): outside edge of the left prints to outside edge of the right prints, at right angles to the line of travel 75%.
  5. Group and gap: when prints come in clusters (bound, lope, gallop, stot), measure the length of one cluster and the gap to the next 70%.
  • "Measure several footprints and average the size if possible" (80%, Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife, quoting Halfpenny and Furman 2010).
  • "It is best not to measure claws, as they sometimes register well, other times not at all" (80%, same source).
  • Measure several strides, not one. Animals change pace on slopes and when tired 70%.

• Mud and snow push the rim out, so the top looks bigger 75%.
  • Measure the floor of the print 80%.
More: why the rim lies
  • "Try to measure from the floor (bottom) of the track, not the top edge" (80%, Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife, livestock investigation guide).
  • Soft snow, deep mud and loose sand all spread the top edge. A print in slush can look a third bigger than the foot that made it (Tip).
  • Snow prints also grow as the sun melts them out 65%. See Aging tracks and sign.
  • Best habit: measure the cleanest print in the firmest ground you can find on the trail (Tip).

  • Black bear: North Dakota Game and Fish lists front about 15 cm long by 10 cm wide, rear about 18 cm by 13 cm (80%, converted from 6 by 4 and 7 by 5 inches).
  • Hares: "the back feet are two to four times as long as the front and always land ahead of the front feet" (85%, New York State Department of Environmental Conservation, Conservationist, February 2015).
  • In a direct register walk the hind lands on the front, so you measure a blend. Find a spot where they separate, often on a turn or a slope (Tip).

AnimalFront lengthFront width
White tailed deer3.5 to 10 cm 80%1.3 to 6 cm 80%
Mule deer5.7 to 10 cm 80%4 to 7 cm 80%
Elk7.6 to 12.7 cm 80%6.4 to 11.4 cm 80%
Moose11.4 to 17.8 cm 80%9.5 to 15 cm 80%
  • Deer and elk overlap at the top end. Look at shape too 70%.
More: where the numbers come from
  • North Dakota Game and Fish, Tracks and Signs of North Dakota Wildlife (government brochure), converted from inches: white tail front 1 3/8 to 4 inches long, 1/2 to 2 3/8 wide; mule deer front 2 1/4 to 4 long, 1 5/8 to 2 3/4 wide; elk front 3 to 5 long, 2 1/2 to 4 1/2 wide; moose front 4 1/2 to 7 long, 3 3/4 to 6 wide (85% for the reading, 80% for use in BC).
  • These ranges include fawns and calves. An adult deer is usually in the upper half (Tip).
  • Maine Inland Fisheries and Wildlife pocket card gives an adult white tail at 6.4 to 7.6 cm (2 1/2 to 3 inches) and moose at 11.4 to 14 cm 85%.
  • Elk tips are blunter and rounder; "adult bulls will have blunt hoof tips" for moose too (80%, North Dakota Game and Fish).
  • Prints splay (toes spread) on slopes, in mud and when running, which makes them wider (80%, North Dakota Game and Fish). Measure a relaxed print on flat ground.

AnimalFront lengthFront width
Coyoteabout 6.4 cm 80%about 5 cm 80%
Wolfabout 11.4 cm 80%about 10 cm 80%
Cougarabout 7.6 to 9 cm 75%about 9 cm 80%
Black bear (front)about 15 cm 80%about 10 cm 80%
  • Cougar: as wide as long or wider 75%.
More: paw sources and cautions
  • North Dakota Game and Fish (converted): coyote front 2 1/2 by 2 inches; gray wolf front 4 1/2 by 4; mountain lion front 3 long by 3 1/2 wide; black bear front 6 by 4 80%.
  • Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife track boxes (length = toe pad to heel pad): wolf about 4 inches wide by 4.5 long (10 by 11.4 cm), coyote about 2.5 by 2.5 (6.4 cm), cougar about 3.5 by 3.5 (9 cm), domestic dog about 3 by 3 and variable 80%.
  • One BC note: grizzlies live in the Thompson. Bear tracks have their own toe line test in Tracks.

• Front 10 cm or longer, or hind 9 cm or longer, no claws: likely wolf 80%.
  • Big dog breeds overlap. Read the trail as well 80%.
More: the rule in full
  • "Tracks were likely made by wolves if either of the following is true (82% of dogs have feet smaller than this): Hind foot length 3 1/2 inches or longer without claws; Front foot length 4 inches or longer without claws" (85%, Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife, citing Halfpenny and Furman 2010).
  • In centimetres: hind 8.9 cm or more, front 10.2 cm or more 85%.
  • Breeds in the wolf range: Irish wolfhounds, Akitas, Saint Bernards, Newfoundlands, Great Danes and mastiffs (85%, same source).
  • "Gaits and track patterns around kills and carcasses are often confusing and not diagnostic" (85%, same source).
  • Tracker lore: a wild canid walks a straight purposeful line; a dog wanders and visits everything 60%.

• Direct register: hind in the front print. One print shows 85%.
  • Overstep is faster than direct; understep is slower 75%.
More: register in full
  • Direct register: "the hind foot lands in the same spot as the front foot, leaving only one print" (85%, New York State Department of Environmental Conservation).
  • Indirect register: the hind lands near but not in the front print 80%.
  • Overstep: hind lands past the front. Understep: hind lands short. Understep walks are probably slower than direct register walks, and both slower than overstep walks (70%, tracking literature via search preview).
  • Deer and elk at a walk or trot usually put the hind hoof on or near the front hoof print on the same side 70%.
  • Cats direct register; a fox walking directly registers (80%, New York State Department of Environmental Conservation).
  • A direct register print can look like a double print with a small offset. Do not read it as two animals (Tip).

• Walk, trot, lope or gallop, bound. Each leaves its own shape 85%.
  • Faster: longer stride, narrower straddle 85%.
More: definitions from a wildlife agency
GaitDefinitionTrail
WalkEach limb moves on its own, never all off the ground 85%Alternating prints, short stride, wide straddle 85%
TrotDiagonal legs move together 85%Longer stride, narrower straddle 85%
Lope2 moments with all 4 feet in the air; a slow gallop 85%Groups of 4 on a slant 75%
GallopFastest gait, at least one moment with all feet off the ground 85%Groups of 4 in a line, long gaps 80%
Bound or jumpHind feet land and push off side by side 85%Hind pair lands ahead of the fronts 85%
  • Source: New York State Department of Environmental Conservation, Wildlife Tracking Skills presentation (Matt Walter) and Winter Tracks (Conservationist, 2015) 85%.
  • "Trotting creates a longer stride and a narrower trail width than walking" (85%, same source).
  • "As speed increases, prints space farther apart" (85%, same source).
  • Rabbits, squirrels, mice and rats are jumpers 85%.
  • A side trot is a trot with the body angled, so front and hind prints land in pairs side by side. It is mostly a dog and fox gait 70%.

• Mule deer walking: about 38 to 64 cm 80%.
  • Stot groups: about 2.4 to 4.6 m apart 80%.
More: the stride table and the catch
  • North Dakota Game and Fish "walking stride" ranges, converted: white tail 33 to 66 cm; mule deer 38 to 64 cm; elk 46 to 89 cm; moose 71 to 112 cm; black bear 43 to 64 cm; coyote 34 to 43 cm; wolf 33 to 61 cm; cougar 48 to 81 cm; bobcat 15 to 36 cm (85% for the reading).
  • The catch: those numbers look like print to next print (a step). The New York agency shows a white tail trail at about 84 cm (33 inches) same foot to same foot, with a straddle of about 13 cm (5 inches) 80%. My reading: North Dakota measured steps, New York measured strides 60%. Compare like with like.
  • Mule deer stot: "tracks are separated by an 8 to 15 foot stride" (85%, North Dakota Game and Fish). That is about 2.4 to 4.6 m.
  • White tailed deer prints may be angled 10 to 20 degrees outward from the line of travel (80%, New York State Department of Environmental Conservation).
  • When a deer runs scared, dewclaws print behind and the toes spread (85%, New York Conservationist).

• Zig zag walk, browse nips: relaxed and feeding (Tip).
  • A sudden change in pattern marks a moment. Look around it (Tip).
More: mood reading in full
PatternLikely moodWhat you do
Wandering walk, stops, browseFeeding, relaxed (Tip)Slow down. Bed may be close
Straight walk or trot on a trailTravelling with purpose 65%Find where the trail goes: bed or feed
Feet together, then stot or gallopSpooked 80%Look back: was it you?
Long trot, nose to ground lineBuck in the rut on a doe trail (Tip)Rut lesson: The rut
  • Feet bunched together at a stop, then a gallop: the animal stood and looked, then fled (Tip).
  • Read 20 m before and after any change. The cause (your scent, a coyote, a vehicle) is usually there (Tip).
  • Speed check: stride grows and straddle shrinks as it speeds up (85%, New York State Department of Environmental Conservation).

ClueTells you
StraddleBody width and weight 70%
Walking strideLeg length 70%
Print depth vs your bootWeight (Tip)
Drag marks in snowShort legs or deep snow 70%
  • Wide straddle and deep prints: a heavy animal (Tip).
More: size reading and buck lore
  • "A wide straddle often indicates a heavy bodied animal like a bear or a badger; a narrow straddle usually belongs to efficient walkers like foxes or coyotes" (65%, tracking guide via search preview).
  • Depth test: step beside the print with full weight. A print deeper than your boot in the same ground came from an animal heavier than you (Tip).
  • Buck or doe from one print: not reliable 60%. Tracker lore from the Benoit family (Maine white tails): bucks worth following usually leave prints at least 7.6 cm (3 inches) wide (60%, Outdoor Life).
  • A wide straddle with toes pointed out and a heavy, dragging walk in snow is the classic big buck story. It is lore, not proof 60%.

• 8 lines per trail. Photo with your knife (Tip).
  • Your own notes become your best size table (Tip).
More: why logging matters
  • Record the ground: "sand, snow, soil, wet mud, stone", plus date, time, location, weather, and how clear the track was (70%, Jack Raven Bushcraft via search preview).
  • Use the app Journal. One line per fact.
  • After 20 logged trails you will know what a Heffley Creek mule deer walk looks like in your own numbers (Tip).
  • Photograph straight down with the scale object flat beside the print, then one photo from low and to the side to show depth (Tip).

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law): One print tells you who. Ten prints tell you how. Measure both.

Common mistakes
  • Measuring the top rim in soft snow, then calling a doe a big buck.
  • Mixing up step and stride, so your numbers never match a table.
  • Naming a wolf from one big print without checking for a dog trail.

Do this in the field

Find one walking deer trail. Measure 3 prints, 3 strides and the straddle. Then find where it speeds up and measure again.

More: the drill step by step
  1. Pick a trail in mud or fresh snow.
  2. Measure 3 front prints on the floor. Average them.
  3. Measure 3 strides, same foot to same foot. Average them.
  4. Measure the straddle.
  5. Walk the trail until the pattern changes. Measure the new stride and straddle.
  6. Write: what changed, and why you think so. Photo both.

• LWSSG: Length, Width, Stride, Straddle, Group.
  • Faster = longer and narrower.
  • Wolf: front 10, hind 9 (centimetres, no claws).
More: more hooks
  • "Floor, not the rim." Say it every time you kneel.
  • "Two steps make a stride."
  • "Hare: hind feet first." The big feet land ahead.
  • Number trick: a mule deer stot gap is about the length of your truck, 2.4 to 4.6 m (Tip).

  • New York State Department of Environmental Conservation, Wildlife Tracking Skills, Matt Walter and Winter Tracks, Conservationist February 2015, read directly, checked 2026-10-11 85%: gait definitions, register, stride and straddle, deer print angle, hare feet.
  • Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife, Livestock injury and mortality investigations, read directly, checked 2026-10-11 85%: wolf or dog rule, measuring tips, track sizes.

• Maine Inland Fisheries and Wildlife, Pocket guide to Maine animal tracks, read directly, checked 2026-10-11 85%: adult deer and moose print sizes.

rs-track-aging:
Why it matters

Old sign shows where animals were. Fresh sign shows where they are. Only one of those fills a tag.

  • Five age bands: minutes, hours, today, days, a week or more.
  • Always give a range and say why (Tip).
More: what this session covers
  • Tracks and Reading sign gave the quick aging clues. This session is the full method.
  • You will learn: the control print, weather clocks (rain, frost, dew, wind, snowfall), debris and insects, broken twigs and crushed plants, how each ground type ages, scat, beds, rubs and scrapes, and how to decide if sign is fresh enough to hunt.
  • Honest warning: even expert trackers sort sign into broad bands like "fresh" and "old" more easily than into hours (65%, Original Wisdom, trailing deer). Aging is a skill you calibrate, not a formula.
  • Aging means judging the time since sign was made "taking into consideration vegetation damage, rain, sun, and other natural elements" (65%, tracking glossary via search preview).

#Key point
1Your own boot print is the clock (Tip)
2Rain pits or frost inside: made before that weather 70%
3Dark trail in dewy grass: made after the dew formed (Tip)
4Mud ages slowest; sand and dust fastest 65%
5Shade and cold keep sign crisp for days 65%
6Use moisture and shine, not colour, for scat (Tip)
7Know the last 72 hours of weather (Tip)
8Give a range, never a minute (Tip)
  • Learn these 8, then the detail.

Age a track in 4 steps1 of 4
  • Your print is minutes old. Theirs looks the same? It is fresh (Tip).
  • Every patch of ground ages differently. Test it 65%.
More: why it works
  • Ground varies so much that "the only way to truly understand how a particular track has aged is to test that spot and get a feel for its nature and how it weathers" (65%, tracking source via search preview).
  • Tracking schools teach aging with a tracking box or a strip of open ground: make prints each day and compare them through different weather 65%.
  • Make the control print with the same pressure and in the same light. A sun print and a shade print age at different speeds (Tip).
  • After a long dry spell, hard ground takes poor prints and even rain does not reset it as you expect (60%, Original Wisdom).

• Crisp walls: hours. Rounded: days. Debris inside: a week (Tip).
  • In fine dust a fresh print has a thin raised rim that slumps within hours 60%.
More: edge details
  • As a track ages, "bits of disturbed soil will dry and the track edges will round out" (65%, Nature Mentor via search preview).
  • Fresh: sharp walls, crisp toe dividers, the ridge between the two hoof halves still standing (Tip).
  • A day: edges softening, loose crumbs sliding in (Tip).
  • Days: walls rounded, the ridge between the toes gone (Tip).
  • A week or more: debris, spider web or insect trails inside 70%.
▶Hunting Tips: How to Age TracksSharp edges mean fresh. Rounded and filled means old.
Outdoor Life, YouTube, 1 min. Needs internet.

• Pits inside the print: made before the rain 70%.
  • A clean print on pitted ground: made after 70%.
More: rain in full
  • Rain pits inside a print mean it was made before the rain. A clean print on rain spattered ground is after the rain (70%, from Tracks).
  • Heavy rain softens and fills prints, so old tracks look days older than they are (Tip).
  • Rain also makes blood look lighter than it was (65%, Bowhunter). See Blood, hair and tissue.
  • Know when it last rained. Write the time in your notebook or check the Environment Canada history for Kamloops when you get home (Tip).

• Frost crystals inside: made before the frost 65%.
  • Print cut through frost: made after it, often this morning 65%.
More: frost and snow in full
  • Frost crystals grown inside a print mean it was made before the frost, usually last night or earlier 65%.
  • A print that cuts through the frost crust was made after the frost formed 65%.
  • Fresh snow inside a track: made before or during the snowfall. If it stopped snowing 4 hours ago and there is snow in the track, it is at least 4 hours old (60%, hunter source via search preview).
  • No new snow in the track after an overnight snowfall: made after the snow stopped 60%.
  • A frozen or icy floor usually means older, made before the freeze 60%.
  • Sun melts snow prints out bigger and rounder over days 65%. Measure with care: Measuring tracks.
  • Full snow method: Snow tracking and Sign in snow, mud, sand and dust.

• A dark line through silver dewy grass: made after the dew formed (Tip).
  • Dew inside a print in bare ground: made before dawn (Tip).
More: dew in full
  • In the morning, "look for signs of dew in the tracks to determine whether the tracks were made this morning or last night" (65%, Nature Mentor via search preview).
  • "Dew knocked off vegetation" is a classic sign of passage (65%, tracking glossary).
  • Dew forms on clear calm nights. A dew trail you can see from 50 m at sunrise often leads to a feeding or bedding spot (Tip).
  • Glass dewy meadows at first light from above. The dark lines show where deer walked off the field (Tip). See Glassing.

ClueMeansCertainty
Leaves or needles fell inTime passed, often a day plusTip
Insect trails across the floorAt least a nightTip
Spider web over the printAt least hours, often a nightTip
Wind blown sand or snow in itIt survived a wind65%
  • Debris inside means time has passed 70%.
More: debris in full
  • Leaves, needles, insect trails or spider web inside a print mean time has passed (70%, from Tracks).
  • "Broken cobwebs" across a trail are sign of passage (65%, tracking glossary). An intact web across a trail: nothing walked here since the spider spun it (Tip).
  • Fall leaf drop covers tracks fast in aspen and cottonwood bottoms in October (65%, Original Wisdom).
  • Wind leaves its own mark: drifted sand or snow on the downwind side of the print (Tip). Check when the last wind blew.

• Fresh break: pale, moist, maybe sap. Old: grey and dry (Tip).
  • Crushed grass slowly stands back up 65%.
More: plants in full
  • "Healing" is the term trackers use for crushed live vegetation repairing itself, and it is used to age sign (65%, tracking glossary).
  • Crushed or bruised vegetation, mud spattered on clean leaves, or broken sticks reveal passage (65%, Outdoor Life via search preview).
  • A turned leaf shows its paler underside until it dries or flips back (Tip).
  • Fresh browse: torn end pale green or white and moist. Old browse: grey and dry (Tip, from Reading sign).
  • Stones kicked out of their beds show a damp, darker underside that dries in hours in sun (Tip).

• Mud is the slowest ager: it can look fresh for days 65%.
  • Sand and dust age fast at the edges 65%.
More: each ground in full
  • Mud "is typically the slowest aging substrate", so tracks look fresh long after the animal has gone (65%, Nature Mentor via search preview).
  • Sand: "its edges dry out fast", so tracks are "highly susceptible to drying out in sun, wind and rain" (65%, Point Reyes Light via search preview).
  • Dust: shows fine detail but holds it only until the next breath of wind 60%.
  • Forest duff and leaves: hardest to age. Look for crushed moss and flipped leaves instead of edges (Tip).
  • In warm weather "a fresh track is hard to tell from one that is several hours old" (60%, hunter source via search preview).
  • Shaded north banks stay cold and keep tracks crisp for days 65%. Cold still nights in the Interior do the same 65%.

• Wet and shiny: hours. Dry crust: a day or two. Faded, mould: weeks 60%.
  • Colour depends on diet. Read moisture and shine (Tip).
More: scat aging in full
  • Hours: wet, shiny, strong smell, flies 60%.
  • A day or two: dull, dry crust, soft inside 60%.
  • Days to a week: dry, lighter, cracked 65%.
  • Weeks: faded, crumbling, moss or mould, insect holes 60%.
  • North Dakota Game and Fish notes deer scat "can be light brown when deposited but turn dark brown a day or two later" 80%. Other hunting sources say fresh pellets are dark and glossy 60%. Colour changes with diet, so do not age by colour alone (Tip).
  • Cold slows everything. Frozen pellets can look fresh for a week (Tip).
  • Break one pellet with a stick: moist and green inside is recent; dry and fibrous throughout is older (Tip).
  • Full species guide: Droppings deep dive.

SignFreshOld
BedWarm, flat, hair, frost free floor (Tip)Grass standing back up (Tip)
RubWet wood, curled bark, sap 65%Grey, dry, edges darkened 65%
ScrapeDark damp soil, urine smell (Tip)Leaves blown back in (Tip)
BrowsePale moist end (Tip)Grey dry end (Tip)
  • Mixed ages in one place: they live here 60%.
More: sign aging in full
  • In snow a used bed melts and refreezes into an icy bowl. A dry crisp floor with no refreeze is recent (65%, from Reading sign).
  • Fresh rub: bright wet wood, shredded bark curls on the ground, sap beading on conifers (Tip). Rubs grey and darken over weeks 65%.
  • A scrape that has been reopened shows fresh pawed soil over older leaf cover (Tip). Deep dive: Rubs and scrapes.
  • Beds deep dive: Beds and bedding areas.

• Every print survived some weather and not other weather (Tip).
  • Note rain, frost, wind and snow times each day of your trip (Tip).
More: how to run a weather log
  • Write it in the Journal: time of last rain, last frost, last wind, last snow.
  • Ask: did this print go through the frost? The wind? The rain? Each "yes" pushes its age back past that event (Tip).
  • Night temperature matters most in the Interior: a hard frost at Heffley Creek in late October can hold a print crisp into the afternoon on a north slope (Tip).
  • See Weather, moon and seasons for reading fronts.

• Under 24 hours and the wind is right: hunt it at dawn or dusk (Tip).
  • Older: log it, keep scouting for fresher (Tip).
More: the decision in full
  • Fresh sign beats a good map (Grandpa's rule from Reading sign).
  • Pick the freshest sign on your walk and hunt within 300 m of it at dawn or dusk (Tip).
  • Lots of mixed age sign in one place means the animals live there; they did not just pass through (60%, hunter lore).
  • Very fresh sign (minutes): stop moving. The animal may be watching you. Glass ahead before you take another step (Tip). See Following a track.

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law): Old sign is history. Fresh sign is news. Hunt the news.

Common mistakes
  • Calling a crisp mud print fresh. Mud keeps a fresh look for days.
  • Aging by scat colour alone. Diet changes colour.
  • Forgetting last night's frost and rain, so every print looks the same age.

Do this in the field

Build an aging lab on your first trip: 6 boot prints, sun and shade, mud, dust and sand. Photo at 1, 6, 24 and 72 hours.

• Pits inside, before the rain. Frost inside, before the frost.
  • Mud lies, sand tells.
  • Your boot is the clock.
More: more hooks
  • D W I G: Dew, Webs, Insects, Grey wood. Four clocks you can read with no tools.
  • "Shine is time": shiny wet scat means hours.
  • "Range, not a minute": always say "4 to 8 hours", never "6 hours".

  • Original Wisdom, The beauty of trailing deer and observations on track ageing, read directly, checked 2026-10-11 65%: hard ground, leaf fall, broad age bands.

  • Bowhunter, blood variations (search preview, 65%): rain lightens blood.
  • Tips and Grandpa's rules are opinion.
  • Research log: research/2026-10-11-rs.md.
rs-droppings:
Why it matters

A dropping tells you who was here, what it ate, how long ago, and whether it stood, walked or lay down.

• Shape, size, contents, place, age. In that order (Tip).
  • Gloves and a stick, every time 80%.
More: what this session covers
  • Reading sign gave the quick tables. This session goes species by species and teaches you to read the contents and the placement.
  • You will learn: scat safety, a 4 step reading method, pellets to scale (hare, cottontail, deer, elk, moose), how diet changes shape, bear, cougar, wolf, coyote and dog, small mammals, birds (grouse, quail, ducks, geese, owl pellets), what the contents mean for your hunt, and where droppings lie.
  • Aging scat is in Aging tracks and sign.

#Key point
1Gloves and a stick; canid scat can carry a tapeworm 85%
2Pellets: hoofed animals, hares, rabbits, porcupines 80%
3Tapered rope: dog family. Blunt segments: cat family 80%
4Big pile, never covered: bear 80%
5Measure the diameter; wolf over 2.5 cm, coyote under 65%
6Contents are the menu: hair, bone, seeds, insects 80%
7Scattered: moving. Piled: standing or bedded 80%
8White cap: a bird dropping 80%
  • Eight points. Detail follows.

• Gloves on. Open droppings with a stick 80%.
  • Wash with soap before you eat 85%.
More: why canid scat matters
  • Echinococcus multilocularis is a tapeworm that lives in wolves, coyotes and foxes and sheds eggs in their feces. In people it causes alveolar hydatid disease, "a deadly infection in people and dogs" (85%, Western College of Veterinary Medicine, University of Saskatchewan, 2015).
  • BC's first known case was a dog near Quesnel in 2009. The parasite was later found in coyotes and foxes there, and surveys of hunter and trapper samples found it in new areas of BC (85%, same source).
  • People get it by "accidentally swallowing tapeworm eggs from contaminated food or water, or from handling infected animals" (85%, Alberta Health, MyHealth Alberta).
  • Alberta Health advises "disposable gloves if you are handling a coyote, fox, or other wild animal (dead or alive)" and washing hands with soap and water before touching food 85%.
  • Risk to people is "very low" and "it's rare that people get it" (85%, Alberta Health). Low risk, easy prevention: gloves, stick, soap.
  • Wash wild berries you pick on a hunt (85%, Alberta Health).
  • Keep your dog from rolling in or eating wild scat 85%.

Read a dropping in 4 steps1 of 4
  • Then age it (Tip). See Aging tracks and sign.
More: the 4 steps in full
  1. Shape. Pellets (hoofed animals, hares, rabbits, porcupines). Rope with tapered ends (dog family). Segmented tube with blunt ends (cat family). Soft pile (bear, or a grazer on green feed) (75%, Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife, North Dakota Game and Fish).
  2. Size. Diameter is steadier than length, because length depends on how it broke (Tip). Write it in centimetres.
  3. Contents. Hair, bone chips, seeds, berry skins, insect parts, grass, wood fibre 80%.
  4. Place. Middle of a trail, beside a bed, under a roost, in a scrape, on a rock (Tip).
  5. Age. Moisture, shine, crust, mould 60%.

ShapeFamilyCertainty
PelletsDeer, elk, moose, hare, rabbit, porcupine80%
Tapered ropeCoyote, wolf, fox, dog75%
Segmented, bluntCougar, bobcat, lynx75%

  • Bears "seldom, if ever, cover" their scat 80%.
More: shape families, quoted
  • Bears: "Scats are highly variable... may be large and tubular in shape with relatively blunt ends or they may be relatively small and round/oval... Bears often deposit scats in large piles and seldom, if ever, cover them with debris" (85%, Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife, livestock investigation guide).
  • Cats: "scats often appear segmented with blunt ends. Cats often scratch out areas and deposit scat in this spot then they may or may not cover scats" (85%, same source).
  • Dogs: "scats often have a tapered end" (85%, same source).
  • Coyote: "usually in a single cord and pointed at the ends... often contains hair... up to five inches long" (85%, North Dakota Game and Fish). That is up to about 13 cm.

• Deer: about 1.3 cm, pointed at one end 85%.
  • Moose: about 1.9 cm across and 2.5 to 3.8 cm long 80%.
