  • Big deer and small elk overlap. Use the tracks beside the pile (Tip).
  • Mule deer and white tail pellets look the same 60%.

• Green summer feed: soft clumps and patties 70%.
  • Woody fall and winter feed: hard separate pellets 70%.
More: seasons in full
  • Deer on green feed drop soft clumps; in fall and winter, firm separate pellets (70%, from Reading sign).
  • Moose: dry distinct pellets in winter, softer clumps or patties in summer 65%. Winter moose pellets look like pressed sawdust 65%.
  • Elk on lush grass drop patties like a small cow pie 65%.
  • In October in the Thompson you will see both: patties near green irrigated hay or riparian grass, pellets on dry slopes (Tip).
  • Cattle pies are much bigger and flatter than any elk patty. Region 3 grasslands have lots of cattle (Tip).

• Tube about 4 to 6 cm across, or a loose pile in berry season 65%.
  • Fresh berry scat on your trail: make noise (Tip).
More: bear scat in full
  • Black bear: tube about 4 to 6 cm across and 13 to 30 cm long, often a loose pile in berry season (65%, from Reading sign).
  • Grizzly: the same but bigger, often over 5 cm across, with roots and meat 60%.
  • Contents follow the season: grass and green plants in spring, berries in late summer and fall, plus insects, roots, meat and hair 70%.
  • Bears often deposit scat in large piles and do not cover it (85%, Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife).
  • Fresh bear scat, overturned logs and dug up anthills are "fresh signs that indicate recent bear activity" (85%, Alberta Environment, Be BearSmart for hunters).
  • See the berry calendar and Bush safety.

• Segmented, blunt ends, often in a scratched scrape 75%.
  • Deer hair and bone chips inside 65%.
More: cougar scat in full
  • Cougar: segmented tube about 2.5 to 4 cm across and 10 to 15 cm long, blunt ends (65%, from Reading sign).
  • "Cats often scratch out areas and deposit scat in this spot then they may or may not cover scats with ground debris. Scats may contain large amounts of hair and/or bone. Cougar scats will often be larger than bobcat" (85%, Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife).
  • Cougar scrapes: a small pile of needles or dirt, scraped back with the hind feet, on a ridge trail 65%.
  • Cougar sign means deer country. It also means a kill may be near. See Predator sign and kill sites.

• Thumb wide and full of deer hair: wolf 65%.
  • Finger wide, twisted, mouse hair: coyote 65%.
More: canid scat in full
AnimalDiameterContents
CoyoteUnder about 2.5 cm 65%Mouse, vole and hare hair, berries, small bones 70%
WolfOver about 2.5 cm, up to 4 cm 65%Deer, elk or moose hair and bone 70%
DogAny sizeOften uniform, kibble, little hair (Tip)
  • Dog family scat often tapers at the ends and twists like rope 75%.
  • Coyote scat "contains hair, which is more identifiable as the scat ages" (85%, North Dakota Game and Fish).
  • Canids leave scat in the middle of trails and at junctions as a marker (Tip).
  • Measure at the widest point. One wide wolf piece and one thin coyote piece can overlap; look at several (Tip).
  • Gloves: this is the tapeworm group 85%.

AnimalDroppingWhere
Snowshoe hareFlat ball 1.2 cm, sawdust inside 70%Runways in brush
CottontailPea size 85%Brushy cover
PorcupineCurved pellets, piles 85%Den mouths, under feeding trees
Red squirrelNot scat: cone piles (middens) (Tip)Under conifers
  • Hare pellets in piles mean it fed there a long time 65%.
More: small mammal details
  • Hares drop pellets singly; piles only where they fed for a long time (65%, from Reading sign).
  • Hare twigs are cut clean at 45 degrees 75%. See Reading sign.
  • Porcupine scat is "often found in large piles at the mouth of an underground den or under a tree in which it has been feeding". Bark stripped high in a tree is porcupine sign too (85%, North Dakota Game and Fish).
  • Snowshoe hares are small game in BC with their own season. Check BC rules and the Rule Book before you hunt them.

• White cap: a bird. Birds pass urine and feces together 80%.
  • A pile of grouse droppings: a night roost 70%.
More: bird droppings in full
  • Upland bird droppings "have a distinctive white coloration which is the result of dried urine products"; scat is often found "in large groups where birds have roosted overnight" (85%, North Dakota Game and Fish).
  • Grouse: curved cylinders about 2 to 3 cm long, pencil thick, brown with a white tip, in piles at roosts 70%.
  • Grouse also leave soft, dark cecal droppings, often at a different roost from the hard fibrous ones (65%, quoting Elbroch and Marks, Bird Tracks and Sign, via search preview).
  • Canada goose droppings: green cylinders of grass 75%. Lots of fresh green droppings in a field means geese fed there recently (Tip). Geese drop about 6 times an hour while feeding (60%, Royal Society for the Protection of Birds (RSPB) blog via search preview).
  • Owl pellets are not droppings. They are coughed up balls of hair and bones, light grey, under a favourite perch (85%, North Dakota Game and Fish).
  • Bird sign deep dive: Bird sign.

• Berries in the scat: the berry patch is a feeding spot (Tip).
  • Deer hair in predator scat: deer use this area (Tip).
More: how to use the menu
  • Coyote scat full of rose hip seeds in October: rose thickets nearby. In the South Okanagan, rose thickets are quail cover too (Tip). See Habitat tour: quail and grouse.
  • Bear scat full of fresh berries: a bear fed here in the last day. Go loud, spray on the belt (Tip).
  • Wolf scat full of deer hair on a ridge trail: deer are using the drainage below (Tip).
  • Pellets full of green fibre in October: deer are on green feed, often near water or irrigated fields (Tip).

• Scattered along a trail: moving 80%.
  • A pile: it stood or bedded there 80%.
More: placement in full
  • Deer scat "is generally found in piles where they have bedded or where they were standing. Scat may also be found deposited along a trail as the animal moved" (85%, North Dakota Game and Fish).
  • Deer drop about 13 to 34 pellet groups a day, so piles are not a count of deer (70%, from Reading sign).
  • Biologists count pellet groups on set plots to compare deer use between areas 70%. You can do a rough version: count fresh groups per 100 m of trail on two ridges and compare (Tip).
  • Grouse piles under a tree: a roost. In snow, a hole with droppings inside: a snow roost 70%.
  • Cougar scat in a scrape on a ridge: a marking spot 65%.

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law): The animal tells you its dinner, its address and its schedule. Read the whole letter.

Common mistakes
  • Picking up coyote scat bare handed.
  • Calling elk from one pellet pile without looking at the tracks beside it.
  • Reading an owl pellet as a predator scat.

Do this in the field

Find 3 droppings from 3 different animals. Gloves on. Shape, diameter, contents, place, age. Photo with your knife for scale.

• SSCPA: Shape, Size, Contents, Place, Age.
  • Taper dog, blunt cat, pile bear.
  • Thumb wolf, finger coyote.
More: more hooks
  • "Pea, marble, olive, grape, walnut": cottontail, hare, deer, elk, moose, smallest to biggest (Tip).
  • "White hat, bird scat."
  • "Piled is parked." A pile means it stood or lay there.

  • Western College of Veterinary Medicine, University of Saskatchewan, Researchers hunt for tiny worm in BC wildlife, read directly, checked 2026-10-11 85%.
  • Alberta Health, Echinococcus tapeworm, read directly, checked 2026-10-11 85%.
  • Alberta Environment, Be BearSmart: hunting in bear country, read directly, checked 2026-10-11 85%.

rs-beds:
Why it matters

Deer spend most of the day bedded. Find the bedroom and you know where the day starts and ends.

• A bed tells you who, how big, how long, and which way it left.
  • Read beds when the animals are out. Hunt the trails, not the bedroom (Tip).
More: what this session covers
  • Reading sign showed what a bed looks like. Trails and funnels showed the daily loop from bed to feed. This session goes deep on beds.
  • You will learn: reading a single bed in 4 steps, where deer pick beds and why (research and lore), weather and beds, does versus bucks, elk and moose beds, bedding areas, how to find them by map and by glass, 3 ways to hunt them, and how not to ruin them.
  • Most of this is about deer, the owner's first big game. Elk and moose are covered briefly.

#Key point
1Deer bed: oval 0.9 to 1.2 m, flattened, hair, pellets 70%
2Deer like beds near conifers with cover on some sides 75%
3Temperature and cover drive bed choice 75%
4Lore: top third of a slope, wind behind, view below 60%
5Hot days: shade and north slopes. Cold: sun (Tip)
6Many beds, trails, mixed age pellets: a bedding area (Tip)
7Beginner lean: ambush the trail, do not walk the beds (Tip)
8Warm bed means minutes. Freeze and glass (Tip)
  • Detail follows.

• Flattened oval, knee marks, hair, pellets, exit tracks 70%.
  • North Dakota Game and Fish: beds "a couple feet long", oval 85%.
More: bed sizes in full
  • A deer bed is an oval of flattened grass, duff or snow about 0.9 to 1.2 m long, often with pellets and a few hairs (70%, from Reading sign).
  • North Dakota Game and Fish: "Deer beds are a couple feet long and generally an oval shape. There may be several in one location. In vegetation, they are recognized by flattened grass. In snow, they may be recognized by melted snow and ice or exposed earth" 85%. A couple of feet is about 0.6 m: a curled up deer or a fawn makes a smaller bed than a stretched out adult (Tip).
  • Elk beds: about 1.2 to 1.5 m, in groups 65%. A Roosevelt elk bed may run up to about 1.8 to 2.4 m long (60%, general website).
  • Moose beds: bigger again, often alone, in willow or timber near water 60%. Exact size: VERIFY.

Read a bed in 4 steps1 of 4
  • Bounds leaving the bed: it was spooked, maybe by you 80%.
More: the 4 steps in full
  1. Size. Compare with the table above. A small bed beside a big one: doe and fawn (Tip).
  2. Hair. Grey brown hollow hair: deer. Long coarse black: bear. Lots of hair: it lay a long time or it is moulting (Tip).
  3. Pellets and urine. Deer often stand, stretch, urinate and drop pellets when they get up (Tip). Lore says a buck urinates in the middle of the bed and a doe behind it (50%: not proven, VERIFY before you trust it).
  4. Facing and exit. The body shape shows where the head lay. Walking tracks out: it left on its own to feed. Stot or gallop groups out: something spooked it 80%. See Measuring tracks.
  5. Warm bed test: hand in the bed. Warm means minutes (Tip).

StudyFindingCertainty
Utah mule deer, 1986Bed under or near conifers; less visibility on north and west sides75%
Forest day beds, 2004Site temperature and canopy closure mattered most75%
Arizona desert mule deerMost thermal cover at beds in summer75%
  • Beds are about comfort and safety: temperature and cover 75%.
More: the studies, quoted
  • Great Basin Naturalist (1986), Rocky Mountain mule deer: "Deer appeared to prefer bedding under or near conifers, and visibility was lower on the north and west sides of deer beds in both community types than on the south and east sides" (75%, abstract via search preview).
  • Germaine and others (2004), mule deer summer day beds: "Site temperature and canopy closure were the most influential attributes in bed site selection" (75%, abstract via search preview).
  • Arizona study, desert mule deer: thermal cover at beds was highest in summer, and thermal cover helps "thermoregulation, escape, and fawn protection" (75%, abstract via search preview).
  • White tailed deer in winter in central Ontario were studied for bed site choice too (Armstrong and others, 1983) (70%, title via search preview).
  • What it means for you: in October heat, check shady conifer patches; on cold mornings, check sunny spots with cover behind them (Tip).

• Hunter lore: a bench in the top third, near trees, wind behind, view below 60%.
  • The deer smells what comes from above and sees what comes from below 60%.
More: lore and its limits
  • Day beds sit where the animal can see below and smell what comes from above: benches, the top third of a slope, under a tree with a view (hunter lore) (60%, from Reading sign).
  • Deer often travel with the wind at their back or side so they can smell behind and look ahead (60%, from Wind and thermals).
  • Morning thermals rise uphill and evening thermals sink. A deer bedded high in the morning gets rising air from below, so it can smell you coming from below even though it is "looking" there (75% for thermals). See Wind and thermals.
  • Lore is a starting point. Your own logged beds at Heffley Creek beat any rule (Tip).

• Come in from the side or from above with the wind in your face (Tip).
  • Approach from below only when thermals carry your scent away (Tip).
More: approach rules
  • Never walk straight up at a bed from below in the morning: rising thermals push your scent to the deer (75% for thermals, Tip for tactic).
  • In the evening, falling thermals: approaching from above sends scent down to it. Come across the slope (Tip).
  • Steady crosswind is the easiest wind for a stalk (Tip). See Moving quietly.

• Temperature drives bed choice 75%.
  • Wind and rain push deer into thick cover and lee slopes (Tip).
More: weather in full
  • Hot sun: shade, north and east slopes, conifer patches, cool draws near water (Tip, supported by the temperature studies, 75%).
  • Cold and clear: south and west slopes in the sun, with cover at their back (Tip).
  • Strong wind: lee side of ridges, low draws, thick timber. Deer get nervous in wind because they cannot hear well (Tip).
  • Rain or wet snow: thick conifers, under big Douglas fir (Tip).
  • Late October around Heffley Creek can bring frost mornings and warm afternoons. Deer may bed in sun early and move to shade by midday (Tip).

• Groups of small beds: does and fawns (Tip).
  • One big bed alone on an edge: maybe a buck. Lore, not proof 60%.
More: buck bed lore
  • A mature buck often beds alone in a bigger bed on an edge, with thick cover or a drop behind it for escape (hunter lore, 60%).
  • Rub lines often lead toward buck bedding areas. See Rubs and scrapes.
  • Big beds can be big does. Use tracks, rubs and what you glass to confirm (Tip).
  • A fawn bedded alone is not abandoned. The doe is nearby (85%, from the photo caption). Leave it.

• Elk: many beds together, near water and wallows 65%.
  • Moose: often alone, willow or timber near water 60%.
More: elk and moose in full
  • Elk beds are about 1.2 to 1.5 m and come in groups (65%, from Reading sign).
  • In late winter, moose "significantly chose areas with shallow snow for bed sites" (75%, Alces journal, Michigan winter bed sites, via search preview).
  • Snow 45 to 50 cm deep makes elk move to shallower snow (70%, Rangelands journal via search preview).
  • Most Region 3 moose and elk hunts are LEH (Limited Entry Hunting). See The rut and the Rule Book.

• Many beds, trails between them, pellets of mixed age (Tip).
  • A main trail out to feed: your ambush line (Tip).
More: what makes a bedding area
  • Bedding areas have many beds, trails between them, and pellets of mixed age (Tip, from Reading sign).
  • Look for cover that hides a standing deer within about 20 to 30 m, next to food within a few hundred metres (Tip).
  • "Bed in the trees, feed in the grass, you on the line" (Grandpa's rule from Trails and funnels).
  • The daily loop: Trails and funnels.

Find a bedding area in 4 steps1 of 4
  • Watch deer walk to bed at sunrise, from far away (Tip).
  • Glass for parts: an ear, an antler tip, a leg line (Tip).
More: finding in full
  • Map: look for benches, saddles and the shady side of ridges within a few hundred metres of feed and water (Tip). See Map scouting.
  • Morning glass: at first light deer feed, then walk to bed. Mark where they disappear (Tip). See Glassing.
  • Midday glass: bedded deer show "just heads and ears" (from the photo caption). Look at shade under trees, slowly (Tip).
  • Check on foot only once, ideally when deer are out feeding or after the season, with the wind right (Tip).

• My lean for a beginner: option A, ambush the trail between bed and feed (Tip).
More: options with pros and cons
OptionProsCons
A: Ambush the trail at dawn or duskLow risk of spooking, safe shooting lanesDeer may use another trail
B: Still hunt into the bedding areaWorks in wind, rain or soft snowEasy to bump deer; shots are quick
C: Spot and stalk a bedded buckOpen country, you see him firstNeeds wind, cover and patience; he may stand and leave
My lean (opinion)

My lean: A first. Sit on the trail between the bedding cover and the feed, wind in your face, at first and last light. Try C only after you have glassed a buck bedded and have a safe stalk route and backstop.

  • Shot at a bedded deer: only a clear, safe shot with a backstop. Many bedded deer show only head and neck. Wait for it to stand if unsure (Tip). See Shot placement.

DoDo not
Check beds once, wind rightWalk through every week
Scout when deer are outScout at noon when they are in
Glass from far awaySit 50 m away "to watch"
Leave quietly the way you cameCut through the middle
  • Bumped deer often move to another bed or go nocturnal (Tip).
More: why it matters
  • "Walking through a bedding area at noon to check for beds. You just evicted the deer" (common mistake from Reading sign).
  • Pressure pushes deer into thicker cover and later movement (Tip). See Weather, moon and seasons.

• Hand in the bed: warm means minutes (Tip).
  • Freeze, glass ahead and to both sides before you move (Tip).
More: what to do next
  • A warm bed means the animal left in the last few minutes, often because of you (Tip).
  • Look for it standing behind cover 50 to 150 m away, often watching its back trail (Tip).
  • In snow: a fresh bed has a dry crisp floor; an old bed melted and refroze into an icy bowl 65%. See Aging tracks and sign.
  • No shot? Mark the bed, note the time, back out. Come back on a better wind (Tip).

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law): Read the bedroom once. Hunt the hallway every day.

Common mistakes
  • Walking the bedding cover at noon every weekend to "check it".
  • Approaching a hillside bed from below on a morning uphill thermal.
  • Calling every big bed a buck bed.

Do this in the field

Find 3 beds. For each: size, hair, pellets, facing, exit, age. Pin each on the map, then look at what they have in common.

• Eyes below, nose behind.
  • Hot north, cold south.
  • Read the bedroom once, hunt the hallway.
More: more hooks
  • SHPE: Size, Hair, Pellets, Exit. The 4 things to read in a bed.
  • "Top third, near a tree": the lore spot to check first.
  • "Warm bed, cold feet": stop moving.

• North Dakota Game and Fish Department, Tracks and Signs of North Dakota Wildlife, read directly, checked 2026-10-11 85%: deer bed description.
  • Search previews (abstracts), checked 2026-10-11, 70% to 75%: Great Basin Naturalist 1986, mule deer beds; Germaine and others 2004, mule deer day bed sites; Bed site selection by desert mule deer, University of Arizona; Armstrong and others 1983, white tailed deer winter beds, Ontario; Alces journal, winter bed sites of moose in Michigan; Rangelands, elk and snow depth.
  • eWash, Roosevelt elk beds (search preview, 60%): elk bed length.

• Earlier figures from Reading sign; thermals from Wind and thermals.
  • Hunter lore lines are labelled Tip or 60% or less.
  • Research log: research/2026-10-11-rs.md.
rs-rubs-scrapes:
Why it matters

Rubs and scrapes are bucks writing notes to other deer. Learn to read the notes and you learn the buck's route and schedule.

• Rubs show where a buck travels. Scrapes show where deer meet 65%.
  • Most scrape visits happen at night 65%.
More: what this session covers
  • Reading sign and The rut introduced rubs and scrapes. This is the deep dive.
  • You will learn: why bucks rub, the season, reading one rub in 4 steps, rub lines and signpost rubs, deer versus elk versus moose, scrape anatomy, the camera research on when scrapes are visited, edge versus cover scrapes, how to hunt them, and the BC rules that touch them (cameras, lures, baiting).
  • Region 3 mule deer make fewer rubs and rarely scrape; white tails do both 60%. Learn both: you may hunt white tails in the North Thompson and the Fraser Valley.

#Key point
1Rubs leave scent from forehead glands 70%
2Older bucks make more rubs; yearlings about half as many 65%
3Rub height says more than tree size 60%
4Rubbed side faces where the buck came from 60%
5Scrape: pawed soil under a licking branch 1.2 to 1.5 m up 65%
6About 80% of scraping: mid October to mid November 65%
785% of buck scrape visits at night 65%
8No bottled deer urine from outside BC 95%
  • Detail follows.

• Velvet off, then rubbing, then scrapes peak before the rut 70%.
  • Bars are approximate and shift with latitude (Tip).
More: timing in full
  • About 80% of scraping in the north happens from mid October to mid November (65%, from Reading sign).
  • In a Georgia study, bucks 2.5 years and older visited scrapes most in the week of 15 to 21 October (65%, Buckmasters reporting on University of Georgia research). Georgia is far south of BC; timing here may differ (Tip).
  • BC deer rut timing: The rut has the Region 3 timeline.
  • Rubs stay visible for years. A fresh rub in October is this year's buck (Tip).

• Forehead glands are most active in autumn 70%.
  • Higher ranking mature bucks secrete more 70%.
More: the science in full
  • Research by Atkeson and Marchinton found white tails have forehead skin glands that are most active in autumn, and mature, high ranking bucks tend to secrete more from them (70%, Deer and Deer Hunting, The Science of Buck Rubs, via search preview).
  • Rub activity tracks testosterone, which rises with age and rank. Prime age bucks reach higher levels and make more rubs (65%, same source).
  • "Yearlings make only about half as many total rubs as prime age whitetails", even with no mature bucks around (65%, same source).
  • Bucks also rub a licking branch above a scrape with the gland near the eye (preorbital gland) (80%, North Dakota Game and Fish).
  • Other deer smell and lick rubs. A rub is a sign and a scent post (Tip).

Read a rub in 4 steps1 of 4
  • Photo every rub with your knife for scale, and pin it (Tip).
More: the 4 steps in full
  1. Height. Most rubs sit about 30 to 105 cm above the ground. A rub centred 75 cm or higher suggests a mature buck 60%.
  2. Tree size. 2.5 to 5 cm trees are often yearlings; over 10 cm is usually an older buck 60%. Rub height says more about buck size than tree size 60%.
  3. Fresh or old. Fresh: bright wet wood, curled bark shavings on the ground below, sap on conifers (Tip). Old: grey, dry, darkened edges 65%. See Aging tracks and sign.
  4. Side. The rubbed side usually faces where the buck came from 60%.
  5. Tine scratches above the main rub and broken branches hint at a wide or heavy rack (Tip).

ClueYoung buck (Tip)Older buck (Tip)
Rub heightBelow kneeWaist or higher 60%
Tree diameter2.5 to 5 cm 60%Over 10 cm 60%
DamageLight scuffDeep gouges, broken limbs
  • Young bucks rub big trees too. Height is the better clue 60%.

• A line of rubs facing one way: his route between bed and feed 60%.
  • Rubbed side toward the beds: he walks that way in the evening (Tip).
More: using rub lines
  • A line of rubs facing one way is his route between bed and feed (60%, from Reading sign).
  • Rubs facing the feed: made on the morning walk back to bed. Rubs facing the beds: made in the evening heading out (Tip).
  • Follow the line backward toward thick cover to find the bedding area, once, with the wind right (Tip). See Beds and bedding areas.
  • Rub lines through a funnel or saddle are prime ambush spots (Tip). See Trails and funnels.

• A big tree rubbed year after year 60%.
  • Mature bucks keep them going; other deer visit 60%.
More: signposts in full
  • "Typically, especially during the rut, mature bucks make most signposts to advertise their presence" (60%, Bowhunter via search preview).
  • "The oldest bucks typically make the largest rubs, whereas younger bucks and females may visit and interact with the rub, but rarely maintain it" (60%, Outdoor Nebraska via search preview).
  • Older bucks re rub traditional rubs year after year (60%, Buckmasters on research by Grant Woods, via search preview).
  • A signpost rub means a buck uses this area every year. It does not mean he walks past at noon (Tip).

• Deer: knee to waist. Elk: over your head. Moose: thrashed brush 65%.
More: species in full
AnimalRubOther sign
White tailed deerMany rubs, saplings, 30 to 105 cm 65%Scrapes, rub lines
Mule deerFewer rubs, small conifers and shrubs 60%Rarely scrape 60%
ElkBigger trees stripped, often above your head (Tip)Wallows, bugling 65%
MooseThrash willow and alder, strip saplings 65%Rut pits soaked in urine 65%
  • Bulls thrash shrubs and small trees with their antlers many times an hour in the rut (65%, from Reading sign).
  • Porcupines also strip bark high in trees (85%, North Dakota Game and Fish). No antler gouges, tooth marks instead (Tip).
  • Bears claw and bite trees too. Look for claw marks and hair (Tip). See Predator sign.

• Pawed bare soil under a licking branch 1.2 to 1.5 m up 65%.
  • The buck chews the branch and urinates in the scrape 70%.
More: scrape anatomy in full
  • A is a pawed bare oval of dirt under an overhanging licking branch about 1.2 to 1.5 m up (65%, from Reading sign).
  • "Scrapes are created by bucks in the early fall as a place to leave their scent so other deer know they are in the area. Scrapes are most often made below overhanging branches. To leave scent, a buck will rub on an overhanging branch with a scent gland near the eye called the preorbital gland" (85%, North Dakota Game and Fish).
  • Fresh scrape: dark moist soil, pawed leaves thrown back, urine smell, chewed and broken branch tip (Tip).
  • White tails scrape; mule deer rarely do 60%.

• 85% of buck visits and 75% of doe visits at night 65%.
  • Does visited nearly twice as often as bucks 65%.
More: the camera studies
  • University of Georgia trail camera study (6 traditional scrapes, about 1,375 ha managed property, 2 years): 85% of buck visits and 75% of doe visits were at night (65%, Buckmasters and Outdoor Life via search preview).
  • Reported as about 562 visits: 31 per scrape per season, only about 5 in daylight 65%.
  • "Nearly twice as many does visited the scrapes as bucks" 65%.
  • A Missouri study by Grant Woods also found most scrape visits at night; the top daylight windows were about 8:45 to 10:15 a.m. and 3:45 to 5:15 p.m. 60%.
  • What it means: sitting over a field edge scrape all day is usually a poor bet (Tip).

• Edge scrapes: mostly night visits (Tip).
  • Scrapes near bedding cover: better odds of daylight (Tip).
More: why location matters
  • Bucks feel safer close to cover in daylight. Scrapes deep in or near bedding cover get a higher share of daylight visits (Tip, consistent with the camera studies at 60%).
  • Four of the six Georgia scrapes were on field edges and two deeper in the woods 65%.
  • A row of scrapes along a trail between cover and feed is a scrape line. Hunt the cover end at first and last light (Tip).

OptionProsCons
A: Ambush a rub line near coverDaylight movement, simpleNeeds the right wind every sit
B: Camera on a scrape firstLearn timing without disturbingWireless camera rules (see below)
C: Mock scrape with synthetic lureDraws local bucksLots of night visits; lure rules
  • My lean: A, with a non wireless camera to learn timing (Tip).
More: options in detail
My lean (opinion)

My lean: find a fresh rub line between bedding cover and feed. Sit near the cover end with the wind in your face at first and last light. Put a normal memory card camera on the nearest scrape to learn which buck and when.

  • Enter and leave on routes that do not cross the rub line (Tip).
  • Check cameras at midday, quickly, once a week, with gloves and rubber boots (Tip).
  • Do not use urine lures. See the rules below.

Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

RuleWhere
No wireless camera for hunting, 1 August to 10 December 99%Synopsis page 11, item 30
No deer, elk, moose or caribou part or derivative from outside BC for hunting 95%Synopsis page 12, item 51
No baiting ungulates within 200 m of homes or schools, Region 3 95%Synopsis page 33
More: the rules in full
  • Province wide: it is unlawful to use a wireless camera for the purposes of hunting from 1 August to 10 December in every region except Region 1, where wireless cameras for hunting are banned all year (99%, synopsis page 11, item 30, and page 20). A normal camera with a memory card is not a wireless camera (85%, interpretation). From Reading sign.
  • It is unlawful to use, for the purpose of hunting wildlife, any part or derivative of a deer, elk, moose or caribou that originated outside BC (95%, synopsis page 12, item 51). Bottled deer urine is almost always from outside BC (85%, interpretation). From The rut.
  • Region 3: it is unlawful to intentionally bait or feed ungulates within 200 m of a dwelling, school yard or playground (95%, synopsis page 33).
  • Full rules: BC rules and the Rule Book in phase 7.

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law): A rub tells you where he walked. A scrape tells you where he wants to be. Your watch tells you he did it in the dark.

Common mistakes
  • Sitting all day over a field edge scrape.
  • Calling a big tree rub a big buck without looking at the height.
  • Hanging a bottle of store deer urine over a mock scrape.

Do this in the field

Find 5 rubs. Measure height and tree size, age them, note the rubbed side, pin them. Connect the pins: is it a line?

• High rub, big buck (maybe).
  • The bark points home.
  • Scrapes sleep by day.
More: more hooks
  • "H S F S": Height, Size, Fresh, Side. The 4 rub reads.
  • "Lick, paw, pee": the 3 parts of a scrape.
  • Number trick: licking branch about 1.2 to 1.5 m, roughly your belt to your chest (Tip).
