rs-bird-sign:
Why it matters

Grouse, quail, ducks and geese leave sign every day. Read it and you walk to the birds instead of hoping.

  • Tracks, dust bowls, droppings, roosts, feathers, feeding sign.
  • Feathers can tell you who killed a bird 60%.
More: what this session covers
  • Reading sign gave grouse sign in brief. This session covers all your birds: grouse in the Thompson, California quail in the South Okanagan, ducks and geese in the Fraser Valley and the Interior.
  • You will learn: bird tracks, walkers versus hoppers, dust bowls, droppings and roosts, feeding sign, moult feathers versus kill feathers, plucking spots versus mammal kills, wing marks in snow, waterfowl field and shore sign, and how to mark a bird you shot.
  • Droppings in detail: Droppings deep dive.

#Key point
1Game birds walk: one print ahead of the next 65%
2Grouse dust bowl about 20 cm; quail bowls 7 to 15 cm 65%
3White capped droppings piled up: a roost 80%
4Plucked whole quills: a bird of prey. Bitten shafts: a mammal 60%
5Fresh green goose droppings: a field fed on today (Tip)
6Wing marks in snow: a take off, or a strike 65%
7Mark every fall and retrieve: it is the law for migratory birds 99%
  • Detail follows.

• Grouse: 3 toes forward, 1 short back, about 5 cm 85%.
  • Duck 5 to 7.6 cm, goose 7.6 to 10 cm, webbed 85%.
More: tracks in full
  • Ruffed grouse track about 5 cm (2 inches) (85%, Maine Inland Fisheries and Wildlife pocket card).
  • Grouse: 3 toes forward, 1 short toe back, about 5 to 7 cm long; the bird walks in a line, often zig zag (65%, from Tracks).
  • In winter grouse grow comb like fringes on their toes, so the snow track looks wider 65%.
  • Waterfowl: "Duck: 2 to 3 inches long; Goose: 3 to 4 inches long; Swan: 6 to 7 inches long" (85%, North Dakota Game and Fish). That is about 5 to 7.6 cm, 7.6 to 10 cm, and 15 to 18 cm.
  • Quail prints are smaller than grouse prints; when running, prints space further apart (65%, Bear Tracker via search preview).
  • Ground birds walk, one print ahead of the next. Many songbirds hop, leaving prints side by side in pairs 65%.

• Grouse: one round scrape about 20 cm, a feather or two 65%.
  • Quail: many small 7 to 15 cm bowls together 65%.
More: dust bowls in full
  • A grouse dusting bowl is a round to oval scrape in dry fine soil, about 20 cm across, often on a trail or road edge, with a few feathers in it (65%, from Reading sign).
  • Quail: "circular indentations left behind in the soft dirt, some 7 to 15 cm (3 to 6 in) in diameter"; birds pick sunny spots with newly turned or soft soil (65%, Vancouver Island University biology blog and Wikipedia via search preview).
  • Upland birds dust "to help minimize body parasites"; dust bowls are found where soil is exposed (85%, North Dakota Game and Fish).
  • A cluster of small fresh bowls near rose or chokecherry thickets in the South Okanagan: a covey uses this spot (Tip). See Habitat tour: quail and grouse.

• A pile of curved white capped droppings: a night roost 70%.
  • Snow roost: a hole in soft snow with droppings inside 70%.
More: droppings and roosts in full
  • Upland bird droppings are "often found in large groups where birds have roosted overnight" (85%, North Dakota Game and Fish).
  • Grouse: curved cylinders about 2 to 3 cm long, pencil thick, brown with a white tip 70%.
  • Grouse that snow roost for a long time defecate in one spot, making a small latrine (65%, Ruffed Grouse Society biologist via search preview).
  • In deep soft snow ruffed grouse dive in and roost under the snow for warmth (80%, from Habitat tour: quail and grouse).
  • Quail roost in trees or thick cover at night (75%, from Quail, chukar, partridge, pheasant).
  • A drum log with a pile of droppings on it: a ruffed grouse displays there (Tip).

BirdFeeding signWhere
Ruffed grouseClipped buds and catkins, winter 75%Aspen, birch, willow
Grouse, fallBerries, rose hips, leaves 75%Edges, burns, cut blocks
QuailScratched soil and litter patches 65%Under shrubs near cover
GeeseGrazed shoots, droppings, feathers 75%Fields, pasture, lawns
DucksDabbled mud, floating feathers (Tip)Shallow marsh edges
  • Fresh sign plus food plus cover: come back with the shotgun (Tip).
More: feeding sign in full
  • Quail feed "on the ground, often scratching at the soil" (65%, search preview). Look for scratched patches near cover.
  • Goose grazing can look very similar to deer feeding in a field. Check for droppings and tracks (65%, North Carolina State University extension via search preview).
  • Ruffed grouse eat aspen buds in winter (75%, from the photo caption of the aspen grove).
  • Before you carry the shotgun: grouse, quail and waterfowl all have their own seasons and limits. See BC rules and the Rule Book.

• One or two feathers on a trail: often moult or preening (Tip).
  • A pile of feathers: something died here 75%.
More: feathers in full
  • "It's sometimes possible to narrow it down to an avian or mammalian predator by looking at the method of feather removal, with plucked feathers pointing to a bird of prey and chewed off feathers to a mammal" (60%, bushcraft forum via search preview).
  • Mammal: teeth leave holes in the vanes, blunt or cut shafts, saliva, feathers stuck together 60%.
  • Raptor: bills leave cut or crushed shafts near the base, or whole quills pulled clean 60%.
  • "Carcasses are scavenged too, so if you come across older remains then more than one type of sign may be seen" 60%. Read the whole site.
  • A cat grabs a mouthful of feathers and shakes its head, scattering them (55%: Tip).

• Ring of feathers on a stump or open spot, breastbone left: a raptor 60%.
  • Scattered feathers, tracks, maybe a carcass gone: a mammal 60%.
More: kill sites in full
  • A raptor often leaves the breastbone and the wing bones, often still attached (60%, forum via search preview).
  • Goshawks pluck their prey; reports on great horned owls are mixed (55%: Tip).
  • A coyote or fox may carry the bird away and leave only a few feathers (Tip).
  • Lots of grouse kill sites in one area: lots of grouse, and lots of predators (Tip).
  • Mammal predators and kill sites in detail: Predator sign and kill sites.

• Tracks end in a fan of wing marks: it flew 80%.
  • Wing marks where mouse tracks end: an owl or hawk strike (Tip).
More: snow wing marks
  • Wing prints in snow mark where a grouse took off or landed (80%, from Reading sign).
  • A burst of wing marks beside a hole: a grouse came out of a snow roost 80%.
  • Wing marks with a small hole and no bird tracks: an owl or hawk dropped on a vole (Tip).
  • Snow tracking in detail: Snow tracking and Sign in snow, mud, sand and dust.

• Fresh green droppings in a field: geese fed there today (Tip).
  • Feathers and droppings on a bar: a loafing spot (Tip).
More: waterfowl sign in full
  • Geese roost on water overnight and at first light often fly out to feed on crop fields or pasture (65%, onX via search preview).
  • Hunters scout the field geese use late in the afternoon and set up there the next morning (60%, hunting source via search preview).
  • Geese drop about 6 times an hour while feeding, so fresh droppings pile up fast where they fed (60%, Royal Society for the Protection of Birds (RSPB) blog).
  • Moulted flight feathers on a lake shore in late summer mark a moulting area (Tip).
  • Fraser Valley fields near home: get landowner consent before you walk any field 95%. See Landowner permission.
  • Ducks and geese in depth: Ducks, Geese, Habitat tour: ducks.

• A puff of feathers means a hit 75%.
  • Line the fall up with a tree or rock. Walk straight there (Tip).
More: marking and the law
  • A bird that flies on after a puff of feathers may be hit. Watch it until it is out of sight; it may drop far away (Tip).
  • Line up the fall with something tall behind it. Do not shoot again until you have marked the first bird (Tip).
  • Mark the fall spot with your hat or a blaze orange item, then search in small circles (Tip).
Migratory Birds Regulations, 2022, s. 42

"A person must not hunt migratory game birds unless they have adequate means at their immediate disposal for retrieving any such bird that they kill or injure." "An individual who wounds a migratory game bird must ensure that the bird is killed and retrieved as soon as the circumstances permit." 99%

  • BC adds for all game: make "all reasonable effort to locate, dispatch, retrieve and include it in their bag limit" (99%, synopsis page 12).
  • Full text: Migratory birds in BC. Shotgun skills: Shotgun skills.

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law): Find the dust, the droppings and the berries in one place, and the birds are within a gun shot.

Common mistakes
  • Reading one feather on a trail as a kill site.
  • Walking a goose field the morning you want to hunt it.
  • Shooting a second bird before you marked where the first one fell.

Do this in the field

On your first grouse or quail walk, find 3 kinds of bird sign: tracks, a dust bowl and droppings. Photo, pin and age each.

• Pulled clean, a bird. Bitten, a mammal.
  • White cap, bird scat.
  • One big bowl grouse, many small quail.
More: more hooks
  • D D R F: Dust, Droppings, Roost, Feathers. The 4 bird signs.
  • "Puff, fall, mark": the 3 things to watch after a shot.
  • Number trick: duck track about the length of your thumb, goose track about your palm width (Tip).

• North Dakota Game and Fish Department, Tracks and Signs of North Dakota Wildlife, read directly, checked 2026-10-11 85%: waterfowl track sizes, dust bowls, upland droppings and roosts.
  • Maine Inland Fisheries and Wildlife, Pocket guide to Maine animal tracks, read directly, checked 2026-10-11 85%: ruffed grouse track size.
  • Migratory Birds Regulations, 2022, s. 42, as quoted in Migratory birds in BC 99%.

• Search previews, checked 2026-10-11, capped at 55% to 65%: Bushcraft UK, sign question; Seabrooke Leckie, murder in the woods; Bird Forum, pile of feathers; Vancouver Island University biology blog, California quail; Wikipedia, dust bathing; Bear Tracker, California quail; Northern Woodlands, tracking ruffed grouse; WXPR, grouse snow roost latrines; onX, types of geese; North Carolina State University, goose feeding damage; Mississippi Sportsman, scouting geese.
  • Research log: research/2026-10-11-rs.md.
rs-predator-sign:
Why it matters

Predator sign tells you where deer are and where danger is. A kill site can be the most dangerous spot in the woods.

• Read predator sign from a distance. Never walk up to a covered carcass 75%.
  • Ravens and magpies in one spot: a carcass, maybe a bear 85%.
More: what this session covers
  • Reading sign gave kill site basics. Predators covers the species, seasons and rules. This session goes deep on reading predator sign and kill sites, and on safety around them and around your own kill.
  • You will learn: predator sign to look for, cougar, wolf, bear and coyote kill styles, killed versus scavenged, a 5 step drill when you find a carcass, when surprise encounters are likely, how to hang meat, and how to come back to your own kill.
  • Not covered here (open owner question): how to set up on the wind when calling coyotes. See Predators.

#Key point
1Covered carcass: a cache. The owner is close and coming back 75%
2Cougar: tidy, dragged to cover, covered 85%
3Wolf: messy, at the kill, bones cracked, scattered 85%
4Bear: raked mound, ground torn up, defends it 70%
5Birds circling or calling in one spot: a carcass 85%
6Your own kill: gut pile away, meat hung high, come back loud 85%
7Moved or buried meat: leave and report 85%
  • Detail follows.

• Torn logs, dug anthills, fresh scat, tracks: recent bear activity 85%.
  • Ravens, magpies, crows or jays: maybe a carcass that drew a bear 85%.
More: sign in full
  • Alberta's hunter bear guide lists "fresh signs that indicate recent bear activity: tracks, scat, overturned logs or dug up anthills" and areas where bears may be feeding: berry patches, digging sites, near animal carcasses, grain fields (85%, Alberta Environment, Be BearSmart).
  • "Watch for ravens, magpies, crows or jays. These birds could be at a carcass or gut pile that may have also attracted a bear" (85%, same source).
  • Claw marks on aspen: a bear climbed (80%, photo caption). Bites and rubbed trees with hair: bear marking 65%. See the video below.
  • Cougar scrapes: a small pile of needles or dirt with scat or urine on it, on a ridge trail (65%, from Reading sign).
  • Tracks and scat to scale: Tracks, Droppings deep dive.
▶How to Track for Signs of Bear While Hunting - MeatEater with Steven RinellaBear sign: scat, torn logs, tracks, rubbed trees.
MeatEater, YouTube, 3 min. Needs internet.

• Little sign of a chase; kill dragged to cover and covered neatly 85%.
  • A cougar stays near and feeds for 6 to 8 days 70%.
More: cougar kills in full
  • Stalking predator: "Requires cover"; "Attacks occur over limited distance with little or no chase"; "Kills may be drug or carried considerable distance to an area of cover" (85%, Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife, livestock investigation guide).
  • Attack zones: neck, throat, head, shoulder. "Crushed neck, windpipe, skull"; "Knife like wounds and lacerations with very clean edges" 85%.
  • Feeding: "efficient, tidy"; "Hair removed by sheering or plucking"; "Entry behind shoulder or just behind ribs"; "Internal organs consumed first (heart, liver, lungs)"; "Caching of kill" 85%.
  • Claw scrape marks on a cougar kill are long, about 61 cm (24 inches) or more; bobcat marks are short, 41 cm (16 inches) or less (80%, same source).
  • Cats "Usually carry or drag prey item away from kill site, often to an area of dense cover. May then cache prey by carefully scraping the surrounding area and covering the prey item with ground debris" 85%.
  • It stays nearby and feeds for 6 to 8 days (70%, from Reading sign).

• Chase, bites to the rear and flanks, fed on at the kill 85%.
  • Big bones cracked, remains spread out on older kills 85%.
More: wolf and coyote kills in full
  • Wolf: "coursing predator"; "Potential for prolonged chase and attack"; "Kills rarely moved from attack location" (85%, Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife).
  • Wolf attack zones: hindquarters, groin, tail, front armpits, throat 85%.
  • Wolf feeding: "messy"; "Internal organs consumed first, then generally progresses from rear to head"; "Rumen often busted open"; "Large bones cracked open and marrow consumed (older carcass)"; "Prey remains spread across site (older carcass)" 85%.
  • Coyote: "Typically attack at or near the throat"; "Smaller bones broken and chewed"; kills rarely moved 85%. Coyotes mostly take small prey, fawns and weak animals (Tip).
  • A dog pack: "Relatively indiscriminate in attack location"; "Seldom feed on carcass" 85%.
  • Wolves tend to chase and bite to bring prey down, so a struggle may show at the scene 85%.

• Dirt and debris raked over the carcass; ground looks rototilled 85%.
  • Bears defend caches 70%.
More: bears at kills in full
  • Bears are "More variable than cougars": they "May or may not carry or drag prey item away from kill site. May or may not cache prey. If prey is cached, bears will use ground debris as well as dirt and ground may appear as if it was roto-tilled around the prey item" (85%, Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife).
  • Bear attack signs: bites along the spine between the shoulder blades and to the head or neck; possible claw lacerations 85%.
  • Bears may chase prey a short distance then use size and strength 85%.
  • Grizzly bear sites are generally in more open habitat, black bear sites in denser habitat (80%, same guide).
  • A bear may bed close to a cache. Investigators photographed a grizzly bed site near a kill 85%.

• Cat tidy, wolf messy, bear raked (Tip, built on 85% source).
More: cautions
  • The guide warns that wound patterns alone may not separate predators, and that "Figure should be used for general reference only" 85%.
  • Many predators visit one carcass. A cougar kill may be fed on by bears, coyotes and ravens later 85%.
  • You do not need to solve it. You need to know it is a kill site and leave (Tip).

• Blood, broken brush and trampled plants: killed here 85%.
  • Little blood, no struggle: maybe died first, then fed on 85%.
More: predation versus scavenging
  • "Wolves, coyotes, dogs, cougars, bobcats, and bears all take advantage of scavenging opportunities" (85%, Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife).
  • Signs of a struggle: "trampled vegetation, broken branches on nearby trees or shrubs, spilled or sprayed blood on ground or nearby vegetation" 85%.
  • Investigators confirm a live attack by bite marks with bruising (haemorrhage) under the hide. Bites with no bruising were made after death 85%. You will not skin a carcass you find; this is for understanding only.
  • A dead deer with no predator sign may be a wounded animal another hunter lost, or a disease death. Report unusual dead deer; CWD testing matters (Tip). See CWD.

Found a carcass: 5 steps1 of 5
  • Never kneel over a covered carcass for photos (Tip).
More: the 5 steps in full
  • A covered carcass means a cougar or bear is close and will come back. Do not touch it. Back out the way you came, talking loudly, and tell your brother where it is (75%, from Reading sign).
  • Bear spray in hand, safety clip off only when needed. See Bush safety.
  • If you see a bear at the kill, leave. Do not try to haze it away (85%, Alberta guidance for hunters).
  • Danger to people: call RAPP (Report All Poachers and Polluters) 1 877 952 7277, 24 hours, for wildlife conflicts where public safety is at risk (95%, synopsis page 2, from the Rule Book).
  • Avoid the area for the rest of the day. Change your plan (Tip).
▶How to Use Bear Spray - Banff National ParkRemove the clip, aim low, spray a cloud between you and the bear.
Parks Canada, YouTube, 2 min. Needs internet.

• Loud water, wind, low light and thick cover: make more noise 85%.
  • Hunters move quietly, so they surprise bears more than hikers 85%.
More: why hunters are at higher risk
  • "Being quiet, using animal attractants and calls and travelling alone mean that hunters place themselves at a heightened risk of a bear encounter" (85%, Alberta Environment, Be BearSmart).
  • Be extra cautious when noise levels are high near rivers and streams, in wind or heavy rain, at dusk, night or dawn, and where sightlines are short because of heavy cover, bends in trails or hills (85%, same source).
  • "Distress or mating calls, decoys and cover scents can attract bears as well as game" 85%.
  • "Be cautious when tracking a wounded animal. Bears may also be attracted to animals that are wounded. When possible, have a partner keep watch" 85%. See Blood, hair and tissue.
  • In Alberta, self defence actions by hunters have been the top cause of death for grizzly bears since 2006 (85%, same source). Prevention protects you and the bears.

• Bears are often drawn to the gut pile first 85%.
  • Move the carcass at least 200 m from the gut pile before you leave 85%.
More: working at your kill
  • "While field-dressing the carcass, be aware the scent may be attracting a bear. Make noise so nearby bears know you are in the area. If possible, have someone stand watch for bears while you handle the carcass" (85%, Alberta Environment).
  • "If you need to leave the carcass and return later, separate the carcass from the gut pile. If you can, move the carcass at least 200 metres from the gut pile before you leave" 85%.
  • Your brother watches with the rifle and spray while you work. Swap jobs (Tip). See Field dressing and Packing out.
  • Do not drag the carcass back to camp: it lays a scent trail to where you sleep 85%.

• At least 3.5 m up and 1.5 m from trees, in plain view 85%.
  • Store harvested animals at least 100 m from camp 85%.
More: hanging in full
  • "Hang the carcass. The carcass should be suspended at least 3.5 metres off the ground and 1.5 metres from nearby trees in an area easily seen from a distance" (85%, Alberta Environment).
  • "Store harvested animals at least 100 metres away from camp" 85%.
  • Plain view lets you glass it from far away before you walk in (Tip).
  • Meat care while it hangs: Meat care.

• Approach from upwind, glass first, make lots of noise 85%.
  • Moved, buried or partly eaten: leave right away and report 85%.
More: returning in full
  • "When returning to the kill site, use caution. Approach the site from upwind, use binoculars to see if the site is clear and make as much noise as possible" (85%, Alberta Environment). Coming from upwind lets a bear smell you before you arrive, so it is not surprised.
  • "If you see a bear at your kill site or if the carcass has been moved or buried, do not approach. Leave the site immediately" and report it 85%.
  • If you find the carcass partly eaten, leave the area immediately: a bear may have claimed it and will defend it (85%, Alberta government page via search preview).
  • In BC, report to the RAPP line (Report All Poachers and Polluters) 1 877 952 7277 95%.
  • Meat is replaceable. You are not (Tip).

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law): If something covered it, something is coming back for it. Be gone when it does.

Common mistakes
  • Kneeling over a covered carcass to take photos.
  • Leaving meat beside the gut pile overnight.
  • Walking back to your kill at first light, quiet, into the wind, straight to the meat.

Do this in the field

On every scouting walk, note one predator sign: track, scat, scrape, claw marks or birds circling. Pin it. Ask: what does it eat here, and where are the deer?

• Covered means coming back.
  • Cat tidy, wolf messy, bear raked.
  • 3.5 up, 1.5 out, 200 away.
More: more hooks
  • S L R B T: Stop, Look and listen, Read from afar, Back out, Tell. The carcass drill.
  • "Birds over a spot, bear on the spot" (Tip).
  • "Upwind and loud when you come back": the one time you want to be smelled.

• Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife, Livestock injury and mortality investigations, read directly, checked 2026-10-11 85%: predator signatures, caching, struggle, scavenging.
  • Alberta Environment, Be BearSmart: hunting in bear country, read directly, checked 2026-10-11 85%: bear sign, risk factors, carcass handling, hanging, returning.
  • Government of Alberta, bears and hunters (search preview, 80%): partly eaten carcass.
  • BC Hunting and Trapping Regulations Synopsis, RAPP line, as quoted in the app Rule Book 95%.
  • Earlier figures from Reading sign (cougar feeding 6 to 8 days, scrapes).
  • Not used: Alberta and Idaho phone numbers and self defence rules, which do not apply in BC.
  • Research log: research/2026-10-11-rs.md.
rs-blood-hair-tissue:
Why it matters

The first 3 m after the shot hold the answer to how long to wait and where to look. Read them before you take one step down the trail.

  • Hit site first: hair, blood, bone, tissue, dug in hoofs (Tip).
  • Then read the land: where would a hurt deer go here? (Tip)
More: how this fits with Blood trailing
  • Blood trailing is the step by step recovery lesson: watch, wait times, flags, grid search, the law on hours and lights, private land. Read it first. This lesson goes deeper on two things: reading the evidence, and reading the terrain.
  • You will learn: a 5 step hit site search, what each kind of blood, hair and tissue means, blood drop direction, where blood sits on brush, how much blood is a lot, why trails dry up, where wounded deer go, a recovery plan by hit, and bear safety on a blood trail.
  • Wait times and hit reads are hunter education opinion, not law 70%.

#Key point
1Search the hit site and the bullet path before you trail (Tip)
2Pink froth and spongy tissue: lungs 70%
3Green or brown matter with a smell: gut. Back out 70%
4Blood drop tails point the way the animal went 75%
5Blood darkens as it dries; rain lightens it 65%
6No blood does not mean no hit 70%
7Wounded deer head downhill, to thick cover and water 70%
8Bears come to wounded animals too. One watches, one tracks 85%
  • Detail follows.

Search the hit site in 5 steps1 of 5
  • Do this after your wait, not before, on a doubtful hit 70%.
More: the 5 steps in full
  • Walk to where the animal stood and flag it. Look for blood, hair, bone chips, scuffed ground, a bullet furrow (70%, from Blood trailing).
  • Pick the landmark while you are still at your shooting spot. Things look different up close (Tip).
  • Dug in hoof prints show the launch spot and first direction (Tip). See Measuring tracks.
  • Exit spray, hair and tissue can land metres behind the animal, on trees and brush in the bullet path (Tip).
  • On a heart or lung hit you may go to the hit site after about 20 to 30 minutes; on a doubtful hit, wait longer first (65%, Deer and Deer Hunting via search preview).

• Read everything together: blood, hair, tissue and the reaction 65%.
  • Stomach matter beats blood colour for calling a gut hit 65%.
More: evidence in full
  • Lung hit: "light coloured blood, blistered blood, and soft and light coloured lung tissue on the ground" (65%, Norma Academy via search preview).
  • Bright pinkish, frothy blood is "a positive indication of a solid lung hit" (65%, Realtree via search preview).
  • Gut hit: green or brownish plant matter 65%; "green digested plant material, sometimes liver, grainy, dark red blood as well as a strong smell" (65%, Norma). A paunch hit "will likely leave a sparse trail of small drops and pinpricks of blood mixed with stomach content"; back off and wait at least 8 hours (70%, Pennsylvania Game Commission, Game News, April 2016, via search preview).
  • "Greenish matter smeared on the shaft, usually with white fatty tissue, means a paunch hit" (65%, Realtree, bowhunting).
  • Bone chips: a bone was struck. Bone, marrow and light fur at the strike point suggest a front leg hit (65%, Norma).
  • Pink blood plus bone chips can mean a shoulder or rib hit that also caught the lungs 60%.
  • Full colour chart and wait times: Blood trailing.

ConditionWhat happensCertainty
DryingDarker, duller, brown when dry65%
FreezingDarker and dull65%
On soilLooks darker than on leaves65%
RainLooks lighter, washes away65%
  • Read colour on fresh blood, soon after the shot 65%.
More: colour in full
  • "The longer any blood is on the ground, the darker it appears, particularly after it dries" (65%, Deer and Deer Hunting via search preview).
  • Blood that dries or freezes darkens and looks dull; blood on soil looks darker than on leaves; rain can make it look lighter (65%, Bowhunter via search preview).
  • "Dried blood usually has a brown color and can be difficult to spot on brown grass or leaves" (70%, hunter education course, Nebraska, via search preview).
  • Colour "is most accurately determined if you can inspect it soon after the shot" (65%, Bowhunter).
  • Hydrogen peroxide fizzes on blood you cannot see in leaves (70%, from Blood trailing).

• A drop that hits at an angle grows a small tail on the far side 80%.
  • That tail points the way the animal was moving (Tip).
More: the physics
  • Forensic research: for low impact angles, bloodstains "can include an asymmetric tail that bloodstain analysts can use qualitatively to establish directionality" (80%, Physics of Fluids 2023 via search preview).
  • The tail forms in the last moments of spreading and keeps its shape as it dries (80%, same source).
  • Field use: drops from a moving animal fly forward, so the tail points the direction of travel (Tip, built on 80% physics).
  • Round drops with no tails: the animal was standing or moving slowly (Tip).
  • On slopes and leaf litter, gravity and texture blur the tails. Use tracks too 75%.

• Blood high on both sides: a pass through, bleeding well (Tip).
  • Low on one side: maybe no exit. Expect less blood (Tip).
More: brush in full
  • Blood sprayed on brush both sides of the trail: a pass through, bleeding well (Tip, from Blood trailing).
  • Blood only low and on one side: maybe no exit hole. Expect less blood (Tip, same).
  • The height of blood smears on brush tells you how high on the body the wound is (Tip).
  • A fine mist of tiny drops on leaves at nose height often comes from blood breathed out: a lung sign (Tip).
  • Look up: blood on the underside of leaves and on twigs at chest height is easy to miss when you only look down (Tip).

• Blood volume is about 7% of body weight 60%.
  • A deer may need to lose about a third before shock or death 60%.
More: volume in full
  • "The blood volume of most animals is approximately 7 percent of body weight" (60%, hunting magazine via search preview). A 60 kg deer: about 4.2 L.
  • "A deer must lose about a third of its blood to go into a state of shock or die" (60%, search preview); the threshold varies with how fast it is lost (60%, Buckmasters citing Texas bowhunter education).
  • Hunters often guess blood loss badly; estimates in a bowhunter class were "all over the map" 60%.
  • Deer often die from trauma to vital organs faster than from blood loss alone 60%.
  • Practise: pour one cup (250 mL) of water with red food colour on leaves. See how big a cup looks. Then you will not panic at a "lot of blood" (Tip).

• Clotting is the most common reason a trail fades 60%.
  • No blood does not mean no hit. Look for tracks 70%.
More: dry trails in full
  • "When you initially find blood, and then it disappears, in most cases clotting is the reason" (60%, Deer and Deer Hunting via search preview).
  • Fat or hair can plug a small hole; a high hit with no exit bleeds inside (Tip).
  • Gut hits bleed little outside: "much less external bleeding" and the deer often beds "in the first few hundred yards" (60%, Outdoor Life on Jeanneney's book, via search preview).
  • Hair but no blood at all: back out and give it more time (70%, from Blood trailing).
  • When the blood ends, switch to tracks and disturbed ground (Tip). See Following a track.
▶Tracking Beyond the Blood Trail - how to find wounded deer, elk and other GameWhen the blood stops, look for tracks and disturbed ground.
Clay Hayes, YouTube, 7 min. Needs internet.

• Hair tells you how high you hit (Tip).
  • After recovery, compare the hair to where you hit. Learn your own reads (Tip).
More: hair in full
  • Long white fine hair: belly or brisket, a low hit. Short brown or grey with dark tips: side of the chest. Long coarse grey brown: top of the back, a high hit. White with a dark band: tail or rump (Tip, from Blood trailing).
  • Cut hair at the hit site means a bullet passed close or through the hide (Tip).
  • Lots of cut hair and no blood: maybe a graze. Look hard and wait (Tip).
  • Keep a small bag of hair from your hit sites with notes in the Journal. Over years it becomes your reference set (Tip).

• Downhill, to water, into thick cover, often on a game trail 70%.
  • Look ahead for the animal, not only down for blood (Tip).
More: terrain in full
  • Wounded animals head downhill and to water, often on a game trail. Check creeks (70%, National Deer Association, from Blood trailing).
  • A rifle hit in the heart or lungs: the deer is usually dead within about 137 m (150 yd) (70%, National Deer Association).
  • Gut hit deer often bed early, within a few hundred metres, if not pushed 60%.
  • Before you start, look at the map: where are the nearest thick patch, creek bottom and downhill trail? Plan the likely route (Tip). See Map scouting.
  • Around Heffley Creek, check the timbered draws below open grass slopes first (Tip).
  • Note private land boundaries before you follow. The Trespass Act has no tracking exception (95%, from Blood trailing).

• Waits are opinion from hunter education, not law 70%.
  • Rain or snow coming: go sooner (Tip).
More: the plan in full
  • Wait table with sources: Blood trailing. Hunter education and the National Deer Association differ on liver and gut waits; this app shows the hunter education numbers 70%.
  • Lungs: often a short trail. Follow slowly, look ahead.
  • Liver: dark blood, then often a bed. Back out quietly and come back after the wait 70%.
  • Gut: thin blood with stomach matter. Back out at least 6 to 8 hours 70%. Pennsylvania Game Commission says at least 8 hours 70%.
  • Leg or muscle: may travel far. Get help: your brother, a leashed dog (dogs on deer must be leashed in BC, 95%).
  • Warm afternoon on a gut hit: the meat clock fights the wait clock. Wait less, trim more (Tip).

• Bears may be drawn to wounded animals 85%.
  • One person tracks, one watches with spray and rifle 85%.
More: safety in full
  • "Be cautious when tracking a wounded animal. Bears may also be attracted to animals that are wounded. When possible, have a partner keep watch" (85%, Alberta Environment, Be BearSmart).
  • Talk while you track in grizzly country. A quiet tracker on a blood trail into thick cover is the classic surprise setup (Tip).
  • Finding your deer covered or buried: leave and report 85%. See Predator sign and kill sites.

Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

RuleCertainty
All reasonable effort to locate, dispatch, retrieve 95%Synopsis page 12
No hunting from 1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise 95%Synopsis
No hunting with a light 95%Synopsis
  • Tracking with a firearm after hours or with a light is hunting. Do not (85%, my reading).
More: the law in full
  • "No person shall kill, cripple or wound game without making all reasonable effort to locate, dispatch, retrieve and include it in their bag limit" 95%.
  • "Hunt" includes "following after or on the trail of" wildlife "while in possession of a firearm or other weapon" 95%.
  • Lost the light on a lung hit: call the RAPP line (Report All Poachers and Polluters) 1 877 952 7277 and ask for direction (lean from Blood trailing).
  • Full text: Blood trailing and the Rule Book.

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law): The deer writes its own report at the hit site. Read it slowly before you go chasing the last page.

Common mistakes
  • Walking straight down the blood line and trampling the hit site.
  • Calling it a miss because there was no blood in the first 10 m.
  • Trailing into thick cover in grizzly country alone and quiet.

Do this in the field

Before season: lay a practice trail with your brother. Coloured water drops, a cup splash, a bit of hair. Each of you finds and reads the other's trail.

• Pink froth, lungs. Green bits, gut.
  • Tails point the trail.
  • Down, dark, wet: downhill, thick cover, water.
More: more hooks
  • H B B T S: Hair, Blood, Bone, Tissue, Scuffs. The 5 things in the 3 m circle.
  • "A cup looks like a bucket": small amounts of blood look big on leaves.
  • "No blood, still look": no blood does not mean a miss.

• Search previews, checked 2026-10-11, capped at 60% to 70%: Norma Academy, shot analysis and wounded game recovery; Realtree, expert blood trailing; Pennsylvania Game Commission, Game News April 2016; eWash, where you shot a deer; Deer and Deer Hunting, the first 50 yards; Bowhunter, blood variations; Hunter Ed, Nebraska, trailing shot game; Buckmasters, how much blood can a deer lose; MeatEater, lies about blood trailing; Deer and Deer Hunting, why blood trails dry up; Outdoor Life on Jeanneney's book.

• Bloodstain physics: United States National Institute of Justice, bloodstain tails and AIP Publishing, written in blood (search preview, 80%).
  • Alberta Environment, Be BearSmart: hunting in bear country, read directly, checked 2026-10-11 85%.
  • Law lines and wait tables as sourced in Blood trailing (synopsis, Hunter Ed, National Deer Association).
  • Research log: research/2026-10-11-rs.md.
rs-track-following:
Why it matters

Most trails end with the animal watching you go by. Good trackers look ahead, match the pace, and know when to leave the trail.

  • Track with your eyes ahead, not at your feet 60%.
  • Wind first: never walk your scent up its trail (Tip).
More: what this session covers
  • Snow tracking covered backtracking versus following in snow. This session is the full technique on any ground: picking a track, light, the track stick, losing and finding the trail, pace, wind, the hook before the bed, working as a pair, when to quit, and safety.
  • Following a fresh trail with a rifle is hunting: legal hours, land status and all hunting rules apply 95%.
  • Honest note: big woods trackers walk a buck all day and fail more often than they succeed (Tip, from Snow tracking). Patience is the skill.

#Key point
1Pick fresh, legal, worth it; skip doe and fawn wanderings 60%
2Glance down, then look 40 to 100 m ahead (Tip)
3Low side light shows faint tracks 65%
4Track stick: step and stride bands find the next print 65%
5Lost it: flag the last track, circle 10 m, then 20 m (Tip)
6Match its pace: feeding means slow right down 60%
7Trail turns downwind or hooks: leave it, swing wide (Tip)
8Know when to quit: light, weather, land, legs (Tip)
  • Detail follows.

• Fresh, the right animal, and legal light left (Tip).
  • Skip meandering doe and fawn trails if you want a buck 60%.
More: choosing in full
  • "A common mistake is following the first set of tracks you see. Usually, those belong to a doe and her fawns" (60%, MeatEater via search preview).
  • Benoit family lore (Maine white tails): bucks worth following usually leave tracks at least 7.6 cm (3 inches) wide, the best near 8.3 cm (3 1/4 inches) (60%, Outdoor Life via search preview). A Region 3 mule deer buck is bigger bodied; build your own numbers (Tip).
  • Aging the track: Aging tracks and sign. Measuring: Measuring tracks.
  • Check the season and your licence for that animal before you start 95%. See BC rules.

• Bend to deer eye level and watch the terrain ahead 60%.
  • When it slows to feed, slow down a lot and scan every direction 60%.
More: looking ahead in full
  • When following a buck track, put yourself "in the animal's hooves", bend to eye level, and look ahead while following (60%, Realtree via search preview).
  • "Once he slows down and begins to feed, you need to slow down exponentially as well. Really start to look over the terrain ahead of you in every direction" (60%, MeatEater via search preview).
  • Look ahead, not down. Every few steps stop and glass the cover ahead and above (Tip, from Snow tracking).
  • Rule of thumb: 3 seconds down for the next track, 10 seconds ahead (Tip).
  • See Glassing and Moving quietly.

• Get low and look toward the light: faint tracks show as shadows 65%.
  • Early and late light is best for tracking (Tip).
More: light in full
  • Trackers call it side heading: get low, eyes near the ground, facing the light, to see tracks and grit compressions on hard surfaces (65%, Wildwood Tracking via search preview).
  • Be at "as low an angle to the tracks as possible" (65%, same source).
  • Midday overhead sun flattens tracks. Walk so the trail is between you and the low sun (Tip).
  • At home, practise with a flashlight held low across a dusty floor. Never use a light to hunt or track with a firearm: that is hunting with a light 95%. See Blood trailing.

Use a track stick in 4 steps1 of 4
  • A walking stick or ski pole with 2 rubber bands or O rings 65%.
More: the track stick in full
  • A common build is a dowel or old ski pole about 0.9 to 1.2 m (3 to 4 feet) long, with rubber O rings or bands as movable markers (65%, Bear Tracker and Wildwood Tracking via search preview).
  • Set the first mark at stride length, heel to heel; a second mark can show print length to confirm you are on the right trail 65%.
  • Place the tip over the last clear print and sweep in an arc while looking for the next track under the mark. Keep the stick above the ground so you do not disturb sign 65%.
  • "Stride varies with terrain and fatigue", so reset the bands every so often 65%.
  • Look for crushed needles, bent grass, moved pebbles. Mark found prints with tape so you can backtrack 65%.
  • Measure the step and stride first: Measuring tracks.

• Never wander ahead making new tracks over the trail 70%.
  • The trail must cross your circle somewhere (Tip).
More: the circle in full
  • Lost the line? Walk a slow circle 10 m out around the last clear print and find where the trail leaves the circle (Tip, from Tracks).
  • Lost the blood? Go back to the last flag. Never wander ahead making a second set of tracks (70%, from Blood trailing).
  • Check the likely ways first: the game trail, the easy downhill, the gap in the brush (Tip).
  • Two people: one stays on the last flag as a fixed point, the other circles (Tip).

• Travelling straight: you can move faster (Tip).
  • Feeding, wandering, beds: it is near. Creep 60%.
More: pace in full
  • "The trail tells you when you are close: feeding turns to walking, then a single line going uphill, then a bed" (hunter lore, 60%, from Snow tracking).
  • In crunchy snow, walk like a deer: a few quick steps and a stop, maybe a soft grunt or bleat (60%, Hal Blood in Outdoor Life via search preview). Check calling rules for your species and area first.
  • Stot or gallop groups: it is alarmed. Give it time to settle, sometimes an hour (Tip).
  • Gait reading: Measuring tracks and reading gait patterns.

• Follow with the wind in your face or across you (Tip).
  • Trail turns downwind: leave it and loop around (Tip).
More: wind in full
  • If the trail turns downwind, loop around rather than walking your scent to the bed (Tip, from Snow tracking).
  • Thermals change through the day: morning air rises, evening air sinks 75%. Recheck the wind every few minutes with a puffer or thread (Tip). See Wind and thermals.

• A buck may loop back and watch you walk past 60%.
  • When the trail starts to hook, swing wide and glass the bed area (Tip).
More: hooks in full
  • "You might cover five miles of broken terrain just to realize the buck you're following looped back and watched you walk past from a ridge" (60%, Realtree via search preview).
  • Hunter lore says deer often hook back before bedding so they can watch or smell their back trail (Tip; not confirmed by a study in this research).
  • Big woods trackers walk a buck track until he beds, then stalk the bed from above (Tip, from Snow tracking).
  • Beds in detail: Beds and bedding areas.

Track ageAnimal likelyYour plan (Tip)
MinutesWithin sight or soundFreeze, glass, wind check
A few hoursBedded, often within 1 to 2 kmSlow follow, glass often
A day or twoStill in its home rangeBacktrack to learn, not to catch
  • A white tailed buck's home range is often only about 26 to 31 km² 60%.
More: home range in full
  • Benoit Tracking School: white tailed bucks "tend to have their own home territory... that usually isn't more than 10 or 12 square miles", so a track a couple of days old can still lead to a buck close by (60%, Outdoor Life via search preview). That is about 26 to 31 km².
  • Mule deer home ranges in BC vary by season and herd. See Mule deer and How animals move.
  • Backtrack to learn its life. Follow to catch it (Tip, from Snow tracking).

• Tracker reads the trail. Spotter watches ahead and to the sides (Tip).
  • Swap every 30 minutes; eyes get tired (Tip).
More: working as a pair
  • Agree on hand signals before you start: stop, animal, bear, come here (Tip).
  • Only one person shoots, on a safe agreed angle. Know your zone of fire (95% for the safety principle). See Firearm safety.
  • In bear country the spotter carries spray in hand (Tip). See Predator sign and kill sites.

• Any "no" means stop, flag it, and come back (Tip).
  • Pin the last track. Tomorrow you can start there (Tip).
More: quitting in full
  • Legal light: no hunting from 1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise 95%. Leave enough light to field dress and pack out (Tip).
  • Weather: rain erases sign; fresh snow can restart the hunt (Tip).
  • Land: the trail does not give you consent to cross a fence. The Trespass Act has no tracking exception 95%. See Maps: land status.
  • Your legs: the walk back is as long as the walk in. Set a turnaround time (Tip).

▶Hug-A-Tree & Survive filmLost? Stop. Stay put. Shelter and signal.
AdventureSmart, YouTube, 12 min. Needs internet.
  • Pin the truck before you start. Record your track on the GPS (Tip).
  • Tell someone your area and return time (Tip).
More: navigation in full
  • Following a trail pulls your attention to the ground for hours. It is the classic way to get turned around (Tip).
  • Check your map every 15 minutes: where am I, where is the truck, how long back? (Tip). See Maps: navigation.
  • Leave a trip plan with someone at home (Tip). See Bush safety.

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law): The tracks are behind the animal. Your eyes should be in front of it.

Common mistakes
  • Staring at your feet and walking right past the bedded buck.
  • Following the trail straight downwind into its bed.
  • Wandering ahead when you lost the trail, and stamping out the next print.

Do this in the field

Make a track stick. Follow one deer trail for 30 minutes, flagging every lost and found print. Swap tracker and spotter with your brother.

• Glance down, look ahead.
  • Lost it? Flag, circle, widen.
  • Its pace sets your pace.
More: more hooks
  • F L A W: Fresh, Light, Ahead, Wind. The 4 checks before every follow.
  • "3 down, 10 ahead": 3 seconds on the track, 10 seconds on the cover ahead.
  • "Hook means look": when the trail curls, stop and glass.

• Search previews, checked 2026-10-11, capped at 60% to 65%: Bear Tracker, tracking stick; Wildwood Tracking, track stick; Wildwood Tracking, side heading; Realtree, scouting deer in the snow; MeatEater, how to track down a buck fast; MeatEater, tracking a buck in different snow; Outdoor Life, Making Tracks (Benoit); Outdoor Life, Hal Blood snow tracking.
  • Legal hours, lights and trespass as sourced in Blood trailing 95%.
  • Earlier lines from Snow tracking and Tracks.
  • Research log: research/2026-10-11-rs.md.
rs-sign-substrates:
Why it matters

The same deer leaves a perfect print in mud, a hole in powder, and nothing on rock. Know the ground and you know what to trust.

• Wet grounds show detail. Dry grounds hide it 65%.
  • Every ground ages at its own speed 65%.
More: what this session covers
  • Snow tracking is the full snow method. Aging tracks and sign covers aging clocks. This session compares the grounds you will hunt: snow of every kind, mud, sand, dust, grass, leaves, duff and rock.
  • You will learn: what each ground shows and hides, snow types, melt out, mud traps, wet and dry sand, dust roads and the tire trick, reading leaf litter, natural track traps, and safety on snow and ice.
  • Your country: dusty grassland roads around Kamloops and the South Okanagan, mud and sand by Interior creeks and lakes, Fraser Valley mud and dyke edges, and November snow at Heffley Creek (Tip).

#Key point
1Wet snow captures detail; powder captures little 85%
2Sun melts snow prints out bigger 65%
3Mud shows toes and nails, and ages slowest 65%
4Wet sand shows detail; dry sand makes bowls 65%
5Dust shows fine detail until the wind blows 60%
6No prints? Read flipped leaves, moss, duff, stones 65%
7A print on top of a tire mark came after the vehicle (Tip)
8Crossings are natural track traps (Tip)
  • Detail follows.

• Soft and damp grounds hold the best prints 65%.
  • Track appearance varies hugely with ground and speed 85%.
More: the table in full
  • "Depending on the substrate (snow, mud, dust, sand, etc.) and the speed the animal was moving, tracks may show great variability in their appearance" (85%, Maine Inland Fisheries and Wildlife pocket card).
  • Mud: "great for seeing the clear details in tracks like toes, pad shape and toenails" and "typically the slowest aging substrate" (65%, Nature Mentor via search preview).
  • Sand: greatest detail when wet; edges dry fast in sun, wind and rain (65%, Nature Mentor and Point Reyes Light via search preview).
  • Dust: "great detail can be seen in the fine grain of dust, but suitable tracks are rare" (60%, search preview).
  • Small animals need finer, crisper ground than big ones to leave readable prints 60%.

• Wet snow captures a print well; dry powder does not 85%.
  • Crust: few prints and loud walking (Tip).
More: snow types in full
  • "Wet snow captures a paw print well, whereas dry powdery snow captures a less defined print pattern" (85%, New York State Department of Environmental Conservation, Conservationist, February 2015).
  • "A thin layer of wet snow shows the best tracks, but as the snow ages, the edges of the track will soften. Hard, crusty, or wet snow, or strong wind, can make tracks nearly empty" (65%, search preview).
  • Powder: you read depth, spacing and drag marks, not shape (Tip).
  • Crust: animals may break through (deer) or walk on top (coyotes, hares). Your steps are loud; slow down or wait for a softer day (Tip).
  • Snow depth and movement: deer struggle past about 30 cm, moose to about 40 cm, elk between (65% to 75%, from Food, water and cover).

• After sunny days a print can look much bigger and rounder 65%.
  • A melted out fawn print can fool you into "elk" (Tip).
More: melt out in full
  • In snow "an older track will increase in size and round off" (65%, search preview); after a few days prints "can appear huge with melting" 60%.
  • South facing slopes melt prints fastest; north slopes keep them crisp (Tip).
  • Measure only crisp fresh prints, on the floor: Measuring tracks.
  • Shape clues survive melt better than size: toe count, claws, pattern (Tip).

• Water seeping into the floor and a shiny rim: fresh (Tip).
  • Mud ages slowest: a crisp mud print can be days old 65%.
More: mud in full
  • In mud, fresh means the walls are still shiny and wet (Tip, from Tracks).
  • Morning frost freezes mud prints solid; they thaw and soften by afternoon (Tip).
  • Mud splashed onto clean leaves or rocks beside a crossing: something passed recently 65%.
  • Elk rub wallow mud on nearby trees (65%, from Reading sign).
  • Muddy creek crossings and pond edges in the Fraser Valley and Interior: check for webbed duck and goose tracks too (85% sizes). See Bird sign.

• Wet sand by water: clear shapes 65%.
  • Dry sand: read the spacing and pattern, not the print (Tip).
More: sand in full
  • Sand "holds tracks well", but "its edges dry out fast", so freshness checks look at whether the raised edges are still moist (65%, Point Reyes Light via search preview).
  • Wind ripples fill dry sand prints within hours on an exposed bar (Tip).
  • Lake beaches and river bars are classic places to learn tracks: walk them at dawn (Tip).
  • In dry sand the gait still shows: Measuring tracks and reading gait patterns.

• Dust shows fine detail, until the wind blows 60%.
  • A print on top of a tire tread: made after that vehicle passed (Tip).
More: dust and roads in full
  • In fine dust a fresh print has a thin raised rim that collapses within hours (60%, from Tracks).
  • The overlap rule: whatever mark lies on top was made last. A track printed over a tire tread came after the vehicle; a tread over a track came after the animal (Tip, simple logic).
  • If you know when a vehicle passed (yours, last evening), the overlap brackets the age of the track (Tip).
  • Dusty grassland roads near Kamloops: drive slowly at first light and look for fresh crossings, then come back on foot (Tip). Never shoot from or across a road; see the Rule Book.
  • Dust bowls from grouse and quail: Bird sign.

• Leaves, duff and rock show disturbance, not prints 65%.
  • Crouch low and look along the ground toward the light 65%.
More: litter, grass and rock in full
  • Sign of passage in litter: "displaced vegetation or stones", "turned over leaves", "dew knocked off vegetation", broken cobwebs (65%, tracking glossary via search preview).
  • Grass: bent stems lie the way the animal moved (65%, from Tracks). A dark line through dewy grass is a fresh trail (Tip). See Aging tracks and sign.
  • Rock: look for scuffs of soil carried onto clean rock, moss scraped off, pebbles knocked out of their beds (Tip).
  • Use low side light: Following a track.

• Creek crossings, road edges, fence lines and field edges collect tracks (Tip).
  • Check them first on any new piece of ground (Tip).
More: traps in full
  • Animals funnel through the easy places: low spots in fences, shallow creek crossings, gaps in brush. Those are where prints pile up (Tip). See Trails and funnels.
  • Fence crossings collect hair too (65%, from Reading sign).
  • Road edges: walk the soft shoulder of a quiet forest service road (FSR) at first light. Read which way crossings go and how fresh they are (Tip).
  • Smooth a strip of dirt on a trail with your boot one evening and check it in the morning: a homemade track trap (Tip).
  • Private land and consent rules still apply at fences 95%. See Maps: land status.

• Avalanche terrain starts around 30 degrees once there is enough snow 70%.
  • November river and lake ice is not trustworthy (Tip).
More: safety in full
  • Avalanche terrain starts around 30 degrees of slope once there is enough snow to slide. Open slopes, gullies and the run outs below them can slide in November (70%, from Snow tracking).
  • Check the Avalanche Canada forecast before snow country trips (Tip).
  • Do not cross river or lake ice to save a kilometre (Tip). Cold water: Water safety.
  • Set a turnaround time; leave a trip plan (Tip). See Bush safety.

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law): Ask the ground how honest it is before you ask the track how old it is.

Common mistakes
  • Measuring a melted out snow print and calling it an elk.
  • Calling a crisp mud print fresh because it looks perfect.
  • Giving up on leaf litter because there are no prints.

Do this in the field

Find one deer print in 3 different grounds: mud, dust or sand, and snow or grass. Photograph each with your knife. Compare detail and age.

• Wet tells, dry hides.
  • Sun grows snow prints.
  • On top came last.
More: more hooks
  • M S D L: Mud, Sand, Dust, Leaves. Each has its own trap: too fresh looking, shapeless, wind erased, no prints.
  • "Crossings collect": check every creek, fence and road crossing.
  • "Powder shows depth, wet snow shows toes."

• New York State Department of Environmental Conservation, Winter Tracks, Conservationist February 2015, read directly, checked 2026-10-11 85%: wet versus powder snow.
  • Maine Inland Fisheries and Wildlife, Pocket guide to Maine animal tracks, read directly, checked 2026-10-11 85%: substrate variability.
  • Search previews, checked 2026-10-11, capped at 60% to 65%: Nature Mentor, where to find animal tracks and how to tell if tracks are fresh; Point Reyes Light, tracking; Northern Illinois University, tracking; Outdoor Life, animal tracks; Hunting BC forum archive and bowhunting forum (melt out); Bear Tracker glossary.

• Snow depth, avalanche and ice lines as sourced in Food, water and cover and Snow tracking.
  • Research log: research/2026-10-11-rs.md.
fronts-and-movement:
Why it matters

Camp talk says "hunt the front". The collars say something more useful. Learn which weather really moves deer, ducks and birds, so you hunt the right place on the day you have.

  • Strong: snow and cold, the rut, hunting pressure, freeze up.
  • Weak: barometric pressure. Near zero: the moon.
  • Weather picks where you hunt, not whether you go (Tip).
More: what this session covers and how sure we are
  • This session goes deeper than Weather, moon and what moves game. Read that one first if you have not.
  • Here: what a front is, what collared deer did around 30 storms, the one weather factor that keeps showing up (temperature), how freeze up moves ducks, how storms change geese and upland birds, and how to turn a forecast into a plan.
  • The bar chart is my rating of the studies below (Tip). The studies themselves carry their own certainty on each screen.
  • Most good collar data is on white tailed deer in the United States. Interior mule deer may differ (Tip). Where a study is on mule deer or BC birds, it says so.
  • Moon and daylight have their own session: Moon and daylight.

• A : cold, heavy air pushes under warm air 80%.
  • Before: south wind, falling pressure. After: northwest wind, colder, rising pressure 70%.
More: the front, in plain words
  • A cold front is the edge of an advancing mass of cooler, denser air that replaces warmer air (80%, US National Weather Service glossary, via the Weather Prediction Center).
  • Typical sequence in the Northern Hemisphere (70%, general meteorology, US National Weather Service forecast office page, search preview):
    • Before it: wind from the south or southwest, clouds thicken, pressure falls.
    • At it: a band of rain or snow showers, gusty wind, a quick wind shift.
    • After it: wind from the west or northwest, colder and drier air, pressure rises, skies clear.
  • A warm front is the opposite: warm air rides up over cold air, with a long spell of light rain or drizzle ahead of it (70%, general meteorology).
  • In the BC Interior, mountains bend the wind. The valley wind on your slope may not match the forecast arrow (Tip). Thermals still rule the first and last hours: see Wind and thermals.
  • Forecast source: use the official Canadian forecast for Kamloops or the nearest station. This app does not repeat forecasts (Tip).

• The wind swings from south to northwest as the front passes 70%.
  • During the storm, deer moved less 80%.
  • Glass the first calm hours after it (Tip, not proven).
More: what the animation shows, line by line
  • The rain cloud crossing the hill is the front. The wind dial swings from south to northwest (70%, general meteorology).
  • The deer beds in cover while the storm is on: in the Penn State study, collared does moved less during storms 80%.
  • After the storm the deer feeds. That part is a hunter's tip, not a study result. No study found for this session measured movement right after a front (VERIFY if you see one).
  • Your scent: the wind shift moves your scent cone too. A stand that was perfect at dawn can be wrong by noon after a front (Tip). Plan a second seat for the new wind.

• 30 winter storms, collared does: no real change before the storm 80%.
  • They moved less during it 80%.
More: the Penn State storm study in full
  • Penn State Deer Forest Study, "Spidey sense", read directly 2026-10-02 and rechecked in this session's notes: collared does through 30 winter storms, 2015 to 2017 80%.
  • Their words: "Data show no statistical or biological significance of oncoming winter storms on behavior or movement of our collared deer." 80%
  • The deer slowed during the storms, not before them 80%.
  • Limits: white tailed does in Pennsylvania forest, winter storms. Bucks, mule deer, fall fronts and the BC Interior were not tested (Tip: treat it as a strong hint, not a law).
  • Penn State preliminary notes: bucks moved less in rain than does (65%, preliminary blog notes).
  • So the "feed before the front" rule is not supported by the best collar study found. It may still happen on your hill. Log it and see (Tip).

• One Oklahoma collar study: temperature explained most of the change in movement 65%.
  • South Carolina collars: weather effects were real but smaller than the daily rhythm 65%.
More: temperature studies and what to do with them
  • Mississippi State team, Oklahoma collar study: temperature explained most of the change in deer movement; no clear barometric pattern (65%, search preview via Mossy Oak).
  • Goethlich thesis, Auburn University, South Carolina GPS (Global Positioning System) collars: weather, temperature, wind speed, pressure and moon each affected activity in some seasons and hours, but "responses to abiotic factors were typically less pronounced than circadian fluctuations in activity" (65%, search preview). Plain English: the time of day matters more than the weather.
  • Penn State October data: deer moved about 120 to 140 m an hour at dawn and dusk, under 50 m an hour in the day and about 60 m an hour at night (75%, Penn State Deer Forest blog, read directly). Dawn and dusk beat any weather effect.
  • A hot October spell: deer bed in shade (north and east faces, timber) and move at the very edges of legal light (Tip).
  • A cold snap after mild weather: hunters report more daylight feeding. No study found for the Interior; log it (Tip).
  • Trend beats hour: compare today to the last 3 days, not to 6 am (Tip).

• Snow and cold trigger the fall move to 85%.
  • Trouble near 30 cm of snow; deer leave slopes near 50 cm 75%.
More: snow, cold and migration timing in full
  • Trigger: snow and cold, not the rut (85%, Monteith and others 2011, Ecosphere, via research notes).
  • Wyoming GPS collars, 2016 to 2018: temperature and snowfall set migration timing in both sexes; the rifle season added only about 2% to the chance a doe migrated and under 0.01% for bucks (85%, Rodgers and others 2021, Journal of Wildlife Management, abstract read directly).
  • BC deer account: deer "have difficulty moving through snow deeper than 30 cm" 85%. A UBC (University of British Columbia) thesis: deer leave slopes near 50 cm 80%. Use 30 to 50 cm as the range 75%.
  • Southern Interior Mule Deer Project: most collared deer were back on winter range in October and November; one year nearly all by mid October 85%.
  • So for a mid to late October hunt near Heffley Creek: the first real snow up high is the best weather news you can get (Tip). See Migration routes in BC.

• Cold days add up, ice locks the food, dabblers leave 75%.
  • Interior freeze up ends most BC fall migration by late November 75%.
More: the weather severity index and BC timing
  • Schummer and others 2010, Journal of Wildlife Management: in Missouri 1995 to 2005, a cumulative weather severity index best explained changes in mallard and dabbling duck numbers. It adds up mean temperature, the run of days at or below 0 °C, snow depth and the run of snow cover days (75%, abstract read directly).
  • Why it works: cold costs energy; snow and ice hide food (75%, same study).
  • BC: "The fall migration largely concluded by late November, coinciding with freeze-up in most of the province." (75%, Ducks Unlimited 2024 field report, quoted with its hyphen)
  • Plateau lakes freeze first, valley rivers later. When the high potholes ice over, ducks pack onto open valley water (Tip, consistent with the freeze up pattern).
  • Daily flights by weather: see Waterfowl daily flights.

• Stormy days: geese flew more through the whole day 70%.
  • Worse weather pushes pheasants deeper into cover 70%.
  • Heavy snow pushes chukar lower and onto south slopes 75%.
More: the bird studies and sources
  • Canada geese, Crab Orchard refuge, Illinois, about 40,000 birds over two winters: geese "usually fly to feeding areas in the early morning and late afternoons but undertake increased flight activity throughout the day when it is stormy" (70%, Raveling, Crews and Klimstra, Wilson Bulletin, search preview).
  • Pheasants: Minnesota DNR (Department of Natural Resources): worse weather pushes birds deeper into cover (70%, read directly). Pheasants in BC: Okanagan and Georgia Depression, chiefly below 500 m (85%, BC Breeding Bird Atlas).
  • Chukar: "moving from higher elevations to lower terrain during heavy snows", may move onto south facing slopes (75%, USDA Fire Effects Information System). In BC: "Prolonged cold temperatures plus deep snow" are the chief threat (80%, Demarchi thesis via research notes).
  • Ruffed grouse dive into soft snow to roost 80%. See Habitat tour: quail and grouse.
  • Upland daily patterns by terrain: Upland birds' daily pattern.

Read a forecast in 5 steps1 of 5
  • Wind first, always (Tip).
  • Write the plan the night before (Tip).
More: the 5 steps in full
  1. Wind: direction and speed for dawn, midday and dusk. Your whole approach depends on it (Tip). Thermals: up in the morning as the slope warms, down in the evening 80%.
  2. Temperature trend: falling 3 days in a row, or a warm spell? Warm: shade and the edges of the day. Cold: sunny faces in the morning (Tip).
  3. Rain or snow, and the freezing level or snow line. Fresh snow up high pushes mule deer down over days to weeks (85% for the trigger; timing varies).
  4. Front timing: if rain or snow hits at 10 am, glass hard from first light to 9:30, sit tight in cover during, and glass the first calm after (Tip).
  5. Spot A for the forecast wind, spot B for the other wind. Check both against closures and the Region 3 Rule Book before you go.
  6. The night before checklist lives in Weather, moon and what moves game.

More: how each row was built
  • Clear and cold: deer on sunny faces at dawn is hunter practice (Tip); dawn and dusk movement peaks are measured 75%.
  • Storm on: deer moved less during storms 80%. Lee slopes for wind shelter is a tip.
  • Geese flying all day in storms: Illinois study 70%.
  • First snow and freeze up: mule deer trigger 85% and duck freeze up 75%.
  • Ducks seeking calm water in wind is a waterfowler's tip, not a study result here (Tip).

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Grandpa's rule (wisdom): The front tells you where to sit, not whether to go. Go, then let the wind pick the seat.

Common mistakes
  • Staying home because the barometer "looks wrong".
  • Keeping the dawn seat after a front swung the wind.
  • Hunting high ground after the first big snow.
More: the mistakes explained
  • The barometer: weak and mixed evidence. Losing a free day to it costs more than any pressure effect found (Tip).
  • The wind swing: a front can turn a south wind into a northwest wind in minutes 70%. Your scent goes with it (Tip).
  • After snow up high, many mule deer start down toward winter range 85%. The high bench can go empty (Tip).

Do this in the field

Every trip: log wind, temperature trend, front timing and what moved. Compare at Christmas.

• "South wind before, northwest wind after, pressure low then higher." The front passes.
  • "Storm: still. Calm: fill." Deer moved less in storms 80%; glass the calm (Tip).
  • 30 and 50: snow trouble starts near 30 cm, deer leave near 50 cm 75%.
  • SCRaP: Snow and cold, Rut, and Pressure from hunters move deer most. "Pressure" here means people, not the barometer.
  • Ice is the eviction notice for ducks 75%.

  • Rodgers and others 2021, Sex specific behaviors of hunted mule deer during rifle season, Journal of Wildlife Management, abstract read directly 2026-10-11 85%.
  • Schummer and others 2010, weather related indices of dabbling duck abundance, abstract read 2026-10-11 75%.
  • Ducks Unlimited 2024 migration and wintering habitat update, BC section, via research notes 2026-10-03 75%.

• Raveling, Crews and Klimstra, Wilson Bulletin, Canada goose flights, search preview 2026-10-11 70%.
  • Minnesota DNR pheasant hunting tips, read directly 2026-10-11 (70% applied to BC).
  • USDA Fire Effects Information System, chukar, via research notes 2026-10-03 75%.
  • Goethlich thesis, Auburn University and Mossy Oak on the Oklahoma study, search previews 65%.
  • US Weather Prediction Center front definitions, search preview 2026-10-11 (70 to 80%).
