pressure-push:
Why it matters

Your first hunts are in October, with everyone else. Pressure is the one force you can predict on a map. Learn where people stop, and you will know where the deer went.

  • Most hunters stay within half a kilometre of a road (90%, Pennsylvania).
  • Hunted deer go thick, steep, far, or into the night (65 to 85%).
More: what this session covers
  • is people in the woods: trucks, quads, boots, voices, scent, shots.
  • This session: where hunters actually go (a measured study), what deer, mule deer and elk do about it (collar studies), where pushed game ends up, how to use other hunters, and how not to be the pressure yourself.
  • The short version is in Weather, moon and what moves game. This is the full version.
  • Most measured data comes from the United States. BC hunters face the same pattern on roaded Crown land (Tip: no BC collar study on hunter pressure was found for this session).

• 73% of hunters were within 0.5 km of a road 90%.
  • Each 1 km closer to a road: about 3 times more hunters 90%.
  • Average farthest point from a road: 0.84 km 90%.
More: the Pennsylvania study in full
  • Luloff and others, Penn State final report, August 2004: aerial counts of hunters on 45,907 ha of public forest, plus interviews (90%, read directly).
  • "Hunters on our study area were not distributed uniformly (73% were ≤ 0.5 km from a road)". 90%
  • Each kilometre closer to the nearest road made an area nearly 3 times more likely to be hunted; each 10 degrees flatter, 1.25 times 90%.
  • "The average maximum distance hunters reached from a road open to public vehicles was 0.84 km", and they walked an average of 5.48 km a day 90%.
  • Morning: 72% sat still. Afternoon: more walked and stalked 90%.
  • 16% of the area was over 1 km from a road; "there were substantial portions of the study area where little or no hunting occurred" 90%.
  • Applied to BC: an assumption. Assumption: BC hunters on Crown land behave like this. Check it with your own eyes on opening weekend.

• Trucks arrive. Hunters spread near the road (90% pattern).
  • Deer slide to thick, steep cover. Sit the trail between (Tip).
More: what the animation shows
  • The hunters stay close to the road: the measured pattern above 90%.
  • The buck walks up a trail to the timber: hunted deer select security cover away from motorized routes (85%, Wyoming mule deer bucks).
  • You sit the trail before first light: a tip. It works only if you get there first and the wind is right. See Wind and thermals.

• Move less, in smaller areas 65%.
  • Bucks go to security cover away from roads 85%.
  • More of their moving shifts into the dark 65%.
More: the deer studies
  • Oklahoma, 1,861 ha, controlled hunter numbers: deer "reduced movements and used smaller areas more intensively"; displacement ended about 3 times lower after the season than at the start (65%, Little and others 2016, Basic and Applied Ecology, search preview).
  • Same project: bucks recognized pressure quickly at both low (1 hunter per 250 acres, about 1 per 100 ha) and high (1 per 75 acres, about 1 per 30 ha) density and moved less (60%, popular summary).
  • Wyoming mule deer, GPS 2016 to 2018: "Males selected security habitat away from motorized routes during hunting season"; females stayed on better feed (85%, Rodgers and others 2021, abstract read directly).
  • Hunted deer shift activity to night and to thick cover; one study saw the shift within 48 hours of the opener (65 to 70%, search previews, see Weather, moon and what moves game).
  • Popular claim: bucks avoid a stand for about 3 days after it is hunted. One researcher's report, secondary source 50%. Treat it as a Tip.

• Hunting season, Oregon: mule deer 190 m from closed roads, 1,250 m from open ones 70%.
  • Closed roads are quieter. Walk them (Tip).
More: roads, traffic and the BC rules that help you
  • Curtis and Du Toit 2017, Wildlife Society Bulletin, Oregon forest, GPS collared mule deer, August to October 2015 (70%, Conservation Evidence summary). Site comparison: association, not proof.
  • Elk at the Starkey research site in Oregon: traffic as low as 1 vehicle every 12 hours changed where elk were (60%, review citing Starkey work).
  • Oregon elk used habitat within 500 m of open roads half as much as expected (60%, same review).
  • In BC Region 3, no ATV (All Terrain Vehicle) for hunting in MUs (Management Units) 3-28, 3-29 and 3-30 from 1 September to 10 December (99%, synopsis page 33). Hunters there walk from the truck. My lean: those quiet road ends are worth the walk (Tip).
  • Look for gated roads and roads shown as closed on the maps. Then walk them at first light (Tip). Check the Region 3 Rule Book first.

• Utah: elk on public land dropped from up to 64% to 29% in rifle season 80%.
  • They moved onto private land where hunting was limited 80%.
More: the elk studies
  • Sergeyev and others, Journal of Wildlife Management, reported by The Wildlife Society (March 2022): 445 GPS collared elk on about 43,000 km2 in central Utah, 2015 to 2017. "As soon as the hunt opens, they all move en masse onto private lands." 80%
  • When Utah opened private land hunting in 2016, public land use rose from 29% to 41% 80%.
  • Montana: elk used private land closed to hunting as refuges; limited hunting there cut both the share of the herd and the time spent (75%, Burcham, Edge and Marcum, Wildlife Society Bulletin, search preview).
  • Elk are few near Heffley Creek (85% for about 1,350 in the Thompson Okanagan in 2000). The pattern teaches you about deer too (Tip).
  • Private land is closed to you without permission. A refuge is a place to watch from the edge, never to cross. See Land status.

• Thick, steep, far, closed to hunting, or dark (Tip, built on the studies).
  • Your job: find the nearest refuge to the road crowd (Tip).
More: the four refuges near Heffley Creek (Tip)
  • Thick: north facing Douglas fir timber, dense draws with aspen and shrubs (Tip). Deer bed in hiding and thermal cover 80%.
  • Steep and far: the steep side of a draw, more than 1 km from the nearest open road (Tip, from the 0.84 km figure).
  • Closed to hunting or shooting: Sun Peaks within 400 m of lifts and runs (Map C11), City of Kamloops lands, private ranches (99% rules). Deer that live there can feed out onto Crown land at the edges (Tip).
  • Dark: if you only see deer at last light, they may be leaving a refuge. Back off and sit the edge earlier (Tip).
  • Rules for each: Local plan: Heffley Creek.

Find the pressure gap in 5 steps1 of 5
  • Do it on the map at home, then check it on foot (Tip).
More: the 5 steps in full
  1. On the Hunt Map, turn on Forest Service roads, motor vehicle closures and private land. Mark every road a truck can use (Tip).
  2. Shade about 1 km around each open road. In the Pennsylvania study, 73% of hunters were inside 0.5 km and the average farthest point was 0.84 km 90%.
  3. Beyond the shade, find steep slopes, dark timber or brushy draws (Tip). Contours close together mean steep: see Maps 1: reading terrain.
  4. Find the trail, saddle or draw that links the crowd to the refuge. That is your seat (Tip). See Trails and funnels.
  5. Arrive 30 minutes before legal light. Big game is legal from 1 hour before sunrise (99%, synopsis page 11). You want to be still before anyone else moves.
  6. Building the full map: Build your own hunting map.

• Opening morning: the crowd is your drive (Tip).
  • Sit still between the road and the timber (Tip).
More: how to use other hunters, safely and fairly
  • Many hunters still hunt and walk in the afternoon (90%, Pennsylvania). Deer that move away from them use trails (Tip).
  • Sit a seat with a safe backstop, never facing a road or another hunter's route (Tip). Wear orange where others hunt (Tip; see Firearm safety).
  • Do not crowd another hunter's seat. It is unlawful to "block or harass" a legal hunter (99%, synopsis page 12, item 45).
  • Midweek has less pressure. Hunt Tuesday to Thursday if you can (Tip).

• Every walk in leaves scent and noise (Tip).
  • Bumped a spot twice? Rest it (Tip).
More: keep your own pressure low (Tip)
  • Walk in on the downwind side, along the bottom, and never across the feeding area (Tip). See Moving quietly.
  • Same seat every morning: deer can learn it. Rotate 3 or 4 seats by wind (Tip).
  • Glass more, walk less. A glassing seat 600 m away puts no scent on the deer (Tip). See Glassing.
  • After a missed shot or a bump, note it in the Journal: wind, time, route. Patterns show up over a season (Tip).

Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

  • No ATV for hunting in 3-28, 3-29, 3-30, 1 September to 10 December 99%.
  • Never use a vehicle or boat to herd or harass wildlife 99%.
More: the rules in full
  • Page 33: "ATV for Hunting Closed Areas: from Sept 1 - Dec 10 in MUs 3-28, 3-29, 3-30, and that portion of MU 3-17 shown on Map C3." 99%
  • Page 11, item 25: unlawful "To use a power boat, aircraft, or motor vehicle or other mechanical device to herd or harass wildlife." 99% Driving at deer to push them is that offence (95%, my reading).
  • Page 12, item 45: do not block or harass a legal hunter or trapper 99%.
  • Page 33: all motor vehicles except snowmobiles banned above 1,700 m in Region 3 except on existing roads and trails 99%.
  • Full text: Region 3 Rule Book and It is unlawful.

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Grandpa's rule (wisdom): Walk past the last boot print, then sit where the boot prints push the deer.

Common mistakes
  • Hunting the first 500 m from the truck on opening day.
  • Calling it "no deer here" after one pressured weekend.
  • Walking the same route into the same seat every morning.
More: why each one hurts
  • The first 500 m is where 73% of hunters were 90%. Deer there have learned (Tip).
  • Hunted deer move less and shift to night 65%. They are still there, just not where the trucks are (Tip).
  • Same route, same scent, same time: you become the pattern (Tip).

Do this in the field

This week: on the map, find one spot over 1 km from any open road in MU 3-27. Find the trail to it. Walk it midweek with binoculars, no rifle.

• "Half a K holds the crowd." 73% within 0.5 km 90%.
  • "0.84": the average farthest a hunter got from the road 90%.
  • TSFD: Thick, Steep, Far, Dark. Where pushed deer go (Tip).
  • "Closed road, close deer": 190 m versus 1,250 m 70%.
  • 3 times per km: each kilometre nearer a road, about 3 times the hunters 90%.

• Luloff and others 2004, A Comparison of Hunter Movement, Activities and Opinions During Two Pennsylvania Hunting Seasons, Penn State final report, read directly 2026-10-11 90%.
  • Little and others 2016, Hunting intensity alters movement behaviour of white tailed deer, Basic and Applied Ecology, search preview 2026-10-11 65%.
  • Rodgers and others 2021, Sex specific behaviors of hunted mule deer during rifle season, abstract read directly 2026-10-11 85%.
  • Conservation Evidence: Curtis and Du Toit 2017, close roads in defined seasons, read directly 2026-10-11 70%.
  • The Wildlife Society: When hunters arrive, elk seek safer territory, read directly 2026-10-11 80%.

• Backcountry Hunters and Anglers literature review: roads and elk, search preview 2026-10-11 60%.
  • Montana elk private land refuges, Burcham, Edge and Marcum, search preview 75%.
  • BC Hunting and Trapping Regulations Synopsis 2026 to 2028, 2 October 2026 edition, pages 11, 12 and 33, as carried in the Rule Book 99%.
  • Tips and Grandpa's rule are opinion.
bc-migration-routes:
Why it matters

Your October hunts fall right in the fall move. Know who is leaving the high country, when, and by which road, and you hunt where the animals will be next week, not where they were last month.

  • Four patterns: long distance, up and down, short shifts, stay home.
  • October to November is moving month for mule deer and ducks (70 to 85%).
More: what this session covers and where the data lives
  • The overview is in How animals move through the year. This session is the route detail: numbers, timing, elevations and how to find a route yourself.
  • Every month and elevation here comes from the app's migration data file (data/migration.json, updated 2026-10-03) and its sources. Each species there carries its own certainty.
  • Strong data: mule deer (BC collar study), snow geese (Reifel sanctuary counts), moose snow limits (BC account).
  • Weak data: elk near your bases (few animals), ducks month by month in the Interior (no local counts), black tailed deer in the Fraser Valley (Vancouver Island data). Those lines say so.
  • The Hunt Map has month layers for mule deer, white tails, moose, elk and sheep (general pattern, 60%). Open it at #/map.

• 74% of collared deer migrated, about 47 km a year 85%.
  • Longest: 102 km in a straight line 85%.
More: the Southern Interior Mule Deer Project in full
  • BC Wildlife Federation project page: 30,000 km2 study; "74 per cent were migratory, travelling an average of 47.2 km per year" 85%.
  • Winter update, 11 March 2020: "78% of our deer migrated. Most deer moved to summer range April-May and returned to winter range in October-Nov. On average the collared deer migrated 55 kms" (85%, quoted with its hyphens).
  • Update, 13 November 2019: a doe collared near Apex Mountain, west of Penticton, left on 1 May and arrived west of Aspen Grove on 12 May, 102 km in a straight line 85%.
  • Same update: "By mid-October this year, nearly all the collared deer in each study area were back in their winter range." 85%
  • Study areas: West Okanagan, Cache Creek, Boundary. Cache Creek is the closest to Heffley Creek 85%.
  • Some deer stay low all year: residents (85%, BC deer account).

• "Most of the deer choose nearly the same path" both ways 85%.
  • Down in October and November, up in April and May 85%.
More: route facts and what they mean for you
  • Same path: SIMDeer winter update, 2020 85%. Strong home range fidelity year to year (85%, deer research notes).
  • Trigger for the fall move: snow and cold, not the rut (85%, Monteith and others 2011).
  • Wyoming collars: temperature and snowfall timed migration; hunting season barely changed it (85%, Rodgers and others 2021).
  • Older BC account: Interior deer "often remain at high elevations until December" (85% as written). It conflicts with the collar data. Use October to December as the window, earlier in deep snow years (75%, research notes reading).
  • A route crosses ridges, saddles and draws. Those are the funnels: see Trails and funnels.
  • My lean: in a mild October, hunt mid slope fir and burn edges; after the first real snow up high, drop to the winter range edges (Tip).

• Snow trouble near 30 cm, deer leave near 50 cm 75%.
  • Track the snow line every trip (Tip).
More: snow depth by species
  • Deer: "difficulty moving through snow deeper than 30 cm" (85%, BC deer account); leave slopes near 50 cm (80%, UBC (University of British Columbia) thesis).
  • Moose: "little or no difficulty" to 40 cm, "only slight difficulty" at 40 to 70 cm, and they "commonly winter in areas with 50 cm or more" (85%, BC moose account).
  • Elk "usually keep to regions where the snow remains shallow on winter ranges" (85%, BC elk account).
  • So the same snowfall moves deer first, elk next, moose last (75%, my reading of the three accounts).

• Shaded columns: your hunting months.
  • Mule deer and ducks are moving; moose are still high (70 to 85%).
More: the month detail from the data file
  • Mule deer: October "Fall migration: collared deer came back in October and November" 70%; November "Most deer on or near winter range. Rut in November and early December." 75%.
  • Elk: September rut, most cows bred mid to late September 70%; October "autumn snow pushes herds back toward winter range" 60%.
  • Moose: October rut early in the month; "Moose stay high longer than deer, elk or sheep" 70%; November slow drift down 65%.
  • Ducks: peak fall passage through the Interior in October; freeze up in late November ends most Interior migration (60 to 65%).
  • Snow geese: arrive on the Fraser delta by early October; best numbers mid October to mid December; shift to the Skagit late December (70 to 75%, Reifel).
  • Dusky grouse: moving uphill into dense conifers in September and October 60%.

• Mule deer drop from about 400 to 1,800 m in October to 300 to 1,100 m in December (70 to 75%).
  • These bands come from habitat zones, not collar data 65%.
More: the elevation bands and zone names
  • Mule deer: October 400 to 1,800 m (Ponderosa Pine, Interior Douglas fir, Montane Spruce zones); December 300 to 1,100 m (Bunchgrass, Ponderosa Pine, Interior Douglas fir) (70 to 75%).
  • Near Kamloops the studied winter range is below about 760 m (80%, Willms 1976).
  • Moose: October 800 to 1,900 m; December 400 to 1,600 m (65 to 70%).
  • Elk: October 600 to 2,000 m; December 0 to 1,200 m across BC including coast herds (55 to 60%).
  • White tails: about 300 to 1,000 m in October, 300 to 900 m in December, valley bottoms all year (60 to 65%).
  • Zone elevations: Meidinger and Pojar 1991, Ecosystems of BC (90% for the zone ranges; 65% when used as an animal's range).
  • Rough heights near your base: valley about 370 to 450 m, Heffley Lake about 950 m, Sun Peaks village about 1,250 m (55%, VERIFY on the Hunt Map elevation readout).

• White tails: short moves along or across valleys 85%.
  • Coast black tails: some migrate within a watershed, some stay 80%.
More: the details
  • White tails: "Seasonal movements are mostly upstream or downstream along the major valleys, or cross-valley from north-facing slopes in summer to south-facing sites in winter." (85% as written, Kootenay data; 65 to 70% for the Thompson). Quoted with the source's hyphens.
  • "Within areas that have a suitable climate, whitetails prefer valley bottoms with farmland." 85%
  • Near Heffley Creek: North Thompson hayfields and cottonwood bottoms (75%, local reading).
  • Black tails, coast: migrant annual range about 1,770 ha versus about 140 ha for residents (80%, Vancouver Island data). Winter below about 1,000 m in old forest 80%. Weak for the Fraser Valley (55 to 70%).

• Moose leave the high country last 85%.
  • Elk are few near Heffley Creek (85% for the 2000 count).
More: moose and elk in full
  • Moose in mountains "usually migrate between winter-spring ranges in valley bottoms and higher-elevation summer ranges, but some Moose remain in the valleys year-round" (85%, quoted with hyphens).
  • In autumn they "stay on high-elevation ranges much longer than Elk, deer, or mountain sheep" 85%.
  • Plateau moose winter "along river valleys that cut through the plateaus and in burns, logged areas, and wetland complexes" 85%.
  • Seasonal home range "seldom exceeds 5 to 10 km2" 85%.
  • Bonaparte Plateau, north of Kamloops: provincial moose research area since 2012 90%. No movement results were found in the report read.
  • Elk: Interior Rocky Mountain elk "tend to be more migratory"; "Autumn snowfalls push the Elk back to their traditional winter ranges" 85%. About 1,350 elk in the Thompson Okanagan in 2000 (85% for that date).

winter-range-legal:
Why it matters

In November the deer you want stand on winter range. Know what that land is, which rules cover it (and which do not), and how to hunt its edges without pushing deer that need every calorie.

Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

  • : low, steep, sunny slopes with shrubs and old fir 85%.
  • An official winter range order is a forestry rule, not a hunting closure (85%, my reading).
More: what this session covers
  • Part 1, the land: what winter range is, why old fir matters, where the official ones are near Heffley Creek.
  • Part 2, the law: four different rule books touch winter range. Only the hunting rules (seasons, closures, access) decide if you may hunt (85%, my reading).
  • Part 3, the hunt: how to hunt the edges in November without wasting deer energy.
  • Background: Food, water and cover, Migration routes in BC, Land status.

• Steep south and west faces, broken rock, shrubs, old Douglas fir 85%.
  • Near Kamloops the studied range is below about 760 m 80%.
More: the biology in full
  • BC deer account: Interior winter range is "shrublands in the dry forest zone and on steep south and west facing sites with broken terrain" 85%.
  • Snow decides it: deer have "difficulty moving through snow deeper than 30 cm" 85%. Sunny slopes melt first; broken rock and steep ground shed snow (75%, my reading).
  • Kamloops study (Willms 1976): Dewdrop range below 760 m north of Kamloops, and Jamieson Creek. Douglas fir in the diet peaked in December and January; shrubs early fall and late winter (80 to 85%).
  • Browse on Kamloops winter range: Douglas fir, saskatoon, Oregon grape, red osier dogwood, rose, bitterbrush, rabbitbrush, sagebrush 80%.
  • Aspect: south and west, old Douglas fir (85%, Armleder 1994 via research notes).
  • Moose winter "along river valleys that cut through the plateaus and in burns, logged areas, and wetland complexes" 85%.

• Big fir crowns catch snow; the ground below stays walkable 80%.
  • That is why winter range orders protect old fir (99% for the order wording).
More: why the cover matters
  • Order u-3-003 makes forest users keep enough "snow interception cover (SIC)" in each winter range planning cell (99%, order read directly).
  • Plain English: old, big crowned Douglas fir catches snow, so deer can walk and feed under it in deep snow years (80%, my reading of the BC deer account and the order).
  • Fir is also food: Kamloops deer ate the most Douglas fir in December and January 80%.
  • In the field: a south slope with scattered big fir and a shrub understory is the classic look (Tip).

• A UWR (Ungulate Winter Range) order covers logging and roads 99%.
  • Hunting is set by the Wildlife Act and its synopsis 99%.
More: who makes which rule
  • UWR: made under "sections 9 and 12 of the Government Actions Regulation" of the Forest and Range Practices Act (90%, BC Ministry of Environment UWR page, read directly).
  • A 2004 order lists the species a winter range may be made for: mule and black tailed deer, white tailed deer, elk, mountain goat, caribou, bighorn sheep, thinhorn sheep and moose (99%, order read directly, 6 May 2004).
  • Seasons, bag limits, closed areas and No Shooting areas: the BC Hunting and Trapping Regulations Synopsis, 2026 to 2028 99%.
  • WMAs (Wildlife Management Areas) and other conservation lands: "Before hunting in a Conservation Land, please contact your regional office." (99%, synopsis page 9)
  • Motor vehicle closures: synopsis maps by MU (Management Unit) 99%. See Where you can hunt.
  • So: a UWR on the map does not by itself close hunting (85%, my reading of the order and synopsis). Check the other three every time.

• Order u-3-003, Merritt TSA (Timber Supply Area), mule deer 99%.
  • Rules for timber harvest, silviculture and roads. Nothing on hunting 99%.
More: the order, read directly
  • "ORDER: UNGULATE WINTER RANGE #U-3-003, Merritt TSA, Mule Deer", given under "sections 9(2) and 12(1) of the Government Actions Regulation" 99%.
  • "Primary forest activity" means timber harvesting, silviculture treatments, and road construction, maintenance and deactivation 99%.
  • General Wildlife Measure 1: forest activities must not drop snow interception cover below the order's Table 1 amounts 99%.
  • Signed 21 January 2008 by the Deputy Minister of Environment 99%.
  • The order has no hunting, firearm or motor vehicle wording (99%, read all 2 text pages). Other orders may differ: read the one for your area (Tip).

• Around Heffley Creek: no approved UWR polygons 90%.
  • Nearest mule deer orders: u-3-003 south toward Merritt, u-8-001 North Okanagan side 90%.
More: the layer query and the Dewdrop WMA
  • Layer "Ungulate Winter Range, Approved", queried 2026-10-03 for a box around Kamloops and Heffley Creek (longitude 120.7 to 120.0 west, latitude 50.6 to 51.1 north): zero approved polygons 90%.
  • Mule deer orders nearby: u-3-003 (latitude 50.12 to 50.51, south of Kamloops toward Merritt and Logan Lake), u-8-001 (North Okanagan side) 90%.
  • Dewdrop Rosseau Creek WMA, north shore of Kamloops Lake, MU 3-29: "winter range for Mule Deer and California Bighorn Sheep" (90%, BC WMA page). Map C16: motor vehicles on open lines only, year round 99%.
  • Lac du Bois and Dewdrop: Map C15, vehicle access only on highlighted roads, year round 99%.
  • So near the base, use the habitat rule: south and west slopes, grassland and dry fir below about 1,000 m 75%.
  • On the Hunt Map: turn on the "Mule deer winter range" layer (95% for the layer itself). Open #/map.

• Season, closures, land owner, vehicles: in that order (Tip).
  • Then hunt on foot, quietly.
More: each question and its rule
  • Season: Region 3 mule deer in your MUs: any buck 1 to 31 October; 4 point bucks only 1 November to 10 December (99%, synopsis page 34). White tailed bucks 10 September to 10 December; antlerless white tails 10 to 31 October 99%.
  • No Shooting and closed areas: Map C7 Kamloops, C11 Sun Peaks, C12 McQueen Lake, C17 Tranquille; Kamloops city limits 99%. See Local plan: Heffley Creek.
  • Land owner: "A person is not permitted to hunt on cultivated land or on Crown land which is subject to a grazing lease while the land is occupied by livestock, without the consent of the owner, lessee, or occupant of the land." (99%, page 9) Leased land falls under the Trespass Act whether or not cattle are there 99%. Much Kamloops grassland is grazing lease (Tip: check before you walk it).
  • Reserves: "Indian Reserves are private land. Permission must be obtained" (99%, page 9).
  • Vehicles: ATV (All Terrain Vehicle) for hunting closed in 3-28, 3-29, 3-30, 1 September to 10 December; snowmobile for hunting closed in 3-28 from 1 April to 14 December 99%.

More: the exact words
Item 25, page 11

"To use a power boat, aircraft, or motor vehicle or other mechanical device to herd or harass wildlife."

  • A snowmobile or quad run at deer on winter range is that offence (95%, my reading).
  • No loaded firearm in or on a motor vehicle, and no shooting from one (99%, page 11).
  • After 10 December, Region 3 deer seasons in your MUs are closed (99%, page 34). Winter is for scouting from a distance (Tip).
  • Full list: It is unlawful.

• Disturbance makes deer burn energy and lose feeding time 70%.
  • Hunt the edges, take your shot, leave (Tip).
More: the fact sheets
  • Utah and Wyoming winter range fact sheet: human disturbance forces mule deer to use more energy and "can reduce their body condition to levels that influence survival or reproduction" (70%, search preview).
  • US Forest Service winter range page: deer that flee use reserves needed to get through winter (70%, search preview).
  • Wyoming: as few as 2 to 6 vehicle passes a day displaced mule deer on average 2.61 km (60%, Sawyer and others 2009 as summarized by Backcountry Hunters and Anglers).
  • Some studies found mule deer hide in cover rather than run, which still costs feeding time (60%, Wisdom and others 2004 via the same summary).
  • The fat bar in the animation is an illustration, not a measurement.

• Dogs strongest, then machines, then people off trail 70%.
  • Leave the dog home on winter range (Tip).
More: details
  • Fact sheets: ATVs and mountain bikes cause a stronger flight response than hiking or horseback riding; off trail use causes more avoidance than on trail; dogs increase stress (70%, agency fact sheets, search previews).
  • Dogs in some WMAs must be leashed unless lawfully hunting (99%, WMA Use and Access Regulation, research notes). Check the WMA's own rules.

Hunt a winter range edge in 5 steps1 of 5
  • Glass, do not walk the range (Tip).
More: the 5 steps in full
  1. Hunt Map: winter range layers, MU lines, closures, private land and WMAs (95% for the layers).
  2. Season and class for today: from 1 November a Region 3 mule deer buck needs 4 points on one antler (99%, page 34). Count before you shoot: see Legal to shoot.
  3. Park at an open road. No ATV for hunting in 3-28, 3-29, 3-30 until 10 December 99%.
  4. Glass the edge where timber meets open slope at first and last light, from 400 to 800 m across a draw (Tip). See Glassing.
  5. One clean shot within your range, or back out the way you came. Do not push the same deer twice (Tip).

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Grandpa's rule (wisdom): Winter range is a pantry. Take what the law allows, then close the door behind you.

Common mistakes
  • Thinking a winter range layer means "no hunting".
  • Walking a grazing lease with cattle on it without asking.
  • Driving roads on winter range to spot deer, then chasing them.
More: why each one hurts
  • UWR orders set forestry rules (99% for the order read). Hunting is set by the synopsis 99%.
  • Grazing lease with livestock: consent needed (99%, page 9).
  • Chasing with a vehicle is item 25 99%. Repeat flights cost deer fat 70%.

Do this in the field

This month: open the Hunt Map, turn on the winter range and closure layers, and find one south facing slope under 1,000 m within 45 minutes of the base. Glass it at dusk from across the draw.

waterfowl-daily-flights:
Why it matters

Ducks and geese keep a timetable. Learn where they sleep, where they eat and when they commute, and you can be under the flight line instead of guessing at a pond.

  • Dabblers often feed at night and rest by day 65%.
  • Geese: fields at dawn and late afternoon, water at midday 70%.
  • Legal duck hours: half an hour before sunrise to half an hour after sunset 99%.
More: what this session covers
  • The four parts of a waterfowl day: roost, feed, loaf, commute. Then how wind, storms and cold change it, how to scout the spot, and the rules on the water.
  • Species ID, calls and decoys: Ducks, Geese, Your first duck hunt.
  • Places: Habitat tour: ducks and Local plan: Heffley Creek.
  • Most daily flight studies are from the United States and Europe. BC birds use the same rhythm on different water (Tip: watch your own birds).

• Ducks commute between a safe roost and a feeding area (65 to 85%).
  • Louisiana mallards: 3.1 to 15 km between day and night sites 85%.
More: the commute in full
  • Dutch GPS (Global Positioning System) mallards made "regular commuting flights at dusk and dawn between a fixed day roost and one or several fixed nocturnal foraging sites", visiting 2 to 4 feeding areas a night (65%, search preview).
  • Louisiana: 126 radio tagged female mallards, 2,455 paired day and night locations, 2004 to 2006. Moves between day and night sites ranged from 3.1 to 15.0 km by land type (85%, Link and others 2011, Waterbirds, abstract read directly).
  • Distances were longer from some refuges as the season went on (85%, same).
  • Flights got longer when fresh water was scarce and as temperatures fell toward 0 °C (65%, Dutch study, search preview).
  • Roost: calm, safe water with little disturbance (Tip). Loafing: sunny, sheltered shore, sandbars, logs (Tip).

• Missouri mallards: about 3 km a day on average, most under 13 km 65%.
  • So the field they feed in is usually within sight of a map's reach (Tip).
More: details
  • Ducks Unlimited satellite tracking, Missouri and Mississippi corridors: "local movements of satellite-marked mallards averaged only about two miles, and most were less than eight miles" (65%, quoted with its hyphen).
  • On your phone map, draw a 15 km circle around a roost lake. The feeding fields are almost certainly inside it (Tip, based on the 3 to 15 km range).
  • Canada geese: roost on a big lake, feed on crop and pasture land nearby (70%, Illinois study).

• Morning flight to fields, back to water, out again late afternoon 70%.
  • Stormy days: flights all day 70%.
More: the goose study and BC places
  • Crab Orchard refuge, Illinois, about 40,000 geese, two winters: geese "usually fly to feeding areas in the early morning and late afternoons but undertake increased flight activity throughout the day when it is stormy" (70%, Raveling, Crews and Klimstra, Wilson Bulletin, search preview).
  • Fraser Valley: Bert Brink WMA (Wildlife Management Area) "open fields are partly flooded in the winter and attract foraging wigeon and Canada geese" (90%, BC WMA page). Its hunting status: VERIFY with the regional office.
  • Thompson: Tranquille is goose and swan staging, and a No Shooting area 90%.
  • Canada and cackling geese, Region 3: 1 October to 23 December, 10 a day (99%, synopsis page 34).
  • Field hunting needs the landowner's yes. Cultivated land: consent always (99%, page 9).

More: landing and decoy setup

  • Ducks Unlimited: choose a blind so the wind blows from your back, directly or quartering 70%.
  • Put decoys where you do not want birds to land; leave an open hole. About 20 yards (18 m) out is a common landing zone advice (65%, Ducks Unlimited Source).

More: why it works and when it does not
  • A bird landing into the wind slows down and drops; with the wind at your back, that drop happens in front of you (70%, landing into wind; Tip, the shot angle).
  • Quartering wind (from behind one shoulder) also works: birds slide across in front (65%, Ducks Unlimited).
  • Wind straight in your face: birds finish behind you or land short. Move the blind or the spread (Tip).
  • Safety: never swing on a bird past your hunting partner. Agree on zones of fire first: see .

  4. Arrive in the dark. Be set and still 30 minutes before legal light (Tip). Wind at your back 70%.
  5. Shooting a roost every day drives the birds off (Tip). Hunt it every few days at most.

upland-daily-pattern:
Why it matters

A covey at 8 am and the same covey at 1 pm are in different places. Learn each bird's clock and its ground, and you walk where the birds are now.

  • Feed early and late, hide midday, roost at dusk: the common pattern 75%.
  • Each bird does it on different ground (75 to 85%).
More: what this session covers
  • Four birds you will hunt: California quail (South Okanagan), chukar (Thompson and Okanagan rock), ruffed grouse (aspen and creeks near Heffley Creek), dusky and spruce grouse (higher forest). Pheasant as a bonus (Okanagan).
  • ID and limits: Grouse, Quail, chukar, partridge and pheasant. Places: Habitat tour: quail and grouse.
  • Daily timings are patterns from agency and research sources, mostly outside BC (65 to 75%). Your own Journal will beat them within one season (Tip).

• Seldom more than 15 to 30 m from cover to feed 75%.
  • Roost in dense trees or shrubs 75%. Need water in hot weather 75%.
More: California quail in full
  • California Department of Fish and Wildlife life history (Ahlborn), read directly: "Yearlong, diurnal activity." "Seldom ventures more than 15-30 m (50-100 ft) from cover to feed." Brush and trees "provide cover for feeding, escape, movement, and roosting." (75%, quoted with its hyphens)
  • Water: "In hot weather, requires free water daily." "Gathers near water in dry weather, and disperses when green vegetation and water are abundant." 75%
  • Home range: winter coveys averaged 10.5 ha (6.9 to 18 ha); "Not migratory" 75%.
  • BC: Okanagan and Kettle valleys; below 750 m, most at 250 to 500 m; Ponderosa Pine and Bunchgrass zones (85%, BC Breeding Bird Atlas).
  • Most valley bottom quail ground is private or reserve land: ask first 75%. See Local plan: Okanagan.

build-hunting-map:
Why it matters

Everything in Reading the Land ends up on one map: the law, the roads, the pressure, the habitat, the terrain, the wind and your own sign. Build it once, keep it alive, and every trip starts with a plan.

  • Six layers, bottom up: law first, your sign last (Tip).
  • Use the app's Hunt Map at #/map, plus the Rule Book.
More: what this session covers
  • A method, not a single map: the same 6 layers work for Heffley Creek deer, Okanagan quail or a Fraser Valley slough.
  • Tools: the Hunt Map in this app (layers, waypoints, lines, areas, range rings, scent cone, elevation profile, slope and aspect shading, offline areas), iMapBC from the BC government, the Rule Book, and your Journal.
  • Each layer links back to the session that teaches it.
  • Start small: one area you can walk across in a morning, about 2 to 5 km2 (Tip).
  • Next session puts it to work: Field drill: read a piece of land.

• Each layer answers one question (Tip).
  • Can I? Can I get there? Will they be there? How do I come in?
More: the questions each layer answers
  1. Legal base: can I hunt here at all? (MU, land status)
  2. Closures: can I shoot here, and where can I not drive?
  3. Access and pressure: how do I get in, and where will other hunters be?
  4. Habitat and season: will the animal be here this month?
  5. Terrain and wind: where exactly, and from which side do I come in?
  6. Your sign and seats: what did I actually see, and where do I sit?

• Hunt Map for building; Rule Book for checking; Journal for truth (Tip).
  • Download the area offline before you go (Tip).
More: the tools in full
  • Hunt Map layers in this app include: private land, parks, reserves, city and town limits, WMAs (Wildlife Management Areas), MUs (Management Units), LEH (Limited Entry Hunting) zones, motor vehicle closures, Forest Service roads, recreation sites and trails, winter range by species, burns by year, cutblocks by age, wetlands, habitat zones, month layers for big game, duck waters, quail habitat, candidate spots, routes and camps. Each shows its source, data date and certainty (90 to 95% for official layers, 60% for pattern layers).
  • Hunt Map tools: waypoints with hunting icons (parking, glassing point, bed, rub, stand and more), lines with distance and climb, areas in hectares, range rings at 100, 200 and 300 m, scent cone from the forecast wind (Tip), elevation profile, slope and aspect shading, legal light and moon at a point, GPX and KML import and export, offline areas.
  • iMapBC: the BC government map viewer for land status and official layers 90%.
  • No Shooting maps (C7, C11, C12, C17 and others) live in the synopsis and the Region 3 Rule Book. Draw them on your map yourself (Tip).

Build the map in 6 layers1 of 6
  • Layer 1: which MU, and whose land (99% rules).
  • Near the base, the North Thompson is the MU line: 3-27 east, 3-28 west (85 to 90%).
More: layer 1 in full
  • Turn on Management Units and their numbers, then private land, parks, reserves, city limits and WMAs.
  • Your MU sets your season and class: see Local plan: Heffley Creek. In October any mule deer buck is legal in your MUs; from 1 November a buck needs 4 points (99%, synopsis page 34).
  • River rule: where a river is an MU line, the line follows the right bank as you face downstream (98%, Management Unit Regulation). At Heffley Creek the water is in 3-27 (80%, interpretation).
  • Private land: no hunting without permission. Cultivated land and grazing leases with livestock need consent (99%, page 9). "Indian Reserves are private land." (99%, page 9)
  • Parks: some allow hunting in season (Lac du Bois outside the city line, Roche Lake, Bonaparte), some do not (Paul Lake: treat as closed) (95 to 99%).
  • Conservation lands and WMAs: "Before hunting in a Conservation Land, please contact your regional office." (99%, page 9)

• Draw the No Shooting maps and a 100 m ring round every house and barn 99%.
  • Mark motor vehicle closures 99%.
More: layer 2 in full
  • No hunting or shooting within 100 m of a dwelling, or a farm or ranch building occupied by people or animals (99%, page 10). The Hunt Map range rings (100 m) make this quick (Tip).
  • Not within 15 m of the centre of a numbered highway or 2 lane public road (99%, page 10).
  • Near the base: Kamloops city limits (no firearm discharge at all), Map C7 Kamloops band, Map C11 Sun Peaks (400 m from lifts, runs and facilities), Map C12 McQueen Lake (1 km), Map C17 Tranquille 99%.
  • Motor vehicle closures: Map C15 Lac du Bois and Dewdrop, Map C16 Dewdrop Rosseau Creek WMA, Map C13 Skull Mountain 99%. ATV (All Terrain Vehicle) for hunting closed in 3-28, 3-29, 3-30 from 1 September to 10 December 99%.
  • Paint all of it the same "no go" colour (Tip).

• Mark every open road, gate and parking spot (Tip).
  • Shade about 1 km around open roads: that is where most hunters are 90%.
More: layer 3 in full
  • Forest Service roads and recreation sites from the Hunt Map; check closures and road notices before each trip (99% for the need to check; see the Local plan for links).
  • Pressure band: 73% of hunters within 0.5 km of a road, average farthest 0.84 km (90%, Pennsylvania). See Hunting pressure.
  • Route in and route out: draw them as lines, and check the climb with the elevation profile (Tip).
  • Parking: wide pullouts, never a blind corner (Tip).

• Winter range, burns, cutblocks, wetlands, water (95% layers).
  • Then the month: where will they be this week? (60 to 85%)

  • Mule deer in October: mid slope fir and burn edges if mild; lower south and west slopes after the first real snow (75 to 85%). See Migration routes in BC and Winter ranges.
  • Burns and cutblocks by age: a south facing burn or cutblock with 5 to 15 years of regrowth is a classic deer glassing target (Tip).
  • Water in a dry fall, and edges where food meets cover: see Food, water and cover.
  • Ducks: plateau ponds until freeze up, then valley water 75%. Upland: aspen and creek bottoms for ruffed grouse, rock for chukar (75 to 85%).

  • Thermals: up in the morning, down in the evening 80%.

  • Turn on aspect shading: south and west faces warm first and hold winter range (85% for winter range aspect).
  • Turn on slope shading: steep, broken ground is where pushed deer and chukar go (Tip).
  • Mark benches, saddles and draws: the funnels deer travel. See Maps 1: reading terrain and Trails and funnels.
  • For each glassing point, write the wind it needs. Morning: glass from above; evening: from below or across (Tip). See Wind and thermals.
  • Scent cone tool: shows where your scent goes with the forecast wind. A guide, not a promise: valley winds swirl (Tip).

  • Two seats per area: one for each common wind (Tip).

  • Waypoint icons: glassing point, bed, rub, stand, parking and more. Add the date and a note (Tip).
  • Range rings from a seat: 100, 200 and 300 m (109, 219, 328 yd). Know your distances before an animal shows up (Tip).
  • Sign tells you more than any layer. Fresh sign moves your seat (Tip). See Reading sign.
  • Rules for gadgets: no drone on the trip, and no drone information from less than 6 hours before it (99%, page 11, item 36). No wireless (cell) trail camera for hunting from 1 August to 10 December outside Region 1 (99%, item 30). No hunting on location info from an aircraft (99%, item 34).

• Red: no go. Tan: pressure. Green: habitat. Pins: your sign (Tip).
  • This example is a made up area.
More: how to read the example
  • The glassing point sits across from the south facing burn, with a note: "AM: N wind". Assumption in the example: a north wind carries your scent away from the burn.
  • The trail from the burn to the road has two fresh sign pins: the route is in use.
  • The private block is painted no go, so the deer that feed there are hunted only where they cross onto Crown land, and only with a safe backstop (Tip).
  • Park well away from the trail so your truck and scent stay off it (Tip).

• Check it the night before; update it the night after (Tip).
  • 1 November changes the mule deer class in Region 3 99%.
More: what changes during your season
  • 1 November: mule deer bucks need 4 points in your MUs 99%.
  • Road closures and fire restrictions change during the fall: check the Thompson Rivers road safety page and BC Wildfire Service (99% for the need; see Local plan).

Grandpa's rule (wisdom): A good map is half law, half dirt. Draw the law at home and the dirt with your boots.

  • Trusting the month layer over fresh sign.
  • Never updating the map after a trip.

  • Month layers are a general pattern 60%. Fresh tracks are today (Tip).
  • An old map leads you to last month's deer (Tip).

This week: build all 6 layers for one area of MU 3-27 within 45 minutes of the base. Then walk it once and add 10 pins.

land-drill-heffley:
Why it matters

Reading land is a skill you only learn by doing. This drill walks you through one full day, stop by stop, with a question at each stop. Do it on paper first, then on the ground.

Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

  • Six stops: park, walk in, glass, read sign, sit, walk out.
  • The terrain in the pictures is made up. The place and the rules are real.
More: how the drill works and what is real
  • Real: Heffley Creek, MU (Management Unit) 3-27, the Sullivan Lake (Knouff) recreation site, Sun Peaks, Paul Lake, the season dates, the closures and the times of day. Each carries its source and certainty.
  • Made up: the ridge, bench, draw, private block, deer and sign in the pictures. They are a practice scenario. On the real ground, use the Hunt Map to see what is actually there.
  • Assumption: the drill day is Saturday 24 October 2026 and the forecast is clear, cold and a light north wind. That forecast is invented for practice.
  • Where: Crown land near a recreation site that lists hunting as an activity, in MU 3-27. The Sullivan Lake (Knouff) site, location "Heffley", is one such site (90%, BC recreation site data layer, via research notes). Check land status around it before you go: VERIFY.
  • The skills come from earlier sessions: Build your own hunting map, Glassing, Tracks, Reading sign, Wind and thermals.

• Legal deer hunting about 6:37 to 18:52 on 24 October (85% times, 99% rule).
  • Glass early, read sign mid morning, sit late (Tip).
More: the times and the moon
  • Heffley Creek, 24 October 2026: sunrise about 7:37, sunset about 17:52, Pacific Daylight Time (85%, my calculation with the NOAA solar method; check the NRC calculator).
  • Big game: from 1 hour before sunrise to 1 hour after sunset (99%, synopsis page 11). So about 6:37 to 18:52.
  • Moon: full moon falls about 26 October 2026 (70%, my calculation, about a day either way). It barely matters for deer movement: see Moon and daylight.
  • Deer pattern: Penn State October collars moved most at dawn and dusk, 120 to 140 m an hour 75%. The bedded block midday is a tip.
• Do each stop in order. Answer the question before you open the answer.
The drill in 6 steps1 of 6

• Question: what is legal in MU 3-27 on 24 October?
  • Question: where can you not shoot near here?
More: the answers
  • Mule deer: any buck, 1 to 31 October, in 3-12 to 3-20, 3-26 to 3-44 and 3-46 (99%, synopsis page 34). One mule deer a year, Regions 3 to 8 combined 99%.
  • White tailed deer: bucks 10 September to 10 December; antlerless 10 to 31 October 99%.
  • Grouse (dusky, ruffed, spruce): 10 September to 30 November, 5 of each, 10 in total a day 99%. Black bear: 1 September to 30 November, with a bear species licence 99%.
  • No shooting: City of Kamloops (no firearm discharge at all), Map C11 Sun Peaks (400 m from any lift, run, facility or development), Map C7 Kamloops band 99%. Paul Lake Park lists no hunting: treat as closed 95%.
  • Recreation sites: no firearm "on or into the developed portion", which is the structures plus a 100 m buffer (99%, Forest Recreation Regulation s. 11, via research notes). No game offal, hides or bones in the developed portion (99%, s. 10).
  • 100 m from any lived in house or occupied barn; 15 m from the centre of a 2 lane public road (99%, page 10).
  • Score: 4 points if you got all of these before opening the answer.

• Question: where do you park, and when do you load the rifle?
More: the answers
  • Park in a wide pullout or a signed parking area, never on a blind corner or blocking a gate (Tip).
  • Not inside the developed part of the recreation site if you will shoot nearby: walk well past its 100 m buffer before you load (99% rule; Tip for where you load).
  • Load only at legal light and only once you are walking in to hunt (Tip). No loaded firearm in or on a vehicle (99%, page 11).
  • Walk in on the downwind side of where you expect deer (Tip). With a north wind, that is the south side.
  • A headlamp to walk in before light: point it at your feet and switch it off before you start looking. Using any light to hunt is unlawful (99%, page 11, item 38). Whether walking in with one is an issue: VERIFY with the Conservation Officer Service.

• Question: how many deer can you find? Which is the buck?
  • Grid it in 3 strips. Take 3 minutes before you open the answer.
More: the answer
  • Three deer (made up picture):
    • One at the timber edge, top centre, just leaving the open slope (antlers not visible).
    • One bedded under the tree on the right: a body shape and an ear, no legs showing.
    • One standing by a shrub, lower left, with antlers: the buck.
  • Real glassing: look for parts, not whole deer: an ear, a leg, a flicking tail, the white rump, a horizontal line in vertical timber (Tip). See Glassing.
  • Order: the app shows near first and far first as two options; pick one and stick to it (Tip).
  • Score: 1 point per deer found, 3 maximum.

• Question: who made it, which way did it go, how old is it?
  • Question: what does the rub add?
More: the answers
  • A: a deer track line. The pointed tips lead, so the deer went up and to the right, toward the timber (85% for direction rule). Edges crisp in cold ground can last days, so do not over age it 65%.
  • B: shiny pellets: fresh, likely hours, not days (Tip; see Reading sign).
  • C: a fresh rub: a buck has been here (85% that rubs are made by bucks). Mule deer rub less than white tails 60%.
  • Story (Tip): a buck fed on the bench at night and walked up into the timber at dawn to bed. He may come back down at last light.
  • Score: 4 points if you told the who, which way, how old and the story.

• North wind blows down from the ridge; the morning thermal rises up the slope.
  • Question: route A from below, or route B from the side?
More: the answer
  • Morning thermals rise as the slope warms; evening thermals sink 80%.
  • Here the forecast wind (from the north, downhill) and the morning thermal (uphill) fight. Near the ground the thermal can win on a sunny slope (Tip).
  • Route B, across the slope from the side, keeps your scent off the bench either way (Tip). Check with a puff bottle every 100 m.
  • For the evening sit, the thermal sinks: sit below or across from the bench, with the bench above and upwind of you (Tip).
  • Range: use the Hunt Map range rings from your seat. Know 100, 200 and 300 m marks before you sit (Tip).
  • Score: 4 points for route B and a sound evening plan.

• Leave the way you came, quietly. Write the Journal the same night (Tip).
  • Add your total. 16 or more: you are reading land (Tip).
More: the debrief
  • Journal: date, place, weather, wind by hour, every animal with the time, every sign with a pin, what you would do differently (Tip). See Hunt journal guide.
  • Update map layer 6 with the pins (Tip).
  • Score 5 points for a full Journal entry the same night.

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Grandpa's rule (wisdom): Walk the land once with no rifle. You will see twice as much when you are not busy wanting to shoot.

Common mistakes
  • Skipping the night before checks because "it is close to home".
  • Walking straight up the slope at the bench with the morning thermal rising.
  • Leaving the Journal until next week.
More: why each one hurts
  • Close to home is where the city line and the Sun Peaks map sit (99% rules).
  • Morning thermals carry scent uphill 80%.
  • Memory fades fast. A same night entry is worth ten later ones (Tip).

Do this in the field

Before your first hunt: do this drill for real, without a rifle, in MU 3-27 on Crown land you have checked. Score yourself honestly.

moon-and-daylight:
Why it matters

The moon gets blamed for empty days. Daylight is what really runs the deer year, and the clock of legal light runs your hunt. Spend your planning on the right one.

  • Moon effect: about 4 to 6 m an hour. Dawn and dusk: 120 to 140 m an hour 75%.
  • Time of day beats moon phase by a mile (Tip, on the data).
More: what this session covers
  • Part 1: the moon. What collar studies found, and what nobody has tested.
  • Part 2: daylight. How shortening days set the antler cycle and the rut, and how fast your hunting day shrinks in October and November.
  • Part 3: legal light. The only light rule that is the law.
  • Short version: Weather, moon and what moves game.

• Mississippi bucks: moon effect about 4 m an hour, inside GPS error 75%.
  • Penn State does: about 6 m an hour more at new moon than full moon 75%.
More: the moon studies in full
  • Mississippi State University Deer Lab, 48 GPS (Global Positioning System) collared bucks, September to February: moon effects of about 4 m (4 yd) an hour, within the collar error. "The moon has no effect on buck movement." (75%, read through a MeatEater article)
  • Same data: buck travel nearly doubled in the rut 75%. Rut beats moon.
  • Penn State Deer Forest blog, 9 August 2017: adult does on three state forests, October 2015 and 2016. Deer were about 6 m an hour more active at new moon than full moon; the author calls it neither statistically nor biologically meaningful (75%, read directly).
  • A 2016 paper in the Journal of the Southeastern Association of Fish and Wildlife Agencies: peer reviewed work has "failed to document any association between lunar phase and white-tailed deer activity" (65%, search preview, quoted with its hyphen).
  • A review found only four peer reviewed papers on big game and moon phase, all on white tailed deer (60%, search preview).
  • One North Carolina State study reported a dawn movement peak around the new moon (55%, search preview). Treat it as a Tip until you can read it.
  • No mule deer or elk moon study was found for this session (VERIFY if you find one).

• Dawn and dusk: the real peaks 75%.
  • Midday under 50 m an hour; night about 60 m an hour 75%.
More: the Penn State hourly numbers
  • October does: about 60 m an hour at night, under 50 m an hour in daylight, rising to 120 to 140 m an hour at dawn and dusk; single hours ranged from 0 to 2,748 m (75%, read directly).
  • An Oregon study of mule deer and elk found activity peaks at about 4 to 9 am and 5 to 9 pm (85%, Stewart 2002, via deer research notes).
  • So: be on a glassing point at first light whatever the moon (Tip).

• Longer spring days: melatonin falls, antlers grow 80%.
  • Shorter fall days set the breeding season (70 to 80%).
More: photoperiod in full
  • University of Georgia extension: "In whitetail deer, the increase in photoperiod length causes a decline in melatonin levels." "As melatonin decreases, antler growth is initiated." Then testosterone rises and "The velvet is sloughed off". "Shortly after whitetail breeding season, testosterone levels begin to decline in bucks." (80%, read directly)
  • Mississippi State Deer Lab: white tailed deer are "short-day breeders"; the rut builds as days shorten (65%, via a hunting site summary, quoted with its hyphen).
  • Weather changes how hard the rut shows, not when it starts (60%, extension style summary). Tip: the rut window in an area is about the same each year.
  • Mule deer rut in BC: November and early December (85%, BC deer account); peak mid November 80%.
  • See The rut.

• Full moons about 26 October, 24 November, 24 December 70%.
  • The rut window does not follow them (Tip, on the photoperiod evidence).
More: how the dates were made
  • New and full moon dates: my calculation from the mean lunar cycle (29.53 days from the new moon of 6 January 2000), about a day either way 70%. The Hunt Map's Insights panel shows today's phase with the same method.
  • Mule deer rut mid November to mid December 80%.
  • So in 2026 the rut overlaps a full moon around 24 November. Hunt it anyway: the rut nearly doubled buck travel in the Mississippi data 75%.

• 11.7 hours on 1 October; 9.8 hours on 31 October 85%.
  • About 3.8 minutes less light every day in mid October 85%.
More: the numbers and what they mean
  • Heffley Creek (50.86 N, 120.27 W): 1 October 11.7 h, 15 October 10.8 h, 31 October 9.8 h, 30 November 8.3 h, 21 December 7.9 h (85%, my calculation with the NOAA solar method).
  • Less light means less time to glass, stalk, gut and pack out. Plan the pack out before the shot (Tip). See Packing out.
  • Cold mornings come with the short days. Dress for the 2 hours you sit still at dawn (Tip). See What to wear.

Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

  • Game: 1 hour before sunrise to 1 hour after sunset 99%.
  • Migratory birds: 30 minutes before sunrise to 30 minutes after sunset 99%.
More: the rule, the clock change and the calculator
Items 37 and 38, page 11

"To hunt migratory game birds from 1/2 hour after sunset to 1/2 hour before sunrise."

"To hunt game, except migratory game birds from one hour after sunset to one hour before sunrise."

  • The moon changes nothing: no hunting outside these hours, and no light of any kind to hunt by (99%, page 11, items 37 and 38).
  • Sunrise and sunset: the synopsis names the National Research Council calculator or a local newspaper 99%.
  • BC no longer changes clocks: the 8 March 2026 spring forward was the last change, so there is no fall back on 1 November 2026 (95%, BC government news release, 2 March 2026). Legal hours follow the sun, not the clock.
  • Heffley Creek windows (my calculation, 85%): 15 October 6:22 to 19:11; 31 October 6:49 to 18:39; 1 November 6:51 to 18:38; 30 November 7:39 to 18:00 (no clock change). Ducks: 30 minutes less at each end.

Plan the day in 4 steps1 of 4
  • Legal light is not always enough light to identify (Tip).
More: why each step
  1. Legal times change daily; write them on your hand or the Journal (99% rule).
  2. Moving in the dark spooks less than moving at first light (Tip).
  3. Dawn is the movement peak 75%.
  4. Before every shot: positive ID, target, what is beyond. If you cannot see it clearly, do not shoot (Tip; see Firearm safety). Legal light ending does not change that.

• Many ducks feed at night anyway; species differ 65%.
  • No study found that isolates the full moon for ducks (VERIFY).
More: the bird evidence
  • Ducks Unlimited: research shows "a variety of nocturnal feeding behaviors in ducks"; some species feed mostly after dark, others do not (65%, search preview).
  • Hunter belief: ducks feed all night under a full moon and fly late in the morning. No controlled study found for this session (Tip, VERIFY).
  • Upland birds are active in daylight: California quail have "yearlong, diurnal activity" 75%.
  • See Waterfowl daily flights.

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Grandpa's rule (wisdom): The moon is for poems. The sun is for hunting. Know when it rises, and be sitting when it does.

Common mistakes
  • Skipping a free weekend for a full moon.
  • Guessing legal light from how bright the morning looks.
  • Planning a long stalk at 4 pm in late November.
More: why each one hurts
  • The measured moon effect is about 4 to 6 m an hour 75%. A free weekend is worth more (Tip).
  • A bright moon does not move legal light 99%.
  • On 30 November the day is about 8.3 hours long and legal light ends at about 17:00 85%. Leave time to recover the animal (Tip).

Do this in the field

All season: log the moon phase and the first and last time you saw deer each day. In January, check if the moon made any difference to your own sightings.

  • "One for deer, half for ducks": hours before sunrise 99%.
  • "Lose 4 minutes a day in October." 85%
  • "Sun clock, not moon clock."

land-in-weather:
Why it matters

Your October days will not all be dry and calm. Rain dates tracks, wind shows you shelter, snow shows you everything. Bad weather is a reading lesson if you dress for it.

  • Rain dates tracks. Wind shows shelter. Snow shows everything (Tip, on the tracking rules).
  • Dress for it first: cold and wet is the real danger 75%.
More: what this session covers
  • How each kind of weather changes what you can read on the ground, where animals go, and how you move.
  • The weather science (fronts, storms, temperature) is in Weather fronts and game movement. This session is the boots on the ground side.
  • Tracking basics: Tracks, Snow tracking.
  • Safety: Bush safety and What to wear.

• Rain pits inside a track: made before the rain 70%.
  • Clean track on spattered ground: made after it 70%.
More: rain and tracks in full
  • "Rain pits inside the print mean it was made before the rain. A clean print on rain spattered ground is after the rain." (70%, Tracks session)
  • So the time the rain stopped is your clock. Check the overnight record or ask your brother what time it quit (Tip).
  • Mud after rain: fresh prints have shiny wet walls (Tip). Soft ground also shows prints that dry ground hides (Tip).
  • Blood trails wash out in heavy rain: if you hit an animal and rain is coming, follow up sooner rather than later, within the rules in Blood trailing (Tip).

• Deer moved less during storms 80%. Bucks moved less in rain than does 65%.
  • Rain softens your steps and leaves (Tip).
More: details
  • Penn State: collared does moved less during storms 80%; preliminary notes: bucks moved less in rain than does 65%.
  • Light rain: wet leaves and grass are quieter underfoot. A good still hunting day (Tip). See Moving quietly.
  • Scent: hunters say rain knocks scent down and humid air carries it close to the ground. No study found for this session (Tip).
  • Optics fog and rain spots blur glass: keep lens caps on and a soft cloth in a dry pocket (Tip).
  • After a long rain, glass the first dry, calm hours (Tip).

• Strong wind: glass sheltered lee slopes and timber (Tip).
  • A swirl forms just past a ridge top (Tip).
More: wind and shelter
  • Lee slopes and thick timber break the wind. Hunters find deer bedded there in gales (Tip).
  • Swirls and eddies near ridge tops and in draws carry your scent in odd directions: see Wind and thermals.
  • Thermals still run early and late on light wind days: up in the morning, down in the evening 80%.
  • Noise: strong wind hides your steps but also hides an animal's steps from you. Look more, listen less (Tip).
  • Safety: dead trees and big limbs fall in strong wind. Do not sit under a dead snag in a windstorm (Tip).

• Three studies, three answers: mixed evidence (55 to 65%).
  • Do not stay home for wind. Change where you look (Tip).
More: the three studies
  • Oklahoma, 7 years of GPS (Global Positioning System) collars (Noble Foundation): very little change in distance travelled with wind speed; temperature mattered more (60%, magazine summary, search preview).
  • South Carolina GPS thesis (Goethlich, Auburn): wind speed and other weather affected activity in some seasons and hours, less than the daily rhythm (65%, search preview).
  • South Texas radio collars, 25 bucks, 1980s: movement dropped at 15 to 19 mph (about 24 to 31 km/h) and came back up above 20 mph (32 km/h) (55%, magazine summary). Treat it as a Tip.
  • Shooting in wind: bullets drift. Know your drift at 200 m before the season: see .308 ballistics.

• A track on top of new snow was made since the snow stopped 70%.
  • Old tracks under it are older than the snowfall (Tip).
More: reading fresh snow
  • Fresh snow tells you who moved since it stopped, how many, which way and where they bedded (Tip, built on the tracking rules).
  • Cold, still nights keep tracks crisp for days, so crisp does not always mean fresh 65%.
  • Snow falling while you track fills prints from the edges: watch them soften (Tip). See Snow tracking.

• Trails, beds, urine, grouse snow roosts (65 to 80%).
  • Snow moves mule deer down: trouble near 30 cm, gone near 50 cm 75%.
More: snow sign and snow depth
  • Beds melt an oval to the ground or to a crust (Tip). Count beds to count deer (Tip).
  • Ruffed grouse dive into soft snow to roost and burst out leaving wing marks 80%.
  • Mule deer: snow and cold trigger the move to winter range 85%; trouble near 30 cm, leave near 50 cm 75%.
  • Moose: little trouble to 40 cm; often winter in 50 cm or more 85%.
  • Chukar move lower and onto south slopes in heavy snow 75%.
  • Avalanche terrain is real on steep open slopes with snow. See the avalanche screen in Snow tracking.

Read a weather morning in 4 steps1 of 4
  • Fresh sign since the change is your best clue (Tip).
More: the 4 steps in full
  1. When did rain stop, snow end, or wind swing? That is your clock (Tip).
  2. Sign made after the change is fresh: clean tracks on spattered mud, tracks on top of new snow 70%.
  3. In wind, lee slopes and timber edges (Tip).
  4. On snow, deer bodies and dark legs stand out; so do you. Wear white or break your outline in the open, with blaze orange where others hunt (Tip).

• Fog: close range only. Never shoot at a shape (Tip).
  • Wait for it to lift, then glass hard (Tip).
More: fog details (Tip)
  • Valley fog often burns off by mid morning on clear fall days in the Interior (Tip). Use the time to walk to a higher glassing point.
  • Fog plays tricks on distance and colour. Positive ID of a legal animal and a safe backstop come first (Tip). See Legal to shoot.

• You do not need frost to get hypothermia; wind and rain raise the risk 75%.
  • Fumbles, mumbles, stumbles, grumbles: turn back 75%.
More: hypothermia and the stop rules
  • Fraser Health: it does not need to be below freezing to get hypothermia; wind chill and rain raise the odds (75%, health authority handout, search preview).
  • Mild signs: shivering, cold, and the "umbles": fumbles, mumbles, stumbles, grumbles (75%, Bush safety session).
  • Shivering that stops with confusion and stiffness is severe hypothermia, an emergency (Bush safety session).
  • Keep a dry warm layer in a dry bag in your pack, eat and drink every hour, and turn back early (Tip). Full detail: Bush safety.
  • On the water, cold water is a bigger danger again: Water safety.
  • Snow and ice on Forest Service roads: check road reports and carry chains or traction aids (Tip). Highways: DriveBC.

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Grandpa's rule (wisdom): Bad weather writes the freshest news. Dress warm enough to sit and read it.

Common mistakes
  • Calling every crisp snow track fresh on a cold, still morning.
  • Glassing the windy open face in a gale.
  • Pushing on while cold and fumbling.
More: why each one hurts
  • Cold, still air keeps tracks crisp for days 65%.
  • In a gale, deer use sheltered ground (Tip).
  • Fumbling hands mean mild hypothermia has started 75%. Turn back together.

Do this in the field

The first rainy or snowy morning this fall: write down when it stopped, then find 3 tracks made after and 3 made before. Photo each with your knife for scale.

• "Pits before, clean after." Rain and tracks 70%.
  • "On top is new." Tracks on fresh snow 70%.
  • "Gale? Go lee." (Tip)
  • "Umbles mean go home": fumbles, mumbles, stumbles, grumbles 75%.
  • "30 trouble, 50 gone": snow depth for mule deer 75%.

  • Outdoor Life, the truth about hunting whitetails in wind and Grand View Outdoors, can deer move in high winds, search previews 2026-10-11 (55 to 60%).
  • Goethlich thesis, Auburn University, search preview 65%.
  • Fraser Health, hypothermia handout, search preview 2026-10-11 75%.
  • Snow depth: BC deer account and BC moose account 85%; chukar: USDA Fire Effects Information System 75%.

mule-deer:
Why it matters

The mule deer is the deer of the hills around Heffley Creek. Learn its day and you will know where to sit at first light.

  • The main deer of the southern BC Interior 85%.
  • Your first hunt, mid to late October, is the pre rut 70%.
More: what this session covers
  • Mule deer are the main deer of the southern BC Interior 85%.
  • Your first hunt is mid to late October. That is the pre rut: bucks start to roam, the big breeding push is still weeks away 70%.
  • This session: how to tell one, where it is hour by hour, what it eats, how it hides, and how you hunt it.
  • The deep dive on senses and alarm is in How a deer thinks.

• Big ears, forks on forks, thin black tipped tail 85%.
  • No clear antlers? Not a buck (Tip).

More: the full ID list
  • Ears: very big, like a mule. That is the name 85%.
  • Antlers (buck): forks that fork again, like a "Y" on a "Y" 85%.
  • Tail: thin, white, rope like, with a black tip 85%.
  • Rump: big white patch around the tail 85%.
  • Doe: same body, no antlers, smaller neck 85%.
  • Fawn: born in early summer; by October it has lost its spots and is about half the doe's size 75%.
  • Metatarsal gland (scent patch on the outside of the hind leg): long, 10 to 15 cm 85%.
Tip (opinion)

A buck in October has a thick neck. A doe has a thin neck and a long, narrow face. If you can't see antlers clearly, you have not identified a buck.

ClueMule deerWhite tail
AntlersForks that fork againOne main beam, single tines up
TailThin, white, black tipWide, brown on top, white under
Running awayStots: all 4 feet hit and push together, bouncing 85%Gallops, tail up like a white flag 85%
EarsVery bigMedium
Leg glandLong, 10 to 15 cm 85%Small 85%
More: licences and hybrids
  • Both deer live near Heffley Creek. They need separate (page 14) 99%.
  • Hybrids exist but are uncommon 70%. When in doubt, do not shoot (Tip).

• Peaks: about 04:00 to 09:00 and 17:00 to 21:00 85%.
  • Be glassing 45 minutes before legal light (Tip).

More: the hour by hour detail
  • Night (about 21:00 to 04:00): feeds on and off in open grass and brush, rests between bouts 75%.
  • Before first light (04:00 to 07:00): a strong activity peak. Feeding, moving 85%.
  • Legal light starts: 1 hour before sunrise (page 11, item 38) 99%. Mid to late October sunrise near Kamloops is about 07:30 to 07:50 (calculated) 75%. Use the Legal light screen in Field Mode.
  • Sunrise to about 09:00: last feeding, then drifts uphill toward cover 85%.
  • Midday (10:00 to 15:00): bedded. Chews cud. Gets up briefly to stretch, nibble, and re bed 80%.
  • Late afternoon (16:00 to 18:00): rises, browses near the bed, then moves toward open feeding slopes 80%.
  • Sunset (about 17:40 to 18:00) to 21:00: second peak. Out in the open 85%.
  • Peaks from a telemetry study: about 04:00 to 09:00 and 17:00 to 21:00 85%.
Do this in the field

Be on your glassing spot 45 minutes before legal light. The first and last hour are when you will see deer.

• A browser that chews cud, then beds 85%.
  • Shiny pellets = fresh (Tip).
More: the detail
  • Eats: a browser. Twigs, leaves and buds of shrubs, plus forbs (small leafy plants), with little grass in fall 85%.
  • Chews cud: a ruminant. It fills up fast, then lies down to chew again 85%.
  • Poops: piles of oval pellets, about 1 to 1.5 cm long. Firm and dry in fall and winter 70%.
  • How often: roughly 13 to 34 pellet groups a day 70%.
  • Sleeps: in short naps, often with head up or curled, waking often 70%.
  • Walks: slow, stopping to look and listen. Often walks the same trails each day 75%.
  • Drinks: in dry fall weather, near water at dusk or dawn. With green feed and dew, it needs less (Tip).

• Learn 3 plants: saskatoon, red osier dogwood, Oregon grape (Tip).
More: the stomach study and the plant list
  • Study of deer stomachs near Kamloops, September to April 85%:
    • Grass was under 10% of the diet until spring.
    • More forbs in fall.
    • Shrubs important in early fall and late winter.
    • Douglas fir needles peak in December and January.
  • Key browse: Douglas fir, saskatoon, Oregon grape, red osier dogwood, willow, rose, bitterbrush, rabbitbrush, sagebrush, snowbrush 80%.
  • Late October menu: last green forbs, shrub leaves and twigs, fresh green grass shoots after fall rain 75%.
Tip (opinion)

Learn 3 plants this week: saskatoon, red osier dogwood (red stems) and Oregon grape (holly like leaves). Find them chewed and you are in a feeding area.

• High in summer, low sunny slopes in winter 85%.
  • Elevations are rough: check a map (Tip).

More: local reading, elevations and winter range maps
  • Mule deer like steeper, higher, open, broken ground. White tails like valley bottoms and farm fields 85%.
  • Local reading 75%:
    • Grassland and open Douglas fir benches above the valley.
    • Up toward Heffley Lake, Paul Lake and Sun Peaks in summer and early fall.
    • Lower, sunnier slopes as snow comes.
  • Winter range: south and west facing slopes with old Douglas fir 85%.
  • A study of winter range north of Kamloops used slopes below about 760 m 80%.
  • Rough elevations (Tip, VERIFY on a map): valley 370 to 450 m, Heffley Lake about 950 m, Sun Peaks village about 1,250 m.
  • Ungulate winter range maps: view the "Ungulate Winter Range, Approved" layer in iMapBC 85%. Near Kamloops there may be no approved mule deer areas (VERIFY).

• Snow and cold start the move, not the rut 85%.
  • Snow up high? Hunt below the snow line (Tip).

More: the migration numbers
  • About 74% of tracked mule deer in a southern Interior study migrated 85%.
  • Collared deer in the Southern Interior Mule Deer Project moved an average of about 47 to 55 km between summer and winter range, the longest about 100 km (85%, BC Wildlife Federation project pages).
  • They use the same route every year 85%.
  • What starts the move down: snow and cold, not the rut 85%.
  • Timing: back on winter range October to November; in one year nearly all were back by mid October 85%.
  • Another BC account: interior deer often stay high until December 80%.
  • Deer have trouble in snow deeper than about 30 cm and leave slopes where it passes about 50 cm 75%.
My lean (opinion)

Early snow up high in October? Hunt the mid slopes below the snow line. No snow yet? Glass the high benches and openings near Heffley Lake and Paul Lake first.

• Nose first, then ears, then eyes 85%.
  • Wind in your face, quiet gear, slow moves (Tip).
More: what scares, calms and attracts them
  • Nose: strongest sense. Wind at your back toward the deer ends the hunt 85%.
  • Ears: hear about 115 Hz (hertz) to 54 kHz (kilohertz), best at 4 to 8 kHz 85%. That is the range of zippers, Velcro, nylon swish and metal clicks.
  • Eyes: see blues well, no red cone, so blaze orange looks dull to them 75%. They catch motion and outline fast 85%.
  • Scares them: human scent, a skyline outline, sudden moves, metal clicks, voices, a slammed truck door (Tip).
  • Calms them: slow natural walking rhythm, other relaxed deer, steady breeze (Tip).
  • Attracts them: fresh green feed, does in heat (in the rut), other deer 80%.
  • Lights: a headlamp beam swinging across a slope will move deer. Use red light and keep it on the ground (Tip).
  • Full story: How a deer thinks.

• Rut: mid November to mid December 80%.
  • Late October: bucks spar, rub and check does 70%.
More: groups, rut and antlers
  • Does live in family groups: mother, daughters and fawns 85%.
  • Bucks spend summer in bachelor groups of 2 to 4. These break up in October 80%.
  • Groups are mostly 5 or fewer. In winter 5 to 8, up to 15 to 30 75%.
  • Deer return to the same home range year after year 85%.
  • Rut (breeding season) for mule deer: mid November to mid December, peak mid November 80%.
  • Late October: bucks spar (push antlers, not real fights), rub small trees, and start checking doe groups 70%.
  • In the rut: a buck tends one doe at a time, follows her, and fights rivals 75%. Bucks get careless in daylight.
  • Antlers fall off in winter and regrow each year 85%.
• Deer bed where they see below and smell above (Tip).

More: bed detail
  • Day beds give hiding cover and shelter 80%.
  • Warm days: north facing timber, benches, draws, shade 80%.
  • Cold days: sunny south and west slopes, out of the wind 80%.
  • Lore: bucks bed in the top third of a slope, looking down, with wind from behind (hunter lore) 60%.
  • A bed is an oval of flattened grass or scraped earth, about 1 m long, often with pellets and hair nearby 70%.
  • Deer bed where they can see danger below and smell danger above (Tip).

• One track can't tell mule deer from white tail 60%.
  • A stotting trail can 85%.

More: track and sign detail
  • Track: heart shape, 2 toes, pointed end shows direction of travel 85%.
  • Mule deer front track: about 5.7 to 10 cm long 60%.
  • You can't tell mule deer from white tail by one track. Too much overlap 60%.
  • Stotting leaves groups of 4 prints, 2.4 to 4.6 m apart 60%.
  • Browse sign: deer tear twigs (no upper front teeth). Hares cut clean at 45 degrees 75%.
  • Rubs: mule deer make fewer rubs than white tails, on small conifers and shrubs 60%.
  • Fresh sign: shiny wet pellets, crisp track edges, green stem ends on browse (Tip).

Spot and stalk in 5 steps1 of 5
▶Remi Warren Breaks Down His Mule Deer Stalking TechniquesPlan the stalk from where you glassed: landmarks, wind, cover.
OutdoorClass, YouTube, 2 min. Needs internet.

OptionProsCons
A: spot and stalkClassic, see lots of countryHard, easy to bump deer

  • My lean: Option B on the first trip (Tip).
More: the three options in full

Option A: spot and stalk

  • Glass from a high point at first light, find a buck, then sneak in with the wind in your face.
  • Pros: the classic mule deer method; you see lots of country (hunter consensus) 60%.
  • Cons: hard on a beginner; long stalks; easy to bump the deer.

Option B: sit and glass a feeding slope

  • Sit at the edge of a grassy slope or opening at dawn or dusk. Let them come.
  • Pros: quiet, safe, steady shot from a rest, great for learning.
  • Cons: needs the right spot and patience.

Option C: still hunting through timber

  • Walk slowly through bedding cover. 10 steps, stop 1 minute.
  • Pros: works midday when deer are bedded.
  • Cons: deer usually see you first; shots are quick and close.
My lean (opinion)

Option B for the first trip. Dawn and dusk on a slope with a long view. Midday, scout with binoculars and learn the trails.

• .308 Winchester, 150 to 165 grain expanding bullet (Tip).
  • Limit: a 15 cm plate, 9 of 10 (Tip).

  • Mule deer do not need magnum power. They need one good hit (Tip).
Tip (opinion)

Your maximum range is the distance where you can hit a 15 cm (6 in) plate 9 times out of 10 from a field rest. For most beginners: 200 m (219 yd). Past that, get closer.

  • Wind, angle and a racing heart make field shots much harder than the bench (Tip).

White tails live in the North Thompson valley bottoms, close to roads and farms. The antlerless season may be open during your October hunt.

More: the three options in full

Option A: stand or ground blind

  • Sit on the trail between bedding and food, downwind, before light or 2 hours before dark.
  • Pros: you are still, deer come to you, easy steady shot.
  • Cons: needs scouting and permission on farm land; cold; patience.

Option B: still hunting

  • Walk 10 steps, stop and look for a minute or more. Wind in your face.
  • Pros: covers ground; works in thick bottoms midday.
  • Cons: white tails are hard to sneak on in thick cover; quick close shots.

Option C: rattling and grunting

  • Clack antlers together and grunt to sound like bucks fighting.
  • Pros: can pull a buck in close.
  • Cons: works best in early November, not mid October. One Texas study saw about 65% of bucks respond, best on cool, calm, overcast mornings 70%.
My lean (opinion)

Option A. Get permission on one hayfield edge, find the main trail, and sit it at dusk.

Same limit as mule deer: only shoot as far as you can hit a 15 cm (6 in) plate 9 times out of 10 from a field rest. For most beginners, 200 m (219 yd).
