deer-mind:
Why it matters

A deer's whole life is staying alive. Think like a scared prey animal and you stop spooking them.

  • Nose first, then ears, then eyes (Tip).
  • Wind and thermals (air sliding up or down a slope) carry your scent 80%.
More: the key points
  • A deer trusts its nose first, then its ears, then its eyes (Tip, ranking based on the facts below).
  • Its nose almost never lies. Its eyes are great at motion, poor at detail 85%.
  • Wind and thermals (air sliding up or down a slope) decide where your scent goes 80%.
  • Alarm has stages: alert, stamp, snort, run. You can sometimes stop it at stage 1 (Tip).
  • Cougars kill more southern Interior mule deer than any other cause. Deer are built around that fear 85%.
  • Hunters change deer too: pressure pushes them into thicker cover and night movement 70%.

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

You can fool the eyes. You can quiet your feet. You can never fool the nose. Play the wind.

  • Motion and outline give you away, not colour 85%.
More: cones, UV and lights
  • Deer have 2 colour cones, peaking near 455 nm (blue) and 537 nm (green). No red cone 85%.
  • So blaze orange looks dull, close to grey or brown, to a deer 75%.
  • Deer pick up more ultraviolet (UV) light than we do 75%.
  • Some laundry detergents add UV brighteners that may glow to a deer (Tip) 65%. Use unscented, no brightener soap.
  • Motion and outline give you away, not colour 85%.
  • Lights: a moving headlamp or phone screen in the dark is pure motion. Red light, pointed at the ground (Tip).

• Zips, Velcro and metal sit right in its best band 85%.
  • Walk, stop, walk, like a deer (Tip).
More: hearing details and the walking tip
  • Deer hear about 115 Hz (hertz) to 54 kHz (kilohertz). Best around 4 to 8 kHz 85%.
  • That band is exactly zippers, Velcro, nylon swish, metal on metal, and snapping twigs 85%.
  • Each ear swivels on its own to point at a sound 75%.
  • Natural sounds (a squirrel, a deer walking, wind) are filtered out. Odd rhythms and metal are not (Tip).
Tip (opinion)

Two legged walking is a steady "crunch crunch crunch". A deer walks, stops, walks. Copy that rhythm.

• Smell is its strongest sense 85%.
  • Cover scents help a little. The wind helps a lot (Tip).
More: scent sources, folklore and the lure rule
  • Smell is a deer's strongest sense 85%.
  • The often quoted "297 million scent receptors" figure is folklore, not a measured fact 45%.
  • Your scent comes from breath, skin, clothes, boots and your truck (Tip).
  • Cover scents and scent control help a little. The wind helps a lot (Tip).
  • Deer and elk urine lures from outside BC are banned for hunting (page 12 item 51) 95%. The synopsis warns that urine based scents can spread (Chronic Wasting Disease) (inside back cover) 99%.

• Morning: approach from above or the side 80%.
  • Evening: hunt from below or the side 80%.
More: thermal details, my lean and the wind check
  • Sun warms the slope in the morning. Warm air rises, so scent drifts uphill 80%.
  • Slopes cool in the evening. Cool air sinks, so scent drifts downhill 80%.
  • At dawn before the sun hits, air often still sinks. It flips after sun warms the slope 75%.
  • Draws and saddles swirl the air. Your scent can go everywhere (Tip).
  • Main wind usually beats thermals when it blows hard (Tip).
My lean (opinion)

Morning: approach from above or from the side. Evening: hunt from below or the side, and leave before the cold air drains your scent down to the bedded deer.

Do this in the field

Carry a puffer bottle of unscented powder or a thread on your rifle. Check it every 10 minutes.

5 stages of alarm1 of 5
  • Stared at? Do not move a finger. Count to 100 (Tip).
More: each stage in words
  1. Alert: head up, ears forward, stare. Freeze until it looks away (Tip).
  2. Head bob: drops the head as if to feed, then snaps it up to catch you moving (hunter lore) 70%.
  3. Foot stamp: stamps a front hoof. Warns other deer and tries to make you move 70%.
  4. Snort or blow: a loud whoosh of air. All deer nearby are now on alert 70%.
  5. Escape:
    • Mule deer stot: bounces on all 4 feet, good for steep broken ground 85%.
    • White tail flags and gallops to cover 85%.
  • Mule deer often stop and look back from about 150 to 300 m (hunter lore) 65%.

If a deer stares at you, do not move a finger. Count to 100. Most deer go back to feeding if nothing else happens.

  • So deer bed where they can see below and smell above (Tip).

  • Against wolves and dogs (chase hunters), deer use rugged steep slopes 80%.

moose:
Why it matters

A moose is the most meat you will ever carry out of the bush, and the easiest animal to break the law on. The antler rule decides everything.

  • Region 3: spike fork bulls only 98%.
  • Every licence holder reports by 31 March 98%.
More: what this session covers
  • Moose are the biggest member of the deer family. A big bull in most of Canada can weigh up to 600 kg (search preview) 80%.
  • Region 3 general open season: spike fork bulls only. Cows, calves and bigger bulls are closed unless you hold an (Limited Entry Hunting) authorization 98%.
  • Dates depend on your (Management Unit). The three Region 3 blocks run 20 September to 31 October, 15 October to 15 November, and 1 to 15 November 98%.
  • Every moose holder must file a Mandatory Hunter Report by 31 March, hunt or no hunt 98%.
  • The antlers must travel with the species licence 98%.
  • Your .308 Winchester can do it at modest range with heavy premium bullets (Tip).
  • Hunt moose with your brother. One person cannot pack a moose out alone in a day (Tip).

Warning

An antlerless moose in Region 3 is closed to you without an LEH draw. Cow or calf, it does not matter. No antlers, no shot.

More: the full ID list
  • Bull: antlers. By late August or early September the velvet is off and the antlers are hard (search preview) 75%.
  • Young bull: a spike or a small fork on each side. This is the legal class in Region 3 (Tip).
  • Cow: no antlers, about 1.8 m at the shoulder, 340 to 420 kg (synopsis definition, page 3) 98%.
  • Calf: under 12 months old 98%. "Much smaller" with "a distinctly stubby face" 98%.
  • Synopsis warning: "not all moose in the accompaniment of a larger moose are necessarily calves. Be sure of your target" 98%.
  • Bell: the flap of skin under the throat. Both sexes have one, so it does not prove a bull 65%.
  • Mature bulls usually drop antlers in November. Some young bulls keep theirs until April (search preview) 75%.

• Spike fork: no more than 2 tines on one antler 98%.
  • Region 3 and Region 8 use this class only 98%.

More: the synopsis definitions

Synopsis definitions, pages 3 and 4 98%:

  • Spike fork bull: "a bull moose having no more than two tines (points) on one antler. (Includes tines on main antler and brow palms.) Does not include a calf."
  • Tripalm bull: "at least one antler with a brow palm bearing three or more tines (points)." The brow palm is split from the main palm by the deepest bay.
  • 10 point bull: "at least one antler with a minimum of ten tines (points), including the tines on the brow palm."
  • : at least 2.5 cm long and longer than it is wide 98%. Rounded bumps on top of the palm "may not constitute a point" 98%.
  • Region 3 and Region 8 general seasons use the spike fork class only 98%.
  • Tripalm and 10 point classes appear in other regions. Region 7B Peace rows (page 62) open for spike fork, tripalm or 10 point bulls; the Haines Highway area in Region 6 (page 50) does the same 98%.
Tip (opinion)

The test is on one antler. Read literally, a bull with 2 points on one side and 3 on the other fits the spike fork definition (interpretation) 85%. My lean: if you are counting that closely, let it walk.

• Wetlands, willow flats, young cutblocks (Tip).
  • Your MU (Management Unit): VERIFY on the map.
More: numbers, closures and local reading
  • Moose live across most of the BC Interior. Region 3 estimate: 7,000 to 9,000, stable (2022 provincial estimates, search preview) 80%.
  • Local reading (Tip): North Thompson wetlands, willow flats and young cutblocks toward Barriere and Clearwater; lake edges and subalpine basins in early fall.
  • Wells Gray Park is MU 3-45. Hunting and the discharge of firearms are prohibited there (page 33) 98%.

More: trichinosis, care and yield
  • Skin fast. The fat layer and thick hide trap heat (Tip). A bear shot on a warm October afternoon and left whole can spoil by morning (Tip).
  • Trim the fat and render it separately. It is fine lard (Tip).
  • Trichinosis: a parasitic worm in muscle. Bear is the usual source of human cases from wild game in Canada (CMAJ, Canadian Medical Association Journal, search preview) 75%.
  • Cook every cut to an internal 71 C (160 F) with a meat thermometer. Colour is not a sign of doneness (CDC, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and CFIA, Canadian Food Inspection Agency, guidance, search preview) 80%.
  • Freezing does not make bear safe: the northern species, Trichinella nativa, survives freezing for months or years 75%.

  • The synopsis sends you to the BC Centre for Disease Control for diseases you can get from wildlife (page 80) 98%.

More: the three options, pros and cons, and the retrieval law

Option A: the straight line walk

  • Two hunters 15 to 25 m apart, walking slowly through cover edges, stopping every 20 steps (Tip). The stop makes nervous birds flush.
  • Pros: works for quail, partridge and pheasant. Cons: running birds slip ahead; you need to mark every fall.

Option B: pinch the cover

  • One hunter walks a hedgerow or draw toward the other, who stands at the end in the open (Tip). Birds flush toward the blocker.
  • Pros: cuts off runners. Cons: the blocker is in the line of fire. Agree a no shot arc before you start (Tip).

Option C: chukar from above

  • Climb above the slope on an old road, then work down and across. Chukar run up and flush down, so being above them turns a 300 m chase into a shot 65%.
  • Pros: real chukar odds. Cons: steep, loose rock, long days.
  • No dog means every bird must fall where you can find it. Shoot only over short cover and walk straight to the spot, eyes on it (Tip).
  • Retrieval is the law: "No person shall kill, cripple or wound game without making all reasonable effort to locate, dispatch, retrieve and include it in their bag limit." 99%

A ram is the hardest legal animal in BC to judge. Shoot one a quarter curl short and you have broken the law, not bent it.

More: the law, word for word
The rule

Full curl bighorn (plain English): seen square from the side, a horn tip must rise above a line from the centre of the nostril to the lowest back edge of the horn base 98%.

"MOUNTAIN SHEEP - Full Curl Bighorn Ram - means any male bighorn mountain sheep, the head of which, when viewed squarely from the side, has at least one horn tip extending upwards beyond a straight line drawn through the centre of the nostril and the lowest hindmost portion of the horn base." (Synopsis page 4) 98%

The rule

3/4 curl bighorn (plain English): a horn tip must reach forward past a line through the back of the eye opening, drawn at right angles to that nostril to horn base line 98%.

"MOUNTAIN SHEEP - 3/4 CURL BIGHORN RAM - means any male bighorn mountain sheep, the head of which, when viewed squarely from the side, has at least one horn tip extending beyond a straight line drawn through the back of the eye opening and at right angles to a line drawn between the centre of the nostril and the lowest hindmost portion of the horn base." (Synopsis page 4) 98%

The rule

Full curl thinhorn: the ram is 8 years old by true horn rings, or a horn tip rises above the line of the nose bridge. Mature bighorn ram uses the same nose bridge test 98%.

"MOUNTAIN SHEEP - FULL CURL THINHORN RAM - means any thinhorn ram mountain sheep that has attained the age of 8 years as evidenced by true horn annuli as determined by the regional manager or his designate, or whose horn tip, when viewed squarely from the side at right angles to the sagittal plane of the skull, extends dorsally beyond the nose bridge plane." (Synopsis page 4) 98%

  • The synopsis adds: do not use horn rings to age a ram in the field, because false rings may be present 98%.
  • The skull test at inspection uses the back edge of the eye socket, so a ram that looks borderline alive can fail on the table 95%.

• A young ram: nowhere near legal. Learn this look first.

  • LEH: main draw deadline June 23, 2026; you need the resident hunting licence and the goat species licence as well as the authorization 98%.
  • Horns must not be altered until the carcass reaches a meat cutter, home or CI 98%.

• Plan 2 to 3 pack loads for a billy. Skin and salt the hide the same day (Tip).
More: meat and cape care
  • A billy field dresses heavy; expect a hard pack out of 2 to 3 loads (Tip).
  • Meat is good, though old billies in rut can be strong; grind and braise (Tip).
  • The hide is thick and the hair long; skin it the same day and salt it if you want a mount (Tip).
  • Keep horns, CI data sheet and species licence together for life 95%.

Common mistakes
  • Shooting the first white goat you see. The first one is often a nanny with a kid out of view.
  • Shooting a goat above a cliff. It falls, the horns break, and the meat is gone.
  • Climbing in running shoes. Loose rock and wet grass kill goat hunters.
More: one more
  • Also: no spotting scope, no rope, and no partner (Tip).

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

A nanny is a goat factory. Leave her, and you will have goats to hunt in ten years.

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Never shoot a goat where it stands unless you would be happy to stand there yourself.

caribou-bison:
Why it matters

These are the two "someday" animals of BC. Both are draw only, both live far from Heffley Creek, and both come with rules that trip up good hunters.

  • Caribou: every hunt is a LEH (Limited Entry Hunting) draw 98%.
  • Bison: a short season in parts of three Peace MUs (Management Units), plus draws 98%.
More: the key points
  • Caribou: BC's herds fell from about 40,000 to about 17,000; recovery work has them near 19,000 95%.
  • Every caribou hunt in BC is LEH (Limited Entry Hunting). The regional tables say "LIMITED ENTRY HUNTING ONLY" 98%.
  • Bison: one wild plains bison herd at Pink Mountain and three small wood bison herds in the northeast 85%.
  • Bison have a short general open season in parts of three Peace MUs (Management Units), plus LEH shared hunts 98%.
  • Both need Mandatory Hunter Reporting or Compulsory Inspection, and special gear rules apply to bison 98%.

• Both sexes grow antlers. Antlers alone never make it a bull 85%.
  • Most northern draws are for a 5 point bull 98%.
More: every identification clue and the 5 point rule
  • A medium sized deer family animal with a white neck mane, big concave hooves and a rich brown or grey coat 85%.
  • Both sexes grow antlers. Only in caribou do females carry antlers 85%. A small antlered animal may be a cow.
  • Bulls: a big rack of amber antlers, a shovel over the face, shed in November or December 85%.
  • Cows keep antlers into winter, so late season "antlered" is not "bull" 85%.
  • 5 point bull in law: one antler bears at least 5 tines, including the tip of the main beam above the rear point; if the rear point is missing, the first rear facing point is used as the rear point 98%.
  • Most northern LEH hunts are for "5 pt Bull"; some Cariboo hunts are "Bull" meaning any bull regardless of antlers 98%.

• Draws in Regions 5, 6, 7A and 7B. None in Region 3 98%.
  • Seen one? Shut off the quad and let it pass 95%.
More: status, draw areas and odds
  • Southern Mountain and Boreal caribou are listed as "Threatened" under the federal Species at Risk Act; Northern Mountain caribou are "Special Concern" and many northern herds are abundant 95%.
  • Region 3 has no caribou season and about a million hectares of Crown land closed to snowmobiles for mountain caribou recovery 98%.
  • LEH caribou hunts in 2026: Cariboo Region 5 (MUs 5-01 to 5-03 and 5-15), Skeena Region 6 (Spatsizi, Level, Horseranch, Little Rancheria, Atlin and more), Omineca 7A (7-37, 7-39 to 7-41), Peace 7B (7-50 to 7-54), Aug 15 to Oct 15 in the north 98%.
  • 2025 first choice odds ranged from under 1 to 1 (Spatsizi, early) to 118 to 1 (Omineca 7-37) 95%.
  • Spatsizi also offers a combination moose and caribou hunt 98%.
  • Caribou live on lichen in winter and move between forested winter slopes and alpine summer range 85%.
Tip (opinion)

If you see caribou while hunting anything else, shut off the quad and let them pass. Disturbance in winter costs them energy they cannot spare 95%.

Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

  • Report by March 31 even if you never hunted 98%.
More: every caribou rule
  • Species licence: $20.00 resident 98%. Not valid until 2 days after issue 90%.
  • Provincial bag limit: 1 98%.
  • Weapons: centrefire rifle, bow A, C or D. No rimfire, no shotgun, no air gun 98%.
  • Dogs must be leashed 98%.
  • Compulsory inspection within 30 days: the incisor (front) tooth, the antlers, and for a caribou without at least one main beam over 60 cm (24 in), the hide with evidence of sex attached 98%.
  • Mandatory Hunter Report by March 31 for everyone who buys a caribou licence, hunted or not 98%.
  • Evidence of sex for transport: the tail or a piece of hide at least 6 cm square, plus a testicle or part of the penis, or part of the udder 98%.
  • CWD (Chronic Wasting Disease) rule: no parts of deer, elk, moose or caribou killed outside BC may come in except clean meat and cleaned hide, antlers and skull plate 98%.
  • Hunting caribou is prohibited in parts of MUs 7-39 and 7-40 (Map G25) 98%.

• Strays near Kamloops are not a hunt. Report them 98%.
More: size, herds and the report line
  • Massive forequarters, a hump, a bearded head and short black horns; bulls weigh about 550 to 900 kg, cows 320 to 545 kg 85%.
  • Wood bison: slightly larger and darker than plains bison, with a taller hump and shorter hair on the front end 85%. Listed Threatened under the federal Species at Risk Act 85%.
  • Plains bison: about 50 escaped near Halfway River in 1971 and grew into the Pink Mountain herd of over 1,000 85%.
  • Wood bison herds in BC: Nordquist (Liard River), Nahanni and Etthithun; Etthithun was estimated near 400 in 2020 to 2021 80%.
  • Highway collisions along the Alaska Highway kill bison every year 85%.
  • Region 3 asks hunters to report any bison on public land to RAPP 1 877 952 7277 98%. Those are strays, not a herd you may hunt.

• General: Sept 1 to Jan 31, parts of MUs 7-42, 7-57, 7-58, Map H25 98%.
  • Draws: groups of up to 4 may apply together 98%.
More: every season detail and odds
  • General open season (Region 7B): either sex, Sept 1 to Jan 31, bag limit 1, restricted to portions of MUs 7-42, 7-57 and 7-58 shown on Map H25 98%.
  • LEH (Liard): either sex, two week windows from Oct 1 to Jan 31 in zones of 7-42, 7-57 and 7-58; single applicants or shared groups of up to 4 98%.
  • 2025 LEH odds ran from 72 to 1 up to about 494 to 1 95%.
  • The LEH synopsis warns: "BISON AUTHORIZATIONS ARE CURRENTLY UNDER REVIEW AND SUBJECT TO CHANGE." 98%
  • Snow machines are often needed for November and December access 98%.

Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

  • 175 grain or heavier, and 2,712 joules left at 100 m 98%.
More: every bison rule
  • Species licence: $70.00 resident 98%. Provincial bag limit: 1 98%.
  • Rifle rule: the bullet must be 175 grain or heavier and still carry 2,712 joules (2,000 ft lb) at 100 m 98%. Your .308 with 165 grain loads does not qualify (Tip, check the box).
  • No rimfire, no shotgun, no air gun 98%. Bow E only: at least 22.6 kg pull, arrow over 26 g, broadhead over 8.1 g and 2.2 cm wide 98%.
  • Shared hunt: any member may kill the authorized animal; everyone carries the Harvest Report 98%.
  • Evidence of sex: a testicle or part of the penis, or part of the udder or teats 98%.
  • The LEH synopsis reminds you that you must make every reasonable effort to retrieve a wounded bison; "this is particularly important with Bison" 98%.

• Within 100 m, broadside, and stay ready after the shot (Tip).
More: caribou and bison tactics
  • Caribou: glass ridge tops and lichen flats, then move in across open ground with the wind; they are curious but drift fast (Tip).
  • Bison: find the herd, pick a single animal with a clear backstop, get within 100 m, wait for broadside (Tip).
  • A bison shot in the lungs may stand for a minute. Reload, stay ready, do not approach until it is down and still (Tip).
  • Bring help: a bison is 4 to 6 pack loads of meat and must not be wasted (Tip).

• Caribou: behind the shoulder, one third up 75%.
  • Bison: lower and farther forward than the hump suggests (Tip).
More: where to aim
  • Caribou: heart and lungs behind the shoulder, one third up, broadside 75%.
  • Bison: the lungs sit lower and farther forward than the hump suggests; aim behind the front leg, low third, broadside (Tip).
  • No head or neck shots; the skull and hump absorb bullets (Tip).

• Take the neck, ribs, four quarters and loins 98%.
More: meat care
  • Caribou meat spoils fast in the warm August season; skin, quarter and hang in shade or cool water the same day (Tip).
  • Bison yields several hundred kilograms of beef like meat; arrange a meat cutter before the hunt (Tip).
  • Edible portions must be removed: neck, ribs, four quarters and loins 98%.

Common mistakes
  • Counting a cow caribou as a bull because it has antlers.
  • Bringing a deer rifle to a bison hunt and failing the 175 grain, 2,712 joule rule.
  • Forgetting the Mandatory Hunter Report by March 31 and losing next year's licence options.

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Draw animals are earned in June on the computer, not in September on the mountain. Apply every year.

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

A bison is a truck with hair. Treat every one as if it is still alive until you have touched the eye.

wild-turkey:
Why it matters

A spring gobbler is the loudest, most exciting bird in BC and the only one you hunt by talking to it. It is also the one hunt where another hunter can mistake you for the bird.

  • No turkey season in Region 3. Nearest: Region 8, then Region 4 95%.
  • Spring: bearded birds only. Fall: any turkey 98%.
More: what this session covers
  • BC's turkeys are Merriam's wild turkeys, introduced and spread from the United States 75%.
  • Strongest numbers in the Kootenays (Region 4), then the south Okanagan (Region 8) and parts of Vancouver Island 75%.
  • Region 3 has no turkey season 95%. Your nearest hunt is Region 8, then Region 4.
  • Spring seasons are bearded birds only; fall seasons are any turkey 98%.
  • No species licence; a turkey is an upland game bird on your basic licence 98%.
  • A shotgun or a .22 rimfire is legal; a centrefire rifle is not 98%.

• Look for the beard first, then the head (Tip).
  • Merriam's: white tips on the tail fan 75%.

More: every mark, and the legal meaning of bearded
  • Tom (gobbler): big, dark, bronze body, bare red, white and blue head, a beard of bristles on the chest, spurs on the legs, a full round tail fan 75%.
  • Hen: smaller, duller brown, blue grey head, usually no beard 75%. A few hens grow a thin beard and are legal in a bearded season (Tip).
  • Jake: a year old tom. Short beard about 5 to 10 cm, short spurs, uneven fan with longer centre feathers (hunter lore) 65%.
  • Merriam's have white tips on the tail fan and rump feathers 75%.
The rule

The spring class is "Bearded". In law, a bearded turkey has a tuft of hair like feathers on the chest that grows larger with age 98%. Any bird with a visible beard qualifies; sex does not matter.

"BEARDED TURKEY - means a turkey with a tuft of hair-like feathers on the chest that grow larger with age." (Synopsis page 3) 98%

• Kootenays and the south Okanagan. Roosts in big pines on ridges 75%.
My lean (opinion)

From Heffley Creek: Region 8 is 2 to 3 hours away and has a short spring season in the MUs (Management Units) listed below. Region 4 is a longer drive but has three times the season.

More: history, numbers and habitat
  • First release: James Island near Vancouver Island, 1910 75%.
  • 1960s: birds spread north from Washington, Idaho and Montana into southern BC 75%.
  • 1980s: the province moved birds from the Creston Valley to the East Kootenay 75%.
  • Now: the valleys of the East and West Kootenay and the southeast Okanagan, with about 4,000 to 5,000 birds in 2004 and more since (search preview) 75%.
  • Region 4 hunters took about 620 turkeys a year from 2016 to 2020 (search preview) 70%.
  • Habitat: open conifer and deciduous forest edges in foothills; roosts in large pines on ridges 75%.

Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

  • Region 8: 1 in spring, 1 in fall, 2 a year 98%.
  • Region 4: 1 in spring, 2 in fall, 3 a year 98%.

More: every rule in full
  • Spring is a bearded only season: the beard must stay attached to the carcass, along with one feathered wing, until the bird is home 98%.
  • Hours: no hunting from 1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise 98%.
  • Weapons: shotgun, air gun or .22 rimfire allowed; centrefire rifle is for grouse or ptarmigan only, not turkey 98%. Bows B, C and D allowed 98%.
  • Lead shot is still legal for upland birds including turkey 98%.
  • Recorded or electronic calls and live decoys are unlawful for game birds 98%. Mouth, box and slate calls are fine (Tip).
  • No species licence for residents; a non resident needs the $50 upland game bird licence 98%.

• Down from the roost at first light, back up at dusk 75%.
More: spring, fall and snow
  • Roosts in tall trees at dusk, flies down at first light, feeds and travels through the morning, loafs midday, feeds again late afternoon 75%.
  • Spring: toms gobble on the roost and strut for hens from mid April; breeding and nesting run through May 75%.
  • Fall: flocks of hens with young, and separate groups of toms; birds scratch for seeds, acorns, insects and waste grain (Tip).
  • Snow pack often lingers until a week or two before the spring opener 75%.

More: sign in full
  • Roost sites: piles of droppings and feathers under big pines on ridges; roosts are used year after year 75%.
  • Scratching: leaf litter raked back in patches (Tip).
  • Tracks: three long toes, about 10 cm, in mud and snow (Tip).
  • Dust bowls on dry banks and logging roads (Tip).

• Find the roost the evening before. Set up 100 m away before light (Tip).
My lean (opinion)

Option A in Region 8 on opening week. Scout the roost two days before.

More: the three options, pros and cons

Option A: roost and call at dawn

  • Locate a roost the evening before. Set up 100 m away before light with a hen decoy, call softly as the sun comes up.
  • Pros: the classic hunt; a gobbler often flies down to your decoy 75%.
  • Cons: one mistake in setup and the birds go the other way.

Option B: run and gun with locator calls

  • Walk ridges midday, use an owl or crow call to make a tom "shock gobble", then move close and call.
  • Pros: finds birds when roost hunts fail 75%.
  • Cons: more walking, more chance of bumping birds.

Option C: fall flock busting

  • Find a flock, scatter it, sit down and call the young birds back.
  • Pros: works in October with no gobbling.
  • Cons: easy to break the law on bag limits with a flock in front of you.

• Head and neck only. Max about 40 m (Tip).
More: loads, patterns and the .22
  • A 12 gauge with a full or turkey choke, patterned at 30 and 40 m (33 and 44 yd) (Tip).
  • Shot sizes 4, 5 or 6 lead, or heavier tungsten loads (Tip). An example from an experienced hunter: 2 ounce loads of number 5 shot patterned to 50 m 75%.
  • Maximum range: where 8 or more pellets land in the head and neck of a paper turkey, usually 40 m (Tip).
  • Aim at the head and neck, never the body; body shots waste the bird and often fail (Tip).
  • A .22 rimfire is legal; it is a precise tool for a still bird's head at short range, not a flying shot (Tip).

• You sound like a turkey. Dress so no one thinks you are one (Tip).
More: safety in full
  • Never wear red, white or blue; those are a tom's head colours (Tip).
  • Sit with your back against a tree wider than your shoulders (Tip).
  • Never stalk a gobble. Another hunter may be making it (Tip).
  • When carrying a dead bird, wrap it in blaze orange (Tip).

More: meat in full
  • Pluck or skin, keep the wing and beard attached until home 98%.
  • Breast is lean; brine it. Legs and thighs are tough; braise them (Tip).
  • Save the beard, spurs and fan for your wall (Tip).

MistakeDo this instead
A second bird in Region 81 per season there

More: the mistakes in full
Common mistakes
  • Shooting the second bird in a flock in Region 8, where the limit is one per season.
  • Calling too much and too loud. Hens call little; toms come to quiet, confident calls.
  • Standing up when the gobbler goes silent. He is probably walking in.

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

If he gobbles at your call, stop calling. Let him come looking.

More: one more rule, and this spring's field task
Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

See the beard, then the head. If you cannot see both, you cannot shoot.

Do this in the field

This spring: drive to the south Okanagan on a weekend in early April, listen at dusk for roosting birds, and mark the roost on your map.

predators:
Why it matters

Predator seasons are the longest seasons in Region 3, and the easiest place for a beginner to make a legal or ethical mistake. Know the animal, the paper and the reason before you shoot.

• Five predators with Region 3 seasons. Wolverine: none here 98%.
  • Learn to skin before you hunt. Fur is the product (Tip).
More: the key points
  • Region 3 has seasons for cougar, wolf, coyote, bobcat and lynx; wolverine has no season here 98%.
  • Wolf has no closed season in MU (Management Unit) 3-17 and MUs 3-26 to 3-44, and coyote is open Sept 1 to June 30 with no bag limit 98%.
  • Cougar needs a $30 species licence, Compulsory Inspection (CI) and a kitten rule 98%.
  • Bobcat and lynx need an $8 licence each, bag 1, and a Compulsory Report in Region 3 98%.
  • You may use unleashed dogs and electronic calls for these animals 98%.
  • Fur is the product. Learn to skin before you hunt, or bring the animal to someone who can (Tip).

• Cougar: long heavy tail, a third of the body, black tip 85%.
More: cougar details
  • Cougar: light brown cat, compact head, long heavy tail about a third of the body with a black tip 85%. Tracks show no claws 85%. Kittens are spotted 85%.

• Watch the tail when it runs: out is wolf, down is coyote 85%.
More: wolf and coyote details
  • Wolf: 30 to 50 kg in BC, females about 20% smaller; tail carried out behind when running; big feet, broad muzzle 85%.
  • Coyote: 9 to 23 kg, bushy black tipped tail usually carried down when running, slim pointed muzzle, tall ears, small feet 85%.
  • A big dog at 200 m looks like a wolf. A hunter shot a neighbour's dog is a story that ends in court (Tip).

• Check the tail tip: black all round is lynx 70%.
More: lynx and bobcat details
  • Lynx: long ear tufts, huge furry paws, long legs, grey coat with few markings, short tail with a fully black tip 70%.
  • Bobcat: smaller, spotted tan coat, black bars on the front legs, short ear tufts, tail black on top only with a white underside 70%.

• Spots or under 1 year: a kitten. Hands off it and its mother 98%.

The rule

A cougar kitten is any cougar with spots or under one year old. You may not hunt a kitten or any cougar in its company 98%. You may not hunt a lynx or bobcat that is with another lynx or bobcat 98%.

  • Thoroughly cook wild game before eating 85%. A hare with a swollen, spotted liver or spleen goes in the bin, not the pot (hunter lore) 60%.
  • A sick looking, slow hare is a hare you do not touch 95%.
  • Check yourself for ticks after hunting brush in spring and fall 85%.

Why it matters

The coast an hour from Mission holds ducks you will never see at Heffley Creek, and one goose with a ten day season. The rules change at the tide line.

  • Brant: open only in MU (Management Unit) 2-4, March 1 to 10, 3 a day, 9 in possession 98%.
  • MU 2-4 and the Mission portion of MU 2-8 need the Fraser Valley Special Area licence and $1,000,000 liability insurance 98%.

gallery-deer:
Why it matters

You will see most deer for two seconds, half hidden, from the side or from behind. Learn every angle here so your eyes know the animal before your brain does.

  • This session is pictures first. Each screen shows one view: side, front, rear, running, bedded, in cover, far away.
  • Read the caption, then look for the one or two marks it names.
  • BC has three deer you can hunt: mule deer, white tailed deer and black tailed deer 85%.
  • The law treats black tailed deer as mule deer: the synopsis says "Mule (Black tailed) Deer" (99%, page 4, 2 October 2026 edition).
  • Photos are illustrations. The written field marks are the source of truth.
  • Photos come from many places in western North America. Captions say where.

• Ears: huge, about three quarters the length of the head 85%.
  • Antlers: each main beam splits into two, and each branch can split again 85%.
  • Face: pale, with a dark patch on the forehead in fall (Tip).

• The rear view is the fastest ID: white rump, small white tail, black tip 85%.
  • A mule deer tail hangs down, even when the deer runs 85%.

• A spooked mule deer often : all four feet hit and push off together, like a pogo stick 85%.
  • It often stops on a ridge and looks back (Tip).

• In cover, look for parts, not a whole deer: an ear, the white throat, a leg, an antler tip (Tip).
  • Sagebrush, bunchgrass and open pine are classic mule deer country in the BC Interior 85%.

• Past 300 m (328 yd), use binoculars, then a spotting scope. Never use the rifle scope to look at deer (Tip).
  • Colour fools you at distance. Shape, rump and ear size are steadier clues (Tip).

• A doe has no antlers. A (male fawn) has only bumps under the hair 85%.
  • Fawns lose their spots by early fall 80%.

• White tail antlers: one main beam with single tines growing up from it. They do not fork like a mule deer's 85%.
  • Ears are smaller than a mule deer's 85%.
• White tails gallop with the tail raised 85%. Mule deer bounce with the tail down 85%.

ClueMule deerWhite tailed deer
TailThin, white, black tip 85%Wide, brown on top, white below 85%
EarsVery large 85%Medium 85%
AntlersFork, then fork again 85%Tines off one main beam 85%
RunningStots, tail down 85%Gallops, flag up 85%
• Black tailed deer live on the coast and in the Fraser Valley, the deer you would meet around Mission 85%.

• Tail: wider than a mule deer's and dark or black down the whole top (Tip).
  • Antlers fork like a mule deer's, so the 4 point rules apply to them too (99%, page 4).
Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

"MULE (BLACK-TAILED) DEER - FOUR POINTS OR GREATER BUCK - means any buck having at least four tines, excluding the brow tine, on one antler."
  • Plain English: count one antler. Four or more true tines, not counting the , and he is a (99%, page 4, 2 October 2026 edition).
  • A must be at least 2.5 cm long and longer than it is wide (99%, page 4).
  • A spike or a fork horn (2 points) or a 3 point is not a 4 point buck (99%, page 4).

• Some seasons are for 4 point bucks only. The class column of the season table for your MU (Management Unit) says which (90%, my reading).
  • Cannot count the points for sure? Do not shoot (Tip).

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Look at the back end first, then the head. The tail tells you the species, the antlers tell you if he is legal.

Common mistakes
  • Calling a deer from its colour. Grey, brown and red coats all happen in every species.
  • Counting the brow tine on a mule deer. It is excluded from the 4 point count.
  • Shooting at a deer in cover when you only saw a leg or an ear. Wait for the whole animal.

Do this in the field
  • Every deer you see this week, say out loud: species, sex, and which view you had.
  • For every buck, count the points on the near antler through binoculars before you touch the rifle.
  • Note which mark you saw first. Most days it will be the rump or the ears.

gallery-waterfowl:
Why it matters

Ducks come in fast, in poor light, and some have their own bag limits. You must name the bird before you pull the trigger, from the side, from below and in the air.

  • Each screen shows one species group: drake (male), hen (female) and, where we found one, a flight shot.
  • In fall, many drakes are still in drab early in the season and look like hens 80%.
  • Learn the wing patch, the : it shows on both sexes and in flight 80%.

• Learn the shape too: jump straight up off the water; run along the surface to take off 80%.
  • Photos are illustrations. The written field marks are the source of truth.

• Drake: white forehead and crown, so hunters call it baldpate 80%.
  • Both sexes: short blue grey bill with a black tip 80%. In flight the drake shows a big white patch on the front of the wing 80%.

• The smallest dabbling duck in BC. Flocks twist and turn in tight bunches 80%.
  • Blue winged teal mostly leave BC early in fall (Tip).

• The only puddle duck with a white speculum 80%.
  • A gadwall hen looks like a mallard hen. Check the wing: white, not blue 80%.
• The bill is longer than the head and wide at the tip 80%. Flies with the bill pointed slightly down (Tip).

• Lives on wooded ponds, beaver ponds and sloughs with trees 80%.
  • In flight: long square tail, head held up, bill pointed down (Tip).

• Ring necked drake: black back. Scaup drake: grey back 80%.
  • Ring necked ducks like small ponds and marshes; scaup like big lakes and the coast (Tip).

• Goldeneye wings whistle in flight 80%.
  • Goldeneyes have their own limit inside the duck bag: 2 a day, Barrow's and common together (99%, page 12, 2 October 2026 edition).

• Both fly fast and low over open water, often in small groups (Tip).
  • Black and white small diver with a white head wedge: bufflehead. Bigger, with a round white face spot: goldeneye drake 80%.

• Profile tells them apart: canvasback forehead runs straight into the bill; redhead has a round head 80%.
  • Canvasback has its own limit inside the duck bag: 4 a day (99%, page 12).

• Puddle ducks spring straight up. Divers patter across the water first 80%.
  • Never shoot into a flock. Pick one bird you have named (Tip).
• A is a separate species from the Canada goose, not a young one 85%.
• Both sit in the dark goose bag in BC; check your district's goose limits (VERIFY for your area).
• White geese show black wing tips in flight. A swan is all white and much bigger 80%.

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.
  • Loons and grebes have no open season. They are protected 90%.

• Swans: no open season in BC (VERIFY in the ECCC, Environment and Climate Change Canada, BC migratory bird summary). An all white bird bigger than a goose, with no black wing tips, is a swan 80%.
  • Harlequin duck is legal in BC, but only 2 a day inside the duck bag (99%, page 12).

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

If you cannot name it, it is not a duck yet. Let it go and wait for the next one.

Common mistakes
  • Shooting at a dark shape at first light before you can see the wing patch.
  • Calling every small white duck a bufflehead. Check the head pattern.
  • Shooting a grebe or a loon that dove and came up near the decoys.

Do this in the field
  • Sit at a marsh with binoculars for an hour. Name each duck: species, drake or hen.
  • Watch how each one takes off. Jump up, or run along the water?
  • Count how many goldeneyes and canvasbacks you would have in a bag of 8.

gallery-upland:
Why it matters

Upland birds flush at your feet and are gone in a second. If you know the shape, the tail and the habitat before you go, you name the bird as it lifts.

  • Each screen shows one bird or one group, male and female where we found both.
  • Habitat is half the ID: aspen and birch for ruffed grouse, dark conifers for spruce grouse, open ridges for dusky grouse, rock and cheatgrass for chukar 80%.
  • Some look alikes have no season at all. Those are on the last photo screen.
  • Photos are illustrations. The written field marks are the source of truth.

• Grey and red (brown) colour phases. The tail band is the same in both 80%.
  • Wide dark band near the end of a long fan shaped tail 80%.
  • Explodes off the ground with a roar of wings 80%.

• The biggest forest grouse in BC 80%.
  • Sooty grouse is the coast form; the synopsis lists it in Region 2 as "SOOTY (Blue)" 99%.
• Male: plain slate grey with a pale grey band at the tail tip 80%.

• Dark conifer forest, often on the ground near spruce and lodgepole pine 80%.
  • Very tame; it often just sits and watches you 80%.
  • In southern BC the male shows white spots above a dark tail: the form 80%.

• Sharp tailed grouse: pale, with a short pointed tail that shows white in flight 80%.
  • White tailed ptarmigan: white tail in every season; willow and rock ptarmigan have black tails 80%.
  • Both are legal only in listed MUs (Management Units) and places 99%.

• Both sexes carry the teardrop plume; the male's is bigger and black 80%.
  • They live in a and run before they fly 80%.
• Legal in Region 8, not in Region 3 (99%, Region 3 page 34 has no quail row).

• Chukar: steep rocky slopes and cheatgrass; runs uphill, flies downhill 80%.
  • Pheasant: farm edges, ditches and cattails. Check your region's rules on hens (VERIFY for your region).

• Spring seasons are for bearded birds only (98%, turkey session).
  • A bearded turkey has a tuft of hair like feathers on the chest (98%, page 3). A few hens grow beards 80%.

• Turns white in fall and brown in spring, by day length, not snow 80%.
  • In a snowless fall a white hare stands out on brown ground (Tip).
Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

• Sage grouse: no season row anywhere in the synopsis, so no open season in BC (90%, my reading). It is also listed as gone from BC (Tip).
  • Mountain quail: "No open season on mountain quail" (99%, Region 1, page 21). It has a straight plume, not a curled one 80%.
  • Sharp tailed grouse outside the listed MUs: no season 99%. See the Grouse session.

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Name the bird by its tail and its trees. If it flushed from the wrong habitat, look twice.

Common mistakes
  • Shooting a sharp tailed grouse because it "looked like a grouse" in an MU with no season.
  • Calling a dusky hen a ruffed grouse. Look for the black tail band.
  • Shooting a hen pheasant where only roosters are legal.

Do this in the field
  • Every bird you flush, call out the tail: fan with a band, plain dark, pointed, or white.
  • Note the trees and ground where it rose. Match it to the habitat on this screen.
  • For turkeys in spring, find the beard through binoculars before anything else.

gallery-big-game:
Why it matters

Big animals still fool beginners: a cow moose for a bull in thick willows, a brown black bear for a grizzly, a coyote for a wolf. One wrong call can be a protected animal.

  • Each screen shows one animal or one comparison, from several angles.
  • Read the caption, then find the mark it names in the photo.
  • Bears: colour does not tell you the species. Shape does 85%.
  • Photos come from western North America unless the caption says otherwise.
  • Photos are illustrations. The written field marks are the source of truth.
• Biggest deer in the world; black brown, with a long face and a under the throat 85%.

• Young bulls carry spikes or small forks; big bulls carry wide palms 85%.
  • Some seasons are for only: no more than 2 points on one antler (99%, page 3, 2 October 2026 edition).
• A cow has no antlers. A calf stays with her through its first winter 85%.
• A is a moose in its first year; it is never a spike fork bull (99%, page 3).

• Elk: tan body, dark brown neck and legs, pale rump patch 85%.
  • Bigger than a deer, smaller and much paler than a moose 85%.
• Antlers sweep back over the body with long tines; count the brow tine on elk (99%, page 3).
• Black bears come in black, brown, cinnamon and blonde 85%.
• No open season on the white (Kermode) or blue (Glacier) phases (98%, page 80, Notice to Black Bear Hunters).
Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

• Unlawful: "To hunt a black bear less than 2 years old or any bear in its company" (98%, page 11, item 14).
  • Plain English: no cubs, no yearlings, and not the sow with them 98%. Watch any bear for several minutes before you decide (Tip).

• No open season on grizzly bears anywhere in BC (98%, page 19).
  • Marks: , , short round ears, long pale front claws 85%.

ClueBlack bearGrizzly
ShoulderNo hump 85%Big muscle hump 85%
FaceStraight from forehead to nose 85%Dished 85%
EarsTall, pointed 85%Short, round 85%
Front clawsShort, dark, curved 85%Long, pale, straighter 85%

• Bighorn: brown body, white muzzle, white belly and rump patch 85%.
  • Ram horns are heavy and curl; ewe horns are short and thin, like a goat's 85%.

• Mountain goat: all white, black dagger horns on both sexes, black hooves 85%.
  • A sheep's horns are amber or brown, never black 85%.

• Cougar tail is long, about a third of its body 85%. Lynx and bobcat tails are short 85%.
  • Lynx tail tip is black all around; bobcat tail is black on top, white under 70%.
• Wolf: 30 to 50 kg in BC; coyote: 9 to 23 kg 85%.

• Wolf: broad blocky muzzle, short rounded ears. Coyote: narrow pointed muzzle, tall pointed ears 85%.
  • Coyotes run with the tail down; wolves carry it straight out (Tip).

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Bears: look for the hump and the face, never the colour. If you are not sure, it is a grizzly, and you do not shoot.

Common mistakes
  • Calling a brown or cinnamon bear a grizzly, or a black grizzly a black bear. Check hump, face and ears.
  • Shooting a cow moose in willows because only the body showed. Wait to see the head.
  • Shooting a lone bear without waiting for cubs to show up behind it.

Do this in the field
  • Every bear you see: say "hump or no hump, dish or straight, ears tall or round" before anything else.
  • Every moose: find the head and count points on one antler.
  • Every canid: weigh it in your head. Mallard sized head and slim legs, coyote. Big blocky head, wolf.

shooting-skills:
Why it matters

The rifle is zeroed from a bench. Deer are shot from dirt, snow and sticks. The gap between the two is the shot you miss.

• Steadiest first: prone, sitting, kneeling, standing 85%.
  • A rest beats a position. Sticks make standing work (Tip).
  • Your max range is a number you tested, not a feeling (opinion).
More: all key points
  • Four standard rifle positions: prone, sitting, kneeling, standing. Prone is the steadiest. Standing is the hardest 85%.
  • Get closer if you can. Get steadier if you can. A rest beats a position (Tip).
  • Sticks or a tripod turn a standing shot into a real option in tall grass and brush 70%.
  • Five fundamentals: aiming, breath control, movement control, trigger control, follow through 85%.
  • Dry fire builds the trigger press for free. Tikka says use a snap cap 95%.
  • Your max ethical range is a number you tested, not a feeling. The 20 cm test is on a later screen (Hunt Mentor method, opinion).
  • Four weeks and about 60 rounds gets a beginner there (Tip).

Four positions, step by step1 of 4
  • Prone is steadiest, standing is hardest 85%.
  • Offhand only when the deer is close and there is no time to sit (Tip).

  • Sitting. Both arms supported by your legs. Next to prone, the steadiest 85%.

My lean (opinion)

This is Hunt Mentor's method, an opinion, not a law. It is stricter than most hunters' habits on purpose.

  • Target: a 20 cm circle. A paper plate. Deer vitals are about 20 to 25 cm (8 to 10 in) across, so the plate gives margin 70%.
  • Cold. First shots of the day. No warm up, no sighters. A deer gives you none (Tip).
  • Field position. Sitting or sticks, whichever you will really use. Not the bench (Tip).
  • Timed. From standing with the rifle slung: get down, 3 shots, 90 seconds (Tip).

shot-placement:
Why it matters

One bullet through both lungs is a dead animal within sight. One bullet a hand too far back is a night of tracking and often a lost animal.

Find the spot in 3 steps1 of 3
  • Aim for both lungs, just behind the shoulder 85%.
  • Broadside is best, quartering away is second 85%.
  • No head, neck or rear end shots 85%.
More: all key points
  • The target is the heart and lungs: in the chest, just behind the front shoulder, about one third of the way up from the bottom of the chest 85%.
  • Broadside is the best angle for deer, elk, moose and bear. Quartering away is second 85%.
  • Aim for both lungs, not the heart. The lungs are the biggest vital target and give the most room for error 85%.
  • Quartering to, head on and rear end shots: beginners wait (Tip). Rear end shots: nobody takes them 85%.
  • Head and neck shots: small targets, small margin, lost animals. Not for you 85%.
  • Bears: the heart sits low, the lungs reach well back, and the hair fools your eye. Halfway up, tight behind the shoulder 85%.
  • After the hit, read the reaction and the blood. It tells you how long to wait 85%.

• Lungs fill the chest behind the shoulder: your target 85%.
  • Heart sits low. Liver and paunch behind the lungs are slow kills 85%.
More: each organ in detail
  • Heart: low in the chest, just above and slightly behind the front leg. Small and deadly 85%.
  • Lungs: fill the chest above and behind the heart. On a deer the pair is about the size of a volleyball 75%.
  • Shoulder bones: the shoulder blade and upper leg bone sit over the front of the chest. A .308 bullet breaks them. An arrow does not 85%.
  • Liver: just behind the lungs. A hit there kills, but slowly 85%.
  • Spine: runs along the top of the back, a little below the hair line. A hit drops the animal. A near miss above it is a clean miss 75%.
  • Paunch: behind the liver. Stomach and guts. A hit there is a slow death and a hard track 85%.
  • Hunter Ed's rule: find the near front leg, go straight up its back edge, aim one third of the way up from the bottom of the chest 85%.

• Broadside: best. Quartering away: good, exit the far shoulder 85%.
  • Quartering toward: wait for the turn (Tip). Facing away: never 85%.

A shotgun is pointed, not aimed. The bird is where it will be, not where it is. Most misses are behind the bird and over the top of it.

  • Cut cleanly with a knife or scissors. Make the notch obvious. Tip.
  • Carry a pen. Some fields may be written, not cut. VERIFY on your own licence before the hunt.
  • Notch first, then confirm dead with the eye touch, then knife. Phase 1 Session 13 had the order right.

• Keep the papers until the meat is eaten 95%.
More: the carry rules, word for word
  • "You must carry all your species licences while hunting, both cancelled and uncancelled" (95%, p. 5).
  • Unlawful: "To hunt without carrying all species licences, including cancelled species licences, issued during the licence year" (95%, p. 12).
  • Lost one? Replace it at FrontCounter BC or Service BC for $10. You must declare the harvest from the cancelled original (95%, p. 8).
  • "Hunters must keep all documents under which an animal was taken until the animal has been consumed" (95%, p. 7).
  • Mounted head or tanned hide: keep the licence "in a safe place indefinitely" (95%, p. 7).

• Unskinned tail AND the sex organ, on meat you carry 95%.
  • The antlered head does not replace them 95%.
More: the law, word for word
The rule

Deer: leave "naturally attached to the carcass or one part of the carcass in the person's possession" the "unskinned tail, AND: i. If the animal is male, a testicle or part of the penis, ii. If the animal is female, a portion of the udder and teats" (95%, p. 15).

  • Both parts. Tail and sex organ, attached to meat you are carrying 95%.
  • The antlered head is not a substitute for the tail and testicle on a deer (95%, p. 15; Hunting Regulation s. 15).
  • "Unskinned" means the tail keeps its hide. Do not skin the tail 95%.
  • When can it come off? "after it arrives at a person's normal dwelling place and is butchered and stored there", "after it is taken to a meat cutter or the owner or operator of a cold storage plant", or "after it has been inspected by a qualified Compulsory Inspector" (95%, p. 15).

• Plan the cut before you start (Tip).
More: the gutless tip in full
  • Gutless method: leave the tail on a strip of hide on one hind quarter, and the testicle or penis attached to that same quarter. Plan the cut before you start (Tip, my practical reading of "one part of the carcass").

• Antlers are never evidence of sex, deer or moose 95%.
More: every species, word for word
  • Caribou, elk or moose: "the animal's tail or another readily identifiable part of the hide not less than 6 cm2, AND" a testicle or part of the penis, or "a portion of the udder or teats" (95%, p. 15).
  • Antlers are not evidence of sex for moose either. BC lists only the tail or hide patch plus the organ 95%. Alaska says the same in plain words: "Moose antlers are not proof of sex" 80%.
  • Black bear: not on the evidence of sex list for Regions 2 and 3 (95%, p. 15 lists caribou, elk, moose, deer, bison, goat, sheep, cougar).
  • Black bear still has its own rules: no possessing or trafficking a gall bladder or paws separated from the carcass (95%, p. 12). Leave the gall at the kill site, or dispose of the gut pile within 48 hours (95%, p. 12).
  • Cougar: skull and hide with evidence of sex attached, plus compulsory inspection (95%, p. 15, p. 17).

• Region 3 mule deer: 4 point seasons in September and Nov to Dec 10. October is any buck 95%.
More: the law and the Region 3 seasons, word for word
The rule

"A person must, while returning from hunting, keep the antlers or horns, naturally attached to a portion of the upper skull, of wildlife killed during an antler/horn restricted season (e.g., 6 pt, full curl, spike fork, etc.) and the species licence under which the wildlife was killed, together and available for inspection by an officer" (95%, p. 15).

  • Region 3 mule deer: seasons Sept 10 to Sept 30 and Nov 1 to Dec 10 in most s (Management Units) 3-12 to 3-20 and 3-26 to 3-44. "The antlers must accompany the species licence" (95%, p. 34).
  • Region 3 mule deer Oct 1 to Oct 31: "Bucks". Any antlered buck, no point rule (95%, p. 34). Your first October hunt falls here.
  • Region 3 moose: spike fork bulls only. "Antlers must accompany the species licence" (95%, p. 34).
  • Unlawful to "alter or tamper with horns or antlers" from a restricted season until the carcass reaches a meat cutter, cold storage, your home where it is butchered, or compulsory inspection (95%, p. 12).
  • Antlers "altered or tampered with in any way" are no longer "naturally attached" (95%, Hunting Regulation s. 15.1).
• Four or more tines on one antler, brow tine not counted (99%, page 4).

• Upland birds: one feathered wing. Ducks and geese: a wing or the head 95%.
More: the bird rules, word for word
  • Grouse, quail and other non migratory game birds: "must leave attached to the carcass one feathered wing" (95%, p. 15). Turkey in a bearded season: the beard too.
  • Ducks, geese and other migratory game birds: "one feathered wing or the feathered head" (95%, p. 15).
  • Game bird : "both breasts" (95%, p. 3). The legs are yours to take too. Tip.

• Region 3 deer and black bear: no inspection, no report 95%.
  • Moose licence? Report by March 31 even if you never hunted 95%.

field-dressing:
Why it matters

Meat starts to spoil the minute the heart stops. The next hour with a knife decides what ends up in your freezer.

Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

MethodWhat it isLean
GuttedGuts out, carry it wholeDeer within 300 m of the truck
GutlessMeat off, guts stay inFar in, or any moose
  • Licence notched first. See Session 6.
More: the two methods and the law parts
  • Two ways to open a deer: the gutted method (classic) and the (skin and take the meat, leave the guts in).
  • Both are skills, not law. The law parts: notch first, evidence of sex, edible portions, bear galls, safe meat handling.
  • Everything below assumes the licence is already notched. See Session 6.

• One sharp fixed blade knife plus a backup (Tip).
  • Cloth game bags, never plastic 80%.
  • Gloves: provincial advice for disease safety 95%.
More: the full tool list
  • One sharp fixed blade knife, 8 to 10 cm, and a replaceable blade knife as backup. Tip.
  • A small sharpener. A dull knife is the one that cuts you. Tip.
  • Bone saw or folding saw: only for the skull plate and ribs. Tip.
  • Game bags: 4 for a deer, 8 for a moose. Cotton or synthetic, never plastic (80%, Alaska Department of Fish and Game).
  • Nitrile gloves, plus a cut resistant glove for the off hand. Gloves are also provincial advice for disease safety (95%, synopsis p. 18).
  • Tarp, 10 m of rope, a small pulley for moose, headlamp, paper towel, zip ties for tagging bags. Tip.
  • Zip bags for the heart and liver if you want them (80%, Penn State Extension).

More: before the knife in detail
  • Notch the licence. Photograph it beside the animal (95%, Session 6).
  • Decide which hind quarter keeps the unskinned tail and the testicle or udder. Cut around them, never through them (95%, Session 6).
  • Rifle unloaded and set where it will not fall, be lost in the dark, or get blood in the action (70%, BC Outdoors Magazine).
  • Animal on its back, head uphill, braced with rocks or a rope to a tree. Tip.
  • Gloves on. Headlamp on if light is going. Tip.
  • Bear country: bear spray on your belt, not in the pack (70%, BC Outdoors Magazine).

Gut a deer in 8 steps1 of 8
  • Do not cut the paunch. Do not cut off the evidence of sex (Tip).
  • Gut contents on meat: wash that spot and dry it at once 80%.
More: the 10 written steps
  1. Cut around the anus, free the rectum 10 cm in, and tie it off with string or a zip tie. A bag over it stops leaks (80%, Penn State Extension).
  2. Pinch the belly skin at the pelvis. Small cut, then two fingers inside guiding the blade up, edge up, to the bottom of the breastbone. Skin and muscle together, no stomach 80%.
  3. Roll the paunch and intestines out to one side. Do not pull hard yet. Tip.
  4. Cut the diaphragm free along the ribs on both sides (Tip, common practice).
  5. Reach up into the chest. Cut the windpipe and gullet as high as you can. Pull heart and lungs down and out (Tip).
  6. Pull the tied rectum through the pelvis from inside. No need to saw the pelvis or the breastbone (80%, North Dakota State University Extension).
  7. Save the heart and liver in a zip bag on ice if you want them 80%.
  8. Tip the carcass to drain. Wipe the cavity with a dry cloth or paper towel. Trim any gut contents and the bloodshot meat (80%, Penn State Extension, Alaska Department of Fish and Game).
  9. Prop the chest open with a clean stick. Hang it, or lay it on logs in the shade (80%, Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife).
  10. Clean your knife and hands. Wash before you eat anything (95%, synopsis p. 18).
  • Gut contents on the meat: wash that spot with clean water and dry it right away. Otherwise do not wash. Water removes the blood glaze that slows bacteria (80%, Alaska Department of Fish and Game).
▶How to Field Dress a Deer with Steven Rinella - MeatEaterGut a deer step by step, blade up, no punctured gut.
MeatEater, YouTube, 7 min. Needs internet.

Gutless in 8 steps1 of 8
  • Never leave the guts in overnight. It spoils regardless of temperature 80%.
  • Neck, ribs and loins still come out 95%.
More: the 10 written steps
  1. Animal on its side. Cut around the hocks, down the inside of each top leg, and up the midline from the pelvis to the chin. Cut around the genitals and leave them attached (80%, Alaska Department of Fish and Game).
  2. Skin the top half back past the spine. Short knife strokes, blade angled shallow, inside of hide to outside. Spread the hide: it is your clean mat 80%.
  3. Front quarter: lift the leg, cut into the armpit through the loose tissue, follow it up to the shoulder blade and cut it free. No bone to cut 80%.
  4. Hind quarter: from the inner thigh follow the seam down to the pelvis, fillet the muscle off the pelvis to the hip joint, cut the ligaments, free it 80%.
  5. Backstrap: knife flat against the vertical spine, cut from pelvis to neck. Second cut along the horizontal bones out over the ribs. Peel it off 80%.
  6. Ribs and flank: cut the rib meat off the bone or saw the ribs off. Take the flank between the ribs and the rear leg 80%. In BC the ribs are legal edible portions 95%.
  7. Tenderloin: inside the cavity, behind the last rib, under the backbone. Shallow cut, work it free with fingers, cut both ends. Do not puncture the gut 80%.
  8. Roll the animal onto the clean hide and repeat on the other side 80%.
  9. Neck: skin to behind the ears and fillet the neck meat off, or take the whole neck 80%.
  10. Head: saw the skull plate with antlers through the eye sockets, or take the whole head with 8 cm of neck for a (Chronic Wasting Disease) test (95%, BC CWD page; Session 10).
  • Every piece goes straight into its own game bag. Hang the bags, never stack them 80%.
  • Never leave the guts in overnight and come back. It "will cause spoilage regardless of outside temperature" (80%, Alaska Department of Fish and Game). Gut it instead.
  • The gutless method does not excuse you from the neck, ribs and loins. The rule is the same 95%.
My lean (opinion)

Deer within 300 m of the truck or ATV (all terrain vehicle): gut it and drag or carry it whole. Deer a kilometre into the timber, or any moose: gutless, into bags, pack it out. Gutless keeps the paunch away from the meat but you must still reach in for the tenderloins.

▶The Gutless vs Gutting Method for Field Dressing a DeerGutless method: take the meat, leave the guts inside.
Montana Knife Company, YouTube, 8 min. Needs internet.
• Same order every time and you will not forget a loin (Tip).

• Legs come off at the joints. No saw needed 80%.
  • Bone in or boned out: both legal if all edible portions come out 95%.
More: quartering details
  • "Quartering" for a packer means: four leg quarters off, then backstraps, tenderloins, neck meat and rib meat, in bags (70%, MeatEater).
  • Legs come off at the joints. No saw needed: shoulder through the armpit, hind leg through the hip ball joint (80%, Alaska Department of Fish and Game).
  • Bone in quarters keep meat cleaner and drier. Boned out meat weighs half as much. Both are legal in BC as long as the edible portions all come out 95%.
  • Leave the lower legs on until the quarter is off. They are handles 80%.
  • A gutted deer can be split in half across the spine behind the ribs for two people to carry. Tip.
▶How to Quarter and Pack Game out of the Backcountry - Conservation Field Notes with Steven RinellaQuarter the animal so you can carry it out.
MeatEater, YouTube, 4 min. Needs internet.

• Hang by the hind legs. Fist and pull, knife as little as possible 80%.
  • Above freezing on a big animal or a bear: skin it soon 80%.
More: skinning details
  • Hang by the hind legs on a gambrel through the tendon and hock (80%, North Dakota State University Extension).
  • Cut around the hocks, down the inside of the legs, up the belly. Then fist and pull. Use the knife as little as possible 80%.
  • Keep hair off the meat. Knife moves from hide side out. Wipe hair off immediately 80%.
  • Head off at the atlas joint: the first joint behind the skull 80%.
  • Hide on or off? On: insulation in hard cold, protection on the drag. Off: faster cooling. Above freezing on a big animal or a bear, skin it as soon as you can (80%, Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife, Penn State Extension).
  • Skin it before it freezes stiff. A frozen hide is a long job. Tip.
▶Skinning a DeerSkin a hanging deer and keep hair off the meat.
Farmstead Meatsmith, YouTube, 10 min. Needs internet.

• Decide before any cut forward of the shoulders 70%.
  • Never cut the throat or brisket on a mount 70%.
More: caping details
  • Decide before any cut forward of the shoulders. A throat cut or a brisket cut ruins the mount (70%, Outdoor Edge pro staff).
  • Ring cut around the body well behind the front shoulders. The taxidermist wants 20 to 30 cm (8 to 12 in) of hide behind the shoulder 70%.
  • One cut up the centre of the back of the neck to between the antler bases. Never down the throat 70%.
  • Peel the cape forward over the shoulders and neck to the back of the skull. Cut the head off at the atlas joint with the cape still on it 70%.
  • Leave the ears, eyes, lips and nose to the taxidermist. Cool it fast. Freeze or salt within 24 to 48 hours 70%.
  • Antler restricted season: antlers stay on the skull plate with the licence (95%, Session 6). Evidence of sex stays with the carcass, not the cape 95%.
  • More in Session 13, Trophy care.

• Meat never touches the ground. Hide, then tarp (Tip).
  • No plastic bags on warm meat. Ever 80%.
More: keeping meat clean in detail
  • Clean, cool, dry. Dirt, hair, moisture and gut contents are the enemies (80%, Alaska Department of Fish and Game).
  • Hide as a mat. Tarp as a second mat. Meat never touches the ground. Tip.
  • Trim blood clots and bloodshot meat at the site. Less weight, less spoilage 80%.
  • Let the meat form a dry crust in the bag. It slows bacteria and stops flies laying 80%.
  • No plastic bags on warm meat. Ever (80%, Alaska Department of Fish and Game, Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife).
  • Clean the knife often. Wash hands and tools when done (95%, synopsis p. 18).

More: cold weather details
  • Below freezing the meat is safe for a long time, but a whole carcass can freeze before it cools inside. Open it, prop it, and get the heat out first. Tip.
  • Hide on protects the meat from drying and from freezing solid on a long drag (80%, Penn State Extension).
  • Skin and quarter before the hide freezes on. Tip.
  • Snow in the cavity works like ice packs. Bagged is better than loose (80%, Penn State Extension).
  • Coyotes and ravens find a hanging deer by morning. Hang high or take it home. Tip.

• A valley afternoon in October can hit 20°C: a spoilage day (Tip).
  • Skin, quarter, bag, shade. Cooler the same day 80%.
More: warm weather details
  • A valley afternoon in October can hit 20°C. That is a spoilage day (Tip).
  • Gut or go gutless within the hour. Skin it. Quarter it. Bags. Shade. Air 80%.
  • Bags of ice in the chest cavity if the air is above 4°C (5°C per Penn State) (80%, Penn State Extension).
  • To a cooler or a cold room the same day (80%, Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife).
  • Never a tarp or a closed truck canopy on a warm carcass. Open air on the drive 80%.
  • Bears: thick coat and fat hold heat. Skin a bear right away in any weather above freezing (80%, Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife).

More: the law in full

  • Evidence of sex stays naturally attached to one part you possess (95%, p. 15).
  • Take all the edible portions: "neck, ribs, four quarters and the loins" (95%, p. 3, p. 12).

meat-care:
Why it matters

Nobody loses meat to a bad shot. They lose it to a warm afternoon, a tarp and a closed truck.

Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

  • One target: meat below 4°C (40°F), as fast as you can 80%.
More: where these numbers come from
  • Four enemies: heat, moisture, dirt, gut contents (80%, Alaska Department of Fish and Game).
  • One target: meat below 4°C (40°F), as fast as you can (80%, Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife).
  • Food safety numbers here come from state and university food safety sources, not BC law. BC adds the handling advice on synopsis p. 18.

• Danger zone 4 to 60°C. Freezer minus 18°C. Cook to 71°C (80 to 95%).
  • Best: in a cooler the same day as the kill 80%.

  • Hide on while aging protects the meat from drying (80%, Penn State Extension, aging at 0°C to 3°C with hide on).
  • Do not age: a young animal, one shot in warm weather and not chilled fast, one that ran hard or was trailed for hours, one with heavy wound damage, or a dirty carcass 80%.
  • Slime, mould or off smell: stop, trim, freeze at once 80%.
  • No cold room? Skip aging. Cut and freeze within a few days at fridge temperature. Tip.

• Rain: a tarp as a roof, with an air gap. Never wrapped 80%.
  • Flies: bags, plus pepper or citric acid on the surface 80%.
More: flies, rain and warm days in detail
  • Flies: a skinned carcass in cheesecloth or a game bag. Black pepper or food grade citric acid on the surface helps (80%, Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife).
  • A dry crust on the meat "deters egg laying insects" (80%, Alaska Department of Fish and Game).
  • Rain: tarp as a roof above, with an air gap. Never a tarp wrapped around 80%.
  • Wet meat spoils faster. Dry it with paper towel and keep it in bags under cover. Tip.
  • Warm day plan: skin, quarter, bag, shade by noon. Cooler by evening. Tip.
  • Night cold, day warm: hang it out at night, cooler by day. Tip.

• Ice on the bottom, bagged meat on top. Drain melt daily (Tip).
  • Thermometer inside: under 4°C or add ice 80%.
More: cooler details
  • Two coolers: one for quarters, one for loins, neck and trim. A 70 litre cooler holds a boned deer with ice. Tip.
  • Frozen water jugs or bagged ice on the bottom. Meat in game bags on top. Drain the melt water daily. Meat never sits in water. Tip.
  • Keep the lid closed and the cooler in the shade of the truck, not the cab. Tip.
  • A cheap thermometer inside. Under 4°C or add ice (80%, Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife target).
  • Transport: carcass "clean and dry", "out of direct sunlight", with air flow. Chill fully before any plastic 80%.
  • Long drive from Heffley Creek to Mission in October: boned meat in coolers with ice, not a whole deer on the roof. Tip.

More: what spoils meat in detail
  • Heat: the cavity, the hide, the sun, the truck 80%.
  • Moisture: rain, washing, condensation inside plastic 80%.
  • Dirt and hair: wipe off at once, keep meat on the hide or a tarp 80%.
  • Gut contents: a cut paunch or bladder. Wash the spot, dry it, trim it 80%.
  • Delay: slow gutting and "failure to cool the carcass promptly" are the usual causes of strong flavours (80%, North Dakota State University).
  • Stress: an animal run hard before it died is tougher and ages badly (80%, Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife).

  • Cook all bear meat to at least 71°C 95%.
More: the federal advice in full
The rule

Not a BC hunting rule, but federal food safety advice: "All wild game meat, pork and horse meat should be cooked to an internal temperature of at least 71°C" (95%, Canadian Food Inspection Agency).

  • In Canada "the primary risk for acquiring trichinellosis is through the consumption of undercooked or raw meat from wildlife species such as bears and walruses" 95%.
  • "Most species of Trichinella found in wildlife are resistant to freezing" 95%. Freezing a bear roast does not make it safe.
  • "Curing (salting), drying, smoking or microwaving the meat does not consistently kill infective larvae" 95%. No bear jerky unless cooked to 71°C first.
  • Washington goes higher: 74°C (165°F) for all game, 77°C (170°F) for bear 80%.
  • Skin a bear fast. The coat and fat hold heat 80%.
  • Bear fat renders well. Trim it off the meat for storage. Tip.
  • Bear meat is a legal edible portion in BC like any big game (95%, synopsis p. 3).

More: bird care details
  • Gut and remove the crop as soon as you can. It opens the cavity for cooling (80%, North Dakota State University).
  • Cool to 2°C to 4°C (35°F to 40°F) fast. Do not pile warm birds. Keep them apart in the cooler (80%, Penn State Extension).
  • Keep one fully feathered wing on grouse and quail, a wing or the feathered head on ducks and geese, until home (95%, synopsis p. 15).
  • Pluck ducks if you will roast them. The skin keeps the meat moist (80%, Penn State Extension).
  • Grouse and quail: soak 1 to 2 hours in cold water to pull blood out, then fridge 80%.
  • Age birds no more than 2 to 3 days at 4°C or less (80%, Penn State Extension).
  • Cook birds to 74°C (165°F) (80%, North Dakota State University).

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

If you would not leave a steak on the dashboard, do not leave a deer in the truck.

  • Aging a gut shot deer that was trailed for 5 hours in the sun.
  • Freezing bear meat and calling it safe. Freezing does not kill wild Trichinella.

Thermometer in the cooler. Check it when you check the ice. Under 4°C, every time you look.

Why it matters

A deer is one hard trip. A moose is a weekend. Plan the pack out before you plan the shot.

Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

  • Every edible portion comes out, however many trips 95%.
More: the three ways out
  • Three ways out: on your back, on a sled, on the (all terrain vehicle).
  • The ATV has its own rulebook: the Wildlife Act, the Off Road Vehicle Act, and federal firearm transport rules.
  • The one rule that never changes: every edible portion comes out, however many trips it takes 95%.

• Big game: neck, ribs, four quarters and loins come home 95%.
  • Birds: both breasts 95%. Bones, hide, head and guts can stay 95%.
More: the law in full
The rule

Unlawful: "To kill wildlife (with the exception of a fur bearing animal other than a black bear) and fail to remove from the carcass the edible portions (see definitions section) to the person's normal dwelling place or to a meat cutter or the owner or operator of a cold storage plant" (95%, synopsis p. 12).

  • for big game: "the edible portions of the neck, ribs, four quarters and the loins of the animal" (95%, p. 3).
  • Game birds: "the edible portions of both breasts of the bird" (95%, p. 3).
  • You may hand the animal to someone else who then takes the edible portions home. The duty moves with the meat (95%, p. 12).
  • Boning out is fine. Bones, hide, head and guts can stay at the site, or go to a landfill (95%, p. 12; p. 81 on landfill disposal of cervid parts).
  • Not within municipal boundaries and not where people go: a carcass is an attractant (95%, p. 9, p. 15).

• ATV (all terrain vehicle): no live round in the chamber or attached magazine 99%.
  • No hunting from it. Check closures for your MU (Management Unit) 95%.
  • Region 3: MUs 3-28, 3-29, 3-30 and part of 3-17 closed Sept 1 to Dec 10 95%.
More: the Wildlife Act rules in full
  • An ATV is a "motor vehicle" under the hunting rules (95%, p. 4 definition).
  • Unlawful: a firearm "containing live ammunition in its breech or in its magazine attached to the firearm, in or on a railway car, motor vehicle, sleigh, aircraft, bicycle or other conveyance" (99%, page 11, item 28 (2 October 2026 edition)).
  • So: magazine out, chamber empty, before you touch the ATV. Clip with rounds in the rifle counts as loaded (95%, p. 3).
  • Unlawful "To hunt wildlife from a motor vehicle" (99%, page 11, item 22 (2 October 2026 edition)).
  • Motor Vehicle for Hunting Closed Area: using a motor vehicle "to hunt, transport wildlife, transport equipment and supplies which are intended for or in support of hunting, or transport hunters to and from the location of wildlife is prohibited" (95%, p. 10).
  • "Unless specifically exempted, all motor vehicle prohibitions include private land" (95%, p. 10).
  • Region 3 ATV for Hunting Closed Areas: "from Sept 1 - Dec 10 in MUs 3-28, 3-29, 3-30, and that portion of MU 3-17 shown on Map C3" (95%, p. 33).
  • Stake Lake cross country ski trails near Kamloops: closed to ATVs and snowmobiles (95%, p. 33).
  • Maps for every closure: gov.bc.ca/motorvehicleprohibitions (95%, p. 10). Signs may be missing. "The regulation is the final authority" 95%.

More: the ORV Act in full
  • The (Off Road Vehicle) Act "applies to ORVs on Crown land and prescribed private land" (95%, p. 9).
  • "Mandatory registration applies to ORVs. The plate or sticker must be clearly displayed on the front, back or left side of the ORV" (95%, p. 9). Registration is through the Insurance Corporation of British Columbia (95%, ORV Act s. 4).
  • "Mandatory safety laws apply to all ORVs; this includes helmets for ride astride ORVs and seatbelts (if installed). People under 16 must be supervised by an adult at least 19 years" (95%, p. 9).
  • "While travelling on a Forest Service Road, operators of ATVs are required to hold a valid driver's licence and carry a minimum of $200,000 third party liability insurance" (95%, p. 9).
  • Carry government photo ID if you are 12 or older (95%, BC ORV page).
  • Fines: $230 for an unregistered ORV, $368 for careless operation (95%, BC ORV page).
  • Spark arrestor required during wildfire conditions. $460 ticket without one (95%, BC ORV page).
  • Crossing or riding a public highway needs ICBC basic insurance and a free police issued operation permit where it applies (90%, BC ORV page and search summary). VERIFY with ICBC for your route.

• Rifle unloaded in transport. It goes with you, not on the parked quad (95%, Tip).
  • Licence travels with the meat. Brother's deer: his Record of Receipt 95%.
More: firearms and game in detail
  • Federal transport rule: a non restricted rifle may be transported only if "it is unloaded" (95%, SOR/98-209 s. 10).
  • Unattended ATV with the rifle on it: no lockable trunk, so the rifle must be "not visible from outside the vehicle" and the compartment "securely locked" (95%, s. 10). Practical answer: the rifle goes with you, not on the parked quad. Tip.
  • Carrying your own game on an ATV: no extra rule in the synopsis beyond closures (85%, my reading). The licence travels with the meat (95%, p. 15).
  • Carrying your brother's deer alone: his Record of Receipt in your pocket (95%, p. 15).
  • Strap quarters in game bags on the rear rack, meat away from the exhaust. Tip.
  • Whole deer across the front rack: head up, belly cavity open, drive slowly. Tip.
  • A loaded rack changes the handling. Low speed, no side hills. Tip.

• 20 to 30 kg per trip is sustainable for a fit adult (Tip).
  • Going back to a cache: wind in your face, make noise 70%.
More: packs, sleds and drags
  • A pack frame with a load shelf carries a quarter or two bags. Strap the load high and tight to your back. Tip.
  • Fit adult, rough ground: 20 to 30 kg per trip is sustainable. 40 kg is a one trip hero load. Tip.
  • "A load that blocks your view or pulls you off balance is too heavy" (70%, BC Outdoors Magazine).
  • Sleds: a plastic game sled or kids toboggan on snow, with a rope harness. Whole deer in one pull downhill. Tip.
  • Drag a whole deer by the antlers or a rope around the neck, head first, hide on. Tip.
  • Return trips: approach the cache with the wind in your face and make noise. Bears claim meat (70%, BC Outdoors Magazine).
