named-areas:
Why it matters

These are the places that government pages, magazines and forums name. Learn them for the rules and the country, and expect company.

Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

• Every card shows species, MU (Management Unit), access and certainty.
More: how to read this session
  • A public name means more hunters. Every place here is named online or in print, so plan on it being busier (Tip).
  • The quiet spots are not on this list. They come from the Spot Finder map's candidate spots, built from land status, roads, closures and habitat, and from your own scouting. Not from the internet (Tip).
  • Each place shows what it is known for, the access type, the source type and a certainty.
  • Access types: Park (the BC Parks page says firearms are permitted for hunting in open season), WMA (Wildlife Management Area: rules vary, so contact the regional office first), Rec site (recreation site: no shooting within 100 m of camp structures), Permission (private or reserve land), Closed.
  • Forum and blog mentions are capped at 60%. Treat them as leads to check, not facts.
  • MU (Management Unit) numbers are point checks on the official layer at the place name 90%. Check the boundary on the MU map before you hunt.

Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

  • Parks open, Tranquille and Wells Gray closed (85 to 99%).
More: named by government, in full

Named by government

  • Lac du Bois Grasslands Protected Area. Bighorn, mule and white tailed deer, moose, waterfowl, sharp tailed grouse. Park, but no shooting in the part inside Kamloops city limits; ATVs (all terrain vehicles) closed for hunting 1 Sep to 10 Dec. BC Parks, synopsis page 33 95%.
  • Dewdrop Rosseau Creek Wildlife Management Area, north shore of Kamloops Lake, Management Unit 3-29. Winter range for mule deer and bighorn. Motor vehicle closed, Map C16. BC page, synopsis page 33 90%.
  • Tranquille Wildlife Management Area, head of Kamloops Lake. Geese and swans stage here spring and fall. Closed: No Shooting, Map C17 85%.
  • Bonaparte Provincial Park. Moose, mule deer, black bear, waterfowl, ruffed and spruce grouse. Park; logging roads up Jamieson Creek or float plane. BC Parks 95%.
  • Tunkwa Provincial Park, Tunkwa Lake in Management Unit 3-18. Moose, mule and white tailed deer, Canada goose, mallard, snipe. Park; vehicles on designated trails only. BC Parks 90%.
  • Dunn Peak Provincial Park. Mule deer, mountain goat, black bear. Park. BC Parks 90%.
  • Wells Gray Park, Management Unit 3-45. Closed: no hunting, no firearms. Synopsis page 33 99%.

More: rec sites, in full

Rec sites that list hunting

  • Rec site rule: no shooting within 100 m of camp structures 99%.
  • These sites have hunting among their first 3 listed activities in the provincial data 90%.
  • Near Heffley Creek: Community Lake Southwest and Sullivan Lake (Knouff), Management Unit 3-27. Toward Sun Peaks: McGillivray Lake West, Morrisey Lake West 90%.
  • North and west: Pass Lake (Management Unit 3-29), Fishtrap Creek, Dunsapie Lake and Gorman Lake (Management Unit 3-28), Mayson Lake (Management Unit 3-30) 90%.
  • Leads to check, not facts (50 to 85%).
More: hunter talk, in full

Hunter talk: leads, not facts

  • Jamieson Creek, Management Unit 3-28 at its mouth. A 1976 study used it as Kamloops deer winter range 80%. Forum: mule deer 50%. Land status VERIFY.
  • Barriere Lakes and the Chu Chua road ridges, Management Unit 3-38. Blog, 2011: "Moose, Mule Deer and Black bear", ridges after snow 55%. Land status VERIFY.
  • Deadman River, Red Lake, Criss Creek, Management Unit 3-29. Blog, 2011: "mule deer hunting, some moose" 55%.
  • Little Fort to Clearwater. Blog, 2011: "heavily hunted but success ratios are good" 55%.
  • Paul Lake, Pinantan, Heffley, Management Unit 3-27. Forum mention: mule deer 50%.
  • Bonaparte Plateau. A provincial moose research area since 2012 85%. Research, not a hunting tip.
  • The same blog calls Tunkwa Management Unit 3-19; the official layer puts Tunkwa Lake in Management Unit 3-18 90%. Trust the layer.

Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

• MU 2-4 and Mission: special licence and insurance 99%.
More: the special licence and named by government, in full
  • Management Unit 2-4, and the parts of Management Unit 2-8 inside Mission, Maple Ridge, Pitt Meadows and Coquitlam, need the Fraser Valley Special Area licence and $1,000,000 liability insurance (99%, synopsis page 29). See Local plan: Mission.

Named by government

  • Pitt Addington Marsh Wildlife Management Area, Pitt Marsh, Management Unit 2-8. Wintering and migrating waterfowl, sandhill cranes. Waterfowl hunting only, on Saturdays, Sundays and Wednesdays in the general season, only in the marked parts; blinds come out each day. No vehicles, camping or fires (85%, BC page, Fraser Valley Special Area brochure 2023/2024, synopsis page 27).
  • Boundary Bay Wildlife Management Area, Management Unit 2-4, west edge of the area. Pacific Flyway hub, over 1.5 million birds. Closed to snipe; no lead shot on the Delta and Surrey dykes; no camping or fires 85%.
  • Bert Brink Wildlife Management Area, Management Unit 2-4. Wigeon and Canada geese on flooded winter fields. No vehicles, camping or fires. Hunting status VERIFY 85%.
  • Lhá:lt Harrison Chehalis Wildlife Management Area, Harrison Mills. Wintering and migration wetlands. No camping or fires. Hunting status VERIFY 85%.
  • Pinecone Burke Provincial Park. Black tailed deer, goats, black bear; Widgeon Slough waterfowl. Park. BC Parks 90%.
  • Skagit Valley Provincial Park, south of Hope. Black tailed deer and black bears seen along the road. Park. BC Parks 90%.
  • Herrling Island near Hope, Management Unit 2-3. Resident white tailed deer, but no open season for them. Synopsis page 27 99%.
More: hunter talk, in full

Hunter talk: leads, not facts

  • Roberts Bank, "the Ladner Marsh", Delta, west of the area. Early season and snow goose hotspot, "busy at the beginning of the season, particularly on the weekends". Tidal: waders and tide charts (65%, BC Outdoors 2013).
  • Pitt Marsh. "some of the best duck hunting the Lower Mainland has to offer", and the hardest public marsh: boat and blinds (65%, BC Outdoors 2013).
  • Chilliwack River valley. Black tailed deer, a few blue grouse up high (forum mention, 50%). Land status and road shooting limits VERIFY.
  • Harrison Lake west side. Deer in cutblocks off the main road (forum mention, 50%).
  • Stave Lake area, Management Unit 2-8. Occasional blue grouse (forum, 50%); elk released in the Stave watershed (news, 65%). Mission bylaw areas apply.
  • The same magazine: "Much of the local waterfowl hunting takes place on private land" 65%.
  • Only 1 of 39 rec sites in this area has hunting among its first 3 listed activities: Scuzzy Creek near Boston Bar, closed until further notice (90%, provincial data).

Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

  • Quail: 1 Oct to 30 Nov, 10 a day 99%.
More: the quail season and named by government, in full
  • Quail in Region 8: Management Units 8-1 to 8-15 and 8-21 to 8-26, 1 October to 30 November, 10 a day, 30 in possession (99%, synopsis page 68, 2 October 2026 edition).

Named by government

  • South Okanagan Grasslands Protected Area: Kilpoola (Management Unit 8-2), Mount Kobau (Management Unit 8-1), Chopaka. Bighorn range, class 1 mule deer winter range. Park; vehicles only on Kruger Mountain Road and the Mount Kobau road 95%.
  • White Lake Grasslands Protected Area, Management Unit 8-1. Mule deer and bighorn winter range, lambing. Park; no vehicles; no hunting at the Seacrest toboggan hill and Scout camp; much access is through private land 95%.
  • Vaseux Protected Area, east of Vaseux Lake. Bighorn winter range. Park, next to the closed sanctuary 90%.
  • Vaseux Lake, Management Unit 8-1. Wintering waterfowl and swans, coots in fall. Closed: bird sanctuary and National Wildlife Areas. Synopsis page 67 99%.
  • Osoyoos Oxbows, Management Unit 8-1. Waterfowl habitat in an old basin study 65%; quail filmed on the trail (news, 55%). No shooting or hunting 1 March to 30 September; vehicles on established roads only. Synopsis page 69 99%.
  • South Okanagan Wildlife Management Area, Vaseux Lake to Osoyoos Lake. Species at risk, antelope brush, river oxbows. Hunting status VERIFY with the Penticton office 85%.
  • McTaggart Cowan nsək'łniw't Wildlife Management Area, east of Skaha Lake. Bighorn lambing and winter range; deer, elk and goat winter habitat. Hunting status VERIFY 85%.

• Cultivated land and reserves need consent 99%.
More: why most birds are on private land, in full

Quail: why most birds are on private land

  • California quail live on valley farm, orchard and suburban edges, mostly below 750 m 85%.
  • More than 40% of the remaining South Okanagan grasslands are private and 10% are reserve land (75%, SOSCP (South Okanagan Similkameen Conservation Program)).
  • The big tame flocks inside towns are off limits (60%, news).
  • Hunter talk: Osoyoos quail are mostly on private property, so door knock early in the year (forum mention, 50%).
  • The law: no hunting on cultivated land, or on grazing lease land with livestock on it, without the owner's or lessee's consent. Reserves need the band office's OK (99%, synopsis page 9).
  • Crown parcels: use the map's candidate spots and ParcelMap BC. See Local plan: Okanagan quail.

Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

  • Check fire bans and closures before every trip 99%.
More: the camping rules, quoted
  • Crown land: "Any person may camp on Crown land for up to 14 consecutive calendar days." Leave with your gear for 72 hours to reset the count (99%, Crown land Permission policy, section 2). No fee or application (my reading, 85%).
  • Rec sites: same 14 day limit (99%, Forest Recreation Regulation section 13). "Most recreation site campsites are available on a first-come, first-served basis"; fees at some sites, cash to the operator 99%.
  • At a rec site: no shooting within 100 m of camp structures, no gut piles, no taking firewood (99%, sections 10, 11, 14).
  • No camping and no fires in Pitt Addington Marsh, Boundary Bay, Bert Brink, Harrison Chehalis and Serpentine Wildlife Management Areas (99%, B.C. Reg. 24/2015).
  • Campfires: follow BC Wildfire Service bans; a campfire is at most 0.5 m by 0.5 m with water or a hand tool ready 99%. On 3 October 2026 campfires were allowed in the Kamloops and Coastal fire centres (99% for that day only).
  • Check before every trip: the BC Wildfire map, the park page and Recreation Sites and Trails BC closures 99%.

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Wisdom, not law: if you read about it, so did everybody else. Use the name to learn the country, then walk past the parking lot.

Common mistakes
  • Driving to a named spot on opening Saturday and expecting it empty.
  • Thinking a Wildlife Management Area is open because it is public land. Some are closed, some open only on set days.
  • Trusting a forum MU (Management Unit) number. Check the official map: Tunkwa Lake is MU 3-18, not 3-19.

Do this in the field

Pick one named place from this list and one candidate spot from the map in the same MU (Management Unit). Visit both on a weekday. Count the trucks at each trailhead and write the counts in your Journal.

  • Crown land Permission policy, rec site fees and rules, fire bans, read 2026-10-03 99%.
  • BC recreation site layer and official Management Unit layer (BC Data Catalogue), and BC Geographical Names, queried 2026-10-03 90%.
  • BC Outdoors Magazine, Lower Mainland duck hunting, 2013 65%.
  • Hunting BC blog, Region 3, 2011 55%. HuntingBC forum threads, search previews only 50%.

Why it matters

The law gives everyday words exact meanings. "Loaded", "hunting" and "4 point" decide whether you are legal before you ever pull a trigger.

More: what this session covers
  • Source: BC Hunting and Trapping Regulations Synopsis 2026 to 2028, edition dated 2 October 2026.
  • This session carries every definition from the Definitions section, pages 3 to 5 of the synopsis, in alphabetical order 99%.
  • Each entry: the term in bold, the official words in quotes, then one plain English line.
  • Printed page numbers are cited. Page 3 and 4 hold nearly all of them; the last four spill onto page 5 99%.
  • The pictures in the synopsis (caribou, elk, moose, sheep, mule deer, tine) are described in words under the term they belong to.
  • Terms with the same word are grouped as the synopsis groups them: three moose classes together, four mountain sheep classes together.

WordIn plain words
ATV (All Terrain Vehicle)Quad, side by side, dirt bike. Not a snowmobile 99%
AntleredDeer family, over 1 year, visible antlers 99%
AntlerlessNo visible antlers. A button buck counts 99%
More: the official words
  • Accompany (99%, page 3, 2 October 2026 edition)
Official definition

"ACCOMPANY - means to remain in the company of the other person, able to see the other person without the aid of any device other than ordinary corrective lenses and able to communicate by unamplified voice with that person."

  • Plain English: stay with the person, close enough to see them with your own eyes (glasses are fine, binoculars are not) and to talk without a radio or a shout 99%. This is the test for supervising a youth or initiation hunter and for a permit to accompany a non resident (95%, my reading).
  • All terrain vehicle, (99%, page 3, 2 October 2026 edition)
Official definition

"ALL TERRAIN VEHICLE (ATV) - means a wheeled vehicle or tracked vehicle propelled by motorized power, and capable of travel on or off a highway, including motorcycles but not including a snowmobile or motor vehicle that is licensed for highway travel under the Motor Vehicle Act."

  • Plain English: a quad, side by side or dirt bike is an ATV (All Terrain Vehicle). A snowmobile is not, and neither is a truck or bike with highway plates 99%.
  • Antlered animal (99%, page 3, 2 October 2026 edition)
Official definition

"ANTLERED ANIMAL - means a member of the deer family over one year of age bearing visible bony antlers."

  • Plain English: a deer, moose, elk or caribou older than 1 year with antlers you can see 99%.
  • animal (99%, page 3, 2 October 2026 edition)
Official definition

"ANTLERLESS ANIMAL - means a member of the deer family bearing no visible antlers. The small skin or hair covered protuberances of male fawns and calves do not constitute antlers."

  • Plain English: no visible antlers means antlerless. A button buck, a male fawn with skin covered bumps, counts as antlerless 99%.

WordIn plain words
BaitAnything put out to draw animals. A decoy is not bait 99%
B.C. residentMain home in BC, and enough time here: see the rule 99%
Bearded turkeyAny turkey with a visible beard 99%
Big game13 named animals, wolf and bobcat included 99%
More: the official words
  • Bait (99%, page 3, 2 October 2026 edition)
Official definition

"BAIT - means anything, including meat, cereals, cultivated crops, restrained animal or any manufactured product or material, that may attract wildlife and includes plastic or other imitation foods, but does not include a decoy as described under these regulations."

  • Plain English: anything put out to draw animals in, fake food included. A decoy is not bait 99%.
  • B.C. resident (99%, page 3, 2 October 2026 edition)
Official definition

"B.C. RESIDENT - means a person who is a Canadian citizen or permanent resident of Canada, and whose only or primary residence is in British Columbia and who has been physically present in B.C. for the greater portion of each of 6 calendar months out of the 12 calendar months immediately before doing a thing under the Wildlife Act, or if not a Canadian citizen or permanent resident of Canada, but whose only or primary residence is in British Columbia, and has been physically present in B.C. for the greater portion of each of the 12 calendar months immediately before doing a thing under the Wildlife Act."

  • Plain English: a citizen or permanent resident whose main home is in BC and who was physically in BC for more than half of each of 6 of the last 12 months 99%. Not a citizen or permanent resident? Then your main home must be BC and you must have been here more than half of each of the last 12 months 99%.
  • Bearded turkey (99%, page 3, 2 October 2026 edition)
Official definition

"BEARDED TURKEY - means a turkey with a tuft of hair-like feathers on the chest that grow larger with age."

  • Plain English: any turkey showing the beard tuft on its chest. The definition goes by the tuft, not the sex of the bird 99%.
  • Big game (99%, page 3, 2 October 2026 edition)
Official definition

"BIG GAME - means any mountain sheep, mountain goat, bison, caribou, elk, moose, deer, black bear, cougar, wolf, bobcat, lynx, wolverine or other animal designated by regulation."

  • Plain English: 13 named animals, plus any other the regulations add. Wolf, bobcat, lynx and wolverine are big game too, not only the hoofed animals 99%.

WordIn plain words
BoltA crossbow arrow 99%
BowIncludes a crossbow 99%
Brow tineFirst point forward or up, lower third. Not counted on a mule deer 4 point 99%
Buck or bullDeer, moose, elk: visible antlers. Caribou: a male with antlers 99%
More: the official words
  • Bolt (99%, page 3, 2 October 2026 edition)
Official definition

"BOLT - means a shaft or missile designed to be shot from a crossbow or catapult."

  • Plain English: a crossbow arrow 99%.
  • Bow (99%, page 3, 2 October 2026 edition)
Official definition

"BOW - means a longbow or crossbow."

  • Plain English: in BC law a crossbow is a bow 99%. Compound and recurve bows fall under longbow (90%, my reading).
  • (99%, page 3, 2 October 2026 edition)
Official definition

"BROW TINE - means the first tine (point) projecting forward or upward in the lower 1/3 of the antler of a moose, caribou, elk, or deer."

  • Plain English: the first point that sticks forward or up in the bottom third of the antler 99%. It does not count toward a 4 point mule deer buck, and it does count for elk and moose 99%.
  • Buck or bull (99%, page 3, 2 October 2026 edition)
Official definition

"BUCK OR BULL - with reference to deer, moose or elk means one bearing visible bony antlers but does not include a calf; with reference to caribou means a male bearing visible bony antlers but does not include a calf."

  • Plain English: for deer, moose and elk the law goes by visible antlers, not by sex. For caribou it must be a male with antlers, because cow caribou grow antlers too 99%.

WordIn plain words
CalfUnder 1 year old 99%
Cancelled species licenceCut or notched as the licence shows 99%
Caribou 5 point bullCount points above the rear point 99%
More: the official words
  • (99%, page 3, 2 October 2026 edition)
Official definition

"CALF - means a moose, elk, or caribou less than twelve months of age."

  • Plain English: under 1 year old 99%.
  • Calf moose (99%, page 3, 2 October 2026 edition)
Official definition

"CALF MOOSE - a moose less than twelve months of age usually less than 1.5 m at shoulder height weighing 135-180 kg."

  • Plain English: a first year moose, usually under 1.5 m at the shoulder and 135 to 180 kg 99%.
  • What the picture shows: a cow moose standing with a calf at her side, the calf much shorter and with a short, blunt face. The caption says calves are much smaller and show a distinctly stubby face, that not every moose walking with a larger moose is a calf, and to be sure of your target 99%.
  • Cancelled species licence (99%, page 3, 2 October 2026 edition)
Official definition

"CANCELLED SPECIES LICENCE - means a Species Licence that has been cancelled as indicated on the licence."

  • Plain English: a (tag) you have cut or notched the way the licence itself shows, after a kill 99%.
  • Caribou, 5 point bull (99%, page 3, 2 October 2026 edition)
Official definition

"CARIBOU - 5 POINT BULL - has one antler which bears at least 5 tines (points), including the tip of the main beam above the rear point. If rear point is missing, the first rear-facing point will be used as the rear point."

  • Plain English: on one antler, count the points above the rear point. The tip of the main beam counts as one 99%.
  • What the picture shows: two caribou antlers drawn side by side, each with an arrow to its rear point, the tine that sticks backward low on the main beam. Everything above that is what you count 99%.

WordIn plain words
Compound crossbowA crossbow with cams or pulleys 99%

"COMPOUND CROSSBOW - means a crossbow on which the bow string runs through pulleys."

  • Cougar kitten (99%, page 3, 2 October 2026 edition)

"COUGAR KITTEN - means any cougar with spots or any cougar under one year of age."

  • Plain English: spots or under 1 year old, either one makes it a kitten 99%.
  • Cow moose (99%, page 3, 2 October 2026 edition)
Official definition

"COW MOOSE - a female moose recognizable by having no antlers and being 1.8 m at shoulder height weighing 340-420 kg."

  • Plain English: an adult female, no antlers, about 1.8 m at the shoulder and 340 to 420 kg 99%.
  • Crossbow (99%, page 3, 2 October 2026 edition)
Official definition

"CROSSBOW - means a bow fixed across a stock with a groove for the arrow or bolt and a mechanism for holding and releasing the string. (NOTE: The use of crossbows is permitted during special bow only seasons.)"

  • Plain English: a crossbow is legal in bow only seasons 99%.

WordIn plain words
DecoyMade to look like an animal or bird 99%
Deer familyDeer, moose, elk, caribou 99%
DroneAny pilotless aircraft 99%
Electric bicycleA pedal bike with a motor 99%
More: the official words
  • Decoy (99%, page 3, 2 October 2026 edition)
Official definition

"DECOY - means any material or manufactured product that simulates the appearance or has the form of wildlife."

  • Plain English: anything made to look like an animal or bird 99%.
  • Deer family (99%, page 3, 2 October 2026 edition)
Official definition

"DEER FAMILY - moose, caribou, deer, and elk."

  • Plain English: the four antlered species. Rules that say "deer family" cover all four 99%.
  • Drone (99%, page 3, 2 October 2026 edition)
Official definition

"DRONE - means an aerial vehicle that (a) is not occupied or operated by a person within the vehicle, (b) is operated by (i) remote control, (ii) pre-programmed software, (iii) onboard computer autonomy or artificial intelligence, or (iv) any combination of (i) to (iii) and is capable of attracting, searching for, chasing, pursuing, following after or on the trail of, stalking, spotting or monitoring wildlife."

  • Plain English: any pilotless aircraft, remote controlled or self flying, that could be used to find, follow or watch wildlife 99%.
  • (99%, page 3, 2 October 2026 edition)
Official definition

"EDIBLE PORTIONS - with respect to big game, excluding wolf, lynx, bobcat and wolverine, means the edible portions of the neck, ribs, four quarters and the loins of the animal and with respect to game birds, means the edible portions of both breasts of the bird."

  • Plain English: the meat you must not waste. Big game: neck, ribs, all four quarters and the loins. Game birds: both breasts. Wolf, lynx, bobcat and wolverine are exempt 99%.
  • Electric bicycle (99%, page 3, 2 October 2026 edition)
Official definition

"ELECTRIC BICYCLE - a wheeled device (a) on which a person may ride, (b) with pedals or hand cranks that allow it to be propelled with human power, and (c) with an electric motor."

  • Plain English: a bike you can pedal that also has an electric motor 99%.

Official definition

"ELK - SIX POINTS OR GREATER BULL - means any bull having at least six tines on one antler."

  • Plain English: count one antler. Six or more tines, brow tine included, and he is a 99%.

"ELK - THREE POINTS OR GREATER BULL - means any bull having at least three tines on one antler."

Official definition

"EXISTING ROAD OR TRAIL - means (a) a road or trail with a paved surface, (b) a cross-country or downhill ski route marked in a ski area by the owner of the ski area, (c) a road used for logging or mining, (d) a road or trail used for access to fences, power lines, wind generators or communication towers, or (e) a trail on which there is no vegetation except on a strip that, if present, can be straddled by a 4-wheel vehicle."

  • Plain English: this matters in motor vehicle closed areas where you may only drive on existing roads and trails. A paved road, a logging or mining road, a service road to a power line or tower, a marked ski run, or a bare two track with at most a grass strip down the middle all count 99%. A game trail or an overgrown track does not (90%, my reading).

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

If a word in a season table looks ordinary, it probably is not. Flip to the definition before you decide an animal is legal.

Common mistakes
  • Counting the brow tine on a mule deer buck. It is excluded. Count it on elk and moose.
  • Calling a rifle unloaded because the chamber is empty while a loaded magazine is clipped in.
  • Thinking "hunting" starts at the shot. It starts when you search with a weapon in hand.

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

Why it matters

The right animal in the right place is still illegal with the wrong gun, the wrong shell or at the wrong hour.

More: what this session covers
  • Source: BC Hunting and Trapping Regulations Synopsis 2026 to 2028, edition dated 2 October 2026.

Legal Hunting Methods, Firearms, page 12

"It is unlawful to hunt with a firearm that has an electronically controlled firing mechanism."

"It is unlawful to use a firearm that is designed, altered, or intended to be aimed and fired by the action of one hand OR that has a barrel less than 305 mm in length."

• No set gun, ever 99%.

More: every step from page 18
  • Incisors sit only at the front of the lower jaw. Pulling one does not spoil a mount (99%, page 18, 2 October 2026 edition).
  • Do it while the jaw is fresh. A dried jaw may need a soak in warm water 99%.
  • Steps 99%:
    1. With a thin, sharp knife, cut down through the gum on both sides of the root of one of the centre teeth. They have the biggest root and age best.
    2. Push the tooth out with your thumb. If it sticks, use pliers with a twisting pull. Clean off the soft tissue and bone.
  • Never cut into the root, and never send a tooth with a broken root. The root is what ages the animal 99%.
  • Do not send the whole jaw. No gum, muscle or hide on the tooth. No plastic bag: dry it in a paper envelope 99%.
  • Label the envelope: species, date of kill, region, MU, FWID and which tooth, I1 or I2 99%.
  • The drawing shows the front incisors from the front: two centre teeth marked I1, the next two marked I2, each with its crown at the top and root below, and dashed cut lines down each side of the root 99%.

  • Handling game meat safely, as page 18 recommends (99%, page 18, 2 October 2026 edition):

Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

Why it matters

Ducks and geese run on federal dates, not BC dates. Mission and Heffley Creek open a month apart, and the phone has to know which one you are standing in.

"south of 60° north latitude during the period commencing half an hour after sunset on any day and ending half an hour before sunrise on the next day unless otherwise specified in Schedule 3."

s. 37(1)(c)

"a shotgun not larger than number 10 gauge that either (i) is designed to be capable of holding no more than three cartridges, or (ii) has had its capacity reduced to three cartridges in the magazine and chamber combined, by means of the cutting off or the altering or plugging of the magazine with a one-piece metal, plastic or wood filler that cannot be removed unless the gun is disassembled."

s. 36(1)

"A person must not hunt for migratory game birds within a radius of 400 m from any place where bait has been deposited unless the place has been free of bait for at least seven days or the bait was deposited in accordance with subsection 6(3) or (4) or an aviculture permit."

s. 39(1)

"A person must not hunt a migratory game bird using (a) live birds, including non-migratory birds; or (b) electronic bird calls, except in an area that is set out in column 1 of Table 2 in the relevant Part of Schedule 3 for which the use of an electronic bird call is set out in column 6."

  • Bait means "any feed, or imitation feed, that may attract migratory birds" (99%, s. 1). No hunting within 400 m (437 yd) of bait until it has been gone 7 days (99%, s. 36(1)).

"AHD was first identified in the fall of 2020 on several Gulf Islands (Galiano, Mayne, Pender, and Salt Spring) and southern Vancouver Island as far north as Merville. AHD is a highly contagious and often fatal disease, particularly in black-tailed deer."

"Although there is no known risk to human health from AHD, hunters are advised not to consume meat from animals found dead, obviously ill or acting abnormally prior to death. To help prevent the spread of AHD, dispose of carcasses by deep burial, do not move infected, dead or live deer to new areas, and prevent aggregations of deer at artificial feeding or water sources."

"Help protect B.C. ungulates by understanding these risks, helping to increase awareness, and submitting your deer, elk, moose or caribou for testing. Learn more about the BC CWD Program at www.gov.bc.ca/chronicwastingdisease and AHD at www.gov.bc.ca/wildlifehealth."

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

On the Island, the map decides the gun. Rifle, shotgun slug, shot only or bow: find your spot on the map before you load.

Common mistakes
  • Shooting an antlerless black tail in rifle country because "the deer bag is 3". Antlerless is Special Areas, youth seasons or a draw only.
  • Setting a wireless trail camera in Region 1 in July, thinking the 1 August date applies. Region 1 bans them for hunting with no dates.
  • Hunting a Gulf Island without the Special Area Licence, the $100,000 insurance or the owner's permission.
Do this in the field

Before each Island trip: name your MU, check the bow only and shot only maps for that MU, then read its rows on the season screens.

Why it matters

More: the page 15 words
Carcass Transport Restrictions - Prevent Spread of Chronic Wasting Disease, page 15

"A person who kills a deer, elk, or moose within M.U.s 4-1 to 4-8 and 4-20 to 4-25 (the CWD Management Zone, see page 36) must not ship or transport, or engage another person to ship or transport, outside of the CWD Management Zone, the brain tissue or the spinal column, including the vertebrae and central nervous system tissue but not including the tail."

"There is a 24-hour exemption after harvest for deer, elk or moose harvested in M.U. 4-7, M.U. 4-8, and M.U. 4-25 that require travel outside of the CWD Management Zone to immediately access a designated CWD freezer. This exemption applies only to the routes below."

  • Killed a deer, elk or moose in the zone? The brain and the spinal column, vertebrae included, may not leave the zone. The tail may (99%, page 15).
  • You may not get someone else to carry them out either 99%.
  • Exception: from MUs 4-7, 4-8 and 4-25, you have 24 hours to drive the whole animal to a CWD freezer, on the listed routes only 99%.

• From MUs (Management Units) 4-7, 4-8, 4-25 only, on these routes only 99%.

More: the page 37 box
Page 37 box

"Chronic Wasting Disease was confirmed in white-tailed deer and mule deer populations in the Kootenay Region in January 2024."

"An emergency response has been initiated to prevent spread and access samples to better understand the extent of the outbreak."

"A high risk boundary (the CWD Management Zone) that includes MUs 4-1 to 4-8 and 4-20 to 4-25 has been defined based on animal movement and proximity to CWD cases in BC, Alberta and Montana."

"Mandatory testing is expanded to include deer, elk and moose harvested within the CWD Management Zone and samples must be submitted to a designated freezer before leaving this area. For freezer locations see www.gov.bc.ca/CWDdropoff"

"There is a 24-hour exemption after harvest on specified routes for deer, elk or moose harvested in M.U. 4-7, M.U. 4-8, and M.U. 4-25 that require travel outside of the CWD Management Zone to immediately access a designated CWD freezer. See page 15 for specific routes."

"Brain tissue and spinal column (except for the tail) from deer, elk and moose harvested within the CWD Management Zone cannot be transport outside of this boundary. It is recommended to leave these parts at or near the kill site or dispose of them at a landfill before leaving the area."

"We encourage hunters to continue hunting in the affected areas; hunting can help to suppress transmission and spread by removing infected animals from the landscape. It is estimated that less than 1% of cervids currently have CWD in these areas."

"Hunting is the most important tool for managing CWD as it helps to suppress disease prevalence and provides essential information to support science-based management of CWD."

"For more information visit: www.gov.bc.ca/chronicwastingdisease"

  • Testing is mandatory for every deer, elk and moose taken in the zone 99%.
  • Drop the head sample at a designated freezer before you leave the zone 99%. Freezer list: www.gov.bc.ca/CWDdropoff 99%.
  • Leave the brain and spine at the kill site or at a landfill inside the zone (99%, a recommendation).
  • Under 1% of deer family animals in the zone are thought to carry CWD. Keep hunting there 99%.
  • The season tables repeat it: "Mandatory submission of deer heads for CWD testing in highest risk areas", and the same for elk and moose (99%, page 39).

"Grouse: The daily aggregate bag limit for grouse: blue (dusky), spruce (Franklin), and ruffed is 5."

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

In the Kootenay, the deer is not done when it is down. Head to the freezer, spine stays in the zone.

Common mistakes
  • Driving a Cranbrook buck home to Heffley Creek with the head on. The brain and spine may not leave the CWD (Chronic Wasting Disease) zone.
  • Shooting a mule deer buck on 20 November because white tails run to 30 November. Mule deer close 10 November.
  • Putting out a salt block for deer anywhere in Region 4. Feeding or baiting ungulates is unlawful region wide.
Do this in the field

Hunting the zone: find the nearest CWD freezer before you go, pack a saw, and plan to leave spine and skull at the kill site or landfill.

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

Up north the map is the law. Know your zone letter, your elevation and your road before you leave the truck.

Common mistakes
  • Shooting a Haida Gwaii deer and carrying 6 in the freezer. Possession is 5.
  • Taking a snowmobile to hunt in 6-9 in January. Hunting from it is banned there all year.
  • Shooting a near white black bear on the coast. White and blue phases are closed.
Do this in the field

Before each trip: name your MU, read its rows, then its maps. In the north, check the Map F40 zones and the elevation closures. Screenshot the screen for no signal.

Grandpa's rule (wisdom, not law)

In the Omineca, the bull you can shoot is a spike fork. Count tines twice, pull the trigger once.

Common mistakes
  • Shooting a 3 point bull moose because it "looked small". Only spike fork bulls are open.
  • Running the quad out at 6 am in September in MU 7-12. The ATV hours ban covers that.
  • Shooting a 2 point mule deer buck near Prince George in October. MUs 7-12 to 7-14, 7-24 and 7-25 are 4 point only.
Do this in the field

Before each trip: name your MU, read its rows, then the access hours. Note the time the ATV ban lifts that day.

More: ID by sex and age, the full list
  • Ears: large, about two thirds the length of the head, black edged, white inside (90%, BC deer account 2000).
  • Face: dark brown forehead, whitish face, black muzzle, white throat patch 90%.
  • Rump and tail: large white rump patch, narrow tail with a black tip 90%.
  • Coat: tawny brown in summer, dark or grizzled grey brown in winter 90%.
  • Buck (male): antlers grow April to August in velvet, hard from about September, drop January to March 90%. Chapter 5 has the antler year.
  • Doe (female): no antlers, slimmer neck, longer looking face (Tip).
  • Fawn (under 1 year): born late May through June with white spots 90%. Spots fade with the first fall coat 75%. By October about half a doe's size (75%, quick lesson).
  • Yearling buck (about 1.5 years): most have 2 points a side (90%, BC account).

• Yearling: most have 2 points a side 90%.
  • Point count is a poor age guide. Read the body 90%.

More: antlers, body and the 4 point count
Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

  • BC account 90%:
    • Most yearling mule deer have 2 points on each side.
    • Two year olds grow large forks or 3 points.
    • Older bucks have 4, 5 or more points plus a small eye guard (brow tine) near the base.
    • "The number of antler points is not a reliable way to determine the age."
  • Mule deer antlers fork once about 15 to 25 cm (6 to 10 in) above the base, then each branch forks again. Brow tines are small or absent, even on mature bucks (85%, Mule Deer Working Group fact sheet 27).
  • By about age 4, antlers reach about 80 to 90% of their peak size (85%, Mule Deer Working Group fact sheet 24).
  • Body clues for an older buck: deep chest, thick neck that blends into the shoulders, belly that sags, legs that look short for the body (Tip, hunter consensus). A young buck looks like "a doe with antlers" (Tip).
  • Legal count: a has at least 4 tines on one antler, not counting the (99%, synopsis page 4, see Region 3 rules). Count one side. Then count again.

• Mule deer, black tail, white tail: separate seasons 99%.
  • Not sure which? No shot (Tip).

More: size details and what it means for you
  • BC numbers (90%, BC deer account 2000):
    • Mule deer stand 90 to 95 cm at the shoulder.
    • Bucks 68 to 113 kg; bucks in peak condition up to 180 kg.
    • Does 50 to 75 kg.
    • Black tailed bucks 48 to 90 kg; does 40 to 65 kg. Sitka black tails are smaller and darker.
    • Fawns weigh 2.7 to 4 kg at birth.
  • US park figures for comparison: bucks 57 to 114 kg, does 45 to 60 kg, 1.2 to 2.1 m nose to tail (80%, US National Park Service, Bryce Canyon).
  • Weight swings a lot by season: bucks lose weight in the rut 90%. Chapter 2 has the fat year.
  • What it means for you: a field dressed buck is still a heavy load for one person. Plan a partner or quarter it (Tip). Meat math is in chapter 10.

• Interior: mule deer. Coast: black tails. Haida Gwaii: Sitka 90%.
  • The Coast Range splits them, mostly in winter 90%.
More: the three races and hybrids
  • One species, Odocoileus hemionus, three races (subspecies) in BC (90%, BC deer account 2000):
    • Mule deer (O. h. hemionus): most of the interior, east of the Coast Mountains to Alberta.
    • Columbian black tailed deer (O. h. columbianus): the coast, Vancouver Island, Fraser Valley, Sechelt Peninsula.
    • Sitka black tailed deer (O. h. sitkensis): north coast. Introduced to the Queen Charlotte Islands (Haida Gwaii) in the early 1900s.
  • Where ranges meet they interbreed; deer in some intermediate valleys look mixed 90%.
  • The BC account calls the black tail "a species in the making" because of its long isolation on the coast 90%.
  • Mule deer are most common in the southern interior and the northeast (85%, BC habitat model 2003).
  • Your bases: Heffley Creek and the South Okanagan are mule deer country. The Fraser Valley near Mission is black tail country (85%, my reading of the ranges above).

• About 100,000 to 170,000 in BC 85%.
  • Harvest is far below the 1960s peak 90%.
More: numbers, trend and why
  • BC account 2000: the interior "has about 165,000 Mule Deer"; 20,000 to 25,000 on northern ranges 90%.
  • WAFWA (Western Association of Fish and Wildlife Agencies) 2020 status report: BC mule deer 100,000 to 170,000; harvest 9,986, 87% males; 58,230 hunters (tags) 85%.
  • Black tailed deer: 150,000 to 250,000 in recent decades (90%, BC account 2000).
  • Deer harvest peaked in the late 1960s at about 75,000 (mule and black tailed), then fell to about 20,000 a year by 2000 90%. The account blames habitat loss, predation and fewer hunters, not over hunting.
  • Trend worries: buck to doe ratios are close to or below the provincial goal of 20 bucks per 100 does after the hunt (85%, WAFWA 2020).
  • The Southern Interior Mule Deer Project (SIMDeer, BC Wildlife Federation and partners) studies the decline across 30,000 km2 of the southern Interior 85%. Cougars were the top cause of death of collared adult does and older fawns 85%.
  • In the Thompson study area, almost entirely burned in 2017, adult doe survival was 82% and overwinter fawn survival 63% over two years (85%, WAFWA 2020).

• MU (Management Unit) 3-27: about 1 in 3 hunters got a mule deer, 2020 to 2024 90%.
  • Average: about 22 hunting days per deer (90%, computed).

  • Old hand's rule (opinion): "Read the body before the bone." Neck, belly and legs age a buck faster than the rack.
Common mistakes
  • Forgetting that a Fraser Valley deer is a black tail under the Region 2 rules.
  • Counting both antlers together for a 4 point buck. Count one side.
  • Judging age by points alone.
Do this in the field

Next drive at dusk: for every deer you see, say out loud "buck or doe, age, how many points a side".

mc-mule-deer-02:
Why it matters

Know where the lungs, heart and bones sit and you will place one clean shot and save the meat.

  • Lungs fill the front of the chest; heart sits low behind the leg (75 to 85%).
  • Rumen and gut fill the belly behind 85%.
More: what this chapter covers
  • Bones that matter for a bullet, how a deer breathes, the heart and big vessels, the four chamber stomach, coat and body heat, the fat year, teeth and age, and what all that means for your shot and your meat.
  • Anatomy facts come from hunter education and wildlife agency sources. Drawings are simplified, not to scale 75%.
  • Previous: Chapter 1, Meet the animal. Next: Chapter 3, The senses.

• Shoulder blade covers the front of the chest 75%.
  • Aim behind it, one third up from the brisket 85%.
More: the bones in detail
  • The shoulder blade (scapula) is a broad flat bone over the front of the rib cage, joined to the upper leg bone (humerus) (75%, hunter education drawings).
  • When the near front leg steps forward, the shoulder moves forward and opens the chest behind it (85%, shot placement).
  • Ribs are thin. A hunting bullet passes them easily; a heavy shoulder joint can stop or deflect it (85%, Texas Parks and Wildlife hunter education).
  • Spine runs high along the back, well above the lungs. A miss high over the lungs can graze it or miss clean (Tip).
  • Aim: up the back of the front leg, one third up the chest 85%.
  • Quartering to you: the near shoulder is in the way. Beginners wait for a better angle (85%, Texas hunter education: "wait for a better angle").

• The lungs are the biggest vital target 85%.
  • A hole in the chest lets the lungs collapse 70%.
More: lungs, diaphragm and what a lung hit looks like
  • Lungs fill most of the chest cavity above and around the heart. That makes them the largest vital target (85%, Texas and Massachusetts hunter education).
  • The diaphragm is the dome of muscle behind the lungs. When it pulls back, air rushes in (75%, general mammal anatomy).
  • The diaphragm slants: its top sits farther back than its bottom 75%. A shot too far back slips behind it into the liver or rumen.
  • Lung hit blood: bright red, often frothy or bubbly (70%, National Deer Association via the blood trailing session).
  • Double lung deer: often run hard, under about 100 m (85%, shot placement).
  • A newborn fawn's resting heart rate averages 177 beats a minute and drops to about 60 when a person comes close, while it holds its breath (85%, Mule Deer Working Group fact sheet 26). Adult rates: no reliable source found (VERIFY).

• Heart: low in the chest, just behind the front leg 85%.
  • Aorta runs back under the spine 65%.
More: heart, vessels and hit reactions
  • The heart sits low, just above and slightly behind the front leg (85%, hunter education).
  • Heart hits: deer often bolt hard, sometimes with a jump or kick; rarely over about 50 m (85%, shot placement).
  • The aorta, the main artery, arches from the heart and runs back just under the spine. A high chest hit can cut it (65%, hunter education guides). Do not aim for it; it is a bonus, not a target (Tip).
  • The big veins (vena cava) run back from the heart along the chest floor and up through the liver (70%, general anatomy).
  • Aim for the middle of the lungs and you have margin for the heart below and the big vessels above (Tip).

• One stomach, four chambers: rumen, reticulum, omasum, abomasum 75%.
  • Fill up fast, then bed and chew cud 85%.
More: how a ruminant eats, and what it means for you
  • A ruminant (cud chewer): the rumen is a fermentation vat where microbes break down plant cell walls (75%, extension and biologist sources).
  • Food is swallowed fast, brought back up as cud, chewed again, then passes on through the reticulum, omasum and abomasum 75%.
  • Mule deer are selective feeders. Rumen bacteria are specific to their foods, so a sudden new food can kill: winter fed deer can "die with full stomachs" (85%, Mule Deer Working Group fact sheet 2).
  • Browse (twigs and leaves of shrubs and trees) is the bulk of the year's diet (85%, BC habitat model). Chapter 7 has the plants.
  • The rumen is big: it fills the middle of the belly. A shot behind the diaphragm usually hits it (Tip).
  • Gut hit sign: thin, green brown blood with stomach matter and a sour smell; the deer often hunches and walks off (70 to 85%, blood trailing). Wait hours, not minutes.
  • Why it beds midday: a full rumen needs rest time to chew cud (85%, quick lesson).

• Tawny summer coat, grey brown winter coat 90%.
  • In winter it keeps warm mostly by picking warm slopes 85%.
More: how it handles heat and cold
  • Coat: reddish or tawny brown in summer, dark or grizzled brown in winter (90%, BC deer account).
  • Winter hairs are hollow with larger air pockets than summer hairs (mule deer: about 26 vs 13 micrometres) (60%, Utah Tech conference poster). Good insulation.
  • The main way mule deer manage winter cold is habitat choice: warm south and west aspects, gentle to moderate slopes, low elevations, Douglas fir cover (85%, BC habitat model 2003).
  • Mule deer have "little requirement for summer thermoregulation" in the habitat model; summer cover is about hiding 85%.
  • Moult timing follows day length, and deer in good condition moult earlier (65%, Massachusetts wildlife agency, search preview).
  • For you: on hot October afternoons look in shade, on north facing slopes and in timber; on cold mornings look on the first sunny slopes (80%, bedding studies via the quick lesson).

• Fat peaks in fall; lowest in spring (60 to 65%).
  • Bucks burn fat in the rut and enter winter thin 90%.
More: fat, winter and survival
  • Deer eat less and lose weight in winter even in good conditions (85%, Mule Deer Working Group fact sheet 17).
  • Wyoming mule deer does used their fat about 2.5 times faster in November and December than in late winter (65%, study data summary).
  • Fat stores tend to build through summer, peak in late autumn and bottom out in spring (60%, white tail study, same pattern expected).
  • After the rut "bucks have lost weight and some have wounds or broken antlers, and they tend to hide and rest" (90%, BC deer account).
  • Snow costs energy: walking in 25 cm of snow takes about 50% more energy; 41 cm about 150% more (85%, BC habitat model citing Parker 1984).
  • Starving deer use up the last fat in the bone marrow: healthy winter marrow is pale and fatty; marrow under 10% fat is red and jelly like (65%, Massachusetts, search preview). You may see this in a winter kill.
  • People disturbing wintering deer make them burn reserves they need (85%, fact sheet 17).
  • For you: a late season buck is lean. Do not expect fat on the meat (Tip).

• No upper front teeth: it tears browse 85%.
  • Few live past 8 to 10 years 90%.
More: teeth, ageing and lifespan
  • Deer have 6 lower incisors plus incisor like canines, pressed against a hard upper pad. No upper incisors (85%, Mule Deer Working Group fact sheet 35). That is why browse looks torn, not cut (75%, chapter 8).
  • Age by the lower jaw (85%, fact sheet 35):
    • 1.5 years: tooth 3 (the last premolar) still has 3 cusps and is worn; the last molar is not fully up.
    • 2.5 years: tooth 3 has 2 cusps; the last molar is fully up.
    • 3 to 5: a brown band of dentine shows on the back cusp of the last molar.
    • 6 to 8: tooth 4 (first molar) worn flat.
    • 8 plus: tooth 4 worn to the gum.
  • Tooth wear is good to about 3.5 years; past that a lab count of cementum rings is more accurate 85%.
  • Yearlings in October are 15 to 17 months old (85%, Idaho Fish and Game).
  • Few mule deer live more than 8 to 10 years (90%, BC account). 45 to 70% of fawns normally die 90%.
  • The Region 3 pages ask hunters to submit deer heads for CWD (Chronic Wasting Disease) testing; details in the Rule Book, Region 3 (95%, via the rut).

• Broadside: behind the leg, one third up, both lungs 85%.
  • Wait for the leg to step forward 85%.
More: shot and meat notes
  • Broadside: up the back of the front leg, one third up the chest. Both lungs and the top of the heart (85%, shot placement).
  • Quartering away: aim so the bullet exits the far shoulder 85%.
  • Vital zone with margin: about 20 to 25 cm (8 to 10 in) 75%.
  • A shot through the shoulder blade wastes meat and can deflect (85%, Texas hunter education).
  • A gut hit taints meat near the wound; gut and cool fast once you recover it (Tip, field dressing).
  • Rutting bucks carry thick necks and shoulders: aim behind the shoulder, not in it 75%.
  • Full meat chapter: Chapter 10.

• Rhyme: "Up the leg a third of the way; lungs and heart are where you lay."
  • Number trick: 4 chambers, 3 cusps at 1.5 years, 2 cusps at 2.5 85%.
  • Old hand's rule (tradition): "Shoot the lungs, eat the shoulders."
More: more hooks
  • Rhyme: "Hollow hair and a sunny slope keep a mule deer's winter hope."
  • Number trick: 25 and 41: centimetres of snow that cost 50% and 150% more energy 85%.
  • Number trick: 8 to 10: few mule deer live longer 90%.
  • Number trick: 177: a newborn fawn's resting heart rate; 60 when you walk up 85%.
  • Old hand's rule (widely taught, opinion): "Aim small, miss small." Pick one hair behind the leg, not the whole deer.
  • Old hand's rule (opinion): "Too far back, wait it back." A gut hit means hours of waiting.
Common mistakes
  • Aiming at the middle of the deer. That is the rumen.
  • Aiming at the shoulder of a quartering to deer.
  • Expecting fat on a December buck.
Do this in the field

Next deer you see: picture the lungs and heart inside it. Say "leg, third up" out loud.

mc-mule-deer-03:
Why it matters

A mule deer is a nose with ears and eyes on top. Beat all three and you get close.

  • Nose first, ears second, eyes third (Tip, from the facts below).
  • You can fool eyes and ears. Only the wind beats the nose (Tip).
More: what this chapter covers
  • The nose and how your scent moves with wind and , the ears and the sounds that carry, the eyes (colour, motion, night, field of view), how a deer combines them, and how to beat each one.
  • The short version is in How a deer thinks. This chapter goes deeper.
  • Previous: Chapter 2, The body. Next: Chapter 4, The mind.

• Smell is a deer's strongest sense 85%.
  • Downwind of you = smelled. No exceptions (Tip).
More: how the nose works
Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

  • Smell is the strongest deer sense (85%, research notes). The often quoted "297 million receptors" figure is folklore (45%, not a fact).
  • Deer also have a second scent organ, the vomeronasal organ in the roof of the mouth. A rutting buck curls his lip (the flehmen face) to pull a doe's urine scent into it (65%, University of Georgia researcher via fishgame.com; Outdoor Life).
  • Deer scent glands send messages to other deer (90%, BC deer account):
    • Metatarsal (outside of the lower hind leg): alarm scent. Large on mule deer (10 to 15 cm) 85%.
    • Tarsal (inside of the hock): recognition; bucks rub urinate on it in the rut 90%.
    • Interdigital (between the toes): leaves a scent trail as it walks 90%.
  • Your scent comes from breath, skin, clothes, boots and the truck (Tip).
  • Scent spreads downwind and widens with distance, like a cone (Tip). The Hunt Map draws it: Scent cone in the wind tools.
  • Deer, elk, moose or caribou parts from outside BC cannot be used for hunting, and urine scents can carry CWD (Chronic Wasting Disease) (99%, synopsis page 12 item 51 and inside back cover, see deer mind).

• Sun on the slope: air and scent drift uphill 80%.
  • Evening cooling: scent slides downhill 80%.
More: thermals in detail
  • Sun warms a slope in the morning; warm air rises, so scent drifts uphill 80%.
  • In the evening slopes cool; cool air sinks, so scent drifts downhill 80%.
  • At dawn before the sun hits a slope, air is often still sinking. It flips after the sun warms that slope 75%.
  • A shaded north slope can still be draining while a sunny south slope is rising (Tip).
  • A strong main wind usually beats thermals (Tip).
  • Valley air near Heffley Creek sinks at night and in the evening and rises in late morning (80%, Heffley Creek).
  • Full lesson with drills: Wind and thermals.
My lean (opinion)

Morning: approach from above or from the side once the sun is on the slope. Evening: hunt from below or across, and leave before cold air drains your scent onto bedded deer.

• Draws, saddles and ridge backs swirl the air (Tip).
  • Check the wind every few minutes in broken ground (Tip).
More: swirls, eddies and how to read them
  • Wind pouring over a ridge can curl back down the lee side in an eddy (Tip, basic air flow).
  • Saddles funnel wind and swirl it; deer like to cross there, and so does your scent (Tip).
  • Mule deer often bed on the leeward (downwind) side of a roll in the ground, where they can smell the slope behind them (65%, Steven Rinella, MeatEater).
  • Incoming weather and clouds quickly kill a steady wind direction; plan stalks for stable wind (65%, Rinella).
  • Tools: a puffer of unscented powder, a light thread on the rifle, or milkweed fluff (Tip). The Hunt Map Weather and wind tool shows the forecast wind (Tip).

• Hears 115 Hz to 54 kHz, best 4 to 8 kHz 85%.
  • That band is zips, Velcro, nylon and metal clicks 85%.
More: what the ears catch
  • Deer hear about 115 Hz (hertz) to 54 kHz (kilohertz), best at about 4 to 8 kHz (85%, D'Angelo and others 2007).
  • People hear about 20 Hz to 20 kHz, so deer hear much higher pitches than you do 85%.
  • That best band holds zippers, Velcro, nylon swish, metal on metal and snapping twigs 85%.
  • Big ears swivel to point at a sound 75%. A mule deer's ears are about two thirds the length of its head 90%.
  • Natural sounds (wind, a squirrel, another deer walking) blend in. Steady two legged crunching, voices and metal do not (Tip).
  • Truck doors, tailgates and loud voices at the pullout can clear a slope (Tip).

• About 310 degrees without turning the head 80%.
  • Poor depth and detail; superb at motion 80%.
More: field of view, depth and motion
  • Eyes set on the sides of the head see about 310 degrees without moving the head (80%, Penn State Deer Research).
  • Depth perception is poor; the zone seen by both eyes is narrow and straight ahead 80%.
  • Horizontal pupils, typical of prey animals, gather a wide strip of the horizon 80%.
  • Many more rods than cones. Rods are better motion sensors 80%. So: motion and outline give you away, not colour 85%.
  • Straight behind is a small blind spot 80%. Do not count on it; deer turn their heads all day (Tip).
  • Nervous mule deer walk in a "stiff and jerky manner" (80%, US National Park Service). That walk means it has noticed something.

• Two colour types: blue and yellow green. No red cone (80 to 85%).
  • Blaze orange looks dull; blue and UV (ultraviolet) stand out 75%.
More: colour, ultraviolet and night
Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

  • Deer have 2 cone types, peaking near 455 nm (blue) and 537 nm (green). No red cone (85%, Jacobs 1994 via research notes).
  • They can tell blue from red but not green from red (80%, Penn State).
  • So blaze orange looks dull, close to yellowish grey 75%. The colour chart is a rough sketch, not exact (Tip).
  • Deer lack a UV (ultraviolet) filter in the eye, so they may pick up UV glow (80%, Penn State). UV brighteners in some detergents may glow to a deer (65%, Tip). Wash in unscented, no brightener soap.
  • Low light: rods are more than 1,000 times as sensitive as cones (80%, Penn State). A reflective layer behind the retina (tapetum) sends light back through the receptors; that is the eyeshine in your headlights 80%.
  • Lights: a moving headlamp or phone screen in the dark is pure motion. Red light, pointed at the ground (Tip). Hunting with a light is unlawful (99%, page 11, see legal methods).

• Hears it, looks for it, tries to smell it, then goes (Tip).
  • Freeze while it is only ears and eyes (Tip).
More: the sequence and the alarm stages
  • A sound or motion gets its attention; it stares, bobs its head, stamps, and often tries to circle downwind to smell you. Once it smells you, it leaves (Tip, built on the alarm stages in How a deer thinks).
  • The 5 alarm stages: alert stare, head bob, foot stamp, snort, escape (70%, hunter lore and research notes).
  • The metatarsal gland releases alarm scent that warns other deer (85%, BC account; biologists via Buckmasters).
  • Other deer watch each other: one alarmed deer alerts the group (Tip).
  • A deer that cannot see or smell what it heard may come closer to look (Tip). Curiosity is a mule deer weakness (see chapter 4).
5 stages of alarm1 of 5

• Nose: wind. Ears: rhythm and soft fabric. Eyes: stillness (Tip).
  • Use cover and shadow, never the skyline (Tip).
More: the full kit and drills
Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

  • Nose: keep the wind in your face or quartering; plan by thermals; check the wind every 10 minutes; leave if it turns (Tip).
  • Ears: walk, stop, walk, like a deer; soft wool or fleece; tape sling swivels; no talking, use signals (Tip, chapter 9).
  • Eyes: move only when its head is down or behind cover; stay below ridgelines; sit in shadow with something behind you; glass, do not walk (Tip).
  • The BC synopsis has no hunter orange requirement (90%, via What to wear). Wear it anyway for safety (Tip). It looks dull to deer 75%.
  • Drill: sit 20 minutes on a slope at dusk with the wind checker out. Note every time it changes (Tip).

• Rhyme: "Nose knows, ears hear, eyes see the move. Wind in your face, slow is smooth."
  • Number trick: 310 degrees of view; 4 to 8 kHz best hearing; 2 colour cones (80 to 85%).
  • Old hand's rule (tradition): "You can fool the eyes, you can fool the ears, you will never fool the nose."
More: more hooks
  • Rhyme: "Sun on the hill, scent climbs still; sun goes down, scent slides down."
  • Number trick: 115 Hz to 54 kHz: the deer's whole hearing range 85%.
  • Number trick: 1,000: rods are over 1,000 times more light sensitive than cones 80%.
  • Old hand's rule (widely taught, opinion): "Wind first, then the deer. If the wind is wrong, go somewhere else."
  • Old hand's rule (opinion): "When it stares, you are a stump."
Common mistakes
  • Checking the wind once at the truck.
  • Hunting a draw in the evening from above.
  • Moving while a deer is staring at you.
Do this in the field

This week: sit one evening on a slope with a puffer bottle. Write the time the air started to drain downhill.

mc-mule-deer-04:
Why it matters

A mule deer survives cougars, coyotes and hunters with a few habits. Learn them and you can predict its next move.

  • Built around cougar fear: cougars kill the most 85%.
  • Its habits are predictable: stot uphill, stop, look back (65 to 70%).
More: what this chapter covers
  • Alarm signals, flight and the famous look back, flight distance and hunting pressure, how it learns and remembers, family life, mother and fawn, old bucks versus young bucks, and the mistakes it keeps making.
  • Previous: Chapter 3, The senses. Next: Chapter 5, The year.

5 stages of alarm1 of 5
  • Stage 1 or 2? Freeze and you may win (Tip).
  • Stiff, jerky walk = it has noticed you 80%.
More: each signal and what to do
  • Stare: head up, ears forward. Freeze until it looks away (Tip).
  • Head bob: drops the head as if to feed, then snaps it up to catch you moving (hunter lore, 70%).
  • Foot stamp: a front hoof stamp warns other deer and tries to make you move 70%.
  • Snort or blow: a loud whoosh through the nose; all deer nearby go on alert (70%, mostly white tail sources).
  • Stiff, jerky walk: nervous mule deer walk "in a stiff and jerky manner" (80%, US National Park Service).
  • Alarm scent: the metatarsal gland on the hind leg releases alarm scent (90%, BC account).
  • Tail: a mule deer does not flag like a white tail; a tail held out or flicked while it stares means tension (Tip).
  • Stared at? Do not move a finger. Count to 100. Most deer go back to feeding if nothing else happens (Tip).

• Mule deer flee uphill into rough ground 70%.
  • Many stop on the rise and look back 65%.
More: the stot and the look back
  • The stot: all four feet land and push off together. Each bound covers 2.7 to 5.2 m, up to about 40 km/h (80%, US National Park Service).
  • Stotting suits steep, broken, brushy ground; it may also let the deer see over brush on its escape route (60%, Wild About Utah summary).
  • In Alberta studies, mule deer confronted by coyotes moved up slopes; white tails ran down and away (70%, Lingle, search previews).
  • The look back: after a few hundred metres a mule deer often stops on a rise to check on what spooked it (65%, Rinella; Outdoor Life; hunter consensus).
  • Big, mature bucks are often the exception: they leave and keep going (65%, Rinella).
  • What to do: when a deer stots off, do not chase. Get a rest, find the skyline it will cross, and wait. Only shoot a standing, broadside deer you have fully identified (Tip).

• Hunted deer run from farther away 65%.
  • Off trail walkers and dogs scare deer most 85%.
More: flight distance, pressure and what deer do about it
  • A 2008 review of hoofed animals: hunted populations flee people at greater distances than unhunted ones; predictable disturbance gets a smaller response than surprise (65%, Stankowich 2008 via citing papers).
  • People off trail cause more avoidance than people on trails; people with dogs cause even more (85%, Mule Deer Working Group fact sheet 17).
  • "If deer are moving away from you, you are too close" (85%, fact sheet 17).
  • Under hunting pressure, mule deer studied in Arizona did not leave their home ranges; they moved into better escape cover 65%. A Montana study found more use of timber in hunting season 65%.
  • Roads and access raise buck harvest risk: Idaho names open road density as the biggest driver, plus less hiding cover, gentle terrain and hunting during the rut (65%, Idaho Fish and Game, search preview).
  • Mule deer are more open country deer and more vulnerable to harvest than white tails (65%, Montana Fish, Wildlife and Parks policy).
  • For you: walk 500 m to 1 km past roads; close the truck door with your hip; no voices (Tip).

• Same migration route every year 85%.
  • Learned places pass from mother to fawn 85%.
More: memory, learning and habit
  • GPS (Global Positioning System) collars show mule deer use the same migration route year after year (85%, Mule Deer Working Group fact sheet 12).
  • Most SIMDeer (Southern Interior Mule Deer Project) deer "choose nearly the same path" each year (85%, BC Wildlife Federation 2020 update).
  • Deer return to the same home range year after year (85%, research notes). Mature deer are highly faithful to their ranges; yearling males are not (60%, Montana study, search preview).
  • Learned behaviour passes on: winter fed deer learn feeding sites and share them with each year's offspring (85%, fact sheet 2).
  • A deer spooked from one spot returns to its range; spooking is not forever (85%, quick lesson). But it may use that spot only at night for a while (Tip).
  • Habit you can use: the same trails, the same benches, the same crossing in the same wind (Tip).

• Doe clans: related females. Bucks: unrelated 90%.
  • Sparring is bonding, not fighting 90%.
More: groups, rank and the rut
  • "The social system consists of clans of females that are related to each other by maternal descent and bucks that are not related" (90%, BC deer account).
  • Mule deer mostly travel alone or in small groups, but "sometimes form larger groups" 90%. Groups are mostly 5 or fewer; winter 5 to 8, up to 15 to 30 (75%, research notes).
  • Bucks spend summer in bachelor groups of 2 to 4; these break up in October 80%.
  • Dominance display: a dominant buck circles a rival with deliberate steps, back arched, head low, tail flicking; the smaller one often bolts 90%.
  • Bucks also show dominance by "violently thrashing the bushes with their antlers" 90%.
  • Sparring between unequal bucks, especially yearlings and 2 year olds, is pushing and twisting, and "actually result[s] in social bonding" 90%.
  • In the rut, mature bucks of equal size fight head to head 90%. Older dominant bucks do most of the breeding; does cluster around the largest bucks 90%.
  • Does in groups have more eyes and ears 85%. When you glass one deer, look for the others (Tip).

• Fawns hide over 95% of the time; mother stays near 85%.
  • Mule deer does fight coyotes to defend fawns 70%.
More: fawn life and the doe's defence
  • Newborn fawns are "hiders": alone, licked clean, spotted, still (85%, Mule Deer Working Group fact sheet 26).
  • Days 1 to 3: head and ears flat, motionless even if touched. Days 4 to 6: hide, then bolt. By a week: run from farther. At 2 to 3 weeks: follow the mother 85%.
  • The doe nurses a few times a day and stays a few hundred metres away 85%. Deer milk has nearly 3 times the fat and protein of cow milk; fawns gain 5 to 10% of their birth weight a day 85%.
  • Before giving birth, does drive off last year's young and find a secluded spot (90%, BC account). Twins are the rule; young does often have one 90%.
  • Mule deer does vigorously defend fawns against coyotes; white tails rely more on flight (70%, Lingle, American Naturalist 2008, search preview).
  • Mule deer and white tail mothers respond to recorded fawn distress calls, even of other species in the right pitch (70%, Lingle 2007 and 2014).
  • Found a fawn? Leave it. The mother is near (85%, fact sheet 26).
  • Most fawn deaths in the first 15 weeks in SIMDeer (Southern Interior Mule Deer Project) were bears; cougars led for adult does and older fawns (85%, BC Wildlife Federation 2021 update).

• Young bucks wander and look back (60 to 65%).
  • Old bucks hold tight and slip away 65%.
More: personality by age
  • Yearling males are not faithful to a range; mature deer are (60%, Montana).
  • Young bucks are easier to see: daylight, open slopes, curious, look back (Tip, hunter consensus).
  • Big mature bucks often do not look back (65%, Rinella).
  • After the rut, bucks are thin and "tend to hide and rest" (90%, BC account).
  • By about 4 years antlers are 80 to 90% of peak size (85%, fact sheet 24). A big old buck may not carry the biggest rack.
  • Older bucks drop antlers first in winter (90%, BC account).
  • Buck survival is lower where roads are dense and cover thin (65%, Idaho).
  • Old hand's view (opinion): old bucks bed where they see below and smell above, often alone, and move in the last minutes of light (Tip).

• The look back, curiosity, and the rut (60 to 75%).
  • Same trails, same benches, same time (Tip).
More: the list an old hand uses
  • The look back on a rise 65%.
  • Curiosity: a deer that cannot place a sound may walk closer to see it (Tip).
  • Routine: same trails, crossings and beds when undisturbed (85% for routes; Tip for daily beds).
  • First light in the open: feeding on open slopes at dawn, then drifting to the bed (85%, chapter 6).
  • The rut: bucks travel in daylight and focus on does (75%, the rut session). "Without a doubt, the greatest time to hunt mule deer is during the rut" (65%, Rinella).
  • Snow: snow pushes them down onto winter range, where they gather 85%.
  • Group trust: a relaxed doe group calms a buck; spook one and they all go (Tip).
  • Use each one legally and fairly: no chasing with vehicles, no lights (99%, legal methods).

• Rhyme: "Up the hill, then stand and stare; old bucks don't, so be aware."
  • Number trick: 95% hiding fawn, few hundred metres to mum 85%.
  • Old hand's rule (tradition): "When a mulie bounces off, sit and count to 60."
More: more hooks
  • Rhyme: "Cougar fear made the mule deer: high and open, eyes in the rear."
  • Number trick: 2.7 to 5.2: metres per bound in a stot; 40 km/h top 80%.
  • Number trick: 1 clan of does, 2 to 4 bachelor bucks, groups mostly 5 or fewer (75 to 90%).
  • Old hand's rule (widely told, opinion): "Big bucks don't look back."
  • Old hand's rule (opinion): "If they are moving away, you are too close." (Also fact sheet 17 advice, 85%.)
Common mistakes
  • Chasing a deer that stotted over the hill.
  • Moving during the head bob.
  • Expecting an old buck to behave like a young one.
Do this in the field

Next time a deer stots away: stay put, rifle on a rest, watch the next rise for 2 minutes. Note if it looked back.

mc-mule-deer-05:
Why it matters

The same slope holds deer in one month and none the next. The calendar tells you which.

  • Day length drives antlers and the rut 85%.
  • Snow and cold drive the move down 85%.
More: what this chapter covers
  • January to December: winter survival, antler drop, green up, migration, fawns, velvet, hard antlers, the October shift, the rut, the post rut.
  • Two clocks run the year: day length (antlers, rut, fawning, very steady year to year) and weather (snow, green up, timing of migration, varies a lot) (85%, Mule Deer Working Group fact sheets 26 and 27; Monteith 2011).
  • Previous: Chapter 4, The mind. Next: Chapter 6, The day.

• Low, sunny, Douglas fir slopes; eat less, move little 85%.
  • Bucks drop antlers, old bucks first 90%.
More: winter in detail
Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

  • Winter range: low elevations, warm south and west aspects, gentle to moderate slopes, Douglas fir with snow catching crowns (85%, BC habitat model).
  • Snow over about 50 cm shuts deer out; 25 to 30 cm hinders them 85%. Trouble begins near 30 cm (90%, BC account).
  • Winter diet near Kamloops shifts to tall shrubs and trees as snow deepens; Douglas fir needles peak in December and January (85%, Willms 1976).
  • Deer eat less and lose weight in winter, even in good years; they move little to save energy (85%, Mule Deer Working Group fact sheet 17).
  • Antlers drop January to March, older bucks first (90%, BC account).
  • Main killers: predators (cougars first in SIMDeer, the Southern Interior Mule Deer Project), plus starvation in hard winters (85 to 90%).
  • No general mule deer season runs in MUs (Management Units) 3-27 and 3-28 after 10 December (99%, page 34, see Region 3). Winter is for scouting sheds and sign from a distance (Tip).
  • Keep away from wintering deer: "if deer are moving away from you, you are too close" (85%, fact sheet 17).

• April: deer on low south facing grass slopes 90%.
  • April to May: migrants head up to summer range 85%.
More: spring in detail
  • "The best time for viewing Mule Deer is April, when they move to low elevation, south facing grassy slopes in search of the first hints of green." The BC account names the Dewdrop Range near Kamloops 90%.
  • Most SIMDeer (Southern Interior Mule Deer Project) deer moved to summer range in April and May (85%, BC Wildlife Federation 2020 update).
  • Migrations can take 2 to 4 months, most of it spent at stopover sites following the green up (85%, Mule Deer Working Group fact sheet 12).
  • Bucks take longer than does on spring migration, about twice as long in one Wyoming and Colorado GPS (Global Positioning System) collar study (70%, USGS, United States Geological Survey, 2021).
  • Antlers start growing in April 90%.
  • 74% of SIMDeer deer were migratory, average 47.2 km a year; the longest about 100 km 85%. Some deer stay low all year 90%.
  • Spring diet: grasses and forbs like balsamroot, clover, wild strawberry, fireweed (90%, BC account).

• Fawns born late May through June 90%.
  • Twins are the rule 90%.
More: fawning in detail
  • Gestation about 203 days (85%, BC habitat model citing Robinette 1977); "six to seven months" (90%, BC account).
  • Fawns born late May through June 90%. In western provinces most are born in June (85%, fact sheet 26).
  • Birth sites: gentle terraces and benches between winter and summer range, with cover, food and nearby water (85%, BC habitat model).
  • Birth weight 2.7 to 4 kg. Twins are the rule; young does often have one; triplets now and then 90%.
  • Over 90% of adult does give birth each year 90%.
  • Most does breed as yearlings and have their first fawn near their second birthday 90%.
  • 45 to 70% of fawns normally die 90%. In SIMDeer (Southern Interior Mule Deer Project), bears caused most fawn deaths in the first 15 weeks 85%.
  • Does chase off last year's young before giving birth 90%. That is when you see lone yearlings (Tip).

• Antlers grow in velvet April to August 90%.
  • Deer are high: moist, high country, burns and meadows (85 to 90%).
More: summer in detail
  • Antlers are bone grown under velvet, a skin full of blood vessels and nerves (85%, fact sheet 27).
  • Testosterone is low while antlers grow; it rises in autumn and hardens them 85%.
  • Bucks hold bachelor groups of 2 to 4 in summer 80%.
  • Most deer leave the dry valley side ranges for moister, higher ground in summer (90%, BC account).
  • Summer diet: forbs and leaves of many shrubs; cut blocks and burns grow good summer food (85%, BC habitat model; the 2020 WAFWA (Western Association of Fish and Wildlife Agencies) report notes that recent burns boosted summer forage).
  • Summer is your scouting season: glass basins and burn edges at first and last light (Tip).

• Velvet comes off in 24 to 48 hours 85%.
  • 4 point bucks open 10 to 30 September in 3-27 and 3-28 99%.
More: September in detail
Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

  • Rising testosterone dries the velvet; the buck rubs it off on saplings and bushes, usually within 24 to 48 hours (85%, fact sheet 27). Bark tannin and blood stain the antlers brown 85%.
  • Bucks are still on or near summer range 85%.
  • Feeding hard: fat peaks heading into fall (60 to 65%, chapter 2).
  • Rule recap (study aid only): MUs (Management Units) 3-27 and 3-28 general season, 4 point bucks or better, 10 to 30 September (99%, page 34, Region 3).

• Pre rut: bachelor groups split, rubs, sparring (70 to 80%).
  • First snow up high starts the move down 85%.
More: the October shift in detail
Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

  • Bachelor groups break up in October 80%. Bucks spar and thrash brush 90%.
  • Snow and cold trigger the move to winter range, not the rut (85%, Monteith 2011).
  • SIMDeer (Southern Interior Mule Deer Project): most collared deer returned to winter range in October and November; in 2019 "by mid October ... nearly all the collared deer in each study area were back" 85%.
  • The 2000 BC account says interior deer "often remain at high elevations until December" 90%. Both are true in different years: the snow decides (75%, my reading).
  • Late October: bucks start checking doe groups at dawn and dusk 70%.
  • Rule recap (study aid only): 1 to 31 October in MUs (Management Units) 3-27 and 3-28 is any buck (99%, page 34).
  • My lean: no snow yet, glass high benches and burns at first light; snow up high, hunt mid slopes below the snow line (Tip, quick lesson).

• Rut mid November to mid December, peak mid November 80%.
  • Bucks follow does in daylight. Hunt the does 65%.
More: the rut in detail
Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

  • Mule deer rut "in November and early December" in BC (90%, BC account). Peak about mid November 80%.
  • Mule deer bucks rut on winter range, so snow and rut bring them to the same open slopes (80%, the rut).
  • Courtship is a tending bond: a buck stays with one doe and keeps other bucks away until she breeds or another buck displaces him (90%, BC account).
  • A doe is receptive for about a day; if not bred she cycles again about 4 weeks later (60%, white tail sources).
  • Rutting bucks smell doe urine and lift the lip (flehmen) 65%.
  • Equal mature bucks fight; bucks show up in daylight; they eat little (90%; 65% eat little).
  • "Find does and wait," and hunt all day: bucks stay active longer in the rut (65%, Rinella).
  • Rule recap (study aid only): 1 November to 10 December, 4 point bucks or better, MUs (Management Units) 3-27 and 3-28 (99%, page 34).

• Bucks thin, tired, hiding to rest 90%.
  • A smaller second rut can follow about 4 weeks later 60%.
More: December in detail
Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

  • "Following the rut, bucks have lost weight and some have wounds or broken antlers, and they tend to hide and rest" (90%, BC account).
  • Unbred does cycle again about 28 days later; some late breeding in December (60%, white tail sources; Kentucky wildlife agency).
  • Deer gather on winter range; deeper snow pushes them lower 85%.
  • The general season in 3-27 and 3-28 ends 10 December (99%, page 34).
  • Deer use fat fastest in November and December (65%, Wyoming does). Leave wintering deer in peace after the season (Tip).

• Rhyme: "April green on the low south hill; June brings fawns; October chill; November rut."
  • Number trick: 203 days pregnant: mid November rut, early June fawn 85%.
  • Old hand's rule (tradition): "First snow up high, hunt down low."
More: more hooks
  • Rhyme: "Velvet in summer, bone by fall; snow brings them down, the rut brings all."
  • Number trick: 1, 3, 4 to 8: drop antlers January to March; grow April to August 90%.
  • Number trick: 24 to 48: hours to strip velvet 85%.
  • Number trick: 74 and 47: percent of SIMDeer (Southern Interior Mule Deer Project) deer that migrate, and kilometres a year they travel 85%.
  • Old hand's rule (widely taught, opinion): "In the rut, hunt the does."
  • Old hand's rule (opinion): "Day length sets the date, weather sets the show."
Common mistakes
  • Hunting high country after the first big snow.
  • Expecting the rut in October.
  • Counting the rut as the trigger to migrate. It is snow.
Do this in the field

Keep a Journal note each trip: date, snow line elevation, deer seen and where. After 3 seasons you have your own calendar.
