mc-mule-deer-06:
Why it matters

Most mule deer are seen in two short windows a day. Be in the right seat for both.

  • Peaks about 04:00 to 09:00 and 17:00 to 21:00 85%.
  • Bedded about 10:00 to 15:00 80%.
More: what this chapter covers
  • Bed to feed to water, the hours, and how wind, rain, snow, cold fronts, barometric pressure, the moon and hunting pressure change the day.
  • Each claim carries its evidence level. Much of what hunters say about weather is lore, not tested (see the evidence screen).
  • Previous: Chapter 5, The year. Next: Chapter 7, Where they are.

• Dawn: feed on open slopes, then drift up to bed 85%.
  • Dusk: down to feed, water in dry weather (80%, Tip).
More: the daily loop
Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

  • Night: feeds on and off in open grass and brush, rests between bouts 75%.
  • Before first light to about 09:00: a strong activity peak (85%, Stewart and others 2002, Oregon telemetry).
  • Then it drifts uphill or into cover to bed (85%, quick lesson).
  • Mule deer "tend to bed not far from a food source" (65%, Rinella).
  • Midday: bedded, chewing cud; gets up to stretch, nibble and re bed 80%.
  • Late afternoon: rises, browses near the bed, then moves to open feeding slopes 80%.
  • Sunset to about 21:00: second peak 85%.
  • Water: in dry fall weather near water at dusk or dawn; with green feed and dew, less need (Tip).
  • Deer activity is highest within about 3 hours of sunrise and sunset (85%, Mule Deer Working Group fact sheet 17).
  • Legal hunting hours: 1 hour before sunrise to 1 hour after sunset (99%, page 11, see legal methods).

• Warm day: shade, north slopes, timber 80%.
  • Cold day: sun, south and west slopes, out of wind 80%.
More: where it beds and why
  • Day beds give hiding cover and shelter (80%, Germaine 2004).
  • Warm days: north facing timber, benches, draws, shade 80%.
  • Cold days: sunny south and west slopes out of the wind 80%.
  • On a slope it often beds facing downhill with the wind at its back, on the leeward side of a roll (65%, Rinella).
  • In a desert study, bed sites had the most overhead cover in summer (60%, Arizona 2001). Temperature and canopy decide summer beds 60%.
  • Lore: bucks bed in the top third of a slope (60%, not a rule).
  • Midday is the time to find beds with binoculars and plan a stalk (Tip, chapter 9).

• Strong or shifting wind ruins stalks 65%.
  • Most weather effects on deer are weakly tested (50 to 55%).
More: weather, one by one
  • Wind: strong wind makes deer edgy and hard to approach (Tip, hunter lore 55%). Clouds and incoming weather kill a steady wind; back out and wait (65%, Rinella).
  • Rain: light rain dampens your noise and scent; deer often feed through it (Tip). Heavy rain: bedded (Tip).
  • Snow: fresh snow shows every track (Tip). Deep snow pushes deer down and limits movement (85%, chapter 5).
  • Cold: cold, crisp mornings put rutting animals on their feet in daylight; warm wind hides them (70%, the rut).
  • Heat: warm October afternoons push deer into shade and timber 80%.
  • Cold fronts: hunters say deer feed hard before a front and move after it (Tip, 50%). Not well tested for mule deer.
  • In GPS (Global Positioning System) studies of white tails, weather had an inconsistent effect within a season (70%, Webb and others 2010).

• Moon phase: GPS (Global Positioning System) collar studies found no effect 70%.
  • Barometer: no solid evidence (40%, Tip).
More: the evidence, honestly
  • Moon: 32 GPS collared white tails in Oklahoma over 7 years. Moon phase had no effect on daily, night or day movement (70%, Webb and others 2010). Other GPS work found small or no moon effects 65%.
  • Earlier studies that found moon effects used older radio collars (65%, Penn State).
  • No mule deer moon study found. Treat moon tables as entertainment (Tip).
  • Barometric pressure: one white tail study tied very high pressure to more winter buck movement, with caveats; others found little (50%, search previews). Not a fact for mule deer.
  • What does move deer, with good evidence: light (dawn and dusk), snow and cold, the rut, hunting pressure (70 to 85%).
  • My lean: hunt every day you can. Log weather and sightings in the Journal and find your own pattern (Tip).

• Pressured deer use thicker cover and more night (65 to 70%).
  • Weekends and roads push deer away (Tip).
More: pressure in detail
Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

  • Pressured deer move more at night and use thicker cover (70%, quick lesson).
  • Arizona: hunted deer shifted to better escape cover as the season went on 65%. Montana: more use of timber in hunting season 65%.
  • Hunted populations flee people at longer distances (65%, Stankowich 2008).
  • Roads and ATVs (all terrain vehicles) raise buck vulnerability (65%, Idaho Fish and Game).
  • Off trail people and dogs disturb more than on trail (85%, fact sheet 17).
  • For you: be in your seat before first light, stay through midday on busy weekends, and hunt the quiet weekdays if you can (Tip).
  • Rule recap (study aid only): no ATV (all terrain vehicle) for hunting 1 September to 10 December in MUs (Management Units) 3-28, 3-29 and 3-30 (99%, page 33, Region 3). Fewer quads, calmer deer (Tip).

  • Rut days are long days: stay out (65%, Rinella).
  • Post rut bucks hide 90%.
More: why
  • Peaks at dawn and dusk come from the Starkey study 85% and agency advice (85%, fact sheet 17).
  • Rut: bucks travel and show in daylight (75%, the rut); "hunt all day" (65%, Rinella).
  • Post rut: "they tend to hide and rest" (90%, BC account).

  • Plan on light, snow, rut and pressure. Log the rest (Tip).
More: how to read this
  • Strong: several studies or agency sources agree.
  • Good: one or two studies, or agency advice.
  • Lore: widely told by hunters, not tested for mule deer.
  • Weak or not supported: tested, little or no effect found, mostly in white tails.

• Rhyme: "Four to nine and five to nine; between them deer lie down in line."
  • Number trick: 3 hours: peak activity within 3 hours of sunrise and sunset 85%.
  • Old hand's rule (tradition): "Be on the glass before the light."
More: more hooks
  • Rhyme: "Hot day, shady slope; cold day, sunny hope."
  • Number trick: 04 to 09, 10 to 15, 17 to 21: active, bedded, active (80 to 85%).
  • Number trick: 32 deer, 7 years, no moon effect 70%.
  • Old hand's rule (widely taught, opinion): "Hunt the weather you have." Go every chance you get.
  • Old hand's rule (opinion): "Noon is for finding beds, not for napping."
Common mistakes
  • Walking in at daylight. The deer were already up and leaving.
  • Planning around the moon.
  • Leaving at 10:00 on a cold rut day.
Do this in the field

Each trip, log: time of each deer seen, temperature, wind, cloud, moon. After 10 trips, sort by hour.

mc-mule-deer-07:
Why it matters

Deer are not everywhere. They are where food, cover and safe ground meet, at the right height for the month.

  • Summer high, winter low on sunny slopes (85 to 90%).
  • An edge animal: food next to cover 85%.
More: what this chapter covers
  • Habitat needs, key BC plants by season, winter range, elevation by month, your three areas (Heffley Creek, Fraser Valley, South Okanagan), and step by step how to find deer country on the Hunt Map.
  • Zones on the drawing are BEC (Biogeoclimatic Ecosystem Classification) zones: BG bunchgrass, PP ponderosa pine, IDF interior Douglas fir, MS montane spruce, ESSF Engelmann spruce subalpine fir (90%, BC zone names). The order is right; the heights are a sketch (Tip).
  • Previous: Chapter 6, The day. Next: Chapter 8, Sign and tracking.

• Needs food, hiding cover and winter thermal cover close together 85%.
  • Hunt the edges where they meet (Tip).
More: habitat needs in detail
  • Mule deer are an "ecotonal species" that favour high contrast forest edges with lots of forage close to escape and thermal cover (85%, BC habitat model 2003).
  • Typical habitats: open conifer forest, climax brush, aspen stands, steep broken terrain and river valleys 85%.
  • Security (hiding) habitat: rugged broken terrain, wooded valleys, shrubby draws, steep slopes, dense trees or shrubs 85%.
  • Good hiding cover hides about 90% of a deer at 60 m or less, in patches 180 m or more across (80%, Thomas 1979 via the model).
  • Fire and logging open the forest and grow shrubs; burns and young cutblocks are good summer food 85%.
  • The 2017 and 2018 fires boosted summer forage but cut winter cover in places (85%, WAFWA, Western Association of Fish and Wildlife Agencies 2020).

• Browse is the bulk of the year's diet 85%.
  • Winter near Kamloops: Douglas fir peaks December and January 85%.

More: the plant table
SeasonMain foods (certainty)
SpringNew grass, forbs: balsamroot, clover, wild strawberry, fireweed 90%
SummerForbs and leaves of many shrubs 90%
FallForbs, shrub leaves and twigs, fresh grass after rain; grass under 10% near Kamloops 85%
WinterShrubs and Douglas fir: big sagebrush, bitterbrush, rabbitbrush, snowbrush, saskatoon, rose 90%
  • Kamloops stomach study (Willms 1976, September to April): grass under 10% until spring; more forbs in fall; shrubs early fall and late winter; Douglas fir peaks December and January 85%.
  • Central interior winter ranges: diets 45 to 76% conifers; Douglas fir 24 to 73% (85%, Waterhouse 1994 via the model).
  • Winter diet elsewhere: 79% browse, 15% grasses, 6% forbs (85%, Cowan 1947 via the model).
  • Other important plants: willow, chokecherry, soopolallie, snowberry, Oregon grape, aspen, rose, alfalfa (85%, model table; quick lesson).
  • Learn 3 by sight first: saskatoon, red osier dogwood, Oregon grape (Tip).

• South and west slopes, low, gentle, old Douglas fir 85%.
  • Crowns catch snow; canopy about 65 to 70% 85%.
More: winter range in detail
  • Interior winter range: shrublands in the dry forest zone and steep south and west facing broken terrain (90%, BC account).
  • Thermal habitat: warm aspects, gentle to moderate slopes, low elevations, Douglas fir dominant (85%, BC habitat model citing Bunnell 1990 and Armleder 1986).
  • Good stands: long crowns that intercept snow; canopy about 65 to 70% closure with small openings; layers of younger fir underneath 85%.
  • Snow over about 50 cm shuts deer out; 25 to 30 cm hinders 85%.
  • Some interior provincial benchmark winter habitats are rated class 1 in the ponderosa pine and very dry interior Douglas fir zones (85%, model table).
  • Winter range is fragile. Respect closures and do not push wintering deer (85%, Mule Deer Working Group fact sheet 17).

• Low in winter, high in summer, moving in spring and fall (85 to 90%).
  • Snow sets the timing each year 85%.
More: elevation in detail
  • "In summer, most deer migrate to higher elevations ... but some remain at low elevations all year" (90%, BC account).
  • In mountains of BC, mule deer use upper elevation and alpine habitats in summer, lower valleys and south slopes in winter (85%, BC habitat model).
  • A Kamloops winter range study area sat below about 760 m (80%, Willms 1976).
  • Near Tranquille, ponderosa pine and Douglas fir zones run about 610 to 1,160 m (70%, ecological reserve description, search preview).
  • Rough local heights (VERIFY on the map): valley about 370 to 450 m, Heffley Lake about 950 m, Sun Peaks village about 1,250 m 55%.
  • No snow yet in October: bucks often mid slope, about 900 to 1,500 m, on open fir and burn edges (75%, Heffley Creek).
  • Use the Hunt Map elevation profile and the BEC (Biogeoclimatic Ecosystem Classification) zone layer rather than fixed numbers (Tip).

• Kamloops and the North Thompson rank among BC's best mule deer areas 85%.
  • No mapped official winter range right around Kamloops 90%.
More: Heffley Creek in detail
Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

  • The BC habitat model lists the highest reported mule deer densities (over 1 deer per 0.2 km2) in places including the North Thompson River, the City of Kamloops and Copper Creek in the Thompson Basin 85%.
  • Approved ungulate winter range polygons: none in a box around Kamloops and Heffley Creek (90%, BC data check, research notes 2026-10-03). Use the habitat rule instead: south and west slopes, bunchgrass, ponderosa pine and Douglas fir below about 1,000 m 75%.
  • Dewdrop Rosseau Creek WMA (Wildlife Management Area), north shore of Kamloops Lake, is winter range for mule deer and bighorn sheep 90%. The synopsis lists it as a motor vehicle closed area (90%, page 33 via research notes; check Region 3).
  • Lac du Bois Grasslands: mule and white tailed deer (95%, BC Parks). Hunting rules there: see the Heffley Creek session and the Rule Book.
  • Local reading 75%: grassland and open Douglas fir benches above the valley; up toward Heffley Lake, Paul Lake and Sun Peaks in summer and early fall; lower, sunnier slopes as snow comes.
  • MU (Management Unit) 3-27 success 20 to 41% a year, 2020 to 2024 (90%, chapter 1).
  • Closest SIMDeer (Southern Interior Mule Deer Project) study area: Cache Creek and Bonaparte. Mule deer were the most abundant mammal on cameras there 85%.

• Here the deer is the black tail, same species 90%.
  • Spring and summer: logged openings. Winter: old growth higher up 90%.
More: black tail country in detail
  • Columbian black tailed deer live along the coast, west of the Coast and Cascade summits (90%, BC account).
  • They "make frequent use of logged habitats during spring and summer" 90%.
  • Old growth forest is key winter range for coastal black tails, more so northward and at higher elevations; steep south to west facing sites are best winter range 90%.
  • Winter and early spring foods: Douglas fir, western redcedar, red huckleberry, salal, deer fern, tree lichens. Late spring to fall: grasses, trailing blackberry, fireweed, pearly everlasting, willow, salmonberry and maple leaves 90%.
  • Black tailed deer breed in November and early December (80%, BC wildlife report).
  • Region 2 resident "mule deer" (black tail) success: 41% in 2024, 2,708 hunters (90%, harvest statistics).
  • Skagit Valley Provincial Park lists mule and black tailed deer along the road and campgrounds (90%, BC Parks, research notes).
  • Rules differ from Region 3: see Region 2 and Mission.

• Grassland and dry pine slopes are prime mule deer winter range (85 to 95%).
  • White Lake and the South Okanagan grasslands are named winter range 95%.
More: South Okanagan in detail
  • BC Parks: South Okanagan Grasslands Protected Area is "class 1 mule deer winter range"; White Lake Grasslands is "mule deer winter range" (95%, research notes 2026-10-03).
  • Provincial benchmark winter habitat is rated class 1 in the very dry ponderosa pine and Douglas fir zones of the South Okanagan Basin and Okanagan Range (85%, BC habitat model).
  • The Okanagan River area is listed among the highest mule deer densities 85%.
  • Access to White Lake is largely through private land; ask first (95%, BC Parks). Rules: Region 8 and South Okanagan.
  • Region 8 resident mule deer success: 23% in 2024 (90%, harvest statistics). MU (Management Unit) 8-1: 38% in 2024 90%.
  • One mule deer buck for Regions 3 to 8 combined: a Heffley Creek buck uses up your Okanagan buck (95%, bag limits).

Find deer country on the Hunt Map1 of 6
  • Open the Hunt Map. Pick the month at the top of the layers panel (Tip).
  • Then go and check on foot (Tip).
More: step by step in words
  1. Layers: turn on "Mule deer" season layer (pick the month), mule deer ungulate winter range, burns, cutblocks and BEC (Biogeoclimatic Ecosystem Classification) zones. Land status layers on: Crown land, private land, parks, closures (Tip). The season layer is a general pattern from studies, not mapped corridors (app layer note).
  2. Terrain tools, Slope direction (aspect): south and west faces for October to winter; north faces for hot afternoon beds (85%, chapter 6).
  3. Slope steepness: benches (flat) under steep ground are classic beds and feeding edges (Tip). Steep red and purple ground is escape terrain (Tip).
  4. What can I see from here (viewshed): drop a pin on a ridge or knob; the map shades what you can see. Pick seats that see several benches and openings (Tip).
  5. Sun and shade: set the time to sunrise; slopes that get first sun on a cold morning get early feeding deer (Tip).
  6. Weather and wind, scent cone: check the forecast wind and draw your scent cone. Approach so it misses the slope (Tip).
  7. Add a waypoint for each seat. Check land status and closures for every spot (Tip, see land status).
  8. Then walk it: sign, beds, glassing at first light. The map finds country; your boots find deer (Tip).

• Rhyme: "Food by cover, sun on the slope; that's where mule deer winter in hope."
  • Number trick: 90 at 60: good cover hides 90% of a deer at 60 m 80%.
  • Old hand's rule (tradition): "Hunt the edges, not the middles."
More: more hooks
  • Rhyme: "South and west when the snow falls; north and shade when the heat calls."
  • Number trick: 65 to 70: percent canopy of good fir winter range 85%.
  • Number trick: under 10: percent grass in fall and winter diets near Kamloops 85%.
  • Old hand's rule (widely taught, opinion): "Find the food, find the deer."
  • Old hand's rule (opinion): "Map the country at home, read it on foot."
Common mistakes
  • Glassing the middle of big open grass at midday instead of the edges.
  • Hunting high basins after a big snow.
  • Trusting a map layer without checking land status.
Do this in the field

This week: on the Hunt Map, mark 3 glassing seats on south or west slopes within 1 hour of Heffley Creek. Check each with "What can I see from here".

mc-mule-deer-08:
Why it matters

Sign is the deer's diary. Read how fresh it is and you know whether to sit, stalk or move on.

  • Tracks, pellets, beds, browse, rubs: who, which way, how long ago (Tip).
  • Fresh sign beats old memories (Tip).
More: what this chapter covers
  • Tracks to scale, gaits and trail patterns, droppings, beds, rubs and thrashed brush, browse sign, how fresh, and how to follow a trail.
  • Mule deer do not dust like grouse or call like elk; their sign is tracks, pellets, beds, browse and rubs (Tip).
  • The general lessons: Tracks, Reading sign, Snow tracking.
  • Previous: Chapter 7, Where they are. Next: Chapter 9, How to hunt them.

• Split heart, 2 toes; the point shows the way it went 85%.
  • Front track about 5.7 to 10 cm long 60%.
More: track details
  • Two toes, heart shaped; the pointed end shows the direction of travel 85%.
  • Mule deer front track about 5.7 to 10 cm long (60%, research notes). Front tracks are usually a bit bigger than hind 75%.
  • Dewclaws (two dots behind the print) show in soft ground, snow or when running (Tip).
  • One track cannot tell mule deer from white tail; too much overlap 60%. The trail pattern can (chapter screen below).
  • Measure, never guess: carry a tape or know your knife length (Tip).
  • Splayed toes and deep prints: running or a heavy animal on soft ground (Tip).

• Stot: groups of 4 prints, bounds 2.7 to 5.2 m (60 to 80%).
  • A stot trail means alarm. A walk means calm (Tip).
More: gaits in detail
  • Walking: prints in pairs or one line, short even steps; the hind foot often lands in the front print (Tip, see Tracks).
  • Trot: longer, straighter steps (Tip).
  • Stot: all 4 feet push off together; groups of 4 prints 2.4 to 4.6 m apart (60%, research notes); park service gives 2.7 to 5.2 m per bound 80%.
  • A white tail bounding gallop leaves groups too, but long and low with the hind feet landing ahead of the front (70%, Tracks). The bouncy stot is the mule deer mark 85%.
  • A stot trail near you: you or something else spooked it. Do not follow at once (Tip).

• Oval pellets about 1 to 1.5 cm 70%.
  • Dark, shiny, moist: hours old 60%.
More: pellets in detail
  • Pellets: oval, about 1 to 1.5 cm long, often with a small point; firm and dry in fall and winter 70%.
  • Summer on green feed: softer, clumped (Tip).
  • A deer drops roughly 13 to 34 pellet groups a day 70%. Lots of piles = lots of deer time there (Tip).
  • Hours: wet, shiny, maybe warm. Days: dull with a crust. Weeks: faded, crumbling, mouldy 60%.
  • Cold slows ageing: frozen pellets can look fresh for a week (Tip).
  • Mixed ages in one spot: a bed or feeding area used again and again (Tip).

• Oval about 1 m, pellets and hair nearby 70%.
  • Melted frost or a warm bed: minutes to hours (Tip).
More: bed reading in detail
  • A deer bed is an oval of flattened grass, needles or snow about 0.9 to 1.2 m long 70%.
  • Beds sit where a deer sees below and smells above: benches, under a tree with a view, the lee side of a roll (60 to 65%, hunter lore and Rinella).
  • Mule deer often bed facing downhill (65%, Rinella).
  • Several beds together: a doe group. A lone big bed away from others: often a buck (Tip).
  • In snow, an old bed melts and refreezes into an icy bowl; a dry, crisp floor is recent (65%, Reading sign).
  • Frost: a dark green oval in a white frosted slope at 08:00 means it just got up (Tip).
  • Warm bed: the deer may be watching you. Freeze and glass ahead (Tip).

• Mule deer rub less than white tails, on small conifers and shrubs 60%.
  • Thrashed brush in October: a buck is near (90% for the behaviour, Tip for the meaning).
More: rubs in detail
  • Bucks rub velvet off on saplings and bushes in late August and September; velvet strips in 24 to 48 hours (85%, Mule Deer Working Group fact sheet 27).
  • Bucks show dominance by "violently thrashing the bushes with their antlers" (90%, BC account).
  • Mule deer make fewer rubs than white tails, mostly on small conifers and shrubs 60%.
  • Rub height says more about buck size than tree size; a rub centred 75 cm or higher suggests a mature buck (60%, Reading sign).
  • Scrapes are mostly a white tail sign; mule deer rarely scrape 60%.
  • Fresh: wet white wood, curled bark shavings, sap; old: grey, dry wood (Tip).

• Deer tear twigs; hares cut them clean at 45 degrees 75%.
  • Green stem ends = fresh (Tip).
More: browse in detail
  • Deer have no upper front teeth, so browsed twigs look torn and ragged (75 to 85%, chapter 2).
  • Snowshoe hares clip twigs clean at about 45 degrees 75%.
  • A browse line: shrubs eaten up to about head height on winter range shows heavy deer use (Tip, Reading sign).
  • Fresh browse: green, moist stem ends; old: brown, dry (Tip).
  • Check saskatoon, red osier dogwood, bitterbrush and rose (85%, chapter 7).

• Read 3 clues, not 1: track edges, pellets, bed (Tip).
  • Note weather: rain and frost reset the clock (Tip).
More: freshness checklist
  • Track edges sharp, no debris or frost in the print: fresh (Tip).
  • Last rain or frost: a print on top of it is newer than the weather (Tip).
  • Pellets shiny and soft: hours 60%.
  • Bed with no frost while the slope is frosted: very fresh (Tip).
  • Browse ends green and wet: today (Tip).
  • Decide: fresh sign plus good wind = slow down and glass; old sign = mark it in the Journal and move (Tip).

Follow a mule deer trail1 of 4
  • Follow slow. The deer is usually ahead, watching back (Tip).
  • Snow is the best classroom (Tip).
More: following in detail
  • Mark the last sure track with flagging and a phone pin; you will need it if you lose the trail (Tip, blood trailing).
  • Walk beside the line so you do not wipe out sign for a second look (Tip).
  • Glass ahead every few steps; a following hunter usually sees the deer only if he looks up (Tip).
  • A trail that turns uphill and slows, with the deer stopping to look back, often leads to a bed on a bench (Tip).
  • Mule deer often bed where they can watch their back trail (hunter lore 60%). Follow the trail from the side and above (Tip).
  • Lost it: back to the last flag, then circle in small then bigger loops (Tip).
  • Wounded animal tracking is its own skill: blood trailing.

• Rhyme: "Point shows the way, shine shows the day."
  • Number trick: 1, 1 to 1.5, 5.7 to 10: a 1 m bed, 1 to 1.5 cm pellets, 5.7 to 10 cm tracks (60 to 70%).
  • Old hand's rule (tradition): "Fresh sign beats a good map."
More: more hooks
  • Rhyme: "Torn twig, deer; clean cut, hare."
  • Number trick: 4 prints per group in a stot; 2.7 to 5.2 m between (60 to 80%).
  • Number trick: 13 to 34 pellet groups a day 70%.
  • Old hand's rule (widely taught, opinion): "Look up from the track." The deer is ahead, not under your boots.
  • Old hand's rule (opinion): "A warm bed means freeze, not sit."
Common mistakes
  • Calling species from one track.
  • Following with eyes on the ground.
  • Trusting pellets alone for freshness in frost.
Do this in the field

Next scouting walk: find 3 pellet piles and age each one. Photograph them with your knife for scale. Check your guesses against the sign drill.

mc-mule-deer-09:
Why it matters

Mule deer are hunted with the eyes first and the feet last. Every method here starts with glass and wind.

  • Glass first, then choose the method (Tip).
  • Wind decides which slope, every time (Tip).
More: what this chapter covers
  • Scouting, glassing, spot and stalk, still hunting, sitting a trail or edge, calling and rattling, hunting with a partner, the day's decisions, ethics, and what a 40 year hunter does differently.
  • Tactics are opinion (Tip). Each one is built on the biology in chapters 2 to 8 and on advice from hunting educators and the Mule Deer Foundation.
  • Rules in this chapter are a study aid only; the official regulations are the law. Full rules: the Rule Book.
  • Previous: Chapter 8, Sign and tracking. Next: Chapter 10, Shot to table.

Scout a new area in 5 steps1 of 5
  • Scout in the off season and the week before (Tip).
  • Log every deer: time, slope, which way it faced (Tip).
More: scouting in detail
  • Use the Hunt Map at home (chapter 7), then confirm on foot (Tip).
  • Drive the Heffley Lake road at dusk with binoculars; note every deer, the time, the slope and which way it faced (Tip, quick lesson field task).
  • Summer scouting shows where bucks live, but snow can move them before your hunt (85%, chapter 5). Scout again the week before (Tip).
  • Walk midday for sign: tracks, pellets, beds, rubs, browse (chapter 8). Stay off the slopes you plan to hunt at dawn (Tip).
  • Check land status, closures and No Shooting areas for every spot (Tip, land status).
  • Use the Journal: after 10 trips you have your own pattern (Tip).

• Sit on a rest before first light; glass shadows and edges (Tip).
  • Look for white rumps, ears, antler tips, a flick (65%, Tip).
▶Glassing for Mule Deer with Jordan Budd | MeatEater ClipsSit, rest the optics, and pick the slope apart.
MeatEater Clips, YouTube, 3 min. Needs internet.
More: glassing in detail
Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

  • Be on the seat 45 minutes before legal light (Tip, quick lesson). Legal light starts 1 hour before sunrise (99%, page 11, legal methods).
  • "Glass from a distance and let the spotting scope do the walking" (60%, Mule Deer Foundation, M. Luby). Set up before first light and glass into the shadows 60%.
  • In snow free country you often find mule deer by their whitish rumps; in snow, look for brown bodies (65%, Rinella).
  • Bedded deer: scan for heads, necks, ears and antler tips above brush (65%, Rinella).
  • Grid method: split the slope into squares, near to far, 1 to 2 minutes per square (Tip, Glassing).
  • Steady optics on a tripod or pack; 10x42 binoculars are a good first optic (Tip, Mule Deer Foundation).
  • Glass again the same slope; deer stand up and appear all morning (Tip).

Spot and stalk in 5 steps1 of 5
  • Plan with landmarks, wind and sun before you move (60%, Tip).
  • From above if you can: they bed facing down 65%.

▶Remi Warren Breaks Down His Mule Deer Stalking TechniquesPlan the stalk from where you glassed: landmarks, wind, cover.
OutdoorClass, YouTube, 2 min. Needs internet.
More: stalking in detail
  • Use terrain, wind direction and the sun to your advantage, and stay out of sight lines (60%, Mule Deer Foundation).
  • Mule deer bed facing downhill, so "starting the stalk above the deer" is a huge advantage (65%, Rinella).
  • Mule deer bed on the leeward side of rolls; plan for the wind they are using 65%.
  • Landmarks look different up close. Pick 2 or 3 near the deer (a dead tree, a rock, a bush) and photograph them from the glassing seat (Tip).
  • Morning thermals rise once the sun is up: come from above or the side then. Evening: from below or across (80% thermals; Tip approach).
  • Leave the pack, slow to a crawl the last 100 m, check the wind every 20 m (Tip).
  • Bedded buck: wait for it to stand if the angle is bad; deer usually stand to stretch in the afternoon (80%, chapter 6).
  • If the wind turns: back out and come back another day (Tip).

• Slow walk into the wind through bedding cover (Tip).
  • Works midday and in timber; deer often see you first (Tip).
More: still hunting in detail
  • A few steps, stop, look for a minute; walk like a deer, not a person (Tip, Still hunting).
  • Into or across the wind only (Tip).
  • Look for parts: an ear, a leg, a horizontal back line in vertical timber (Tip).
  • Best on damp, quiet ground, in wind or light rain (Tip).
  • Shots are quick and close: shoot only standing deer you have fully identified (Tip).
  • Mule deer in rough broken ground are better glassed than still hunted (Tip, hunter consensus).

• Sit between beds and feed at dawn and dusk (Tip).
  • Quiet, steady, great for a first season (Tip).
More: sitting in detail
  • Deer feed on open slopes at dawn and dusk and drift to beds (85%, chapter 6). Sit the edge where they cross (Tip).
  • Pick a seat with the wind blowing from the deer to you, a rest, and a safe backstop (Tip).
  • In the rut, sit a saddle or bench between doe groups from first light (Tip, the rut).
  • Pros: quiet, rested shot, learn deer behaviour. Cons: needs the right spot and patience (Tip).
  • My lean for your first trip: sit and glass a feeding slope at dawn and dusk; scout midday (Tip, quick lesson).

• Mouth calls are allowed; electronic calls are not (95 to 99%).
  • Rattling works less well for mule deer (50%, Tip).
More: calls in detail
Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

  • Recorded or electronic calls are unlawful for hunting wildlife except wolf, coyote, cougar, lynx, bobcat and Schedule C birds (99%, page 12, legal methods).
  • Mouth calls, grunt tubes and rattling antlers are not recorded or electronic, so they are allowed (95%, my reading in the Rule Book).
  • Rattling pulled bucks in about 65% of sessions in a Texas white tail study 70%, but it is less reliable for mule deer 50%.
  • A soft grunt or doe bleat can stop a walking buck for a shot (60%, hunter lore).
  • Mule deer does respond to fawn distress calls (70%, Lingle). That is a reason not to blow distress calls carelessly: you may pull does, not bucks (Tip).
  • Deer urine lures: banned if from outside BC; urine scents can carry CWD (Chronic Wasting Disease) (99%, page 12 item 51, inside back cover).

• One glasses and signals, one stalks (Tip).
  • Agree zones of fire and signals before you split (Tip).

More: partner tactics in detail
Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

  • Spotter and stalker: the spotter stays on the glassing seat and guides with hand signals; the stalker follows landmarks (Tip).
  • Two seats: you and your brother glass two slopes and meet at 10:00 (Tip).
  • Push a draw: one hunter walks a draw with the wind at his back while the other sits the escape route up the slope; mule deer often flee uphill (70% for uphill flight; Tip for the tactic). Never with either hunter in the other's .
  • Blaze orange on both of you when moving (Tip; not required by the BC synopsis, 90%).
  • Only one shooter at a time (Tip). The hunter who kills the deer cancels his own species licence right away (99%, page 11 item 1, via the quick lesson).
  • Dogs: allowed for deer only on a leash (99%, page 12, legal methods). That includes a dog tracking a wounded deer (90%, my reading in the Rule Book).

• Wind wrong? Change slope (Tip).
  • Not sure? No shot (Tip).
More: decisions in detail
  • Before dawn: check the forecast wind and thermals; pick the slope where both work (Tip).
  • First light: glass. No deer by about 10:00? Walk for sign or move to the next seat (Tip).
  • Deer bedded: plan the stalk, or note the spot and come back for the evening (Tip).
  • Snow fell overnight: drop elevation and look for fresh tracks (85% for deer moving down; Tip for the tactic).
  • Before any shot: legal species, sex, points counted on one side, safe backstop, inside your tested range, broadside or quartering away (99% for the legal parts via the Rule Book; Tip for the rest).
  • Long day plan: dawn seat, midday sign walk, afternoon stalk or seat, dusk seat (Tip).

• Sits and glasses more, walks less (Tip).
  • Lets a bad chance go (Tip).
More: the old hand's habits and ethics
Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

  • Glasses for hours, walks for minutes (Tip, widely taught).
  • Checks the wind all day and walks away from a bad wind (Tip).
  • Walks 500 m to 1 km past roads and pullouts (Tip).
  • Knows each slope by month and snow (chapter 5) and keeps a journal (Tip).
  • Waits for a standing broadside deer inside a tested range; passes on running, skylined or quartering to shots (Tip, shot placement).
  • Counts points twice in a 4 point season (99% rule; Tip habit).
  • Expects the look back, and is ready on a rest 65%.
  • In the rut, hunts the does and stays out all day (65%, Rinella).
  • Ethics: fair chase, no lights (99%, page 11), and a real effort to recover every hit animal (95%, blood trailing). The full list of unlawful acts: Rule Book.
  • Respect land: ask permission on private land and ranches (Tip, landowner permission).

• Rhyme: "Glass at first light, stalk at noon, sit at dusk under the moon." (Tip)
  • Number trick: 45, 10, 100: be seated 45 minutes before light; glass till 10:00; crawl the last 100 m (Tip).
  • Old hand's rule (tradition): "Glass more, walk less."
More: more hooks
  • Rhyme: "Wind in your face, landmarks in mind; from above the bed, you'll be hard to find."
  • Number trick: 2 landmarks near the deer, 1 shooter at a time (Tip).
  • Old hand's rule (widely taught, opinion): "The deer you see first is the deer you can stalk."
  • Old hand's rule (opinion): "If the wind is wrong, go home or go elsewhere."
  • Old hand's rule (opinion): "When it beds, you plan; when it stands, you shoot."
Common mistakes
  • Walking ridgelines all day and seeing only rumps.
  • Starting a stalk without landmarks.
  • Talking on the glassing seat.
Do this in the field

First trip plan: dawn seat, midday sign walk, dusk seat. Agree 4 hand signals with your brother before you leave the truck.

  • Steven Rinella, MeatEater (2018), A guide to hunting mule deer, checked 2026-10-11 65%
  • Lingle (fawn distress calls), ScienceDaily 2007, search preview 70%
  • BC Hunting and Trapping Regulations Synopsis 2026 to 2028, via the Rule Book: page 11 (hours, lights), page 12 (calls, dogs, item 51) 99%; calls my reading 95%
  • Hunt Mentor sessions: Glassing, Still hunting, the rut, What to wear, shot placement, legal methods.
  • Research notes: research/2026-10-01-deer.md (rattling study), research/2026-10-11-masterclass-mule-deer.md.
mc-mule-deer-10:
Why it matters

The hunt is not over at the shot. A calm hour after it decides whether you find the deer and how good it tastes.

  • Shot, watch, wait, track, notch, cool, hang, cut, cook (Tip).
  • Notch the licence before you handle the deer 99%.
More: what this chapter covers
  • Shot placement and range, reactions to the hit, waiting and tracking, field care, meat care, yield and cooking, a rules recap that links to the Rule Book (no new rules), the one page cheat sheet, and links to every chapter.
  • Full lessons: shot placement, blood trailing, field dressing, meat care, cooking.
  • Previous: Chapter 9, How to hunt them.

• Broadside: up the back of the front leg, one third up 85%.
  • Your limit: the range where you hit a 15 cm plate 9 of 10 (Tip).

More: placement and range in detail
  • Broadside: up the back of the front leg, one third up the chest; both lungs and the top of the heart 85%.
  • Quartering away: aim so the bullet exits the far shoulder 85%.
  • Quartering to: not for your first season (Tip). Head, neck, running, skylined: no (Tip).
  • Wait for the near front leg to step forward; it opens the chest 85%.
  • Vital zone with margin: about 20 to 25 cm (8 to 10 in) 75%.
  • Your .308 Winchester with a 150 to 165 grain expanding bullet is plenty for mule deer (Tip, quick lesson).
  • Maximum range: where you hit a 15 cm (6 in) plate 9 of 10 from a field rest; for most beginners about 200 m (219 yd) (Tip).
  • Mule deer often stop and look back: be on a rest and ready, but only shoot a standing deer you have identified and counted (65%; Tip).

• Kick and hard low run: often heart or lungs 70%.
  • Hunched, slow walk: often a gut hit 70%.
More: reactions in detail
  • Keep the rifle on the deer until it is out of sight. Reload, safety on (Tip).
  • Mule kick, then a hard low run: often heart or lungs (70%, National Deer Association via blood trailing).
  • Heart: rarely over about 50 m; both lungs: under about 100 m (85%, shot placement).
  • Hunched back, short run, then a walk: often a gut hit 70%.
  • Hard run with a limp: often a leg hit 70%.
  • Listen for a crash. Fix the last spot you saw it: a tree, a rock (Tip).
  • Drop a phone pin where you shot from and where it stood. Note the time (Tip).

• Heart or lungs: wait 30 minutes (70 to 85%).
  • Liver: 4 to 6 hours. Gut: 6 to 8 hours or overnight (70 to 85%).
More: waiting and tracking in detail
Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

  • Wait times are opinion from hunter education, not law (70 to 85%, blood trailing).
  • Mark the exact spot where it stood with flagging before you move 85%.
  • Read the hit site: blood colour, bubbles, hair, stomach matter (70 to 85%):
    • Bright red, bubbly: lungs.
    • Dark red, no bubbles: liver.
    • Thin, green brown, smells: gut.
  • Track slowly beside the trail; glass ahead (Tip, chapter 8).
  • Lost blood: go back to the last sign and grid search (Tip).

Why it matters

You cannot hunt what you cannot name in half a second. This chapter makes a white tail obvious at 200 m.

  • 10 chapters. This is chapter 1: who the white tail is.
  • Quick version first? White tailed deer.
More: what the 10 chapters cover
  1. Meet the animal (this one): ID, look alikes, size, BC numbers.
  2. The body: bones, lungs, heart, rumen, fat.
  3. The senses: nose, ears, eyes and how to beat each.
  4. The mind: alarm, pressure, family life, old bucks.
  5. The year: month by month, antlers, rut, fawns.
  6. The day: bed, feed, weather, moon, pressure.
  7. Where they are: habitat, foods, your 3 regions, the Hunt Map.
  8. Sign and tracking: tracks, beds, rubs, scrapes, following.

  10. Shot to table and the rules: placement, tracking, meat, rules, cheat sheet.
  • Each chapter ends with memory hooks and a 5 question quiz.
  • Flashcards: the White tail Masterclass deck.
  • Mule deer share most of the body plan. Their Masterclass is chapter by chapter alongside this one, for example Mule deer Masterclass 2.

• Buck: antlers September to winter 85%.
  • Doe: no antlers. Fawn: spots fade by fall 75%.

More: ID by sex and age
  • Buck (male): hard antlers from about September until they drop, January to March (75%, see chapter 5).
  • Doe (female): no antlers. Longer, slimmer face (Tip).
  • Fawn (under 1 year): born late May or June with white spots (85%, BC account). Spots fade with the first fall coat 75%.
  • Button buck: a male fawn with two small bumps, not antlers. Counts as antlerless (99%, synopsis page 3, via the quick lesson).
  • Yearling buck (about 1.5 years): often a spike or small fork, thin neck, "a doe with antlers" (65%, National Deer Association via Field and Stream).

• White tail: wide brown tail, white only underneath 85%.
  • Up and waving = the flag 85%.
More: tail, rump and run
  • White tail: tail is wide, brown on top, bright white underneath and on the edges (85%, Alberta Institute for Wildlife Conservation).
  • Rump: only a small white patch, hidden when the tail is down 80%.
  • Alarm: tail goes straight up and waves 85%.
  • Mule deer: thin white rope tail with a black tip on a big white rump 85%.
  • The run: white tails gallop low and smooth to cover. Mule deer stot, bouncing on all 4 feet 85%.

• One main beam sweeps forward. Tines rise off it 85%.
  • Mule deer antlers fork, and fork again 85%.
More: how to read white tail antlers
  • Main beam: grows back from the base, then curves forward and in 85%.
  • Brow tine (G1): short tine just above the base. Most white tail bucks have one 70%.
  • Tines G2, G3, G4: rise straight up from the main beam, like teeth on a comb 85%.
  • Counting points: hunters count each tine about 2.5 cm (1 in) or longer, plus the beam tip (Tip, scoring custom). For legal antler definitions use the Rule Book only.
  • Antler size grows with age and food, but a young buck on good feed can fool you. Judge age by the body (next screen) 65%.

• Body first, antlers second 65%.
  • Yearling: thin neck, long legs, "a doe with antlers" 65%.
More: aging on the hoof
  • Yearling (1.5 years): lanky, clear break between neck and shoulders, narrow waist 65%.
  • 2 to 3 years: chest deepens, neck swells in the rut, hindquarters and shoulders even out 60%.
  • 4 years plus: deep chest, belly sags, thick neck blends into the shoulders, legs look short 65%.
  • Old bucks may show loose skin on the face and neck and a sway back 60%.
  • Hindquarters bigger than the shoulders: almost always a 1 or 2 year old 60%.
  • Not an exact science. Get more than one view (65%, Kip Adams, National Deer Association, via Field and Stream).
  • Easiest in late pre rut and the weeks after, when bucks are in peak shape 60%.

• Mule deer: separate species, separate licence and seasons 99%.
  • Button buck = antlerless. Know which class is open 99%.

mc-white-tailed-deer-02:
Why it matters

Know what is under the hide and you know where to aim, how far it runs, and how to save the meat.

  • Lungs and heart sit just behind the front leg 85%.
  • Same plan as a mule deer, a bit smaller 80%.
More: what this chapter covers
  • Bones and muscles that matter for the shot and the meat.
  • Breathing: lungs and diaphragm.
  • Heart and big blood vessels.
  • Digestion: the rumen and its 4 chambers.
  • Body heat, coat and the fat cycle through the year.
  • How long white tails live.
  • Shared deer anatomy is drawn in more detail in Mule deer Masterclass 2. This chapter stands alone and adds what is white tail specific.

• Shoulder blade covers the front of the lungs 80%.
  • Aim tight behind it, one third up 75%.
More: skeleton and muscles that matter
  • The front leg hangs from the shoulder blade by muscle only. Deer have no collarbone, so the shoulder slides as the leg moves 75%.
  • A forward leg (walking) pulls the shoulder forward and opens the lungs. A back leg covers more lung (Tip, hunter education).
  • The heavy leg bone (humerus) runs from the shoulder joint down to the elbow. Hitting it can stop a bullet short of the lungs (Tip).
  • Biggest meat: the hindquarters, then the backstraps along the spine, then the shoulders 75%.
  • A shoulder shot wastes the most front meat (Tip).

• The diaphragm pulls the lungs open 85%.
  • Hit both lungs: fast, humane collapse 75%.
More: breathing detail
  • Like all mammals, a deer breathes with its diaphragm, a sheet of muscle between chest and belly 90%.
  • The diaphragm moves back, the chest gets bigger, air rushes in. It moves forward, air goes out 90%.
  • A bullet hole through the chest wall lets air in around the lungs, and they collapse 80%.
  • Both lungs hit: the deer runs on stored oxygen, often 50 to 100 m, then falls (Tip, quick lesson; National Deer Association says usually within 137 m, 150 yd) 70%.
  • Breath shows on cold mornings. A steaming breath in the brush can give a bedded deer away (Tip).

• Heart sits low, between the elbows 80%.
  • Main artery runs under the spine 85%.
More: heart and vessels detail
  • The heart sits low in the chest, roughly level with the elbow 80%.
  • Aim one third up the chest to take both lungs and the top of the heart (75%, standard hunter education).
  • The aorta (main artery) runs from the top of the heart back under the spine 85%.
  • A shot high in the lungs can cut the big vessels under the spine, but also risks a spine hit and a deer that drops and gets up again (Tip).
  • Heart shot deer often bolt hard, then crash (Tip). See chapter 10.
  • Link: vitals diagram.

• 4 chambers. Microbes do the digesting 85%.
  • Eats 2 to 4% of body weight a day, dry 80%.
More: rumen detail
  • White tails are ruminants with a four chambered stomach (85%, Montana State University Extension).
  • Chamber 1, the rumen, holds bacteria and protozoa that break plants down 85%.
  • The microbes specialise. A sudden diet change (like hay in a hard winter) can leave a deer starving on a full stomach until the microbes adjust (80%, Montana State University Extension).
  • A deer needs 2 to 4% of its body weight in dry matter a day. Mature bucks peak at about 2 to 3 kg (4.5 to 6.5 lb) a day in spring; does peak at about 1.4 to 2.7 kg (3 to 6 lb) in fall 80%.
  • They are selective browsers: a narrow muzzle picks buds, leaves and twigs 85%.
  • They chew cud lying down, which is why a bedded deer stays put for hours 75%.
  • Meat note: a gut shot spills rumen and gut contents. Clean the cavity fast and trim (Tip). See field dressing.

• Red summer coat, grey brown winter coat 80%.
  • Deep snow over about 40 cm makes travel hard 85%.
More: heat, coat and winter
  • Summer coat: thin and reddish. Winter coat: thick, grey brown, hollow hairs that trap heat 75%.
  • Walking in 40 cm (16 in) of snow costs a small deer 7 to 8 times the energy of bare ground (85%, US Forest Service species review).
  • In 30 cm (12 in) of snow in New York, about 97% of food was buried (85%, US Forest Service species review).
  • In hard winters, white tails yard up: they stay in a few hectares of dense conifer cover and pack trails (80%, Montana State University Extension).
  • Deer cut their own food intake in winter and lower their energy use (75%, studies on northern deer).
  • The metatarsal gland is bigger in northern deer. One idea is that it helps with temperature, but its role is unclear 60%.

• Bucks: fattest in September, burn it in the rut 75%.
  • Everyone is leanest in late winter 80%.
More: fat cycle detail
  • Bucks fatten through late summer, then nearly stop eating in the rut and lose a lot of weight 75%.
  • Does are leanest after nursing fawns in summer and late winter, and fatten in fall 75%.
  • A white tail that enters winter fat can lose about 30% of its weight and live (60%, popular press, Tip).
  • A rut worn buck enters winter thin. Hard winters kill more old bucks and fawns 70%.
  • Meat note: an October deer carries more fat than a December buck (Tip). Deer fat tastes strong. Trim it before you freeze (Tip, see cooking).

• Few pass 10 years 85%.
  • A 4 year old buck is already old for a hunted herd (Tip).
More: lifespan detail
  • White tails can live past 20, but few pass 10 (85%, US Forest Service species review).
  • One review: most die by age 4 or 5 80%.
  • Heavily hunted Pennsylvania: average life expectancy about 2 years for males and 3 for females (85%, US Forest Service species review).
  • Idaho Fish and Game: a deer that eats well and avoids predators may live to 9 or 10 80%.
  • Exact age needs tooth wear or a tooth section in a lab 75%.

• Aim behind the shoulder, one third up 75%.
  • No shoulder bone, no gut: more meat, faster death (Tip).

  • Number trick: 4 chambers, 1 diaphragm, one third up.
  • Old hand's rule (tradition): "Shoot the shoulder crease, not the shoulder."

  • Number trick: 2 to 4% a day. A 90 kg buck eats about 2 to 3.5 kg of dry food a day.

  • Aiming too high "for the heart" and hitting above the lungs.

Why it matters

Every white tail you ever get close to, you got close by beating its nose, ears and eyes in that order.

  • Nose first, ears second, eyes third (Tip, ranking).
  • Valley white tails live where wind swirls and air pools (Tip).

  • Nose and how scent travels with wind and thermals.

More: nose detail
  • A deer's nose is its best sense 85%. The often quoted "297 million receptors" is folklore (45%, not a fact).
  • Your scent comes from breath, skin, clothes, boots and your truck (Tip).
  • It spreads downwind as a cone: narrow at you, wide far away (80%, physics of drifting air).
  • Light wind swirls the cone. Steady wind keeps it tight and predictable (Tip).
  • White tails often bed and travel so the wind brings them news from where they cannot see (Tip, hunter observation).
  • The Hunt Map has a Scent cone tool: set the wind and see where your scent goes (Hunt Map).

• Evening: cool air drains downhill to the bottoms 80%.
  • Morning sun: air rises up the slopes 80%.
More: thermals for white tail country
  • Sun warms slopes in the morning, warm air rises, scent drifts uphill 80%.
  • Slopes cool in the evening, cool air sinks, scent drifts downhill 80%.
  • In a valley, that cool air pools along the river at dusk and dawn, right where white tails bed in willow and cottonwood (Tip, from thermal physics).
  • So an evening stand on the slope above a river bottom can leak your scent down to the deer (Tip).
  • Better: sit on the field edge with the bottom upwind, or on the bottom's downwind side (Tip).
  • At dawn before sun hits, air still sinks. It flips once the slope warms 75%.

• Hears about 115 Hz (hertz) to 54 kHz (kilohertz) 85%.
  • Best at 4 to 8 kHz: zippers, Velcro, metal clicks 85%.
More: ears detail
  • Deer hear from about 115 Hz (hertz) to 54 kHz (kilohertz), best around 4 to 8 kHz (85%, D'Angelo and others 2007).
  • That best band is exactly zippers, Velcro, nylon swish, metal on metal and snapping twigs 85%.
  • Each ear swivels on its own to point at a sound 75%.
  • Natural rhythms (a squirrel, another deer: step, stop, step) pass. Steady two legged crunching does not (Tip).
  • Idaho Fish and Game: white tails have very good hearing for danger and give a loud snort when alarmed 80%.

• Sees about 310 degrees without turning its head 80%.
  • Poor depth and detail; great at motion 80%.
More: field of view detail
  • Eyes on the sides of the head give about a 310 degree view (80%, Penn State Deer Research; some sources say 300).
  • The blind spot is a narrow wedge straight behind 80%.
  • Only a narrow zone in front is seen by both eyes, so depth judgement is poor 80%.
  • Horizontal pupil: a wide slit that scans the horizon, typical of prey animals 80%.
  • Rods give strong motion detection and good low light vision 80%.
  • A reflective layer behind the retina (tapetum lucidum) brightens dim light. That is the eye shine in headlights 75%.

• No red cone: blaze orange looks dull 75%.
  • Motion and outline give you away 85%.
More: colour detail
  • Deer have 2 colour cones, peaking near 455 nm (blue) and 537 nm (green). No red cone (85%, Jacobs and others 1994).
  • So blaze orange looks dull, close to grey or brown 75%. Blue stands out more (65%, Tip: skip blue jeans).
  • In low light, deer are most sensitive to blue and blue green (80%, Penn State).
  • Deer see more ultraviolet (UV) than we do 75%. Unscented soap without UV brighteners (Tip, 65%).
  • A moving phone screen or headlamp in the dark is pure motion (Tip).

• Height takes you out of the main view (Tip).
  • Deer do look up. Stillness still matters most (Tip).
More: stands and eye level
  • A white tail scans the horizon at its own eye level (80%, horizontal pupil).
  • A tree stand or a ground blind with a dark back wall hides your outline (Tip, hunter consensus).
  • Ground hunters: sit in shadow with something behind you, not on the skyline (Tip).
  • Deer that have been hunted from stands learn to look up (Tip).
  • Tree stand safety: wear a full body harness and stay clipped in from the ground up (Tip, widely taught tree stand safety). Ground blinds avoid the fall risk (Tip).

• Ears and eyes raise doubt. The nose decides (Tip).
  • Unsure white tails often circle downwind (Tip).
More: how they combine
  • A white tail often hears you first, then looks for motion (Tip, hunter observation).
  • If it sees something odd but cannot smell it, it may stamp, head bob or stare to make you move 70%.
  • Many hunters report unsure white tails circling to get downwind (Tip, widely reported, not measured).
  • Once the nose confirms: snort, flag, gone 80%.
  • The full alarm ladder (alert, head bob, stamp, snort, run) is in How a deer thinks and chapter 4.

SenseBeat it withNever
NoseWind and thermals 80%Hunt a bad wind (Tip)
EarsWool, slow feet (Tip)Zippers, Velcro 85%
EyesStillness, shade 85%Skyline, quick moves (Tip)
  • Check the wind every 10 minutes (Tip).
  • Move only when its head is down or behind cover (Tip).
More: the full plan
  • Nose: pick stands by the wind for the hour you sit. Have a plan B stand for a different wind (Tip).
  • Nose: walk in on a route your scent will not cross the trail (Tip).
  • Ears: quiet outer layer, tape metal on sling and pack (Tip).
  • Ears: walk like a deer: step, step, stop (Tip).
  • Eyes: shade, a background, slow hands (Tip).
  • All three: arrive early and let the woods settle (Tip).
  • Deer urine lures from outside BC are banned for hunting (95%, synopsis page 12 item 51, via How a deer thinks). Wind beats lures anyway (Tip).

• Rhyme: "Nose knows, ears hear, eyes see what moves near."
  • Number trick: 310 degrees, 4 to 8 kHz, 2 cones.
  • Old hand's rule (tradition): "Hunt the wind, or hunt somewhere else."
More: more hooks, mistakes and field drill
  • Rhyme: "Sun up, scent up. Sun down, scent down."
  • Old hand's rule (widely taught, opinion): "You can fool the eyes and the ears. You can never fool the nose."
  • Number trick: 360 minus 310 = a 50 degree blind spot behind.
Common mistakes
  • Sitting an evening stand above a river bottom: your scent drains down to them.
  • Unzipping a pack when a deer is in sight.
  • Turning your head quickly when you hear a step.
Do this in the field

Next sit: hang a thread on your rifle. Note the wind direction every 10 minutes in the Journal, plus when it flips.

mc-white-tailed-deer-04:
Why it matters

A white tail is a nervous homebody. It knows every bush in its range and learns your habits fast.

  • Lives its whole life in a small home range 75%.
  • Learns pressure in a day, and hides rather than leaves 70%.
More: what this chapter covers
  • Alarm signals: body, tail and voice.
  • Flight: where it runs and when it stops.
  • How it learns and remembers pressure.
  • Family life: does, fawns, bachelor bucks, dispersing yearlings.
  • Old buck vs young buck.
  • Mistakes white tails make that you can count on.
  • Mule deer behave differently in open country. Compare Mule deer Masterclass 4.

5 stages of alarm1 of 5
  • Stamp and snort are tests: freeze (Tip).
  • Relaxed tail flicks side to side: calm deer (Tip).
More: alarm detail
  1. Alert: head up, ears forward, stare 75%.
  2. Head bob: drops the head as if to feed, then snaps it up (70%, hunter lore).
  3. Foot stamp: stamps a front hoof. It may also leave extra scent from the gland between the toes 60%.
  4. Snort or blow: a loud whoosh, a bit like a whistle. It means danger (80%, Idaho Fish and Game).
  5. Escape: tail up (the flag), smooth gallop to cover 85%.
  • Tail flicking side to side while feeding usually means calm (Tip, hunter observation).
  • Tail half up, stiff legged walk: suspicious, about to go (Tip).

CallWhoMeans
SnortAllDanger 80%
GruntBucks, doesContact, low threat 80%
Grunt snort wheezeRut bucksBig challenge 80%
Tending gruntBuck with doeRut 70%
BleatDoes, fawnsContact, distress 70%
  • Researchers recorded 12 white tail calls 80%.
More: voice detail
  • Atkeson, Marchinton and Miller (1988) recorded 12 white tail vocalizations and analysed 10 80%.
  • Agonistic (fighting) calls: the low grunt, the grunt snort (grunt plus 1 to 4 snorts), and the grunt snort wheeze, typical of dominant bucks in the breeding season 80%.
  • Tending grunt: longer and drawn out, made by a buck with a doe (70%, Marchinton via Realtree).
  • Bleats: fawns and does call to stay in touch, and fawns bleat in distress 70%.
  • How you use this: a few soft grunts in late October and November (chapter 9). Never snort wheeze at a small buck: it can scare him off (Tip).

• Why it flags is still debated 70%.
  • A flag means it is leaving. Let it go (Tip).
More: why the flag
  • Ideas: warn other deer, tell the predator "I see you, do not bother", or a beacon for fawns to follow 65%.
  • Caro and others (1995) found little support for the "warn other deer" idea 70%.
  • Idaho Fish and Game teaches it as a warning and a beacon for fawns in thick brush (80%, agency education).
  • For you: a flagging deer is in full flight. No shot (Tip, matches the quick lesson's rule).

• Runs to the nearest thick cover, not over the hill 75%.
  • Often stops just inside to look back (Tip).
More: flight detail
  • White tails rely on cover close by. They gallop to it, often along a trail they know 75%.
  • They can make an almost 90 degree turn at full speed (60%, Field and Stream).
  • Standing jump of about 2.4 m (8 ft) is reported (60%, Tip).
  • Swims of over 3 km (2 miles) are documented 60%.
  • Many hunters see a spooked white tail stop just inside cover and look back (Tip). That look back is not a reason to rush a shot through brush.
  • No flight distance study for white tails was found. VERIFY any number you hear.

• GPS deer reacted the day before opening 70%.
  • They hide inside their home range. They do not leave 70%.
More: pressure detail
  • Penn State satellite collar study (Diefenbach): deer began reacting to hunters the day before season opened (70%, news and radio reports).
  • Deer found cover within their home range during hunting hours. One doe moved to a steep hillside refuge once rifle season began 70%.
  • Adult males were the hardest of all to kill and reacted fastest 70%.
  • Deer return to the same home range year after year, so pressure is not forever 85%.
  • Pressured white tails move more at night 70%.
  • More: Hunting pressure.

• Does live in family groups with their daughters 80%.
  • About 70% of yearling bucks leave home 80%.
More: social detail
  • Doe groups are matrilineal: an old doe, her daughters and their fawns 80%.
  • Yearling does often rejoin their mother and her new fawns after fawning and stay until the next spring (80%, Montana State University Extension).
  • Bucks form bachelor groups of 2 to 4 in summer (80%, Montana State University Extension). They break up in September and October 75%.
  • About 70% of yearling bucks disperse, mostly in October and November in Pennsylvania (80%, Pennsylvania Game Commission). Missouri: 77% of buck fawns left at about 1 year, average about 14 km (9 miles) 75%.
  • Dispersing yearlings go farther where there is less forest 80%.
  • Does hide newborn fawns alone and return only to nurse 85%.

• Bucks spar after velvet comes off, then sort out rank 80%.
  • White tail bucks fight more than mule deer bucks 75%.
More: hierarchy detail
  • After antlers harden, bucks spar and form a dominance hierarchy that decides who breeds in the November rut (80%, Montana State University Extension).
  • Bucks mark areas with rubs and scrapes but do not defend a territory. They defend the doe in heat 80%.
  • Combat is common among dominant bucks in the same area 80%.
  • Montana State University Extension: white tail bucks are more aggressive toward each other than mule deer bucks 75%.
  • That is why rattling (fake fight sounds) works on white tails (70%, chapter 9).

• Old bucks: smaller home range, thickest cover, night moves 65%.
  • Young bucks: daylight, careless, easy to see (Tip).
More: old and young in detail
  • A review of 15 years of collar studies found mature bucks' home ranges get smaller with age, not bigger (65%, Boone and Crockett).
  • A South Texas study of 33 bucks: home range shrank from yearling to 3 years, then grew in mature bucks 65%. Results differ by place.
  • A Mississippi study of 60 collared bucks: the average buck used 31 bedding areas in a season. The few beds used again and again had dense screening cover (65%, Field and Stream).
  • Mature bucks are most at risk in the rut search phases, before and after peak breeding 65%.
  • Yearlings disperse, wander and move in daylight (80% dispersal; daylight Tip).

• Rut bucks move in daylight chasing does 75%.
  • Same trail, same field edge, evening after evening (Tip).
More: mistakes you can count on
  • Rut: bucks cover far more ground and move midday in late October and November 75%.
  • Habit: a calm white tail uses the same trail from bed to food night after night (Tip, hunter consensus).
  • Curiosity: a buck may come to a soft grunt or rattling near the rut 70%.
  • Following a doe: a buck trailing a hot doe walks into the open (Tip).
  • Funnels: deer squeeze through the same pinch points: creek crossings, fence gaps, brush necks (Tip, see Funnels).
  • Return: a deer spooked once is often back in a few days if you leave it alone (Tip).

• Rhyme: "Stamp and stare, freeze right there."
  • Number trick: 12 calls, 2 to 4 bachelors, 70% of yearlings leave.
  • Old hand's rule (tradition): "Pressure him and he hides at home."
More: more hooks, mistakes and field drill
  • Old hand's rule (opinion, widely repeated): "An old buck didn't get old by being careless." Matches collar findings that adult males react fastest.
  • Rhyme: "Does in the family, bucks in a gang; yearlings wander when the rut bells clang."
Common mistakes
  • Moving when a doe stamps at you.
  • Hunting the same stand every day until the deer pattern you.
  • Using a loud snort wheeze call on young bucks.
Do this in the field

Watch one family group of does at a field edge for an evening. Note who leads, where they enter, and what makes heads come up.

mc-white-tailed-deer-05:
Why it matters

The calendar tells you where a white tail is and what it wants. October and November change everything.

  • Antlers: drop in winter, grow in summer, hard by September 75%.
  • Rut peaks in November. Fawns: late May or June 85%.
More: what this chapter covers
  • January to December, one screen per season.
  • October and November in detail: rubs, scrapes, rut phases, the doe's heat.
  • The antler cycle.
  • Winter survival.
  • Mule deer migrate much farther. Compare Mule deer Masterclass 5.

• Valley bottoms, south slopes, dense conifer in deep snow 85%.
  • Bucks drop antlers January to March 75%.
More: winter detail
  • Snow depth is the main factor in where white tails can live (85%, BC account).
  • Winter range: south to southwest slopes, fans and terraces with shrubs; cottonwood and willow groves early in winter; conifer patches when snow is deep (85%, BC account, East Kootenay data).
  • In winter they are active most of the day, not just dawn and dusk (85%, BC account).
  • In hard winters they yard up in dense cover and pack trails 80%.
  • Deer can use snow as water in winter (80%, Montana State University Extension).
  • Antlers drop after testosterone falls, about January to March 75%.
  • Winter browse near Kamloops: Douglas fir peaks in December and January in deer rumens (85%, Willms 1976, mostly mule deer data).
  • Leave wintering deer alone: every run costs fat they cannot replace (Tip).

• Fields and riverbanks green first 60%.
  • Fawns born late May or June, hidden about 2 weeks 85%.
More: spring detail
  • Antlers start growing in April, in velvet 75%.
  • Pregnant does drive off last year's young before giving birth 70%.
  • Gestation is about 202 days, roughly 7 months (80%, Montana State University Extension; US Forest Service species review range 187 to 213 days).
  • Fawns are born late May and June (85%, BC account; Montana State University Extension). Twins are normal 80%.
  • Fawns weigh 2 to 4 kg (5 to 8 lb) 80%. Does choose 0.4 to 2 ha (1 to 5 acre) patches with low shrubs and trees to give birth (80%, Montana State University Extension).
  • The doe hides the fawn and comes back only to nurse, about 4 to 6 times a day 75%. Fawns lie still about 95% of the day for the first 10 to 14 days (75%, Virginia DWR, Department of Wildlife Resources).
  • Fawns have almost no scent at first, and the doe licks them clean 75%.
  • Found a lone fawn? It is not abandoned. Leave it (Tip, agency advice).
  • The fawn photo above is a mule deer fawn: white tail fawns look the same at this age 75%.

• Bucks in bachelor groups, antlers in velvet 80%.
  • Fawns start following the doe at 3 to 4 weeks 70%.
More: summer detail
  • Summer: floodplains, river terraces, hay and alfalfa fields (85%, BC account; data/migration.json).
  • Bucks in velvet avoid fights and stay in cool, secure, insect free spots (80%, Montana State University Extension).
  • Bachelor groups of 2 to 4 bucks 80%.
  • Summer activity peaks at dawn and dusk (85%, BC account).
  • Fawns lose spots as their first winter coat comes in, in late summer and fall 70%.

• Velvet comes off in early to mid September 75%.
  • Bachelor groups break up. Sparring starts 75%.
More: September detail
  • Rising testosterone, driven by shorter days, hardens the antler and the buck rubs the velvet off (75%, University of Georgia).
  • First rubs appear on saplings 70%.
  • Bachelor groups split up through September and October 75%.
  • Buck season opens. Region 3: bucks 10 September to 10 December 99%. Region 8: bucks 10 September to 30 November 99%. Details in chapter 10.
Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law. Region 3 page 34, Region 8 page 68, 2026 to 2028 synopsis.

• Rubs early, scrapes late in the month 65%.
  • Bucks start moving in daylight late October 70%.
More: October detail
  • Early October: sparring, rubs, bucks still on summer feeding patterns 70%.
  • Mid to late October: scrapes appear and get worked at night 60%.
  • Late October: the seeking phase. Bucks cruise for the first does in heat (60%, hunter guides).
  • Yearling bucks disperse, mostly October and November (80%, Pennsylvania).
  • Antlerless white tails: Region 3 and Region 8, 10 to 31 October, no draw (99%, pages 34 and 68).
  • Food shifts: hay regrowth, last green forbs, then browse 75%.
  • Hunter's move: hunt trails between bedding and food, add soft grunts late in the month (Tip, chapter 9).

• Peak breeding mid November 80%.
  • Old bucks move midday. Be out all day (Tip).
More: November detail
  • The BC account puts the white tail rut peak in November 85%.
  • Penn State: most does conceive about 13 to 17 November 80%. The Thompson peak is not measured: VERIFY local dates.
  • Northern white tails breed in a tight window of about a month (85%, US Forest Service species review).
  • Chasing in early to mid November, then tending (lockdown) when bucks stay with does (60%, hunter guides).
  • Bucks barely eat and lose weight fast 75%.
  • Rattling and grunting work best now 70%.
  • Region 3: bucks open to 10 December. Region 8: bucks close 30 November. Youth only either sex 1 to 30 November in both (99%, pages 34 and 68).

• In heat about 24 hours 80%.
  • Not bred? Heat again about 28 days later 80%.
More: estrus detail
  • A doe is in heat (estrus) about 24 hours (80%, Montana State University Extension; US Forest Service species review says 24 to 48 hours).
  • A buck tends her for 1 to 3 days before and 2 or 3 days after 80%.
  • Not bred: she comes back into heat at about 28 day intervals (80%; US Forest Service species review gives 21 to 30 days).
  • So a small second rut shows in mid December (Tip, from the 28 day cycle).
  • Doe fawns on good feed can breed at 6 to 7 months, often later than adults (80%, Montana State University Extension).

• Bucks worn out, feeding hard, back in cover 70%.
  • Snow pushes deer to winter range 85%.
More: December detail
  • Post rut bucks rest, feed and stay tight to cover 70%.
  • Early winter: river groves first, then south slopes and conifer patches as snow deepens (65%, data/migration.json).
  • Region 3: bucks to 10 December, then bow only either sex 11 to 20 December (99%, page 34).
  • Region 8: bow only either sex 1 to 20 December (99%, page 68).
  • Late season deer are lean. Food is the key: find the best remaining browse (Tip).

• Rhyme: "Spring in velvet, fall in bone; November bucks won't leave does alone."
  • Number trick: 202 days, 24 hours, 28 days.
  • Old hand's rule (tradition): "When the leaves are down and the frost is hard, the old bucks walk in daylight."
More: more hooks, mistakes and field drill
  • Number trick: 13 to 17 November: most does bred (Penn State). Count back 202 days: early June fawns.
  • Old hand's rule (opinion, widely repeated): "Hunt rubs in October, scrapes before peak, does in the rut."
  • Rhyme: "Antlers drop when days grow long; velvet's off when the rut's song's strong."
Common mistakes
  • Hunting only weekends in November and missing the midweek peak.
  • Expecting a rut on a fixed date every year.
  • Pushing wintering deer for photos or shed antlers.
Do this in the field

From 15 October, log every rub, scrape and chasing buck you see, with date and place. In 3 years you will know your valley's rut.

mc-white-tailed-deer-06:
Why it matters

Most white tails are seen in the first and last hour of light. Be in place before those hours, not during them.

  • Peaks near dawn and dusk 85%.
  • Midday: bedded and chewing cud 75%.
More: what this chapter covers
  • Bed to feed to water: the daily loop.
  • How the day shifts with season.
  • Weather: wind, rain, snow, cold fronts, barometric pressure, with the evidence level for each.
  • The moon. Hunting pressure.
  • A hunter's day plan.
  • Mule deer days in open country: Mule deer Masterclass 6.

• Feed in fields late afternoon into the night 75%.
  • Back to willow and cottonwood beds by first light 75%.
More: the daily loop
  • Evening: leave bedding cover, stage at the edge, enter the field near dark 75%.
  • Night: feed in hay and alfalfa, browse along edges 75%.
  • Dawn: drift back to bedding cover at or before first light 75%.
  • Midday: bedded, chewing cud, getting up to stretch and nibble now and then 70%.
  • Water: deer drink about 3 lb of water per lb of dry food, but only half a pound per lb of green food (80%, Montana State University Extension). In a valley bottom water is never far (Tip).
  • Penn State October data: about 120 to 140 m an hour at dawn and dusk, under 50 m an hour midday, about 60 m an hour at night (75%, via Weather fronts).

SeasonPattern
SummerDawn and dusk 85%
FallDawn, dusk, night fields 75%
RutAny hour, midday too 70%
WinterActive most of the day 85%
  • Winter deer feed in the warm midday sun (Tip).
More: why the pattern shifts
  • BC account: "In summer, they are more active at dawn and dusk, but in winter they are active most of the day" 85%.
  • Starkey, Oregon (deer and elk): activity peaks about 04:00 to 09:00 and 17:00 to 21:00 (85%, Stewart and others 2002).
  • Rut bucks search for does at all hours 70%.
  • Winter: short days and cold push feeding into the warmest hours (Tip).

• Time of day and season beat any weather effect 75%.
  • Weather effects are real but small and mixed 70%.
More: the studies
  • Auburn University thesis (South Carolina GPS, Global Positioning System, collars): weather, temperature, wind, pressure and moon mattered only in some seasons and hours, and less than the daily rhythm (75%, search preview).
  • Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries and Parks: across many deer and a whole season, weather effects are weaker than hunters think. Very high barometric pressure went with more winter buck movement 70%.
  • Penn State: does through 30 winter storms showed no change before storms and moved less during them (80%, via Weather fronts).
  • Oklahoma collar study: temperature explained most of the change in movement 65%.
  • Rating in the chart is my reading of these studies, not a published score (Tip).

• Strong wind: deer bed tighter, move less 60%.
  • Light rain: deer often still move (Tip).
More: wind, rain, snow
  • One South Texas radio collar study: movement dropped sharply at about 24 to 31 km/h (15 to 19 mph) wind, then rebounded above about 32 km/h (60%, secondary report).
  • An Oklahoma collar study found little change in distance moved with wind speed (60%, secondary report).
  • So wind effects are mixed. Wind matters most because it carries your scent and covers your sound (Tip).
  • Rain: Penn State preliminary notes: bucks moved less in rain than does 65%.
  • First snow: fresh tracks show exactly where deer are moving. Great scouting (Tip, see Snow tracking).
  • Deep snow over about 40 cm pushes white tails onto winter range and packed trails 85%.

• "Feed before the front" is not proven 75%.
  • A hard cold snap after a warm spell: watch for daylight feeding (Tip).
More: front detail
  • Penn State storm study: no change before winter storms 80%.
  • Mississippi: very high pressure correlated with more winter buck movement 70%.
  • Hunter consensus: the day after a cold front clears, with rising pressure and cold calm air, is a great morning to sit (Tip, widely repeated, weak evidence).
  • Hot October days: deer bed in shade and move at the edges of legal light (Tip).
  • Log temperature, pressure and wind in the Journal each sit. Your own valley data beats any article (Tip).

• collar studies: dawn and dusk win in every moon phase 75%.
  • Moon effects, if any, are small 75%.
More: moon studies
  • Texas King Ranch: 43 collared bucks showed no moon phase pattern (65%, via Outdoor Life).
  • North Carolina State: over 22,000 collar locations, deer moved most at dawn and dusk regardless of phase, with only small midday upticks near the full moon 65%.
  • Auburn and SEAFWA (Southeastern Association of Fish and Wildlife Agencies) 2016: 38 collared bucks. Small solunar effects that changed with the moon phase; the authors warn solunar charts "may be misleading" 80%.
  • Penn State: no moon phase link in collared does 65%.
  • The moon does not set the rut. Day length does 75%.
  • My lean (Tip): ignore the moon. Hunt the wind and the time of year.

• Pressure turns white tails nocturnal and into thick cover 70%.
  • Midweek beats the weekend (Tip).
More: pressure detail
  • Penn State collar study: deer reacted the day before opening and hid inside their home range 70%.

You will see white tail sign 50 times for every white tail. Read it right and the sign tells you where to sit.

More: track detail
  • Two toes, heart shaped, pointed end forward 85%.
  • White tail front track about 4 to 10 cm long 70%. Often narrower with tips close together 60%.
  • Dewclaws show in mud, snow or when running 75%.
  • Big, deep, splayed prints with a wide straddle may be a buck, but a big doe fools people (60%, hunter lore).

  • Stot: tight groups of 4 means mule deer 85%.
More: pattern detail
  • Walk: prints in a near line; the hind foot lands in or near the front print 75%.
  • Trot: same line, longer spacing 70%.
  • Gallop: groups of 4 with hind prints landing ahead of the front prints; long gaps between groups 75%.
  • Stot (mule deer): all 4 feet land together in tight groups, groups about 2.4 to 4.6 m apart 60%.
  • A gallop trail leading to cover: you spooked it, or something did (Tip).

• Oval pellets about 1 to 1.5 cm 70%.
  • Shiny and moist = hours old (Tip).

More: droppings detail
  • Pellets oval, often with a point at one end, about 1 to 1.5 cm 70%.
  • Firm separate pellets in fall and winter; clumped, softer in summer on green feed 70%.
  • A deer drops about 13 to 34 pellet groups a day 70%.
  • Lots of pellets in one spot: a bedding or feeding area (Tip).

  • Pellets beside it: the deer stood and dropped them (Tip).
More: bed detail
  • A bed is a flattened oval in grass, leaves or snow, about 1 m long 75%.
  • Does and fawns bed in groups; several beds side by side 75%.
  • A single big bed, often on a little rise with a view and the wind at its back, may be a buck (Tip, hunter observation).
  • Mississippi collared bucks used about 31 bedding areas in a season, and repeat beds had dense screening cover 65%.
  • Never walk through bedding cover to check beds in season. Scout it in late winter (Tip).

More: rub detail
  • A buck rubs bark off small trees and shrubs with his antlers and forehead 75%.
  • The forehead gland between the antler bases leaves scent on rubs 65%.
  • First rubs in September as velvet comes off; most in October 70%.

  • The branch at about 1.2 to 1.5 m is the key 65%.
More: scrape detail
  • A buck paws a patch of bare dirt, often urinates in it, and chews and rubs the branch above with his face 75%.
  • The branch carries scent from the preorbital gland at the corner of the eye and the forehead gland 65%.

More: pros and cons in full
  • Stand or ground blind: you are still, deer come to you, easy steady shot. Needs scouting, permission and patience (Tip).
  • Still hunting: covers ground, works midday in thick cover. White tails in thick brush are hard to sneak up on (Tip).
  • Glass and stalk: great for open fields and broken hills. Valley white tails are often too close to cover for long stalks (Tip).
  • Grunt and rattle: can pull a buck close. One Texas study saw about 65% of bucks respond, best on cool, calm, overcast mornings 70%.
  • Partner push: moves deer out of small cover. Highest safety risk. Never shoot toward your partner (Tip).
