mc-ducks-02:
Why it matters

Know where the heart, lungs and air sacs sit, and you know why some hit ducks drop and others fly off to die.

  • Heart and lungs: high and forward, under the wing roots 75%.
  • The back half is air sacs and gut 80%.
More: the parts that matter to a hunter
  • Lungs: small, stiff, pressed up against the spine and ribs 80%.
  • Air sacs: thin bags in front of and behind the lungs, filling much of the body. They move air but do not take up oxygen 80%.
  • Heart: big for the body, low and forward in the chest, behind the keel 75%.
  • Breast: the big flight muscle on the keel. This is most of the meat 80%.
  • Gizzard: a hard muscle pouch low in the belly, behind the liver 80%.
  • Spine and neck: a pellet here drops the bird at once (Tip, from the vital areas in chapter 10).
  • Anatomy positions are drawn from general bird anatomy, simplified 75%.

• Air flows ONE way through a bird lung 80%.
  • It takes two breaths to move one gulp through 80%.
More: the two breath cycle in plain words
  • Breath 1 in: fresh air goes past the lung, mostly into the rear air sacs 80%.
  • Breath 1 out: the rear sacs squeeze that fresh air forward through the lung 80%.
  • Breath 2 in: the used air moves on into the front air sacs 80%.
  • Breath 2 out: it leaves through the windpipe 80%.
  • So the lung gets fresh air on the in breath and the out breath. Bird lungs get oxygen better than ours, even high up 80%.
  • No diaphragm: the ribs and breastbone pump the air sacs like bellows 75%.
  • Hunter meaning: a duck can fly hard for hours. A lightly hit duck can still fly a long way before it falls (Tip).

• 9 air sacs: 4 pairs plus 1 at the base of the neck 80%.
  • Air even fills the hollow wing bones 80%.
More: what the sacs do
  • The pairs: neck, front chest, rear chest and belly. The single one sits at the base of the neck (the clavicular sac) 80%.
  • Side pockets from the sacs run into bones: the upper wing bone (humerus), the shoulder girdle, the hips and some neck bones 80%.
  • Air in the bones and sacs makes the body light for flight 75%.
  • Divers squeeze air out of the sacs and feathers before a dive (Tip).
  • These details come from anatomy studies on pigeons and kingfishers. Ducks follow the same bird plan with small differences 75%.

• A pellet in the belly mostly hits air sac and gut, not vitals (Tip).
  • Head, neck and the front half kill. Aim at the front 70%.
More: the shot logic, and how sure we are
  • To kill, a pellet must reach a vital area: brain, spine, or heart and lungs 75%.
  • Published lethality tables count 1 to 2 hits in the vitals with the right pellet size as enough for ducks 70%.
  • The lungs and heart sit forward and high. A bird hit only in the rear belly can keep flying and die later, unrecovered (Tip, my reading of the anatomy).
  • A wing hit alone breaks the bird down but leaves it alive: it swims and dives (Tip).
  • Ducks over decoys: Ducks Unlimited advice is to look at and aim at the bill on the first shot 65%.
  • Lost birds: the commonly quoted figure is about 1 in 5 ducks shot but not recovered in the United States 65%.
  • Chapter 10 covers pattern, pellet counts and what to do after the shot: Masterclass 10.

• When a diver goes under, its heart slows for a moment 75%.
  • Forced under, it slows hard to save oxygen 80%.
More: what happens under water
  • Free diving tufted ducks (a European diver) show a short heart slow down at the start of a dive, then the rate comes back near normal within 6 to 8 seconds 75%.
  • On long dives, or when a duck is held under, the heart slows a lot to save oxygen. This drop is stronger in diving ducks than in puddle ducks 80%.
  • Hunter meaning: a crippled diver can stay under a long time and come up far away. Most cripples head for the shore and the bank cover 65%.
  • Old hand's rule (opinion): "A wounded diver is a lost diver unless you shoot it on the water now."

• The keel bone anchors the big flight muscles 75%.
  • That breast is your meat 80%.
More: the flight engine
  • The keel is a ridge down the middle of the breastbone. The downstroke muscle (pectoralis) and the upstroke muscle (supracoracoideus) both attach to it 75%.
  • Divers have legs set far back for swimming. That is why they patter along the water to take off and walk badly on land 80%.
  • Ducks burn about 12 times more energy flying than resting 75%.
  • Breast meat on ducks is dark red, built for long flights (Tip).

• No teeth. The gizzard and grit grind the food 80%.
  • A mallard can stuff about 113 g of grain in its gullet 75%.
More: food in, energy out
  • Ducks have no true crop, but the gullet (oesophagus) stretches to hold food 80%.
  • Order: bill, gullet, glandular stomach (proventriculus: acid and enzymes), gizzard (muscle plus grit), gut and two caeca 80%.
  • The gizzard grows bigger when a duck eats hard food. Divers that eat clams and snails have bigger gizzards for their size 75%.
  • Why they gorge fast: eat quickly in the field, then fly to safe water to digest 75%.
  • Hunter meaning: a duck with a fat gullet of grain tells you what field it fed in. Check the gullet when you clean birds (Tip).
  • Laying wood duck hens may need more than 300 invertebrates an hour for eight hours 65%.

• Warm and cold blood pass side by side in the legs 80%.
  • Feet stay cold, the body stays warm 80%.
More: cold, wind and clear nights
  • The setup is called countercurrent heat exchange. It works so well ducks can stand on ice for hours 80%.
  • Down under the outer feathers holds the warmth. Preened, waterproof outer feathers keep the water out (Tip).
  • Clear, cold nights cost a duck the most energy. Ducks pick sheltered roosts out of the wind 75%.
  • Hunter meaning: on a cold, windy day ducks feed harder and seek calm, sheltered water. Hunt the lee shore (Tip).

• Fall: they fatten before migration 75%.
  • Hens spend their fat on eggs and nesting 75%.
More: the fat cycle and the meat
  • Before fall migration ducks eat more and store fat faster 75%.
  • They reach winter waters fairly lean, then regain fat in early winter on grain and seeds 75%.
  • From mid to late winter body mass usually drops, likely set by the body itself 75%.
  • Hens rely on fat, protein and calcium built up over winter and spring for eggs and incubation 75%.
  • Hunter meaning: late October and November birds are often fat, with a yellow layer under the skin. Pluck them to keep it (Tip). See Cooking.

  • Few wild ducks reach 5 years 75%.

  • Oldest known wild mallard: a drake about 27 years old 70%.
  • Clutch 5 to 15 eggs replaces the losses each year 75%.
  • Young birds of the year are more likely to be shot than adults 80%. More in Masterclass 4.

mc-ducks-03:
Why it matters

Ducks beat you with their eyes. Hide from the eyes and you beat almost every duck.

  • A mallard sees almost all the way around 70%.
  • It can watch the whole sky without turning its head 65%.
More: field of view, and how sure we are
  • Ducks Unlimited describes a mallard's view as a full 360 degree circle 70%. A vision scientist quoted by hunting media calls ducks "an extreme case" of panoramic vision 65%.
  • Ed Yong's book on animal senses, citing vision research, says the mallard field has no blind spot above or behind (60%, secondhand).
  • Some sources say there may be a small blind area right behind the head. Not settled: treat ducks as seeing everything (Tip).
  • Most waterfowl see each side with one eye. Only a thin zone in front is seen by both eyes 75%.
  • Hunter meaning: there is no "behind" a duck. A circling flock sees your hide from every side (Tip).

• Four colour cones; you have three 75%.
  • Shine and glare are your enemy (Tip).
More: what they see that you do not
  • Birds have an extra set of cones that pick up ultraviolet light: "tetrachromatic" vision (75%, Ducks Unlimited).
  • They see reds, yellows and blues more vividly than we do 70%.
  • Ultraviolet helps them see well at dawn and dusk 70%.
  • Feathers reflect ultraviolet. Young pintail drakes reflect it differently from adults 70%.
  • Delta Waterfowl scientists say ducks likely see ultraviolet, and much is still unknown 70%.
  • Hunter meaning: avoid shiny guns, glasses, phones, new plastic and a bare face. Some decoys use ultraviolet dulling paint; how much it matters is not proven (Tip).

• Bird eyes are built to catch motion 75%.
  • They look DOWN into your hide. Keep your head down (Tip).
More: why motion kills a hunt
  • Bird retinas keep blood vessels in one comb shaped structure (the pecten) instead of across the retina. That reduces visual clutter and helps them see motion 70%.
  • Florida's wildlife agency: ducks have great eyesight and are very good at seeing movement; full camouflage and sitting still are the answer 75%.
  • No camouflage pattern hides a hunter who stares up or fidgets (Tip, widely reported).
  • Look with your eyes, not your face. Use a hat brim, a face mask or face paint (Tip).
  • Let one person call the shot. Everyone rises together, once (Tip).

• They see fine detail 2.5 to 3 times farther than you 70%.
  • They judge depth by moving the head 70%.
More: how they judge distance
  • With eyes on the sides, most of what a duck sees is flat. It bobs or turns its head to see an object from two angles, which builds depth 70%.
  • Birds control the shape of both the cornea and the lens. Divers can see well under water 70%.
  • Hunter meaning: a fake looking decoy spread, or a hide that sticks up, is seen from far out. Match the shape of the cover around you (Tip).

• Ducks see well in low light and fly at night 75%.
  • Most migration happens at night 80%.
More: low light facts
  • Ultraviolet sensitivity lets birds work fully at dawn and dusk 70%.
  • Most waterfowl migrate at night. Movement picks up soon after sunset and peaks near midnight 80%.
  • Under hunting pressure ducks fly out to feed at night 80%.
  • Birds see a flickering light as flashes, where we see a steady light 70%.
  • Legal hours for ducks: half an hour before sunrise to half an hour after sunset 99%. See the Rule Book.

• Best hearing: 1 to 3 kHz, where duck calls sit 75%.
  • A clank or a slammed truck door carries (Tip).
More: what the studies found
  • A mallard hearing test (3 birds) found a range of about 66 Hz to 7.6 kHz, with best hearing near 2 kHz 75%. Mallards do not hear the very low sounds that pigeons do 75%.
  • Ten diving bird species, including scaup and ruddy duck, shared their best hearing at 1 to 3 kHz. The ducks had the most sensitive hearing of the group 75%.
  • Duck calls (their own voices) mostly sit in that same 1 to 3 kHz band 75%.
  • Hunter meaning: a mouth call sits right in their best band. Call softly and rarely when birds are close (Tip).
  • Hunter meaning: metal on metal, a dog whistle or loud talk in the hide carries (Tip).

• Duck smell is barely studied. Do not count on it either way (Tip).
  • Wind matters because ducks land into it 80%.
More: what we know about smell
  • The old belief that birds cannot smell is not supported. Reviews list ducks among birds with a working sense of smell 70%.
  • No study found here shows ducks avoid hunters by scent (VERIFY). Ducks Unlimited and state agencies advise on sight and motion, not scent (Tip).
  • Wind still sets your hide: ducks land into the wind, so set the spread with the wind at your back or side (80% for landing into wind; the setup is a Tip).
  • Old hand's rule (opinion): "Play the wind for the landing, not for the nose."

• Edge ducks sleep with one eye open, facing out 80%.
  • Half the brain stays awake 80%.
More: the study
  • Mallards sleeping in a row of four: the two edge birds slept with one eye open about 32% of the time, the middle birds about 12% 75%.
  • The open eye faced away from the group, where a predator would come from. The awake half of the brain reacted fast to threats 80%.
  • This is called unihemispheric sleep 80%.
  • Hunter meaning: a sleeping raft is never fully asleep. Sneaks on rafted ducks rarely work in the open (Tip).

mc-ducks-04:
Why it matters

Ducks put safety first, food second, and they learn fast. Read the flock and you know your next 10 seconds.

  • Necks up and still: they are about to leave (Tip).
  • Freeze the moment you see it (Tip).
More: alarm signals in detail
  • Relaxed birds feed, tip up, preen and sleep. Alert birds stretch their necks, stop feeding, bunch up and swim away from the threat (Tip, widely reported).
  • Hens of most puddle ducks give loud quacks; the whole flock reacts to an alarm (Tip).
  • Mallards put safety first, then food, and keep their trips short (80%, Ducks Unlimited research summary).
  • Old hand's rule (opinion): "When the necks go up, your feet stop."

• No good flush distance numbers for BC ducks (VERIFY).
  • Pressured birds flush sooner and farther (Tip).
More: what we know, and what we do not
  • No published flush distance for hunted BC ducks was found. Do not trust a fixed number (VERIFY).
  • Divers must run along the water to take off, so they tend to swim off or leave early (Tip).
  • Puddle ducks jump straight up, so they often sit tight in cover until you are close, then burst (Tip).
  • In a West Tennessee study, ducks disturbed in their sanctuaries "hunkered down" and moved less rather than spreading out 80%.
  • Hunter meaning: on small water, use cover and the bends to get close. On big open water, decoys work better than sneaking (Tip).

• GPS (Global Positioning System) mallards avoid heavily hunted areas in shooting hours 80%.
  • About 2 flights a day: refuge, food, refuge 80%.
More: the research
  • West Tennessee, winters 2019 to 2022: GPS tracked mallards "clearly avoided heavily hunted areas during shooting hours" and made about two flights a day 80%.
  • Researchers heard more than 339,000 shotgun volleys over three seasons 80%.
  • Mallards moved between refuges only if they were less than about 16 km (10 miles) apart 80%.
  • In Arkansas, tagged mallards stayed away from public hunting areas for the whole season 70%.
  • In heavily hunted areas, ducks rest in no hunting zones by day and fly out to feed at night 80%.
  • Hunter meaning: hunt the flight line between a refuge and food, at first light and last light (Tip).

WeekYour pond

  • "Ducks perceive sanctuary in weeks, not days" 80%.
  • Rest a spot a week or more 75%.
More: resting a spot
  • Ducks Unlimited researchers advise that a property may need a week or more of rest to improve hunting 75%.
  • Short closures (half days, some days off) are a weak substitute for real no hunting areas 80%.
  • Hunter meaning: you and your brother should have 3 or 4 spots and rotate them (Tip).
  • Old hand's rule (opinion, widely taught): "Never hunt the roost." Shooting where they sleep moves them off it.

• Ducks trust other ducks on the water (Tip).
  • That is why decoys work (Tip).
More: flock behaviour
  • Ducks often land where other ducks already sit; decoys copy that (Tip, the basis of all decoy hunting).
  • Mallards in fall flock loosely; teal flocks twist as one; canvasback fly in lines and V shapes 80%.
  • A big flock has more eyes. Small groups and singles decoy more easily (Tip).
  • Hunter meaning: set decoys in small family sized groups with a clear landing hole (Tip). Spreads: Ducks, tactics.

• Mallards pair up in fall and early winter 75%.
  • The drake leaves early in incubation; the hen raises the brood alone 70%.
More: the social calendar
  • Mallard courtship peaks in October and November in a California wintering study. Over 80% of hens were paired by early December 75%.
  • In New York, courtship starts in September and about 90% of hens are paired by November 65%.
  • Green winged teal pair later: 90% of hens paired by early February 75%.
  • The pair flies north together; the hen usually picks the nest site (Tip).
  • After a few days of incubation the pair breaks and the drake leaves 70%.
  • Hunter meaning: in November, drakes and hens often fly as pairs. Name both before you shoot (Tip).

• Young of the year are shot more than adults 80%.
  • Late season adults are wary: hide better, call less (Tip).
More: the evidence
  • Bellrose and others (1961): juveniles are more vulnerable to hunting than adults, and the gap varies by place, time, year and species 80%.
  • The age ratio in the bag rises after a late nesting year 75%.
  • A popular summary says juvenile mallard hens are 2 to 3 times more vulnerable (60%, not checked against the original study). VERIFY.
  • Old hand's rule (opinion): "Opening week teaches you nothing. December teaches you everything."

• They land into the wind 80%.
  • They return to yesterday's field and flight line (Tip).
More: the habits you can use
  • Landing into the wind: you know which way they will come in 80%.
  • Same field, same flight line, day after day while the food lasts (Tip, the basis of field hunting).
  • They leave to feed earlier on moonlit, windy evenings 75%.
  • Fresh birds after a cold front decoy easily (65%, hunter lore).
  • They trust a calm, spread out flock of decoys on the water (Tip).
  • Pressured birds go straight to refuges: the hunter who knows the refuge knows the flight line (Tip).

mc-ducks-05:
Why it matters

The duck you hunt in October is a different bird from the one in December. Know the calendar and you know who is on the water.

  • October: peak fall passage through the Interior 60%.
  • Late November: freeze up ends most Interior migration 65%.
More: the year in one paragraph per season

  • Spring: north again from March; plateau lakes open as the ice goes (55 to 60%).
  • Summer: nesting on Interior wetlands and potholes, broods, then the wing moult 60%.
  • Fall: early migrants in August, well under way by late September, peak in October, mostly over by late November (60 to 75%).

  • Clutch: 5 to 15 eggs, about 9 on average (70 to 75%).
  • Incubation: 26 to 30 days, about 28 75%.
  • Ducklings stay in the nest about 10 hours, then follow the hen to water 65%.
  • They fly at about 50 to 60 days 70%.
  • Breeding in BC: Interior wetlands and potholes, mostly below 500 m for mallards; lesser scaup, canvasback and redhead on plateau lakes at 500 to 1,500 m (85%, BC Breeding Bird Atlas).

  • Flightless for about 3 to 4 weeks 80%.

  • Unlike most birds, ducks, geese and swans lose all flight feathers together after breeding 85%.
  • Mallards: about 24 to 26 days flightless in captive birds, about 23 to 24 days in Dutch field work 75%.
  • Black ducks in Labrador: 27 to 30 days, peak in mid July 75%.

• Teal, shoveler, pintail leave first 75%.
  • Goldeneyes, bufflehead and mergansers go with the ice 75%.

  • Blue winged teal, shoveler and pintail leave breeding areas in August or early September 75%.
  • Green winged teal: September to October; most are south by November 75%.
  • Mallard, wigeon and gadwall: September or October, and stay as long as water is open 75%.
  • Ring necked duck in October; canvasback and redhead October to November 75%.
  • Goldeneyes and bufflehead: with the ice, mid to late October, reaching wintering water in November and December 75%.
  • Common merganser: one of the last, late October to November 75%.
  • Most migration happens at night 80%. With a strong tailwind a mallard can cover about 1,300 km (800 miles) in 8 hours, then needs 3 to 7 days to refuel 60%.

• Colour back, pairs forming, the big push (60 to 75%).
  • Late season: fewer, wiser, fatter birds (Tip).

  • Early October near Kamloops: local mallards, wigeon and green winged teal, plus the first northern birds (Tip, 60%).

mc-ducks-06:
Why it matters

Ducks run on a daily commute: roost, food, rest, food, roost. Be on the route at the right minute.

  • Fields at dawn and late day. Water at midday and night 80%.
  • Legal from 30 minutes before sunrise 99%.
More: the daily pattern
  • Mallards feed early morning and late afternoon in harvested fields, then return to marshes and creeks for the night 80%.
  • Wigeon raft offshore until late afternoon, then move into marshes and ponds to feed 80%.
  • Redheads spend the day rafted on deep water and feed morning and evening in the shallows 80%.
  • Legal hours: half an hour before sunrise to half an hour after sunset 99%. Rule Book.

• Two flights a day: out to feed, back to rest 80%.
  • The first 30 minutes of legal light are prime (Tip).
More: how the clock shifts
  • GPS (Global Positioning System) tracked mallards under pressure made about two flights a day 80%.
  • The clock moves with sunrise. In October sunrise gets later each week, so the dawn flight does too (Tip).
  • Where hunting is heavy, the feeding flight shifts to after dark and the birds are back on the refuge before dawn 80%.
  • Old hand's rule (opinion, widely taught): "Be set up and quiet before the first bird can see."

• Ice, snow and pressure: strong evidence 80%.
  • Barometer on its own: no good study found (VERIFY).
More: the evidence behind each line
  • Freeze up and snow: a Missouri study built a weather severity index from cold, days below freezing and snow cover. When it passed a threshold, mallards were more likely to leave 80%.
  • Warmer winters with less snow are expected to delay fall migration, most for mallards and least for pintails 70%.
  • Wind: ducks land into the wind 80%.
  • Moon: waterfowl leave to feed earlier on moonlit, windy nights than on dark, calm nights 75%.
  • Full moon makes mornings slow because ducks fed all night: hunter lore, not shown in a study found here (Tip).
  • Cold front with a north wind brings new birds: hunter lore, widely repeated 65%.
  • Barometric pressure on its own: no duck study found. Pressure falls before a front, so it may only be a sign of the front (VERIFY).

• Hunt the morning after a front passes (65%, lore).
  • New birds decoy better than the locals (Tip).
More: reading a front
  • A brings a wind shift to the north or northwest, colder air and often clearer skies (Tip).
  • Migrating ducks ride tailwinds. A tracked mallard was clocked at about 165 km/h (103 mph) ground speed on a strong tailwind 70%.
  • Before the front: birds may feed hard (Tip). After it: fresh birds on new water 65%.
  • Check forecasts 3 days ahead and plan your ponds for the morning after (Tip).

• Wind sets the landing direction 80%.
  • Windy days push ducks to calm, sheltered water (Tip).
More: wind and rain in practice
  • Ducks land into the wind; set the spread so they cross in front of you (80% landing, Tip setup).
  • Strong wind: ducks hold on the lee side of ponds and sloughs 65%.

  • Most cripples head for shore; check the bank cover 65%.

Why it matters

A goose cups its wings for half a second. In that half second you must know if it is legal, and which bag it fills.

  • 4 goose groups in BC, each with its own limit 99%.
  • Quick version: Geese. This is the deep version, 10 chapters.
More: what this masterclass covers
  • Chapters: 1 Meet the animal, 2 The body, 3 The senses, 4 The mind, 5 The year, 6 The day, 7 Where they are, 8 Sign and tracking, 9 How to hunt them, 10 Shot to table and the rules.
  • Main bird: Canada and cackling geese. Snow, Ross's and white fronted geese get their own screens because BC has seasons for them (99%, Rule Book: migratory birds).
  • Brant: one screen here, then the Sea ducks and brant lesson.
  • Every chapter ends with Memory hooks and a 5 question quiz. Chapter 10 holds the one page cheat sheet.
  • Certainty: 95 to 100% read in the official text. 80 to 94% official source or a study, some reading. 60 to 79% a good secondary source. Tip: opinion.
  • Assumption: you hunt with your brother, a 12 gauge with steel shot, a 10 ft boat, a kayak and an ATV (All Terrain Vehicle), from your profile.

• Black neck, white chinstrap, white under the tail 85%.
  • Gander and goose look the same 85%.
More: every mark and the sizes
  • Black head and neck, a white chinstrap that runs up behind each eye, grey brown body with pale feather edges, black rump and tail, white upper and under tail coverts, black bill, legs and feet (80%, Ducks Unlimited ID).
  • Sexes look alike 85%.
  • Length about 76 to 117 cm (2 ft 6 in to 3 ft 10 in) (80%, Audubon).
  • Wingspan about 90 cm to 2 m, by race (80%, Hinterland Who's Who).
  • Weight by race: Hinterland Who's Who gives 1.1 kg for the smallest form to 8 kg for the giant form; Ducks Unlimited gives 2.4 to 9 kg (5.3 to 19.8 lb) for the Canada goose races 75%. The quick lesson's 1.35 to 5.45 kg covers most birds you will see 80%.
  • Voice: honks, "ka lunk". About 13 different calls have been described (80%, Hinterland Who's Who).

• Same feathers. The gander is a bit bigger 75%.
  • Watch behaviour: the gander guards and leads 80%.
More: how to tell them apart in the field
  • Ganders (males) are slightly larger than geese (females); otherwise they look alike (75%, Internet Center for Wildlife Damage Management).
  • At the nest the gander stands guard, sometimes several hundred metres away (80%, Hinterland Who's Who).
  • Before a family flies, the gander's head toss gets them up fastest (80%, Raveling 1969). See Chapter 4.
  • Young of the year look like adults by fall 80%. Goslings stay with their parents a full year 80%.
  • In the hand, hunters say young birds have softer, bendier bills and smaller feet (Tip, 60%).
  • The law does not care: no sex or age rules for geese in BC (99%, Rule Book).

• Short neck, stubby bill, high yelp: cackling goose 75%.
  • Same bag as Canada geese: 10 a day together 99%.

More: the numbers
  • A is its own species, split from the Canada goose; it is not a young Canada goose 85%.
  • Bill: cackling 2.8 to 3.8 cm (1.1 to 1.5 in); Canada 4.1 to 5.8 cm (1.6 to 2.3 in) (75%, Ducks Unlimited).
  • Average weight: cackling males about 1.5 kg (1,542 g), females about 0.95 kg (953 g) 75%.
  • In flight a cackler looks mallard sized with a short neck 75%. Its call is a higher "hrooonk" 75%.
  • In the air the two can be hard or impossible to separate 85%. It does not matter for your bag: the law counts "Canada Geese and Cackling Geese, combined" 99%.

  • Hinterland Who's Who counts 11 races of Canada goose; four former races now make up the cackling goose 80%.
  • Ducks Unlimited lists the western race (moffitti) as mostly resident from British Columbia to Manitoba, west and south of the Rockies 75%.
  • The Vancouver race (fulva) breeds from coastal Glacier Bay, Alaska, south to southwest BC 75%.
  • Dusky geese breed in southern Alaska and winter in the lower Columbia and Willamette valleys; they have declined long term 75%.
  • Lesser geese (parvipes) breed from boreal Alaska to Nunavut and winter from western Washington to Mexico 75%.
  • Cackling geese: minima and Taverner's winter in the Willamette and lower Columbia valleys of Oregon and Washington 75%. To get there they pass BC (Tip, 65%).
  • Okanagan nesting geese are hybrids of several races brought in during the 1960s and 70s; they never learned to migrate (85%, Regional District of Okanagan Similkameen).
  • Resident geese in BC towns and valleys are mixed race introductions, often big (85%, quick lesson).
  • Why it matters: a September goose is almost always a local bird. Migrants and cacklers mix in from October (Tip, 65%). See Chapter 5.

• Snow and Ross's count together in one bag 99%.
  • Grin patch on the bill: snow. Stubby, no grin: Ross's 80%.

More: marks, weights and limits
  • Snow goose: white with black wing tips, rose pink bill and feet, a dark "grin patch" on the bill (80%, Ducks Unlimited).
  • Blue morph: white head and neck, grey brown body. Young white birds are greyish with grey pink bills 80%.
  • Lesser snow goose weights: males 1.9 to 2.8 kg (4.2 to 6.2 lb), females 1.7 to 2.9 kg (3.8 to 6.4 lb) 75%.
  • Ross's goose: smaller, short stubby bill, no grin patch, bluish warty base to the bill on older birds 70%. Males 1.1 to 2 kg (2.5 to 4.5 lb) 70%.
  • BC snow geese are the Fraser and Skagit part of the Wrangel Island, Russia, population (85%, Demarchi 2006).
  • Limits: District 3 and District 8, 5 a day (15 in possession) 99%.

  • The synopsis page 12 prints 5 a day outside 2-4 and 2-5. The Region 2 Rule Book marks this VERIFY and says take 5 a day in 2-8 to stay safe (Tip).

• Grey brown, white face band, barred belly: "specklebelly" 70%.

More: marks, voice and range

  • Weight about 1.95 to 3.3 kg (70%, search preview of the Cornell Lab guide).
  • Voice: a high laughing "kow kow kow" from V flocks (80%, quick lesson).
  • Two populations, Pacific and mid continent; they travel the Pacific and Central flyways (70%, Ducks Unlimited).

• Swans: never. No open season 90%.
  • Brant: only MU (Management Unit) 2-4, 1 to 10 March 99%.

More: the look alikes in full

  • Brant: no open season in Districts 3 and 8 99%. In District 2 only in MU 2-4, 1 to 10 March, 3 a day 99%. Not your bird at Mission or Heffley Creek. Full story: Sea ducks and brant.
  • Farm and domestic geese are not wild game. Leave them alone (Tip).

• BC hunters took 15,539 geese in 2016, 6,053 in 2024 (99%, survey).

  • Snow geese: about 1 million in 1970, 19 million in 2013, about 14 million in 2019 75%.

mc-geese-02:
Why it matters

A goose is a flying engine wrapped in muscle, bone and feathers. Know where the engine sits and you know why steel BB, close range and the head matter.

  • Big breast muscle on a deep keel: that is flight, and your meat 80%.
  • Hollow bones join the air sacs 80%.
More: what this chapter covers
  • Skeleton and muscle, breathing with air sacs, heart and big vessels, the gut and gizzard, body heat, the fat cycle, lifespan.
  • Last screen: what it all means for the shot and the meat.
  • Bird body facts here come from general bird biology (Stanford Birds, ornithology lecture notes) plus goose studies. Where a fact is for birds in general, it says so.

• The keel (breastbone) anchors the breast muscles 80%.
  • Legs sit far back: a goose walks and swims well (Tip).
More: muscle and bone
  • A bird's skeleton is light: some bones are hollow and linked to the air sacs; others are dense where strength matters (80%, Stanford Birds).
  • Air spaces in bones are more extensive in large birds than small ones (70%, search preview of a bird anatomy handout).
  • Flight power comes from the breast muscles on the keel. That is why a goose breast is so big 80%.
  • Wing bones and the thick breast stand between a pellet from below and the vital organs (Tip, 65%).
  • Geese fly in V formation (80%, Audubon) and can travel more than 1,000 km in a day (80%, Hinterland Who's Who).

• Birds have 9 air sacs and one way air flow 85%.
  • The breathing system fills about one fifth of the body 80%.
More: how a goose breathes
  • The 9 air sacs: one interclavicular, two cervical, two front thoracic, two rear thoracic, two abdominal (85%, Weber State ornithology lecture).
  • The sacs do not trade oxygen. They are bellows that push air one way through stiff lungs 85%.
  • Breath in: most fresh air goes to the rear sacs. Breath out: the rear sacs push it through the lungs. Used air moves to the front sacs and leaves on the next breath out 80%.
  • About one fifth of a bird's body volume is breathing system, versus about one twentieth in a mammal (80%, Stanford Birds).
  • A bird takes about one breath every 6 to 10 heartbeats; a mammal about one every 4.5 80%.
  • Air sacs also help shed heat in hard flight 70%.
  • What it means for you: a pellet through the body cavity can collapse sacs, but a goose hit only in the sacs can still fly far (Tip, 60%).

• Heart: low and forward, under the base of the neck 80%.
  • Lungs: tight against the back ribs 80%.
More: heart and blood
  • Birds have relatively large four chamber hearts (80%, University of Connecticut lecture notes; Stanford Birds).
  • Resting heart rate in birds: about 150 to 350 beats a minute, higher in flight 80%.
  • Blood pressure can reach 300 to 400 mm of mercury 75%.
  • Big vessels run from the heart up the neck to the head. A neck hit cuts them (Tip, 65%).
  • Heart and lungs sit in the front half of the body, shielded by the keel and breast below and the back ribs above 80%.

• Grit in the gizzard grinds grass 85%.
  • Grass passes in about 1.5 hours 70%. They eat most of the day.
More: digestion in full
  • Path: bill, gullet, glandular stomach (proventriculus), muscular gizzard, intestine with two blind pouches (ceca), vent (85%, FAO poultry digestion chapter).
  • The gizzard is the grinding mill. It needs grit, small stones the goose swallows 85%.
  • A true crop in geese: sources disagree. VERIFY. Hunters often find grain packed in the gullet (Tip).
  • Brent geese passed food in about 1.5 hours (70%, Wildfowl journal). Grazing upland geese digest only 27 to 34% of grass organic matter 70%.
  • One barnacle goose study estimated about 160 droppings a day (60%, crude estimate). Lots of droppings is good sign for you. See Chapter 8.
  • Geese often feed 12 hours a day or more (80%, Hinterland Who's Who).
  • Canada geese on rougher, high fibre food ate less, held it longer and grew bigger guts 70%.

• Birds run warmer than you: about 38.5°C resting, 41°C active 85%.
  • Down traps heat; feet feel less cold 80%.
More: cold and heat
  • Mean bird body temperature: 38.5°C resting, 41.0°C active, 43.9°C in hard activity (85%, Prinzinger and others 1991, search preview).
  • Waterfowl feet have fewer nerves, so they stand on ice and snow for long spells (80%, Ducks Unlimited senses article).
  • Cold changes behaviour: below about minus 9°C (15°F) at sunrise, a big wintering flock usually skipped its morning flight (80%, Raveling and others 1972). See Chapter 6.
  • A shot goose holds heat in its feathers. Cool it fast (Tip). See Chapter 10.

• Hens store reserves for about a month of sitting 80%.
  • Fall: they fatten on grain (Tip).
More: the year in reserves
  • Before nesting, geese feed hard to store reserves that carry the hen through about one month of incubation (80%, Hinterland Who's Who).
  • The hen sits 25 to 28 days and eats little 80%. She is at her leanest after hatch (Tip).
  • Moult costs: a study of Illinois geese found the largest nutrition costs of moult from July to November 70%.
  • The chart shape is a Tip, built from these facts, not a measured curve.
  • For the table: fall birds on grain are often fatter than early September birds (Tip).

AgeWhat it means (80%, Hinterland Who's Who)

  • Most that survive year one live 10 years or more, up to about 24 80%.
  • About half of goslings survive to fly 80%.
More: longevity records
  • A Canada goose banded at the Jack Miner sanctuary in Ontario was at least 23 years old when found (70%, Auk 1955, search preview).
  • Older sources list longer records; the current official banding record could not be read here. VERIFY.
  • Old birds have seen many hunters. They are often the wary ones (Tip). See Chapter 4.

• Head, neck, front body: clean kills (Tip, 65%).
  • Rear body hits: cripples that fly on (Tip).
More: shot and meat notes
  • Thick feathers, big muscle and strong wing bones stop small pellets. Use steel BB for big Canada geese (70%, quick lesson; Ducks Unlimited).
  • Pattern: at least 60 pellets in a 76 cm (30 in) circle at your longest range (65%, Ducks Unlimited).
  • On close decoying birds aim at the head, which is about the size of a dove's body (65%, Ducks Unlimited). Fewer pellets end up in the breast 65%.
  • Max range for you this season: 35 m (38 yd) (Tip, from the quick lesson).
  • Meat: the breast is the prize, about 1 kg boned from a big Canada goose 60%. Legs are worth slow cooking (Tip).
  • Full detail: Chapter 10 and Shot placement.

Memory rhymes (made for this app)
  • "Keel and breast, the engine's chest."
  • "Nine sacs breathe one way: air in, air through, air away."
  • "Heart up front and low: aim the head, and down they go."
  • Number trick: 9, 41, 1.5. 9 air sacs, about 41°C active, about 1.5 hours from bill to dropping.
Old hand's rule (tradition, opinion)

Shoot the head, not the goose. Widely taught by goose guides: aim at the white cheek, not the whole bird.

mc-geese-03:
Why it matters

Deer hunters fight the nose. Goose hunters fight the eyes. Every flock you lose at 80 m saw something.

  • Sight first, hearing second, smell a distant third 80%.
  • Beat the eyes and you beat most geese (Tip).
More: what this chapter covers
  • Eyes: field of view, colour, detail, motion, low light.
  • Ears: what they hear best.
  • Nose: what is known, and what is lore.
  • How a flock combines them: the watchers.
  • How to beat each sense, in one table.

• Almost all the way around, with a narrow blind spot behind 90%.
  • They see ground and sky at once 90%.
More: what the eye studies found
  • Canada geese have narrow blind areas, wide side vision, wide binocular fields and can see their own bill tips (90%, Fernandez Juricic and others 2011).
  • Their sharpest retina band runs at a slant (oblique), not flat. It lets a goose scan the ground and the sky at the same time, or line up with the horizon by tilting its head 90%.
  • Because of this they move their heads less than many birds while watching in open fields 90%. More head movement in cluttered cover 90%.
  • The study summary gives no degree values. Do not trust a number you see quoted without a source. VERIFY.
  • What it means: there is almost no "behind" to hide in on open ground. Hide under cover, not just out of the line of sight (Tip).

• 4 cone types; the shortest tuned to violet 90%.
  • Fine detail 2.5 to 3 times farther than you 80%.
More: the colour science
  • Canada geese have four visual pigments with peaks at 409, 458, 509 and 580 nm (90%, Moore and others 2012).
  • That is a violet sensitive system. Ducks Unlimited describes waterfowl colour vision as running from near ultraviolet to red 80%.
  • The brightest patches to another goose are the cheek, crown, neck and upper tail: the marks they use to keep flocks together 90%. That is why decoy heads and chinstraps matter (Tip).
  • Waterfowl see fine detail 2.5 to 3 times farther than people (80%, Ducks Unlimited).
  • Side set eyes give weak depth sense. Birds move the head to judge distance 80%.
  • What it means: a bare face, a shiny gun, fresh blind fabric and frosted decoys all stand out (Tip, 65%).

• Movement and glare flare more birds than anything 80%.
  • Keep your face down until the shot call (Tip).
More: motion rules from goose guides
  • Waterfowl flare at movement in the blind and at the glint of a gun barrel (80%, Ducks Unlimited senses article).
  • Frosted decoys glare at sunrise. Set decoys as late as you can without missing the first flight (65%, Ducks Unlimited goose guide).
  • Hide hands and face: face mask or paint, gloves, hat brim low (Tip).
  • Watch birds through the mesh or the brim, never by lifting your head (Tip).
  • One hunter calls the shot. Everyone moves at once, then not before (Tip).

LightWhat a wintering flock did (80%, Raveling 1972)
Clear dawnFirst birds 15 min before sunrise, main flight at or just after sunrise
Overcast dawnAbout 15 min later
Clear duskBack between sunset and civil twilight
Cloudy duskBack before sunset
Full moon visibleBack later in the evening
  • Geese fly by light levels: first birds about 15 minutes before sunrise in clear weather 80%.
  • Cloud delays them about 15 minutes 80%.
More: night and the moon
  • A Saskatchewan flock started its morning flight at about 32 foot candles of light (80%, quoted in Raveling and others 1972).
  • Barnacle geese in the Netherlands fed at night only around the full moon (75%, Wildfowl journal). For Canada geese night feeding under the moon is hunter report only (Tip).
  • Your legal shooting light starts half an hour before sunrise 99%. The first geese often come about then (Tip). See Chapter 6.

• Most birds hear best at 1 to 4 kHz (kilohertz), the range of your voice 80%.
  • A slammed truck door is a goose alarm (Tip).
More: hearing in full
  • Bird hearing in air is mostly below 10 kHz, best at 1 to 4 kHz (80%, sea duck hearing paper).
  • Diving ducks tested best at 1 to 3 kHz; lesser scaup best at 2 to 3 kHz 75%. No goose audiogram found. VERIFY.
  • Waterfowl ears have no outer flap; soft feathers cover the openings and cut wind noise (80%, Ducks Unlimited).
  • Hearing keeps mates and families together in noisy flocks 80%. Geese use about 13 calls (80%, Hinterland Who's Who).
  • What it means: your call is heard. So are tailgates, zippers, shell boxes and talking (Tip).

• Smell is weak in waterfowl; they rely on sight 80%.
  • No study found showing geese smell hunters (VERIFY).
More: what is known
  • Waterfowl smell is not as keen as a dog's, but they do detect odours (80%, Ducks Unlimited).
  • Greylag geese can tell food plants from other plants by smell 80%.
  • About 400 taste buds in waterfowl versus about 9,000 in people 80%.
  • Hunter lore says scent control does not matter for geese (Tip). Wind still decides everything, because geese land into it. See Chapter 9.

• Edge birds and ganders keep heads up more 75%.
  • Many heads up at once: they are nervous (Tip).
More: vigilance studies
  • In pre nesting Canada geese, males were more vigilant than females and more so at the flock edge (75%, Wildfowl journal).
  • In white fronted geese, birds watched a road less as flock size grew 70%.
  • Head up does not always mean alarm; some head up time is social 75%.
  • A big feeding flock can feel safe and relaxed. A small group of wary birds is harder to fool (Tip).
  • Count heads up when you glass a field. Rising numbers mean leave them alone today (Tip).

SenseHow to beat it (Tip unless shown)
Eyes, shapeHide in or beside cover; brush the blind with field stubble
Eyes, motionFace down, one shot caller, move together
Eyes, shineMud the blind, matte gun, face mask, late decoys on frost
EarsQuiet doors and gear, mouth call only (electronic calls banned, 99%)
NoseNot the problem. Play the wind for landing
More: why the call rule is in this table
  • Electronic calls and recordings are banned for migratory birds in BC (99%, Rule Book: migratory birds). Mouth calls are fine (95%, my reading in the Rule Book).

Memory rhymes (made for this app)
  • "Eyes first, ears next, nose last: hide well, sit still, stay fast."
  • "Face up, flock up."
  • "Four cones beat your three: if it shines, they see."
  • Number trick: 2.5 to 3. A goose sees detail 2.5 to 3 times as far as you 80%.
Old hand's rule (tradition, opinion)

Hide first, decoys second, call last. Widely repeated by goose guides: concealment is the biggest single factor.

• Fernandez Juricic 2011, Moore 2012, Raveling 1972, Ducks Unlimited senses article, hearing and vigilance studies. Checked 2026-10-11.

mc-geese-04:
Why it matters

A goose flock is a family business with a long memory. Read its moods and you know when to sit still, when to shoot and when to go home.

  • Flocks are families: pairs plus this year's young 80%.
  • Families decide together; the gander leads 80%.
More: what this chapter covers
  • The alarm ladder and the preflight head toss.
  • Flight distance and how geese learn hunting pressure.
  • Family life, pairing and rank.
  • Old birds versus young birds.
  • The habits that put them in front of your gun.

• Heads up, then tall necks, then head tosses, then gone 80%.
  • At step 2, freeze. At step 4 they are leaving (Tip).
More: the signals in full
  • Head up is the main watch posture. It is not always alarm; some of it is social (75%, Wildfowl journal).
  • Tall necks and walking away with honks: rising alarm (Tip, 65%).
  • Head tossing is the preflight signal: side to side or up and down shakes with the neck held straight, before the bird flies or walks to a new spot (80%, Raveling 1969; Black and Barrow).
  • Ganders recruit their family into the air fastest after starting to head toss (80%, Raveling 1969, Smithsonian summary).
  • Ground threat: a gander lowers its head close to the ground and hisses (80%, Audubon).
  • In flight, a flock that starts to climb and swing wide has seen something (Tip).

• See head tosses? The family is about to fly 80%.
  • Shoot only if in range now; never chase them (Tip).
More: how to use it
  • Raveling's study followed 77 marked geese from 10 families, 2 pairs and 35 yearlings, and tied preflight movements to family status 80%.
  • When you watch a field from the road, head tossing means the flock is about to go. Note where they fly: that is tomorrow's flight line (Tip).
  • In a blind, tossing heads on the ground in front of you means your hide or movement has been seen (Tip).

• How close you get depends on the place 70%.
  • On hunt days, tracked geese moved less and flew sooner when a threat came close 80%.
More: the studies
  • Belgium: Canada goose flight initiation distance changed with flock size and other birds, and differed by site; most wary in the least visited reserve, least wary in a busy park (70%, Belgian Journal of Zoology, search preview).
  • Pennsylvania, 2025: 134 GPS tagged female geese stayed on two hunted Wildlife Management Areas through the season, at least 165 times more likely to be on them than off (80%, Beatty and others, Movement Ecology; Penn State news).
  • On hunting days and during hunting hours they took flight less and walked less, but took flight more as a threat got close 80%.
  • Older work in Illinois: geese went alert at shots even inside a refuge and left places where disturbance kept them from feeding 70%.
  • What it means: hunted geese do not leave the area, they get quieter and harder to approach (Tip, 65%).

Pressure signWhat to change (Tip, 65%)
Birds land 200 m off your spreadMove to where they landed next time
Flocks flare at 100 mFix the hide; fewer blinds
Birds stop using the fieldRest it a week
Same flock every huntChange the spread size and shape
  • They avoid fields where they are disturbed again and again 70%.
  • Same spread, same spot, every day: they learn it 65%.
More: the guide advice
  • Hunting the same spot with the same spread teaches local birds to avoid it. Change decoy count and layout through the season (65%, Ducks Unlimited goose guide).
  • Smaller, more realistic spreads in places other hunters do not use 65%.
  • Fewer blinds: with six hunters, three blinds and rotate shooters 65%.
  • "Rest the field" is widely repeated hunter advice. No study measured how long (Tip).

• Young stay a full year; pairs usually last for life 80%.
  • Most first nest at 2 or 3 years old 80%.
More: families in full
  • A goose finds a mate in its second year and usually stays paired for life; a bird that loses its mate will pair again (80%, Hinterland Who's Who; Ducks Unlimited).
  • Fall flocks are families travelling together, from a few families to thousands of birds 85%.
  • Families with young fly as a unit; you will often see 4 to 8 birds in a tight group inside a big flock (Tip).
  • The gander guards the nest and the brood; both parents tend the young (80%, Audubon).
  • About half of hatched goslings survive to fly 80%.
  • Shoot the lead bird of a family and the rest often swing back (hunter lore, Tip). Ethics first: take only clean shots.

• Young of the year decoy more readily (Tip, widely reported).
  • Old birds come in high, circle wide and land short (Tip).
Old hand's rule (tradition, opinion)

Early season and family groups come easy. Late season singles and pairs are the professors. Hunters widely repeat this; no study tested it.

More: what is fact and what is lore
  • Fact: most geese that survive year one live 10 or more years 80%. So many birds in a flock have survived several seasons 80%.
  • Fact: hunted geese change behaviour on hunt days (80%, Pennsylvania study).
  • Lore: old ganders lead the flock away from danger and young birds break off to decoys (Tip).
  • Lore: a lone goose that has lost its family is easier to call (Tip).
  • Use the lore to choose tactics, not to decide what is legal or ethical.

• Every habit is a place to wait for them (Tip).
  • Best one: back to yesterday's field 65%.
More: each habit and its source
  • In the morning geese usually return to the field they fed in the afternoon before (65%, Ducks Unlimited goose guide; quick lesson).
  • They land into the wind, so the wind sets your hide and landing hole (80%, quick lesson; Ducks Unlimited).
  • Cold or cloudy mornings: they fly later (80%, Raveling 1972).
  • They avoid decoys near fence lines, brush piles and ditches that could hide a predator (60%, Outdoor Life search preview).
  • They trust their own kind: decoys work (Tip).
  • Same roost and flight line day after day while undisturbed (Tip, 65%). See Chapter 6.

Memory rhymes (made for this app)
  • "Heads up, sit tight. Necks tall, no fight. Heads toss, take flight."
  • "Yesterday's field is tomorrow's yield."
  • "Families come easy; the old ones come wary."
  • Number trick: 2, 2 or 3, 10. Mate in year 2, first nest at 2 or 3, many live 10 years or more 80%.
Old hand's rule (tradition, opinion)

Never bump a feeding flock off the field. Let them leave on their own, then hunt them tomorrow. A standard rule in goose scouting guides.

mc-geese-05:
Why it matters

The goose year decides which birds are in front of you: big local families in September, migrants in October, wary survivors in December.

  • Nest in spring, moult in summer, move in fall 80%.
  • October and November change the most (Tip).
More: what this chapter covers
  • Month by month, January to December.
  • The nest, the moult and the young.
  • What changes in October and November.
  • Which goose is in BC in which month.
  • Season dates are only quoted from the Rule Book. No new dates here.

• Winter flocks hold open water and fields 80%.
  • Spring moves start as early as February 75%.
More: the months in full
  • Winter: geese feed a few hours in early morning and late afternoon in fields, then rest on water (80%, Hinterland Who's Who).
  • Some populations start north in February; northern breeders arrive late April or early May (75 to 80%).
  • Pairs form in a goose's second year; spring is when pairs settle on territories 80%.
  • In temperate areas nesting can start as early as mid March 80%.
  • Late season days quoted from the Rule Book 99%: District 3 (Kamloops), Canada and cackling geese 1 to 10 March. District 8 (Okanagan), 21 February to 10 March in a year that is not a leap year. District 2 (Mission), 10 February to 10 March 2027.
  • Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

StageNumber 80%
Eggs4 to 7, sometimes 2 to 11
Sitting (incubation)25 to 28 days, hen only
Leave the nest1 to 2 days after hatch
First flight6 to 9 weeks
Survive to flyAbout half
  • The hen sits; the gander guards 80%.
  • Families walk several kilometres in a few days after hatch 80%.
More: the nest in full
  • The hen picks a slightly raised dry spot near water with a good view and builds a shallow bowl lined with down (80%, Audubon).
  • Most geese do not nest until they are 2 or 3 years old (80%, Hinterland Who's Who).
  • In BC Canada geese nest mostly below 500 m (85%, BC Breeding Bird Atlas via the quick lesson).
  • Okanagan towns addle eggs within 14 days of incubation to control introduced geese (85%, Regional District of Okanagan Similkameen). That is a permit program, not hunting.
  • Spring is a time to stay away from nests. No goose season runs in April or May in any BC district (95%, my reading of the Rule Book tables).

• All flight feathers drop at once: 4 to 6 weeks flightless 70%.
  • Non breeders fly north to moult in late May and June 80%.
More: moult in full
  • Hinterland Who's Who gives a 4 to 5 week flightless moult 80%; a city naturalist guide gives 4 to 6 weeks, about the same time the goslings cannot fly 70%.
  • Timing: usually June into August 70%.
  • Non breeding geese make a moult migration, late May to early June (80%, Hinterland Who's Who).
  • Goslings fly at 6 to 9 weeks, the biggest races later (80%, Audubon).
  • You will find moulted flight feathers on lake shores in summer. Good sign for next fall (Tip). See Chapter 8.

• September geese are mostly local, big and in family groups (Tip, 65%).
  • District 3 Canada geese close 21 to 30 September 99%.
More: September in full
  • Early season dates (99%, Rule Book): District 3, 8 to 20 September. District 2, 5 to 15 September 2026. District 8 opens 20 September.
  • Young birds fly by late summer and look like adults by fall 80%.
  • Families are still feeding on hay, pasture and the first grain stubble near their home water (Tip, 65%).
  • Hunter lore: early season birds have not been shot at yet and decoy best (Tip).
  • Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

• Migrants and cacklers join the locals 75%.
  • High lakes freeze and birds crowd the valley water 75%.
More: October and November in full
  • Northern geese leave their breeding areas late August to September and reach wintering areas in October or November (75%, Ducks Unlimited). Some linger in the north until early October (80%, Hinterland Who's Who).
  • Snow geese reach the Fraser delta by early October and peak mid October to mid December (80%, How animals move).
  • Fall migration is well under way by late September and mostly over by late November, when Interior lakes freeze (75%, Ducks Unlimited via the migration lesson).
  • High plateau lakes freeze first; birds then crowd onto open valley water and the coast (60%, my reading in the migration lesson).
  • After weeks of shooting, flocks flare sooner and land farther out (Tip, 65%). Change the spread. See Chapter 4.
  • Heffley Creek in October: District 3 Canada and cackling geese open 1 October to 23 December, 10 a day 99%. Mission: District 2 opens 10 October 2026 99%.
  • Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

• Local Canada geese: all year 85%.
  • Snow geese: Fraser delta October to April, Skagit in deep winter 80%.

More: the details and the gaps
  • Snow geese: Fraser delta by early October, peak mid October to mid December, most shift to the Skagit in Washington late December to February, return mid March to mid April, then fly to Wrangel Island in April 80%.
  • Cackling geese pass BC on the way to the Willamette and lower Columbia valleys 75%; exact Interior dates: VERIFY.
  • White fronted geese: passing flocks in early fall and spring, a Tip 60%. No BC count found.
  • Migrant Canada geese in the Interior: from the first hard frosts of October (Tip, 65%, quick lesson).

• Cold days: geese feed in the warm afternoon 80%.
  • District 2 Canada geese close 23 November to 18 December 99%.
More: December in full
  • Below about minus 9°C (15°F) at sunrise, a big wintering flock usually skipped its morning flight; on the coldest days only a few birds fed (80%, Raveling 1972).
  • In bitter cold geese roost through the morning and feed when it is warmest (65%, Ducks Unlimited goose guide).
  • Snow on fields: geese feed where wind or cattle bared the ground (Tip).
  • District 3 closes 23 December; District 2 reopens 19 December 2026 to 10 January 2027; District 8 reopens 20 December to 5 January (99%, Rule Book).
  • Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

Memory rhymes (made for this app)
  • "March they nest, June they rest, fall they fly, winter they try."
  • "September: big and local. October: new and vocal. December: few and fickle."
  • Number trick: 28, 6, 9. About 28 days sitting, about 6 weeks flightless, young fly by 9 weeks 80%.
Old hand's rule (tradition, opinion)

First hard frost, look up. Hunters across the north watch for the first cold snap to bring new birds. A Tip, not a measured trigger.

mc-geese-06:
Why it matters

Geese run on light, food and safety. Learn their clock and you are hidden and quiet before the first bird leaves the roost.

  • Roost, feed, rest on water, feed, roost 80%.
  • First birds leave about 15 min before sunrise in clear weather 80%.
More: what this chapter covers
  • The daily loop and the flight line.
  • How cloud, cold, storm, wind, moon and pressure change it.
  • How sure we are about each claim.
  • Most timing numbers come from one strong study: about 40,000 wintering Canada geese at Crab Orchard, Illinois, over two winters in the 1960s (80%, Raveling and others 1972). BC birds likely follow the same rules of light and cold (Tip, 70%).

• Feed a few hours morning and late afternoon, rest on water between 80%.
  • Back to yesterday's field in the morning 65%.
More: the loop in full
  • Winter geese feed in fields a few hours early morning and late afternoon, then rest on lakes or big rivers (80%, Hinterland Who's Who).
  • The main morning flight starts at or just after sunrise; evening return between sunset and civil twilight in clear weather (80%, Raveling 1972).
  • Individual families vary inside the flock pattern 80%.
  • Geese often feed 12 hours a day or more when days are long 80%.
  • Legal hours for geese: half an hour before sunrise to half an hour after sunset (99%, Rule Book). Use the Legal light screen in Field Mode.

• Undisturbed geese use the same roost and line day after day (Tip, 65%).
  • The line is where you pass shoot, or where you scout from (Tip).
More: how to use it
  • Watch the line two evenings in a row before you plan a hunt (Tip).
  • Pass shooting: hide under the line, as close to the feeding field as you can (65%, Ducks Unlimited goose guide). See Chapter 9.
  • Never set up on the roost itself. Shooting a roost pushes the whole flock out (hunter wisdom, Tip).

• Cloud: later and longer in the fields 80%.
  • Very cold: no dawn flight; feed in the afternoon 80%.
More: weather in full
  • Overcast skies delayed the light level that starts the flight by about 15 minutes (80%, Raveling 1972).
  • On cloudy days geese stayed longer in feeding areas 80%.
  • Below 15°F (about minus 9°C) at sunrise there was usually no heavy morning flight; from minus 9 to minus 7°C (16 to 20°F) there was sometimes a partial flight 80%.
  • Stormy weather: more flying through the day, and geese sometimes roosted in fields instead of on water 80%.
  • Wind: geese land into it 80%. Hunters say they fly lower and decoy better on windy days (Tip).
  • Rain and fog: hunters report later flights and lower birds (Tip, 60%).

ClaimEvidence
Daylight sets the migration windowWidely stated, general (Tip, 60%)
Cold fronts and north winds push migrantsBlog and hunter reports only (Tip)
A falling barometer makes geese feed hardNo study found (lore)
Frozen lakes push birds to open waterFits Interior pattern 75%
  • A cold snap may move new birds in. Evidence is weak (Tip).
  • Barometric pressure: no study found. Treat it as lore (VERIFY).
More: what to do with weak evidence
  • Ducks Unlimited migration reports show cold snaps shifting some flocks south while others keep moving their own way 60%.
  • Log weather, wind and flocks in your Journal. Your own notes for your fields beat any general rule (Tip).
  • See the Weather and moon lesson for how to read a forecast.

• Full moon visible: geese come back to the roost later at dusk 80%.
  • Night feeding under the moon: proven in barnacle geese, hunter report in Canada geese (Tip).
More: moon in full
  • In the Illinois study, evening flights later than civil twilight usually happened when a full or nearly full moon was visible at sunset 80%.
  • Barnacle geese in the Netherlands fed at night only around the full moon (75%, Wildfowl journal).
  • Hunters report Canada geese feeding at night and showing up late or not at all the next morning after a bright full moon (Tip). Some say heavy cloud cancels it (Tip).
  • Lean (opinion): after a bright full moon, plan an afternoon field hunt as well as a morning one.

DayWhat to expect (Tip unless shown)
Opening weekendMany hunters, birds move around a lot
WeekdaysQuieter, birds settle
After shooting on the roostBirds may leave the area
Hunt days in a studyLess flight and walking 80%
  • Hunted geese stay, but move less and flush sooner when close 80%.
  • Weekends bring more hunters (Tip).
More: pressure in full
  • Pennsylvania 2025: GPS geese on hunted Wildlife Management Areas flew less and walked less during hunting hours and on hunting days 80%.
  • Geese left places where repeated disturbance kept them from feeding (70%, Illinois refuge work).
  • MUs (Management Units) 3-27 and 3-28 near Heffley Creek had under 30 estimated goose hunters a year in the BC survey (99%, survey estimate). Light pressure there (Tip). MU 2-4 had 251 in 2024 99%.

Memory rhymes (made for this app)
  • "Clear and bright, fly at first light. Grey and low, fifteen minutes slow."
  • "Below minus nine, they sleep in fine."
  • "Big moon at night, late birds in sight."
  • Number trick: 15, 15, minus 9. First birds 15 minutes before sunrise, cloud adds 15 minutes, below minus 9°C no dawn flight 80%.
Old hand's rule (tradition, opinion)

Scout in the evening, hunt in the morning. The standard rule in goose guides, built on birds returning to yesterday's field.

mc-geese-07:
Why it matters

Geese need three things close together: safe water, open food and a clear view. Find all three and you have found geese.

  • Roost on big water, feed in open fields nearby 80%.
  • Towns and parks hold geese you cannot hunt (Tip).
More: what this chapter covers
  • Habitat: roost, loafing and feeding ground.
  • Foods by season, with BC habitat photos.
  • Elevation through the year.
  • Your three areas: Heffley Creek (Region 3), Mission and the Fraser Valley (Region 2), the South Okanagan (Region 8).
  • Finding them on the Hunt Map: layers and terrain tools.

• Nest near water; winter where food is within commuting distance of water 80%.
  • Open views: geese avoid feeding next to tall cover 60%.
More: habitat in full
  • Lakes, ponds, bays, marshes and fields; always nests near water; winters where feeding areas are within commuting distance of water (80%, Audubon).
  • Geese spend as much time on land as on water (85%, quick lesson).
  • Many urban and refuge geese are now year round residents (80%, Audubon).
  • Loafing spots: river bars, sandbars, mudflats, points and pond edges (Tip, 65%).
  • Fields: they avoid decoys and spots near fence lines, brush piles and ditches that could hide a predator 60%.

• Almost all plants: grass, sedges, seeds, berries, grain 80%.
  • Fall and winter: waste grain and green grass 80%.

More: foods in full
  • Diet: grass and sedge stems and shoots, water plants, seeds, berries and cultivated grain; rarely insects or small fish (80%, Audubon).
  • Many races feed on waste grain and winter cereal crops (75%, Ducks Unlimited).
  • They graze on land, tip up in water, grub for roots and pick seeds 75%.
  • Snow geese on the Fraser delta dig roots of American three square bulrush and now rely on farm and refuge fields as well (85%, Demarchi 2006).
  • BC farm foods you will see: cut hay and pasture, corn stubble in the Fraser Valley, grain stubble in the Interior (Tip, 65%).

• Nest mostly below 500 m 85%.
  • When high water freezes, birds drop to valley rivers and the coast 75%.
More: elevation in full
  • BC Breeding Bird Atlas: Canada geese nest across the southern two thirds of BC, mostly below 500 m (85%, via the quick lesson).
  • High plateau lakes freeze first; birds then crowd onto open valley water and the coast (60%, migration lesson).
  • Named wintering water: the South Thompson River from Little Shuswap Lake to Kamloops Lake, Vaseux Lake, and the Fraser delta and valley marshes (80 to 90%, migration lesson).
  • Tranquille at the head of Kamloops Lake is spring and fall staging for geese and swans, and it is a No Shooting area 85%. Vaseux Lake is a bird sanctuary with no hunting 99%.

• Look for river bars and hay or grain fields in the valley bottom (Tip, 65%).
  • Light pressure: under 30 estimated goose hunters a year in 3-27 and 3-28 (99%, survey).
More: Region 3 notes
  • Heffley Creek is MU (Management Unit) 3-27 east of the North Thompson and 3-28 west, both District 3 (85 to 99%, Rule Book: Region 3).
  • Canada geese and cacklers are common on the Thompson River all year (70%, first duck hunt lesson).
  • The fields that hold geese are almost all private : written permission first (99% that consent is required).
  • Map C7: no hunting or shooting along the South Thompson band to the Lafarge Bridge, no shooting from there to the Pritchard Bridge (99% rule, 90% map reading). Tranquille (Map C17) is a No Shooting area 85%.
  • Region 3 goose harvest is small: 196 geese in 2024, 614 in 2020 (99%, survey estimate). An open niche for a hunter who scouts (Tip).
  • Local plan: Heffley Creek.

• Most BC geese are taken in Region 2; MU (Management Unit) 2-4 leads (99%, survey).
  • Mission needs the special area licence and insurance 99%.
More: Region 2 notes
  • 2024 survey: MU 2-4 (Delta, Boundary Bay) 251 hunters, 1,028 geese; MU 2-8 (Mission) 109 hunters, 201 geese 99%.
  • Fraser Valley Special Area: all of MU 2-4 and the parts of 2-8 inside Maple Ridge, Pitt Meadows, Mission and Coquitlam need the Fraser Valley Special Area Hunting Licence and $1,000,000 public liability and property damage insurance (99%, Region 2 Rule Book, Map B10).
  • Pitt Addington Marsh (2-8) and Bert Brink Wildlife Management Area (2-4): no motor vehicles all year 99%.
  • Burns Bog (2-4): no hunting 99%.
  • Bert Brink has open fields partly flooded in winter that draw wigeon and Canada geese (90%, habitat tour lesson).
  • Snow geese: the Fraser delta and Westham Island area 80%. MUs 2-4 and 2-5 carry the extra snow goose limit 99%.
  • Local plan: Mission.

• Many Okanagan geese are introduced residents that do not migrate 85%.
  • Orchards and vineyards are cultivated land: consent first 90%.
More: Region 8 notes
  • Okanagan nesting geese are hybrids of races introduced in the 1960s and 70s (85%, Regional District of Okanagan Similkameen).
  • District 8 Canada and cackling geese: 20 September to 28 November, 20 December to 5 January, and 21 February to 10 March in a year that is not a leap year, 10 a day 99%.
  • Vaseux Lake bird sanctuary: no hunting 99%.
  • Region 8 goose harvest: 185 in 2024, 925 in 2023 (99%, survey estimate).
  • Local plan: South Okanagan. Rules: Region 8 Rule Book.

Find goose water and fields in 4 steps1 of 4
  • Open the Hunt Map, then scout from public roads (Tip).
More: layers and tools explained
  • Layers to turn on: "Private land" (permission needed), "Wetlands", "Duck staging and winter waters" (goose roosts too), "Wildlife Management Areas" (WMA) and "City and town limits" (most towns ban shooting) (layer notes in the app, 90%).
  • "Motor vehicle closures" before you drive a farm or dike road (99% that closures apply).
  • Terrain tools: "Slope steepness" and "Slope direction" (aspect), "Sun and shade", "What can I see from here" (viewshed), "Elevation profile".
  • Wind tools: "Weather and wind" and "Scent cone". For geese the wind matters for landing, not scent (Tip).
  • Save each roost, flight line and field as a Spot with the date and the count. See Map scouting.

Memory rhymes (made for this app)
  • "Water to sleep, field to eat, a clear view to keep."
  • "Below five hundred they nest. When lakes freeze, the valley's best."
  • "Red on the map: knock first."
  • Number trick: 3 of 3. Safe water, open food, a clear view: miss one and the geese go elsewhere (Tip).
Old hand's rule (tradition, opinion)

Find the field, not the goose. The goose comes back to the field; you cannot chase it there. From the app's quick lesson and repeated by goose guides.

• Audubon, Ducks Unlimited, Demarchi 2006, BC survey, Rule Book, app habitat and migration lessons. Checked 2026-10-11.

mc-geese-08:
Why it matters

Goose hunters do not track a bird; they track a habit. Fresh droppings on the right patch of a field tell you where to lie down tomorrow.

  • Droppings, tracks, feathers, clipped grass, calls, flocks (Tip).
  • Fresh sign plus birds seen = the X (Tip).
More: what this chapter covers
  • Tracks to scale and how to read them.
  • Droppings and how fresh they are.
  • Feathers, down and grazed ground.
  • Calls as sign.
  • Scouting the X step by step.
  • Following a flock without chasing it.

• Goose track: 10 to 12 cm, three webbed toes 65%.
  • Duck track: half the size, about 5 to 7.5 cm 65%.
More: tracks in full
  • Canada goose print about 10 to 12 cm (4 to 4.75 in) long; one measured about 11 cm by 5.5 cm (65%, naturalist sources).
  • Three forward toes joined by webbing, a small back toe that rarely prints, middle toe longest 65%.
  • Prints turn in a little and alternate left and right, about 15 cm (6 in) apart 65%.
  • Gull tracks top out near 9.5 cm (3.75 in) and are slimmer 60%.
  • Where to look: soft mud at the water's edge, field puddles, sand bars (Tip).
  • Many tracks pointing the same way along a shore: a loafing spot (Tip).

• Tubes 5 to 10 cm long, green on grass 65%.
  • Wet and shiny means today (Tip).
More: droppings in full
  • Tubular, 5 to 10 cm (2 to 4 in) long, a bit thinner than a finger, green when geese graze grass (65%, naturalist and wildlife control sources).
  • They often lie in piles where geese feed and rest 65%.
  • Lots of them: grass passes in about 1.5 hours and grazing geese digest only a third of it 70%. See Chapter 2.
  • Freshness ladder (Tip): wet, bright and shiny today; dull with a skin after a day or two; dry, pale and crumbly when old. Rain softens old ones and frost hardens new ones, so compare several spots.
  • Many fresh droppings in one patch of a big field marks the X (65%, Ducks Unlimited goose guide).

• Body feathers and down on the X (Tip).
  • Grass clipped short, grain picked clean (Tip).
More: what to look for
  • Fresh down caught on stubble or floating at the water's edge: birds were there recently (Tip).
  • Long flight feathers on summer shorelines: a moult site 70%. Geese drop all flight feathers at once in June to August 70%.
  • Grazed grass looks mowed in patches, with droppings among the stems (Tip).
  • Puddles in a field with tracks around the edge: a drinking spot (Tip).

• At dawn and dusk, listen from the road: honks show the roost and the line (Tip).
  • High yelps in the flock: cacklers mixed in 75%.
More: how to listen
  • Geese are very vocal in flight and in big flocks (75%, Ducks Unlimited).
  • Cackling geese call higher than Canada geese 75%.
  • Snow geese give a high "kow luk" 75%. White fronted geese a laughing "kow kow kow" 80%.
  • Stand outside the truck with the engine off for 10 minutes before first light (Tip).

Scout the X in 5 steps1 of 5
  • They usually return to yesterday afternoon's field 65%.
More: the full scouting method
  • Geese usually return to the previous afternoon's feeding spot in the morning (65%, Ducks Unlimited goose guide, Wade Bourne).
  • Wait until the flock flies to roost, walk out (with permission), check for fresh droppings, and save the spot on your GPS (Global Positioning System) or as a Spot on the Hunt Map 65%.
  • Set up in cover 45 to 90 m (50 to 100 yd) off the X if the X itself is bare; hunting from cover often beats lying on the exact spot (65%, Casey Self, Ducks Unlimited guide).
  • Scout where you can see without trespassing: use the "What can I see from here" tool. See Chapter 7.
  • Law: no loaded gun in or on a vehicle while you scout; no shooting from a vehicle or in the (99%, quick lesson rules).

• Drive the roads ahead of the flock, stop, glass (Tip).
  • Note time, field, wind and count in your Journal (Tip).
More: how to do it
  • Goose flocks fly kilometres between roost and field. Use binoculars and public roads; never follow a flock across private land (99% on trespass).
  • Note the direction they leave the roost and the time. Next evening wait farther along that line (Tip).
  • A flock that circles and lands in the same field two days running is your best bet (Tip, 65%).
  • Keep a record: date, time, field, wind, flock size. After a season you will know your fields better than any book (Tip). See Journal guide.

Memory rhymes (made for this app)
  • "Green and wet, the best bet. Dry and white, not tonight."
  • "Glass at dusk, find the X; set at dawn, take the next."
  • "Three toes webbed, ten cm long: a goose walked here and moved along."
  • Number trick: 10, 10, 1.5. Track about 10 cm, droppings up to 10 cm, about 1.5 hours from grass to dropping (65 to 70%).
Old hand's rule (tradition, opinion)

Never bump the birds when you scout. Watch them leave, then walk the field. Standard advice in goose hunting guides.

• Ducks Unlimited goose guide, naturalist track and scat notes, Wildfowl journal, Hinterland Who's Who. Checked 2026-10-11.

  • PEI Untamed, Canada goose tracks and scat and Critter Control, goose tracks, search previews 2026-10-11 65%.
  • Internet Center for Wildlife Damage Management, read directly 2026-10-11 75%.
  • Wildfowl journal, food throughput time, search preview 2026-10-11 70%.
  • Ducks Unlimited ID pages, read directly 2026-10-11 75%.
