mc-geese-09:
Why it matters

Goose hunting is won the evening before and the hour before light: the right field, the right hide, the right wind. The shot is the easy part.

  • 4 ways: field over decoys, water over decoys, pass shooting, sneak (Tip).
  • Field over decoys is the best start for you (Tip).
More: what this chapter covers, and the options
MethodProsCons
Field over decoysClose, slow, feet down birds; dryPermission, decoys, a hide
Water over decoysYour duck gear, boat and kayak workBirds land short; retrieval
Pass shootingNo decoys, little gearHigh birds, long shots, cripples
Sneak on a feeding flockFree, excitingHard on open fields; one chance
My lean (opinion)

Field over a dozen or two decoys, on a field you scouted, with written permission. Your brother calls the shot, you both lie still.

  • Assumption: you hunt with your brother, a 12 gauge with steel, a 10 ft boat and a kayak, no dog yet.
  • Study aid only. The official regulations are the law. Rules recap: Chapter 10.

Ask for a goose field in 6 steps1 of 6
  • No hunting on cultivated land without consent 99%.
  • Farmers often welcome goose hunters on new grass and winter crops (Tip).
More: the law and the goose angle
  • "A person is not permitted to hunt on cultivated land or on Crown land which is subject to a grazing lease while the land is occupied by livestock, without the consent of the owner, lessee, or occupant of the land." (99%, synopsis page 9)
  • Fenced, signed or naturally bounded land is enclosed under the Trespass Act: no entry without consent (99%, page 9).
  • No hunting or shooting within 100 m of an occupied dwelling or farm building (99%, page 10).
  • One yes, one season, unless they say otherwise (99%, page 77). Get it in writing (Tip).
  • Goose angle: ask before you need it. Tell them where you will park, that you will walk in, that you pick up every shell and take the decoys out the same day (Tip).
  • Ask before you dig a blind or drive on a field (65%, Ducks Unlimited goose guide).
  • Full lesson and form: Asking for permission. Law: Where you can hunt.

• Feeders upwind, a landing hole downwind, blinds beside the hole 65%.
  • Geese land into the wind 80%.
More: numbers from goose guides
  • About 80% feeders and 20% active (heads up) decoys. Feeders near the centre, upwind of the landing area; actives downwind in bunches of 3 to 7 (65%, Ducks Unlimited goose guide).
  • Put blinds about 9 m (10 yd) to the side of the landing hole, or parallel to the wind, so the birds see decoys, not blinds 65%.
  • Right handed shooters sit slightly right of the hole: swinging left is easier 65%.
  • Do not mix decoy types (full body, shell, silhouette, windsock) except same brand full bodies and shells 65%.
  • Scatter hunters in small decoy clusters rather than a row of blinds 65%.
  • Quick lesson numbers: 1 to 3 dozen decoys for a start 65%.
  • Keep decoys off fence lines, brush and ditches 60%.

• Open the hole wide enough to land in (Tip).
  • High birds: a few decoys 45 to 55 m downwind pull them down 65%.
More: spread tricks and high birds
  • Six decoys 50 to 60 yd (45 to 55 m) downwind, in two groups on either side of the spread, help pull high birds lower. Do not call until birds commit, then call and flag hard to stop them landing short (65%, Ducks Unlimited goose guide).
  • Change decoy numbers and shape through the season 65%.
  • Late season: smaller, very real looking spreads where nobody else hunts 65%.
  • Frosty mornings: set decoys last to cut glare 65%.
  • Gear and prices: start with what you can carry with a partner; price checks: VERIFY before you buy.
More: the evening before, in order
  1. Last hour of light: find the flock in a field from the road (Tip).
  2. Note field, time, flock size and wind (Tip).
  3. Check tomorrow's wind on the Hunt Map Weather and wind tool. If the wind will swing, plan the hide for tomorrow's wind (Tip).
  4. Call the landowner to confirm (Tip).
  5. Pack the night before: permit with stamp, BC licence, steel shells, plug in, decoys, blinds, mud, stubble straps, flag, call (Tip). See the checklist in Geese.
  6. In the dark: set the blinds first, then decoys, then brush. Be done 30 minutes before legal light (Tip).

Hide a layout blind in 4 steps1 of 4
  • Concealment beats decoys and calling (Tip, 60%).
More: blind craft
  • Hiding is the single biggest factor in goose hunting success (60%, Grand View Outdoors; widely repeated).
  • Dig shallow pits for layout blinds only with permission; pack mud or sand on the edges and add natural vegetation (65%, Ducks Unlimited).
  • Use stubble from the field itself and add more during the hunt; pick up spent shells 65%.
  • Pull stubble about 14 to 18 m (15 to 20 yd) away so the ground right around the blind keeps its colour (60%, Field and Stream search preview). Dig a shallow trench parallel to the rows 60%.
  • Mud the blind with a dirt and water slurry to kill the shine; let it dry first 60%.
  • Snow: use a snow cover and scuff dirt downwind among the decoys to look like feeding 65%.
  • Layout blinds also work on sand bars, mudflats and pond edges 65%.
  • No blind? Lie in a ditch, a fence row or tall stubble 45 to 90 m off the X 65%.

Call a flock in 4 steps1 of 4
▶Mastering the Art of Calling Geese in Fields with Fred Zink from Zink Calls | DUTVRead the flock and call to match it.
Ducks Unlimited, YouTube, 1 min. Needs internet.
  • Calling too much is the top mistake 65%.
More: the four sounds, flagging and the law
SoundMeans (65%, Ducks Unlimited)
HonkRelaxed contact
CluckExcited, short honk
MurmurFeeding and loafing
MoanAll purpose, in flight or on water
  • Far birds: a wall of honks, clucks and moans until they turn. Once they turn: ground talk, murmurs and soft clucks. If they slide away: back to loud, excited calling 65%.
  • Big wind: loud and steady. Calm days and local birds: softer and less 65%.
  • Two callers: one sets the tempo; stop if the flock shies 65%.
  • Flagging: several hunters flag to catch far birds; once they turn only the leader flags; everyone stops on the final approach 65%.
  • Short reed calls are loudest and most versatile but hardest; resonant chamber calls are easiest 65%.
  • Electronic calls are banned for geese in BC 99%. Mouth calls and flags are fine (95%, my reading).

• Set on a bar or point geese use; hide on the bank (Tip).
  • No shooting from a moving motor boat 99%.
More: water rules and the boat
  • Floaters near a bar or point the geese loaf on; hide on the bank (Tip, quick lesson). Pros: your duck gear works. Cons: geese often land out of range, and you need a way to fetch (Tip).
  • Federal and BC: no hunting migratory birds from or using a moving boat with a motor or sail; gliding after the motor is cut still counts as moving (99%, Rule Book).
  • Your kayak, paddled with no motor or sail, is not covered by that rule (95%, my reading in the Rule Book).
  • You must have adequate means at hand to retrieve any bird you kill or injure (99%, s. 42). No boat, waders or dog? Do not shoot birds over deep water.
  • Picking up birds: under paddle, or with the motor off and the gun unloaded, until confirmed (80%, my reading in the Rule Book). VERIFY with a conservation officer.
  • Wear your PFD (Personal Flotation Device). Cold water kills fast (Tip). See Water safety.
  • Mission and all of MU (Management Unit) 2-4 need the Fraser Valley Special Area licence and insurance, foreshore included (99%, Map B10).

• Pass shoot only birds under 30 m (Tip).
  • Sneak with cover and permission, or not at all (Tip).
More: both methods in full
  • Pass shooting: scout the lanes in and out of the feeding field, hide in cover under them as close to the field as you can (65%, Ducks Unlimited).
  • Cons: high birds, long shots and cripples (Tip). Max for you: 35 m (38 yd), better 30 m (Tip).
  • Never shoot the roost itself; it drives the flock away (Tip).
  • Sneak (jump shooting): use thickets, fence rows and dips to get close to feeding geese and shoot as they flush (65%, Ducks Unlimited).
  • On open BC fields a sneak rarely works; a river bend or a dike with cover is better (Tip).
  • Law: never shoot from a vehicle, or within or across the 99%.

• One caller. Two zones. Rise together (Tip).
  • Never swing past the middle line (Tip).
More: partner rules
  • Agree before light who calls the shot and which birds each takes (65%, Ducks Unlimited).
  • Left hunter takes left birds, right hunter right birds. In a boat sit back to back (Tip, shotgun skills).
  • Keep blinds close enough to talk in a whisper 65%.
  • Fewer blinds are better: with two hunters, two blinds side by side (Tip).
  • Count birds out loud as they fall: you each need to know when the limit is reached (99% on the limit; Tip on the method).
  • Earplugs: magnum loads damage hearing 65%.

Old hand's habitWhy (opinion, from goose guides)
Scouts every evening before a huntYesterday's field is tomorrow's spot
Spends more time hiding than callingConcealment wins
Lets birds work, shoots feet downClose birds die clean
Changes the spread oftenLocal birds learn
Hunts weekdays and afternoonsLess pressure
Keeps one field restingBirds keep coming back

Old hand's rule (tradition, opinion)

Let the first flock land. Widely told by goose hunters: a few live birds on the ground are the best decoys you will ever own.

More: where these come from
  • Every habit above is opinion from published hunting writers and guides (Ducks Unlimited goose guide, Outdoor Life, Grand View Outdoors), not a study. Label: Tip.
  • "Let the first flock land" means passing a small group so they pull in the next bigger flock. Your call; some hunters disagree (Tip).
  • Birds show you what is wrong. Fix one thing at a time (Tip).
More: more calls to make
  • Wind swung 90 degrees: turn the spread so the hole is downwind again, and move the blinds beside it (Tip).
  • Flock after flock lands in the next field: next time hunt that field, with permission (Tip).
  • Bright bluebird day, no wind: expect birds to circle; call less, consider an afternoon hunt (Tip). On calm days take good overhead shots near 27 m (30 yd) with BB or larger, because birds rarely commit (65%, Ducks Unlimited).
  • Bitter cold: plan for a late morning or afternoon flight (80%, Raveling 1972).
  • Bag full: unload, pick up, and leave the field as you found it (99% on the limit).

• Feet down, inside 35 m (38 yd). Pick one bird (Tip).
  • Kill and retrieve every wounded bird you can 99%.
More: ethics in full
  • A goose looks close at 50 m because it is big. Wait (Tip).
  • Pick one bird, then the next. Never flock shoot (Tip).
  • Carry steel 2 or 4 shells for finishing cripples at about 14 m (15 yd) 65%.
  • You must kill and retrieve a wounded bird as soon as you can (99%, s. 42). Make all reasonable effort to find it, and it counts in your bag (99%, page 12).
  • Daily limit reached: stop hunting that species for the day (99%, s. 44).
  • Dogs: Ducks Unlimited advises a young retriever gets a year of duck hunting before geese 65%. Without a dog, plan every retrieve before you shoot (Tip).
  • Leave no shells, no garbage, no ruts. The next hunter needs the same farmer (Tip).

Memory rhymes (made for this app)
  • "Hide it, then decoy it, then call it, then enjoy it."
  • "Wind at your back, hole in their track."
  • "Feet down and near, then shoot: not before, my dear."
  • Number trick: 80, 20, 10, 35. 80% feeders, 20% actives, blinds 10 yd (9 m) beside the hole, shots inside 35 m (65% and Tip).
Old hand's rule (tradition, opinion)

When in doubt, call less. Goose guides agree that over calling is the most common mistake.

• Ducks Unlimited goose guide, Outdoor Life, Field and Stream, Grand View Outdoors, Raveling 1972, Rule Book. Checked 2026-10-11.
More: every source and date checked
  • Ducks Unlimited, The ultimate guide to hunting Canada geese (Wade Bourne, Phil Bourjaily and others), read directly 2026-10-11 65%.
  • Grand View Outdoors, 12 tips for goose hunters, Field and Stream, hide your layout blind, Outdoor Life, brush your blind first, search previews 2026-10-11 60%.
  • Raveling, Crews and Klimstra 1972, read directly 2026-10-11 80%.
  • Video card: Mastering the Art of Calling Geese in Fields with Fred Zink (YouTube, link verified by the app's video manifest).
  • Rules: Rule Book: migratory birds, Where you can hunt, Region 2, checked 2026-10-03 and 2026-10-04 99%. Permission: Asking for permission.
  • Full log: research/2026-10-11-masterclass-geese.md.
mc-geese-10:
Why it matters

A clean goose hunt ends with a clean kill, a found bird, cool meat and every rule kept. This chapter ties it all together, with the one page cheat sheet.

  • Decoying, feet down, inside 35 m (38 yd): the shot to take (Tip).
  • Going away high: let it go (Tip).
More: what this chapter covers
  • Load, pattern and range. Leads.
  • What happens after the shot, and finding cripples.
  • Field care, meat care, yield and cooking.
  • Rules recap with links to the Rule Book. No new rules here.
  • The cheat sheet, chapter links, the quick lesson and the planner.

• Steel BB for big Canada geese; BBB or T for longer shots 70%.
  • Pattern: 60 pellets in a 76 cm (30 in) circle at your longest range 65%.

More: loads and chokes
  • Non toxic shot only, and no lead in your pockets or boat (99%, Rule Book).
  • Steel BB is the all round pellet for large Canada geese; BBB and T for longer range (70%, Ducks Unlimited).
  • Steel 1 or 2 for cackling geese and snow geese over decoys (Tip, quick lesson).
  • Your 12 gauge with 3 inch steel is enough (Tip). Modified choke is a usual start with BB steel (Tip). Pattern it: Shotgun skills, Shotgun guide.
  • Max range for you this season: 35 m (38 yd). A goose looks close at 50 m because it is big (Tip).
  • Cripple shells: steel 2 or 4, finish at about 14 m (15 yd) 65%.

• Swing slowly from behind; fire as you see daylight past the head 65%.
  • Too fast a swing and too much lead is a common miss 65%.
More: shooting notes
  • Big birds look slow, so hunters under lead or over lead. Guides suggest a slow swing from behind and firing when daylight shows between barrel and head (65%, Ducks Unlimited, Phil Bourjaily).
  • Head shots at close decoying birds: the head is about the size of a dove's body and fewer pellets reach the breast 65%.
  • On calm days take good overhead shots near 27 m (30 yd) with BB or larger; birds rarely commit fully 65%.
  • Wear earplugs: magnum loads harm hearing 65%.
  • Background: Shot placement, Shotgun skills.

• Watch every bird that leaves until it is out of sight (Tip).
  • Kill and retrieve wounded birds as soon as you can 99%.
More: cripples and retrieval
  • A goose that drops its legs, lifts its head or sails off is hit. Mark the spot it lands with a landmark and a map pin (Tip).
  • On the ground: finish it at once with a cripple shell to the head at close range 65%, or by hand if you know how (Tip).
  • On water: you must have the means to retrieve before you shoot (99%, s. 42). A kayak or boat under paddle, or motor off with the gun unloaded until confirmed (80%, my reading in the Rule Book). VERIFY with a conservation officer.
  • A bird you find dead and keep counts in your daily bag (99%, s. 43(3)).
  • Make all reasonable effort to locate, dispatch, retrieve and count it (99%, page 12).
  • Do not shoot again at the flock while a cripple is running (Tip).

Goose field care in 4 steps1 of 4
  • Wing or head stays on until preserved 99%.
  • Bird flu care: gloves, clean outdoors, wash up 80%.
More: care in full
  • Keep at least one fully feathered wing or the fully feathered head on each bird until it is preserved (99%, s. 52(1)).
  • "Preserved" means plucked and frozen, made into sausage, cooked, dried, canned or smoked away from the hunting area, or mounted (99%, s. 1).
  • Unpreserved birds count toward the possession limit everywhere, home fridge included (99%, s. 46(1)).
  • Avian influenza: wear rubber or nitrile gloves, clean birds outdoors or in a ventilated place, wash hands, do not take birds that look sick, keep away from your own poultry (80%, Oklahoma and California wildlife agencies).
  • A goose holds heat. Breast it or open it within 1 to 2 hours in mild weather (Tip).
  • Giving birds away: label with your full name, address, phone, email if any, the date, your permit number and your signature, or preserve them first (99%, s. 50).
  • Never let edible meat be wasted (99%, s. 55(1)).

• About 1 kg of boned breast from a big Canada goose 60%.
  • Legs and thighs: slow cook (Tip).
More: yield notes
  • A mature Canada goose of about 3.6 kg gives roughly 1 kg of boned breast; single breast halves run about 280 to 450 g (60%, hunter figures, quick lesson).
  • Cackling and snow geese give less (Tip).
  • Pluck only if you will roast it whole; otherwise skin and breast, keeping a wing on until the freezer (Tip; wing rule 99%).
  • Older resident geese can be tough (Tip). Brine, slice thin across the grain, or grind (Tip).
  • More: Meat care, Butchering.

CutHow (Tip unless shown)
BreastSear, slice thin across the grain
Legs and thighsBraise or confit, low and slow
Tough or old birdGrind for sausage or jerky
Food safetyCook to 74°C (165°F) inside, agency advice for bird flu 80%
  • Goose breast is dark, rich meat (Tip).
More: cooking in full
  • Wildlife agencies advise cooking all game birds to an internal 74°C (165°F) because of avian influenza (80%, Oklahoma and Arkansas agency advice in search previews).
  • Many cooks serve goose breast pinker. That is your choice; the agency advice is the safe line (Tip).
  • Remove any shot and feather bits you find in the meat (Tip).
  • More recipes: Cooking wild game.

Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

  • All from the Rule Book. Read your district's page before every trip 99%.

mc-grouse-01:
Why it matters

Name the bird before you pull the trigger. In BC that means six kinds of grouse, three of them with their own rules.

  • Forest grouse: ruffed, spruce, dusky (Interior), sooty (coast) 85%.
  • Own rules: sharp tailed grouse and ptarmigan 99%.
More: what this Masterclass covers
  • Ten chapters: meet the birds, the body, the senses, the mind, the year, the day, where they are, sign, how to hunt, and shot to table with the rules.
  • This is the deep version. The short lesson stays: Grouse and ptarmigan.
  • Every fact carries a certainty %. Under 60% is labelled Tip or VERIFY.
  • "Old hand's rule" lines are hunter tradition and opinion, gathered from hunting writers and educators. They are not law and not science.
  • Weights on the card: ruffed and spruce 450 to 750 g, dusky 880 g to 1.6 kg (80%, Audubon and Hinterland Who's Who), sharp tailed 596 to 1,031 g (85%, BC species account), ptarmigan about 350 g (white tailed) to 800 g (willow) (85%, Hinterland Who's Who).
  • Rules in this course come only from the app's Rule Book. Nothing new is added.

• Unbroken tail band and 2 rump dots: male (70 to 85%).
  • Band broken in the middle, 1 dot: female (70 to 85%).

More: every mark, with numbers
  • Tail: the male's dark band near the tip runs unbroken across all the tail feathers. The hen's band is often washed out or broken in the middle two feathers (85%, Alaska Department of Fish and Game aging and sexing guide). Some males break the rule, so use two clues (70%, Connecticut DEEP).
  • Rump dots: pluck a feather from the rump just above the tail. 2 or more pale dots: male. 1 dot: female (70%, Connecticut DEEP hunter log; widely used by hunters).
  • Middle tail feather length: about 15 cm (6 in) or more is a male; under 14 cm (5.5 in) is a female; in between, use another clue (70%, Connecticut DEEP).
  • Weight: a male is about 500 g; hens are smaller (85%, Hinterland Who's Who). Average about 640 g in one dataset (65%, Animal Diversity Web).
  • Colour phases: grey and red (brown). Both sexes come in both 80%. West coast birds run more reddish brown (85%, Hinterland Who's Who).
  • Neck ruffs: black feather tufts on the neck sides, bigger on the male, flared in display 80%.

• Male black below with a red comb; hen barred grey or rust 80%.
  • Male tail black; hen tail mottled 85%.
More: marks, Franklin's form and young
  • Male: black throat and breast edged in white, scarlet comb over the eye (80%, Idaho Fish and Game).
  • Hen: grey to reddish brown, heavily barred 80%.
  • Southern BC birds are the form: the male shows white spots above a dark tail and lacks the rusty tail tip 80%.
  • Sex by tail: male tail feathers black, hen's mottled tan (85%, Alaska Department of Fish and Game).
  • Age: pluck the innermost flight feather (P1). Quill base under 2.4 mm wide: young of the year; 2.4 mm or more: adult (85%, Alaska Department of Fish and Game).
  • Weight 450 to 750 g 80%.
  • Nickname "fool hen": it often sits and lets people walk close (80%, Idaho Fish and Game).

• Biggest forest grouse in BC 80%.
  • Coast birds are sooty, Interior birds are dusky 85%.

More: the split, and the marks
  • Until 2006 both were one species, the blue grouse. The American Ornithologists' Union split them that year on DNA, voice and display evidence 85%.
  • Sooty grouse: wet coastal forest. Dusky grouse: drier Interior forest 85%. Where exactly they meet in northern BC is less certain 75%.
  • The Rule Book uses the old name in brackets: Region 2 lists "SOOTY (Blue)", Regions 3 and 8 list "DUSKY (Blue)" (99%, Rule Book).
  • Male: plain slate grey, yellow to orange comb, neck air sacs that show in display, dark tail with a pale grey tip band 80%. Dusky sacs reddish purple (75%, Idaho Fish and Game).
  • Hen: mottled brown and grey, dark tail 80%.
  • Sex by tail: male black with a grey tip, often square ended; hen black tail with mottled rump feathers (85%, Alaska Department of Fish and Game, sooty grouse).
  • Weight: 880 g to 1.6 kg 80%. About 50 cm (20 in) long (75%, Idaho Fish and Game).

• Look at the 2 outer flight feathers, P9 and P10 85%.
  • Pointed and frayed: young. Rounded: adult 85%.
More: how the moult makes this work
  • Grouse replace their flight feathers once a year in midsummer, from P1 outward toward P10 (85%, Alaska Department of Fish and Game).
  • Young birds replace only P1 to P8 in their first summer, so P9 and P10 stay as worn, pointed juvenile feathers 85%.
  • If P8 is not fully grown, it is a young bird. If P9 or P10 is still growing in, it is an adult 85%.
  • Ptarmigan: young birds show more black on P9 than on P8 85%.
  • By October, young birds look like small hens of their species (Tip, 65%).
  • Why care: early in the season you shoot mostly young birds; late in the season more adults (75%, Pennsylvania Game Commission). See The mind.

• Biggest to smallest: dusky, sharp tailed, ruffed and spruce, ptarmigan 80%.
  • BC numbers: only sharp tailed has an estimate 85%; the rest VERIFY.
More: weights behind the chart

  • Sharp tailed 596 to 1,031 g, 41 to 48 cm long (85%, BC species account).
  • Ruffed 450 to 750 g, 40 to 50 cm long (60 to 75%, Pennsylvania Game Commission, Wikipedia). Wingspan 56 to 64 cm 75%.
  • Spruce 450 to 750 g 80%.
  • Willow ptarmigan 450 to 800 g; white tailed about 350 g, the smallest grouse; rock ptarmigan in between (85%, Hinterland Who's Who).
  • Meat per bird: see Shot to table.

mc-grouse-02:
Why it matters

Know what is inside the bird and you know where to shoot, how to keep the meat, and why grouse act the way they do.

  • Big white breast for bursts; crop, gizzard and ceca for tough food (75 to 85%).
  • Lungs high on the back, heart low and forward 80%.
More: the body in one list
  • Crop: a stretchy pouch at the base of the neck that holds a meal 85%.
  • Gizzard: a muscular stomach that grinds food with swallowed grit 85%.
  • Ceca: two long blind pouches where bacteria break down woody fibre 75%.
  • Lungs: small and rigid, tucked against the ribs and backbone 80%.
  • Air sacs: thin balloons that move air through the lungs; they also reach into some bones (70 to 80%).
  • Heart: four chambers, low and forward in the chest 80%.
  • Breast: two big flight muscles on the keel bone, white meat 70%.

• The keel is a blade on the breastbone that anchors the flight muscles 80%.
  • White breast: power for a few seconds. Dark legs: walking all day 70%.
More: why white and dark meat
  • Grouse breast meat is white: fast muscle fibres with little myoglobin that run on stored sugar and tire fast (70%, studies on turkeys and chickens, close cousins).
  • That is why a grouse explodes up, flaps hard, then glides: the breast cannot keep flapping long 70%. Pennsylvania notes the glide is usually under 90 m (100 yd) 75%.
  • Leg and thigh meat is darker: slow muscle that works all day as the bird walks 70%. Grouse walk more than they fly (75%, Pennsylvania Game Commission).
  • Bird bones are light; some are hollow and filled with air sac extensions 70%.
  • Meat note: the breast is most of the meat on a grouse. The leg is small but tasty (Tip).

• Rigid lungs, air sacs as bellows 80%.
  • Air flows one way through the lung, in breath and out 80%.
More: the air sac system in plain words
  • A bird's lungs do not swell like ours. The air sacs expand and squeeze to push air through them (80%, 2024 review in a peer reviewed journal; biology textbook).
  • Most birds have about 9 air sacs, in a front set and a rear set 70%.
  • On the in breath much of the fresh air goes past the lung into the rear sacs. On the out breath that air is pushed through the lung. Gas exchange happens only in the lung, not in the sacs 80%.
  • No diaphragm: the ribs and keel move to pump the sacs 75%.
  • Result: fresh air crosses the lung on both in and out breaths. Birds get more oxygen per breath than we do 80%.
  • Hunting meaning: a pellet through the lungs or the big sacs takes the bird's breath; a hit only in the back half often does not stop it fast (Tip, 60%).

• Four chambered heart, big for the body 80%.
  • Brain, spine, heart and lungs are all in the front half 80%.
More: what it means for the shot
  • Bird hearts have two atria and two ventricles, with the two sides fully separate, like ours. The main artery curves right, not left (80%, avian heart review).
  • Birds carry relatively large hearts for flight 80%.
  • Body temperature runs hot: about 41.5 C in captive ruffed grouse, range 40.4 to 42.6 C 75%.
  • .22: the head or upper neck kills cleanly and saves the breast (Tip, 70%). See How to hunt.
  • Shotgun: put the pattern on the head and front half. Pellets in the head, neck and chest stop the bird (Tip, 70%).
  • A grouse hit only in the wing or rear may run and hide. Mark it and go fast (Tip). See Shot to table.

• Crop stores, gizzard grinds, ceca ferment 80%.
  • Open the crop of every bird you shoot: it shows the food (Tip).
More: digestion step by step
  • A grouse can fill its crop with a day's worth of buds in about 20 minutes, then sit somewhere safe to digest (60%, Northern Woodlands).
  • The gizzard uses swallowed grit to grind seeds, buds and needles 85%. That is why grouse pick gravel on road edges and dust bowls 75%.
  • The ceca hold bacteria that ferment fibre from woody food like aspen and birch buds 75%.
  • Ruffed grouse prefer aspen flower buds and avoid birch and alder catkins when they can choose (80%, Guglielmo and Karasov 1995).
  • Field use: slit the crop and look. Clover leaves, kinnikinnick berries, aspen buds or pine needles tell you exactly where to hunt next (Tip, common hunter practice).

• In winter the gut grows longer to handle needles and buds 75%.
  • Spruce grouse: 99% needles once snow covers the ground 75%.
More: numbers
  • Alberta spruce grouse: conifer needles were 79% of the year's diet by dry weight and 99% during the snow season (75%, Pendergast and Boag 1973, via summaries).
  • Gut sections grow about 40% longer in winter 75%. One secondary source says the gizzard grows about 75% (60%, VERIFY).
  • Ceca enlarge in winter when only needles are eaten 70%.
  • Taste: late season spruce grouse living on needles can taste of pine; soak or brine (Tip).

• Grouse run about 41.5 C inside 75%.
  • Soft snow 20 cm deep turns into a shelter 75%.
More: winter survival tools
  • Snow roost: under 20 cm of soft snow, roost temperatures stayed between -3 and -12 C while the air dropped as low as -35 C (75%, Wilson Bulletin).
  • In Maine, grouse plunged into the snow in flight once it was about 40 cm deep 70%. A study found grouse stress hormones fall sharply once snow is deeper than 20 cm 70%.
  • Snow roosts can be 11 to 17 C (20 to 30 F) warmer than open air (75%, Idaho Fish and Game).
  • Snowshoes: in winter grouse grow comb like scales on the sides of their toes, called pectinations (85%, Hinterland Who's Who).
  • Ptarmigan grow feathered feet, unique among chicken like birds 85%.
  • No good snow? A crust or bare cold ground forces grouse into thick conifers; they lose weight and some starve or freeze (85%, Hinterland Who's Who).

• Most chicks die in the first weeks 75%.
  • About half of adults live through each year 75%.
More: survival numbers
  • Over three quarters of ruffed grouse chicks die within 35 days of hatching, most in the first week (75%, Pennsylvania Game Commission).
  • About half of hens lose their whole brood in the first 1 to 2 weeks (85%, Hinterland Who's Who).
  • Adult yearly survival: about 50% in Pennsylvania 75%; 53% in Maryland; 32% for adults and 16% for young birds in Maine 75%. Winter, January to March, is the hardest time 75%.
  • Few ruffed grouse live to age 2 75%. Some are thought to live 11 years 60%.
  • Dusky grouse: about half die in their first year 65%.
  • Fat: grouse carry little fat compared with ducks. They survive winter by eating every day and roosting well, not by living off fat (Tip, 60%).
  • Hunting: in one large study hunting made up 12% of known deaths and looked compensatory, meaning it replaced other deaths 75%.

• Rhyme: "Crop to store, gizzard to grind, ceca to brew what's left behind."
  • Number trick: "41 inside, minus 35 outside, snow between."
  • Old hand's rule (tradition): "Check the crop, find the crop": what is in it grows nearby.

  • "Front half or nothing": brain, spine, heart and lungs are all forward.
  • "Two sets of sacs, one way through."
  • "3 in 4 chicks gone by 5 weeks."
  • The crop check is common hunter practice written up in many hunting guides; the rhymes are made for this course.

mc-grouse-03:
Why it matters

A grouse lives by its eyes and ears. Learn what it sees and hears and you get the close, calm shot instead of a roar of wings behind a tree.

  • Eyes on the sides: a huge field of view, little overlap 75%.
  • Sees colour and motion very well 75%.
More: the eyes
  • Grouse are galliform birds, close cousins of the chicken. Most eye studies are on chickens; treat these as a guide for grouse 75%.
  • Field of view about 300 degrees, with only about 30 degrees seen by both eyes (75%, chicken data; Martin's review of bird visual fields gives 20 to 30 degrees for most birds).
  • A small blind spot sits straight behind the head 75%.
  • Colour: four kinds of single cones (violet, blue, green, red), one more than us. Birds see colours we cannot (75%, PLOS One study on chickens).
  • Motion: a double cone is thought to handle motion 75%. A grouse notices movement before shape (Tip, 70%).
  • Night: grouse roost at night in trees, on the ground or in snow 75%. How well they see in the dark: no source found (VERIFY).

• Move slow, stop behind trees, never skyline yourself (Tip).
  • Look for a shape and a twitch, not a whole bird (Tip).
More: how hunters use this
  • Your blaze orange does not hurt you much: grouse key on movement more than colour (Tip, 60%). Wear what the law and safety need.
  • Walk, stop, look. The stop is when you see the bird and the bird sees no motion (Tip).
  • In trees: scan near the trunk on the sunny side of conifers. A grouse is a dark blob with a tail hanging down (Tip).
  • On the ground: look for a head moving through the leaves, then freeze (Tip).
  • Old hand's rule (tradition): "See the eye, not the bird."

• Most birds hear best at 1 to 4 kHz 70%.
  • Grouse ears are tuned to low sounds 65%.
More: what grouse hear
  • Bird hearing is sharpest between 1 and 4 kHz, about where we hear best (70%, bird hearing reviews).
  • Gallinaceous birds (grouse, quail, chickens) have an inner ear tuned lower, below 1 kHz 65%.
  • Chickens hear very low sounds, under 64 Hz, better than people 70%.
  • The ruffed grouse drum is a very low sound, under 100 Hz 70%. Other grouse hear it a long way off.
  • What carries to a grouse: boots on rock, a slammed truck door, a dropped tailgate, voices (Tip).
  • Tip: close doors gently, talk in a whisper, and do not crunch along a gravel road edge.

• No study found that grouse smell people (Tip).
  • Wind matters for sound and for your dog's nose (Tip).
More: wind and thermals for a grouse hunter
  • Birds of the grouse family are not known for a strong sense of smell. We found no source showing grouse detect hunters by scent (Tip, so treat smell as a minor factor).
  • Wind carries your noise toward or away from the bird (Tip).
  • Wind and rising or sinking air (thermals) carry the bird's scent to your dog. Work a dog into the wind so it meets the scent cone (Tip, common dog handling advice).
  • Thermals: air rises up slopes when the sun warms them and sinks at evening (80%, see Wind and thermals).
  • Strong wind seems to make grouse wild. Hunters blame noise that hides predators (hunter lore, 60%). See The day.

• First defence: camouflage and stillness 80%.
  • Last: a roaring flush and a short glide to cover 75%.
More: the escape plan, in detail
  • Spruce grouse rely on camouflage and stillness and often let people close 80%.
  • Ruffed grouse often walk or run away under cover before they fly (Tip, 65%).
  • The flush is loud on purpose: the roar startles a predator (Tip, 60%).
  • After the flush a ruffed grouse glides, usually under 90 m (100 yd), and often lands in a tree (75%, Pennsylvania Game Commission; Outdoor Life).
  • Then it freezes again. That is why a follow up works (Tip). See The mind.

• Walk slow, stop often: the silence makes the bird nervous (Tip).
  • Be ready when you stop, not when you walk (Tip).
More: why the stop works (hunter lore)
  • Many hunting writers say a grouse holds while you keep walking past, then flushes when you stop, because a stopped predator may have seen it (hunter lore, 60%).
  • Stop next to an opening with room to swing, not in the thick of it (Tip).
  • Hold the gun at ready during the stop (Tip).
  • Circle a lone evergreen: a grouse under it may walk to the far side and flush from there (Tip, Outdoor Canada).

• Rhyme: "It sees you move, it hears you step, it never smells the sweat you've kept."
  • Number trick: "300 to see, 30 to judge": 300 degree view, 30 degrees with both eyes.
  • Old hand's rule (tradition): "Walk like you're late, stop like you're lost."
More: more hooks
  • "Stop where you can swing."
  • "Doors soft, voices low."
  • "Dog into the wind, you behind the dog."
  • These are memory lines made for this course and widely repeated hunter habits, not science.

• Chicken vision and bird hearing studies, Pennsylvania Game Commission, hunting writers. Checked 2026-10-11.

mc-grouse-04:
Why it matters

Grouse are creatures of habit with a few predictable tricks. Read the bird and you know when it will go, where it will land, and why the old ones are hard.

  • A tall neck and a raised crest: the bird is about to go (Tip).
  • Clucks and a fanned tail often come first (Tip).
More: alarm signals
  • Alert posture: neck stretched up, crest raised, head turning; the tail may fan (hunter lore, 60%).
  • Alarm sounds: grouse cluck or "putt" before flushing, say many hunters (hunter lore, 55%: Tip). Exact calls not confirmed (VERIFY).
  • A hen with chicks hisses, fans her tail and ruff, and may run around you or fake a broken wing to lead you off (70%, Macaulay Library recording notes and field accounts).
  • A sooty or blue grouse hen with small chicks clucks, fluffs, droops her wings and may fly at an intruder 65%.
  • In September a bird that walks off fast with a raised crest is not staying (Tip).

• Spruce grouse often sit; ruffed grouse go (75 to 80%).
  • Every grouse gets warier after it is shot at (Tip).
More: what makes the difference
  • Spruce grouse rely on stillness and camouflage and often let people approach closely: the "fool hen" (80%, Idaho Fish and Game).
  • Dusky and sooty grouse are often approachable, especially young birds early in the season (Tip, 60%).
  • Sharp tailed grouse: singles and small groups early in the season are easier; late season flocks flush far and seldom give a second chance (60%, hunting guides).
  • Ruffed grouse: the wary one in most hunters' books (Tip).
  • Habitat counts too: open cover means longer flushes; studies on a European grouse found less visual cover meant longer flush distances 70%.

• Birds near open roads get shot more 75%.
  • Birds farther from roads live longer 75%.
More: the evidence
  • Pennsylvania study: harvest rate was 48% near open roads versus 19% farther away 75%.
  • Male survival was 36% beyond 201 m from roads versus 23% within 201 m 75%.
  • A North Carolina study saw grouse change their movements to avoid areas after flushing and shooting 70%.
  • Hunting pressure did not lower populations in that study's small woodlots from fall to fall 70%.
  • Hinterland Who's Who: most hunted birds are young birds near roads and clearings 85%.
  • Old hand's rule (tradition): "The easy birds live by the road. The good birds live past the first ridge."

• Ruffed: hen raises the brood alone; males live alone 85%.
  • At about 12 weeks the family breaks up and young birds move out 75%.
More: social life, species by species
  • Ruffed grouse males hold a territory for life and drum to claim it (85%, Hinterland Who's Who). Hens range wider and pass through several males' areas 85%.
  • Families break up when the young are about 12 weeks old 75%. Young hens moved about 4.8 km, young males about 2.1 km, over 17 to 21 days in Wisconsin (80%, Small and Rusch 1989).
  • This "fall shuffle" makes young birds restless. Some fly into windows, fences and trees (75%, Pennsylvania Game Commission).
  • Dusky grouse: summer groups of about 6 to 7 (a hen and chicks); winter groups of 15 to 20 seen (65%, Animal Diversity Web).
  • Sharp tailed grouse: males gather on leks to display; in late fall birds bunch into big flocks (60 to 85%).
  • Ptarmigan: in autumn young and adults form small flocks, which can merge (85%, Hinterland Who's Who). Male willow ptarmigan help raise the young, unlike other grouse 85%.

• Early season: mostly naive young birds in the bag 75%.
  • Late season: more adults, who know every escape 75%.
More: the old male
  • Pennsylvania: adults were 34% of the harvest in October, 51% in November, 57% in December 75%.
  • Adult males keep the same territory for life and know every escape route (85% territory; escape routes are hunter lore, Tip).
  • An old bird often flushes wild, at the edge of range, with a tree between you (hunter lore, 60%).
  • Young birds sit longer, fly into the open and land in plain sight (Tip).
  • Old hand's rule (tradition): "September teaches the birds. November tests the hunter."

• They glide a short way and land in a tree 75%.
  • They return to the same food and grit spots (Tip).
More: mistakes you can use
  • Short flight: most ruffed grouse fly under 90 m (100 yd) and land in trees (60 to 75%). Mark the spot and walk straight there.
  • Walking away under an evergreen, then flushing from the far side: circle the tree (Tip, Outdoor Canada).
  • Same spots: grit on the same road edge, dust in the same bowl, drum from the same log again and again (Tip; Hinterland Who's Who notes males hold territories for life, 85%).
  • Young birds in September and October sit on road edges eating clover and grit 75%.
  • Spruce grouse often stay put after the first shot (Tip). Be sure of your species and your bag count before the next.

• Rhyme: "Neck goes tall, bird goes all."
  • Number trick: "12 weeks, then they seek": families split at about 12 weeks.
  • Old hand's rule (tradition): "Mark the tree, go now."
More: more hooks
  • "48 by the road, 19 off it": harvest rates near and away from roads.
  • "Young birds in October, old birds in December."
  • "Fool hen sits, ruffed hen splits."
  • Rhymes are made for this course; the "mark and follow" habit is common advice in grouse hunting writing.

• Pennsylvania Game Commission, Hinterland Who's Who, Small and Rusch 1989, hunting writers. Checked 2026-10-11.

mc-grouse-05:
Why it matters

Where grouse are in October depends on what happened in May. Learn the year once and every season makes sense.

  • Spring: drumming and hooting. June: hatch 80%.
  • Fall: families split, dusky grouse go uphill (75 to 80%).
More: the year in one table
MonthsWhat happensCertainty
Jan, FebBuds and needles, snow roosts, hardest survival75 to 85%
Mar to MayRuffed drum, dusky and sooty hoot, sharp tails dance, spruce strut75 to 85%
May, JunNests; ruffed hatch usually early June85%
Jul, AugChicks grow on insects then plants; adults moult75 to 85%
Sep, OctFamilies split, young birds disperse75 to 80%
Oct, NovDusky and sooty move uphill to dense conifers; ptarmigan turn white70 to 85%
DecWinter food, snow roosts start75%

• Ruffed grouse eat buds; spruce and dusky eat needles (80 to 85%).
  • January to March is when most birds die 75%.
More: winter detail
  • Ruffed grouse: buds and catkins of poplar, aspen, birch and alder (85%, Hinterland Who's Who); aspen flower buds preferred 80%.
  • Spruce grouse: up to 99% conifer needles in the snow season 75%.
  • Dusky grouse: conifer needles, often high in Douglas fir (70 to 75%).
  • Sharp tailed grouse: buds and catkins of deciduous trees and shrubs (85%, BC species account).
  • Ptarmigan: willow, alder and birch buds; white tailed ptarmigan also eat conifer needles 85%.
  • Survival is lowest January to March (75%, Maine study). Monthly survival 80 to 90% then (75%, Pennsylvania).
  • No hunting season in these months for these birds in your regions (99%, Rule Book).

• Ruffed males drum from a log, mostly March to May (75 to 85%).
  • The wings beat the air; they do not hit the log 85%.
More: drumming, every number we found
  • The male stands on a log, braces with his tail and snaps his cupped wings forward and back (85%, Hinterland Who's Who).
  • The beats start slow and speed into a whirr (75%, Pennsylvania Game Commission). About 50 beats in about 8 to 10 seconds (65%, Nova Scotia and Saltscapes accounts).
  • The sound is very low, under 100 Hz 70%, and can be heard about 400 m or more in thick woods (60 to 70%). How far depends on which way the bird faces (70%, Archibald 1974).
  • Peak drumming is in spring; in one study the peak was mid April 80%. Pennsylvania gives March and April 75%.
  • Males also drum in fall (85%, Hinterland Who's Who) and a little all year 65%.
  • Why: to warn off other males and draw hens 85%.
  • Field use: in April, listen at dawn from a quiet road and map every drummer. Those territories hold birds in October (Tip).

• Dusky and sooty hoot; spruce struts and claps; sharp tails dance (65 to 85%).
More: each display
  • Dusky grouse: males inflate neck air sacs and give deep owl like hoots, heard up to about 400 m (75%, Idaho Fish and Game). The sound is so low you may feel it before you hear it 60%. Hooting runs late March to mid July 65%.
  • Sooty grouse: males hoot from high in a conifer, a run of about six deep hoots that can carry about 800 m 65%.
  • Dusky grouse leave the high country in late March or early April for breeding ground lower down (70%, Colorado Parks and Wildlife).
  • Spruce grouse: males strut with red combs up and tail fanned, then make a short flight that ends in two loud wing claps (65 to 75%).
  • Sharp tailed grouse: males dance on a lek at dawn, stamp their feet, rattle their tails and show pink neck sacs 85%. Lek calls carry up to 1.5 km (85%, BC species account). Leks are used for many years if left undisturbed 85%.
  • Ptarmigan males display with red combs: willow gargle, rock snore, white tailed scream (85%, Hinterland Who's Who).
  • Respect: disturbance at leks can make hens abandon them 85%. Watch from far away.

• Ruffed: 7 to 12 eggs, hatch usually early June 85%.
  • Chicks leave the nest within a day 85%.
More: nests, eggs and chicks
  • Ruffed grouse: 7 to 12 eggs, incubation 23 to 24 days, hatch usually early June (85%, Hinterland Who's Who). Pennsylvania gives 6 to 16 eggs, about 24 days 75%.
  • Spruce grouse: clutches average 4.8 in Alberta, the Franklin's form 75%. Median hatch there about 29 June 75%. Chicks fly short hops at about 6 days 75%.
  • Dusky grouse: about 7 to 9 eggs on average 65%, chicks hatch late May to early June 65%.
  • Sharp tailed grouse: first clutch at 11 months old, average 12.8 eggs, one brood a year, often renest if the nest fails (85%, BC species account). Most nests within 1.6 km of a lek 85%.
  • Ptarmigan: 5 to 14 eggs, about 3 weeks 85%. Chicks fly clumsily at about a week 85%.
  • Only the hen sits on the eggs in ruffed grouse 75%. Male willow ptarmigan stay and help 85%.

• Chicks eat insects first, then leaves, flowers and berries 85%.
  • Adults moult their flight feathers (75 to 85%).
More: summer detail
  • Ruffed chicks eat insects first; by August flowers, soft leaves, berries and seeds; clover is a favourite (85%, Hinterland Who's Who).
  • Chicks make low, buzzy flights in week 1 and fly well by week 3 75%.
  • Yearling plumage by 16 to 17 weeks 85%.
  • Adults moult once a year: Hinterland Who's Who says from June, Pennsylvania July into September (75 to 85%).
  • Dusky grouse males leave breeding areas by mid July for high forest with huckleberry (70%, Colorado Parks and Wildlife).
  • Dog training on game birds under supervision is allowed from 1 August (99%, Rule Book).
Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

• Broods break up; young birds wander 75%.
  • Region 3: youth 1 to 9 Sept, everyone from 10 Sept 99%.
More: September detail and dates
  • Families split at about 12 weeks; young birds disperse over 2 to 3 weeks, hens farther than males (75 to 80%).
  • Restless young birds turn up in odd places, roads and yards 75%.
  • Region 3, MUs (Management Units) 3-12 to 3-20 and 3-26 to 3-44: youth only (under 18) 1 to 9 September; general 10 September to 30 November (99%, Rule Book).
  • Region 3 ptarmigan: 1 September to 30 November 99%.
  • Region 2: bow only 1 to 9 September; general 10 September to 15 December (99%, Rule Book).
  • Region 8: youth 1 to 9 September; general 10 September to 30 November; bow only 1 to 10 December (99%, Rule Book).
  • Sharp tailed grouse, Region 3, MUs 3-30 and 3-31: 10 September to 30 November 99%.
Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

• October: young birds on edges, clover and berries 75%.
  • November: birds tighter in conifers, dusky high, snow tells all (70 to 80%).
More: what changes, week by week
  • Early October: leaves still up, short shots. Young birds feed on road edges and cut blocks 75%.
  • Fall drumming: you may hear ruffed males drum on calm October mornings (85% that they drum in fall; timing Tip).
  • Dusky and sooty grouse move uphill into dense conifers and switch to needles (70 to 75%). Some travel tens of kilometres; most much less 70%.
  • Sharp tailed grouse move to deciduous cover, berries, then buds; late flocks get big and wild (60 to 85%).
  • Ptarmigan are mostly white by mid October 85%, easy to see on brown rock before snow and hard to see after (Tip).
  • First snows: grouse sit in conifers and leave tracks (Tip).
  • By late November more of the birds left are adults 75%.
  • Region 3 and Region 8 seasons close 30 November; Region 2 runs to 15 December 99%.
  • Old hand's rule (tradition): "Leaves down, birds up": after leaf fall you see farther and get more open shots.
• Snow roosts start once snow is soft and deep enough (70 to 75%).

• Region 2 open to 15 Dec; Region 8 bow only 1 to 10 Dec 99%.
More: December detail
  • Ruffed grouse dive into snow about 20 to 40 cm deep to roost (70 to 75%).
  • Hard crust or thin snow pushes birds into thick conifers 85%.
  • Region 2 grouse: open to 15 December 99%. Region 8: bow only 1 to 10 December 99%. Region 3: closed after 30 November 99%.
Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

• Rhyme: "April drums, June chicks come, September splits, December's numb."
  • Number trick: "7 to 12 eggs, 24 days": ruffed clutch and incubation.
  • Old hand's rule (tradition): "Find the drummer in April, find the bird in October."
More: more hooks
  • "Dusky goes up when the leaves come down."
  • "12 weeks to split, 3 weeks to fly."
  • "Season 10 to 30": Region 3 opens 10 September, closes 30 November.
  • "Ptarmigan white by mid October."
  • The drummer rule is widely repeated grouse hunting advice; rhymes are made for this course.

• Hinterland Who's Who, Pennsylvania Game Commission, BC species account, Rule Book. Checked 2026-10-11.

  • Pennsylvania Game Commission, Ruffed grouse, read directly 75%.
  • BC species account, Columbian Sharp tailed Grouse, read directly 85%.
  • Idaho Fish and Game 75% and Wild About Utah 60%, read directly.
  • Archibald 1974, The Auk 91 and drumming peak study (Southeastern Association of Fish and Wildlife Agencies), search preview (70 to 80%).
  • Nova Scotia and Saltscapes drumming accounts, search preview 65%.
  • Spruce grouse clutch and hatch: The Condor 77 papers, search preview 75%.
  • Colorado Parks and Wildlife, dusky grouse; Audubon, dusky grouse, read 2026-10-03 70%.

  • Animal Diversity Web, dusky grouse, read directly 65%.

mc-grouse-06:
Why it matters

The same patch of bush can be empty at noon and full at 4 pm. Time and weather move grouse as much as habitat does.

  • Feed early and late, rest midday, roost at night (hunter lore, 75%).
  • Legal: 1 hour before sunrise to 1 hour after sunset 99%.
More: the day, with the evidence level for each claim
ClaimEvidenceCertainty
Feed early morning and late afternoonAgency and hunter accounts75%
Pick grit and dust on road edgesAgency accounts, sign75%
Rest and dust bathe middayHunter accounts70%
Spruce and dusky sit in trees middayHunter accounts65%
Roost in trees, ground or snow at nightAgency accounts75%
Adults move only a few hundred metres a dayPennsylvania Game Commission75%
  • Hours rule: "To hunt game, except migratory game birds from one hour after sunset to one hour before sunrise" is unlawful (99%, item 38, Rule Book).
Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

• First light to mid morning: edges, trails, road shoulders 75%.
  • They need grit for the gizzard 85%.
More: morning detail
  • Grouse pick small gravel to grind food in the gizzard 85%. Road edges and trails supply it 75%.
  • Young birds in September and October feed on clover and berries along road edges and cut blocks (65 to 75%).
  • Sharp tailed grouse use roadsides and landings with clover, dandelion and yarrow heavily in fall (85%, BC species account).
  • Roads are also where the rules bite. See How to hunt before you hunt a road edge.
  • Tip: walk an old closed road or a trail away from traffic at first light.

• Birds loaf in cover and dust bathe 70%.
  • The best time to still hunt sitters with the .22 (Tip).
More: midday detail
  • Dust bathing: shallow bowls in dry dirt on road edges and banks, used to clean feathers 80%.
  • Spruce grouse spend fall and winter days up in conifers (80%, Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife, earlier lesson).
  • Dusky grouse sit in big Douglas fir (Tip).
  • Tip: slow down at midday; look up, not ahead.

• Last 2 hours of light: birds feed again (hunter lore, 70%).
  • Legal light ends 1 hour after sunset 99%.
More: evening detail
  • Late afternoon feeding mirrors the morning: edges, berries, clover, buds 70%.
  • In bitter cold, some hunters see birds feed in the warmest hours, about 1 to 4 pm (hunter account, 50%: Tip).
  • Roost: in trees (often conifers), on the ground, or under soft snow 75%.
  • Thermals sink in the evening, so a dog working uphill gets scent from above (Tip).
  • Shooting light fades fast in timber; your watch says legal, the woods may say no (Tip).

• Wind and rain move birds into shelter (hunter lore, 55 to 60%: Tip).
  • No grouse study found on pressure fronts or the moon.
More: each weather type, with evidence
WeatherWhat birds doEvidence
Strong windWild, flush early; shelter in low, thick coverHunter lore (Tip)
RainUnder middle aged conifersHunter lore (Tip)
Calm overcastMoving and feeding; good huntingHunter lore (Tip)
Fresh soft snowSnow roosts; tracks show everything70 to 75%
Crust, deep coldInto thick conifers; weight loss85%
Falling pressure, cold frontNo grouse study foundVERIFY
Moon phaseNo grouse study foundVERIFY
  • Hunting magazine and blog advice says calm overcast days are best and windy days make grouse skittish (55 to 60%).
  • Keep your own record in the Journal: date, weather, flushes. Your data beats lore (Tip).
  • See also Weather and the moon for deer.

• Birds close to open roads get shot more 75%.
  • Walk past 200 m from the road (Tip, based on the study).
More: detail
  • Pennsylvania: 48% harvest rate near open roads versus 19% farther away; male survival 23% within 201 m of roads versus 36% beyond 75%.
  • Opening weekend and the first snow bring the most hunters (Tip).
  • Weekday mornings on gated roads see the least traffic (Tip).
  • The flip side: birds far from roads are less shot, not less wary (Tip).

• Rhyme: "Gravel at dawn, dust at noon, berries at dusk, roost by the moon."
  • Number trick: "1 and 1": 1 hour before sunrise to 1 hour after sunset.
  • Old hand's rule (tradition): "Wind day, low and thick. Rain day, under the firs."
More: more hooks
  • "Look up at noon."
  • "200 m past the road."
  • "No study on the moon": do not plan around it.
  • Rhymes are made for this course; the wind and rain rules are common hunter advice, not science.

mc-grouse-07:
Why it matters

Each grouse lives in a band of the mountain with its own trees and foods. Find the band, find the food, find the bird.

  • Grass, aspen, fir, spruce, alpine: one grouse for each (80 to 85%).

More: the bands with numbers
  • Sharp tailed grouse: grassland and open forest, breeding at 275 to 1,190 m in BC (85%, BC species account).
  • Ruffed grouse: most abundant at 750 to 1,250 m, aspen and poplar near water (85%, BC Breeding Bird Atlas).
  • Dusky grouse: breed mainly in Douglas fir and spruce fir zones, many seen at 1,500 to 2,250 m, but breeding at 500 to 1,250 m is not uncommon 85%.
  • Spruce grouse: conifer forest with spruce or lodgepole pine, recorded up to 2,500 m 85%.
  • White tailed ptarmigan: alpine, breeding at 1,830 to 2,650 m in the Interior 85%.

• Young forest under about 20 years, aspen, creek bottoms (75 to 85%).
  • Edges where two kinds of cover meet (Tip).
More: food and cover through the year
  • Young forest less than 20 years old gives food, hiding cover and shelter (75%, Pennsylvania Game Commission).
  • Aspen, poplar, birch and alder near water 85%. Aspen flower buds are the top winter food 80%.
  • Fall foods: berries, clover, leaves and seeds 85%. Fruit is over a quarter of the adult diet 65%.
  • Winter roosts under conifers when snow is poor (75 to 85%).
  • Home range a few hectares; adults rarely move more than a few hundred metres a day (75 to 85%).

• Dense spruce, fir and lodgepole pine (80 to 85%).
  • On the ground in summer, up in the trees from late fall 80%.
More: food and cover
  • Conifer specialist: needles of pine or spruce, especially in winter 85%.
  • Summer and fall: green shoots, leaves, berries, flowers and insects (75%, Idaho Fish and Game).
  • Mostly on the ground from late spring to early autumn, then up in the trees eating needles (80%, Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife).
  • Some move up to about 9.5 km between summer and winter range 70%.
  • East of the Coast Mountains in BC 85%.

• Summer: open edges, even sagebrush. Fall: uphill into dense conifers (70 to 75%).
  • Sooty grouse on the coast winter high in conifers 65%.
More: food and cover
  • Breeding season: forest edges and openings; insects, green plants and berries (75%, Idaho Fish and Game).
  • Summer berries: blueberry, huckleberry, chokecherry, gooseberry; grasshoppers 65%.
  • Autumn: most birds move from open breeding areas to dense conifer forest, usually uphill (70%, Audubon). Maximum known travel about 48 km (30 miles) 70%.
  • Winter: fir and Douglas fir needles, perched high in the trees (65 to 75%).
  • Sooty grouse: winter in dense conifers, often higher than their breeding ground; sources disagree in places, so treat direction as likely, not certain (55 to 65%, VERIFY near Mission).

• Grassland with shrubs, aspen and water birch draws 85%.
  • Region 3: only MUs (Management Units) 3-30 and 3-31 99%.
More: food, cover and the rule
  • Key grassland foods in BC: snowberry, rose and dandelion; browse on water birch, trembling aspen, saskatoon and chokecherry (85%, BC species account).
  • Birds in clearcuts use kinnikinnick, juniper, prickly rose and scrub birch 85%.
  • Fall: roadsides and landings with clover, dandelion and yarrow are used heavily 85%.
  • Winter: riparian draws with buds, catkins and berries 85%. Late fall and winter birds may feed high in aspens and birches (75%, Alaska Department of Fish and Game).
  • Rule: "SHARP-TAILED GROUSE | 3-30, 3-31 | Sept 10 - Nov 30 | 5 (10)", and no open season in the part of 3-30 south of the Scottie Creek Forest Service Road, Map C18 (99%, Rule Book).

mc-grouse-08:
Why it matters

Grouse leave small clues everywhere they live. Read them and you hunt where birds are today, not where they were last year.

  • Three long toes forward, one short toe back, about 5 cm 75%.
  • One line, one print in front of the next (75 to 80%).
More: tracks in detail
  • Forest grouse tracks are about 5 cm long: three forward toes and a short hind toe (75%, Elbroch and Marks, Bird Tracks and Sign).
  • In winter ruffed grouse grow comb like toe edges (pectinations), so prints look wider and fringed 85%.
  • Ptarmigan feet are feathered; in snow the print can look fuzzy, with toes hard to see (Tip, 65%).
  • A walking grouse leaves a line of prints, one ahead of the next, gently zig zag 80%.
  • Where tracks end in a spray of wing marks, the bird flew 75%.
  • Hare tracks look very different: see the diagram below.

• Fibrous, curved, pencil thick, white tipped 85%.
  • A pile means a roost or a drum log (75 to 85%).
More: what droppings tell you
  • Normal droppings: long curved cylinders about pencil thick, fibrous and pale tan, with white uric acid (85%, Hinterland Who's Who). Often 2.5 to 4 cm long (70%, Northern Woodlands).
  • Caecal droppings: soft, dark, tar like, from the ceca, passed less often (70%, Elbroch and Marks via Laura Erickson).
  • Fresh caecal droppings are green and turn black quickly in the sun; they break down in days to weeks (65%, Wyoming Game and Fish, sage grouse).
  • Pile under a tree: night roost 75%. Pile on one spot of a log: drum stand 85%.
  • What is in them: needles mean conifer feeding, berry seeds mean a berry patch (Tip).

• Shallow scrapes in dry dirt, a few feathers 80%.
  • Clipped clover and dropped berries on an edge at dawn (Tip).
More: more sign
  • Dust bowls sit in dry, loose dirt on road edges, banks and root holes 80%.
  • Single small body feathers near a bowl or under a roost tree are normal moult or preening (Tip).
  • A burst of feathers with no bird: a hawk or owl kill (Tip). Goshawks and great horned owls take adult ruffed grouse 85%.
  • Feeding sign: clover leaves clipped short, kinnikinnick or rose hips missing from a patch, aspen buds snipped in winter (Tip).
  • Bits knocked from trees onto snow show birds feeding overhead (75%, Canadian Wildlife Federation).

• Hole, short tunnel, second hole with wing marks (75 to 80%).
  • Wing marks on both sides: the bird has left 75%.
More: reading a roost
  • Grouse fly straight into soft snow, so there may be no tracks leading in 75%.
  • Inside: a small chamber, often with a pile of droppings from the night 75%.
  • Exit hole with wing prints on the snow beside it: the bird burst out 75%.
  • An entry hole with no exit: the bird may still be inside. Be ready (Tip, 60%).
  • Snow roost sign needs soft snow about 20 cm or deeper (70 to 75%).

• Big mossy log, open floor, cover overhead, droppings on one spot 85%.
  • A spring drum log means a male lives here year round 85%.
More: using drum logs
  • The drum stand is often a big moss covered log at a forest edge 85%. Stumps, boulders and mounds are used too 75%.
  • A Minnesota study recorded at least 593 logs used by drumming males 75%.
  • The male holds that territory for life 85%. Find his log in April, hunt that patch in October (Tip).
  • Do not disturb drumming birds in spring: no season then, and it is the breeding time (99% no season; respect Tip).

mc-grouse-09:
Why it matters

Grouse hunting is simple: walk the right cover slowly and be ready. The skill is in the details, and the rules are strict on roads.

  • Two tools: shotgun for flushing birds, .22 for sitting birds (95% legal; Tip on use).
  • Every method below is legal in BC as written 99%.
More: legal tools for grouse
Legal Hunting Methods table, page 13, row "Upland Game Birds"

Air rifle "Yes", Rimfire "Yes" with note 2, Centrefire "Yes" with note 3, Shotgun "Yes", Archery "Bow B, C, D". Note 2: "Grouse, ptarmigan, or turkey only." Note 3: "Grouse or ptarmigan only."

  • So your CZ 457 .22 and your 12 gauge are both legal for grouse and ptarmigan (99%, Rule Book).
  • Handguns are not legal for hunting; nor are full metal jacket rifle bullets (99%, Rule Book).
  • Unleashed dogs are allowed for small game, grouse included (99%, Rule Book).
  • Lead shot is legal for grouse; it is banned for ducks and geese 99%.
Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

▶How to Hunt Ruffed Grouse: Key Tips for Success in the WoodsFind young forest, edges and food. That is where grouse are.
Pheasants Forever and Quail Forever , YouTube, 6 min. Needs internet.
  • April: listen for drummers at dawn (Tip).
  • Summer: note broods on roads; fall: walk with no gun first (Tip).
More: a scouting year
  • April and May: drive or walk quiet roads at dawn, stop every few hundred metres, listen for drums and dusky hoots. Mark each on the Hunt Map (Tip). Drums carry about 400 m (60 to 70%).
  • June to August: hen and brood sightings on roads mean a good fall nearby (Tip).
  • September: walk one Forest Service road edge at first light with no gun. Count birds, note time, tree type and height (Tip).
  • Map work: young cut blocks, aspen draws, creek bottoms, berry slopes; then plan a loop away from traffic (Tip). See Where they are.
  • Check the MU, season, closures and private land layers every time (99% rules).

• Walk slow along edges, stop every 20 to 30 steps (Tip).
  • Stop beside an opening with room to swing (Tip).
More: step by step
  1. Pick an edge: aspen against conifer, a cut block margin, a creek bottom, an old road through young forest (Tip).
  2. Walk with the wind in your face or across it so your noise goes behind you (Tip).
  3. Gun at ready, safety on, finger off the trigger (Tip; safety habit).
  4. Every 20 to 30 steps stop for 10 to 20 seconds. Many flushes come during the stop (hunter lore, 60%).
  5. When a bird flushes: mount, swing, shoot only with sky or dirt behind and no person in front (Tip). Next screen.
  6. Miss or no shot: mark where it lands and follow up (Tip).
  • Pros: legal, simple, all forest grouse. Cons: snap shots, many misses at first.
  • Old hand's rule (tradition): "Hunt slow enough to be bored."

Head shot with the .22 in 4 steps1 of 4
  • Legal for grouse and ptarmigan only 99%.
  • Head or nothing: the breast is the meat (Tip).
More: the full rimfire method and rules
  • Rule: rimfire for upland birds is legal only for grouse, ptarmigan and turkey, so never for quail, pheasant or partridge (99%, page 13 note 2).
  • Rule: no full metal jacket bullets in a rifle 99%. Tip: carry hollow point .22 LR (Long Rifle) hunting loads; whether plated round nose counts as full metal jacket: VERIFY.
  • Rule: 400 m single projectile bands along listed highways (for example Hwy 5, the Coquihalla, Hope to Kamloops) ban your .22 there; shotgun with shot is allowed past the road allowance (99%, Rule Book). Hwy 5 north of Kamloops past Heffley Creek is not on that list (95%, my reading).
  • Rule: no shooting within 100 m of an occupied house or farm building, school, church, playground or regional district park (99%, Rule Book).
  • Range: hunters who use .22s on grouse keep head shots short; inside about 25 m (27 yd) is a sensible limit for most shooters (Tip, 55 to 60%). Practise on a 2.5 cm target at that range before the season (Tip).
  • Aim point: the head, or the base of the neck if the head bobs (Tip, hunter advice).
  • Backstop: a .22 bullet can fly over 1 km. Only shoot with dirt behind the bird; never at a bird on a skyline branch (Tip; safety). See Backstop.
  • Ethics: shooting a sitting grouse is legal. Some hunters see it as less sporting; it is also the cleanest meat (opinion).
  • Spruce grouse often stay put after a shot; count your bag by species before the next shot (99% bag rules, Tip).
Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

• Lead 6 or 7.5 shot, improved cylinder choke (Tip, 60%).
  • Most shots are close and fast: under about 25 m (Tip).
More: loads, chokes and the swing
  • Load: 12 gauge, 28 to 32 g (1 to 1 1/8 oz) of No. 7.5 or No. 6 lead. No. 7.5 is the most common grouse load; No. 6 for later, bigger birds like dusky (60%, Project Upland; app gear notes 65%).
  • Lead is legal for grouse 99%. If you also carry steel for ducks: steel 6 works on grouse (Tip).
  • Choke: improved cylinder for close cover; modified for open country, sharp tails and late season 60%.
  • Swing: start the bead behind the bird, move through it, shoot as the bead passes the beak, keep moving (Tip). See Shotgun skills.
  • Most ruffed grouse shots come inside about 25 m through trees (Tip).
  • Safety: low bird, no shot. Never swing toward a partner (Tip). See the video below.
  • Old hand's rule (tradition): "Shoot where the bird is going, not where the bird was."
▶Shooting Tip: Three Different LeadsThree lead methods. Pick one and practise it.
Ducks Unlimited, YouTube, 1 min. Needs internet.

• Partner: one walks the cover, one waits at the end (Tip).
  • Dog: unleashed is legal for grouse 99%.
More: working with your brother and a dog
  • Walker and blocker: the walker pushes along a draw or hedgerow; the blocker stands in the open just past the end, never facing back into the cover (Tip).
  • Each hunter owns a zone of fire and never swings past it (Tip). Talk often so you always know where the other is (Tip).
  • Orange on both hunters in thick cover (Tip).
  • Dogs: "Unleashed dogs may be used to hunt small game" 99%. Training on game birds under supervision: 1 August to 30 April (99%, Rule Book).
  • Flushing breeds (spaniels, labs) push birds up in range; pointing breeds hold them while you walk in (Tip).
  • Work the dog into the wind (Tip). See The senses.
  • A dog finds wounded birds you would lose (Tip).
• No hunting from a vehicle, no loaded gun in it 99%.

• No shooting or hunting in the road allowance of covered roads 99%.
More: the exact Rule Book words
Highway No Shooting or Hunting Areas, page 10

"It is unlawful to discharge a firearm across or to discharge a firearm or hunt within the road allowances of all numbered highways and any two lane or greater public road in B.C. that is maintained by the Ministry of Transportation and Infrastructure (or their contractors), the federal government or another province or territory. The road allowance extends:" "(a) 15 m on either side of the middle of a road with less than three lanes, or" "(b) 15 m from the edge of the paved surface of a highway with three lanes or more, or" "(c) to the boundary of private or cultivated land," "whichever comes first."

Item 22, page 11

"To hunt wildlife from a motor vehicle."

Item 28, page 11

"To discharge, carry or have in possession a firearm containing live ammunition in its breech or in its magazine attached to the firearm, in or on a railway car, motor vehicle, sleigh, aircraft, bicycle or other conveyance."

ATV on a Forest Service Road

"While travelling on a Forest Service Road, operators of ATVs are required to hold a valid driver's licence and carry a minimum of $200,000 third-party liability insurance."

  • Plain English: on numbered highways and two lane or wider public roads kept by the Ministry of Transportation and Infrastructure, its contractors, the federal government or another province or territory, you may not shoot across, shoot within, or hunt within the road allowance (99%, Rule Book).
  • Every road, every vehicle: no hunting from it (item 22) and no loaded firearm in or on it (item 28) (99%, Rule Book).
  • (Forest Service Road): kept by the Ministry of Forests, not Transportation. The quick lesson reads the road allowance wording as not naming FSRs (70%, interpretation): VERIFY with a conservation officer. Items 22 and 28 apply there too 99%.
  • ATV (All Terrain Vehicle) on an FSR: valid driver's licence and at least $200,000 third party liability insurance (99%, Rule Book).
  • Region 3 above 1,700 m: motor vehicles except snowmobiles only on existing roads and trails (99%, Rule Book). Check the Motor vehicle closures layer 99%.
  • Safe habit on every road, FSR included (Tip): stop, engine off, unload check, walk out past 15 m from the middle and off the road surface, then load; never shoot along or across the road.
Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

• Sharp tails: walk grass and shrub draws; late flocks flush far 60%.
  • Ptarmigan: glass first, climb high, light gun (Tip).
More: how each hunt works

Sharp tailed grouse (MUs 3-30 and 3-31 only)

  • Early season: singles, pairs and small family groups hold closer 60%.
  • Late season: big flocks that flush at sight; a modified choke helps 60%.
  • In fall they feed on roadsides and landings rich in clover and dandelion, then in berry draws 85%; in late fall some feed high in aspen and birch 75%.
  • Not in the part of 3-30 south of the Scottie Creek Forest Service Road, Map C18 99%.
  • Bag 5 a day, 10 in possession (99%, Rule Book).

Ptarmigan

  • Glass rocky slopes and willow basins; their camouflage is excellent, so look for movement (Tip, 60%).
  • Fitness and weather: alpine hunts are long climbs with early snow (Tip).
  • A light shotgun is easier to carry; your .22 is legal too (99% legal; Tip).
  • Region 3 ptarmigan: 5 a day, 15 in possession, 1 September to 30 November in MUs 3-12 to 3-20 and 3-26 to 3-44 99%.
  • Sun Peaks: no hunting or shooting within 400 m of lifts, runs and buildings 99%.
Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

• Weather and season pick the cover (Tip).
  • Walk past the road band, follow every flush (Tip, 75% study basis).
More: what a 40 year hunter does differently (hunter wisdom, opinion)
  • Hunts the edges and the thick young stuff, not open timber (classic grouse hunting advice).
  • Walks slower than feels right and stops often (common advice).
  • Walks away from roads: the Pennsylvania road data backs this 75%.
  • Marks every flush and follows up at once (common advice).
  • Circles lone evergreens and blowdowns (Outdoor Canada tip).
  • Opens crops and hunts the food they show (common practice).
  • Keeps a log: date, weather, where birds were. Over years that log is the "40 years of knowledge" (Tip).
  • Passes on shots with no safe background, every time (safety).
  • Knows the bag by species before the second bird (99% rule).

mc-grouse-10:
Why it matters

A clean shot, a fast follow up and cold meat make grouse one of the best meals in the bush. The rules on wings and breasts travel with you all the way home.

  • .22: head or upper neck. Shotgun: pattern on the head and front (Tip, 70%).
  • All the vitals are in the front half 80%.
More: shot placement and range
  • Brain, spine, heart and lungs sit in the head, neck and front of the body 80%. See The body.
  • .22 head shots: inside about 25 m (27 yd) for most shooters, with a rest and a dirt backstop (Tip, 55 to 60%).
  • Shotgun: most grouse shots are inside about 25 m; improved cylinder and No. 7.5 or 6 lead (Tip, 60%).
  • Big game vitals diagrams do not apply to birds; see Shot placement for deer.

• Keep your eyes on the spot, pick a mark, walk straight there (Tip).
  • A head shot bird may flap hard on the ground; that is a reflex (Tip, 60%).
More: reactions and recovery
  • A grouse hit hard falls straight; a wing hit glides or drops and runs (Tip).
  • A runner hides under logs, brush and roots. Search slowly in growing circles from the mark (Tip).
  • A dog finds wounded birds you will not (Tip).
  • Feathers floating but the bird flew on: watch it out of sight; hit birds often land and stay down (Tip).
  • Reload, then go. Do not stop to celebrate (Tip).
  • Dispatch a live bird quickly and humanely; ask an experienced hunter to show you (Tip).

Grouse field care1 of 4
  • Cool fast; heat spoils birds 80%.
  • One feathered wing stays attached 99%.
More: the care details
  • Remove the entrails and the crop soon after the kill; food in the crop can sour (80%, Clemson Cooperative Extension).
  • Cool quickly; above 4 C (40 F) is the main threat to meat quality 80%.
  • Wipe the cavity with a clean cloth or paper towel, not grass or snow 80%.
  • Air around each bird; in hot weather bag each one and keep it on ice; no warm birds piled together 80%.
  • Transport in a cooler; if none, a ventilated car interior, not the trunk 80%.
  • Note species, MU (Management Unit), date and time in the Journal: Region 3 bag limits are per species 99%.
Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

• One feathered wing stays attached until home 99%.
  • Both breasts are edible portions: take them home 99%.
More: the exact words
Possession and Transportation, Game Birds, page 15

"Anyone who possesses or transports a game bird, other than a migratory game bird, must leave attached to the carcass one feathered wing and for turkey, also the beard, if harvested during a bearded turkey only season."

Definitions, page 3

"EDIBLE PORTIONS - ... with respect to game birds, means the edible portions of both breasts of the bird."

  • Breasting in the field: keep the wing attached to the breast you carry (85%, my reading in the Rule Book).
  • Item 44: you must take the edible portions to your home, a meat cutter or a cold storage plant (99%, Rule Book).
  • Possession while hunting or going home: 3 times the daily limit; sharp tailed grouse in Region 3: 2 times (99%, Rule Book).
Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

• A ruffed grouse gives about 200 to 280 g of meat (Tip, 60%).
  • Cook to 74 C (165 F) in the thickest part 80%.
More: cooking notes
  • Fridge at 4 C or colder, use within 3 days; freeze at -18 C (0 F), use within 6 months (80%, Clemson).
  • Food safety guidance for game birds: 74 C (165 F), checked with a thermometer, since colour is not reliable (80%, extension services citing USDA, the United States Department of Agriculture).
  • Grouse breast is lean white meat that dries out fast; many cooks brine it, wrap it, or cook it in a sauce so it stays moist at a safe temperature (Tip).
  • Spruce grouse on a needle diet in late fall can taste of pine; brine or braise (Tip).
  • Pluck for roasting, skin for speed; the legs are small but worth it (Tip).
  • Pick out shot pellets; a pellet hole that looks dark can carry feather bits (Tip).
