mc-quail-01:
Why it matters

A covey goes up in one second. You name the bird by its plume, its face and its size before the gun moves, or you do not shoot.

  • Three small upland birds share the South Okanagan: quail, chukar and gray partridge 85%.
  • Quail is the smallest: 140 to 230 g 75%.
More: what this Masterclass covers
  • Ten chapters, one per session: the bird, the body, the senses, the mind, the year, the day, where they live, sign, how to hunt, and shot to table with the rules.
  • The quick version stays: Quail, chukar, partridge, pheasant and Your first quail trip.
  • Each chapter ends with memory hooks and a 5 question quiz. Chapter 10 has the one page cheat sheet.
  • Focus: California quail in the South Okanagan, Region 8. Chukar and gray partridge get their own screens where you might meet them.
  • Rules are only what the app's Rule Book says. This Masterclass adds no new rules.

• Curled black plume, black face rimmed in white 80%.
  • Scaled belly with a chestnut patch, white streaks on the sides 80%.
More: male marks in full
  • Length 24 to 27 cm, wingspan 32 to 37 cm, weight 140 to 230 g (75%, Audubon).
  • The male's plume is six feathers that curl forward like a comma (85%, BC Breeding Bird Atlas).
  • Male: black face and throat edged with white, buff forehead, brown cap, blue grey breast, scaled belly with a chestnut centre patch 80%.
  • Sides: grey brown with white streaks 80%.
  • He walks with a nodding head, often in the open next to cover (75%, Audubon).

• Both sexes carry a plume. Hers is smaller and brown 80%.
  • She has no black face and no white rim 80%.
More: female marks in full
  • Female: grey brown head and back, no black and white face, smaller plume, the same scaled belly (80%, Audubon and Edgewood notes).
  • In a flushing covey you rarely see the face. Sex does not matter for the bag in Region 8: the row is "QUAIL", 10 a day (99%, Rule Book).
  • Tip: on the ground, count black faces to guess how many cocks are in a covey.

• In fall, most of a covey are young of the year 60%.
  • Buff tips on the wing coverts mark a young bird 70%.
More: aging in full
  • Juvenile California quail keep buff coloured upper primary coverts and pointed outer flight feathers until their first full moult (70%, 1963 Condor aging study, search preview).
  • Hunters across North America use the buff covert tips to age quail of every species (60%, Project Upland, search preview).
  • Many young in your bag means a good hatch. A New Zealand study used the young share of the bag as an index of breeding success (65%, search preview).
  • By October the young look like small, dull females (Tip, 65%, from the quick lesson).

Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

  • Straight plume? Mountain quail. No open season 99%.
  • Brown bird with a long tail? Hen pheasant. Never legal 99%.
More: look alikes in full
  • Mountain quail: long straight plume, chestnut throat, broad white bars on red brown sides (80%, Audubon). The Rule Book: "No open season on mountain quail." Region 1, page 21 99%.
  • The Region 8 row says only "QUAIL". Whether it covers mountain quail: VERIFY. Shoot California quail only (Tip, from the Region 8 Rule Book).
  • Chukar and gray partridge: legal in Regions 3 and 8 99%. Pheasant: cocks only, Regions 2, 3 and 8 99%.
  • Grouse flush from the same draws in September and October. Different rows, different limits (99%, Rule Book).

• 538 to 765 g, red bill and legs, black necklace 75%.
  • Sexes look alike. Young are duller 75%.
More: chukar marks in full
  • Length 34 to 38 cm, wingspan about 51 cm (75%, Audubon).
  • Sandy brown back, grey breast, buff belly. A black band runs from the forehead through the eye and down to a necklace around a cream throat 75%.
  • Flanks: bold vertical bars of black, white and chestnut. Bill, legs and eye ring coral red 75%.
  • Males are a little heavier. Juveniles are mottled grey brown without the sharp head and flank pattern 75%.
  • Call: a loud, fast "chuck chuck chukar" from the rocks 75%.
  • Native to Asia. BC is the only Canadian province where it took hold (65%, BC Outdoors).

• Orange face, chestnut horseshoe, rusty tail in flight 75%.
  • 300 to 500 g. Flushes with a cackle 75%.
More: gray partridge marks in full
  • Length 30 to 33 cm, wingspan 50 to 56 cm (75%, Audubon).
  • Grey below, orange face and throat, chestnut belly patch, rusty outer tail feathers that flash on the flush 75%.
  • The chestnut patch is smaller on the female 75%.
  • Call: a hoarse "kee ah"; a rapid cackle when flushed 75%.
  • The synopsis spells it "GRAY (Hungarian) PARTRIDGE" 99%. Hunters say .

• Quail 140 to 230 g. Hun 300 to 500 g. Chukar 538 to 765 g 75%.
  • A quail is about the weight of a cup of water (Tip).
More: why size matters
  • On the flush, size and wingbeat help name the bird: a quail is half a Hun and a third of a chukar (75%, from Audubon weights).
  • Small bird, small shot: lead 7.5 or 8 are standard for quail (75%, Washington Fish and Wildlife). See chapter 10.
  • About 160 g is a typical BC quail (65%, BC Outdoors).

• Introduced to BC between 1860 and 1912 85%.
  • Two main areas: the Okanagan and Kettle valleys, and southeast Vancouver Island 85%.
More: history, numbers and trend
  • California quail were released on the coast and in the southern Interior between 1860 and 1912, from a native range in California and Baja California (85%, BC Breeding Bird Atlas).
  • Earliest Okanagan record: 1912 (70%, Lewin 1965, The Condor, search preview). The Okanagan birds may also have come north from releases in northern Washington (60%, iNFOnews).
  • The atlas (2008 to 2012) found the Fraser Valley population apparently gone 85%. So no quail near Mission.
  • Breeding Bird Survey trend for BC, 1970 to 2012: up about 5.8% a year, low reliability (85% that this is what the atlas reports).
  • The increase comes mostly from Interior birds; coastal birds are doing less well 85%.
  • BC quail harvest: up to 4,600 birds in the 1970s, under 1,000 a year recently (65%, BC Outdoors 2021).
  • Conservation status: not at risk 85%.
  • Chukar: released in the south central Interior in the 1950s; best on low slopes of the Thompson from Kamloops to Lytton, also the South Okanagan and Similkameen (65%, BC Outdoors and KnowBC).

• Rhyme: "Curl is legal, straight is not; ring on the cock, or hold your shot." (Tip)
  • Number trick: "2, 4, 6": quail about 200 g, Hun about 400 g, chukar about 600 g (75%, rounded).
More: more hooks
  • Face code: black face = cock quail; orange face = Hun; black necklace = chukar (75 to 80%).
  • Old hand's rule (opinion): "Name it in the air or let it go." Hunting educators teach positive ID before every shot (Tip).
  • Date hook: quail came to BC between 1860 and 1912: "sixty to twelve" 85%.

• BC Breeding Bird Atlas, Audubon, Okanagan and BC Outdoors articles, the app Rule Book. Checked 2026-10-11.

mc-quail-02:
Why it matters

Know where the heart and lungs sit, how the bird breathes and what its muscles can do. Then you know where to shoot, how far it will fly, and how to care for the meat.

  • Heart and lungs sit in the front half, under the back and behind the crop 70%.
  • Most of the body is air sacs, gut and breast muscle 70%.
More: how sure is this chapter
  • Quail anatomy is studied far less than chicken anatomy. Quail and chickens are both in the order Galliformes, so this chapter uses poultry anatomy from Poultry Hub Australia (University of New England) and labels it 70% for quail.
  • Where a figure is for the chicken (temperature, field of view), the screen says so.
  • Shot placement and meat care pull this together on the last screens and in chapter 10.

• Breast muscle is mostly white fibre: fast, short, little staying power 70%.
  • So: a whirring burst, a glide, then they land and run 75%.
More: bones and muscle in full
  • Bird bones are light. Some are hollow and connect to the air sacs ("pneumatic bones") (70%, Poultry Hub).
  • The breastbone has a deep keel. The big flight muscles anchor to it 70%.
  • In fowl the breast muscles are mostly white fibres: they lack myoglobin, contract fast and tire fast. Fowl fly short distances with very rapid wingbeats (70%, Poultry Hub muscular system).
  • Quail run rather than fly, and fly as a last resort (70%, Birder's Handbook via Stanford). When pushed they burst into fast, low flight on whirring wings (75%, Audubon).
  • Leg muscles are darker and built for walking and running all day (Tip, 65%: red fibres carry myoglobin for steady work, Poultry Hub).
  • Hunter meaning: a quail flight is short. Watch it down. Singles often land a few dozen yards away (75%, Washington Fish and Wildlife).

• No diaphragm. Ribs and breastbone pump nine air sacs 70%.
  • Fresh air crosses the lung on the breath in and the breath out 70%.
More: the air sac system in full
  • Fowl have nine air sacs: one clavicular, two cervical, two cranial thoracic, two caudal thoracic and two abdominal (70%, Poultry Hub).
  • The air sacs are thin balloons. They hold and move air but do not exchange gas. Gas exchange happens only in the lungs 70%.
  • The lungs are small, stiff and pressed up against the ribs on the back 70%.
  • Breathing: muscles swing the ribs and breastbone forward and back. That changes the body volume and pumps the sacs 70%.
  • One gulp of air takes two breaths to pass through: rear sacs, lung, front sacs, out (70%, Poultry Hub; a vet interview in dvm360 describes the same).
  • Hunter meaning: the lungs sit high in the back between the ribs, right beside the heart. Pellets that reach the front half of the body hit the engine room (Tip).
  • Air sacs fill much of the body cavity. A hit there alone can let a bird fly on (Tip, 60%).

• Four chambered heart, low in the chest, behind the crop 70%.
  • Heart and lungs together: about a thumbnail on a quail (Tip).
More: the heart in full
  • The bird heart has two atria and two ventricles, like ours (70%, Poultry Hub circulatory system).
  • It sits low in the chest with its point to the rear 70%.
  • Big vessels leave the heart forward to the neck and wings and back to the body 70%.
  • The head and neck carry the brain, spinal cord and big neck vessels. That is why the head and front of the bird is the target in chapter 10 (Tip).

• The crop stores a meal. The gizzard grinds it with grit 70%.
  • Open a crop after the hunt: it tells you today's food (Tip).
More: digestion in full
  • No teeth. Food goes from the beak down the gullet to the crop, a stretchy pouch at the base of the neck that holds a meal (70%, Poultry Hub).
  • Then the glandular stomach adds acid and enzymes, and the gizzard, a thick muscle with a horny lining, grinds the food with grit 70%.
  • Two blind pouches, the caeca, ferment tough plant food 70%.
  • Young quail pick up the gut microbes they need by eating adult droppings (65%, BC Outdoors).
  • California quail eat mostly seeds and green leaves; legume seeds lead the list (80%, California wildlife habitat records). Insects are under 5% of the adult diet (70%, Birder's Handbook) but chicks eat many 80%.
  • Grit: Washington Fish and Wildlife says quail pick grit at roadside edges before the morning and afternoon feeds 75%. Gravel lanes next to cover are worth a look.
  • In cool weather, quail can get water from green plants, insects and dew 80%. In hot weather they need free water every day 80%.

• Body heat about 41 to 41.7 °C in fowl 70%.
  • Hot day: they pant and need water daily 80%.
More: heat in full
  • Fowl body temperature: 41 to 41.7 °C; death near 46 °C (70%, Poultry Hub, chicken figures).
  • Feathers and a fat layer under the skin hold heat in the cold 70%.
  • In heat, birds pant and flutter the throat to lose heat by evaporation 70%.
  • California quail roost in dense trees or shrubs, not on the ground (70%, Birder's Handbook). BC winters are hard on them: one Okanagan naturalist says a bad winter is the main thing that knocks them back (60%, iNFOnews).
  • Gray partridge burrow into snow to reach seeds (75%, Audubon). Chukar move down out of heavy snow and onto south slopes (80%, FEIS).

• Few quail live past their first birthday 65%.
  • Most of a fall covey is young of the year 60%.
More: lifespan in full
  • California quail can live about six years, but few live much past one year (65%, BC Outdoors).
  • An early California banding study: of 101 birds, 52 were known alive at 6 months, 15 at one year, 4 at two years and 1 at three years (60%, search preview).
  • Predators: Cooper's and sharp shinned hawks, great horned owls, snakes, ground squirrels, house cats, coyotes, skunks, bobcats and jays (80%, California wildlife habitat records).
  • Numbers rise after wet years with good green growth; rain drives the hatch 80%.
  • Chukar can live up to 10 years in BC, per one writer (60%, BC Outdoors).
  • Hunter meaning: a covey is a renewable crop of young birds. Good spring rain, good fall covey (Tip).

• Fat cycle for California quail in BC: no good data. VERIFY.
  • Tip: birds in late November often feel plumper than in early October.
More: what we know and do not know
  • No source found that measures California quail fat by month in BC. Treat any claim as a Tip (VERIFY).
  • What is known: breeding and moult cost energy in spring and summer; seeds are the main fall and winter food (80%, California wildlife habitat records).
  • Tip: weigh a few cleaned birds early and late in the season and write it in the Journal. Your own numbers beat a guess.

• Small bird, small shot: lead 7.5 or 8, steel 6 or 7 75%.
  • Aim for the head and front half: brain, neck, heart, lungs (Tip).
More: shot and meat in full
  • One small pellet is often enough to bring down a quail (75%, Washington Fish and Wildlife).
  • A pattern that puts several pellets in the head and front body kills cleanly. A shot to the rear catches gut and air sacs: the bird may fly on (Tip).
  • Breast meat is white and lean, so it dries out fast in the pan (Tip). Legs are darker and tougher (Tip, 65%).
  • Gut contents and the crop sour fast in warm weather. Cool birds fast (Tip). Chapter 10 has the steps.
  • Both breasts are and must go home (99%, Rule Book).

• Rhyme: "Front half, fast fall; rear end, no kill at all." (Tip)
  • Number trick: 9 air sacs, 4 heart chambers, 2 breaths per gulp 70%.
More: more hooks
  • Crop check: "What's in the crop is what's on the slope." Open one crop after every hunt (Tip).
  • Muscle hook: white meat flies, dark meat walks (Tip, 65%).
  • Old hand's rule (opinion): "Watch it down. A quail never flies as far as you think." (Tip, backed by short flights, 75%)

• Poultry Hub Australia (University of New England), Audubon, California wildlife habitat records, Washington Fish and Wildlife, BC Outdoors. Checked 2026-10-11.
More: every source and date checked
  • Poultry Hub Australia: respiratory system and thermoregulation, digestive system, circulatory system, skeletal system, muscular system, read directly 2026-10-11. Chicken anatomy applied to quail 70%.
  • dvm360: the unique avian respiratory system, read directly 2026-10-11 70%.
  • California Wildlife Habitat Relationships: California quail (California Department of Fish and Game), read directly 2026-10-11: diet, water, predators, rainfall 80%.
  • Stanford Birds: California quail, from The Birder's Handbook (Ehrlich, Dobkin and Wheye 1988), read directly 2026-10-11: roost, running, diet 70%.
  • Washington Fish and Wildlife: quail hunting, read directly 2026-10-11: grit, singles, shot size 75%.
  • Audubon field guide: California quail and gray partridge, read directly 2026-10-11 75%.
  • US Forest Service FEIS: chukar (Sullivan 1994), read directly 2026-10-11 80%.
  • BC Outdoors: California quail (Harris 2021), read directly 2026-10-11 65%. iNFOnews 2018 60%.
  • Banding study: an early California quail banding study at Hart Park, California, seen only as a search preview 2026-10-11. Exact paper and year: VERIFY 60%.
  • Rules: Rule Book: unlawful acts, item 44, 2 October 2026 edition 99%.
mc-quail-03:
Why it matters

Quail find you with their eyes first and their ears second. A covey has many eyes and one lookout. Beat those and you get close.

  • Eyes: the strongest sense. Ears: strong. Nose: weak (70 to 85%).
  • A covey adds many eyes and a sentinel 70%.
More: how sure is this chapter
  • Bird senses are well studied in general, less in quail. Where a number comes from the chicken or from birds in general, the screen says so (70 to 85%).
  • How to beat each sense is hunter craft, labelled Tip.

• Eyes on the sides of the head see almost all the way around 70%.
  • Only a narrow wedge in front is seen by both eyes 70%.
More: vision field in full
  • In the chicken only about 26° straight ahead is seen by both eyes (binocular). The rest is seen by one eye at a time (70%, Poultry Hub).
  • In most birds the binocular field in front is narrow, about 20° to 30° at most (65%, Martin 2007 review, search preview).
  • A study of black grouse, a galliform cousin, found wide side fields and only a small blind area behind the head (65%, search preview).
  • So a quail feeding with its head down still watches most of the sky and the ground around it (Tip, 65%).
  • Hunter meaning: you cannot sneak up "behind" a quail the way you can behind a deer. Use cover and ground shape, not angles (Tip).

• Birds have four colour cone types, including ultraviolet (UV) 85%.
  • Movement gives you away more than colour (Tip).
More: colour, ultraviolet and motion in full
  • Most birds carry four colour cone types: ultraviolet or violet, short, medium and long wave. Humans have three (85%, Stoddard et al. 2020, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences).
  • So a quail likely sees colours we cannot, including ultraviolet patterns 80%.
  • Some hunters avoid clothes washed in brighteners that glow under ultraviolet light. No study on quail tests this: Tip only.
  • Blaze orange: birds see colour, but safety comes first. Wear it in brush (Tip, from the quick lesson).
  • Fowl are day active and need more light to see than some other birds (70%, Poultry Hub). Quail roost at dusk and leave the roost at first light 70%.
  • Motion: a moving hunter on a skyline is the classic giveaway. Move when the sentinel is out of view, freeze when it looks (Tip).

• Birds hear best at about 1 to 4 kilohertz (kHz) 75%.
  • Voices, boots on gravel and gun clicks fall right in that band (Tip).
More: hearing in full
  • Across many bird species, hearing is most sensitive from about 1 to 4 kHz (kilohertz), with a drop above that; no ultrasound (75%, avian hearing reviews including Dooling 1978).
  • Some songbirds are less sensitive than people in that band, so do not assume a quail hears better than you 70%.
  • Quail live by sound: assembly calls, contact clucks and alarm calls keep the covey together (70%, Edgewood notes from Calkins et al.).
  • Cooper's hawks are known to hunt quail by their calls 70%. Quail fall quiet when a hawk is about (Tip, 60%).
  • Hunter meaning: talk in whispers, use hand signals, close truck doors softly, and do not rattle shells in a pocket (Tip).

• Smell is not highly developed in fowl 70%.
  • Wind still matters: for your sound and for a dog's nose (Tip).
More: smell in full
  • In fowl the olfactory organ is not very highly developed, and smell seems secondary to other senses for finding food (70%, Poultry Hub).
  • No source says quail detect hunters by scent. Treat scent control as low value for quail (Tip).
  • Wind carries your sound. Walk into or across the wind so noise blows away from the cover ahead (Tip).
  • A dog finds quail by scent. Hunt so the wind blows from the cover to the dog (Tip).
  • Windy days: gray partridge shelter behind tree lines, fence rows, boulders and in lee draws (75%, Washington Fish and Wildlife).

• While the covey feeds, one bird, usually a male, watches from a high perch 70%.
  • He gives the alarm and the covey runs for cover 70%.
More: the sentinel in full
  • "During foraging one individual (usually male) often acts as sentinel, sitting on a high perch and giving Contact and Aerial Alarm Calls when it observes danger." (70%, Edgewood notes from Calkins et al. 1999)
  • The male acts as sentry throughout the year (70%, Birder's Handbook).
  • In the breeding season the male watches while the female sits on the nest 70%.
  • Look for him first: a fence post, a stump, a rock or the top of a shrub (Tip). See the habitat tour.

• Many eyes, one lookout, and calls to share the news 70%.
  • Their answer to danger: run first, fly last 70%.
More: combining in full
  • A feeding covey watches in every direction at once. One alarm moves them all 70%.
  • They feed close to cover. California records say they seldom go more than 15 to 30 m (50 to 100 ft) from cover to feed 80%.

  • First answer to danger: run into cover. They fly only as a last resort 70%.
  • Hunter meaning: they rarely let you see the whole covey in the open. Expect to hear them and to see a few birds on the edge (Tip).

mc-quail-04:
Why it matters

A covey thinks as a group: watch, call, run, burst, scatter, regroup. Learn the script and you know their next move before they make it.

  • Quail talk all day: assembly, contact, alarm, advertising and fighting calls 70%.
  • The assembly call, "chi CA go", is the one to learn first 70%.
More: the calls in full
  • Assembly call: three syllables, loudest on the middle one ("cu CA cow" or "chi CA go"). Given when a bird is separated from the group or its mate, and before and during covey moves. Often repeated 10 or more times (70%, Edgewood notes from Calkins et al. 1999).
  • Audubon writes it "ka kah ko" or "Chi ca go", the second note highest 75%. The BC atlas writes "put way doo" 85%.
  • Contact calls: soft notes that keep a feeding covey together 70%. Washington Fish and Wildlife: listen for soft clucking while they feed 75%.
  • Alarm: a quiet "pit pit" warning (60%, Okanagan naturalist in iNFOnews). The sentinel gives contact and aerial alarm calls 70%.
  • Advertising call: a single loud "cow" from a high perch, by unpaired males early in the breeding season 70%.
  • Fighting call: "squill", between males sorting out rank in spring 70%.

• First choice: run. Fly as a last resort 70%.
  • Cover runs out, or you get too close: they burst 75%.
More: alarm and flight in full
  • "Remain on ground and run very rapidly, flying as last resort." (70%, Birder's Handbook)
  • If startled they explode into short, fast flight; given a choice, they escape on foot 70%.
  • How close before they flush: no published number for BC birds. It depends on cover, pressure and the sentinel (Tip, VERIFY).
  • Pressured birds near trees may fly up and perch in the branches (75%, Washington Fish and Wildlife).
  • Hunter meaning: push them toward the end of the cover, not into a big thicket. Cover too big and they just run or stay in it (75%, Washington Fish and Wildlife).

• A flushed covey scatters. Singles land a few dozen yards away and sit tight 75%.
  • Then they call to regroup with the assembly call 70%.
More: scatter and regroup in full
  • "When they scatter, quail may fly long distances, never to be seen again (at least not that day), or they may settle to the ground only a few dozen yards away" (75%, Washington Fish and Wildlife).
  • "Those singles and doubles will sometimes hold very tight once they hit the ground" 75%.
  • "When a covey is scattered, birds will often emit a sort of crowing whistle to locate each other, and a chorus of such calls may erupt around dusk, as birds begin to roost for the night." 75%
  • An Okanagan naturalist: about 10 minutes after a flush the covey has collected itself and is pecking again (Tip, one observer, iNFOnews).
  • Assembly calls also start the covey's move off the night roost in the morning (70%, Edgewood notes).

• Flush, scatter, sit tight, call, regroup (70 to 75%).
  • Late in the day, give them time to gather before dark (Tip).
More: why time matters
  • Singles hold tight right after the flush: your best shooting chance on singles 75%.
  • As calls start, birds move toward each other. Waiting too long means they are a covey again, and wary (Tip).
  • Tall Timbers' Bill Palmer (bobwhite research): "The evidence suggests it's OK to hunt singles... They are so good at getting back together." (60%, bobwhite, Garden and Gun 2022)
  • Same source, a manners rule: stop a bit before dark and give the birds time to gather (Tip).

• Each flush teaches them. The second flush is farther out 75%.
  • Hard hunted birds hold less and run more 60%.
More: pressure in full
  • Gray partridge: "after they've been flushed once, they're likely to flush farther in front of you or your dog on the second approach, still farther out on the third." (75%, Washington Fish and Wildlife)
  • Quail that have not been hunted hard may hold in small patches of cover instead of breaking into the open 75%.
  • "Heavy hunting pressure can change the birds' habits, even moving them off an area." (60%, Missouri Conservationist 1996, bobwhite)
  • Under raptor pressure, quail feed closer to cover and may skip the afternoon feed (70%, Edgewood notes).
  • Hunter meaning: rest a covey. Hunt it once, then leave it a week (Tip).

• Fall coveys: often under 30, sometimes 100 or more in BC 85%.
  • Males hold a rank order. Only ranked males get mates 70%.
More: social life in full
  • BC: coveys "occasionally include 100 or more birds, but more frequently less than 30" (85%, BC Breeding Bird Atlas).
  • California: coveys average 20 to 25 (70%, Edgewood notes); up to 200, rarely over 300, in fall and winter (70%, Birder's Handbook).
  • Washington: a dozen to several dozen birds 75%. Over 1,000 birds together has been reported in BC in fall and winter (Tip, search preview of Sierra Club BC, VERIFY).
  • Families merge: broods join into "communal broods" with several adults (60%, Wikipedia summary).
  • Males have dominance hierarchies that shape mate choice, relations between coveys and brood moves. Only birds in the hierarchy get mates. Dominant birds call more (70%, Edgewood notes).
  • Pairs form from birds of the same covey. If both survive, they tend to pair again the next year 70%.
  • In good years a female may lay a second clutch, leaving the first brood with a male 60%.

• Older birds pair earlier. Adult hens pick adult cocks 70%.
  • Most fall birds are young: they have never seen a hunter (Tip).
More: old and young in full
  • "Older birds generally mate earlier than younger birds, and adult females generally mate with adult males rather than yearling males." (70%, Edgewood notes)
  • Few quail live past one year 65%. An old bird in your bag is uncommon (Tip).
  • Tip: early October coveys full of young often hold better than the same coveys in late November after a few flushes.

mc-quail-05:
Why it matters

Quail do not migrate. The same covey lives in the same draw all year, but its size, its calls and its habits change by the month. Know the month, know the bird.

  • Coveys in fall and winter, pairs in spring, broods in summer (70 to 80%).
  • Season: 1 October to 30 November in Region 8 99%.
More: how sure is this chapter
  • Most timing data come from California studies 80%. BC birds live farther north and dates may run later: VERIFY against BC records.
  • The BC atlas and the app's migration data agree: no migration, the same low country all year (60 to 85%).

• Big coveys near farms, orchards and thick brush 75%.
  • Hard winters are the main killer 60%.
More: winter in full
  • Winter coveys, sometimes very large, near farms, orchards and suburbs with thick brush; same small range all winter (75%, app migration data).
  • In winter they form even bigger coveys, sometimes hundreds of birds (60%, Okanagan naturalist in iNFOnews).
  • California winter home range of four coveys averaged 10.5 ha (26 acres), from 6.9 to 18 ha 80%.
  • Winter movements cover about twice the area used in summer 80%.
  • Snow: Tip, 60%, from the quick lesson: snow after a cold night pushes coveys to sunny slopes and bare ground, closer to houses.
  • No season now. Scout only: drive back roads, listen, note coveys in the Journal (Tip).

• Coveys break up in March. Pairing takes about 2 months 70%.
  • Unpaired cocks give the single "cow" call from a high perch 70%.
More: spring in full
  • "Approximately 2 months elapse between covey breakup in March and complete segregation of birds into pair bonds." (70%, Edgewood notes)
  • Pairs form from March to early May (80%, California habitat records).
  • Spring dispersal: a covey may spread up to 8 km (5 mi) 80%. App data: some birds disperse up to 8 km in April 65%.
  • Males fight with the "squill" call while they sort out rank 70%.
  • Courtship: the male droops his wings, spreads his tail, bobs his head and may rush at the female; courtship feeding by both sexes (70 to 75%).

• About 14 eggs. The hen sits 22 to 23 days 80%.
  • Chicks run at once and fly short hops at about 10 days 75%.
More: nesting in full
  • Nests April to August, peak May and June; most hatch in June (80%, California habitat records).
  • Clutch averages 14 (range 6 to 16, California records) 80%. Audubon: 1 to 21, usually 13 to 14 75%. Two hens sometimes lay in one nest 75%.
  • Laying: about 3 eggs every 4 days; incubation starts when the clutch is complete (70%, Edgewood notes).
  • Nest: a shallow scrape lined with grass and leaves, under a shrub, brush pile or log 75%.
  • The male stands sentinel while the female incubates 70%.
  • Young leave the nest within a day, follow the parents and feed themselves 75%. The hen broods them at night for the first two weeks; they cannot hold their own heat yet 70%.
  • One brood a year, two in good years 75%. In BC, one or possibly two clutches is more likely (65%, BC Outdoors).
  • Rain drives the hatch: high numbers follow wet winters with good green growth 80%.

• Family groups join into coveys (60 to 70%).
  • Coveys of 20 or more by September 65%.
More: late summer in full
  • August: family groups join into coveys (60%, app migration data).
  • September: coveys of 20 or more in brushy draws and farm edges 65%.
  • Broods use only a few acres in the first 2 weeks and 4 to 8 ha by one month (80%, California habitat records).
  • Moult: young birds replace most feathers through late summer but keep buff tipped coverts into fall (70%, 1963 Condor aging study, search preview). Exact moult months for BC birds: VERIFY.
  • Watch broods in August from the road to guess the fall crop (Tip). Count chicks per hen and write it down.

Warning

Study aid only. The official regulations are the law.

  • November: coveys on winter range: brush, farm edges, riparian thickets 70%.

  • Early October: thick leaves, warm days, fresh birds that hold. Late November: thin cover, cold, birds wiser after flushes (Tip).
  • Orchards and vineyards: harvest crews may be working in October. Ask where people are today (Tip, from the quick lesson).

• Season closed after 30 November 99%.
  • Coveys settle on winter range near cover and food 70%.

  • The Region 8 quail season ends 30 November 99%.
  • December: winter coveys in thick cover near feed (75%, app migration data).
  • Use December to clean the Journal: where each covey was, how many birds, what cover (Tip).

mc-quail-06:
Why it matters

A covey keeps a tight daily routine: roost, call, feed, grit, dust, rest, feed, call, roost. Be where they will be, at the hour they will be there.

  • Two feeds: just after dawn and late afternoon 70%.
  • Midday: loaf in cover, dust bathe, drink 75%.
More: the day in full
  • "During the non breeding season, quail feed twice a day, in the morning just after dawn and again in late afternoon." (70%, Edgewood notes from Calkins et al.)
  • Birds leave the night roost, generally off the ground in trees, between first light and sunrise; assembly calls start the move 70%.
  • They pick grit at road and trail edges before the morning and afternoon feeds (75%, Washington Fish and Wildlife).
  • Midday: rest in moderate to heavy cover, dust bathe, or take water in warm, dry weather 75%.
  • Dusk: a chorus of calls as they gather to roost 75%.
  • Legal hunting hours: 1 hour before sunrise to 1 hour after sunset (99%, Rule Book).

From roost to breakfast1 of 4
  • Be in place, quiet, at first light (Tip).
  • Listen before you walk (Tip).
More: mornings in full
  • Roosts: dense trees or shrubs, not on the ground (70%, Birder's Handbook).
  • The morning feed starts just after dawn 70%. Grit before feeding 75%.
  • Feeding stays close to cover: seldom more than 15 to 30 m out 80%.
  • Tip: on a frosty morning, birds may wait for sun on the brush before moving. A late start can pay.
  • Note the legal start: 1 hour before sunrise 99%. It is often too dark to name a quail then. No shot until you can see the plume (Tip).

• Hot, dry day: they need water daily 80%.
  • Midday they rest in thick cover and are hard to flush 60%.
More: midday in full
  • In hot weather quail need free water every day; in cool weather green plants, insects and dew can be enough (80%, California habitat records).
  • They gather near water in dry weather and spread out when green plants and water are plentiful 80%.
  • "During the middle of the day, especially when it's hot, they tend to hold tight in thicker cover." (60%, Field and Stream, search preview)
  • Chukar: feed through the morning, then move to shady slopes and draws, dusting sites and water holes at midday (75%, Washington Fish and Wildlife). They spend the hottest part of the day in shade (80%, FEIS).
  • Tip: a midday break for you too. Clean birds, rest the dog, then hunt the last 2 hours.

• Storms: they feed in the breaks 70%.
  • Cold fronts, pressure and moon: no good data, Tip only.
More: weather in full, with evidence
  • Rain and storms: "During storms they feed sporadically throughout the day during breaks in the storm." (70%, Edgewood notes)
  • Heat and drought: water every day; birds gather near water 80%.
  • Wind: Huns take shelter behind tree lines, fence rows, boulders, buildings, in narrow draws and on lee hillsides (75%, Washington Fish and Wildlife). For quail, wind makes birds hard to hear and flighty: Tip.
  • Snow: chukar gather where snow is thin; south slopes after cold nights 75%. Quail move to sunny slopes and bare ground (Tip, 60%).
  • Cold fronts and barometric pressure: many hunters say birds feed hard before a front. No quail study found: Tip, VERIFY.
  • Moon: no quail data found. Quail are day birds and roost at night 70%, so moon effects are unlikely to matter much (Tip).
  • Cooper's hawk about: quail may skip the second feeding and stay close to cover (70%, Edgewood notes).

• Pressured birds run more and flush wilder (60 to 75%).

  • Quail flushed near trees may fly up and perch. Washington Fish and Wildlife suggests walking away and coming back 30 to 60 minutes later, when they may be back on the ground 75%.
  • Do not shoot sitting birds in trees: it is not sporting and a low shot into branches is a safety risk (Tip).

mc-quail-07:
Why it matters

Quail live in a narrow band: low, brushy, close to food and water, often next to people. Chukar live on the rock above them. Learn the band and you stop walking empty country.

  • Quail: valley floor and first benches, brush beside food 85%.
  • Chukar: steep rock and cheatgrass slopes above 80%.
More: habitat in full
  • BC: quail mostly breed below 750 m, most common from 250 to 500 m, some as high as 1,250 m (85%, BC Breeding Bird Atlas).
  • They prefer the Ponderosa Pine and Bunchgrass zones in the Interior 85%.
  • Habitat: mixed farm and suburban areas with lots of cover for feeding, nesting and roosting, plus riparian, grassland and open pine or broadleaf woods 85%.
  • They need "a mosaic of low, brushy vegetation, with grass and forb openings, taller shrubs, and trees, interspersed with water" (80%, California habitat records).
  • Washington lists: thick tangles near stream beds, small ponds and wetlands; valley bottoms with Russian olive or tall sage; tree lines and fence lines; low brush and tall grass; edges of grain fields 75%.
  • Chukar: open, rocky, dry slopes and canyon walls, usually steep; grass and brush cover with cheatgrass a key plant (75 to 80%, Audubon and FEIS).
  • Huns: cultivated land, hedgerows, bushy pastures and stubble (75%, Audubon).

• Thorny brush beside open feeding ground (Tip).
  • Food: seeds and green leaves, legumes first 80%.

mc-quail-08:
Why it matters

You will hear quail and read their sign far more often than you see them. Tracks, dust bowls, droppings and calls tell you a covey lives here and roughly when it was here.

  • Look for tracks, droppings and dusting holes near cover 75%.
  • Then walk the road edge in short bursts 75%.
More: the sign method in full
  • Washington Fish and Wildlife: "drive or hike back roads, looking for tracks, droppings and dusting holes that indicate there may be birds nearby." 75%
  • "When you find evidence of birds, walk the edge of the road in short bursts, stopping often near patches of roadside cover." 75%
  • Do it legally: no shooting across or within the , and stay off private land without permission (99%, Rule Book).

• Three toes forward, a short hind toe; prints in one line (60 to 75%).
  • Quail track about 3.5 cm long (Tip, VERIFY).
More: tracks in full
  • Quail forage on the ground, so tracks usually fall in a single line, one foot in front of the other (60%, Bear Tracker).
  • Sandy river bars and dusty lanes show quail tracks best 60%.
  • Size: a related quail (Gambel's) track measured about 3.8 by 3.8 cm (1.5 in) (60%, Wildwood Tracking quiz). For California quail, a working figure of about 3.5 cm: Tip, VERIFY with a ruler on a fresh print.
  • Grouse tracks are about 5 cm (75%, the app's habitat tour). Chukar and pheasant tracks are bigger than quail: measure and write it down (Tip).
  • The hind toe often does not show; in fine dust it can 60%.
  • Tracking basics: Tracks and Reading sign.

• Bird droppings: a dark coil with a white cap 70%.
  • A pile under a roost tree marks a covey's bedroom (Tip).
More: droppings in full
  • Birds pass nitrogen waste as uric acid, the white part of the dropping (70%, Poultry Hub).
  • California quail roost in dense trees or shrubs, not on the ground 70%, so look for droppings under thick conifers, junipers or shrub clumps near feeding cover (Tip).
  • "Watch for roost piles... Fresh roost piles often indicate good places to find birds early or late in the day." (60%, Missouri Conservationist 1996, written about bobwhites, which roost on the ground)
  • Chukar roost on the ground under sage or juniper and among rocks, in coveys, sometimes tail to tail (80%, FEIS): piles collect under ledges.
  • Do not handle droppings with bare hands (Tip).

• Quail dust bathe as a group, often at midday (70 to 75%).
  • Round bowls in loose soil with small tracks around them (Tip).
More: dusting in full
  • Dust bathing is a daily communal habit of quail (60%, Wikipedia summary). Washington Fish and Wildlife names dusting as a favourite midday pastime, often at road edges 75%.
  • One summary says the bowls are about 7 to 15 cm across: Tip, the figure is unsourced (VERIFY).
  • Tip: fresh bowls have loose, fluffy dust and a feather or two. Old bowls crust over and catch leaves.
  • Chukar use dusting sites at midday too 75%.

• A small pile of feathers can mean a hawk kill (Tip).
  • Single grey body feathers at a dust bowl: birds were here (Tip).
More: feathers in full
  • Predators of quail include Cooper's and sharp shinned hawks and great horned owls 80%. A plucked pile on open ground often marks a hawk kill (Tip).
  • A pile of feathers is sign of a covey's range, not of where the covey sits now (Tip).
  • Shot birds: find every feather patch where a bird fell and search from there (Tip). See chapter 10.

• Dawn and dusk calling tells you where a covey roosts 75%.
  • Point to the sound, note the cover, hunt it next morning (Tip).
More: calls in full
  • Assembly calls start the covey's move off the roost at first light 70%.
  • A chorus of calls at dusk as birds gather to roost (75%, Washington Fish and Wildlife).
  • Hunters can start the chorus with a quail call and use the answers to find spots for the next morning 75%. A mouth call is legal; recorded or electronic calls are not for game birds (99% for the electronic ban, 95% for mouth calls, Rule Book).
  • Soft clucks while feeding: you hear them only when you are quiet and close 75%.

• Moist and dark: today. Dry and pale: days old (Tip).
  • Note the last rain or wind; it dates every sign (Tip).
More: freshness in full
  • No study gives aging times for quail sign. All of this is Tip.
  • Tracks after rain: crisp prints on a rain pocked surface were made after the rain stopped (Tip).
  • Morning dew: a dark line where birds walked through dewy grass is from this morning (Tip).
  • Write sign in the Journal with the date and the weather. After a season, you know each covey's routine (Tip).

Follow a covey, step by step1 of 4
  • Listen, read, stop and go, mark (Tip and 75%).
  • Two hunters: one on each side of the cover (Tip).
More: following in full
  • Stop at each patch of cover and wait at least 15 or 20 seconds before moving on; hiding quail may get nervous and fly (75%, Washington Fish and Wildlife).
  • Move quickly from patch to patch, but stop at each one 75%.
  • Mark the singles and go to the nearest first. Singles often hold tight 75%.
  • Move slowly and quietly so you can hear a distant covey rise or see birds flying in (60%, Missouri Conservationist).

  • Number trick: "15 to 20": stop 15 to 20 seconds at each patch 75%.

mc-quail-09:
Why it matters

Quail hunting is permission, listening, slow walking and one safe shot at a time. The skill is in the feet and the ears more than the gun.

  • Legal spot and permission first. Then match the method to the cover (Tip).
  • Methods from Washington Fish and Wildlife 75%.
More: every legal method, at a glance
  • Shotgun, air gun or bows B, C and D. No .22 or centrefire rifle for quail, chukar, partridge or pheasant (95 to 99%, Rule Book: legal methods).
  • Walking up (stop and go), pushing and blocking, hunting singles, glass and stalk for chukar, and a dog are all used (75%, Washington Fish and Wildlife).
  • Calls: a mouth call is fine (95%, my reading); "recorded bird calls to hunt game birds" are unlawful 99%.
  • Live bird decoys: unlawful 99%. Bait rules: see the Rule Book.
  • Retrieval is the law: "No person shall kill, cripple or wound game without making all reasonable effort to locate, dispatch, retrieve and include it in their bag limit." 99%

Ask a farmer in 5 steps1 of 5

More: the law and the script, as the app states them
The rule

"A person is not permitted to hunt on cultivated land or on Crown land which is subject to a grazing lease while the land is occupied by livestock, without the consent of the owner, lessee, or occupant of the land." 99%

The rule

"It is unlawful to hunt or discharge a firearm within 100 m of a church, school building, school yard, playground, regional district park, dwelling house, or farm or ranch building that is occupied by persons or domestic animals." 99%

  • Write the OK down with the name, date, area and phone. Keep it in the vest (60%, secondary legal advice).
  • Offer cleaned birds or a hand with a chore. Send a thank you text that night (Tip).
  • Indian Reserves are private land. Permission from the band office is needed to hunt on or across them 99%.

• Walk a few steps, stop 15 to 20 seconds, repeat 75%.
  • Stop near each patch of cover. Be ready on every stop (Tip).
More: stop and go in full
  • "Each time you stop, wait at least 15 or 20 seconds before moving on; if there are quail hiding nearby, they're likely to get nervous and take to the air." (75%, Washington Fish and Wildlife)
  • Works for a lone hunter in open country with scattered patches of low or moderate cover 75%.
  • For chukar, Washington suggests moving quickly, then stopping for 30 seconds near cover 75%.
  • Missouri tip: moving slowly and stopping often can flush a covey or single that would let you walk right by (60%, bobwhite).

Walk a brushy draw with two hunters1 of 4
  • Each hunter owns one side. Never swing through your partner (Tip).
  • A blocker at the end of a narrow strip stops runners 75%.
More: partners, blockers and dogs in full
  • Groups of three or more can "play dog": some push heavy cover, others wait on the flanks or block the far end. Best in small areas and narrow strips; in big cover the birds just run or refuse to fly (75%, Washington Fish and Wildlife).
  • Blocker safety: agree a no shot arc before you start; the blocker is in the line of fire (Tip, from the quick lesson). Diagram: Quail, chukar, partridge, pheasant.
  • Blaze orange hat and vest on both of you in brush (Tip).
  • Dogs: "Unleashed dogs may be used to hunt small game" and quail are fine with an unleashed dog (99%, Rule Book: dogs). Training on game birds under supervision: 1 August to 30 April 99%.
  • A dog that retrieves finds birds a person would never find 75%. Pointers suit low, open cover; a tough flusher suits thick brush (75%, Washington Fish and Wildlife).
  • No dog: shoot only over short cover and walk straight to the fall (Tip).

• Pick one bird. Never shoot "the covey" (Tip).
  • Straightaways: most hunters shoot high. Hold a hair under 75%.
More: the flush in full
  • "Many a quail hunter, suddenly overwhelmed by a cloud of little gray rockets going off in every direction, has stood there stunned" (75%, Washington Fish and Wildlife).
  • Birds may climb steeply into the open or streak low through weeds and limbs 75%.
  • "The tendency of most hunters is to shoot too high, especially at birds that are going straight away. Shooting just under those birds will pay much better dividends." 75%
  • Small birds look faster than they are 75%. Smooth swing, eyes on the bird's head: Shotgun skills.
  • Only birds above head height with open sky or ground beyond. A low bird is a free bird (Tip, from the quick lesson).
  • Mark where the first bird falls before you swing on a second (60%, Missouri Conservationist).

• Right after the flush, singles hold tight: your best shots 75%.
  • Listen for "chi CA go" and walk to the nearest caller (70 to 75%).
More: singles, calls and manners
  • Singles may land only a few dozen yards away and hold very tight (75%, Washington Fish and Wildlife).
  • Mouth calls: hunters can get a covey talking with a quail call and use the answers to find birds 75%. Electronic or recorded calls: unlawful for game birds 99%.
  • One Rokslide hunter: let it settle a few minutes, listen for regroup calls, then imitate them (Tip, one person's experience).
  • Manners rule (opinion): "if three or more birds are harvested out of the rise, then you let the covey go." Quoted by Bill Palmer of Tall Timbers (60%, bobwhite).
  • Same source: the evidence suggests hunting singles from a healthy covey is fine 60%.
  • Stop a bit before dark to give them time to gather (Tip).

• Chukar: get above them, then follow the same contour 75%.
  • Huns: cover a lot of ground; make the first chance count 75%.
More: chukar and Huns in full
  • "Whenever possible, approach chukars from above. While they tend to fly downhill, they usually run uphill." (75%, Washington Fish and Wildlife) Animation: the chukar run.
  • "Most birds will be at the same approximate elevation, so if you flush a covey at one point along a hillside, move uphill a little and continue along that line." 75%
  • Glass distant slopes for feeding or roosting birds, then stalk into position 75%. Listen for the "chuck" calls 75%.

  • Huns: "cover a lot of ground"; they feed at grain field edges and weedy patches and hide in hay, tall grass, brush and fence lines 75%.

mc-quail-10:
Why it matters

A clean kill, a found bird, a cool carcass and a legal bag. This chapter ties the whole Masterclass together and ends with a one page cheat sheet.

  • Shoot high birds with sky behind, about 15 to 30 m (Tip).
  • Lead 7.5 or 8, steel 6 or 7; skeet or improved cylinder choke 75%.
More: shot placement and range in full
  • Aim for the head and front half: brain, neck, heart and lungs (Tip, anatomy from chapter 2, 70%).
  • "One small pellet is often enough to bring down a quail." (75%, Washington Fish and Wildlife)
  • Loads: "Size 7 1/2 and 8 lead shot are standard among quail hunters, and some go as small as 9's. If you're shooting steel, 6's and 7's are the norm." 75%
  • Chokes: "A fairly open choke, skeet or improved cylinder, is well suited to most quail shooting situations." 75% Your 12 gauge works and puts more pellets in the pattern 75%.
  • The quick lesson's loads (Tip): quail and partridge, lead 7.5 or 6, or steel 6; chukar and pheasant, lead 5 or 6, or steel 3 or 4. Huns: lead 6 or 7.5 at 30 to 45 yards (75%, Washington).
  • Range: 15 to 30 m is a Tip, not a rule. Pattern your gun at 20 and 30 m first: Shotgun skills and the pattern math diagram there.
  • Lead shot is legal for upland birds 99%. Plug: no more than 3 shells in total 95%.

• Mark the fall before you look for a second bird 60%.
  • Retrieval is the law 99%.
More: after the shot in full
  • Mentally mark where the bird falls before swinging on another, and drop a hat or handkerchief where you stood (60%, Missouri Conservationist).
  • Walk straight to the spot with your eyes on it (Tip, from the quick lesson).
  • A hit bird may run. Get to it fast; a wing tipped quail can hide in brush (Tip).
  • Dispatch a live bird at once, quickly and humanely (Tip).
  • No dog: shoot only over short cover so every bird falls where you can find it (Tip).
  • Search in a widening circle from the last feather patch (Tip).
The rule

"No person shall kill, cripple or wound game without making all reasonable effort to locate, dispatch, retrieve and include it in their bag limit." 99%

  • Cool birds fast in October sun (Tip).

  • A game vest with a mesh back beats a plastic bag (Tip).
